I was introduced to Shadowrun back in the early 90's with the SNES classic.  I fell in love with the setting almost instantly; sci-fi with magic?  It was my dream game.  I then became more enamoured with the Sega Genesis version once I discovered it, since it allowed for even more freedom, and a glimpse into the true mechanics of the game.  In Junior High I was introduced to the actual tabletop RPG, and it sparked my love of that hobby.
All that aside, Shadowrun is very important and dear to me, will always hold a special place in my heart, and will forever be held at the highest standard for me.
This game does not dissappoint.  At all.  It is amazing.
The setting harkens back to an earlier time of the Shadowrun universe, when Deckers HAD to go with the group, because wireless connectivity, that wasn't even a thing.
Dunkelzahn hadn't become the first Dagon-American President of the UCAS.
The Arcology was still a shining beacon of how the future will be.
The world is perfect.  It shows how and why people live in the shadows, and doesn't leave anything to mystery as to why the world is in the over all crummy condition it's in.
The gameplay, while not the Shadowrun I know and love, still feels amazing.  Spellcasters are appropriately powerful, while not being the rediculous level of game breaking they can be in the tabeltop (lacking Astral Projection and long-term spirit aid.)  Martial-oriented characters are sufficiently amazing (street samurais and adepts both shine,) and whether you're melee, gun happy, or mixed, you have a lot of cool options.
Where the mechanics really shine?  The Matrix play.  It feels very appropriate for what it's supposed to be.  A little world where you wander around and blast programs.
Where the game lacks over all?  While highly customizable, it still feels as though you are cornered into one or to directions.  Healing is challenging, which isn't bad, just something you aren't really made aware of early on.  It also feels that there's a sharp increase to difficulty if you aren't playing a face (social oreinted) character.
All in all, an amazing game, love it, and suggest it to everyone!

So I'll cut right to the chase
This game is great. It's like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of Dead Island, Resident Evil, and Mirror's Edge.
The game runs extremely well considering the sheer number of zombies you can expect, the quality of the environment, and the day/night cycle and shadows. Depending on how quickly you push through, you might get sick of Jade/Ayo remind you to "get inside, night is coming", though they do vary the exact line so it's not that bad.
Speaking of night, EVERYTHING about this game is twice as amazing because the night gameplay. You are incentivized to go do things at night because most XP and DROPs values are increased (OUTSIDE of safe zones, before you go try to exploit that), as is the risk of being dismembered, defenestrated, or outright DESTROYED by even the lowliest biter. The risk is worth it most times, assuming you know your way around and make sure to beeline it for a safe zone if you start to get swarmed...or in a level 2+ pursuit, because that gets insane REALLY quick.
As for the plot, while at first it seems like your standard Zombie Outbreak Pathogenb Scenario, it's actually a lot deeper and pretty fresh and exciting. Some pretty obvious twists, but nothing too badly done.
The sound in the game is pretty amazing, the music fits the mood, and the zombies all sound great.
Combat is actually pretty balanced in terms of difficulty. You're not gonna be able to take down an army with a crowbar, but a small group is fairly easy to kill. The special enemies are where it gets tough, and even knowing how to beat them sometimes isn't enough to actually execute it, especially when it comes to Demolishers (especially when there's MORE THAN ONE in the area). That being said, there are very few places in the game where you're forced into a stand up fight for too long, and the areas you are and usually ripe with alternatives to simply wading in and hacking them all to death
So, overall, this game gets a 9.5/10 from me, the only thing barring it from a 10 being the tendency for a biter to grab you right as a bomber turns the corner >.>
TL;DR, this game is worth the money for the single player ALONE.

Out of all the purchases I've made so far in the Summer Sale (2016), Dead Space 1 is defintely the game that shines. I am always taken a great interest in survival horror games, such titles from the Resident Evil and Silent Hill series, so trying Dead Space is a breath of fresh air in this category since no prominent Survival horror games come to light to me.
In the game, you're constantly under attack by Necromorphs filling the USG Ishimura, followed by heat-pounding music (AND THE CREEPY "Twinkle Twinkle little star" that WILL get stuck in your head) when they pop out at you. Theres also a great sense of claustrophobia that Dead Space emitted to me, epscially when I encountered the
in multiple rooms. Theres always long, narrow hallways and tight rooms where you need to enter that keeps you sweating bullets.
I also liked the puzzle solving and multiple objectives that are put in front of you in the game. The Main Character, Isaac Clarke, has the abilities of Kenesis (moving objects) and Stasis (slowing enemies). Both of these are craftfully used in BOTH combat and tasks throughout the game. It may feel stressful at times when the supporting characters pile more stuff even after 1 objective is completed, but it all adds up to something new. Plus, the Zero Gravity in Dead Space is fun to use, a bit annoying when trying to find a spot to traverse to, but it's needed to complete a lot of the game.
Of course to combat all the nasty bad guys in the Ishimura, Mr. Clarke is given a satisfying inventory of weapons to keep them dismembered. But to get these, your required to find the schematics of the ammo before you can fully use them.  Thankfully, killing more neromorphs keeps you stocked on ammo and credits. I found that the aiming is a bit difficult to begin with, even with the sensitivity on high. This might be to accomodate how you kill the Necromorphs
, but it's manageable.
The story behind the game is great to read/watch upon. I felt a lot of interest in watching the animated movies of Dead Space to learn more behind what happened BEFORE and AFTER Isaac Clarke got there. It's pretty tragic of how the whole downfall goes and how little crew members survived.
- Great Story, keeps me interested throughout
- Nice inventory of weapons
- Spot-On "Survival Horror"
- Puzzle solving
- Replay Value, keeps you playing for hours
- The "Store"
- Aiming is a bit slow and hard to get used to (increase sensitivity)
- Zero Gravity is hard to jump from spot to spot
- Not many "Survival Horrors" like this :(

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

They FIXED the PC version of the game I heard people cry...
Yeah... right... It only took them about 18 months... they could and should have written it from the ground up in that time.
So as I saw it on sale for a very cheap price... I thought I'd try it.
Oh dear... oh dear indeed.
Whilst they have fixed the stuttering issues, they haven't fixed what is a very flawed game.
It's so short, it's so simplistic... it's so obviously aimed at gamers with short attention spans and a basic lack of understanding what good game mechanics actually are. It's a mediocre console game at best, as a PC game far, far, far below mediocre. The actual core game is very basic, and the very repetative side missions offer nothing new except the batmobile and some tanks to fight.
But the biggest gripe is the sheer number of times it crashes... which is roughly 40% of the time you play it. Then there's the graphical glitches, which on my ASUS R9 290X Shouldn't be an issue, it's sure as hell powerful enough and got more than enough memory... and that's another thing. My system uses on average 2 or 3GB of memory, games on average (even the hungry ones) use 2-4GB.... Arkham Knight uses a whopping 8GB of the 16GB I have installed... and that's RAM, not video memory. This game is really, really, really bad optomised. It's one of the worst ports of a game since GTA IV... and you all know how bad that was... if you don't, read up about it and how Rockstar tried to defend the game by saying it was designed to run on hardware that hadn't been invented yet... I nearly wet myself when I read that... In fact I bought the game from new and built a new system just for it and couldn't play it for 3yrs until I built a new one, and even then with a crossfire graphics setup and CPU that didn't exist when the game was made... it still ran like a bag of sand on tar paper. It was only on yet another build in early 2015 that I finally had a system capable of playing it at a sensible frame rate with all the graphics turned up... as I should have been able to do 7yrs earlier.
Anyway... I got sidetracked... back to Arkham Knight... and it's a shame about the game because the rest of the series offered you something more than this does... they should have left it as a trilogy rather than polluting the franchise with this.
It's worth it if you can get it for £5-8 as it'll give you a few hours of distraction... but any more of that is a criminal waste of money that could be better spent on something good... like toilet paper, because this is a steaming turd.

Dying light Is what Dead island should have been, It's fun, It has solid Melee & Gun Mechanics, It has a genuinely Fresh Day/Night system, And it has a surprisingly Competent story.  Overall this seems like an amazing game, BUT It is mirrored by technical issues, Bugs, And optimization issues, For the most part the game was bug free (For me at least) Except for some audio issues and occasional glitches which pulled me out from the experience, and there are some horrible optimization Issues here, The game only fully utilizes 1 core so that means unless you have an FX 9590 The game is near unplayable with AMD CPU Based systems as AMD Is known for having bad single thread performance, And even though Dying light does feature SLI profiling Using SLI Yields no performance increase unfortunately.  So overall the Pro's Outweigh the cons here, I personally wouldn't buy the game until they Patch the engine, But if you have an Intel based system and you are okay with only getting about 16 Hours of gameplay for $60, Then buy this.
TL:DR Version: Unoptimized, but Excellent.

A fan of the horror genre has to appreciate the difficulty that game developers and film-makers have in creating a true horror atmosphere that isn't entirely reliant on gore and jump-scares. With that in mind, as a true-blue horror fan across all mediums, I am VERY forgiving of trash and, in fact, even rather fond of it. Horror can be campy and hilarious, it can be hard-hitting and metaphorical, it can be deeply satirical and subversive or it can be, as I said, mindless gruesome trash and still be entertaining.
Dead Space, however, is not trash.
Dead Space is true horror.
Dead Space is the 21st Century's answer to 1979 masterpiece Alien and it deserves the same status, fandom and accolade.
I played Dead Space when it came out and I still find it to be a fabulously clunky, unrelenting and an unflinching horror masterpiece. In the face of legions of fast, intelligent and resilient ancient alien demons, Dead Space puts you in the shoes of - not a soldier, not a superhero, not a warrior - a ♥♥♥♥ing engineer. As you would expect, prepare to get the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of you. When you play Dead Space you feel every movement. You have to thrash your arms wildly to survive, run like hell and sometimes you have stomp an enemy over and over and over because they just. Will. Not. Die. I love this. It gave me true insight into actually how many times I would die in (God forbid) a situation like this, and how many horrendous ways there are to die. There are many, and they were very creative.
Unfortunately, the series didn't manage to continue the success that Dead Space 1 reached in tone and atmosphere, but I would argue that this game is so good at instilling fear into a player that it can be forgiven for all it's subsequent sins. It is also very hard. It is as much a work of the horror-genre for horror fans as it is a game for gamers.
Casuals need not apply.

Short version: BUY THIS GAME NOW!
UPDATE: After playing hours and hours of this game I have realized that this game is truely an experience like none other, it is one of the darkest and most unique games I have ever played; the open world is larger and more detailed than anything you've ever played and the story is just awesome, a truely engaging an emotionally draining experience. In my review below I make lots of reference to Dead Island and while I hate to say it, those comments are now irrelevant, Dead Island has nothing on this game. This isn't just an evolution in gaming, it's an evolution in story telling.
Long version:
Nothing can describe this game other than perfect. It takes everything that was amazing about Dead Island; the ambience, the exploration, the story and the crafting and adds more to it. The only thing Dead Island lacked was flawless gameplay, it was buggy and filled with graphics glitches, but Techland have really learnt from that experience and they've taken everything that worked and fixed everything that didn't! This game is like a slap in the face for the Cryengine, the graphics are OUT OF THIS WORLD.
I can also forgive Techland for delaying this game to work on the free-running because it was definitely worth it; the exploration in this game is unlike any other because literally, if it looks like you can climb it, YOU CAN.
Another impressive apsect to Techlands work is the emphasis they put on the zombie; in Dead Island they really made zombie's a threat again, unlike other zombie games where they are basically harmless obstacles that you need to knock over. But in Dying Light they've upped the ante again, you REALLY don't want to confront a zombie and that's just during the day, don't even talk to me about night-time! Which brings me to the day and night cycle; this is the first game where it really affects the game. Taking your character out during the day is completely different to taking him out at night. The game brilliantly conditions you to fear the night and believe me, YOU DO. It's easy to lose track of time when you're working a mission and when you suddenly hear the warning over the radio that it's almost night time, it like a kick in the guts, and then you gun it for the nearest safe zone.
There are only two issues I have with the game; the first is that the Be The Zombie mode is slightly unbalanced and consequently no-one who is playing a human takes the challenge against a hunter, but this is merely a matter balancing the hunter a bit and as soon as its sorted out, it will be amazing. My second problem isn't actually a problem with the game but more of a grievance; I loved Dead Island and this game should've been Dead Island, I can't imagine how amazing this game would be if it were set Bonoi, but that takes nothing away from this game and it's not Techland's fault; Deep Silver are just morons.
Ultimately, this game has all the amazing intrigue and charisma that Dead Island had, but adds to that some of the best graphics I've ever seen, an amazing parkour system and a truely dark, disturbing and terrifying experience.
Techland are becoming the masters of zombie games.

Okay.. So this is going to be a semi-proffesional review... I say semi because I've never done one before.
Gameplay: 7/10 There is a bit of input lag, but that could be due to my PC. But overall it has nice controlls and seems a lot like Resident evil 4 but in space.
Atmosphere: 9/10 There are so many noises coming from all sorts of things from broken doors to necromorphs crawling around in the vents. This helps to create tension and also makes you feel almost lost in the ship. There were some points in this game where I would have to quit as soon as I found a save point just because I was so creeped out.
Story: 8/10 It's an okay story with the basic "You need to find out what's going on in here" main quest. I haven't gotten very far in it (As you can see by my hours...) But I am already enjoying the story of it and trying to find all the audio logs is a challenge, but it is very rewarding due to the majority of them giving you an idea of what is going on and who people are.
One of the big things in this game is the "bench" system. Which means you collect power nodes throughout the game and you can upgrade your gear. This is good because you a get a multitude of options on what you can upgrade even at the first bench! This means that you have to prioritise which upgrades you think you'll need to survive E.g. Damage/capacity/reload/speed or how many hits you can take before you die/ how much air you have in vaccums.
Overall this game is good for what it is trying to achieve and has some rather well done horror aspects which keep you on your toes as well as good gunplay and is definately worth giving a go! I bought this game for £2.49 on sale and it is DEFINATELY worth it!

Bad news first, it's hard to get reasonable FPS. After playing around with the settings and reading a number of guides online I managed to get a fairly stable 45 FPS.  According to the listed specs, I should be able to run this game at high settings across the board.
Now the good news. This is the most enjoyable zombie game I've ever played. My son and I have racked up many hours slaying the undead, but this is the first time where I ever felt the tension that should accompany the activity. Typically these games veer towards tedious (How To Survive, Dead Island) or over powered slash fests (Dead Rising). Dying Light aims for the middle, it takes effort to survive but the protagonist is skilled and capable enough to make the effort feel fun and balanced.
Another nice feature is that Dying Light not only gives you a good reason to run from a fight, but it makes it as fun and exciting as the fight might be. Often times more fun. Adding in the day/night cycle, the zombie types, and the hunt/gather crafting system and every venture out into the city feels both necessary, exciting, and worth the effort.
The only down side to thiegame play so far has been that I have not been able to get into a game as a zombie. Unfortunately none of my friends have bought this game yet, so I'm stuck with public games.  Not to many people seem inclined to leave the door open to their world at the moment.

LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is a lot of fun.  Gameplay is basically the same as all the other LEGO games, which in this case is not a bad thing.  It's got the usual mix of puzzles and action, with a wide variety of characters.  There's also the usual LEGO series sense of humor, and of course, since it's Marvel, Stan Lee makes an appearance.
It's worth mentioning that, as is typical of the LEGO series, this is not a difficult game.  Combat is extremely forgiving; a character that is killed reappears in the same place (or nearby, if the death was due to the environment) after a few seconds, with the only consequence being a loss of some studs.  None of the puzzles that must be solved to advance present any real challenge.  In-game hints about which characters' powers are needed are very common (actually too common, in my opinion).  That said, the ability to go back to old levels with different characters to find collectibles does add a good amount of replay value.
The only real fault here is that in combat the targeting can be uncooperative, sometimes making it difficult to hit what you're trying to hit.  Fortunately, the difficulty of the action sequences is low enough that this isn't a gamebreaking problem, but it's a problem that has been around since the first LEGO Star Wars, so it really should have been fixed by now.

"Imagine the gods are playing some great game like chess and you don't know the rules of the game"
Richard Feynman made this analogy to the joyful feeling of discovery in the sciences; in learning the "rules" of the game of physics.  In many ways this quote applies to this game.  We've seen those well crafted puzzle games such as portal or braid that in one way or another explain the entirety of the ruleset that the puzzles are operating right away.  The rest of the game is challenging you on increasingly difficult applications of those axioms.  Antichamber doesn't do that.  It doesn't explain the intricacies of the rule set.  It doesn't even explain the rules.  You're stuck with the only hint ever given to you being the controls and in a way this feels like a much more gratifying puzzle experience than the games I've mentioned above.

Definitely interesting with some really clever outside-the-box puzzles, and definitely not lacking in style.  However this game has some serious pacing problems, that add a ton of undue frustration, and really knee-caps the player's ability to learn constructively.  Puzzle games need to lay out and reinforce core mechanics early, and make the player constantly apply them in new ways.  This game keeps introducing new mechanics right up until the end of the game, making several puzzles completely unsolvable until later on, but never bothers to make that clear to the player.  And worst of all, too many puzzles simply rely on your powers of observation, rather than your ability to think pragmatically. You seldom think through your solutions here, rather you just battle a war of attrition, throwing spaghetti at the wall and checking every nook and cranny until something unexpected happens.
You have to buy the DLCs to get bugfixes and a proper working multiplayer, so yeah this game gets a solid 10/10 from me.

“A few steps backwards may keep you moving forwards.” This is one of many statements that can be found printed on the walls of Antichamber, a labyrinth whose corridors frequently defy the rules of three-dimensional space. In order to overcome all of the self-constructing walls, false passages, and invisible portals of the labyrinth, the player must indeed take a few steps backwards, by abandoning his or her sense of spatial reasoning.
Besides the dead-ends and regressions, there are no enemies in Antichamber, and the only shooting comes in the form of an upgradable, cube-shooting device. Developer Alexander Bruce proves himself a master of extra-dimensional gameplay, creating challenges that push the player further and further beyond the comforts of conventional physics. He also preys on a few gaming conventions, from a tutorial which must be disobeyed in order to advance, to rooms which are best navigated by walking through them backward. One of Bruce's more frequent tricks is to make many divergent paths lead to the same destination, rendering the player's choices irrelevant. To avoid covering the same ground under the illusion of forward progress, the player must move slowly and be perceptive.
Thanks to some incredibly polished audio and visuals, it is quite enjoyable to move slowly. Crisp sounds and rich colors create an other-worldly atmosphere, completed by Siddhartha Barnhoorn's ambient compositions, which feature digitally-manipulated recordings of Japanese instruments. The graphics are functional as well as beautiful, with correct paths often presenting themselves in recurring shapes, colors and sprites. Responsive control guarantees that you'll get around easily, even when building cube stairways or leaping across chasms.
The average player should be able to complete the game in ten to twelve hours (although experienced gamers, Bruce claims, will have a harder time with certain challenges that were designed to counter traditional first-person tactics). Ten hours might be a little more bewilderment than some can handle, and the second half of the game, with its emphasis on cube manipulation, can get particularly dizzying. If you are prone to existential nausea, I would recommend this game in small doses.
What makes Antichamber so absorbing-- and in my opinion, important-- is that it allows us to experience impossible geometry. In Bruce's words: “Things that are completely incomprehensible by looking at mathematical formulas on paper, like quantum mechanics or non-Euclidean space, [are] presented in a way that allows the player to interact with them more directly and understand their ramifications.” In the real world, we will never experience a closed loop with an exit point, or a single door that opens onto an unlimited number of rooms. We will never take a step that moves us in more than one direction, or jump down a chute to find higher ground. Antichamber gives us these mind-altering opportunities.
TL;DR -- An immersive and puzzling, three-dimensional exhibition of four-dimensional space.

So I'll cut right to the chase
This game is great. It's like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of Dead Island, Resident Evil, and Mirror's Edge.
The game runs extremely well considering the sheer number of zombies you can expect, the quality of the environment, and the day/night cycle and shadows. Depending on how quickly you push through, you might get sick of Jade/Ayo remind you to "get inside, night is coming", though they do vary the exact line so it's not that bad.
Speaking of night, EVERYTHING about this game is twice as amazing because the night gameplay. You are incentivized to go do things at night because most XP and DROPs values are increased (OUTSIDE of safe zones, before you go try to exploit that), as is the risk of being dismembered, defenestrated, or outright DESTROYED by even the lowliest biter. The risk is worth it most times, assuming you know your way around and make sure to beeline it for a safe zone if you start to get swarmed...or in a level 2+ pursuit, because that gets insane REALLY quick.
As for the plot, while at first it seems like your standard Zombie Outbreak Pathogenb Scenario, it's actually a lot deeper and pretty fresh and exciting. Some pretty obvious twists, but nothing too badly done.
The sound in the game is pretty amazing, the music fits the mood, and the zombies all sound great.
Combat is actually pretty balanced in terms of difficulty. You're not gonna be able to take down an army with a crowbar, but a small group is fairly easy to kill. The special enemies are where it gets tough, and even knowing how to beat them sometimes isn't enough to actually execute it, especially when it comes to Demolishers (especially when there's MORE THAN ONE in the area). That being said, there are very few places in the game where you're forced into a stand up fight for too long, and the areas you are and usually ripe with alternatives to simply wading in and hacking them all to death
So, overall, this game gets a 9.5/10 from me, the only thing barring it from a 10 being the tendency for a biter to grab you right as a bomber turns the corner >.>
TL;DR, this game is worth the money for the single player ALONE.

"Imagine the gods are playing some great game like chess and you don't know the rules of the game"
Richard Feynman made this analogy to the joyful feeling of discovery in the sciences; in learning the "rules" of the game of physics.  In many ways this quote applies to this game.  We've seen those well crafted puzzle games such as portal or braid that in one way or another explain the entirety of the ruleset that the puzzles are operating right away.  The rest of the game is challenging you on increasingly difficult applications of those axioms.  Antichamber doesn't do that.  It doesn't explain the intricacies of the rule set.  It doesn't even explain the rules.  You're stuck with the only hint ever given to you being the controls and in a way this feels like a much more gratifying puzzle experience than the games I've mentioned above.

Game Name: Sid Meier’s Civilization V (5)
Original Release: 2010
Personal Rating: A
Estimated Playtime: 96 Hours
Multiplayer/Coop?: Yes
Played on: Steam Controller, Keyboard/Mouse
Sid Meier’s Civilization V or also known as “Civ 5” is a strategy game continuing the line of games within the Civilization series. It’s a classic turn-based strategy game with its roots in the 1990’s, starting with the original Civilization.
Controls: When I play this, I mostly use my keyboard and mouse, but I can occasionally use the Steam Controller if I want to sit on the couch and play on my laptop. The controls aren’t really hard to use and it doesn’t really take the dexterity needed in order to play FPS games or MOBAs. Simple point and click.
Graphics: Graphics are pretty decent, but that isn’t the point of the game. It is a couple steps up from the previous versions and that makes it nice when you want to see the vast empire that you will eventually establish.
Music: The music in the game is great. Themed music for each player, in different situations and regular music continuously play throughout the game. It is definitely the type of soundtrack that you can chill to while you play the game.
Overall: Sid Meier’s Civilization V is a complete game. It brings exactly what its audience wants. The gameplay allows for continuous repeated  play-throughs and when you get tired of being dominated by the computer, you can play and suffer against fellow humans online. Beware though. Once you start, it will be hours before you are done.

Definitely interesting with some really clever outside-the-box puzzles, and definitely not lacking in style.  However this game has some serious pacing problems, that add a ton of undue frustration, and really knee-caps the player's ability to learn constructively.  Puzzle games need to lay out and reinforce core mechanics early, and make the player constantly apply them in new ways.  This game keeps introducing new mechanics right up until the end of the game, making several puzzles completely unsolvable until later on, but never bothers to make that clear to the player.  And worst of all, too many puzzles simply rely on your powers of observation, rather than your ability to think pragmatically. You seldom think through your solutions here, rather you just battle a war of attrition, throwing spaghetti at the wall and checking every nook and cranny until something unexpected happens.

Short version: BUY THIS GAME NOW!
UPDATE: After playing hours and hours of this game I have realized that this game is truely an experience like none other, it is one of the darkest and most unique games I have ever played; the open world is larger and more detailed than anything you've ever played and the story is just awesome, a truely engaging an emotionally draining experience. In my review below I make lots of reference to Dead Island and while I hate to say it, those comments are now irrelevant, Dead Island has nothing on this game. This isn't just an evolution in gaming, it's an evolution in story telling.
Long version:
Nothing can describe this game other than perfect. It takes everything that was amazing about Dead Island; the ambience, the exploration, the story and the crafting and adds more to it. The only thing Dead Island lacked was flawless gameplay, it was buggy and filled with graphics glitches, but Techland have really learnt from that experience and they've taken everything that worked and fixed everything that didn't! This game is like a slap in the face for the Cryengine, the graphics are OUT OF THIS WORLD.
I can also forgive Techland for delaying this game to work on the free-running because it was definitely worth it; the exploration in this game is unlike any other because literally, if it looks like you can climb it, YOU CAN.
Another impressive apsect to Techlands work is the emphasis they put on the zombie; in Dead Island they really made zombie's a threat again, unlike other zombie games where they are basically harmless obstacles that you need to knock over. But in Dying Light they've upped the ante again, you REALLY don't want to confront a zombie and that's just during the day, don't even talk to me about night-time! Which brings me to the day and night cycle; this is the first game where it really affects the game. Taking your character out during the day is completely different to taking him out at night. The game brilliantly conditions you to fear the night and believe me, YOU DO. It's easy to lose track of time when you're working a mission and when you suddenly hear the warning over the radio that it's almost night time, it like a kick in the guts, and then you gun it for the nearest safe zone.
There are only two issues I have with the game; the first is that the Be The Zombie mode is slightly unbalanced and consequently no-one who is playing a human takes the challenge against a hunter, but this is merely a matter balancing the hunter a bit and as soon as its sorted out, it will be amazing. My second problem isn't actually a problem with the game but more of a grievance; I loved Dead Island and this game should've been Dead Island, I can't imagine how amazing this game would be if it were set Bonoi, but that takes nothing away from this game and it's not Techland's fault; Deep Silver are just morons.
Ultimately, this game has all the amazing intrigue and charisma that Dead Island had, but adds to that some of the best graphics I've ever seen, an amazing parkour system and a truely dark, disturbing and terrifying experience.
Techland are becoming the masters of zombie games.

“A few steps backwards may keep you moving forwards.” This is one of many statements that can be found printed on the walls of Antichamber, a labyrinth whose corridors frequently defy the rules of three-dimensional space. In order to overcome all of the self-constructing walls, false passages, and invisible portals of the labyrinth, the player must indeed take a few steps backwards, by abandoning his or her sense of spatial reasoning.
Besides the dead-ends and regressions, there are no enemies in Antichamber, and the only shooting comes in the form of an upgradable, cube-shooting device. Developer Alexander Bruce proves himself a master of extra-dimensional gameplay, creating challenges that push the player further and further beyond the comforts of conventional physics. He also preys on a few gaming conventions, from a tutorial which must be disobeyed in order to advance, to rooms which are best navigated by walking through them backward. One of Bruce's more frequent tricks is to make many divergent paths lead to the same destination, rendering the player's choices irrelevant. To avoid covering the same ground under the illusion of forward progress, the player must move slowly and be perceptive.
Thanks to some incredibly polished audio and visuals, it is quite enjoyable to move slowly. Crisp sounds and rich colors create an other-worldly atmosphere, completed by Siddhartha Barnhoorn's ambient compositions, which feature digitally-manipulated recordings of Japanese instruments. The graphics are functional as well as beautiful, with correct paths often presenting themselves in recurring shapes, colors and sprites. Responsive control guarantees that you'll get around easily, even when building cube stairways or leaping across chasms.
The average player should be able to complete the game in ten to twelve hours (although experienced gamers, Bruce claims, will have a harder time with certain challenges that were designed to counter traditional first-person tactics). Ten hours might be a little more bewilderment than some can handle, and the second half of the game, with its emphasis on cube manipulation, can get particularly dizzying. If you are prone to existential nausea, I would recommend this game in small doses.
What makes Antichamber so absorbing-- and in my opinion, important-- is that it allows us to experience impossible geometry. In Bruce's words: “Things that are completely incomprehensible by looking at mathematical formulas on paper, like quantum mechanics or non-Euclidean space, [are] presented in a way that allows the player to interact with them more directly and understand their ramifications.” In the real world, we will never experience a closed loop with an exit point, or a single door that opens onto an unlimited number of rooms. We will never take a step that moves us in more than one direction, or jump down a chute to find higher ground. Antichamber gives us these mind-altering opportunities.
TL;DR -- An immersive and puzzling, three-dimensional exhibition of four-dimensional space.

I am, historically, a LEGO® game fan. Played them througout childhood and have always counted on a game like this one. After completing LEGO® Marvel™ Super Heroes, I walked away with some great feelings. While playing, I experienced some things not expected, for me, in a LEGO® title. This game, in a sense, blew me away.
Firstly, I was astonished with the level design and graphic art portion of the game. In a LEGO game, I was not anticipating such stunningly fun levels and amazing views. When I was casually running through the game, I couldn't help but to sit back and admire the breath-taking sights from a handful of missions. This game is really incredible, and lives up to most of its hype so far. The graphics are really great, some of the best I have seen in an RPG, which they should be for the type of game it is (survival/horror/RPG). I do worry that it may fall into some of the repetitiveness that other RPGs have in the past. This is in regards to what I will call the “side quest grind”, where completing side quests for different people/groups to gain respect/trustworthiness becomes repetitive and stale. So far I will say it has yet to do this. Each side quest has been a unique experience that exposes you to more areas of the map or just opens your eyes to places you may have passed before without a second thought.
There are also random encounters of different types that have kept my attention such as rescuing other survivors (NPC) who are fighting off zombies, defending them while they complete some task, trying to claim air drops as they appear, and reclaiming safe houses that make for excellent midway points for quests (primary or side).
Then ....... there is the night gameplay........ OHHH the night gameplay! It introduces a stealth aspect to the game that I have never experienced before. If you screw up and are seen, prepare to sweat bullets as you run like you have never run before. It is one of the scariest things I have experienced in gaming; even compared to Outlast, although I will say Outlast is based more on jump scares. The night gameplay creates an atmosphere that produces a constant, sweat inducing fear that keeps you on your toes as you work to navigate your way through the dark city streets and rooftops. This is all while being chased by what can only be described as an unspeakable evil that is as swift as a panther and hits like a bear.  If you feel up to the task I challenge you to get this game and experience the beautiful brutality that is Dying Light.

Antichamber (Nth Review)
Okay, toss aside story, enemies, quests, characters and all that fancy stuff. Antichamber is a pure 3-dimensional puzzle platform shooter in the vein of Portal or.... well, Portal 2.
The graphic style is very spartan, yet effective and delivers a very peculiar atmosphere. Especially contrasted with the ambience sound that directly contradicts what you see and subsequently evokes a very surreal overall picture.
The puzzles are very diverse and get successively more difficult as you explore the labyrinth of rooms and corridors, all while the progression is quite naturally regulated by the growing abilities you gain to interact with the environment - though it is sometimes not really obvious if you can already solve a puzzle or not, which can frustrate, but more often than not you have rooms and paths to explore, when you cannot solve a puzzle yet.
Not directly visible, but also really interesting and engaging is the story of Alexander Bruce, the sole creator of Antichamber (safe for some assets, such as sounds). This work and piece of art was a cathartic episode of his life, struggling with the construction of this game and life in general. And it becomes apparent once you realise that the whole game revolves around finding ways, overcoming obstacles and struggling with the environment to reach an aim you cannot even see, nor grasp its meaning. With this in mind, Antichamber becomes almost profund - yet most likely for no one as much as for its creator.
Rating: Highly recommendable! (As a game, as well as a statement!)

Antichamber is a first-person puzzle game. It's not like anything like you've seen before. Looking at the game screenshots you can clearly see that its graphics are awesome. But if you will buy this game, you will experience something more than just brilliant game. Throughout the game the very matter of your mind will change and you will look at things around you differrently. Every room you will encounter will require you to forget all you have learnt throughout your real life. The game itself will crush your common sense just as you will notice that there are no such thing as x, y and z axis. walking through the door can lead you to the room that was above you seconds ago. Besides messing with your brain with mind-twisting puzzles Antichamber guides you through your life with signs you can read after completing each challenge. (Shhh! Antichamber is also full of easter eggs!)  Antichamber is a clearly philosophical game as it doesn't have a plot. (Yes, that's right. You just spawn in the dark room and follow instructions how to enter the Antichamber.) The Antichamber shows the whole life cycle. For example, if at first you knew nothing about the game and the very simple element of the game puzzled you, at the end of the game even the most complex mind-breaker will not take more than five minutes to solve. Antichamber is a definite must-play.
10/10

FTL is also madly in love with random events and the bulk of the gameplay is trying to make the best decisions and benefit from randomized encounters, maps, event outcomes, shop items, etc. FTL has an incredible amount of depth and in spite of all the random events, it's pretty well balanced. My only real complaints are; you can't sell fuel, missiles or drones at shops, and every map is slowly taken over by the rebel fleet which really doesn't give you a lot of time to explore. But those are just two tiny specks of dirt on a very beautiful diamond. FTL is so good it actually made me start watching Star Trek. I know! Weird right?? But seriously you should get it.

There are 40 levels and each level has 10 hands, and each hand has a unique layout; also each level has a set of objectives that you need to achieve before moving on to the next level. This variety along with a few other quirks adds some strategizing that you don't normally get from regular solitaire. Computer solitaire is often only as good as how satisfying the sound effects are when playing and moving cards. This game has excellent sound effects, and on the whole is an enjoyable solitaire game.

I love, love, love this game. The Lego games have always been a lot of fun. The formula has pretty much stayed the same since the original Star Wars games. Solve puzzles. Punch guys. Break stuff. Build stuff. Along the way, a lot of refinements have been made to the system and it's safe to say that each game has been an improvement on the last one. Now at long last we get a game centered around the Marvel Super Hero universe. Super heroes work best with the Lego game mentality of 'break absolutely everything' and what better character to break absolutely everything than the Hulk? The worst thing I can say about the game is that the levels themselves are fairly repetitive. Fight your way through guys and solve puzzles until you get to the boss fight. But does repetitive matter if you're having tons of fun? The past Lego games that I've played have always been pretty linear with a central 'hub' world connecting everything. It's the same here but the central hub world is the whole of New York City! I had no idea when I bought the game. You can literally roam around NYC (flying is the best) finding all kinds of cool stuff to do that has nothing to do with the main game. There are a large number of random Lego pedestrians walking around and it doesn't seem to hurt the framerate one bit which is quite impressive. And yes, you can steal cars GTA style for absolutely no reason at all. If the free roam NYC was the entire game, it would be worth buying just for that.
Fun Fact: The voices for at least a dozen different characters were done by John DiMaggio, the voice of Bender from Futurama!

When I first picked this up on release, I wasn't too impressed.  It felt flimsy, didn't run very smoothly, failed to render graphics after I tabbed out, had an inconvenient save system, and so on.  Since then, all of those problems have been remedied (note: it seems like quicksaving is a feature included only when Dragonfall is installed).  It is now a thoroughly enjoyable cyberpunk RPG, albeit a bit linear, lacking customizable party members, and suffering slightly from a very XCOM-lite combat system.  If you're looking for an ultra-deep PC RPG you may be better off looking to Planescape: Torment, Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura, or even the more readily available (on Steam) Divine Divinity games.  However, if you approach this with the SNES version of Shadowrun in mind you'll most likely find it to be enjoyable.  It's atmospheric and feels very faithful to the aesthetics of '80s and '90s cyberpunk stuff.  I hear Dragonfall is a good bit better and less linear than the base campaign (Dead Man's Switch), too, so grabbing them both while they're on sale would probably be a good idea!  (This review's subject to change after I play more of the game, but I feel good enough about it to give it my approval during the summer sale.)

Game Review by Dragon: Lego Marvel Super Heroes
Stars: ***
Good bits: Lots to do. Heaps of the Marvel characters are playable. Game only _really_ needs two playthroughs.
Bad bits: Many of the (freeplay) side missions are repetitive, boiling down to 'cabby', 'fetch', 'race', 'destroy', and 'obstacle course' (my least favourite). No 'skip' function for Deadpool's intro's (funny, for sure, but once is enough).
Main story: Made as much sense as any real-world Marvel (or DC for that matter) story. :)
Other stuff: I loved the inclusion of so many of the Marvel minor players (Squirrel Girl!!). I would've preferred Deadpool was playable from the get-go (but that's me - he's one of my favourite characters). For a game aimed at little kids, I think some of the missions and puzzles were extremely tough, possibly impossible without a very patient teen or adult 'helper'. That said, I had fun. Worth the price? Yep.

This game is really incredible, and lives up to most of its hype so far. The graphics are really great, some of the best I have seen in an RPG, which they should be for the type of game it is (survival/horror/RPG). I do worry that it may fall into some of the repetitiveness that other RPGs have in the past. This is in regards to what I will call the “side quest grind”, where completing side quests for different people/groups to gain respect/trustworthiness becomes repetitive and stale. So far I will say it has yet to do this. Each side quest has been a unique experience that exposes you to more areas of the map or just opens your eyes to places you may have passed before without a second thought.
There are also random encounters of different types that have kept my attention such as rescuing other survivors (NPC) who are fighting off zombies, defending them while they complete some task, trying to claim air drops as they appear, and reclaiming safe houses that make for excellent midway points for quests (primary or side).
Then ....... there is the night gameplay........ OHHH the night gameplay! It introduces a stealth aspect to the game that I have never experienced before. If you screw up and are seen, prepare to sweat bullets as you run like you have never run before. It is one of the scariest things I have experienced in gaming; even compared to Outlast, although I will say Outlast is based more on jump scares. The night gameplay creates an atmosphere that produces a constant, sweat inducing fear that keeps you on your toes as you work to navigate your way through the dark city streets and rooftops. This is all while being chased by what can only be described as an unspeakable evil that is as swift as a panther and hits like a bear.  If you feel up to the task I challenge you to get this game and experience the beautiful brutality that is Dying Light.

As someone who did not play any of the XCOM games in their childhood, only finding X-COM on Dosbox a few years ago after having heard stories about it, I feel that I am in a uniquely un-nostalgia-biased position to say that this new XCOM is awful.
Well, let me rephrase that; It is a decent, if unremarkable, Tactical-RPG that is in no way deserving of the X-COM name.
Enough of my personal disappointment, on to the review:
Presentation: The story, an aspect that the first X-COM was unashamedly lacking in, comes across as ham-fisted and forced in the form of unskippable voice-acted cutscenes that linearly direct you from objective to objective, always telling you exactly what you need to do next. I won't pretend that UI design hasn't advanced in the nearly two decades since the original X-COM; as would be expected of a modern game, it is considerably better in both usability and accessability. Unfortunately this is marred by a range of bugs, ranging from misunderstanding orders to the game hanging or crashing entirely.
Gameplay: The designers seem to have gone to great lengths to eliminate as many 'bad choices' from the game as possible. In the original X-COM, you might choose to send a soldier into battle with nothing but a rocket launcher and 5 rockets to fire; such a configuration could be very effective in certain situations, though it would be folly to equip all of your soldiers as such. In this new XCOM, there is no inventory system at all, so it's completely impossible to screw yourself over with poor outfitting choices. It's also impossible to shoot your own soldiers in battle; your bullets always all hit the target alien, or go flying off into space, even if there was someone else blocking the line of sight between you and your target. Action points had been dumbed-down to the point of all of your soldiers able to take two 'actions' per turn, regardless of what those actions are. Cover is generally more resilient as well; offering better protection for your soldiers. Though combined with the fact that you can't even manually target cover to open up lines of sight for your soldiers means the aliens will be better protected as well. Unlike in the original, where the aliens would often actively hunt you down, or at least shoot at you if they saw you, in this X-COM all the aliens obligingly wait for you to spot them before playing an unskippable 'surprise!' animation and taking a free move to run for cover. Whereas the original had randomly generated maps, this new XCOM has static maps that will quickly have you saying ‘Oh, here again’ even in your very first playthrough. I could go on and on but I'll wrap this section up; All of the many, many gameplay changes render this game all-but unrecognizable compared to the original X-COM; and result in an experience that is bland and dumbed-down all around. A thin veneer of randomness to make the game feel 'difficult' while ultimately offering no challenge what-so-ever to the player.
Visuals: The graphics are good, if not exceptional. Generally the sort of thing I would expect from a modern X-COM game. There are numerous graphical glitches where the animation will not match the results the games decides: The bullets visually missing the target when the game rolls a hit, or a character pointing his gun in entirely the wrong direction when firing.
Sound: The audio is okay. I found the constant, repetitive voice-overs a bit grating, though some may like the guidance they offer. Some cutscenes don't obey the audio settings of the rest of the game, and will play at whatever volume they feel like, even if you've turned down the volume for the rest of the game. The music is much more forgettable that the original X-COM.
You may have noticed that many of the issues I presented as negatives in this review are the result of unfavorable comparisons to a games that came out nearly two decades ago. Let me just repeat this, for emphasis: Nearly two decades ago, the original X-COM simulated the flight trajectory of each bullet path in 3D to determine if it hit anything along the way, or shot through an open window without breaking any glass. Both things that a modern game bearing the same name nearly two decades later was apparently unable to replicate.
If this did not have the X-COM name, I would say it was a bog-standard average Tactical-RPG. As things are, I have to give it an F for effort and wasted potential.
That said though, I can't really in good faith recommend you go and play the original, it really is showing its age after all these years, so I'll leave you with this as a conclusion: If you really liked the original years ago, don't bother with this, you'll just be disappointed; enjoy the memories you have, or play X-COM again on dosbox. If you've never played X-COM before, you might enjoy it, but I can't really recommend it.

This game is self-improvement that feels like self-abuse, but when you make progress you know you've earned it.
Super Hexagon is entirely a skill game.  Besides the obvious hand-eye-coordination, Super Hexagon heavily affects your ability to focus on several levels.  It hits your brain's ability to track/manipulate a small, moving object, all while subjected to visual distraction and spacial distortion that prevent you from mentally caching information.  It requires you to mentally buffer between 3 and 6 units of movement, with one move falling off the buffer as you perform it and a new move being added to the end at the same time.  It also taps into the brain's ability to slow perception.
You have to personally improve in order to proceed.  The most luck will do is buy you an extra couple units of time before you die and start over.  There is no grinding or level memorization (though there is light
recognition).  You cannot beat this game without being good at it.  Since it is a skill game, though, the abilities you develop to focus and make buffered, rapid decisions will carry over to anything else you do that call for the same things.
I think that's what's so addictive about Super Hexagon.  The knowledge that
while the mental stress and flashing colors are eroding your sanity.  The thing that keeps it from being too frustrating is
When you stop making mistakes you stop dying.
Here are some things you should know about the game play:
*  Epileptics shouldn't even watch the video, let alone play the game.
*  This is basically a randomly-generated maze, except the walls are constantly hurtling towards you, every aspect of the game is designed to cause you to lose track of what you're doing, and death is instant the first time you make an error.  You can't pause or make the walls stop coming.  You just keep navigating your way forever or until you die.
* Everything occurs in what I'll call "units", which will represent 1/6 the amount of time for what's just beyond the edge of the screen to reach the middle.  Each wall is between 1 and 2 units of time in depth (yes, I'm using time as a measurement of depth and yes that makes sense).
*  In playing this game you will maintain a mental buffer of what you'll be doing over 6 units of time.  This is a live action game, so I mean you'll literally be doing this in your head.  Most of the things thrown at you will come in blocks where you have 2 units of time to move (or stay still).
*  As you're executing the current move and removing it from your mental buffer you're also adding 1 - 2 units to the opposite end of the buffer.  Reminder: this buffer exists solely in your own mind.
*  You can do three things in this game: rotate clockwise, rotate counterclockwise, and stay still.  Doing the wrong one usually kills you.
Regarding some complaints I've heard on the controls:
*  I've heard people recommend using a controller.  I don't think that advice is universal.  I found it easier to use the A and D keys from playing a lot of games where you use your left hand and the WASD keys even though I am right-handed.
*  Your control of the triangle/cursor is inexact.  It's important to reverse direction (when possible) to recenter it.  The reason for movement being freeform is because you will occasionally need to move a hair's width over the line to dodge one wall then immediately reverse direction to avoid being killed by the next wall.  If your movement was less twitchy you could not do this.
*  There is a very slight delay between pressing one of the two move buttons and your cursor moving.  If you hold a button down you will move in that direction ("spin") until you release it.  This is faster than tapping to move the same amount of distance because it only has one delay, but requires better timing to avoid killing yourself.  This is not accidental; there will be times when doing anything other than a controlled spin will be too slow (which will kill you).
...
Despite how that might sound, this game is actually a lot of fun because it challenges your brain.  This is purely a game.  Super Hexagon makes no attempt to be art nor is it a medium for art.  It is a work of craft.

This game is self-improvement that feels like self-abuse, but when you make progress you know you've earned it.
Super Hexagon is entirely a skill game.  Besides the obvious hand-eye-coordination, Super Hexagon heavily affects your ability to focus on several levels.  It hits your brain's ability to track/manipulate a small, moving object, all while subjected to visual distraction and spacial distortion that prevent you from mentally caching information.  It requires you to mentally buffer between 3 and 6 units of movement, with one move falling off the buffer as you perform it and a new move being added to the end at the same time.  It also taps into the brain's ability to slow perception.
You have to personally improve in order to proceed.  The most luck will do is buy you an extra couple units of time before you die and start over.  There is no grinding or level memorization (though there is light
recognition).  You cannot beat this game without being good at it.  Since it is a skill game, though, the abilities you develop to focus and make buffered, rapid decisions will carry over to anything else you do that call for the same things.
I think that's what's so addictive about Super Hexagon.  The knowledge that
while the mental stress and flashing colors are eroding your sanity.  The thing that keeps it from being too frustrating is
When you stop making mistakes you stop dying.
Here are some things you should know about the game play:
*  Epileptics shouldn't even watch the video, let alone play the game.
*  This is basically a randomly-generated maze, except the walls are constantly hurtling towards you, every aspect of the game is designed to cause you to lose track of what you're doing, and death is instant the first time you make an error.  You can't pause or make the walls stop coming.  You just keep navigating your way forever or until you die.
* Everything occurs in what I'll call "units", which will represent 1/6 the amount of time for what's just beyond the edge of the screen to reach the middle.  Each wall is between 1 and 2 units of time in depth (yes, I'm using time as a measurement of depth and yes that makes sense).
*  In playing this game you will maintain a mental buffer of what you'll be doing over 6 units of time.  This is a live action game, so I mean you'll literally be doing this in your head.  Most of the things thrown at you will come in blocks where you have 2 units of time to move (or stay still).
*  As you're executing the current move and removing it from your mental buffer you're also adding 1 - 2 units to the opposite end of the buffer.  Reminder: this buffer exists solely in your own mind.
*  You can do three things in this game: rotate clockwise, rotate counterclockwise, and stay still.  Doing the wrong one usually kills you.
Regarding some complaints I've heard on the controls:
*  I've heard people recommend using a controller.  I don't think that advice is universal.  I found it easier to use the A and D keys from playing a lot of games where you use your left hand and the WASD keys even though I am right-handed.
*  Your control of the triangle/cursor is inexact.  It's important to reverse direction (when possible) to recenter it.  The reason for movement being freeform is because you will occasionally need to move a hair's width over the line to dodge one wall then immediately reverse direction to avoid being killed by the next wall.  If your movement was less twitchy you could not do this.
*  There is a very slight delay between pressing one of the two move buttons and your cursor moving.  If you hold a button down you will move in that direction ("spin") until you release it.  This is faster than tapping to move the same amount of distance because it only has one delay, but requires better timing to avoid killing yourself.  This is not accidental; there will be times when doing anything other than a controlled spin will be too slow (which will kill you).
...
Despite how that might sound, this game is actually a lot of fun because it challenges your brain.  This is purely a game.  Super Hexagon makes no attempt to be art nor is it a medium for art.  It is a work of craft.

This review is mainly a KF1 vs KF2 comparison.
On the surface level, KF2 has much higher production values than Killing Floor 1, but when you look deeper, the gameplay, feel, and atmosphere pale in comparison.
KF2 seems somehow much cleaner than KF1, which had a very brutal, gritty feel to it. The lame metalcore soundtrack of KF2 makes this even worse. In KF1, the soundtrack is mainly comprised of brutal, raw death and industrial metal.
The guns, to me, feel like toys, which is surprising since they said that they really wanted to make the guns feel right this time around. There doesn't seem to be much impact to the headshots. In KF1, each one felt satisfying. Here it's just nothing. I'm thinking it's the combination of the visual and the sound effect. In a game where you spend the majority of the time shooting zeds in the head, it'd better feel pretty damn good.
The gameplay in KF2 seems to be more of a cluster♥♥♥♥. In KF1, the gameplay was way more tactical and there was less room for error. This feels way less methodical and more like running around shooting at things.
The new sci-fi-style UI/HUD looks like garbage, and I can't stand it.
Where KF2 wins is the graphics. KF1 looks outdated by today's standards. But to be honest, I liked it because there was less clutter on the screen, and the atmosphere more than made up for the lesser graphical fidelity in technical terms.
This game is still good, but I still prefer KF1. For a newcomer, I don't know. It failed to impress me as a sequel.
tl;dr: Overall, KF1 is better. Better atmosphere, music, and even gameplay. As a KF1 veteran, I didn't enjoy it. I tried to be as objective as possible, without nostalgia glasses. KF2 is still worth getting, though.
---------------------------------------------------
Year(?) after release update:
Now that the game has been polished and a lot of dumb things have been ironed out, I'd say it's equal with KF1 in its own way. It's different, but I wouldn't say either game is straight up better.

Antichamber is a puzzler in the same way portal is a first person shooter... technically it's true, but in execution it has a distinctly different feel to what one would expect. I compare this to portal for reasons that i will go into later, but it really is a good comparison. Antichamber is a game ment to be experienced as blind as possible, so you can feel that satisfying feeling of self-loathing when you look up the answer to one of the puzzles. The game is all about learning the rules and applying them in as meny ways as you can imagine.
And here in lies the justification for the portal reference. You have a lot of freedom in this game. I'm not talking about sandbox-like games where you have a large play pen to be in. In portal, you could put the portals any way you liked, even if it wasn't relevent to the puzzle. Of course you couldn't portal every surface, but the game never felt the need to take away the functionality of the gun with some scripted sequence (for example, when Samus losing some weapons because her armor was damaged in a cut scene). You also had time to complete puzzles. You didn't feel rushed (until the climax of course), and you weren't punished for your failures as you would be in other games (no lost progress, xp loss, or money loss).
Antichamber puts you in an enviornment and says, "Go Nuts" without telling you what to do. Gradually you will learn the rule set, and understand what you need to gather to progress. It's a tad annoying in that respect, (similar to rogue-like games that refuse to tell you what the items in game do) but not unreasonable. Careful observation and random chance will have you discovering new things that will help you progress. As you get the guns, you can really start to screw with the game and do some really neat stuff.
Antichamber is a great experience, and definitly a situational pick-up. If you love puzzlers, it can be a lot of fun; if you want story, go elsewhere; and if you want solid mechanics, you will be held over but not blown away. Just keep in mind that this game is deep, making you think as opposed to making you ask questions. The goal isn't to give a message like, "War never changes", but rather to change your way of thinking. It does a great job at that. It gave me a headache like every classic piece book i've ever read, but had me walking away with something more then just wasted time and a happy disposition. Pick this up if you want some brain food.
Also-- One piece of advice, the map tells you a lot... if you're stuck, go to rooms you haven't been in, using the map as a reference as to where they might be.

TL;DR at the bottom
Shadowrun Returns is an interesting game. Its a tactical game, set in a sci-fi world of interesting technology and a unique blend of elves, orcs and trolls.
Being the sci-fi nerd that I am, I was immediately enthralled by the writing, which despite some grammatical errors (and kind of cheesy sometimes), was interesting to read. The setting FELT sci-fi (which can't be said of alot of games) and the mix of humans with other mythical-humanish creatures was a cool take on a future universe mixed with what is traditionally considered a past-mythical world.
Now onto the gameplay. Its..pretty simple. You get a few abilities depending on class and how you spend your skill points in a mass effect 1ish skill tree. For the most part combat is dry, but just interesting enough to push through the story, which I actually really enjoyed. The game feels kinda short. For example, there is an entire skill tree, that is related to hacking (or "decking" as it's called in this universe) which while has its dedicated time in the story, is largely ignored. It has a really cool concept of a charecter entering the "matrix" of a computer network using their avatar (which is upgraded via skill tree and items) to gather information, disable turrets and fight defensive programs. Really really cool, but the game lacks the options to make it really shine.
Now, I said the writing was good in this game, which is true, however the game presents itself with the illusion of choice. Many diaglogue options will warrant the same response from the NPC you are talking to. Your dialouge options won't change the way people interact with you, nor will it grant you any unique responses. So if your REALLY looking to immerse yourself in this world, then in this aspect you'l be dissapointed. Its less of a "you are the main charecter" kinda game and more of a book being read to you, but giving you the power of editing a few charecter lines.
That was a long winded and unncessarily long anology.
ANYWAY, I liked this game for the setting, the writing, and just enjoyed the ride. As an avid Shadowrun fan, I was psyched when I heard about the kickstarter for Shadowrun Returns. I immediately backed it and kept careful track of the progress. Based on some of the design decisions and the concept art, I was initially concerned. My worry proved to be unfounded though. When I first opened Dead Man's Switch I was immediately pleased with the depth of detail in story and graphics.
It does a respectable job of emulating the pen and paper game feeling. There is room for improvement, and I certainly hope some of the issues are addressed in the future, but there is enough variety for you to at least customize a character to reflect you (combat) style. Lacking stealth is a particularly strong drawback. So is the way social skills like negotiation and con are replaced with etiquette, but a smart modder can work around that and present an experience which will tailor to your needs.
Which brings me to my next point, the editor. Say what you will about the main story, give it a couple months and it won't matter. The game comes with the same editor the developers used to make the game. Based on the community, you can expect some amazing modules to come and I look forward to them in the future! As for the main game, I enjoyed it even though it was fairly linear. It had the feeling of playing shadowrun at a gaming convention, you needed to follow a set script, but there was a decent story to back it up.
One of the biggest concerns myself, and the community had was the lack of a save anywhere feature. Fortunately HBS was quick to implement this after release. They are very attentive to their fans needs. Now if only they could do something to limit ammo!
Overall though, I am happy with Shadowrun Returns. If you are an avid fan, get it. If you are a casual gamer, do your research first. This game is not made by a major studio, you cannot hold it to the same standards as you would something from EA Games. If you want voice acting, amazing graphics, and more options than you can imagine, this is not for you. If you are willing to give the little guy a chance, and want the feeling of playing Shadowrun with your friends, then you will probably be pleased with what you get. At the very least its the best Shadowrun game out there currently.
UPDATE 6/29/14
I was asked about the game's replayability, so here is an update to address that. I will (most likely) better update the review later, but for now here it is.
Most of my hours were spent inside the editor, you can easily spend hundreds of hours making your own mods. If you want to tell your own stories, and share them with the community, this is the game for you. The editor is the same tool used by the devs to make the official modules.
A regular player will get less mileage out of the official campaign. The base campaign, Dead Man's Switch is under 20 hours for a playthrough. I played through it 3 times with different style of characters, but the experience is more or less the same regardless of character type.
The expansion, Dragonfall, was also under 20 hours of playtime. I have only played that campaign once. Its a much more satisfying experience than the base campaign, but still, limited replay-ability. There are a couple optional missions you can play, but they both are fairly linear overall.
The place where you can get strong replay-ability is the fan made modules. Some of them are really incredible. The downside is that being fan made you need to be patient for them to finish. It is entirely likely that you will start one and then finish everything that is there and be stuck waiting for the next installment.

Welcome to dying light, at the beginning you start of clumsy, slow and powerless but after a while you become a prodigy.
Why do you recommend this you say, well I’ll tell you why?
The story is amazing (I’ve only been playing for a bit but for now its godly) the characters are all unique each in their own way and little to no repetitiveness, i do believe the game uses a morale system -like in state of decay- where if you're popular (you become popular by helping) you get discounts at shops and some people even give you special items, the AI is in my opinion good the rebels are agile, smart and manipulative and usually work in teams I’ve rarely seen one alone whilst the zombies are another story, there are 4 types of zombies that I’ve encountered (there's more but I’ve only seen those) they are ; the slow, stupid biters, the fast and agile runners -act like a rebel- the slow and huge demolisher and last but not least the unnatural scary villatoile.
On the other hand every game has cons so this game has a bit:
If you pre-order the game -which i did- you only get 3 exclusives (be the zombie mode, the princess and yet another weapon).Remembering this is a "techland" game we have to look back at their records (dead island) and they were buggy so what are this games bugs. Well i haven’t been playing for a long time but till now I’ve seen 2 minor bugs and 1 major bug. let’s talk about the minors, the first was an un-textured door it was jet black and was out of tone (spotted it 6 buildings away) and the sound stops every now and then but then returns now let’s talk about the major which is lip sync, from time to time the games lip sync slows down or speeds up which is EXTREEMLY disappointing.
Now let’s talk about the performance
*watch totalbiscuit's PORT REPORT for more info
the game itself is beautiful so it might be quite taxing for low tier PC's and PS's that use AMD, FPS is quite high for a AAA title so that was surprising (looking at you far cry 4) although there was an error for the view distance where it does more harm than good, it decreases your FPS and doesn’t do as much prettiness as you'd think.
Now let’s talk about weapons, weapons in this game aren’t hard to find mainly because anything is a weapon, these weapons break, corrode, and lose power over time if they don’t get repaired often thus bringing us to the crafting and blue-prints part of the game you can find the materials from looting items (dead zombies, trash, in vegetation) and the blue prints can be found here and there and bought here and there.
Every now and then the GRA send in a drop that can contain flares, med kits, antizin (the medicine if you’re infected) ammo, food or valuables that you can sell, of course you can choose to take or leave them and if you take them you will then give them to the tower to gain respect, the drops can be dropped anywhere from the top of the highest tower to the depth of the sea.
Let’s talk about the leveling up system, this is what mainly brings up the RPG element unto the game, there are 3 skill trees in game they are: Power, Agility and Survival. Power talks about if you can sustain enough damage and if you can deal enough damage. Agility talks of how fast you can run and for how long and finally the survival tree speaks of things you can do to basically survive. Of course this is all vague because every tree has VERRY interesting perks (vaulting over zombies).
And last but definitely not least the moment we’ve all been waiting for=Parkour.
The Parkour is as good as mirrors edge, yes you start on slow and clumsy but later you become an expert. It’s very flowing and makes you feel free, unfortunately there are a bit of things that I despite for instance you have to look at where you want to grab to hold/grab on to something which if you don’t could lead into your demise (♥♥♥♥ING TOWER, I SWEAR TO GOD I GRABED THAT) but other than that the Parkour runs amazingly (see what I did there “runs” HAHA)
In conclusion the game has an amazing story with even better characters , the performance can be made a bit better  a basic copy of dead islands weapon duration AMAZING AI very nice random events RPG-like skill and skill tree and GODLY Parkour, overall I would recommend this game to people that like zombies Parkour and free roaming.

If you`re more of a stealth player, you can move around during night time, avoiding a lot harder and faster Zombies. Also some missions are required to be completed during night time. You are rewarded by playing night time by giving you double xp on power and agility. You seem to level up skills by using them (Skyrim again). For example, If you do parkour stuff, your agility seems to increase and if you fight, then your power skills get an increase. When you have collected enough xp on certain skill group, you can pick a skill from a tree which might unlock different moves, crafting skills etc. I`m sure you know the drill from other games.
Sometime (a lot of times it seems) during the night time you get invaded by other player. This player occurs as a huge nightmarish creature who will try to pounce on you. Your task is to kill this creatures nests before he kills you. You get awarded more xp and good loot during this 1 vs 1 game. If you win as a human, you seem to get rewarded with a potion that boosts your performance temporarily in the "real" game. You can also play as this creature if you feel like hunting other players moving during night time.
After you have finished introductive mission (takes around 15-30 minutes), you can start playing cooperatively. I have not yet tested this part of the game, but it seems there are a lot of players available on this mode. When you enter an area, the game informs you that there are like 100 other players starting missions from this area. I quickly browsed trough and it seems you can choose which quests you join to cooperative with.
I would give this game 9/10 after 6 hours of gaming. So far i feel like i`m playing fresh Skyrim in different world and with a chance to cooperative and competitive gaming.
