While I have long since grown tired of horror games using HP Lovecraft's "At The Mountains of Madness" like a formula for plot, I'll grudgingly admit that, after taking some time to simmer on the game and replay it, there are SOME elements of Dead Space which earn some praise. The set pieces within the game itself are very cohesive and make sense within the design of the USG Ishimura (even if it is basically the same levels as System Shock 2's Rickenbacker). The user interface is very well made, and even adds to the inescapable darkness of the game by providing weak, almost timid glows around the holograms. The weapons themselves are shaky, because if you really want to scare someone you shouldn't make sure they have a ridiculous cushion of firepower to hide behind the second things get out of hand, but Dead Space finds an odd middle ground. See, by adopting the same firing style as Resident Evil 4, the game forces actually using your weapon to be a challenging balance of coordination and time management, because missing a shot with even the most overpowered weapon can mean a game over. Combat in the game is an illusory safety if you're not playing on the easiest setting. Also, the ease in spotting where enemies will likely spawn makes the player paranoid, because you're never sure which vent or hall window will burst if you get too close.
The only real problem with the game is that the soundtrack tries too hard to play catch-up with the game, sounding like the orchestra is being tazed whenever an enemy jumps out. A good horror soundtrack acts as a supplement to the media, only stepping in when the silence actually needs to be filled or when unease is necessary that the game can't create on its own. As it is, the best way to play the game is with the soundtrack muted so that the silence really does hammer home the claustrophobia of the game, which is a shame because Jason Graves has some great music in here.
Overall, it's a solid 6 out of 10. Not the best if you're looking for a really stellar horror game, but it shows that at least it's trying.

I played Arkham Knight twice, first before the latest fixes and then after the patch. Overall I enjoyed the game, despite the infamous problems with the PC port. In its current state it is definitely playable, even though some problems are still there, especially while driving the even more infamous Batmobile.
Combat is great, however the lack of real boss fights is a big, big flaw. Far too much tank combat, as everyone's been saying since the game's release, and overall too much Batmobile. Great environments and graphics, cool gadgets and combat moves, I only wish there were some non-tank bosses, and there are none.
The story is decent, some parts are really great, however I find the whole Scarecrow plot annoying in a Nolan-like way. You know, there is no hope, the bad guys are invincible, have unlimited resources and will always screw you no matter what you do and so on. No spoilers intended, but the whole game has that "hopelessness & despair" feel that always irritated me in Nolan's second and third Dark Knight movies (I still consider Batman Begins the best movie in the trilogy). All this was far worse than the Arkham Knight's true identity most players and reviewers have been complaining about. IMHO the final showdown makes absolutely no sense, but again, no spoilers. The ending is also very Nolan-ish, again in an annoying way.
However, despite the game's many shortcomings, I still feel like recommending it. It's in no way as good as Asylum or City, and even the largely underrated Origins had those great boss battles and cool gadgets that made it more challenging and enjoyable than Knight. I'd say it's a 7 or 7.5/10 overall.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is still one of my favourite games of all time. Sure, it is turn-based combat and if you really tried, you can find a few faults with it, but the gameplay is tight, fun, brings across the combat from what I know of the original xcom very well and is very engaging and rewarding.
You play as the commander of the XCOM project. An organisation built to defend earth from the encroaching threat of alien invasion. In the base you arrange for a whole host of things to happen; You sort out your soldiers (hiring, dismissing, equipping, promoting, skill selection, customisation etc), your research projects to get better stuff, interrogations of captives, your base expansions, building and improving of equipment, taking requests from other Countries, selling alien objects, sending up satelites etc etc. So basically, you do lots of stuff. It's deep, engaging and you honestly do end up getting absorbed in everything which all ties up nicely and affects your soldiers in the field.
The field operations are turn based assaults, rescues, area securing and other various missions (depending on dlc or not) which take place in different areas which you do get to see a few times, but are infrequent enough and varied enough to still be interesting. The aliens you fight are nicely varied and gradually get more difficult as the game progresses and the whole thing has a nice tie-in with the base gameplay. You capture aliens, alloys, meld (dlc) and sometimes even soldier units in the field, then use those in the base to make more stuff, which then helps in the field next time. It's smooth, intuitive and really engaging.
There are flaws, naturally. Sometimes some of the abilities seem a little abstracted from the map geometry and units can sometimes see or even shoot through walls at times. The randomness of the ways you can get resources can be a limitation if you're out of funds for this month and seriously need to start building more stuff, but it does not affect gameplay negatively to a huge extent.
Overall, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a fantastic game, with a good story, immersive gameplay and great mechanics. It is fun and interesting, which in my book, is a big plus these days!

I don't understand why this game is well-rated on Steam. Don't get me wrong - Dead Space 1 is a great game on consoles, but on PC, they f**ked the port up in a number of ways.
1) Framerate is locked to 30FPS when you have VSYNC enabled in-game
2) Keyboard and mouse control is like steering a boat through jelly. Takes a big movement to register anything (seems to have a large 'dead-zone'), and the sensitivity is way down. You will be scrolling your mouse across your whole desk to turn a full circle in-game. If you turn the sensitivity to max, it's slightly better, but then the cursor flies all over the navigation menus. It's crazy.
People have written guides on how to attempt to remedy this and some people have good success, those with ATI graphics cards have to do additioanl tweaking to get it working if they can get it working at all. None of this is the point though, you shouldn't have to trawl forums and run through trouble-shooting just to fix something that should have been immediately obvious to the developers in testing - the controls are broken.

On the surface level, KF2 has much higher production values than Killing Floor 1, but when you look deeper, the gameplay, feel, and atmosphere pale in comparison.
KF2 seems somehow much cleaner than KF1, which had a very brutal, gritty feel to it. The lame metalcore soundtrack of KF2 makes this even worse. In KF1, the soundtrack is mainly comprised of brutal, raw death and industrial metal.
The guns, to me, feel like toys, which is surprising since they said that they really wanted to make the guns feel right this time around. There doesn't seem to be much impact to the headshots. In KF1, each one felt satisfying. Here it's just nothing. I'm thinking it's the combination of the visual and the sound effect. In a game where you spend the majority of the time shooting zeds in the head, it'd better feel pretty damn good.
The gameplay in KF2 seems to be more of a cluster♥♥♥♥. In KF1, the gameplay was way more tactical and there was less room for error. This feels way less methodical and more like running around shooting at things.
The new sci-fi-style UI/HUD looks like garbage, and I can't stand it.
Where KF2 wins is the graphics. KF1 looks outdated by today's standards. But to be honest, I liked it because there was less clutter on the screen, and the atmosphere more than made up for the lesser graphical fidelity in technical terms.
This game is still good, but I still prefer KF1. For a newcomer, I don't know. It failed to impress me as a sequel.
tl;dr: Overall, KF1 is better. Better atmosphere, music, and even gameplay. As a KF1 veteran, I didn't enjoy it. I tried to be as objective as possible, without nostalgia glasses. KF2 is still worth getting, though.

I had a lot of fun playing Dying Light. I played through the full storyline and did a moderate amount of side quests along the way. Dying Light goes by a 3 skill tree system which breaks down to Survivor, Agility, and Power with each tree branching out into helpful skills to get you through the hordes of zombies.  While the games parkour system was extremely well done and fun to do, Im just not the kind of person to back down from a fight. By the time I'd finished the main story I had 23 levels in Power, and only a measley 14 in agility.
SURVIVOR TREE and AIR DROPS
You receive survior points by completeing quests, retrieving air drops and returning whatever supplies are in to your quartermaster, saving survivors, killing thugs, etc. The survivor tree is related to crafting items, how much you can carry, and bartering. I was both extremely pleased and also slightly disappointed with the air drops. At the very first air drop you are sent to there are a bunch of thugs already there and you are told to avoid them. While naturally at that low a level those thugs would rip you apart in melee combat, however my molotov cocktail had other plans. This left me a half looted supply crate and I was overjoyed when I found a bunch of hand grenades in it. Unfortunately this is only a one time deal since every crate I found afterwards had only disaster relief kits and medical supplies that I could only give to the quartermaster.
AGILITY TREE and NIGHT TIME
The Agility Tree affects your free running ability and how quick you can get out of tough situations. You recieve points in this tree from simply running and climbing, dodging, and sliding. Now at the start of the game you get tired really quickly    from running and you climb rather slowly. However once you reach the second and third tier of the agility tree you unlock the ability to run faster and climb faster simple as that. During night time you receive double points for both your agility and power tree. Night time is DARK! The flashlight is absolutely necessary when it's night time just to see the ground in front of your feet. The flashlight doesn't alert enemies when you point it at them, unless you point the UV flashlight at a volatile (yikes). If you get caught by one of those monsters you will be "pursued" and you need to free run and climb to keep them away from you (they are faster than you and they will catch you if you run in a straight line). You will get bonus agility points if you successfully evade a pursuit and you will receive more points the longer and the more "intense" the pursuit is. However at lower levels I found it extremely difficult to free run away from them with how slow I climbed.
POWER and WEAPONS
The power tree affects your combat stamina and gives special moves for certain weapons. You get power points for killing zombies by any means. Early on you are givin terrible weapons and the only way to get the best weapons are to buy them with cash that you receive from quests or looting zombies or just laying around and selling commodities like cigarettes and coffee. The weapons you have access to at the store are also dependant on what level of Survivor rank you have so early on I could buy an Epic level Claw Hammer for 1500$ and later on I would buy a Legendary Katana for 30000$. In the power tree you can unlock a strong attack and you would hold down the appropriate attack key for a stronger attack that takes more stamina and swings slower. I never found an upside to this ability it was sluggish and a zombie would grapple me while i'm taking my sweet time swinging my wrench. Once I did get my Legendary Katana and I upgraded it with Bolter Poison and gave it Legendary and Epic upgrades I found myself hewing down zombies left and right taking off heads and arms with single swings. The only time I actually had to run away anymore was from the Volatiles at night those guys hit hard and don't go down easy so it's hard to kill one before they start swarming you.
GRAPPLING HOOK and ENDING
The grappling hook is absurd and does not follow the rules of physics... which makes it all the more fun to use. I would throw it in a straight line and my character would be propelled through the air in an equally straight line. Are you falling to your death? Shoot your grappling hook downward and you will be pulled directly downward without taking any damage. Zombies getting generally near you? Shoot your grappling hook up 15 stories of a building and arrive in mere seconds. Grappling Hook to surmise is fun but unrealistic and quirky. The story of Dying Light is a huge plus and I often found myself relating to the main character both emotionally and verbally. Unfortunately the ending (again spoilers ahead) was extremely disappointing. In fact most "boss" fights were disappointing. You would merely kill an absurd amount of Rais's goons and then you would walk into a trap be stripped of all your gear and givin some flimsy piece of metal to fight with and once the mission is over you would get all your stuff back. Once you finally solve an absurd jumping puzzle with many falls to the death you would reach Rais on the top of his tower and you will finally be rewarded with a sorry quick time event totalling in around 9 button presses. I messed up a lot of the quick time events because I was simply awestricken that they would climax this wonderful story with this sorry display of button pressing.
All in all it's a beautiful game with a great story and great gameplay. I would give it a 7.5/10 it would be an 8 out of 10 but that quick time even ending left me with a sour taste in my mouth. I even received an achievement called Bittersweet. Bittersweet indeed.

I hadn't really followed the development of this game until about a week before release.  I know there was a bit of drama just before release due to the late  review codes being sent out.  Rest assured, Dying Light is a good game.
I didn't like Dead Island as I thought it was very unpolished and buggy when I played.  This made me a bit nervous in taking the plunge.   However, over time I found myself more and more enamored by this game.  The combat is relatively simple but can be in depth in its execution.  You need to have situational awareness as even the simplist zombie can hold you down while others pound on you (also to utilize the terrian to your advantage).   You need to be able to switch weapons on the fly depending on the threat and keep good placement to strike when your enemy is most vulnerable.

The gore in this game is something else as well.  You can chop hands, arms, legs, heads off.  You can cut zombies in half horizontally or vertically (left and right or front and back :o).   Very rewarding when you clobber a swarm of zombies, vault over some other ones and keeping the others at bay.  I can't stress enough how simple the concept of combat is but the execution *muah* fantastic!
Co-op is also another great feature to the game.  You and your friends can play most of the campaign together (basically all the way up until the very last mission).   My friends and I had a few nail biting moments at night running acrossed a bridge while volatiles chased on.  Chucking IR flares behind us as we parkoured up to our safe house.
That being said, there are a couple issues I have most minor.  The biggest is the frame rate.  It isn't consistent and this seems to be a problem a lot of PC users are experiencing.  I, by no means, have an antiquated PC yet sometimes without reason my FPS will drop to 15-20 for a few seconds.    First release problems I am sure it will get fixed.  Another gripe I have is with the ranged weaponry.  There is only 5 guns in the entire game.  American 9mm, German 9mm, Police Rifle, Military Rifle, and Double Barreled Shotgun.  As rich as the melee weapons are, I'd have liked a pump action shotgun, a sniper rifle, crossbow or standard bow, or perhaps upgrades for the guns?  Different sights or suppressors?   Flamethrower or RPG?  If anything for the after game just to screw around.
Over all, the random FPS stutters and small choice in firearms keeps it from getting a perfect score.  If you have any doubts about this game, don't.  Push that purchase button and squish some zombie (and people!) heads!

Antichamber is a first-person puzzle game that loves to trick the player with rule changes, visual sleights, false walls and impossible spaces as well as some testing logic problems.
You start the game in a black-walled chamber with the controls printed on the wall next to a clock ticking down from 90 minutes. From here you enter the game's maze, where a staircase can lead to its own foot, walls and floors can vanish when you touch them, a set of rooms can be both horizontally and vertically adjacent to each other and pressing your face against a window can change where you are standing.
The puzzles are well designed and for the most part - difficult.
Antichamber is not a linear game. You will often find yourself bouncing off several puzzles simultaneously in different parts of the maze.
In my opinion is Antichamber a must have for every first-person puzzle game fan.

Super Hexagon is a great game. You are a triangle that circles around a hexagon in the center of the screen. Various obstacles converge towards the center of the hexagon, and you have to dodge them. Also, the screen spins around while you play. There are 6 difficulty levels; you start out with the first three, Hexagon, Hexagoner, and Hexagonest, then you unlock the hyper version of each difficulty level once you've survived for a minute in that difficulty. It sounds very simple, but it's actually extremely hard. Most people can only last 3 seconds starting out. This doesn't deter most people, though; as you play, you'll start to recognize patterns and work out how to dodge everything. It can keep you playing for a long time, due to multiple difficulty levels and constantly trying to beat your high score. I think it's definitely worth the price.
tl;dr: This game is very difficult, but very fun and worth your 3 dollars.

Short verdict: a door opening simulator that pretends to be scary.
Deadspace had a potential. It's, in general, a decent game and there are a few good things in it, but those good things are overshadowed by stupid concepts and suboptimal controls.
I'll start with the good things.
- "Dead Space" is, all-in-all, a well-polished game. It runs smoothly, everything is thoroughly designed. When there's so many buggy and sloppy games out there, it matters. However, I encountered a game-breaking bug at the end of Chapter 11, when I couldn't open a door and it was on stand-by constantly. I had to use another player's save file that I've downloaded from the Internet to finish the game.
- There is a nice set of weapons that you can upgrade. Upgrades are always a good thing, aren't they?
- The level design is intuitive. And even, if you're not sure where to go, you can activate the path marking. That is very handy. It's much better than a mini-map.
- 95% of the time game responds to your needs. Low on health? You get a health pack in the next crate or enemy. Low on ammo? Same thing.
- Apart from shooting enemies, you also have some powers: stasis let's you slow down enemies and time; kinesis allows you to move objects/body parts. There are also zero-gravity areas, where you can walk on the walls and jump over large distances.
Frankly, I didn't enjoy those powers and I absolutely hated the zero gravity missions. I'd rather prefer just shooting the hell out of things. But, at least the devs have tried and variety doesn't hurt. So, I appreciate that.
And, now, (TA-DA-DA-DAAH), the bad things:
- You need to dismember enemies to kill them. No, a headshot is not enough. A body shot does minimum damage. You need to shoot off their limbs/tentacles. It's so unnatural and because of the problematic aiming, also annoying.
- On medium and higher difficulties, the enemies are
damage sponges. To shoot off a fricking tentacle, you need 2+ direct hits.  A fricking tentacle! Not an armored tentacle. Not a metal tentacle. Just a simple, tiny, soft-tissue tentacle! It just doesn't make sense. While playing on medium difficulty, I was constantly low on ammo in the last few chapters.
(Note: on easy, it's a cake walk. You can shoot without any worries about ammo count).
- Controls. The character is slow. Melee animation takes approximately 3-4 seconds to finish. The aiming lags. It's hard to hit a target, especially, in those sequences, when you're grabbed by that gigantic tentacle with the yellow bulb.
Also, I played this game with an Xbox controller. It's easier like that. And, apparently, this game was primarily made with consoles in mind (framerate capped at 30 FPS, unmentioned controller support, cheats work only with a gamepad), BUT, when I need to shoot the asteroids or the monster in the outer space from a cannon, that is accomplishable only with a mouse. In short, this game has some serious camera and sensitivity issues. Some players even say that it's unplayable. And it's not much of an exaggeration.
- Forced and narrow FOV. Unfortunately, Dead Space is not a first-person shooter. You have a very limited field of vision. I understand that the devs did that to prevent the players to notice the enemies that crawl behind, to make it more scary. But it's not scary. It's just inconvenient and, occasionally, annoying, especially, in some puzzles, when you need to oversee a large area, but you can't, because of the FOV.
- The whole dismemberment concept. The idea is that the corpses can't transform into the monsters (necromorphs), if they are dismembered, and some might think that it's cool and gory. Except that it isn't. It's stupid and childish. And, since the human corpse dismemberment doesn't have any impact on the gameplay and, most of the time, you dismember the monsters with weapons anyway, so why bother? I think that it's a failed concept.
- It's not atmospheric, it's not scary. There's nothing "horror" about it. The game overuses jump scares to make it seem scary, but it fails. Without the proper atmosphere, those things just do not work. Also, there are a lot of safe zones in between. So, no sweat. Not that I care, I just like to shoot things. But, for those of you who do care, I recommend F.E.A.R. It does a much, much better job at creating a tense atmosphere.
- The story is mediocre. And many questions are left unanswered. I did understand what happened before and during the events of the game. And there are some explanations of why some characters did what they did, and what is the history with the Marker and the Church of Unitology. But those explanations are bad. It just doesn't make sense to me. I watched this video to find the answers:
But it still seems like a non-sense to me.
- Puzzles. Firstly, puzzles in a shooter? Why? Second, they are boring and all the same: you just need to re-arrange objects. Third, the FRICKING NARROW FOV!!!
It's hard for me to decide, whether to put "thumbs up" or "down", but I think, all-in-all, Dead Space gameplay is so problematic that I can't recommend it. I did not really enjoy playing it, I finished it only because it was not bad enough not to finish it.
My overall rating: 5/10.

The game is fantastic, and it's very much in a playable state. It's entertaining, it's fast (depending on which difficulty you play at combined with your own skill level) and definitely fun.
Tripwire seems to be listening to feedback, though it seems they only will when they get enough negative backlash about a change. There was one major game ruining effect that was added and, after a wave of negative reactions to it, was quickly compromised upon.
Unfortunately, they've had another lapse in judgment, and that's why I'm leaving a negative review.
Tripwire had a clear goal of 10 released classes, or "perks", that they wanted to implement before the game's release. These perks served the purpose of adding variety to gameplay. Some of them were identical in function to others, but, to be fair, it's hard to imagine making a first person shooter experience any more unique without taking away from the sense of realism, or without becoming too silly.
However, I would've prefered something silly to what they actually released for the 10th perk.
They introduced "Survivalist", which, despite the intriguing name, has nothing unique about it. It's a perk that takes a bit of flavor from every existing perk. However, because of the XP/Level-up and Perk Tree systems, Survivalist gains functionality and purpose very slowly as you level up, and even at your maximum potential you're always just under the bar of adequacy compared to the other classes.
This perk is a balancing nightmare, and feels very much like a half-hearted attempt that was made as a last minute decision - because, I assume, they didn't want to incur the wrath of those saying they broke their promises and falsely advertised their end goal.
To me, the game has become much less fun than it was for two reasons:
-First, if you're a completionist, you have to grind through the mundane experience of playing as a Survivalist.
-Second, a disproportionate amount of players are currently playing Survivalist, and contribute much less than they would if they had picked any other class.
I understand why they did it, but I hope they can understand this review will remain negative until they either balance this  rushed perk or replace it with a much more appropriate option.

Note on Performance: For those having issues with performance, I would recommend turning down the texture quality, turning view distance all the way down, and maybe even turn down shadow maps. These are the settings I've found that seem to have the most impact on performance, and turning them down did not detract from the experience. After I did this the game was smooth as butter on my sli 970s. Also try sli compatibility bits 0x080116F5 if you have an sli configuration.
Review: I've put almost 10hrs into the game so far and I'm really enjoying it. It's pretty much what I expected it to be and everything as it should (apart from performance). The characters are fairly interesting, the story isn't too bad, the combat feels good, looting isn't too tedious, crafting is simple and works fine, and best of all, the parkour is really fun! I wouldn't say it's at the level of Mirror's Edge or Titanfall, but it's in a more interesting environment and you can decide where and how you navigate the environment. I don't know if this is game of the year worthy, and it doesn't inovate all that much, but it does what it set out to do which is bring you a fun, open-world, sandbox survival-horror game set in a zombie apocalype, and it does it well. I never played Dead Island so I don't know how it compares, but from the videos of seen, this is much better. If you liked Dead Island, I think you'll really like this game, as long as you aren't burnt out on zombies. For the price, I would definitely recommend this.
Pros:
-Fun, fluid parkour system
-Satisfying combat
-Good voice acting
-Intriguing story
-Environment is well realized and immersive
-Nighttime is genuinely frightening and intense, but rewarding to make it through 'til sunrise
-Music and sound effects fit the setting and sound good
Cons:
-Poor utilization of sli and multi-core processors
-Occassional bugs that break immersion, like zombies clipping through cars/walls
-Limited video options (no choice of AA, either on or off, etc)
-Uses a lot of RAM. Depends on texture settings, but on high it was using about 4-5GB of RAM.

Summary: A South Park game that represents the series in the best way.
Positive: Humor and ambience. The jokes are standard for the show, albeit pushed further with less restrictions than the heavily-censored TV show.
The atmosphere of the town of South Park is enjoyable to walk around in.
You can avoid combat in most situations via action triggers or simple maneuvering.
Negative: Short length of the campaign. You can beat the game in only a few hours.
The game will drop your inputs from time to time. This is obnoxious since almost every action in combat requires timed button pressing to gain the best effect. A minor annoyance since the game is largely lacking in difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty, this game essentially has almost no challenge element. Think of it as an interactive 15 hour episode of South Park rather than a true RPG. There are difficulty options and I'd recommend playing on max difficulty.
Maximum character level is only 15. This is really easy to hit in a casual playtrough without level grinding. Experience points lose all meaning at the level cap (as expected), so combat in the last 3-4 hours of the game is pointless other than to see some jokes.
There are some areas of the game that can only be visited once per playthrough. Missing anything in these restricted-access areas means you cannot complete certain events/achievements.
Overall: 7/10. By far the best South Park game released to date. If you like the show and enjoy videogames this will be fun for you.

Best movie license game I've ever played. I love it. The turn based RPG system fits so well with the animation. This is the game that south park fans deserve. I'll go over the positive aspects and the negative aspects.
Positive:
-This game is incredibly funny. It's raunchy and dirty sense of humor fits me so well. I love it. However, if you are not into that kind of humor, this game will not appeal to you.
-The turned based combat would sound bad, and boring... But it actually has you involved. You don't just choose a move and then watch it play out. It's kind of like the Mario rpg games, where you have to put in some sort of actions to make a "Perfect" hit. The combat is also fairly fleshed out. There are status effects that can be inflicted on enemies. Also the unique ways each buddy can be used to suit your play style. You can even use the enviroment outside of combat using your abilities you get, such as your fart magic, and an anal alien probe. Skipping combat completely, but getting the experience.
-Plenty to explore, and has some replayability. Although I never completed it after doing it twice.
-It is creatively written. The story line is fantastic. Which it should be, being written by the developers of the show themself.
-Due to the kids larping, it makes some creative items. You can literally take a crap in a toilet, and throw it at an enemy to gross them out.
-The story line and all side missions can give you around... 20 hours, even more if you want to replay it.
Negative:
The negative aspects are just me nit picking a bit, but some of these can be an issue for others.
-This game is for south park fans, and for people who are not easily offended. If you are not a south park fan? You might not enjoy this game, and not get most of the jokes.
-The game is too easy on the default difficulty, and even on hard mode, it can be easy. I've found myself never losing a single battle when you follow the story line.
-20 hours is a VERY short rpg game, when it ends, you just feel like you want more.
Do I recommend this game? Yes and no... It is most assuredly a yes if you enjoy south park and LOVE inappropriate humor used in a clever fashion. No, if you are not a fan, and you are easily offended. This game is best for south park fans, and I thank the developers for making a brilliant game, when they could of easily screwed it up. I give it around 8/10. A good experience.

Antichamber's not perfect. Let's start with that. It does things right, it does things wrong.
At the outset, Antichamber is an interesting game. I know it's going to try and trick me, and knowing is half the battle. Once you know you're in a world of trickery, it's easy to work with. Just trick it back and you'll find yourself on the right path. Anybody who plays games and specifically does all of the things the developers didn't intend for you to do should have no trouble, here.
Then it gets confusing. The nonlinear style begins to take its toll, and this where one of the biggest issues becomes a problem. Until you solve a puzzle, you never really know whether you just haven't been going about it the right way, or if you CAN'T go about it the right way because you don't have the necessary equipment, yet. If you'll forgive a very minor spoiler, a lot of the gameplay of the game revolves around a series of matter guns which collect and place little cubes found all over the place. Each gun greatly expands your options for solving puzzles, and it's here another issue presents itself. The game doesn't always teach you everything a gun can do, and sometimes it's not clear that certain things can work in certain ways.
Of course, you might say that this is sort of the point, and in general you'd be right. But while this IS a game built to shrug off spacial normality, there are still rules set in stone which define the gameplay. There have to be, otherwise Antichamber would just be an unplayable mess.
Towards the end, things make much more sense. Once you have all of the guns and you've been around the block enough times to have filled in a fair amount of your map, you no longer feel helpless and lost all of the time. Just dumb. This is where the game all comes together. Things feel like less of a hassle, and more like a puzzle. You're not confused, because you understand how the game works. You can guess what trickery is at work and where, and conjure a counter quickly as you grin cockily like the waddling pedestal of smugness you are.
Actually, what impresses me most is how comfortable one becomes with the wayward nature of the game, something that seems to almost prove the notion that humans can mentally adapt to almost any situation.
I've read a lot of comparisons to Portal. These seem misplaced. Both are first-person puzzle games where you use a gun-like tool to interact with the world around you in specific ways, and there's not a whole lot more to connect beyond that. The mechanics, puzzles, and style are nothing alike. They each contain a certain amount of space-bending, yes, but in entirely different ways. With Portal's being user-controlled and orderly, while Antichamber's are intruding and chaotic. Portal is a game about using logic to solve logical puzzles. Antichamber is a game about using logic to understand and overcome the illogical.
A better comparison, in my opinion, would be Jim Henson's The Cube. But I'm getting off track.
Antichamber's a fun game once you get going. It's not so fun when you hit a wall, and then about 75 more walls and you're not sure which one you have to figure out how to knock down in order to get the tool that knocks down the others. I enjoyed enough of my time with it, though, to recommend it, and so here we are. And here we go. And there we go. ...And there go more of us. Aw man, spacetime sucks.

Experience
When I was a little boy, I remember a tabletop roleplaying game my friend had. It had so interesting looking manual, I couldnt stop browsing it. It had pictures, formulas, almost nude cyborg chicks, mages, lot of guns and swords. It had orcs, elfs, humans, dwarfs, gnomes, giants and minotaurs. My little mind was blown away. I was so excited, I couldnt stop browsing.
Time passed and memories faded. I was a teenager and girls were much more entertaining, than a tabletop roleplaying game. Roleplaying games were nerdy thing to do - girls were the cool thing, and you get to kiss them. You can kiss a rpg manual sure, it just taste like a paper.
Not so long ago, I saw Shadowrun Returns in Steam Store. Something clicked. I had this indescribable feeling in my stomach. It felt so strange and familiar at the same time, I didnt know what to do actually. My mind went to some kind of automated state, and my mouse pointer hovered over the BUY - button. 30 minutes later, I was playing the game.
Universe
Shadowrun Returns is set in an alternate future in which magic returned to the world in 2012. Its cyberpunk themed. High fantasy meets science-fiction. Shadowrunners are the elite criminals for hire. They do your dirty work, for a wealthy payment, ofcourse. Cyberspace, omnipresent computer networks, genetic engineering and cyberware are reality.
Gameplay
Shadowrun Returns is using isometric view, and you get use cover like in XCOM. Gameplay is fluent and fun. You have many races to choose from, and lot of interesting classes. My first playthrough Im using a rigger. You are basicly an engineer with 2 droids to use and control. Im using shotguns and most of my points are in intelligence, drone control and drone combat. Partysize is four, and you have tons of choices. You hire your party members to every missions. Im usually using me ( as a rigger) , a mage, ranged specialist, and a shaman. Enemies vary alot, and story line is amazing. Its so fun, and entertaining. You can create your own campaigns and upload them to Steam. There are many good custom campaigns to download. This game is gonna entertain you a long time. Length of the original campaign is 15-20 hours, and gameplay is linear.
I recommend Shadowrun Returns to all isometric rpg freaks.

This is perhaps one of the best games made in the history of man-kind.  Without question is it one of the greatest computer games to ever be realized. A strategy game of such depth and replay-ability that it proves beyond doubt good ideas trump giant development teams and millions of dollars.
Most of the game takes place on one screen, with two ships doing battle. You are the hunted who hunts, the captain  of a small ship with many enemies out for your blood. It is your duty to determine what your ship will become. Your duty to deal with the RNG gods to build a ship that will save the Federation. Is your crew a group of hardened soldiers slaying the enemy crew in hand to hand combat? Are you the juggernaut that kills from afar, whose shield's cannot be penetrated? The stealthy ship no one sees until it is too late? Weapons charged captain, stealth disengaged, they stand no chance.
You will die. You will die a lot.  How were you supposed to survive, you ask yourself? You never stood a chance! Or did you? As the nuanced micro-management of your crew and systems begin to unravel inside your mind, new techniques and options become clear. What once killed you become a minor nuisance and certain death becomes an opportunity for greater rewards and more power.
FTL will not hold your hand. FTL rewards your hard work with death, sacrifice and destruction, hopelessness and fear. The first time you win ... oh, the first time ... that is the feeling of accomplishment to which few games can ever attest.
Good luck Captain, your crew awaits your orders.

The game stands the test of time even ten years later. Still, in my opinion, the ultimate single-player campaign that truly achieves everything it set out to do: the beginning feels rushed and anxious, the middle slow and creepy, later weird and wide-open and the end comes together just in time to make you feel like a god but never undeservingly-so because it's a hell of a trying journey to get there.
The game drops you non-chalantly into the role of Gordan Freeman and manages to never make the tight-lipped scientist a caricature of himself. As soon as you seem to have the current level format down, the game either elaborates on that or changes it altogether and perfectly timed for the duration of experience. The use of in-game physics towers above virtually all other title's attempts at doing so (minus a couple other Valve games) and has done so for a decade.
The "Kid A" of current videogames: Shaped ten years of content but was never necessarily elaborated on.
I thought it would be neat to review a title ten years to the day that I first installed it (and Steam altogther) but really, what can be said about it? I guess that it's more fun than generally all the games I play today in 2015.

SPOILERS AHEAD BEWARE!!!
I had a lot of fun playing Dying Light. I played through the full storyline and did a moderate amount of side quests along the way. Dying Light goes by a 3 skill tree system which breaks down to Survivor, Agility, and Power with each tree branching out into helpful skills to get you through the hordes of zombies.  While the games parkour system was extremely well done and fun to do, Im just not the kind of person to back down from a fight. By the time I'd finished the main story I had 23 levels in Power, and only a measley 14 in agility.
SURVIVOR TREE and AIR DROPS
You receive survior points by completeing quests, retrieving air drops and returning whatever supplies are in to your quartermaster, saving survivors, killing thugs, etc. The survivor tree is related to crafting items, how much you can carry, and bartering. I was both extremely pleased and also slightly disappointed with the air drops. At the very first air drop you are sent to there are a bunch of thugs already there and you are told to avoid them. While naturally at that low a level those thugs would rip you apart in melee combat, however my molotov cocktail had other plans. This left me a half looted supply crate and I was overjoyed when I found a bunch of hand grenades in it. Unfortunately this is only a one time deal since every crate I found afterwards had only disaster relief kits and medical supplies that I could only give to the quartermaster.
AGILITY TREE and NIGHT TIME
The Agility Tree affects your free running ability and how quick you can get out of tough situations. You recieve points in this tree from simply running and climbing, dodging, and sliding. Now at the start of the game you get tired really quickly    from running and you climb rather slowly. However once you reach the second and third tier of the agility tree you unlock the ability to run faster and climb faster simple as that. During night time you receive double points for both your agility and power tree. Night time is DARK! The flashlight is absolutely necessary when it's night time just to see the ground in front of your feet. The flashlight doesn't alert enemies when you point it at them, unless you point the UV flashlight at a volatile (yikes). If you get caught by one of those monsters you will be "pursued" and you need to free run and climb to keep them away from you (they are faster than you and they will catch you if you run in a straight line). You will get bonus agility points if you successfully evade a pursuit and you will receive more points the longer and the more "intense" the pursuit is. However at lower levels I found it extremely difficult to free run away from them with how slow I climbed.
POWER and WEAPONS
The power tree affects your combat stamina and gives special moves for certain weapons. You get power points for killing zombies by any means. Early on you are givin terrible weapons and the only way to get the best weapons are to buy them with cash that you receive from quests or looting zombies or just laying around and selling commodities like cigarettes and coffee. The weapons you have access to at the store are also dependant on what level of Survivor rank you have so early on I could buy an Epic level Claw Hammer for 1500$ and later on I would buy a Legendary Katana for 30000$. In the power tree you can unlock a strong attack and you would hold down the appropriate attack key for a stronger attack that takes more stamina and swings slower. I never found an upside to this ability it was sluggish and a zombie would grapple me while i'm taking my sweet time swinging my wrench. Once I did get my Legendary Katana and I upgraded it with Bolter Poison and gave it Legendary and Epic upgrades I found myself hewing down zombies left and right taking off heads and arms with single swings. The only time I actually had to run away anymore was from the Volatiles at night those guys hit hard and don't go down easy so it's hard to kill one before they start swarming you.
GRAPPLING HOOK and ENDING
The grappling hook is absurd and does not follow the rules of physics... which makes it all the more fun to use. I would throw it in a straight line and my character would be propelled through the air in an equally straight line. Are you falling to your death? Shoot your grappling hook downward and you will be pulled directly downward without taking any damage. Zombies getting generally near you? Shoot your grappling hook up 15 stories of a building and arrive in mere seconds. Grappling Hook to surmise is fun but unrealistic and quirky. The story of Dying Light is a huge plus and I often found myself relating to the main character both emotionally and verbally. Unfortunately the ending (again spoilers ahead) was extremely disappointing. In fact most "boss" fights were disappointing. You would merely kill an absurd amount of Rais's goons and then you would walk into a trap be stripped of all your gear and givin some flimsy piece of metal to fight with and once the mission is over you would get all your stuff back. Once you finally solve an absurd jumping puzzle with many falls to the death you would reach Rais on the top of his tower and you will finally be rewarded with a sorry quick time event totalling in around 9 button presses. I messed up a lot of the quick time events because I was simply awestricken that they would climax this wonderful story with this sorry display of button pressing.
All in all it's a beautiful game with a great story and great gameplay. I would give it a 7.5/10 it would be an 8 out of 10 but that quick time even ending left me with a sour taste in my mouth. I even received an achievement called Bittersweet. Bittersweet indeed.

I hadn't really followed the development of this game until about a week before release.  I know there was a bit of drama just before release due to the late  review codes being sent out.  Rest assured, Dying Light is a good game.
I didn't like Dead Island as I thought it was very unpolished and buggy when I played.  This made me a bit nervous in taking the plunge.   However, over time I found myself more and more enamored by this game.  The combat is relatively simple but can be in depth in its execution.  You need to have situational awareness as even the simplist zombie can hold you down while others pound on you (also to utilize the terrian to your advantage).   You need to be able to switch weapons on the fly depending on the threat and keep good placement to strike when your enemy is most vulnerable.

The gore in this game is something else as well.  You can chop hands, arms, legs, heads off.  You can cut zombies in half horizontally or vertically (left and right or front and back :o).   Very rewarding when you clobber a swarm of zombies, vault over some other ones and keeping the others at bay.  I can't stress enough how simple the concept of combat is but the execution *muah* fantastic!
Co-op is also another great feature to the game.  You and your friends can play most of the campaign together (basically all the way up until the very last mission).   My friends and I had a few nail biting moments at night running acrossed a bridge while volatiles chased on.  Chucking IR flares behind us as we parkoured up to our safe house.
That being said, there are a couple issues I have most minor.  The biggest is the frame rate.  It isn't consistent and this seems to be a problem a lot of PC users are experiencing.  I, by no means, have an antiquated PC yet sometimes without reason my FPS will drop to 15-20 for a few seconds.    First release problems I am sure it will get fixed.  Another gripe I have is with the ranged weaponry.  There is only 5 guns in the entire game.  American 9mm, German 9mm, Police Rifle, Military Rifle, and Double Barreled Shotgun.  As rich as the melee weapons are, I'd have liked a pump action shotgun, a sniper rifle, crossbow or standard bow, or perhaps upgrades for the guns?  Different sights or suppressors?   Flamethrower or RPG?  If anything for the after game just to screw around.
Over all, the random FPS stutters and small choice in firearms keeps it from getting a perfect score.  If you have any doubts about this game, don't.  Push that purchase button and squish some zombie (and people!) heads!

Tripwire seems to be listening to feedback, though it seems they only will when they get enough negative backlash about a change. There was one major game ruining effect that was added and, after a wave of negative reactions to it, was quickly compromised upon.
Unfortunately, they've had another lapse in judgment, and that's why I'm leaving a negative review.
Tripwire had a clear goal of 10 released classes, or "perks", that they wanted to implement before the game's release. These perks served the purpose of adding variety to gameplay. Some of them were identical in function to others, but, to be fair, it's hard to imagine making a first person shooter experience any more unique without taking away from the sense of realism, or without becoming too silly.
However, I would've prefered something silly to what they actually released for the 10th perk.
They introduced "Survivalist", which, despite the intriguing name, has nothing unique about it. It's a perk that takes a bit of flavor from every existing perk. However, because of the XP/Level-up and Perk Tree systems, Survivalist gains functionality and purpose very slowly as you level up, and even at your maximum potential you're always just under the bar of adequacy compared to the other classes.
This perk is a balancing nightmare, and feels very much like a half-hearted attempt that was made as a last minute decision - because, I assume, they didn't want to incur the wrath of those saying they broke their promises and falsely advertised their end goal.
To me, the game has become much less fun than it was for two reasons:
-First, if you're a completionist, you have to grind through the mundane experience of playing as a Survivalist.
-Second, a disproportionate amount of players are currently playing Survivalist, and contribute much less than they would if they had picked any other class.
I understand why they did it, but I hope they can understand this review will remain negative until they either balance this  rushed perk or replace it with a much more appropriate option.

Summary: A South Park game that represents the series in the best way.
Positive: Humor and ambience. The jokes are standard for the show, albeit pushed further with less restrictions than the heavily-censored TV show.
The atmosphere of the town of South Park is enjoyable to walk around in.
You can avoid combat in most situations via action triggers or simple maneuvering.
Negative: Short length of the campaign. You can beat the game in only a few hours.
The game will drop your inputs from time to time. This is obnoxious since almost every action in combat requires timed button pressing to gain the best effect. A minor annoyance since the game is largely lacking in difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty, this game essentially has almost no challenge element. Think of it as an interactive 15 hour episode of South Park rather than a true RPG. There are difficulty options and I'd recommend playing on max difficulty.
Maximum character level is only 15. This is really easy to hit in a casual playtrough without level grinding. Experience points lose all meaning at the level cap (as expected), so combat in the last 3-4 hours of the game is pointless other than to see some jokes.
There are some areas of the game that can only be visited once per playthrough. Missing anything in these restricted-access areas means you cannot complete certain events/achievements.
Overall: 7/10. By far the best South Park game released to date. If you like the show and enjoy videogames this will be fun for you.

Shadowrun Returns is a turn-based cyberpunk RPG, similar to dungeons and dragons, with a digital dystopian twist. This game is an adaptation of the original table top game and reflects this in the flexibility of character choices and play styles, despite having a fairly limited and linear story line. The overall artistic style is gritty and cyberpunk; reflected in the graphics, music and dialogue. The combat system is tactical and challenging. Best movie license game I've ever played. I love it. The turn based RPG system fits so well with the animation. This is the game that south park fans deserve. I'll go over the positive aspects and the negative aspects.
Positive:
-This game is incredibly funny. It's raunchy and dirty sense of humor fits me so well. I love it. However, if you are not into that kind of humor, this game will not appeal to you.
-The turned based combat would sound bad, and boring... But it actually has you involved. You don't just choose a move and then watch it play out. It's kind of like the Mario rpg games, where you have to put in some sort of actions to make a "Perfect" hit. The combat is also fairly fleshed out. There are status effects that can be inflicted on enemies. Also the unique ways each buddy can be used to suit your play style. You can even use the enviroment outside of combat using your abilities you get, such as your fart magic, and an anal alien probe. Skipping combat completely, but getting the experience.
-Plenty to explore, and has some replayability. Although I never completed it after doing it twice.
-It is creatively written. The story line is fantastic. Which it should be, being written by the developers of the show themself.
-Due to the kids larping, it makes some creative items. You can literally take a crap in a toilet, and throw it at an enemy to gross them out.
-The story line and all side missions can give you around... 20 hours, even more if you want to replay it.
Negative:
The negative aspects are just me nit picking a bit, but some of these can be an issue for others.
-This game is for south park fans, and for people who are not easily offended. If you are not a south park fan? You might not enjoy this game, and not get most of the jokes.
-The game is too easy on the default difficulty, and even on hard mode, it can be easy. I've found myself never losing a single battle when you follow the story line.
-20 hours is a VERY short rpg game, when it ends, you just feel like you want more.
Do I recommend this game? Yes and no... It is most assuredly a yes if you enjoy south park and LOVE inappropriate humor used in a clever fashion. No, if you are not a fan, and you are easily offended. This game is best for south park fans, and I thank the developers for making a brilliant game, when they could of easily screwed it up. I give it around 8/10. A good experience.

Probably one of the best licensed games ever made. Most licensed games are bad for one or more of these two reasons: 1) the game isn’t very well made. 2) The game has almost nothing to do with its source material. Thankfully, Stick of Truth both is a very well made game and captures the feel of the show better than any licensed game I’ve ever seen. That is to say that it is South Park we’re talking about here, the humor can sometimes be very off putting to some people.
With that said, my biggest criticism with the game is that it’s extremely easy, even in the hardest difficulty if you know enough about the game mechanics you can cheese your way through most battles in just a few turns and because of the huge supply of items you get in the game even the toughest enemies aren’t that hard. The hardest time I had with the game was just because I ran out of curing water and my character was “grossed out” which made it so he couldn’t use healing items. But I still didn’t die in the battle, it was still very manageable. I think the game should have made its hardest difficulty even harder so that people like me couldn’t cakewalk their way through just about every battle. So there really wasn’t much of a reason to get all the summons except for the completionest aspect and maybe to see the animations (which is almost worth it to be honest).
As for the game's somewhat short length (I'm more than fine with it honestly) it's all content that doesn't waste your time at all, there's no grinding required, and every quest needed for the main story is fun and comes with a lot of variety.
tl;dr? Best South Park game ever made, might even be the best licensed game; however, combat is way too easy after you figure out all the rules and techniques making sidequest rewards kind of worthless.

Antichamber is a single-player first-person puzzle platform indie game that seems to echo the philosophical phrase, "Looks can be decieving." For Antichamber, this could not be more true. While at first glance, the game may look similiar to Valve's Portal franchise, but a second look will reveal an entirely different beast.
Antichamber was released on Steam on January 31, 2013. It was developed by Alexander Bruce and is known for it's brain-twisting puzzles built around a non-euclidean form of geometry. What this means for those of us that aren't familiar with Euclid is that during the course of the game, players will encounter puzzles built around geometrical impossibilities, such as passages that lead to different locations depending on which way you face or structures that seem impossible within typical three-dimensional space.
In Antichamber, you control an unnamed protagonist from a first-person perspective as they wander through the halls of puzzle chambers, each with their own unique brand of brain teaser. Upon entering a chamber, the player will be presented with a sign on a wall that will offer a cartoonish iconograph that's is somehow related to the puzzle in the following room as well as a small bit of text that often provides some sort of hint as to how to progress through the room. It's about here that Antichamber's similiarities to Portal end: each room is solved in an entirely different way from any other room. The player will move horizontally, vertically, through walls, ceilings, and/or floors, and will occasionally use a gun with varying abilities provided to you in the relevant rooms to help travers the chamber and proceed to the next room. The player may have to step on switches place blocks in relevant areas, step through or avoid laser beams that can set off various game mechanics, utilize both traditional and non traditional platforming methods, and more. When the player finds themselves stuck or unable to continue, simply pressing escape brings them back to the hub, where they can adjust game settings, review previous signs that they've uncovered over the course of their journey, fast-travel to any room that they've set foot in (and see how they are connected, which is nothing short of a three-dimensional hedge maze of confusion) and gaze through large window at their ultimate goal: the exit.
Overall, this is a game that begs to be played, as it is an experience that I simply cannot capture in the span of a review. The game will fascinate and often frustrate you with it's mind-bending puzzles, but perserverance will lead to satisfaction within the walls of Antichamber. Keep in mind that it is not a journey that's for the faint of heart: Antichamber is much more difficult than Portal, and oftentimes, you will be tempted to look up answers online. But for those that have played the Portal series and are begging for more, then Antichamber is the game for you.
A 6 out of 10.
Authors Note: While Antichamber is a fantastic game, I would highly recommend picking it up in a sale. Unfortunately, the $20 price point seems a little too steep, but at $10 or less, the game is a steal.

Platformer meets rogue-lite actioner. As you play you unlock more and more classes, each with different attacks. There are a lot of different items to pick up and use as you fight off the ever increasing waves of monsters, aliens, and other baddies.
When you start a stage your objective is to find the teleporter and activate it. Doing so starts a countdown where you must fight off a boss monster and waves of enemies until everything is dead and you advance to the next area. As you play, the clock in the upper right counts up and the game gets harder and harder. More and more elite enemies start to spawn and eventually (if you take too long) multiple bosses show up.
The game is very much like other rogue-likes as far as difficulty goes. You get one life and if you die you start all over again (and you will die, a LOT). As you learn what items go best with what classes though you will find yourself getting to the end boss more and more often (sometimes just to die to him).
The game has fantastic pixel style graphics which look amazing on each stage, but what really makes this game great is the AMAZING soundtrack. The music on each stage is just absolutely fantastic and really goes well with the great visuals.
The only negative is that the team that developed the game is (as far as I know) a three man team. As a result, sometimes it takes a bit of time to get bug fixes out (like the one that fixed most of the achievements, they wouldn't unlock for a while). Still, I do recommend trying this one out.

Super Hexagon is a simple mechanic polished and sharpened to a beautiful razor point.
It challenges you at first to even attempt to keep up with its fast pace and forbiddingly difficult gameplay, and as you delve further, to recognize and gradually master its bank of tricks and patterns.
This is hardcore twitch gaming at its most pure, and it will have you swearing with near-misses and pumping yourself up for the perfect run. Avoid hitting walls for 60 seconds straight. It sounds easy. It isn't.
Highly recommended for the addictive music and fast-paced gameplay, but make sure you're prepared for the challenge to your reflexes if you buy it.

~Dead Space is one of the First Horror games that i really wanted to complete simply because of the story, although, as you read, it has more to understand than just a Abandoned Space Ship with "Absurd Monsters"....
~This Game is a Defining Space Horror Game, although more action packed than something like Alien: Isolation but the Environment coupled with the Smart Mechanics and Formidable Enemy AI are the strong points of this EA Game!
Alright let’s get Started on The Good Aspects first:
+The Story is Immersive and Deep on the Scale of 3+ games. There’s much to understand, the whole cause of chaos experience in the Ishimura is not only explained in DS1 but also in other forms of media such as Books, Animated Movies, Graphics novels, a Wii Game and even a little Mobile game (How cute).  No Spoilers here but there are many things that contribute to the Plot such as that Universe's Primary "religion" (AKA- Cult) called Unitology.
+Speaking of Story, a Bulk of the Backstory, is found from Logs within the Levels (Well Hidden of course.) This really Helps the Player (Isaac Clarke) understand Many Characters, Events and even teaches them how to play Zero-G Basketball!!
+The HUD is very Realistic; it is Projected outwards in front of Isaac's face when he walks. Want to Rummage through Ammo while a battle is happening? You will most likely Die...
+The Difficulties are very balanced for the types of gamer out there, from a simple run and gun easy difficulty with lots of supplies (i find it too many) to the Impossible mode which has fewer checkpoints, OP Enemies, hardly any Supplies (Just the way i like it), Bad Starting Suits, Few upgrades and a loss of that checkpoint instantly if you close/exit the game at all. That’s for the Hard-core Gamer who prefers a true horror Experience.
+Loading Times? Where?
+Atmosphere is undoubtedly the game’s biggest Strong Point. an almost empty ships filled with Necromorphs (
) that seem to be around every dark corner (There’s quite a few!) The Metallic Clang of Claws in a vent above you, or the Creaking of the Hull, or Heavy Thuds from the Asteroid belt pelting the ship are all some prime examples of how well the game deals with the unique atmosphere. It’s a Mix of Event Horizon, The Thing and even System Shock 2!
+Scares a-plenty!
+Extremely Innovative targeting Mechanic= Strategic Dismemberment, go for the Limbs..
+Sound is Very Realistic and Proportional, some moments you have to stand still and be quiet to hear where the necromorph is crawling...Can you hear that too?
+Weapon Options are plentiful
+Interesting Currency and requirements to get some Credits
+Upgradable Suits (up to 6 levels!)
+HUD is very informative, you will hardly ever get lost with the 3D map Design
+New Game Plus Ability (Definietely Worth it)
+Boss Battles are Excellent and each are around the right length as well.
Huge Alien Creatures vs Puny Engineer with a Bulky Suit but Heavy Weapons and
Badass "Gadgets"= Interesting/Gory Results!
+Death Animations, Mortal Kombat meets the Thing! Blood will be spilled, then
poured and then Splashed! (R18 for this reason!)

The game is fantastic, and it's very much in a playable state. It's entertaining, it's fast (depending on which difficulty you play at combined with your own skill level) and definitely fun.
Tripwire seems to be listening to feedback, though it seems they only will when they get enough negative backlash about a change. There was one major game ruining effect that was added and, after a wave of negative reactions to it, was quickly compromised upon.
Unfortunately, they've had another lapse in judgment, and that's why I'm leaving a negative review.
Tripwire had a clear goal of 10 released classes, or "perks", that they wanted to implement before the game's release. These perks served the purpose of adding variety to gameplay. Some of them were identical in function to others, but, to be fair, it's hard to imagine making a first person shooter experience any more unique without taking away from the sense of realism, or without becoming too silly.
However, I would've prefered something silly to what they actually released for the 10th perk.
They introduced "Survivalist", which, despite the intriguing name, has nothing unique about it. It's a perk that takes a bit of flavor from every existing perk. However, because of the XP/Level-up and Perk Tree systems, Survivalist gains functionality and purpose very slowly as you level up, and even at your maximum potential you're always just under the bar of adequacy compared to the other classes.
This perk is a balancing nightmare, and feels very much like a half-hearted attempt that was made as a last minute decision - because, I assume, they didn't want to incur the wrath of those saying they broke their promises and falsely advertised their end goal.
To me, the game has become much less fun than it was for two reasons:
-First, if you're a completionist, you have to grind through the mundane experience of playing as a Survivalist.
-Second, a disproportionate amount of players are currently playing Survivalist, and contribute much less than they would if they had picked any other class.
I understand why they did it, but I hope they can understand this review will remain negative until they either balance this  rushed perk or replace it with a much more appropriate option.

Well what can I say - its Dead Space and a classic!
Dead Space is probably definitely the best Survival Horror game ever released. While it released in 2008 it has stood the test of time and nothing has come close to beating it IMHO. It always ran well on a mediocre PC and if you play it today you wont be disappointed because graphically it still looks good even for its time.
I wont give any spoilers away but there is a huge Lore surrounding the games premise. Essentially you follow the journey of Isaac Clarke who is no marine♥♥♥♥♥kicker, he's an engineer that finds himself caught up in a living nightmare. As Isaac you'll have to fight your way through the horrors he uncovers while investigating the USG Ishimura, a Planet Cracker mining vessel.
There are psychological stresses and aberrations to face, as well as the physical nightmare of encountering the horrors on-board the Ishimura. The atmosphere of the game is deeply effective and you'll quickly find yourself wanting to know more about what has occurred aboard this ship. You are charged with various engineering tasks in order to save the ship and ultimately yourself. This is a game that will draw you in very quickly and provide a complete immersive experience.
Apart from the visual scares and frights, there are sound effects which will still be making you jump after many many playthroughs. Its one of those games that manage to pace itself extremely well, getting harder and more difficult as you progress. There is no hand holding in this game and making mistakes early on will soon end your journey. Be prepared to die often especially if you play on hard. This isn't a game for the faint hearted and if you want a game that requires thought at every level and the accomplishment of surviving this horror will be reward enough I assure you!
Isaac Clarke remains mute all through the game and while this appears strange, you will soon realise that this somehow adds to the intrigue and experience. To get the most from this game search areas thoroughly and read and listen to everthing you find even though it will be♥♥♥♥♥♥scary, you will be rewarded for your efforts. Play late in the evening with the lights off and headphones on and if you thought you've played horror before you'll soon realise that this tops anything you've previously encountered.

One of the biggest disappointments this year for me. This review is about Shadowrun Returns not the expansion that probably has fixed some of the problems I felt this game had.
My first impression was that the artsyle is cute and cartoonish but after some time it started looking a bit cheap in my eyes. A bit like mobile games one could say. This is of course about taste so I'll stop here.
Secondly I was very intimidated by the character creation since I didn't have a clue how I was supposed to be "leveling up" my character. Turned out it was quite the opposite, offering very few meaningful choices for my "runner".
I liked the writing and was infact a intriqued by the storyline though the gameplay didn't hold up to it. There were some "ambushes" and "don't let this important person die" kind of moments that just felt poorly conducted. Making it even worse the tactical battle feels more like "choose who shoots whom" and then wait for them to shoot you back. There's a cover system that relies on your characters to just be next to a wall or block, crate etc. You also have some usable items like bandages and grenades with neither of those feeling original at all.
Original or not the game is also very easy (I'm not the only one saying this) and you can just storm through the plot with not much challenge.
After all these negative attributes I can't really recommend Shadowrun Returns to anyone, since it's no challenge, gameplay lacks in all aspects and there's not much to do besides following the story. I can't even consider buying the second iteration after this one since for me it was all about the story.

Shadowrun is cyberpunk meets fantasy, all mashed together with the kitchen sink thrown in. Character classes include shamans (clerics), street samurai (fighters, melee or gun-based), mages, adepts (magical martial arts fighters), deckers (computer hackers) and riggers (who control drone robots). Player character races include humans, orcs, trolls (extra large orcs), elves and dwarves.
The world includes lots of fantasy monsters from spirits and giant scorpions to great dragons, and also plenty of security personnel itching to die at your hands.
Decking (computer hacking), and the way computers and the Internet work in general, doesn't make any sense at all. But this is totally consistent with the Cyberpunk genre, which was generally written by people with no real computer knowledge. Inside Cyberspace, you battle ICE (Intrusion Countermeasures) and even Black ICE (ICE that can kill you in real life).
I've played through the original plot of Shadowrun Returns (Deadman's Switch) and also Dragonfall. I thought that both games had really engaging stories, and were generally well-paced, had good dialogue and interesting characters. The scenes and themes fit well with a cyberpunk "high tech, low life" motif.
Dead Man's Switch was very linear, with little more than dialog choices (nice answer, neutral answer, mean answer). Playing it is a lot like reading a good book that has interactive fight scenes and some inventory management.
Dragonfall was less linear, with some limited ability for the player to make world-changing choices. The important decisions are all made more toward the end of the game, though. This may annoy you, or you may like it because it gives you the chance to load your game and try a different ending with only 5 minutes more investment. Also, Dragonfall has much more lively NPCs, which makes for a game that feels a bit more social and less isolating.
That having been said, it's great that the stories are good, but 90% of your time in the game will be spent in fights. Almost all of the skills that you increase with experience (which Shadowrun calls "karma") are combat skills, although they have some limited utility in conversation (especially Charisma). All the equipment is combat or quest related.
In Shadowrun, the fighting is turn-based, with each character on a side getting a turn (with 2 or 3 Action Points) before the next side gets to act. The huge array of options can be overwhelming, especially at first. Fighting takes place in a large variety of locales and against a wide variety of foes. Sometimes your opponents get a surprise turn against you, which can be very annoying if your main character is squishy (has few HPs), as you see the entire enemy team attack your character (who is not under cover) before you get to act. I was once killed outright this way without even having a chance to react. Fortunately, I had an item that automatically resuscitated me.
The fighting in Shadowrun Returns can get pretty repetitive fairly quickly, though. Once I figured out the ideal strategy (see next paragraph), it was just a question of repeating the same operations every fight. The same strategy works every fight. The only variation is a bit of difference in tactical positioning depending on how the enemy is approaching you and the layout of cover. Take cover, buff your main damage dealers, and kill your opponents. If your opponents bunch up use grenades and area effect spells against them. Rince and repeat.
SPOILER WARNING the best strategy is to take a mage and buy spells that do area effect damage or reduce AP. In a 1v1 duel you can easily steal all of your opponent's AP and just damage them every turn without ever being hurt. Other viable options include a rifle/shotgun specialist or a high-Intelligence decker/rigger. The melee characters are particularly underpowered. Use shamans as support to boost your main damage dealers with AP, HP and accuracy. SPOILER WARNING END
The game is a bit buggy. I frequently have trouble with character equipment, where items will switch in or out of my backpack spontaneously, or I'll see different items when in combat or out of combat. I've had rare situations where I click on a HUD button and my character moves on the map instead--wasting a turn. I encountered no critical bugs that crashed the game or prevented story completion, however.
There are some usability issues. There doesn't seem to be any way to manage drone equipment. It can be awkward to manage objects found in the world, since only the character accessing the container can pick up the item, and outside of combat you only have control over your main character. The game often requires extra unecessary clicks, like when using abilities that can only be used on yourself, you're still forced to click on your sprite to self-select.
Overall, I consider this game worth buying and playing, especially if you're a fan of computer role-playing games.

Antichamber is a single-player first-person puzzle platform indie game that seems to echo the philosophical phrase, "Looks can be decieving." For Antichamber, this could not be more true. While at first glance, the game may look similiar to Valve's Portal franchise, but a second look will reveal an entirely different beast.
Antichamber was released on Steam on January 31, 2013. It was developed by Alexander Bruce and is known for it's brain-twisting puzzles built around a non-euclidean form of geometry. What this means for those of us that aren't familiar with Euclid is that during the course of the game, players will encounter puzzles built around geometrical impossibilities, such as passages that lead to different locations depending on which way you face or structures that seem impossible within typical three-dimensional space.
In Antichamber, you control an unnamed protagonist from a first-person perspective as they wander through the halls of puzzle chambers, each with their own unique brand of brain teaser. Upon entering a chamber, the player will be presented with a sign on a wall that will offer a cartoonish iconograph that's is somehow related to the puzzle in the following room as well as a small bit of text that often provides some sort of hint as to how to progress through the room. It's about here that Antichamber's similiarities to Portal end: each room is solved in an entirely different way from any other room. The player will move horizontally, vertically, through walls, ceilings, and/or floors, and will occasionally use a gun with varying abilities provided to you in the relevant rooms to help travers the chamber and proceed to the next room. The player may have to step on switches place blocks in relevant areas, step through or avoid laser beams that can set off various game mechanics, utilize both traditional and non traditional platforming methods, and more. When the player finds themselves stuck or unable to continue, simply pressing escape brings them back to the hub, where they can adjust game settings, review previous signs that they've uncovered over the course of their journey, fast-travel to any room that they've set foot in (and see how they are connected, which is nothing short of a three-dimensional hedge maze of confusion) and gaze through large window at their ultimate goal: the exit.
Overall, this is a game that begs to be played, as it is an experience that I simply cannot capture in the span of a review. The game will fascinate and often frustrate you with it's mind-bending puzzles, but perserverance will lead to satisfaction within the walls of Antichamber. Keep in mind that it is not a journey that's for the faint of heart: Antichamber is much more difficult than Portal, and oftentimes, you will be tempted to look up answers online. But for those that have played the Portal series and are begging for more, then Antichamber is the game for you.
A 6 out of 10.
Authors Note: While Antichamber is a fantastic game, I would highly recommend picking it up in a sale. Unfortunately, the $20 price point seems a little too steep, but at $10 or less, the game is a steal.
