1. If you're a fan of the original and have a "back in my day" attitude: better leave it alone.
2. If you're a fan of the original and have an open mind: buy it. Its main drawbacks for you will most likely be:
-no multiple bases, no base defense missions (in the vanilla version)
-no action points, instead a soldier can only move once and attack once (there are exceptions though)
-soldiers can carry fewer items than in the original, no inventory, no looting corpses or exchanging items in the middle of the mission
Other than that, it's a streamlined, polished and somewhat simplified (but not made easier) remake of the original. I actually found it much harder than UFO Defense (but not than TFTD). I like it and recommend you buy it if you crave more of the same, but with a different flavor.
3. If you never played the original but like tactics games: a certain buy. Pretty complex from a tactical standpoint, and very fun, if challenging.
4. If you're not a fan of tactics games: it's going to be pretty hard for you, though if you manage to overcome the somewhat steep learning curve, you'll find a highly enjoyable and replayable game underneath.

An enjoyable game with a lot to do. Crafting is fun, and there's plenty of reason to forage and explore. Combat is solid, though it does dissuade using items that make noise, firearms and explosives, as they spawn zombies on use. This means you're likely going to be using melee weapons for most of the game, which break often and easily. By mid to late game, durability becomes a non issue, but still, anything you make has a shelf-life. There is never going to be a point you make a weapon and are done, it will only degrade. That said, once you're out of the early game, you'll likely be replacing weapons with better versions as opposed to breaking them, and all weapons can be broken down to repair, upgrade, or create other items.
Co-op, while very fun, is a bit funky. While you can change your characters clothes (from a list of outfits), you're all the same dude, so theres just 4 identical jackasses running around. But it is entertaining, as, once online, anything becomes an activity. If there's an airdrop, for example, players are given a prompt to race to it, if they desire. Zombie-heavy areas prompt killing contests, and there are lots of spots for footraces.
It's really good for what it is, an open world zombie game. Up to you if that's worth what they are asking.

Maybe I'll change this later on, but several hours in I just cannot recommend this game. The story is absolutely idiotic, one of the worst I've ever seen in a game. The entire premise is just ludicrious, and not because of the zombies. The world ended because of some strain of rabies that has made people go insane.. or resurected the dead. Not quite sure there, but there are plenty of zombies walking around with quite fatal wounds that don't seem to bother them in the least. You're dropped in a city that's mysteriously made up of buildings in worse shape than the zombies, with many oddly only half constructed and the rest in a state of seriously decomposition. No idea why. You play errand boy, running around doing everyone's bidding.. for example, picking up air dropped supplies that are oddly only dropped just before nightfall. No idea why, as night is for some reason much more dangerous than day. Oh, and for some reason you don't carry a flashlight. Have fun stumbling through any dark rooms.
My weapons degrade so fast most seem to disappear before I can kill two zombies with them. I've never seen steel pipes dissolve in the blood of my enemies so quickly. You'll be stopping to duct tape your weapons back together every couple kills, and they can only be fixed a couple times before they're useless. This means you'll never invest in decent weapons.. why bother, as they'll evaporate before you really get any use out of them anyway. So far pocket knifes with 9 volt batteries duck taped to them seem to do the job just fine, as they appear to conjour small lightning storms around my enemies and leave them spasming on the ground for half a minute after I hit them. Odd, that. Don't recall 9 volt's packing quite that much punch.
In all honesty though, weapons aren't even really worth bothering with anyway. The zombies are so terribly stupid and slow they're no challenge to avoid and you can almost ALWAYS walk right past them without any difficutly. I don't think I've encountered a single enemy so far that I actually HAD to fight. Any that I did fight was solely by choice.
The fights themselves basically go like this. Click, click. Take step back. Click. Click. Out of stamina. Walk backwards till it comes back. Click. Zombie died. Weapon broke. Loot for money that everyone mysteriously still uses despite it having no value at all.
The main difference between this game and Dead Island is that this game plays more than a bit like Mirror's Edge. You can climb on literally anything, and spend your time sprinting around the city leaping from place to place. Of course, in reality this is extremely impractical and dangerous.. and nobody in their right mind would attempt to survive by acting in this manner, but hey.. it's a game. That said, you'll quickly grow tired of the camera slamming into walls as you repeatedly climb over every obstacle in the game in first person. This system also effectively eliminates any shred of challenge the zombies may have represented, as the vast majority do not climb at all and will not really react to you if you're above them. I've encountered several zombies that could climb and move many times faster than the others, but I'm not sure if this is intended or not. I imagined that such zombies would exist in the game to counter the ability to climb given to the player, but these zombies looked and moved exactly like all the others, and the game hasn't acknoweldged or explained  their existance in any way.. so I wonder if this was simply a bug.
In all, after only a couple hours I'm quite tired of watching the camera climb over ledges in first person, I'm tired of waiting on stamina to regenerate every swing or two, I'm tired of dealing with the inventory system, I'm tired of spamming Q to activate my "survivor sense" so I can detect nearby lootable items, I'm tired of looting said items, and I'm tired of suspending my sense of reality to such a rediculous degree. Or maybe sense of reality isn't the right term. It's more the logical inconsistencies present in almost all parts of the game. People made insane by a virus is good. Zombies resurrected from the dead by a virus is good. Pick one, stick with it. If the zombies are reanimated dead that can ignore the obviously utterly fatal wounds they have.. why on Earth would a bloody throwing star of all things do anything at all to them?

Past those two missions, day/night becomes very real, and incredibly terrifying. /endRant
Gameplay:
I'm sure it's been said before, but this is what Dead Island should have been. Everything from the parkour to the combat just feels incredibly fluid. Running around is great fun, and jumping into abandoned houses and exploring/finding loot is constantly fun. And this is where I got caught in my first night phase. I was running towards my objective when "oh look another shelter, let me go secure it," then "oh look there's an air drop nearby, let me go grab it," then again another shelter nearby, on top of random houses and zombies (sorry, "biters") to loot, and before I knew it, I got my last radio call telling me I should get to a shelter quick (mind you, the Tower warns runners a few times before nightfall to get home, but I just have to keep scrounging for loot). I checked my map and realized I was pretty damn far from the closest shelter, so I just booked it. This is where freerunning gets exciting. With how seemless and smooth it is to run around/through buildings and across rooftops, the run to my shelter didn't feel annoying or like a chore, but more like a challenge to find the smoothest route (very similar to Mirror's Edge). Long story short, night fell, I♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants and crouched my way from rooftop to rooftop, listening to the horrifying screams of the nighttime biters as I eased my way into my little shelter. I've since tried to go out at night and see if I can tackle a nighttime bonus objective of a quest, and I can tell you, as of right now, I am definitely not prepared... but I'm damn excited to finally face the challenge.
+ Fluid, seemless parkour
+ Combat is fun
+ Enemy AI is surprisingly smart
+ Terrifying and exciting night cycle
+ Scavanging every nook and cranny for loot
Characters:
Some characters are well-performed while others just aren't. Gazi's performance, in my opinion, is laughably bad, but I began to think that it may have been intentional? And Rahim... he must have played a lot of Jak and Daxter back in the day, all he needs to do is dye his hair yellow. Brecken, Jade and Lena are among my favorite so far, with Lena reminding me a lot of Cassandra from DA:Inquisition with her hair and accent. Overall, characters are decent, and that's all that really needs to be said, so far at least.
+ Some interesting characters
- Some poor performances
Technical:
Graphics are gorgeous, and surprisingly undemanding even on my single GTX 970 with everything cranked to max and at 1920x1080. Though many report a huge framerate difference by changing the View Distance option, I can barely see much of a difference in-game with that option set to half or max. The only issue I've noticed is that very very rarely, when you're fighting biters with melee weapons, the game randomly hitches, then continues normally. It only happens in combat, but not often enough to be annoying and that might just be my system. Overall, everything looks great, and the graphics and effects are wonderful. For an ugly game, the visuals are surprisingly beautiful.
Sound:
Music is great, but my only comment is that the music that plays when you're outside has one part where a random singer begins to chant, and I swear it scares the crap out of me every time. Bashing biters with blunt weapons sounds very satisfying, and you can tell when you've hit the right spot, while hitting the chest is usually a muffled thump. I've yet to get a gun though (I've spent a lot of time just wandering around so I'm not too far into the campaign) so I can't comment on that. Also, make a little bit more noise and you'll hear bone-chilling screams in the distance of the more agile biters coming to get you. Very satisfying sound work overall.
Story:
I haven't gotten far into the story so I'll hold off until I've completed it to fill this section.

There are good games, there are brilliant games, there are classic games and there are one-of-a-kind games. Antichamber is one of a kind. If I was to compare it to any other games I have played, the closest would be the Portal franchise, but even that is only similar in first impression, usage of a non-lethal weapon-like instrument and making you use your brain. There, the similarity ends.
While in most other titles the game teaches you in the beginning about its own peculiarities, Antichamber does not. You are never prepared for the quirks of its play with spatial dimensions, unstable matter or anything else you encounter. You are to figure out everyrhing by yourself. And this is one of it's many beauties.
This is not a game just about puzzles. It is a game about self-exploration through solving puzzles. The philosophical pictures and phrases that you find while solving puzzles don't only help you understand the weird world of Antichamber, but can also help you in the weird real world.
Nowadays there are many games, ranging from Crysis to Portal that to a smaller or greater extent make you think out of the box in order to overcome a certain obstacle. Well, Antichamber isn't one of those. It has NO BOX. You can never be sure about what you will find if you keep walking forward. Or if you turn. Or even if you look back. Or if you look forward again after looking back. Sometimes, you fell as if the only way to solve a puzzle is by tricking the game mechanic and after solving it, you realise that this is exactly the way the puzzle was intended to be solved. At the same time, unlike many other games of similar genre, it strangely feels alive on its own. The rooms, the dimensions do not just stay there where you left them. It leaves an impression that while you are absent from the rooms and corridors, they continue to live on their own. The cubes move around, the walls relocate. As soon as you appear in that strange, distorted universe, you feel alien in there. But this alienation is not of a menacing kind, but of a kind that encourages you to explore the world around you. And as you do that, the Antichamber more and more feels more than an strange trans-dimensional labyrinth. It feels like it is a being that functions independently and when you come there, it decides to interact with you.
addictive

1. If you're a fan of the original and have a "back in my day" attitude: better leave it alone.
2. If you're a fan of the original and have an open mind: buy it. Its main drawbacks for you will most likely be:
-no multiple bases, no base defense missions (in the vanilla version)
-no action points, instead a soldier can only move once and attack once (there are exceptions though)
-soldiers can carry fewer items than in the original, no inventory, no looting corpses or exchanging items in the middle of the mission
Other than that, it's a streamlined, polished and somewhat simplified (but not made easier) remake of the original. I actually found it much harder than UFO Defense (but not than TFTD). I like it and recommend you buy it if you crave more of the same, but with a different flavor.
3. If you never played the original but like tactics games: a certain buy. Pretty complex from a tactical standpoint, and very fun, if challenging.
4. If you're not a fan of tactics games: it's going to be pretty hard for you, though if you manage to overcome the somewhat steep learning curve, you'll find a highly enjoyable and replayable game underneath.

Shadowrun Returns is a fun return to the venerable Shadowrun universe.  It has a healthy retro flair to it, both using a classic Shadowrun time period and an interface that would not be out of place in RPGs from the turn of the millenia.
The included base campaign "Dead Man’s Switch" makes for a good entry point for those new to Shadowrun.  The treatment of the Shadowrun setting is excellent and is one of the high-points of the game.  Classic Shadowrun character archetypes are represented, a few familiar faces from previous Shadowrun stories make appearances, and the cyberpunk-meets-fantasy world is generally a joy to explore.  The writing is fittingly hardboiled, if sometimes a bit campy, for the neo-noir plot.  The soundtrack compliments the setting well and there are some very clever musical references to the classic Shadowrun game on the Super Nintendo.
Regrettably, "Dead Man’s Switch" is a rather linear experience.  The writing style is engaging, yet the plot feels somewhat stock.  Most unfortunate, however, is the lack of balance for all character types; certain builds are less useful than others.  Hackers in particular seem to be short changed, as they rarely have opportunities to use their specialities.  Lastly, the game is a bit on the easier side, great for folks either new to the genre or people who are interested only in following the story, but it does include a scaleable difficulty for those who would rather their time in the shadows to be lived on a razor’s edge.
Beyond the included campaign "Dead Man’s Switch," Shadowrun Returns hosts a series of mod tools to allow for player created adventures and content.  As of this writing, there are already some very fun player created missions and campaigns available on the Steam Workshop.
Overall, I really enjoyed Shadowrun Returns.  Though it has some shortcomings, I found them to be far outweighed by the games strengths.  It’s a game I can easily recommend, especially for fans of RPGs like Fallout, Neverwinter Nights, or the old Infinity Engine games.  And should you have an interest in discovering the world of Shadowrun this is a great place to start.

After 150 hours of playtime and writing the Handbooks to Every Survivalists, I think I've played enough to write a review on this.
What I enjoyed from Risk of Rain:
-The graphics are really nice, tiny pixels but lots and lots of details!
-The soundtrack is divine, really helps for immersion
-The "Time=Difficulty" feature is great, requiring the player to manage his time correctly or else die
-The amount of items is gigantic, making every run unique (Unless you've got Command..)
-Talking about Command, the artifacts change the whole game and makes you play very differently
-10 different characters that all plays completely differently
-The game is hard. At least at first, as I don't feel challenged at all anymore, even in Monsoon (Sadly!)
What I didn't like:
-The Multiplayer doesn't work very well, extremely prone to crashes mid-game and unable to join back
-As much as I love the artifacts, you'll only ever use 3 of them after a while (Glass, Command and Sacrifice mostly.)
What I think this game needs:
-A randomize button. Press it, and it chooses you a character and artifacts randomly! Since every Artifact and every Character radically change the way you'll play, that'd make Risk of Rain a game where you truly need to adapt to what you have and surely increase the playtime I have on it of another 20 hours minimum.
-Less lag on multiplayer. I am unable to do runs of over 40 mins because of crashes on my friends' PCs, and if they fixed just the crashes I would play this forever.
-Nerfing Command would be a good idea, because at this point it completely kills the RDM of the game. Maybe make it you can choose but you get a LOT less items on the run, so you get those you want but not as much?
It's sad they don't update this game anymore, because it isn't optimized correctly, at least for multiplayer. One of the last updates greatly reduced lag on the Risk of Rain level which I am extremely grateful for, but crashes on Multiplayer kills the online fun..
Still, even though I said some bad of this game, it remains an extremely good single player game with tons of replayability (140 of those hours were on solo..) and it is able to make you change your playstyle really often. Get this if you're a fan of any hard game!

The prospect of a South Park video game has been around since the series' creation. Kids were forbid from watching the show, but clearly the game couldn't be so bad! Well, it wasn't bad in terms of violence or cursing, just gameplay. No one has really been able to do justice to the series while also making a half-way decent game.
From the most unlikely of developers comes "The Stick of Truth!" Finally, a South Park video game that captures the charm, wit and hilarity of the series while also being quite a decent game. Functioning like a classic JRPG while also mixing up a few elements, Stick of Truth ends up being quite a good time.
While your party can only consist of two members at any given time, the ability to use items and attack in the same term makes for some great strategic elements. It also lightens the difficulty a bit for newcomers (which a South Park game is clearly trying to draw in). Now you can attempt some crazy combos or dramatic spells while screwing up won't spell game over for you.
The melee combat takes a form similar to the Paper Mario series. While everything is turn based, you are given glints and sparkles for when to press attack to maximize damage. Systems like this always keep you engaged as you never want to miss an opportunity to one or two shot an opponent.
The entire town of South Park is rendered very faithfully. This game runs on the engine that the show is now created with, so everything is literally the same as the show. Textures and effects look like they are ripped straight from the new Blu-rays and all of the audio is recorded with the main staff. If the gameplay elements were stripped out, you'd swear this was another episode.
It also helps that the plot never takes itself seriously. Gone are the preachy stand-offs from the newer seasons; this is simply a silly little adventure that has you basking in the insanity that ensues. You won't have your concious dissected or be questioned about religion. It makes for a game that feels epic while also quaint (kind of like a child's view of the world).
As for negatives, the game is incredibly short. While brevity can make for some engrossing titles, this game just feels a bit too short for an RPG. While you will hit max level a tiny bit before the finale, the fact that you can only reach 15 is underwhelming. All of that build-up to simply just stop for an arbitrary reason.
Like I said above, the game is also quite easy. A difficulty slider in the options menu lets you increase the difficulty, but that seems to just doll out more damage on you and your party. You still have the same attack and defense, meaning the difficulty slider becomes pointless after the half-way point.
If you can forgive those little deficiencies, then I'd heartily recommend South Park: The Stick of Truth. It is very humorous, outlandish and crass. It is also quintessential South Park. Never has a video game came so close to capturing the spirit of it's source material.

Hello nostalgia, my old friend. The world of Shadowrun (a classic console title) returns in this updated crowdfunded version, and gives you two absolutely good reasons to slap down the nuyen for it.
The first campaign that the game is packaged is Dead Man's Switch, a noir tale where you investigate a friend's demise, taking you from across an alternate Seattle as you uncover an intricate web of conspiracies. For good or ill, the game streamlines your progression, segmenting maps into pseudo-chapters, where you explore and investigate an area as much as you like, and then leave it completely, moving on to the next area. This is to the game's benefit as it does away with tedious backtracking and nook/cranny-exploration, keeping you in the thick of the plot.
If you're not familiar with the genre of RPGs like Shadowrun, then know that this is not a loot-oriented game. Item/equipment acquisition is never random, always deliberate and often simply purchases from store NPCs. Instead, it is focuses on the (well-told) and the character, The primary method your character grows is through the development of skills. These skills are cheap to start (1 skillpoint for first blip), but become expensive to master (10 skillpoints for the 10th blip), so beginning players have plenty of room to experiment.
However, there may be aspects you will dislike. Respecs are not available (unless you mess with the game code itself) so you may wind up getting skills that become obsolete or boring to you. Also, because this is a fixed campaign with no random encounters, certain types of skills will become more useful than others, so you may feel cheated in that department. In a sense, this is oldschool RPGing, before game devs were compelled to streamline and optimize the player experience. Also also, this being a fixed largely-linear campaign, playing through Dead Man's Switch around twice should show you everything it has to offer.
The campaign itself is enjoyable and most certainly a worthy purchase, despite what I've listed previously. Mind you, all the compliments that I've paid to Shadowrun Returns so far? I count them all as
.
: This game is supported by the Steam Workshop, which means user-created content can multiply the amount of time and enjoyment you get out of Shadowrun Returns significantly. This does mean that the level of quality may diminish, but hell, now you could even make your own Shadowrun adventures if you have the time and stamina for it!
I heartily recommend Shadowrun Returns for those players who enjoy tactical turn-based gameplay, strong storylines, and noir settings. And if you like the game as well, definitely consider looking at Shadowrun: Dragonfall, a second campaign currently offered as purchasable DLC!

Antichamber is probably the definition of a mysterious game.  While this game's objective, solve puzzles to find a way out of the maze you are in, is simple, that is the only straightforward thing about this game.  Antichamber has a logic of its own when it comes to puzzles.  Pathways can loop around into themselves, going back may lead to areas you haven't seen before, and merely looking or not looking at something can change the result between success or failure.
Fortunately, it's surprisingly intuitive, and a handy map viewable from the initial room (which you can teleport to at any time,) helps immensely in keeping track of your progress through the labyrinth.  The puzzles themselves are pretty fun, with an engaging atmosphere that draws you in, and are highly rewarding when you work out the solution.
The only downsides are that the game is pretty short and that once the puzzles are solved, there isn't much else to do.  Even so, Antichamber is a unique experience that should be played by any puzzle enthusiast.

I gotta admit I didn't think much about this game before I started playing it. I had heard of it, I have seen memes about it, but I had never thought about it as a great game.
Well, I was pretty wrong. This game is amazing. Somehow, it reminds me both of Half-Life and Bioshock.
The gameplay is solid. Zero gravity rooms and having to cut alien's limbs of to kill them is pretty nice. When you're scared, you instinctively shoot their torso, but after a couple of shots you realize that won't work at all.
The story is nice. It's not a masterpiece, but it's pleasant. The graphics are great, for a 2008 game, and the sound is very well done.
But the reason why this game is so good is the atmosphere. Writings on the wall with blood. Hearing whispers when you're alone. Knowing that the people in the spaceship got allucinations, and that you're probably having them too.
You turn the corner certain that an alien will jump right in front of you, and for a second you are relieved that none did. You step forward and then an alien actually jumps right in front of you and that moment of safety and relief vanishes as quickly as it came.
I'm already recommending it to a few friends.

This game is basically Dead Island with parkour and nighttime zombie supercharge gimmick thrown in. I enjoyed the game but not unreservedly, there are upsides and downsides to it.
Pros:
- Graphics are excellent, even on medium settings.
- Parkour adds a new dimension to the game and for the most part well executed.
- Decent melee gameplay, weapons and feedback feel right.
- Gunplay is good.
- Good melee upgrade system.
- Well executed and believable city.
- Interesting and rewarding skill trees.
Cons:
- Story is boring and predictable.
- Characters are bland and instantly forgettable.
- Melee weapons are treated as consumables - that orange quality sword you spent 12 grand on, it will become worthless after 5 repairs.
- Parkour feels underdone compared to AC.
- Nighttime gameplay is poorly executed, odds are stacked too heavily in favour of zombies, if you love the feeling of being hunted you will probably enjoy it though.
- As far as I can tell range weapons are not up-gradable like they were in Dead Island.
- The prologue drags on for an hour during which it will take you a few minutes just to kill a simple biter.

All I truly play now adays is survive games. I have always wanted a good zombie game though, where food and water were a must, shelters and bases were able to be built, and so forth. Now to start, I must say I HATE special infected zombies. (Keep reading this isn't a negative review) They just annoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. I can't stand left for dead. They throw special infected every wave, and not just 1 or 2 but like 10. You get fisted by a charger and the moment you deal with that you coughed on,♥♥♥♥♥♥on, and then pounced while being attacked by 15 other zombies.
~My view of zombies in general~
First off I want to start with the zombies. Like I said a bit ago, I cannot STAND special super zombies. I am a original, I believe zombies should be slow, stupid, and only have power in numbers. Dying light doesn't just♥♥♥♥♥♥on you with special infected. I like that there are the OG zombies. They walk, they groan, and they don't ninja stealth the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you like they do on movies and other games (where they just so happen to not make noise until they are close enough to shove their dangled decayed rod in your butt hole). They gradually get stronger, I can tolerate an acid spitter here and there, and the big brutes that guard safe houses sometimes. I like it. They have a truly good balance between the number of S.E. and normal zombros.
Now night time, night time I get. As long as I have the OPTION to go out at night, or wait until day, I am happy. Night scares the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. I don't even like standing near the fence even though I am safe. They truly create a horrific feeling at night. I don't mind the super crazy op zombies at night time, because they give me the option to bypass it. Now at night, more zombies sprint than walk. I get that. I don't mind running into a couple during the day that run, I can handle it. I personally just jump on a roof, and when they try to get up, I just kick their little asses right back down. It's fun and easy to find humor in. The characters aren't hard to develope likings too. You will feel actual hate, intensity, urge, adrenaline, and all that zambie stuff. Some characters you end up not really caring about but it's okay. The AI is truly awesome. I like running into bandits at air drops, and they seem to all have their own personalities because sometimes they are cocky and try to jump you, but when you have a gun on them, some of them put their hands up, back off, and let you take the air drop, because they wont want to get lit the ♥♥♥♥ up, they are actually smart enough to understand they can lose the fight, unlike some game ai that will just always attack you. You can even attempt to do this with an unloaded gun too. It's cool to be able to attempt to pull off these things and have a different outcome each time.
~Skill Tree~
You will eventually get all skill points there is to get but you have to do certain things to level up in each tree. For agility you have to jump around and things, for combat you kill things, for survivalist you play the game.
~Crafting~
Most games have very, very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ crafting systems. This game actually GIVES you good weapons and items when you craft, items that you will go out and hunt for to craft things and you will eventually remember what you need to craft things. I am not going to spoil the things you can craft so moving onward.
~Story~
The story mode is alright. It's not a skyrim story. Skyrim had everything a story mode could need and beyond. This game is quite a fetch game, but if you feel like doing something else you can, so there is an escape method from fetching. Plus you get easily distracted. It's good enough.
~Characters~
I honestly haven't had a super big caring connection to any of the main characters. You just don't spend enough time with or around them to gain a liking to them. It is rather easy to develope a sense of hate though.
~Fighting, Guns~
Melee weapons are obviously the most common thing you will find here. The melee system is great. Camera control isn't super shaky or fast moving and landing hits feels satisfying. Aim is good too and well applied. Guns are easy to use, easy to aim. Moving and shooting is hard though. Head shots are VERY rewarding and usually are one hit kills. They reward head shots perfectly in my opinion. They should always be one hit kills in the head. The only thing I don't like too much is how many hits normal zombs take. A basic zombie takes about 4 to 7 direct blunt hits to the head to kill. It's just.... too much. There are too many zombies at one time to have to sit there and hit each one 7 times, you just get overwhelmed too fast epecially since you can only swing 3 or 4 times until you are out of breathe and have to wait.
~Movement~
You can run from anything if you know how. The hardest thing to run from however is the night time infected because they don't get winded period. You can only sprint for so long but I think at night, when you are being chased, your character strives and runs as long as he can. Climbing is easy, there is one weird thing that happened to me though. I was climbing a radio tower and just, glitched directly under the map and pretty far away from the tower. I managed to get back above ground though by simply walking to a low terrain area and jumped back through. Odd, I know. The running is smooth, climbing is fun, and you get a feeling of safety when up high. The only zombies that can climb are the viral sprinters, and the night time ones. The rest you can look down at and laugh then move on.
I would rate the game 9/10. The only thing I feel that needs to change are the "fetching quests", the "You have to do this at night" quests, and the fact normal zombies take 10 hits to kill.
It's worth buying so go get it and have fun with it.

If you're into the shadowrun universe and played the tabletop/SNES game then you'll mostly enjoy this. It's good, but like the SNES game it's different than the tabletop, which is to be expected since they're different mediums of entertainment. The mechanics are mostly solid, but your experience can be largely determend by which build you decide to start with. If you choose shaman your going to feel useless as all hell; largely the same with decker. They try to make those too more rewarding by giving special dialogue options based on charisma, biotech knolwedge, and intellect, but they're few and far between with combat being the larger focus. Speaking of combat, it's almost as brutal as it is in the tabletop's, but only for enemies. You'll find that you and your teamates are super beefy. I played a mage and with decent positioning and my heal spell I largely never dipped below half HP with crappy body and strength. So, in that sense it's a bit easy. However, it tries to compensate for this by screwing with your dice on hit chances. I can't conferm this, but the only decernable differences between the difficulty settings seemed to be the HP of enemies, how much damage they dealt, and how much the game blatantly lies to you about hit chance. I'm not kidding, I've had people standing point blank with a shotgun miss three 95% chance to hits more than once. I might just be paranoid, it might just be bad programming, but that sort of thing defeintly seems to happen more than it should on the harder difficulties. Anyway, the story is pretty "pink mohawk" as is to be expected from a Shadowrun game, but the writing and character dialogue is actually fairly above average. Despite it's downsides and such it's still pretty good. Everything about the combat other than what I mentioned is either fine or good, and there are a lot of other dialogue options and some cool things you can do out of combat to make your life easier. There's also a fair bit of level exploration, and it functions a bit like an isometric point and click adventure game when you're not bashing skulls.
Yeah, that's about it.

--UPDATED REVIEW--
No doubt about it, Shadowrun Returns is a Shadowrun roleplaying game engine (built on Unity), not a game. The first campaign released was Dead Man's Swtich. The second campaign is Dragonfall. They are fully standalone campaigns and are really where you find the game of Shadowrun Returns. Dragonfall is not "DLC". It is, in fact, a more robust, more ambitious and (at least as I played it) twice-as-long campaign compared to its predecessor.
This is really important to recognize, especially if you haven't played through Dead Man's Switch, or maybe you didn't like it. It's like playing a roleplaying campaign under two different GMs with two different encounter design styles and stories to tell. You definitely don't have to play Dead Man's Switch at all to enjoy Dragonfall.
Since I played Dead Man's Switch, many things have been improved / patched. For instance, scripting in the game's dialog has allowed you to often call on your teammates' skills to help interject in a hacking (decking!) or knowledge based problem. It's not perfect, but it's much, much better. The save system is also now fully featured, which was my biggest complaint about Shadowrun Returns (save when you want, OMG!).
I don't really like how little influence you have over your party's inventory, but I kinda like the narrative implication that they are in charge of themselves, and you're fully in charge of what characters get to come with you on your runs.
The art style, the characters, the rules, the format, etc. they're all the same as you'd remember from Dead Man's Switch. Where Dragonfall shines uniquely is in providing an environment that is far more free than the campaign of its predecessor. I believe most computer roleplaying game fans will greatly prefer Dragonfall. There is a town hub where you are free to shop and pick up side quests, unlike the compact hideout in Dead Man's Switch. Many combat situations have multiple approaches compared to what Dead Man's Switch offered. The characters are more interesting, have more personality, are more plentiful (and more useful), and are better written than those in the prior campaign (reminds me a lot of Mass Effect 2). The story also goes from the small criminal raids of a simple shadowrunning team to the gigantic world-changing epic story that RPGs are famous for.
That said, Dead Man's Switch is still a friendlier, smaller, and more digestible introduction to the Shadowrun world, so I really do recommend playing that campaign first if you're just diving in for the first time.
I'd also like to add that in Dead Man's Switch I played a shotgun-toting, robot-driving hacker, which is basically my ideal cyberpunk character idea. I had a great time! I was originally a little underwhelmed with Dragonfall when I started as a melee fighter because it lacked the gimmicks of my prior loadout (but I'll be darned if I only play one archetype in an RPG). In fact, the lackluster start is what kept me from really even playing the game for 4 months. But in the end, I was really impressed with my troll, and he was just as important to my party as my prior character.
So yes! If you like RPGs and good writing, play Dragonfall. DO IT!
--ORIGINAL REVIEW--
This is only the second Kickstarter game I've played. I'm pretty impressed with it, and it really is the kind of game that most publishers would never fund, so I'm excited to have had the opportunity to play it.  I've so far only finished the Dead Man's Switch campaign, so the following points are regarding that campaign only.
Here's some bullet points:
* The visuals are adequate but not compelling. The high-res handpainted isometric art is impressive for the skill required to execute it. It's retro without being pixillated or limited in palette. VFX are adequate.
* Really cool music, though not enough of it. Never became obnoxious but I was blown away in the first couple hours, but heard basically the same music for the rest of the game. Adequate sound, but no voice acting, which would've pushed the reception of the game's narrative over the edge!
* The story was really cool with some great twists, though it is linear. It's a lot like a great pen-and-paper campaign. You normally wouldn't replay something like that, so a surface-level appearance of choice and nonlinearity is enough, and as a result I found myself happy with the game. However, if you're looking for the story to change dramatically as a result of your choices, you will be disappointed. There are a few dialog options that will change based on your choices, but they are for flavor only. That's OK with me.
* The gameplay is fun. I love turn-based RPG tactics, I just do. I love the positioning and the AOE attacks and managing action points. I like buffs and line-of-sight and overwatch. The game is fully featured in terms of the amount of relevant (and effecitve) skills and choices you have available. You are not locked into a class. Where the gameplay falls short is the dice rolling (like most direct tabletop RPG-to-videogame translations). I hate it when I have an 83% chance to hit a guy and miss twice in a row. Further, I hate when an enemy has a 21% chance to hit me, and it lands. I want my performance to be more predictable and tactical and less dependent on luck. Usually things play out like you'd expect, and so it's okay, but every time the odds are in your favor and you fail, you feel cheated. I hate that.
I would be very comfortable recommending Shadowrun Returns except one thing: The abysmal save system. This game will only autosave when you go from one area to another. There is no other way to save than autosaving. Further, as the story and quests are linear, you can't just abuse the auto-save system by going back and forth between locations. The result is that whenever the designer decides that you'll be in one area for a really long time, it means you can't save that whole time. This is remarkably, and frequently, inconvenient. That said, as the game is turn based, most of the time you take are decisions you mull over. Your progress is the result of choices, not usually execution. So losing progress isn't so bad when you die, as you'll quickly be able to repeat your choices that you've already thought through. Still though, in this day and age in gaming, it's a pretty egregious oversight.
That said, I would still recommend Shadowrun Returns if only for the wonderful and rare cyberpunk videogame setting, choice driven character systems, and tactical RPG combat.

This is kind of odd for me to write a review for.  I really wish that steam had a middle option between thumbs up and thumbs down.
It's definatly not bad, and it plays like a lego game, but as far as I've gotten I've noticed quite a few patterns that i didn't see in previous titles that make the game seem rather lazy.  It is definatly a huge game, with quite a few playable characters, but the story levels seem to be lacking.
As an example, every boss I've encountered so far has played out the exact same.  You fight a horde of enemies, then you're allowed to his the boss once, then another horde of enemies, then you can hit the boss again, then another horde of enemies and then you hit the boss again and win.  I've gone through quite a few bosses and since every one has played the same, I don't see them changing it up later.  Needless to say it gets rather boring rather quick.
The humor also seems to be lacking, and I am comparing this to the lego star wars.  Now I haven't played lego lord of the rings, so I don't know if it also has voice acting, but I feel like the voice acting and actual dialouge has really taken away a lot of the humor.  Each character that talks has a single character trait and tends to just repeat it in differant ways.  Spiderman just won't shut up about all the teen-angst he's having to go through.  I don't think I've sat through a conversation with him where he didn't mention having to do homework.  Again it gets very tired very quickly.  The funniest parts tend to be the deadpool cameos.  Those are done in the old lego game style, through humerous movements and noises.
The game is also far too story focused.  There are few games where I'd consider this a bad thing, but this is one of them.
There is a bleeding cutscene every 4 minutes, and this game sufferes from one of the worst features in all video games.  Unskippable cutscenes.  That is almost as bad as micro transactions.  People like me don't care about the story of a lego game.  The story is also incredibly redundent.  There are cosmic bricks from the silver surfer's surfboard and Dr. Doom wants them to rule the world.  There that's the plot.  Be prepared to have that drilled into your brain in every single unskippable cutscene.
All that being said there is still a really nice charm to playing a lego game.  Playing as the characters and seehing how they're differant to each other is really great fun.  I love being able to swing around New York as Venom (so few games have Venom as a playable character and I don't understand why.  Venom is amazing).  I like being able to go insanely fast as iron man (although, I won't lie, he's an utter pain to control while flying).  That's the main driving point to continue playing; seeing what new character you'll unlock, or working twords unlocking your favorite marvel character.
It's a really weird situation writting a review like this, because if you play it the way you're supposed to (the story mode) it's really rather boring, but if you play it just dicking around as the characters you unlock, it's rather great fun.   If you don't get bored easily or you like constantly doing the same thing, go for it.  Otherwise I'd say it's safe to avoid unless you're a massive Marvel fan.

Antichamber is amazing. It's combat system is intuitive, the battles are envigorating, the storyline is majestic, except...there isn't any of those.
They're practically nonexistent.
There is no combat, enemies, characters, story, or even damage.
Then why did I recommend this game?
For that exact same reason.
Antichamber is, in it's entirety, a mind game. Not a puzzle game, a mind game. It takes what you know about normal First-person exploration games...then flips it on it's head. Hallways will change when you look away, walkways will spontaneusly appear underneath your feet, walls will dissappear as soon as you step toward them, and rooms will change by the simple act of looking through a window.
Antichamber is a mind game.
You start off in a large, black room with the only useful information being how to move, look around, and interact with things. That's the only straightforward information the game will EVER directly give you. Everything else is found through discovery.
If this sounds much too mind-boggling for you, have no fear, there are little hints left for you throughout the game. For example, let's say you come to what looks like a dead end. A normal person would just turn away, assuming there is nothing to be found here. Instead, there will be a sign that says "sometimes the easiest path is straight forward," implying that you should walk straight through the wall. Alas, when you walk toward the wall, it dissappears and you move on forward.
Antichamber is a fun and somewhat humerous way to mess with your head, but can be a little confusing at times.

I don't write many reviews, but I'll make an exception for this.  This is just going to be a performance review for the most part.  I can't speak for everyone so I'm just going to run down how it performs on my rig.
Core i7 4770k
SLI GTX 970's
16 gb RAM
30" 2560x1440 60hz monitor
For starters, this game doesn't support SLI, so it's only using one card.  I have texture and shadows set to medium, everthing else on high, AA on, Vsync off.  I have rain and light shafts physx settings on, smoke/fog and debris settings off.  With these settings I get a solid 60fps in most areas with occasional dips to around 45-50.  Nothing game breaking by any means.  The only time it really hitches is when driving around in the batmobile, but it's so slight that I usually don't notice with everything else going on.  Battle mode is solid 60fps.
The game itself looks beautiful and the story is excellent.  My only real gripe is the lack of boss battles.  There really are none, which is disappointing, but the combat has been even more fine tuned than it was in Arkham City and executes exceptionally well.
I definitley recommend this title as long as your rig is similar or better than mine.  Again, I can't speak for others, but I have no problems running this game at the settings mention above with consistant 60fps.  I was actually surprised how well it runs on a single 970 at 1440p given all the terrible reviews.

The game is COMPLETE. It has an entertaining story, with developed characters, and pretty decent amount of depth for the main story. There is emotions all over the place. Anger, humor, pity... It also progresses at a good pace. The challenges of starting, mid game, and end game are perfect. Harder zombies are introduced as you go along at just the right pace.
For the most part the controls feel pretty natural. However at times (when zombies lunge forward, or when you are dropping on them from above, or trying to exexcute a "finish") they can be a tad clunky, leaving you unsure when you were supposed to time the button press or where you were supposed to aim.. One time it may work, but not the next.
I'm not a big fan of climbing around. The early A.C. games were fun because it was innovative, but once it became manditory and forced, I didn't enjoy it anymore. This game has just the right amount of forcing you to climb and "platform" around. Enough variety that it is different, but not annoying. Also not annoying is the respawns. Once you go through an area, it is pretty safe. Although there is freeclimbing to pretty easily avoid the zeds, once you clear an area it is pretty safe for the remainder of the game. Some stragglers but you really feel like to accomplished something after a big fight.
The weapons have some variety, and you can build a bit towards how you'd like to play with your weapons. I find the elemental additions to be a little more desired. 90% of the fighting is vs zombies, so some elements are pointless, and when you kill them you have to wait for the element to run its course before looting the body, or you will take damage. After the 1000th zombie, that's annoying.
It has a bit of Farcry, mixed with a bit of Fallout, and Dead Island (from this studio).
I love the "Survivor Sense". It's a small area radar that shows you things to interact with. Really nice mechanic so you aren't running around trying to loot things you already looted, or trying to find the right spot to open the trunk. It's one of those elements that makes the game run more efficient. Not hold your hand, but cut down on time wasting.
Overall, I love the game. I honestly can't think of anything that I really DISLIKE about the game, but I do have some improvements that I'd like to see.
1) The main characters have very unique faces. However everyone else in the game is very generic. I've seen this one character's face about 10 times (he looks like my friend so I notice). Also the zed models are the same way. Maybe 5 unique models for the most common zeds, and then 1 model for each specialty zed. All in all you're killing less than 10 models of zombie the entire game.
2) Sometimes the zombies feel hard to distract. It's like only 10 can focus on something at a time, and the rest just stand there. When using a firecracker, I'd expect every zombie from sidewalk to sidewalk to come to it.
3) The "runner" zombies can get annoying. These are the ones that can climb and chase you, and come when there is a loud noise. I like them to keep you on your toes, but sometimes they just keep coming, one by one by one seemingly forever. I just fought a pack, and I want to grab the loot and move on, but the runners keep on coming.
4) I spent the last 8 hours doing side quests. Although I got some skills from levels, the money/weapons seems to just scale. So it's all relative. Theoretically you could beat the game with the same ease at lvl 5 as lvl 30. I guess the point is just seeing the content.
5) I wish it wasn't such a linear story. I had hoped there would be at least 1 decision to make that would make a difference. It also wouldn't hurt to maybe have some factions or relations of some sort. No decisions, no factions, and just freerunning around doing random stuff is not as fun as other "open world/sandbox" games.
6) Multiplayer... Coop is okay.. But the "hunter" thing, just a huge annoyance. My first night in the game, someone dropped in and we did the Vs. thing. He was actually a kind player and told me how to fight him. It was a decent fight, but I wanted to get back to my game. Before I could turn it off, ANOTHER player jumped in. Fought again. Then ANOTHER.. By that time I said screw it and just left the game. That's just insane.. The reward is minimal and the annoyance is through the roof.. Probably the only truely BAD thing I can say about the game.
In conclusion, I'd like to say that this game has the polish of a real quality 2nd game of a franchise. Most times I see the first installment of a series and the best I can say is "it has a bright future", but this game is great RIGHT NOW AS IS. The next installment can just expand on this game, not worry about going back and fixing things.

The only gripe I have is a very small gameplay detail regarding a change in fleshpound AI from the first game. In this game, the fleshpound's rage and boredom meters are removed and substituted for a simple timer of when it will enter an enraged state. For people who took the time to learn how to use the rage and boredom meters from the first game, this is a disappointment, but not a deal breaker.

South Park has been a favourite of mine since I was a child, and it's something I've grown up with over the last 18 or so years. Previous SP games I've played, especially during the PS1/N64 era, have been lackluster to say the least, so I approached TSoT with a ton of cautious optimism.
It turns out that I shouldn't have worried at all, because The Stick of Truth is the best use of a film/TV IP since KOTOR2.
When drawing on almost two decades of a classic cartoon, it'd be pretty easy & understandable for a third party to miss out on the essence of the source material, even if they're fans of the series. Thankfully, Obsidian are masters of their craft, and with the help of series creators Matt & Trey, TSoT perfectly captures all the best bits of one of TVs longest enduring cartoons, and condenses it all into 10 hours of hallmark insanity.
The combat is a little basic, and the gameplay is pretty simple to solve (gross out & fire beats all, basically), but the environments, questing, weapons, and armour, are all varied enough to keep the game more than interesting.
Perhaps not a title for everyone, but for South Park fans? It's an absolute no brainer. One of the most enjoyable games of 2014, with plenty of laugh-out-loud moments, memorable scenes, and flat out insane scenarios. The perfect South Park game.

Antichamber is, in it's entirety, a mind game. Not a puzzle game, a mind game. It takes what you know about normal First-person exploration games...then flips it on it's head. Hallways will change when you look away, walkways will spontaneusly appear underneath your feet, walls will dissappear as soon as you step toward them, and rooms will change by the simple act of looking through a window.
Antichamber is a mind game.
You start off in a large, black room with the only useful information being how to move, look around, and interact with things. That's the only straightforward information the game will EVER directly give you. Everything else is found through discovery.
If this sounds much too mind-boggling for you, have no fear, there are little hints left for you throughout the game. For example, let's say you come to what looks like a dead end. A normal person would just turn away, assuming there is nothing to be found here. Instead, there will be a sign that says "sometimes the easiest path is straight forward," implying that you should walk straight through the wall. Alas, when you walk toward the wall, it dissappears and you move on forward.
Antichamber is a fun and somewhat humerous way to mess with your head, but can be a little confusing at times.

A love letter to South Park fans. Nearly everything from past episodes is referenced somewhere in the world, and the attention to detail goes above and beyond what I'd expect a game. Specific characters who you can completely avoid might make a joke if you do something specific, like farting or changing to a buddy (like swapping to Butters when you're in Professor Chaos' lair). The attention to detail on such small things is not something you see in many games. It feels just like an episode of South Park, comedic pacing and all.
I had a few problems with the game. The shop system was probably made for a gamepad, since selling things takes too long. You'll find items which only exist to be sold, and you get them in bulk. You have to double click each and every single one, or if it's in a stack, select the item, then left click "sell stack". It's not horrible but it takes longer than it needs to. The more important problem is that the game is just too damn easy. At the 10 hour mark I put the game on hardcore difficulty (which I never do because I'm a filthy casual), and I still ended up destroying every boss in 3-6 turns, minus the final boss which was only slightly longer, but by no means difficult. Also my character kept cutting out during the pre-final boss cutscene, which kind of took me out of the experience.
Regardless it's still one of the best JRPGs I've ever played, and it's totally worth your time and money.

So my review of Dying Light is as follows: There are issues with some of the gameplay at times, at least from my experiences. An example is the jumping can sometimes be weak. Like when I go to jump on a car, or from car to car, and I tap the jump button because it's not a big jump, the character fails in the jump. Sometimes the grabbing on the ledge gameplay can be a little frustrating because the character doesn't grab onto the ledge at first and you have to attempt again. That may not sound like a big deal (which it really isn't) BUT with a few zombies lingering in your direction and you want to get the hell up off the road, it gets to be a pain.  I was bummed to read the negative reviews about the issues involving people with AMD's, AFTER I had purchased the game. The first hour or two I played through the issue because I waited so long to play this game and I didn't want to let framerate drop (really bad at times) hold me back from playing Dying Light. So after a bit I decided to try changing settings to the setting of "Best Performance", which is the lowest settings for the game. Now I had the same issues with Far Cry 4 when it came out, where the framerate would drop and takeaway from the gameplay. I tried the lowest settings then and it didn't improve, so that's why I was hesitant on trying it on Dying Light. WELL after changing to the lowest settings, the game has been running so much better. I'd like to eventually play the game with all the settings maxed out, that's  if they ever put a patch out for the AMD users. But for now the game is running a lot better and so much more enjoyable.  So with these issues I still LOVE the game! So far it's pretty freaking badass! When the night falls and the Volatiles come out, the intensity picks up as you try to creep roof top to roof type, or across the ground level without alarming them. I alarmed them twice when they were first introduced, and tried to out run them to the safe zone. Needless to say BIG MISTAKE. I turned around to see how far they were behind me and like 10 of them were scaling the roof top behind me getting ready to jump to the roof top I was on, and moments later I was dead lol. So far though I'm enjoying the game and recommend it to people. If you don't like the idea of having to scale down to the lowest settings because your PC is equipped with AMD, then I'd wait to see if they patch it. If you don't care like me, then I'd say BUY the game...

This game is like Dead Island - Only, it's actually good,
This game is like Mirrors Edge - Only, it's actually good.
Although I am not usually a fan of the First Person perspective, this game is just done right. The immersion is fabulous.
Combat just feels right, one or two zombies, no problem. Mob of 5? Pushing it a little but manageable unless you find yourself cornered or haven't planned an emergency escape route. Once you get the hang of it though Zombie killing becomes second nature. Darting through even large mobs, quickly kicking one out of your way and smashing anothers skull with your wrench just to let them know you mean buisness. The special zombies in the game also add a nice variety and more of a challange too, especially if they have a bit of a mob with them. Loud noises also attract 'Virals', Zombies on steriods, suddenly that gas bottle you just used to blow up an entire mob doesn't seem like it was such a good idea, it's best to leave the area asap or prepare for a really rough fight.
However as storylines such as the 'Walking Dead' have warned us, it may not be the dead that pose the biggest threat in an apocolypse... its other Humans.
In an open world with limited supplies its no surprise bandits are rife, a bit harder to deal with than mushy headed dead walkers. Usually out numbered the threat already feels very real, and of course with working brains and quicker reflexes they are able to evade and dodge. Taking on these guys is a frantic mele battle where reactions are essential and wits are put to the test. Take them head on or plan a more complex strategy? the open world makes the choice yours.
Then just when you think you might have got the hang of it, it gets dark. Warned in advance of the approaching gloom via your watch or your radio, you better hope you've cleared out a safe house or there's some live traps nearby because things are about to get real. Turn on your torch and attract everything nearby or stumble through the darkness hoping to stay out of sight. Virals roam freely at night, with thier cone of vision visable on your map its possible to avoid them with careful espionage-like gameplay. Get seen however and you better start running. With double XP during the night it can be fruitful to stay out past dark, providing of course you can actually evade the nighmares chasing you. Urgency and panic create a further immersion that many other survival games just don't pull off. I have yet to be invaded by another real player, though I imagine its terrifying.
The three skills trees gain XP independently and offer various paths to suit your style of gameplay. The crafting system is also fairly indepth. Modify your base weapons with elemental damage by finding weapon blueprints and crafting materials. You can also create throwables, medkits and lockpicks.
So far having a great deal of fun, worth a play for any survival/zombie fan.
I have not yet tried the Multiplayer Co-op or 'Be the Zombie', however I already feel this was worth the preorder.

Tommy Vercetti, a loyal former member of the Forelli Family, has just been released in 1986, serving 15 years for killing 11 men in the Harwood District of Liberty City in early 1971, earning him the nickname The Harwood Butcher.[3] Tommy's old boss, Sonny Forelli, fears that Tommy's presence in Liberty City will heighten tensions between the other Liberty City families and bring unwanted attention to his organisation's criminal activities.[4]
To prevent this from happening, Sonny ostensibly promotes Tommy to a capo and sends him to Vice City under the guardianship of a crooked lawyer and Sonny's contact Ken Rosenberg to act as their buyer for a series of cocaine deals for Sonny, whose interest is to expand his family activities down the South and to overrun the Liberty drug market with the high-end cocaine from Vice City, hoping to create a monopoly on the Liberty City drug ring to establish the Forelli Crime Family on the top.[5]
Soon, Tommy and his bodyguards are awaited at the Escobar International Airport by Ken, who gives them an info about the deal and takes them to the docks, where they are awaited by the Vance Crime Family, prominent drug kingpins of Vice City led by Victor Vance, who arrive in the chopper with Diaz. As they settle the deal, they are ambushed by several armed and masked men, who kill Victor and Tommy's bodyguards. Tommy narrowly escapes with Ken from the docks, and as a result, he ultimately loses both Forelli's money and the cocaine in the process. Ken drives to his office, while Tommy returns to his hotel.[6]
When Tommy informs Sonny of the ambush, Sonny loses his temper and threatens Tommy with the consequences of attempting to cheat the Mafia. Tommy promises to retrieve the money and the cocaine and kill whoever was responsible for the ambush.[7] Towards this end, Tommy meets up again with Ken at his office, who leads Tommy to retired Colonel and mid-level drug dealer named Juan Garcia Cortez, who was Victor Vance's contact and who organised the deal between the Vances and the Forellis. Cortez expresses regret about Tommy's bad deal and promises that his own lines of inquiry are being made to find out who masterminded the ambush plot. Tommy also meets Cortez's daughter Mercedes, who becomes Tommy's confidante shortly thereafter.
While Tommy waits for the outcome of Cortez's investigation, he meets cocky 21-year old British record producer Kent Paul, real estate mogul Avery Carrington, and a mysterious man, who introduces himself as Lance Vance, younger brother of Victor and the underboss of the now-defunct Vance Crime Family, who wants revenge for the death of his brother and also wants the Vance Crime Family back on the map.[8]
As time passes, Tommy befriends Cortez and begins to do regular work for him as an errand boy and hitman. On one such job, Tommy is called in with Lance to protect the deal of a drug baron named Ricardo Diaz during a deal with the Cubans, looking to buy some high-end cocaine. During the deal, Diaz is ambushed by a gang of Haitians, but Tommy is able to kill them and save the deal, as well as Diaz's life. Consequently, Diaz begins hiring Tommy for his own agenda. Tommy takes this work because it pays well, in spite of his distaste for Diaz. On another errand for Cortez, he plans to meet a French courier to retrieve missile chips stolen from the French government. The deal is ambushed by several French agents and Tommy later kills the courier, who fled the ambush with the chips, retrieving the items.
Tommy learns from Cortez that Cortez's own lieutenant, Gonzalez, was partially responsible for the ambush on Tommy's cocaine deal since he is the only person besides Cortez to know about the deal, and Cortez asks Tommy to kill Gonzalez as a favour, since he was a man who he did distrust and was working behind his back. Afterwards, Cortez voices his suspicion that Diaz might have been behind the ambush. Tommy initially continues the status quo to prepare for his attack, but his hand is forced when Lance attempts to take revenge by himself and fails, forcing Tommy to rush across the city and rescue him from the junkyard in which he is held. With the die cast, the two move quickly to raid Diaz's mansion and execute Diaz. With Diaz dead, and Colonel Cortez fleeing the country to escape the French, the established drug empires in Vice City quickly crumble and Tommy and Lance personally take over, becoming Vice City's drug kingpins.
Tommy becomes the head of his own organisation, the Vercetti Crime Family, distancing himself from the Forelli Family and Liberty City and more interested in personally controlling Vice City than being Forelli's puppet. But the more powerful and rich Tommy gets, the more Lance begins to exhibit paranoia and sociopathic behaviours, to the point that he begins to abuse his own bodyguards and constantly calls Tommy in states of hysteria, losing his mind over being just a powerless second-in-command as he was under his brother for the past 2 years. Tommy begins to suspect that Lance is up to something.
Tommy makes alliance with Umberto Robina's Cubans against Auntie Poulet's Haitians, even though he is at the same time hypnotised by Poulet's voodoo into helping the Haitians as well. However, Tommy and Poulet part ways Tommy and the Cubans sneak explosives into the Haitian drug factory disguised in Haitian gang cars and blow it up, effectively ending the conflict and putting the Haitians out of business, enabling the Cubans to take over Little Havana. Umberto then becomes Tommy's partner. He also becomes friends with Big Mitch Baker, a leader of the biker gang and a Vietnam veteran, with both the bikers and the Cubans becoming protectors of Vercetti family business.
As his drug business expands, Tommy buys assets in nearly bankrupt companies such as a car lot named Sunshine Autos, a cab depot Kaufmann Cabs, a popular night club called The Malibu, a local boathouse, a print shop, Print Works, an ice-cream company, and an adult film company, all of which he turns back into competitive businesses. He also becomes a personal bodyguard to glam metal band Love Fist, and pulls a major bank heist. He starts to control almost all the assets and ties of Vice City: Sunshine Autos as a chop shop, Kaufmann Cabs for money laundering, The Malibu Club for dispatching drugs, the ice-cream company for the production of drugs and the film company to control the underground movie scene.
Eventually, the Forelli family discovers that Tommy has gained control over entire Vice City and without having sent a single dime back to them. Sonny is enraged that Tommy has become independent and is hustling him, and sends collectors consisting of high-ranking Forelli members to force money out of Tommy's assets. Tommy disposes of them, but after they injure the elderly operator of his print shop of counterfeit money, he decides to cut Sonny and the Forelli family out of his business, severing his ties with the Forelli family.
An angered Sonny arrives in Vice City with a small army of mafiosi, intent on taking their tribute by force. Sonny and his henchmen soon arrive at the Vercetti Estate. Just as Tommy attempts to give them their tribute in counterfeit money, Sonny reveals he is the one who set Tommy up fifteen years before, sending him to kill the eleven men who were expecting him since he was feeling that Tommy would himself take over Sonny's business. Lance then exposes himself as a traitor, revealing Tommy's attempt to fool Sonny, and also admitting to informing Sonny about Tommy's activities in Vice City. Lance explains that he did it because Tommy started to disown him and didn't treat him equally, and wanted him dead so he could rebuild the Vance Crime Family and the fortune he had with his brother. An enraged Tommy starts a gunfight.
In the ensuing battle, Tommy first chases, ridicules, and finally kills Lance, then storms downstairs, where he faces off with Sonny,

Antichamber is a first-person puzzle game somewhat like Portal except Antichamber is not linear and has a higher focus on exploration. The game's non-Euclidean space/geometry often means conventional logic won't work, and you'll often have to "think outside the box" in order to solve a room (or find a different exit to a room you previously solved). Additionally, part of the fun of Antichamber is just trying to figure out what the goal of the game is.
I enjoyed the game very much and believe it is one of the best games of the year.  I would absolutely recommend it to a friend, especially if that friend enjoyed Portal.
PROS:
-The game is fun and each room has a unique puzzle or trick to it.
-Non-linear design means if you get stuck you can try a different direction/room.
-The puzzles struck a good difficultly balance and were difficult but not impossible to figure out on my own.
-The game is completely non-violent and is ideal for casual gamers, children, and those normally turned off by video games due to violence.
CONS:
-The game is single-player only.
-The story is minimal.
-The game has little replayability because the puzzles are set. There is no way to create/share/download new puzzles.

LEGO usually does fantastic with its games, but they out did themselves for LEGO Marvel Superheroes. The story is exciting and different. A usual good vs evil conflict with classic characters ending with some awesome plot twists. Through the whole story which took me about 8 hours to complete you don't see the same level repeting itself. The different locations you go to always keep it exciting, but the one flaw I have about the story is the lack of characters used in it. You play as majoy heroes and fight major villians, but never the less known characters. Deadpool likes to hide around the levels which was dissapointing because he would have added some great lines, which you get to see at the end. In the game you get to explore an open city with notable cities like Stark Tower, X-Men Manor, Avengers Mansion, Baxtor Building and many more. Even better is that there are hours of side quests to unlock new characters and vehicles. They don't take to long either so it can be fun for a short session. The characters you can unlock are amazing, big characters like the Guardians of the Galaxy and Ant-Man and Carnage to small unknown characters like Squirrel Girl and AIM Henchmen. Hours upon hours can go into this game without it feeling like you're doing the same thing over and over. Only two complaints I had throughout the game is the lack of characters in the story, and lack of DLC. The DLC contained big characters like Thanos but LEGO for some reason doesn't like DLC on PC. Other then that, best LEGO game ever, and best Marvel game in a long long time. 9.5/10

Better than I expected, very few flaws which are minor (ignoring physics ones / mechanical failures that get you killed).
Guns! Fun to use, not worth using because of the horde they draw in. Virals are not fun to fight, and I usually just cheese the fights by climbing a ledge with only 1 way up and executing them as they jump up 1 at a time.
Easter eggs! That plants vs zombies easter egg was over the top and awesome! Intentionally unbalanced, probably.
Zombies are in an awkward place right now in terms of difficulty. They are nearly completely backwards! The normal walkers have a crazy amount of vitality. The virals rarely suffer recoil and there's no 'invincibility frames' doing execution kills so I frequently die from several zombies attacking me while the slow execution moves are going off. The spitter zombies are annoying from afar since they can lob shots over obstacles and hit you with a poison DOT, but since they take like 1 kick to the head to put down, they're not too bad to deal with. The bulky zombies are way easier than the virals or biters to kill because they move slowly and predictably. The demolisher is the easiest zombie type to take down due to the amount of time it cools down for after charging into an object. The nightmares at night pose no threat if you can take them on 1 at a time. Using a farmer scythe and a UV light together, they go down in 3 hits.
Virals man. Freaking virals. For every one you shoot, two more come back. They basically outrun you, hit you so you can't run, and then you're dead. You can't kick stun them or charge up a hit and knock them back, they ignore all of that and attack you while you attack. The only way to take on more than 2 at a time without giving up a lot of health is to sit on a small ledge where they can be executed as they climb up. They need a little tuning or a limit in their gun related spawning because guns are not worth using at this time because of them.
Gameplay 9/10 - meeting or beating expectations
Story 4/10 - beyond predictable, no real connection to characters, and no more new air drops... If the final mission is focused on your struggle with slowly turning into a zombie and your character and female-lead-name deciding who lives and who turns... then what's the player supposed to think during the post game free roam? Throughout the story, the player occasionally begins to turn and needs a shot of antizen. Now it's never encountered again in free roam and there's no more air drops. Did everyone suddenly become immune? It kind of invalidates all of the character deaths, struggles and pretty much the entire plot up to the ending. Rais wouldn't hold any power if Brecken knew that in a few days/weeks of your arrival, everyone would suddenly be immune & cured.
But we don't play zombie games for the story, we play for the zombie slaying! For this game specifically, we came to see dead island done better with some mirror's edge thrown in :)
Still great graphics even for today's standards, difficult AI good storytelling overall good game

To clarify, what this is not, is a sprawling open-world RPG with endless space to explore and fight and level up with the same character until you become and unstoppable behemoth that Blizzard is targeting premium content at on a daily basis. If you want that, look elsewhere.
Yes the graphics are a little retro, personally it works for me, it may not for everyone, if it doesn’t for you - since there are a huge number of videos and photos available to see before purchasing the game, I find whining about it a little childish, no?
What this is, is a fun and engaging storyline and an amazing opportunity for user generated content to provide a huge wealth of different experiences. To challenge yourself to find different solutions and to challenge yourself to myriad different play styles.
The user generated content will get there, and when it does, there will be so much to this game (that the studio could never have afforded to produce) that I foresee loosing many many hours blissfully jacked in.
If you doubt any of this look at the amount of user generated content for the dungeon crawler Legend of Gimrock, what you buy is a single campaign that takes a day or so to complete, what you get access to is a vast wealth of user generated dungeons created by people who, with the intricacy of their level design and fiendishness of their traps and puzzles, make the guy in the Saw films look like he really wasn't trying. If that can happen with this game (which I’m sure it will so long as the level creation and modding tools are there) it will be awesome.
