Your name is Crane and you are working for some people at a place called the Tower and they have given you orders to reboot the electric grid while the sun is setting....now for most that doesnt mean much but for you it means everything.  You need to reboot the grid before a select group of superhuman zombies who can only be described as nightmare fuel emerge from their hidey holes and rip off your ♥♥♥♥ing face like a swarm of zombie locusts.  You flip the switch and the screen completely locks up but the sound keeps going....whats going on? you hear a loud bursting of a door or a wall and what sounds like a boss monster.  You dont see any of that though because the screen is still fixated on the electric box.  Suddenly the game jumps to life and you see a zombie with a Rebar sledgehammer much like in Fallout swinging wildly towards you,  You have to kill this giant grizzly beast of a man on a time limit with the added benefit of him slamming down his sledge to attract more zombies. The only thing is that the game will periodically freeze frame while the game will play in the background.
Thats right folks you will be in the middle of fighting a horde of zombies, be near a environmental hazard you dont want to stand in or jumping from rooftop to rooftop like a ghetto Batman and the game will say "This looks like far too much fun for you to handle, let me just go ahead and kill you" and lock up.  This is a debilitating, crippling, game killing bug that needs to be sorted out immediately for the game to even be playable.
Besides that fact the game is incredibly fun to play and makes a effort to build the world and make it halfway believable and not weighing you down or forcing you through the story like Call of Dookie or the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game adaption of the movie Red Dawn, Homefront.  A lot of the models, textures, and game mechanics from Dead Island are copy pasted into the game but it doesnt take away from Dying Lights right to have its own name.  Aside from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t bug this game can stand on its own and not pay any mind to the people who say its just Dead Island 1.5.
I would put this game as a must buy for anybody who is a loot ♥♥♥♥♥, people who like sandbox games, or light RPG / combat mechanics.  I would sugguest that you just wait for the patch to get rid of the terrible awful frame rate drops before you pick it up so you wont rage quit after the game decides to freeze beside a soon-to-be exploding vehicle.  Good luck out there in Zombieland!

If you came here looking for a classic x-com game, you came to the wrong place. The aliens may be the same, and in fact I'd say they did a good job of updating all the aliens to be something new and unique, but this has almost none of the traditional x-com charm and difficulty. Everything is based on a very simple cover system... either you're in cover, or you're not. You don't shoot in the direction of enemies, like you do in the original games, but rather you shoot at a single enemy, and either you hit, or you miss. If you miss, you might get lucky and blow up their cover.
The game operates on a mob group system. Aliens are in groups, and if they spot you, they get a cinematic in which they run in to cover. This means that if a group of aliens has not seen you this turn, they will not shoot you during their turn, so the threat is minimal. Even at the start of the game, you're fielding a squad of 4 guys vs. many aliens. Later on you go up to a whopping 6, making the aliens feel very weak... how are we even losing this war?
All that said, if you take away the xcom, the game is a functional TBT. It's fairly decent, and can be quite enjoyable. If you're looking for x-com, skip it and go buy xenonauts, or go help out with any of the open source fan projects out there.
Sadly, the game is also riddled with bugs. Sometimes you will be unable to shoot an enemy, even though they can shoot you. Sometimes your troops will end up walking somewhere they can't go, resulting in them being stuck for the mission if they can't fly. There's many others, especially in multiplayer, so only get it if you're interested in TBT. It's a good introduction of the genre to those who wouldn't normally play such.

Being a big fan of the Lego games, especially after the epic advenure the Lord of the Rings one was, I was super psyched to see my super heroes in a game.
Straight to the point, keeping in mind I'm only an hour or two into it, it's been a major let down. The voice acting could have been much better. The voices chosen for each weren't really well picked and don't really fit some of the characters at all. The characters that are portrayed in the newer movies all have that voice people are used to. Lego Lord of the Rings brought all the original cast to re-voice the characters. They should have done the same for this as well seeing as they more than likey would have had the money.
The gameplay has been pretty spot on as you would have hoped. Flying around and shooting energy balls with Iron Man, Hulk Smashing your foes with the Hulk, shooting webs with Spiderman are all a blast. Spiderman's web slinging could have been more interactive ( I sitll think the Spiderman 3 game has the best web slinging controls ever) but it IS a kid's game so, no points docked there.
What reaaallly gets me the most, is the "story". It just doesn't have that Marvel-esque touch that the comics and cartoons had. The story just feels broken and uninteresting. Nothing to get you hyped about playing anyone, just, oh here's some chaos happening, have these 3 particular heroes and deal with it. Another issue, for me personally is I hate Fantastic 4, they're boring, uncreative and just irritating and too much of a portion of the game in the beginning has to deal with them, again that's a personal issue.
The biggest irritation, is in all the lego games you had to destroy structures to release blocks to build something to aid you. They always had that "tell" that you could just look around and spot it and say "ya..I bet I have to break that thing". Here, everything blends in too well, everything looks normal. You will spend more time breaking everything in an area to reveal the blocks to build something than you do spending playing the game for the story. It's almost like they're forcing the "break everything" on you.
Is it a good game? Probably my least favorite of all of them, which hurts to say because I love Marvel comics. Is it worth the price tag even on sale? Hell no. If it was 10 bucks maybe. At it's current price and Thanksgiving sale, I'd be much happier buying a second copy of Lego Lord of the Rings.

In Dead Space, you play as Isaac, a space engineer who ran away from his fanatic b*tch of a mother before she could sacrifice him to the Unitologist church.
You will thus proceed to explore the dark basement of the USG Stone Village, a spaceship that resembles a metallic wiener flying around your mom's womb (probably an allegory of your missing father).
During your exploration, you will come across a varied cast of your grotesquely disfigured siblings - from the wailing anorexic to the morbidly obese, and even the unborn ones - so jealous of your fancy suit they will all try to murder you. Isaac won't have a choice but to cry a lot on them, although reluctantly, to either dismember them or slow them down while he epic slaps them with heavy tools.
Exploring the basement and bringing your murderous siblings to peace will earn you gifts and monies that will allow you to upgrade your tears and pajamas (light RPG mechanics) how you want to better handle the situation further on, as Isaac will have to come to terms with his mom by destroying her heart, her cancer and finally her giant foot (out of her womb?!) by dropping a fiery meteor on it.
The game explores many different fears most children experience on their early life, like solitude, fear of the dark, hospitals, lack of oxygen, drifting into the empty space, swarms, loss of limbs, girlfriends on their period, and babies with tentacles.
Mainly babies with tentacles.
Overall, a great sci-fi action experience that still holds up well to today's gaming standards despite being almost 8 years old (the age of Isaac).
Stellar atmosphere and gorgeous soundscape, with an enjoyable gameplay.

Let's get one important thing out of the way: Shadowrun Returns *needs* the Dragonfall DLC. [EDIT: Now that Dragonfall can be purchased standalone, this game has no real reason to exist] Without it, you're doomed to a story-on-rails campaign built to satisfy gun-monkeys and leave less combat-oriented classes in the dust, to say nothing of an inferior save system.
Basically, Dead Man's Switch should be considered bonus content. Dragonfall is the real game.
And what a game it is. Characters feel real, like they've been lived in for a while, not just plopped all one-dimensional and tabula rasa into the story. They have motivations, interesting origins, disagreements, and so on. They feel like actual people. And those people breathe life into the story -- a conspiracy yarn full of magic, intrigue, and high-tech low-lives. Choices are difficult. There's often a clear division between the morally right and wrong choices, but the consequences muddy it up. Is it better to spare some schlub for the sake of conscience if missing a payday means you can't stop far greater evil down the line?
Combat is kind of a stripped-down X-Com affair with turnbased isometric squad stuff. It's serviceable, but the real treat is the writing.

As one of my favorite games, Risk of Rain is highly recommended.
Most modern gamers will be confused by the graphic, but honestly if this game is built 2.5D in Cry Engine your game will crash so bad, my point: the gameplay is the most important part you should be looking at. Risk of Rain can be very addicted, everytime you start from the beginning with default data and you work your way to become a badass and with the new (kind of new) artifacts system, this game generate so much varieties that I can not count. Basically you chose one of the unique characters blaze through every stage and stock items, level up and build up your character and the objective is to beat the final stage.
One of the main features is the game's difficulty, it grows as the time pass. A decent gameplay management is required as the game can be tough to beat for a new player. RoR will keep surprising you with new contents (characters, items) that you will unlock, varieties tend to increase as you explore more. Which keep a well loop and create a high 'replayability'. RoR also contains several small secrets waiting for you to discover.
I have seen people complaining about the multiplayer experience, which was tough to me as well. Since the developers of RoR are independent developers, a server can be luxury indeed. Simply learn how to port forwarding will be enough to host. No hamachi required, I can prove it myself but who ever is hosting need a decent internet efficiency.
Despite lack of official server (some people actually host servers look it up), RoR is a pick up and play, rogue like action game, with very intriguing item and character design, and it is constantly updating. I can't illustrate how frustrated I feel when the game beat me and some ironic words pop out mocking my failure, or how awesome and satisfied it can be, when I beat the game with tons of items I collected. In other word RoR provide really nice difficulty options where things can get nasty require you to pay some attentions in order to beat it, or you can just sit back, relax, enjoy the show.
If you are available to play co-op, co-op is not too different from single player, which just add some additional chaos on your screen. The soundtrack in RoR is another feature to enjoy, musics in the background certainly polish the game into a another level it is simply astonishing and perfect. You can find all the little details proving that there are people (devs) who care about their games, and it is tons of fun when you are relaxing and reading some introductions of the item you've been using in the game, as well as the monster logs. Sometimes the game can crash if data overloaded (because it's the nature of the game), or some minority bugs happen to get in your way but overall RoR is a must-have game, and trust me you need to go deeper to witness the sorrow of the rain.

This is an addictive game for having such a simple premise.  Spawn on a planet, clear the stage, gather loot, and continue on.  Each time you play, you select a character with specific skill sets (think MOBA).  Each of the characters feels quite unique and really helps to increase the gameplay.  The game stays fast-paced, especially since the longer you play the more dangerous the enemies become.
There are some quirks, though.  The game lets you zoom out to see more of the screen, to the point where the pixel art is 1:1 (your character becomes like 16 pixels tall on the screen).  The GUI and all menus also zoom out, which is unnecessary.  The game loses some of its appeal when zoomed out that much, and you don't feel like you're in as much danger when you can see things coming.  So just don't play zoomed out like that, right?  You get such an advantage in the game while zoomed out that the game just becomes unnecessarily more difficult (and sometimes annoying with faster or long-ranged enemies).
Like others, I also had a game breaking bug twice where your character eternally falls through the world.  Thankfully this rarely happens, and only at the beginning of a run (so all you have to do is restart).

In Dead Space, you play as Isaac, a space engineer who ran away from his fanatic b*tch of a mother before she could sacrifice him to the Unitologist church.
You will thus proceed to explore the dark basement of the USG Stone Village, a spaceship that resembles a metallic wiener flying around your mom's womb (probably an allegory of your missing father).
During your exploration, you will come across a varied cast of your grotesquely disfigured siblings - from the wailing anorexic to the morbidly obese, and even the unborn ones - so jealous of your fancy suit they will all try to murder you. Isaac won't have a choice but to cry a lot on them, although reluctantly, to either dismember them or slow them down while he epic slaps them with heavy tools.
Exploring the basement and bringing your murderous siblings to peace will earn you gifts and monies that will allow you to upgrade your tears and pajamas (light RPG mechanics) how you want to better handle the situation further on, as Isaac will have to come to terms with his mom by destroying her heart, her cancer and finally her giant foot (out of her womb?!) by dropping a fiery meteor on it.
The game explores many different fears most children experience on their early life, like solitude, fear of the dark, hospitals, lack of oxygen, drifting into the empty space, swarms, loss of limbs, girlfriends on their period, and babies with tentacles.
Mainly babies with tentacles.
Overall, a great sci-fi action experience that still holds up well to today's gaming standards despite being almost 8 years old (the age of Isaac).
Stellar atmosphere and gorgeous soundscape, with an enjoyable gameplay.
Recommended for the whole family as an alternative to Disney's classics marathon nights.

I tried the lowest settings then and it didn't improve, so that's why I was hesitant on trying it on Dying Light. WELL after changing to the lowest settings, the game has been running so much better. When someone mentions the word LEGO in a game title, I'm sure most people will think this is a game just for little kids. They could not be further from the truth. The LEGO games are actually fun for pretty much all ages, due to the reference material they use. We've had LEGO games ranging from Star Wars to Harry Potter to Batman, and more. And now we move on to something odd. Marvel Super Heroes. I say odd, because this is a WB game. WB which owns the rights to publish DC related stuff. DC which is a rival company of Marvel. And Marvel, which is now owned by Disney. So this is indeed an dd pairing. Traveler's Tales are just such big fans of Marvel (and who can blame them) that they wanted this to be made. And here it is. And here is probably the best LEGO game to date. A labor of love from fans of Marvel, made for fans of Marvel.
LMSH is a completely original story in the Marvel universe, which borrows characters from the Marvel movie universe and also the comic universe. In fact, it has a roster so massive, it is the biggest roster of any LEGO game to date. You'll find all of your favorites, ranging from the Avengers, X-Men, Fantastic Four, Blade, Daredevil, Spider-Man, and more, and even an assortment of odd picks like Howard the Duck (who even has his own achievement) and more. Of course what's a superhero game without supervillains. So yes, you can play as a number of baddies as well. Normal sized characters have normal LEGO scaling, and the big bruisers like The Incredible Hulk, Colossus, and others have been turrned into bigger LEGO characters called "big figs". And your larger than life characters like Galactus have been given the normal mini fig versions when you want to play as them.
LMSH features a msssive hub world recreation of comic and real world fused Manhattan, complete with a wide assortment of side missions, challenges, and unlockables to discover along the way. You can run, jump, fly, or ride vehicles to get around the city at your own leisure. and when not tackling main story missions, there is a ton of things to do. Even after tackling the main story, you will find so many things to unlock, from characters to vehicles and new mission. Some things will warrant replays through missions with different characters, shooting replayability through the roof.
As for gameplay, LMSH offers the most refined combat of any lego game to date, mixed with the usual puzzle solving based on character powers. It's fun, varied, and easily the most satisfying in the series. The game also puts a huge emphasis on combat more than any LEGO game to date.
My only complaints on this game are the unispired soundtrack, which pales in comparison to previous LEGO games. And also the character creator. It's sloppy. It lacks full customization. And unless you want to unlock a couple of achievements, is completely unnecessary.
Pros:
- Biggest roster to date
- Best moveset to date for individual characters
- Big fig characters!
- So much content packed in. Even after completing the game, there is so much to do.
Cons
- Boring soundtrack
- Character creator is not good
10/10 Very fun.

This game is like Dead Island - Only, it's actually good,
This game is like Mirrors Edge - Only, it's actually good.
Although I am not usually a fan of the First Person perspective, this game is just done right. The immersion is fabulous.
Combat just feels right, one or two zombies, no problem. Mob of 5? Pushing it a little but manageable unless you find yourself cornered or haven't planned an emergency escape route. Once you get the hang of it though Zombie killing becomes second nature. Darting through even large mobs, quickly kicking one out of your way and smashing anothers skull with your wrench just to let them know you mean buisness. The special zombies in the game also add a nice variety and more of a challange too, especially if they have a bit of a mob with them. Loud noises also attract 'Virals', Zombies on steriods, suddenly that gas bottle you just used to blow up an entire mob doesn't seem like it was such a good idea, it's best to leave the area asap or prepare for a really rough fight.
However as storylines such as the 'Walking Dead' have warned us, it may not be the dead that pose the biggest threat in an apocolypse... its other Humans.
In an open world with limited supplies its no surprise bandits are rife, a bit harder to deal with than mushy headed dead walkers. Usually out numbered the threat already feels very real, and of course with working brains and quicker reflexes they are able to evade and dodge. Taking on these guys is a frantic mele battle where reactions are essential and wits are put to the test. Take them head on or plan a more complex strategy? the open world makes the choice yours.
Then just when you think you might have got the hang of it, it gets dark. Warned in advance of the approaching gloom via your watch or your radio, you better hope you've cleared out a safe house or there's some live traps nearby because things are about to get real. Turn on your torch and attract everything nearby or stumble through the darkness hoping to stay out of sight. Virals roam freely at night, with thier cone of vision visable on your map its possible to avoid them with careful espionage-like gameplay. Get seen however and you better start running. With double XP during the night it can be fruitful to stay out past dark, providing of course you can actually evade the nighmares chasing you. Urgency and panic create a further immersion that many other survival games just don't pull off. I have yet to be invaded by another real player, though I imagine its terrifying.
The three skills trees gain XP independently and offer various paths to suit your style of gameplay. The crafting system is also fairly indepth. Modify your base weapons with elemental damage by finding weapon blueprints and crafting materials. You can also create throwables, medkits and lockpicks.
So far having a great deal of fun, worth a play for any survival/zombie fan.
I have not yet tried the Multiplayer Co-op or 'Be the Zombie', however I already feel this was worth the preorder.

My wall of text:
At first Killing Floor 2 seems superior to it's predecessor in every way. But, after you spend some time with it, you can notice that it still loses to original game in some ways. It doesn't mean that KF 2 is worse than KF, no, actually, for me, it's opposite. And when you launch it for the first time after playing original Killing Floor, sequel looks incredible. It's beautiful and everything has that "Umph!" that just makes it feel right.
Aside from new characters you have your classic characters like Mr Foster or Classic Masterson. But this time you can customize them. Good stuff, right? Well, if you are willing to pay 2,49$ to get yourself a key to open some weird crate or "decode an USB" - it sure is. I never liked systems like this, but if it keeps game going - whatever. Still, RNGesus is everywhere and in my opinion - it's pretty bad. Of course, you can get a random skin/cosmetic for free, after you finish an operation or 2, but so far I only got 2 common AA-12 skins and 4 Bandanas. So yeah, bring out your dosh or pray to RNGesus and grind your♥♥♥♥♥off. Some people might say that cosmetics do not matter, but I can't agree with them on that, simply because these still affect you in some way, for example - these items affect your overall enjoyment of the game.
Now that we're done with CS:GO stuff, let's move to guns themselves. Guns look, sound and feel
! Each weapon, aside from starting pistol, looks powerful and usually, get's it's job done. But! There are simply not enough weapons. And because weapons are linked to Perks(classes), it affects gameplay greatly. Take Support Perk(guy that provides team with ammo, locks up doors and uses shotguns), for example. You start the game with a SG-500 pump action shotgun, you kill stuff, get through waves, you buy yourself a Double-barreled Boomstick. You kill even more stuff and you have to decide - you can buy yourself a M4 shotgun, OR you can skip it, save the money, and buy AA-12. No matter what you choose, during last waves you will probably have Double-barreled Boomstick, AA-12 and something else, if your carrying capacity allows. There is simply no reason to NOT get yourself an AA-12, aside from personal preferences. Also, I just listed all of the support weapons in the game. Yep. 4 shotguns. That's it. At first it doesn't sound so bad - straight-forward upgrade of your main weapon. But then you get through 50 games with the same setup and it just feels boring. Of course, you can switch Perks and all that, but that doesn't change anything. Because most Perks have same issue. There are simply no "sidegrades" for them, only direct upgrades(in terms of weaponry). And as you level up, it get's harder and harder not to notice that.
Perks themselves are a little bit different from the ones that were presented in the original game. Sharpshooter doesn't use pistols anymore. Gunslinger does. There are also new perks, Gunslinger, like I already said, is the perk that uses pistols, mostly akimbo pistols. SWAT - SMG perk with some defensive and offensive abilities. And Survivalist - Jack of all trades, that is not released at the moment of me writing this review. Leveling up is not as grindy as it was before. Each five levels you can pick 1 skill out of 2, that will sometimes greatly affect your playstyle - that system is not as straightforward, as it sounds. You have to decide between dealing damage or being able to withstand more damage, carrying more ammo/having larger clip capacity, or being able to reload Perk weapons faster. However, you can change your skills in-between waves, so don't worry about reading guides on how to not screw your character. I, myself, like that system, but some Perks feel much weaker than others to me. But that's probably my own issue, I just have to "git gud". And I am also sulking over Gunslinger and Sharpshooter not being as easy to play as, as before.
Killing Floor 2 does a much better job at being truly difficult, compared to the original game. Of course, bullet-spongy Zeds have their charm, but to me, it was always just a big pile of bs. Killing Floor 2 makes enemies faster, deadlier and smarter with each difficulty step up. On normal enemies just rush at you, making it easy to kill them off or just run past them. On hard difficulty enemies are a bit faster and deal more damage, but still are pretty easy to deal with. But on Suicidal you will notice how movement patterns of enemies change. Alpha Clots will buff and speed up weaker zeds around them, while rushing at you, jumping over obstructions. Slashers will dodge-roll your shots, getting closer and closer to you, before unleashing powerful attacks. Crawlers will spread around you, move out of your line of fire when you aim at them, or even when you turn on your flashlight. Gorefasts, Bloats(after Bloat explodes it will leave acid mines on the ground - walk over it and you know what's going to happen), Scrakes and Fleshpounds use their metallic weapons to protect their heads. Husks use their flame cannons as flamethrowers that melt both your armor and health at close range. They can also go full kamikaze at low health, running up to you, and exploding in blazing inferno. And Stalkers - those are the worst. Not only they move extremely fast, they also dodge your attacks constantly and appear from your left or right, even though second ago they were right in front of you. They jump and spin during their attacks, sometimes making it hard to hit them with anything, unless it's a giant hammer, shotgun or a grenade launcher. There are currently 2 bosses - good ol' Patriarch(not that different from one in the original game) and Dr. Hans Volter. Bosses, however, do not change as much, considering the difficulty settings. Just like in the original game, their health scales with the amount of players. Aside from that - they are preatty easy to deal with.
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is a great game. I couldn't enjoy it to it's fullest, because none of my friends have it and I had to play alone or with randoms. But even so, I like that game and consider it to be a great sequel to it's predecessor.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes does what it says on the tin; it's a Lego game involving the plethora of characters from the Marvel universe. But what this tin doesnt include is all of the 'icky' features that have been introduced into this game.
Story:
Just like Lego Batman 2, LMSH has its own custom story to offer players as they scatter around manhattan to rescue Cosmic Bricks from the hands of various villians. Its a nice simple story that has been injected with a dose of unwanted seriousness that makes it very jarring. Sure its not a doom and gloom story but when you try to do that with quirky characters, it just doesnt work.
LMSH plays it very safe with the story. Dont expect to be moved by it.
Although in a game where you smash enemies into little Lego pieces WHO NEEDS A STORY?!
3/10
Visuals:
LMSH visuals are outstanding. Compared to the bland look of Lego Star Wars and the dark feeling in Lego Batman, LMSH really brings life back to this series. Metals glisten and reflect wonderfully, shadows are sharp and the animation...dont get me started on the animation, but to sum it up, it's bloody fantastic (the most fluid animation I have seen in a lego game by far.).
Such a breath of fresh air in the Lego series.
5/5
Gameplay:
LMSH plays like every other Lego game
-one button to hit
-one button to jump
-one button to switch character
-one button for a special move
Plain and simple and there's nothing wrong with that. Each character has their own special ability (just like in Lego Batman 2) this ranges from Thors electricity to charge power supplies or Spidermans spider sense to reveal hidden objects to interact with. Flying is much more satisfying than Lego batman 2. Here you have one button to go up and one to go down, much better than the target system in the previous game.
Stud collection in this game is a LOT more forgiving than the previous games. In LMSH, if you rack up a combo you can collect times that amount...get it? Lemme break it down, if your character kills 5 guys in a row they get a 5x combo which allows every stud you collect to be 5x more value.
This didnt bother me as much as the secret red brick options...
The Lego Star Wars series is a perfect example of good red brick secrets, each one was unlocked that you could only get through a free play when you have got (nearly) all of the characters. In LMSH you have some already unlocked for you, the biggest annoyance being 'Score x2 ready to buy'.
This zapped all of the excitement out of having a second playthrough to find all those little secrets. It was like the game was holding my hand.
Fun aspects, nothing new at all, slightly repetitive
3/5
Combat:
*pssst* press X to hit guys.
Although two problems did bother me with the combat.  The first being instead of an optional ability to preform a special move on enemies, your character does it automatically..wethere you like it.or.not. I found that this ruined my gameplay slighty by being stopped mid fight and mid combo just to do a special move (although they are pretty cool)
The second problem being the life bar. In Lego star wars I feared for my character when it was up against multiple Stormtroopers or even 2 Droideka's but in this game I feel like hoards of enemies are just a nuisance due to only loosing a life one every 2 hits. It just makes the game very dumbed down compared to ints counterparts.
Simple Combat with some annoying factors
3/5
Overview
Lego Marvel Super Heroes, to me, is the baby of the Lego branded games.
At the core of this game, LMSH is very fun and an experience I have enjoyed...to a certian extent.

A good attempt to modernize X-Com for a newer audience, but one that suffers from many of the pitfalls of today's gaming mentality. The game is full of cute additions that quite quickly become incredibly annoying. The constant talking heads (some of which can be disabled in the expansion apparently), the little cutscenes, the soldier voice acting; they simply make the game less enjoyable as you go along. You can disable them, but you'd think they'd make "fluff" less aggrivating. There are other "features" that I found offputting, useless, or hindered my enjoyment. The entire "Ant Farm" base being a good example of something that serves absolutely no function.
Gameplay is simplified from the original X-Com quite a bit, sometimes with artificial limitations that don't make sense when looked at critically. My honest opinion about the game was that the AI cheated, or the game had no idea how to computate odds for various actions. Which is odd, given that the original X-Com; a very difficult game never felt like it cheated. It comes down to the difference in presentation: One soldier in X-Com means nothing. In Enemy Unknown it means everything. That one soldier can be the difference between failure and loss; making the AI "cheating" or being "cheap" incredibly frustrating.
Also has to be mentioned that 2K promised mod support prior to release, but then changed their tune once the game came out, including making the game "call home", which nukes mod support unless you run it offline or without autoupdate. Not a cool move. There's also the bugs, which last I played were quite bad and patch support was very slow.
Despite that, it's still a solid strategy game. In no way do I think it is anywhere near the original game, but it's a solid attempt. For me, there are enough issues and questionable design decisions that I don't know if I'll ever get the enjoyment I could have out of it. If you don't have any illusions for X-Com, or just want a solid modern strategy game, it's worth a look. I'd still recommend the original over the remake.

Risk of Rain is a passable addition to what I like to think of as the 'randomized indie' pantheon of games, joining titles like Binding of Isaac, Dungeons of Dredmor and Cave Story (the latter of which RoR totally feels like, down to the eerie music and exotic weaponry). The player progresses through a series of semi-randomly generated maps, mowing down all enemies in their path until they reach the titutar spaceship and escape the hazardous planet they have literally been dropped on.
Pros: Each playable character feels unique, which can be a tall order in games like this. The Bandit and Commando are similar, but one has AoE and the other has knockback; HAND-E and the Merc are similar, but one has evasion and the other has healing (and nothing is really like Acrid or CHEF at all). The in-game monsters are adorable and intimidating all in one., supplemented by a gloriously presented bestiary and item log. The items combo spectacularly and there is a real sense of satisfaction as you learn the various combos and modes that the game allows you to overlay onto your experience. Games can last as long or be as short as you like. CO-OP MODE. WITH CONTROLLERS. THAT ISN'T FINICKY TO SET UP.
Cons: After a few games, replaying the first levels are like pulling teeth, and it is totally possible to reach what I like to think of as the Point of Owning: for Drizzle difficulty, it's a row of items; for Rainstorm, it's two, and for Monsoon it's three rows. Once you've reached that point, the game becomes a little more trivial for the experienced platformer. The game is not even remotely balanced around Artifact of Glass or drones, even if both are insanely entertaining. Drones are also the usual culprit for screen tearing or lag, which this game has a ton of once you get a heap of items (the last possible time you'd want to lag after all that investment). The Steam achievements are very buggy and pointblank refuse to update; nor are they very reflective of the actual achievements the game offers.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes does what it says on the tin; it's a Lego game involving the plethora of characters from the Marvel universe. But what this tin doesnt include is all of the 'icky' features that have been introduced into this game.
Story:
Just like Lego Batman 2, LMSH has its own custom story to offer players as they scatter around manhattan to rescue Cosmic Bricks from the hands of various villians. Its a nice simple story that has been injected with a dose of unwanted seriousness that makes it very jarring. Sure its not a doom and gloom story but when you try to do that with quirky characters, it just doesnt work.
LMSH plays it very safe with the story. Dont expect to be moved by it.
Although in a game where you smash enemies into little Lego pieces WHO NEEDS A STORY?!
3/10
Visuals:
LMSH visuals are outstanding. Compared to the bland look of Lego Star Wars and the dark feeling in Lego Batman, LMSH really brings life back to this series. Metals glisten and reflect wonderfully, shadows are sharp and the animation...dont get me started on the animation, but to sum it up, it's bloody fantastic (the most fluid animation I have seen in a lego game by far.).
Such a breath of fresh air in the Lego series.
5/5
Gameplay:
LMSH plays like every other Lego game
-one button to hit
-one button to jump
-one button to switch character
-one button for a special move
Plain and simple and there's nothing wrong with that. Each character has their own special ability (just like in Lego Batman 2) this ranges from Thors electricity to charge power supplies or Spidermans spider sense to reveal hidden objects to interact with. Flying is much more satisfying than Lego batman 2. Here you have one button to go up and one to go down, much better than the target system in the previous game.
Stud collection in this game is a LOT more forgiving than the previous games. In LMSH, if you rack up a combo you can collect times that amount...get it? Lemme break it down, if your character kills 5 guys in a row they get a 5x combo which allows every stud you collect to be 5x more value.
This didnt bother me as much as the secret red brick options...
The Lego Star Wars series is a perfect example of good red brick secrets, each one was unlocked that you could only get through a free play when you have got (nearly) all of the characters. In LMSH you have some already unlocked for you, the biggest annoyance being 'Score x2 ready to buy'.
This zapped all of the excitement out of having a second playthrough to find all those little secrets. It was like the game was holding my hand.
Fun aspects, nothing new at all, slightly repetitive
3/5
Combat:
*pssst* press X to hit guys.
Although two problems did bother me with the combat.  The first being instead of an optional ability to preform a special move on enemies, your character does it automatically..wethere you like it.or.not. I found that this ruined my gameplay slighty by being stopped mid fight and mid combo just to do a special move (although they are pretty cool)
The second problem being the life bar. In Lego star wars I feared for my character when it was up against multiple Stormtroopers or even 2 Droideka's but in this game I feel like hoards of enemies are just a nuisance due to only loosing a life one every 2 hits. It just makes the game very dumbed down compared to ints counterparts.
Simple Combat with some annoying factors
3/5

I love this game A LOT because:
1. Teamwork is key! Having other people watch my back is something pretty rare in games nowadays, but it's everywhere here.
2. The guns: every gun is suited and feels amazing when you use it. Whenever you get a kill, it feels like you got that kill and puts you in the mood. Another thing games don't really have!
3. Constant challenges and Weekly Outbreaks. If you ever get tired of regular survival (which I sometimes do), you can just challenge yourself on the Weekly Outbreak! So many rewards and its more fun now that they have added that!
4. Open community: Other communities of games can sometimes be incredibly toxic. However, the only toxic in this game is the Bloat (and that annoying crawler and Hans). There have been so many maps from the community added and published into the real game, as well as TONS of maps on the server list!
5. Whenever I check the comments myself, I used to see a lot of negative reviews about mainly two things: not keeping their promise (for having 3 bosses and a Martial Arts class when the game was published) and the connection to KF1. Personally, this is supposed to be a full-on upgrade from KF1 and I can't really see a giant corruption that they've done. If you want KF1, play KF1, not KF2. Their promise, I have noted, has been broken. We can't hide from facts. But recently, Tripwire has released a new boss: King Fleshpund. This shows that they are still working on that promise made from a long time ago and we have reason to not give up on them. Maybe the Martial Arts class will be released soon. Who knows?
6. Graphics! I love the graphics of this game. If you're too queasy, turn down the gore. There's an option for everyone here. I play on high since that really brings the feel of the game out. The graphics are AMAZING, case closed.
7. Classes and Perks: The Classes and Perks are so entertaining to have! You can go from a regular point-and-shoot Commando/Gunslinger, or you can specialize with melee, explosives, and a whole lot of varying classes. As for the Perks, you can tell they spent quite some time on it. The Tactical Reload is a whole different reload technique and tell me how much they put into balancing this game's little aspects as well as the big ones.
8. The wide variety of Zeds: Zeds are AMAZING in this game and no other game captures it as much as this one. You have  hard to hit Crawlers and HUGE Zeds like the Scrake and Fleshpound. Zeds are continuing to be added, like the Gorefiend and Quarter Pound, and I like the design and feel of both of them.
Overall, I give this game a 11/10 since it is AMAZING to play, with a friend or without. It doesn't even ask that much of your PC, taking up barely 3GB of RAM. This game is incredible and I don't think any other survival zombie game matches up to this one, all of them combined!

GTA: Vice City is probably the goofiest, yet most timeless entry in the GTA series. Bright colours, fast cars, nonsensical missions, funny characters, and great controls made sure that this game is still regarded by many as their favourite in the franchise.
Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is a strange one, even for GTA. The whole game is more or less an 18-hour parody of Miami Vice– a half-forgotten, enjoyably dumb action show of the 80s. Everything is colourful and neon bright, and practically every story mission, every character, every random dialogue is a parody of something (just listen to the two talk show radios; they are full of the weirdest things).
What makes it a masterpiece is that none of these are over the top. The storyline may be silly at some points, but the core of it is deadly serious: you play as a gangster who was sent to Vice City (Miami) to create a foothold for the Mafia drug business. The deal goes belly-up, but by the end of the game you somehow become the de facto crime lord of the city, either by buying or killing any opposition.
The missions that lead to this goal have great variety and design; almost none feel the same and everyone can find their favourites among them. To complete them, you have access to a wider variety of weapons and vehicles, which now include aircraft and motorcycles. Travelling around is quite easy and fun now.
Many old-school game elements like bomb shops and the top-down camera were removed, but they are rarely missed with such improvements as purchasable assets, which all can be turned into a money-making machine after you complete their associated tasks. Although you still cannot spend that money on anything but more assets and weapons.
These smaller and larger touches not only made Vice City a great game, but also probably the most characteristic and memorable one in the GTA franchise, earning it a permanent spot in many of the players’ hearts.

Lego Marvel Superheroes was my dream come true lego game. I always wished that there were a lego game about Lord of The Rings and a Marvel lego game after playing Lego Star Wars, because I really liked the relaxed and easy-to-access gameplay style. And then, multiple Lego games later, including Lord of The Rings, it is finally here. After multiple iterations, has the gameplay changed enough to justify the purchase?
Let's start with the controls. This is my first time playing a Lego game on a keyboard(I do not own a gamepad, sadface). The Lego franchise was definently made for controllers, which I definently noted playing this game. The default controls for moving and doing actions worked fine on a keyboard. My only problems with moving were with the flying in the free-roam section. The flyinf races were just plain annoying to do and caused lots of frustration. I accidentaly kept dropping out of the flying mode while trying to adjust my flight course. But the biggest problem with the controls were the camera controls. The default camera controls were really awkward to use, especially while fighting. I pretty much had to stop either moving or fighting to adjust my camera. This problem is resolved by using a controller, so it's not that big of a deal, but it's still not nice.
The gameplay is the same as in the previous Lego games. You control multiple characters do solve light puzzles and fight goons and villains. Which there is alot. I mean a lot, since there is a 100+ characters to play as. Many of the characters have special abilities to solve puzzles, such as Iron Mans rockets to blow up silver legos, Spider-Mans spider-sense to find hidden stuff and the list goes on. The game captures the feel of the characters through different animations and abilities, which is awesome. Mr. Fantastics animations are a definite plus. This game also includes the new Big-Figs, which include Hulk, Juggernaut, The Thing etc. They have their own things only they can do, which is indicated by green handles. They are a nice inclusion, and fit nicely to the regular sized figures.
The game ofcourse has a ton of collectibles, which are fun to collect. You could say it's addictive. Those are going to take most of your time, since the campaign isn't all that long if you turbo through that, like I did.
In the end, the game is lots of fun to play. I didn't notice any bugs or glitches, which I cannot say for the previous lego game, Lord of The Rings. Experienced a lot of bugs with that game, so it was nice to have a smooth experience with this game. The game doesn't require that much to run smoothly, so pretty much everyone can play this excellent game. It is just pure fun.
The game is really solid, and you should buy it, especially if you like Lego games, or the Marvel license.
PS. This is my first review ever, so apologies if there is any rambling or repetition, for I wrote off the top of my head. Thank you for reading :)

Shadowrun for me is filled with fond memories of tabletop gaming, and lazy weekends with people too clever by half for their own good. Thankfullly, that core is there, and the story they bundle with it is solid. The problem however, lies with the overall brevity of the content given. There are remarkable storytellers out there who have written, and continue to write stories in the setting, [Do browse the UGC for the game!] but the package as a whole for the average gamer may be a little underwhelming.
Mechanically, the pieces are functional, and the experience in terms of actual gameplay is solid enough, but the pace of action and the lack of diversity in its approach may not seem the divine ambrosia to all. X-Com would be a fair parallel to make for the way the gameplay unfolds in action sequences.
Character development allows for specilization, and divesification both, but can feel stiflingly slow compared to the glut of typical loot-and-shoot games. For players who like the idea of being able to poke a few buttons thoughtlessly, toss another point into "strength" and move on to the next fight, the system may prove unsatisfying. For players who constantly look at old saves and think "What if I tried it with _____ build?" the depth of variety allowed is a welcome change of pace.
Graphically, there is a sense of "days gone by", I personally found myself filled with nostalgia for the classics. The atmosphere is there, in all its dirty, decayed charm, and the experience as a whole is such that no single part of the presentation is a jarring disconnect from the rest.
At its core, it holds true to the experiences I remember as a tabletop gamer. I enjoyed and continue to enjoy it and do not regret the purchase.

My wall of text:
At first Killing Floor 2 seems superior to it's predecessor in every way. But, after you spend some time with it, you can notice that it still loses to original game in some ways. It doesn't mean that KF 2 is worse than KF, no, actually, for me, it's opposite. And when you launch it for the first time after playing original Killing Floor, sequel looks incredible. It's beautiful and everything has that "Umph!" that just makes it feel right.
Aside from new characters you have your classic characters like Mr Foster or Classic Masterson. But this time you can customize them. Good stuff, right? Well, if you are willing to pay 2,49$ to get yourself a key to open some weird crate or "decode an USB" - it sure is. I never liked systems like this, but if it keeps game going - whatever. Still, RNGesus is everywhere and in my opinion - it's pretty bad. Of course, you can get a random skin/cosmetic for free, after you finish an operation or 2, but so far I only got 2 common AA-12 skins and 4 Bandanas. So yeah, bring out your dosh or pray to RNGesus and grind your♥♥♥♥♥off. Some people might say that cosmetics do not matter, but I can't agree with them on that, simply because these still affect you in some way, for example - these items affect your overall enjoyment of the game.
Now that we're done with CS:GO stuff, let's move to guns themselves. Guns look, sound and feel
! Each weapon, aside from starting pistol, looks powerful and usually, get's it's job done. But! There are simply not enough weapons. And because weapons are linked to Perks(classes), it affects gameplay greatly. Take Support Perk(guy that provides team with ammo, locks up doors and uses shotguns), for example. You start the game with a SG-500 pump action shotgun, you kill stuff, get through waves, you buy yourself a Double-barreled Boomstick. You kill even more stuff and you have to decide - you can buy yourself a M4 shotgun, OR you can skip it, save the money, and buy AA-12. No matter what you choose, during last waves you will probably have Double-barreled Boomstick, AA-12 and something else, if your carrying capacity allows. There is simply no reason to NOT get yourself an AA-12, aside from personal preferences. Also, I just listed all of the support weapons in the game. Yep. 4 shotguns. That's it. At first it doesn't sound so bad - straight-forward upgrade of your main weapon. But then you get through 50 games with the same setup and it just feels boring. Of course, you can switch Perks and all that, but that doesn't change anything. Because most Perks have same issue. There are simply no "sidegrades" for them, only direct upgrades(in terms of weaponry). And as you level up, it get's harder and harder not to notice that.
Perks themselves are a little bit different from the ones that were presented in the original game. Sharpshooter doesn't use pistols anymore. Gunslinger does. There are also new perks, Gunslinger, like I already said, is the perk that uses pistols, mostly akimbo pistols. SWAT - SMG perk with some defensive and offensive abilities. And Survivalist - Jack of all trades, that is not released at the moment of me writing this review. Leveling up is not as grindy as it was before. Each five levels you can pick 1 skill out of 2, that will sometimes greatly affect your playstyle - that system is not as straightforward, as it sounds. You have to decide between dealing damage or being able to withstand more damage, carrying more ammo/having larger clip capacity, or being able to reload Perk weapons faster. However, you can change your skills in-between waves, so don't worry about reading guides on how to not screw your character. I, myself, like that system, but some Perks feel much weaker than others to me. But that's probably my own issue, I just have to "git gud". And I am also sulking over Gunslinger and Sharpshooter not being as easy to play as, as before.
Killing Floor 2 does a much better job at being truly difficult, compared to the original game. Of course, bullet-spongy Zeds have their charm, but to me, it was always just a big pile of bs. Killing Floor 2 makes enemies faster, deadlier and smarter with each difficulty step up. On normal enemies just rush at you, making it easy to kill them off or just run past them. On hard difficulty enemies are a bit faster and deal more damage, but still are pretty easy to deal with. But on Suicidal you will notice how movement patterns of enemies change. Alpha Clots will buff and speed up weaker zeds around them, while rushing at you, jumping over obstructions. Slashers will dodge-roll your shots, getting closer and closer to you, before unleashing powerful attacks. Crawlers will spread around you, move out of your line of fire when you aim at them, or even when you turn on your flashlight. Gorefasts, Bloats(after Bloat explodes it will leave acid mines on the ground - walk over it and you know what's going to happen), Scrakes and Fleshpounds use their metallic weapons to protect their heads. Husks use their flame cannons as flamethrowers that melt both your armor and health at close range. They can also go full kamikaze at low health, running up to you, and exploding in blazing inferno. And Stalkers - those are the worst. Not only they move extremely fast, they also dodge your attacks constantly and appear from your left or right, even though second ago they were right in front of you. They jump and spin during their attacks, sometimes making it hard to hit them with anything, unless it's a giant hammer, shotgun or a grenade launcher. There are currently 2 bosses - good ol' Patriarch(not that different from one in the original game) and Dr. Hans Volter. Bosses, however, do not change as much, considering the difficulty settings. Just like in the original game, their health scales with the amount of players. Aside from that - they are preatty easy to deal with.
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is a great game. I couldn't enjoy it to it's fullest, because none of my friends have it and I had to play alone or with randoms. But even so, I like that game and consider it to be a great sequel to it's predecessor.

Dead Space is a horror survival game made by the company Visceral. You play as a engineer named Isaac Clarke that goes out to a planet cracking space vessel, The Ishimura,  in search of his girlfriend named Nicole. Obviously though, once you land on the ship, you learn things aren't too nice on the Ishimura.
While the game itself isn't too scary, what will get to you is the atmosphere. You'll feel like you are trapped on a space mining ship out in the middle of nowhere. You'll slowly creep around each corner, waiting for the next enemy to attack you.  Isaac himself, while he doesn't talk, still feels incredibly human. You can tell through his "diary" that he gets scared, worried, and angry.
Overall, this game is definately a buy. Never has being trapped in outer space ever been this fun.
Definately check out the sequel for this game if you are a fan, too.
Rest in peace, Visceral.

One of the best turn-based strategy games I've ever played. It's like Risk with more layers of complexity, but it's surprisingly intuitive once you start playing. You basically start as cavemen, worried about a few measly tiles of land, and by the end you're managing a modern/semi-futuristic, continent-spanning empire. You can even invest in archeology and dig up relics from ancient battles fought by those very same cavemen you started with! It can get pretty complex at times, but that's a positive thing for this kind of game, and makes for a very rich and unique experience every time.
The main thing for a new Civ player to keep in mind is that, although there are a variety of mechanics to utilize and to micromanage, you don't actually need to use everything all the time. Think of it like a tool box. You don't need every tool for every job. It's good to get a general understanding of it all over time, but it's not the end of the world if you don't... or maybe it is! (:P)
There are 5 victory conditions in the game: Domination, Science, Cultural, Diplomatic, and Time (score). You only need to pursue 1, but each relies on the others to a variable extent, and (while it's not an explicit victory path) religion plays a pretty big role as well. The diversity of influential mechanics in the game makes every decision feel important. Sure, you can decide early on that you're going to plow through a domination victory, but you're going to need science to earn the tech you need to gain an advantage on the battlefield. You're going to need culture to maintain order in all of your conquered lands. You're going to want to practice some level of diplomacy to prevent the entire planet from banning together to block your every move. You're also going to want to make decisions in a timely manner as well, because sometimes 1 turn can change the course of the game.
Each victory condition is worth talking about at length, but the way war is handled in the game is something that stands out to me the most. War and conquest is a perfectly viable and satisfying path to victory (XCOM Units and Giant Death Robots, y'all!), but, unlike most games, completely obliterating rival nations can have a game-changing negative impact. That makes war a more strategic, tactical, and political affair. You can still defeat your adversaries without committing genocide, and that's often the better option sometimes. Heck, I've even gone to war with other nations just to liberate conquered cities and revive nations that were previously wiped off the map. Seems counter intuitive at a glance, but restoring balance and leveling the playing field was my best option to achieve the victory types I was going for - Science/diplomatic!
Which brings me to my last point, the choices you have are not illusions. Each victory path is totally viable and sustainable, and the shift of power and influence is a very interesting thing to observe and navigate over time. The way different mechanics interact and influence the game makes for a genuinely unique experience every time. As the game goes on, you start to think very carefully about the impact of every decision. By the time the game has ended, you can't help but feel a connection to the nation you built, and it's sort of bittersweet to say goodbye.

None of it is game-breaking, or even annoying though, I just feel like after all the time put into it, they could have sanded down those rough edges a bit before releasing the final DLC. There's alot of dislike in Enemy Unknown, It's painfully unforgiving, glitchy, infuriating and perhaps a bit too refined.
I can't even begin to count the amount of times iv'e been shot through a wall or 2, by an enemy that had no line of sight on me. Or fighting 1 alien and having another 3 or 4 mobs just appear somewhere they 'logically' shouldnt (such as behind you in a room with only 1 door) And of course the good old 99% hit chance and the soldier misses by an entire postcode.
Yes XCOM can be so infuriating at times that it feels as though the game really is against you, to the extent that it openly laughs in the face of your plans and attempts to break you, by bending it's own rules to screw you over.
But make no mistake, XCOM:EU is a fantastic game and it's flaws are outweighed by all the positives. It's highly addictive, hours can be wasted away taking on the alien menace without even knowing it, you'll be fighting across the globe in a variety of (generic) Locations, such as forests, city streets, motorways and even alien ships, there's alot of places you'll be going and the chances are you'll need a 2nd playthrough to see them all.
When you start teching up, getting new weapons and armour you can't help but get dragged into it all and you'll find yourself  getting attached to your most prized assets ... i mean soldiers.  You watch as you guide them through the world as a lowlife star trek redshirt who couldnt even hit the side of a barn from 1 meter away, right the way up to chuck norris tier where they can shoot the wings off a fly half a mile away (slight exagerations may be included).
The tactics and planning are very intricate, deciding which units to take with you on a mission alone can take ages, do you take a rookie sniper because your best sniper is in sick bay, or do you take another experienced assault and sacrafice your ranged fighting.
On the battlefild it can take 30 seconds minimum to decdie if a 45% chance to hit is enough to take the risk or weither you just sit in overwatch and hope some fool runs into your sights, yes it's safe to say you calculate each and every single move and all the possible outcomes to the point you are scared to do anything. When it goes right you're on top of the world, but when it goes south, thats where you get the true XCOM experience, and being able to pull the cat out of the bag when the situation is beyond dire leaves you feeling like a god.
EU is not for everyone, being a turned base strategy things will likely move too slow for many people to enjoy. But if you show even a passing interest then i'd say it's worth a punt.

Dead Space is a sci-fi, survival horror game that happens to be one of the best and my personal favorite in this ganre. You start on a small ship that's on a repair mission, after reciving a distress call from the USG Ishimura(a giant Planet Cracker-class vessel) and you play as engineer Isaac Clarke who has volunteered for this mission to find his girlfriend that happens to be on the mentioned ship. When all comunications on the ship are blackout, it becomes obvious something is very wrong. Isaac finds himself in a living nightmare where he has to use every tool he can get his hands on to survive.Most of the weapons in the game are actually mining/industrial tools and even Isaac suits is an engineer one that's definetly not designed to protect him against what he finds on the ship, yet it does the job. And so starts the story of the first Dead Space game.
The story is no masterpiace but it's engaging.The ambient sounds can and most likely will give you chills and yes THEY ARE AWESOME! The atmosphere is truely great and will get under your skin. The game is extremly violent and the "action" is fast paced and tense. There is a great options of using difrent tools and objects to more efficiently deal with your enemies. Taking a walk on the lonely coridors and halls(if you don't count the encounters with the necromorphs willing to decapitate your head at any given moment) of the once lively Ishimura will be a experience worth your time.
Pros:
-Great atmosphere , sounds , decent graphics(it's an older game) , engaging story
-Cool and minimalistic HUD, your health indicator is shown on the back of your suit and so on.
-Tense, violent and scary
-Rewarding upgrade system
-Enemy design
Cons:
-Mostly port related
vertical sync makes the game run at 30 fps and the mouse lag becomes a pain
anti aliasing is actually non existant
-The objectives given by Isaac surviving crew makes you feel like an errand boy
Tips:
Rule 1-If it doesn't look human - shoot it
Rule 2-If it looks dead - shoot it to make sure
Rule 3-If it looks human but it has mutated beyond reason - shoot it
Rule 4-Dafuq is this ? - SHOOT IT , empty your ammo on it
Should you buy this game in 2017 ? YES!

My wall of text:
At first Killing Floor 2 seems superior to it's predecessor in every way. But, after you spend some time with it, you can notice that it still loses to original game in some ways. It doesn't mean that KF 2 is worse than KF, no, actually, for me, it's opposite. And when you launch it for the first time after playing original Killing Floor, sequel looks incredible. It's beautiful and everything has that "Umph!" that just makes it feel right.
Aside from new characters you have your classic characters like Mr Foster or Classic Masterson. But this time you can customize them. Good stuff, right? Well, if you are willing to pay 2,49$ to get yourself a key to open some weird crate or "decode an USB" - it sure is. I never liked systems like this, but if it keeps game going - whatever. Still, RNGesus is everywhere and in my opinion - it's pretty bad. Of course, you can get a random skin/cosmetic for free, after you finish an operation or 2, but so far I only got 2 common AA-12 skins and 4 Bandanas. So yeah, bring out your dosh or pray to RNGesus and grind your♥♥♥♥♥off. Some people might say that cosmetics do not matter, but I can't agree with them on that, simply because these still affect you in some way, for example - these items affect your overall enjoyment of the game.
Now that we're done with CS:GO stuff, let's move to guns themselves. Guns look, sound and feel
! Each weapon, aside from starting pistol, looks powerful and usually, get's it's job done. But! There are simply not enough weapons. And because weapons are linked to Perks(classes), it affects gameplay greatly. Take Support Perk(guy that provides team with ammo, locks up doors and uses shotguns), for example. You start the game with a SG-500 pump action shotgun, you kill stuff, get through waves, you buy yourself a Double-barreled Boomstick. You kill even more stuff and you have to decide - you can buy yourself a M4 shotgun, OR you can skip it, save the money, and buy AA-12. No matter what you choose, during last waves you will probably have Double-barreled Boomstick, AA-12 and something else, if your carrying capacity allows. There is simply no reason to NOT get yourself an AA-12, aside from personal preferences. Also, I just listed all of the support weapons in the game. Yep. 4 shotguns. That's it. At first it doesn't sound so bad - straight-forward upgrade of your main weapon. But then you get through 50 games with the same setup and it just feels boring. Of course, you can switch Perks and all that, but that doesn't change anything. Because most Perks have same issue. There are simply no "sidegrades" for them, only direct upgrades(in terms of weaponry). And as you level up, it get's harder and harder not to notice that.
Perks themselves are a little bit different from the ones that were presented in the original game. Sharpshooter doesn't use pistols anymore. Gunslinger does. There are also new perks, Gunslinger, like I already said, is the perk that uses pistols, mostly akimbo pistols. SWAT - SMG perk with some defensive and offensive abilities. And Survivalist - Jack of all trades, that is not released at the moment of me writing this review. Leveling up is not as grindy as it was before. Each five levels you can pick 1 skill out of 2, that will sometimes greatly affect your playstyle - that system is not as straightforward, as it sounds. You have to decide between dealing damage or being able to withstand more damage, carrying more ammo/having larger clip capacity, or being able to reload Perk weapons faster. However, you can change your skills in-between waves, so don't worry about reading guides on how to not screw your character. I, myself, like that system, but some Perks feel much weaker than others to me. But that's probably my own issue, I just have to "git gud". And I am also sulking over Gunslinger and Sharpshooter not being as easy to play as, as before.
Killing Floor 2 does a much better job at being truly difficult, compared to the original game. Of course, bullet-spongy Zeds have their charm, but to me, it was always just a big pile of bs. Killing Floor 2 makes enemies faster, deadlier and smarter with each difficulty step up. On normal enemies just rush at you, making it easy to kill them off or just run past them. On hard difficulty enemies are a bit faster and deal more damage, but still are pretty easy to deal with. But on Suicidal you will notice how movement patterns of enemies change. Alpha Clots will buff and speed up weaker zeds around them, while rushing at you, jumping over obstructions. Slashers will dodge-roll your shots, getting closer and closer to you, before unleashing powerful attacks. Crawlers will spread around you, move out of your line of fire when you aim at them, or even when you turn on your flashlight. Gorefasts, Bloats(after Bloat explodes it will leave acid mines on the ground - walk over it and you know what's going to happen), Scrakes and Fleshpounds use their metallic weapons to protect their heads. Husks use their flame cannons as flamethrowers that melt both your armor and health at close range. They can also go full kamikaze at low health, running up to you, and exploding in blazing inferno. And Stalkers - those are the worst. Not only they move extremely fast, they also dodge your attacks constantly and appear from your left or right, even though second ago they were right in front of you. They jump and spin during their attacks, sometimes making it hard to hit them with anything, unless it's a giant hammer, shotgun or a grenade launcher. There are currently 2 bosses - good ol' Patriarch(not that different from one in the original game) and Dr. Hans Volter. Bosses, however, do not change as much, considering the difficulty settings. Just like in the original game, their health scales with the amount of players. Aside from that - they are preatty easy to deal with.
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is a great game. I couldn't enjoy it to it's fullest, because none of my friends have it and I had to play alone or with randoms. But even so, I like that game and consider it to be a great sequel to it's predecessor.

There's alot of dislike in Enemy Unknown, It's painfully unforgiving, glitchy, infuriating and perhaps a bit too refined.
I can't even begin to count the amount of times iv'e been shot through a wall or 2, by an enemy that had no line of sight on me. Or fighting 1 alien and having another 3 or 4 mobs just appear somewhere they 'logically' shouldnt (such as behind you in a room with only 1 door) And of course the good old 99% hit chance and the soldier misses by an entire postcode.
Yes XCOM can be so infuriating at times that it feels as though the game really is against you, to the extent that it openly laughs in the face of your plans and attempts to break you, by bending it's own rules to screw you over.
But make no mistake, XCOM:EU is a fantastic game and it's flaws are outweighed by all the positives. It's highly addictive, hours can be wasted away taking on the alien menace without even knowing it, you'll be fighting across the globe in a variety of (generic) Locations, such as forests, city streets, motorways and even alien ships, there's alot of places you'll be going and the chances are you'll need a 2nd playthrough to see them all.
When you start teching up, getting new weapons and armour you can't help but get dragged into it all and you'll find yourself  getting attached to your most prized assets ... i mean soldiers.  You watch as you guide them through the world as a lowlife star trek redshirt who couldnt even hit the side of a barn from 1 meter away, right the way up to chuck norris tier where they can shoot the wings off a fly half a mile away (slight exagerations may be included).
The tactics and planning are very intricate, deciding which units to take with you on a mission alone can take ages, do you take a rookie sniper because your best sniper is in sick bay, or do you take another experienced assault and sacrafice your ranged fighting.
On the battlefild it can take 30 seconds minimum to decdie if a 45% chance to hit is enough to take the risk or weither you just sit in overwatch and hope some fool runs into your sights, yes it's safe to say you calculate each and every single move and all the possible outcomes to the point you are scared to do anything. When it goes right you're on top of the world, but when it goes south, thats where you get the true XCOM experience, and being able to pull the cat out of the bag when the situation is beyond dire leaves you feeling like a god.
EU is not for everyone, being a turned base strategy things will likely move too slow for many people to enjoy. But if you show even a passing interest then i'd say it's worth a punt.

Despite a really poor launch, this game has come a long way and is really well optimized now. Running at 3440x1440 at a steady 60 FPS with all settings maxed out and the nVidia special effects - graphics card is a single 980 TI.
This game's graphics are effin' bonkers. I wish I had a more powerful GPU so I could see this game at 4K at a steady framerate (that being above 50 FPS for me). The 980TI can manage about 30 FPS at 4K, but dips frequently to 23-24 FPS during action, so I've decided to stay away from that.
Games coming out NOW and after AK was released don't look as good as this game. Witcher 3 gives it a run for its money, but this game easily beats games like RotR, DXMD and DOOM in the grapics department. Some of the generic enemy NPC textures can look a little janky when zoomed in super close and then texture pops in (and looks better, gotta give it that).
Animation is among the best in the industry. Seriously. The animation, from flying, to landing, to fighting, to getting into your car, to ejecting out and into the air, grappling to a rooftop and leap-of-faith dive-bombing on the other side -- everything is animation to look natural and seemless. There are very few awkward animations in AK, and that's when you have an NPC in an awkard position in a fight (in a corner against a texture that's not just a plain wall - like a small generator on the wall) and you execute a takedown, sometimes it is apparent but it happens rarely.
Combat is still great. If you love the freeflow combat that Prince of Persia started and that Arkham mastered, this is what you're gonna get. Takedowns are as brutal as ever.
Fear Multi-Takedowns are a blast and something you'll actively look for once you understand how to use it. It makes you effin' badass and looks incredibly well-animated.
Music is top notch.
Story is good too. If you're a Batman fan, some things will be super apparent to you from the start. But other twists, especially the main one, is great and welcomed.
I don't know why everyone hated the Batmobile. I thought it was fun and mixed things up.
Also, motion blur is the biggest drain on your system resources. It nearly halved my FPS when executing certain actions. I highly suggest your turn it off immediately.

The transition of survival horror took the meaning of horror in a different direction, wIth Resident Evil 4, we moved from the overall feeling of dread and suspense in the previous titles, to a more generic jump-scare type of horror (with maybe its exception of regenerators). Resident evil 4 was by no means a horror masterpiece, but it was campy and fun, and its gameplay was fantastically implemented, with set pieces oozing from it's pores to thrill the player.
Dead space tried (and failed) in my opinion to bring back any of that tension. Instead we have a linear set of sequences filled with scripted jump scares from monsters overdesigned to look horrific.
There's only a few times of note worthy moments in this game. One in particular was when you enter a room full of dead bodies, and later the game loops around to this room, except now it is populated with a monster which can make monsters from corpses. I had never encountered this monster before I found this room the first time. I instinctively dismembered all of the corpses, and when I came back around it paid off, instead of a dozen monsters I only had to deal with one. That was a moment of rewarding the player for actually playing the game in a way a video game should be played, trusting the player to emergent decisions as opposed to leading them down set routes with set expectations of play. It did that moment once.
So much potential wasted as well. It would have been a lot better if it was more open, Metroidvania. It had the capacity to do that since we have the floor system. And the scripted jump scares could have been randomised or intellegently coded AI which could determine a best attack when the player is at their weakest.
In short, this series is overhyped garbage.
