I was disappointed in Shadowrun Returns.  I bought the title because I am a big fan of turn-based strategy games.  However, what I ended up getting was not everything I was hoping it would be.  But long story short, I'd still recommend the title, but only if the entire complete version cost you $7.50 or less.  (That includes the Dragonfall expansion, the music, etc.)  If I knew what I know now, I'd only pay $4.99 for Shadowrun Returns, complete edition.
That said, I would recommend the game only because it is what you will like in terms of turn-based stategy gaming.  I am sure there are better titles out there in this genre (I want to try out XCOM some day), so I will have to go looking for them.  But I dropped $11.97 for all the Shadowrun stuff when it went on sale.  I believe that I paid double what it was worth, sadly.
The things that frustrate the heck out of me regarding Shadowrun Returns are the following:
*  The melee animations are atrocious.  If you run up and swing your sword on an enemy, it will look slow and akward.  It truly makes me wonder if the developer tested this out or not - very poor presentation.
*  Get used to seeing the word "Missed" a lot.  After having played through the Seattle campaign ("Dead Man's Switch"), I came to learn that there are not enough Karma (experience) points to go around.  That means that you will need to specialize and forego any benefits outside your speciality.  For example, I wanted to have all the conversation options available to me, so I built up for Decking and Charisma.  But then I put into Quickness so that I could use a gun.  Long story short, the highest I think I needed Charisma and Intelligence/Decking was 5.  And even though I put a few more into them, I couldn't hit crap with my gun.  Worse is when you hire mercenaries and they can't hit bad guys, either.  It's like the developer wanted to make the ability to land hits on enemies a challenge, though it is very frustrating.
*  The music was an add-on purchase for me (part of an upgraded bundle).  I have to say, I was ripped off.  It should have been included for free.
*  Also, I ran into a few bugs in the Seattle campaign.  One of them was the inability to act in the Universal Brotherhood scene when we were trying to rescue Marie.  Some buttons could be clicked, but no one moved.  I had to reset before it locked up again (recalling the autosave).
*  One feature I would have loved would have been the ability to save my character from the Seattle campaign and then bring it over to the Berlin one.  Then I could keep leveling him up, so to speak.  But that is not available here.
*  Lastly, while not a super-huge deal, this is a text-intensive video game.  Basically, it plays like a graphic novel/comic book.  So the graphics and the music and the gameplay are really just supposed to lend to storyline.  I suppose everything does as intended.  But there are so many typos, especially towards the end of the campaign, that I was hoping the developer would find somebody in the studio to just sit down and remove them all.  Just polish the thing up.  But like I said, not a super-huge deal.  Just reminds me of the poor melee animations, which makes it seem like the developer did not care as much for this game as I, a paying customer, do.
So if you are up for reading a game, Shadowrun Returns is of that genre.  And believe me - you are going to read!  There are "pathways" in communication here: one decision you make in a conversation can lead to a different path in that conversation.  However, I have noticed that all the pathways really only lead to one end result nearly all of the time.  That is, it doesn't matter on what you click.  If you want to be a smart♥♥♥♥♥character or a polite one or whatever, there are sometimes options for each.  But these by and large do not affect the storyline hardly at all.  There may be a few exceptions, such as deciding the fate of an antagonist.  However, like I said, no matter what you choose, it is going down the same railroad.  Again, this is not a huge deal, especially since this is basically just an electronic comic book.  But just know what you are getting here.
As far as character customization goes, it is a bit limited.  The bigger problem is that you are probably not going to build a truly useful character.  If you specialize, then hope that your hired mercenaries will do their jobs.  Of course, that usually means that you don't need a Summoner, healer, or a multi-class guy.  (I did the whole campaign without anything but ranged attackers by my side.  At Decking level 5, I did all that Matrix stuff.  The only thing I missed out on were all the locked doors.)  But, really, if all you want to do is kill guys, that might be the better build.  (Beware of "Missed"!).
So to close, I simply restate that Shadowrun Returns is worth about $7.50 or less for the full, complete package.  The only benefit to it seems to be the ability to make your own "maps" (scenes) and build your own campaign.  However, this game does not seem to have a boatload of features, so you would probably just be making your own video game comic book, then - like writing your own graphic novel.  I don't know how fun that will be for you, but all I can say is that this entire game package is not worth very much money.  I will search better turn-based games, and I will regret having dropped so much cash on Shadowrun Returns.  Oh, and I will say that the developer's story is a creative one.

So, the Shadowrun world is entirely new to me.  I never played the SNES Shadowrun game, and I definitely didn't know until recently that Shadowrun started out as a Dungeon and Dragons style table top game in the late 80's/early 90's.  Only a few minutes into the game, I could tell that this is a well developed universe, one that could be better appreciated by those who have been involved in the Shadowrun lore for years.  Not to say I'm not impressed.  Like I said, I'm completely new to this world.  But that's what makes this game immediately addicting.  It has it's own world and immediately pulls you right into it.  Yes, you can feel like a foreigner at first, but not for long.  The game starts when you receive a message from an old friend, Sam Watts, who pre-informs you of his death through a video message which is sent to you upon his death.  Your mission is to investigate who killed him and find out who this "Ripper" character is.  As you investigate Sam Watts murder, you get pulled more and more into the underground world of Shadowrun, discovering more of the secrets of Sam Watts, as well as the other characters you meet.
For me, I enjoy a good RPG.  Typically, I have trouble getting into turn based RPGs anymore.  Despite that this game is turn based, there is a strategy element that gives it more depth.  You're not just attacking, healing, and casting magic.  You have to anticipate the movements of your enemies and use your surroundings to your advantage.  There is also a bit of a puzzle element, too, as you must search your surroundings and use items to get past certain areas.
Shadowrun is a nice blend of fantasy with cyberpunk.  I wish I could have emersed myself in this universe before, but I feel fortunate that I can experience it for the first time.  So even if you are not already familiar with Shadowrun, I suggest downloading this game.  It will definitely keep you hooked for hours.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown tries to revive the legendary XCOM series to it´s former glory and in some aspects it even succeeds. It's Cons lie mostly in limited economical and tactical options/behavior but it´s huge strengths are it´s charracter building, strategic and tactical decision making, Immersive cutscenes, events, music and story line. More on these below:
Pros:
+ Music, Voice acting, Immersion.
XCom Enemy Unknown really puts you in the shoes of the Commander. Your key personnel continously brief on important matters and give you comments on new tech, items and mission results. This is boosted by excellent music and cutscenes. One of the most rewarding things is seing the beginning of an alien interrogation knowing that you lost some men to get the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
+ Story Line
This game progresses quite clearly after certain completed missions, research and other key events.
+ Soldier progression
While it isn´t the same as in the old XCOM games. The progression of your soldiers has always been one of the key hooks in these games. To make it even better, all of your soldiers have their own looks & personalities. They throw ballsy comments which makes losing one your best even more (if you are playing in NoLoad mode as these games should be played).
+ Strategic Decisioning
Your choices really count. The losses you take in missions count. Losing a critical mission can hurt you in number of ways, the least of which is getting your best soldiers wiped. The path you take in research, engineering and base develoment count. Your starting continent counts.
+ Tactical skills and weapons
There are lots of AoE weapons like rocket launchers and grenades plus your soldiers skills that can make the difference between life and death. While many of them can only be used once, they are often worth it.
+ Replay value
Each run is different. Your soldiers are different. The events triggered won't be the same / they happen at different times. Mission rewards are different. Your starting continent can be changed (each continent has different bonuses).
Cons:
- Very limited number of Economical choices compared to older XCOM games
You can't really buy much in this game. Inventory management is dummed down and even the country income is not based on your results but only on how many countries you have under your satellite cover.
-Simplified tactical combat
You start with only 4 soldiers. In time you can get this to 6. This is a very low number when you are playing in a noload mode.  (In old X-Com this was around 14). Unless you have certain exp boosts on your soldiers, you can only shoot once per turn. With this in mind a lvl 1 soldier can't really anything usefull in the later game. Combat itself overemphasizes taking cover and flanking enemy cover. Enemies (and your soldiers) are practically free kills.
-No inventory management in tactical combat
our soldiers cannot pick items from fallen soldiers. Have one of your soldiers bleed to death while there is medkit on the ground next to him and you will feel what I mean. You simply can't pick up anything. For alien items this explain: They explode when the wielder dies, but you can't pick them up after you have stunned one either.
- Tactical combat intiations
Most important thing in this game is not to see enemies at the end of your. When you see an enemy, they get to move first. If this is followed by enemy turn, your enemy can move your entire sight radius and get some free kills before you can do anything. After you realize this and start avoiding late turn spotting, the game gets a lot easier and kinda boring. In addition to this you shouldn't trigger more than 1 set of enemies at a time. This is even more important than covering your flank, which makes it quite counter intuitive.
To Sum it Up:
To be honest, if you are looking for a same kind of tactical game as XCOM Apocalypse, XCOM Terror From the Deep or UFO Enemy Unknown, you will be disappointed in one way or another. While this game have some painfull cons, overall it really is a good game to say the least. With some tweaks it would be a great game. Easily worth one or two runs. I strongly recommend starting with normal difficulty and noload mode. It is challenging, but manageble even with no earlier experience.

The forth game in the Arkham series (and the third developed by Rocksteady) is one that is in serious danger of collapsing under the weight of franchise fatigue. Early impressions are that it’s business as usual – A dark, brooding, po-faced adventure where you play a man who dresses as a bat while driving a funny bat themed car. Never is this bizarre tonal contradiction more acute than when you are afflicted with fear gas – after dealing with the terrifying nightmarish journey through your conflicted subconscious you return to reality and you’re still a man dressed as a bat.
Let’s discuss the creaking, oiled leather clad elephant in the room before going any further – the PC port. On a 980ti at 1080p, with almost everything set to it’s highest I managed a mostly stable 60FPS on foot, and an uneven but playable framerate when driving. Turning on enhanced fog and debris brought the framerate crashing down, which puts it on par with most Nvidia specific features in games (hot garbage). So not fantastic, but a far cry from the car crash that the game was at launch.
Let’s also discuss the smaller, leotard wearing acrobat elephant in the room – the batmobile. This is the big selling point of the game, and it’s clear a lot of work has gone into this. The developers are obviously very proud of their creation, and it takes any excuse to pan leeringly over it’s admittedly impressive bodywork, focussing on it’s plates and gears and seemingly extraneous transforming knick-knacks. You’ll be using it a lot whether you like it or not. Virtually every section of the game has a mandatory car section wedged in there, and it is almost entirely to the games detriment. Driving around Gotham is fun in short bursts, though in all honesty grappling and gliding is both faster and typically more entertaining, as well as granting you a superior vantage point to spot the game’s generous helping of side quests.
Really, the bulk of Arkham Knight’s problems rest with the tank. You seem to spend half the game circle strafing enemy drones, and the tank combat never gets any more complex or entertaining. From the first battle, you’ve seen everything the tank has to offer. That half of the boss battles are also tank based just adds insult to injury – there’s nothing here that even approaches the creativity of the Freeze battle in City, a high point among a series rich in excellent set pieces.
The tank also stretches even videogame credulity to breaking point – ploughing into a thug at high speed jolts him (totally non lethally yo) out of the way, and hitting a person with a cannon capable of shredding steel seems to cause nothing more serious than unconsciousness (and presumably the odd shattered pelvis). That’s to say nothing of the unsettling realisation that I’m playing a millionaire using my wealth to hunt the poor and dispossessed – admittedly a problem that has plagued any modern day interpretation of Batman, but it’s at its most crass here.
It’s when the game is most like it’s predecessors that it’s at it’s best – the early portions of the game with Scarecrow are narrow and focussed, and the batmobile still novel enough to be entertaining. The trifecta of stealth, punching and puzzle solving is still engaging (though beginning to sag under the weight of feature creep), and the whole game is so polished you can see your chiselled, scowling face in it. Voice acting is impeccable as ever, though outside of the welcome return of Scarecrow the rogue’s gallery is limp – it was inevitable that by the third game we’d be resorting to repetition or second stringers (with the titular Arkham Knight himself being mostly an extended bum note).
The side quests, featuring more colourful B-Listers (including a welcome appearance by Man Bat) are almost universally more entertaining than the main story – the extended Riddler sidequest in
particular is a high point, though quite how race circuits feature into his battle of wits is not particularly clear. The challenges are however varied and often require you to at least partially engage your brain, more than can be said for the rest of the game. Sadly, some of the other sidequests are Ubisoft tier busywork – including the interminable Riddler trophy ticklist, an exercise in mind numbing masochism which is gallingly required for the true ending.
While this is a review of nothing but complaining, it’s worth noting that Arkham Knight is not a BAD game, not really – just one that is inferior to the games that preceded it, learning all the wrong lessons. Everything new falls flat, and when it sticks to what it knows it can’t help but feel a bit tired. I really need that middle ground rating curiously absent from steam, as this has got 3/5 written all over it – it feels like a cop out to say “If you want more Batman, you’ll enjoy this” but that’s really what it comes down to – more of the same, except the new parts that are a bit rubbish.

It took me a lot of time to have an opinion about this game. Because it's so confusing in the beginning that I lacked solid elements on which to build a judgement. Said judgement began to form halfway through, and never really deviated until the end.
The first thing that strikes about Antichamber is its very unique and distinct graphical personality. It's essentially a black-and-white cell-shaded world made of straight lines, with touches of primary colours here and there, a couple shades of grey, and (almost) no gradient. It sure doesn't look bad in screenshots, but it needs to be experienced rather than just seen to really appreciate it. The graphics are striking, and even though they barely vary throughout the game, Antichamber is short enough that it doesn't become a problem.
Going hand in hand with the unique look is the great soundtrack. I say soundtrack, but in truth there isn't any "song". It's more a collection of ambient soundscapes that blend seamlessly into each other as you navigate the mazes. It's beautiful but also unsettling because, in stark contrast with the cold and precide graphics, the sounds are very organic and often originate from real-life sounds like pigeons cooing, for example. There is a soundtrack CD/digital download (actually, there are two of them) on bandcamp, which I will probably buy at some point even though they are just static renditions of the organic/procedural in-game soundscapes.
So, unquestionably, Antichamber is a great place to explore. But Antichamber is not Proteus: It's a real game, with puzzles to solve. And this is where stuff start to disappoint somewhat.
Puzzles come in two varieties. The first kind involves finding your way in Antichamber's very personal take on geometry. This is not the kind of place where turning left four consecutive times will necessarily take you back to your starting point. Antichamber's space folds on itself in all kinds of intricate ways. Somehow, those puzzles are reminiscent of the parts in games like Dungeon Master (or Legend of Grimrock) where only a specific sequence of moves will let you advance and any other sequence would lead you in circles. And, if your memory of them is similar to mine, these were usually not the best parts. Of course, it's more diverse than that. Strictly speaking, many of the "strange geometry" puzzles involve completely different mechanisms, but the feeling is kind of the same. In essence, those puzzles are less about thinking your way through than about trying everything that crosses your mind.
The second variety involves cube manipulation. Early on you'll get some "gun" that will let you manipulate the small cubes that feature in many puzzles. Those are usually solved by filling some space with the cubes. Achieving this will often unlock doors and let you progress. There are different "guns" that will progressively allow you to manipulate cubes in new ways. These puzzles are much more logical in nature than the first kind. But they're not always well designed. Very frequently, I would solve them in way that felt inelegant. I thought I was using a glitch-like solution and that there must have been a more clever, satisfying way to solve them. Unfortunately, it appears that it isn't always the case: the game's official FAQ acknowledges that some solutions may feel "like a clever exploit of the mechanics" or "like a slow brute force way of doing things".
Antichamber is very non-linear. Not just geometrically, but also in temrs of progressions. You have access to a vast array of unsolved puzzles at all times. The positive consequence is that there wasn't a single moment when I felt completely stuck. Every time I fired the game, however briefly, I would at least solve a couple of puzzles. This is good, and all the better because Antichamber can be approached as a pick-up-and-play experience if one feels like it: It loads lightning-fast and constantly saves your progress.
There is a flipside to this non-linearity: you also have access to many puzzles which you cannot solve because you don't have the right gun. And you have no way of distinguishing them from those you can solve. Another collateral damage of non-linearity is that many times, I solved a difficult puzzle only to find myself at a place I had already reached through another puzzle. It's hard to find a great sense of accomplishment in those cases.
One last grief: NOT EVERYONE HAS A QWERTY KEYBOARD!!! I don't want to change my Windows keyboard settings every time I play a game just because my A and W keys are not where you think they are! Let the user customize the controls.
Overall, I would still recommend Antichamber because it's a unique experience. It's also a beautiful one. The puzzles do get in the way, but because they are not that difficult (despite first appearances)and because Antichamber is short, it's bearable. Just don't expect that the puzzle design will come anywhere near Portal-quality and you should be fine.

For what it's worth, it's not much of a horror game. It's one of those adventure shooters that has ugly enemies. Whenever you pass by vents or see necromorph corpses that hasn't been disfigured, you'll already know that they're just there for jump scares. I will give points for the creepy atmosphere and all the bloody, organic rooms will give you chills. Bosses are also great, even though there's only three. The first one you encounter will let you use one of the game's mechanics of zero gravity jumps to dodge tentacles which makes you seem VERY cool and badass. The second one, I didn't enjoy much since I suck at aiming and then there's the gun overheating. The third and last one was actually a let-down compared the first one, which you'd expected it to be more of an overkill, slightly surviving with a slither of HP. The only thing good that came out of the last boss was how it picked you up and you were forced to use inverted controls to make you panic than you usually would. Then there's the storyline. I feel the twists were from an M. Night Shyamalan movie. You can already foreshadow what'll happen and the twists wouldn't really amuse you. It'll just give you sense of saying, "Welp, more work to do.". Character developement are pretty bad. All you know about the protagonist is that he's here on an adventure to find his girlfriend and slowly becoming loopy while not knowing about it. Really, the only thing that comes out of the storyline is the lore and backstory and most people who comes to shooters just want to use their itchy trigger-fingers and kill everything on sight. All-in-all, this game is just a generic shooter from Point A to Point B. It's a great shooter from its time I'll agree to that; however, it's not a scary game if you're wanting to buy this game for that sole purpose.

This game came as a refreshing suprise after the countless zombie games that have been saturating the market of late. Many would write this game off as "farcry 3 with zombies, mirrors edge with zombies or dead island with parkour" and to be honest, it is all of them, the best parts of all of them to be specific.
Story
I need to stress that I haven't finished the game's main story at the tiem of this review, but I can say that from what I've played so far (20% through the main quest) the story hold up quite well, and is significantly better than their previous installment (dead island for those who live under a rock). The characters are well written, although none of them seemed to be overly interesting (the nieve kid, the evil warlord businessman, the runner). The smaller side quests are where the game shines, as these smaller quests allow for simple stories to keep the action flowing, and the sheer quantity of them will keep you occupied for hours. Random encounters also make an appearance quite oftain, drawing you off the path to your mission to stop some poor guy from getting his ribs kicked in by some gang, or a supply drop where the quicker you get to it, the more stuff you receive. This game kept me so occupied with doing side quests and random encounters, that I've hardly dented the main quest, and in my opinion, that is the formula for a good open world game.
Graphics
The graphics in this game really take advantage of the new generation console's hardware (which means all us PC users get to enjoy better looking cross platform games) Zombies look quite rotten and pale, more detailed facial animations and dynamic skin textures (facial wrinkles) give human and zombie's faces a little more life (and make graphics nuts like me that little bit happier) Skin has a nice soft shader that makes it actually look like skin for a change, water and rain look brilliant (although the ocean has some strange things happen now and then because of its reflection shader, not a massive problem though). The dismemberment system is a lot more detailed than what they had in dead island, although the skin degregation system is no longer present (hitting things with blunt weapons would slowly wear away the skin on zombies in dead island) but has been replaces with a larger number of ways to slice and dice zombies into chunky kibbles. Day and night now take full advantage of an amazing lighting system, throwing shadows from you and your co-op partner's flashlight, car fires, UV light from safehouses, etc. I could probably go on and on about this all day, but I think you get the idea, the game is really pretty.
Gameplay
The game has a very similar style of melee combat to that of dead island (hit them with weapons, dismember, explode heads, degrading weapons, etc) although the breaking of limbs is now absent (there is an ability to break their legs though). Killing zombies is quite satisfying, as you craft new weapons to slice and blugeon them to death. Firearms work the way they're meant to (looking at you dead island) thanks to better feeling controls, but still feel a little weightless due to a lack of visual swey when you look around (more of a graphics issue than a gameplay one). Climbing works a lot like in mirrors edge and it works well, anything you can grab onto, your character will grab onto (except for some things like the outside of a ladder cade, etc). When you begin climbing can be a bit cumbersome due to the fact you need to hold the jump button to grab on, but as time goes on and you learn you become a lot better at this. Optional climbing puzzles appear a lot during the game, but are usually hidden or just part of the sandbox (there's been a few times I've jumped on something to get away from zombies to find a massive climbing puzzle to the top of a building). The different enemy types keep the player on their toes, from ranged enemies to sprinting ones who are as nimble as the player (and will occasionally dodge your attacks!) to human enemies that can block, dodge and occasionally wield firearms (which will attract running zombies when fired). The golden nugget of this game would be the day/night cycle though, which adds an increased challenge to the player, bringing out significantly harder enemies who are stronger, faster and tougher than the player. This is where the game becomes more about stealth than combat, as allerting one of these creatures will alert them all causing a GTA5-like escape to evade their sight until you lose heat. UV light can be used to stun these enemies for a short time, but they will eventually come at you again. Co-operating play is also present, allowing you to play the whole thing with your friends (been having a blast with this). The 'be the zombie' gamemode I believe is where the game falls a little flat. At this point in the game, with so many people playing, you will essentially get invaded every night constantly for the entire night, which will disable all your missions and force you to destroy several hunter nests while the player zombie hunts you. This round is entertaining for what it's worth, but I believe the inability to complete missions at night while still allowing the possibility to be invaded was a poor choice (this is completely my opinion though)
Conclusion
Overall this game suprised me with it's above average story, brilliant graphics, and amazing gameplay. I would highly reccommend it to anyone who is interested in a zombie game that did something new and better for a change.

Risk of Rain is a inde game that you need to understand before going into it. It is esentally a 2D shooter with a RPG leveling up system and power ups you have to buy while on the feild. The catch, you lose EVERYTHING when you die. All powerups, cash, experience, nothing is saved. So the game goes from this crazy shooter into a battle for your life.
Now to many, this would be a instant turn off. What's the point of playing the game if your progress means nothing? Well, the way I see it, this game is a learning experience. You see, when you start, the game literally tells you nothing. power ups arn't labed and monsters just come at you. You don't know what is what. But, after each death, you learn a little more. You find out what powerups give you. You observer monsters attack patterns. You start to realise how to use wepons to better suit survival. And everytime you go through the game, you start to get better and faster. Soon enough, you'll reach the teleporter and be able to expand to the next area and continue to learn.
What makes this game great is how it uses these elements to make the player better and advance more and more every time you start over. If these elements arn't for you, don't buy this game. You'll have a miserable time. But, if you're one seeking adventure and learn from the unkown, then you'll get more bang for your buck.

So I wouldn't quite call myself a horror game enthusiast, but I certainly do enjoy the rush you get when playing games with some quite chilling and terrifying situations. Of all the scary games I have played, Dead Space still stands out in my mind.
500 years in the future, you find yourself in the shoes of everyman engineer Isaac Clarke, who is sent on repair mission to fix communication issues on a deep-space mining vessel, the Ishimura. Little did he and his 5 man crew realize what they were walking into. Within minutes you are deep within the halls of the Ishimura, being attacked by an army of monsters known as "Necromorphs", all the while attempting to repair the heavily damaged vessel and hoping to escape with your life.
Completing this game the first time had me with my jaw on the floor. The characters, the story, the graphics/atmosphere and the twist ending all kept me awake the next couple nights thinking about what I had just played. This game was incredible. I'm going to talk about each of the aforementioned parts of the game, and if I can think of any, criticisms for this game. I will do my best to keep this review spoiler free.
On the characters; Isaac Clarke. Silent protagonist for a sci-fi/horror survival game? Surprisingly effective. It doesn't give his character a lot of depth but there are clever ways to convey his emotion through either gestures or his journal notes. The other two main protagonists are just your normal captain and computer specialist characters. While being average may not seem to be something worthy of praise, the game does a great job selling their situation. Being on a ship in deep space loaded with murderous aliens and a complex mystery is extremely terrifying and life-threatening, and their actors portray how people would act in a lethal situation.
For the story, my god what a compelling one. Where is the crew? Why are these aliens running rampant on this ship? What the hell happened here? All were questions I had in my head throughout the game. As soon as one thing is figured out more questions arise, ESPECIALLY the ending. The depth, the emotional impact and the mystery surrrounding what happened on the ship all make the game that much more enjoyable. I don't want to talk too much about it as I don't want to spoil important plot points :)
Especially for its time being released in 2008 this games graphics hold up pretty well. There are some terribly awful things (notably the hair on the main female protagonist), but aside from that and possibly a few minor things the graphics are terrific. The atmosphere. I swear about 90% of the time playing this game I was on the edge of my seat with my heartbeat off. That's how immersing and gripping this game is. Even when I replay it today I still feel the same way after 70 hours of it. The atmosphere is very convincing as the game is claustrophobic, eerie, dark and truly sells that this is a ship in deep space.
I'm not gonna talk about the ending :) buy the game and enjoy it for yourself don't let me ruin it!
There are only two real criticisms I have about this game and they are more of nit-picks and my own personal feeling after having 70 hours in the game.
The first issue I have is the lack of consistent action, as there are moments throughout the game with lengthy battles, and there are moments of about 5 solid minutes of not shooting something. While a bit disappointing, the horror often times fills up the gaps of action. Now with the horror my issue is it becomes a bit flat as the game progresses. The game uses the same gimick with slight changes for scares repeatedly, sometimes it works, but a couple hours in the game it gets a little stale. However that all changes when the new type of Necromorph is introduced and another curveball is thrown at you. My absolute biggest issue with this game is the controls. I don't know what happened with the conversion from Xbox 360 to PC, or may it's just steam being bad, but there is some SERIOUS input lag with the mouse. There is a grossly notable delay in moving the mouse when compared to Dead Space 2 and Dead Space 3 on Origin. The latter two games are so smooth and crisp, while Dead Space feels like you are dragging the weapon through the dirt when trying to aim at an enemy. The two minor issues are overshadowed by the game itself, but the input lag makes playing on Impossible mode more difficult than it should be, and Necromorphs are not slow... Nevertheless, those are my only criticisms for the game. While the last one is major, it isn't fair to the game to mark it down in its final grade since I certain its a port issue.
Overall rating: A-. I love this game. Love love love it. To this day I still haven't played a game with a compelling enough story to keep me up the way this one did. This game has changed my life and has helped me truly appreciate horror games, and really good games in general. Absolutely check this game out, while is has some serious issues with the controls and minor problems with the pacing of horror and action, this game does a marvelous job at providing a fun, creepy and yet exciting masterpiece that I would recommend to everyone.

I've been waiting since E3 2006 for Dead Island to come out, and I think Techland (With the help of WB Games) has finally made what I wanted for years now. Dead Island and Riptide are much improved upon in this game, but you can still feel how it's similar. Obviously the Zombie element, but conversations with NPCs are similar, although the voice-acting is streets ahead of anything they previously have done. That being said, it is Techland still, so you get the rare zombie clipping into a car or the semi-common falling/moving through an object you shouldn't have. I don't want to go deep into plot due to spoilers and I haven't gotten that far, but you start off by parachuting into the quarantine area to do work for the government. You don't choose from an aray of characters, you are always Kyle Crane - hardcore parkour master, though the parkouring is a bit difficult to get the grasp of at first.
If you liked Dead Island a bit, but didn't care for characters, plot, or the voice-acting - that's all much better in Dying Light. The parkour is an extremely fresh feeling for the game and running for your life at night really does mess with you atleast the first time you do it. Even if you didn't like Dead Island or Riptide, you will probably like this game. The only thing that might stop you is if you hated the combat or the weapon system in those games. The zombies in this game feel much harder to kill, however; it will likely take you awhile to be able to one-shot any of them and running past them usually seems like the better option (unless you need to get somewhere for a mission, obviously.) Zombies aren't your only enemy in the game, as you have to fight some rude individuals as well, which was a difficult fight for me the first time it happened. The AI is very much improved from the previous Techland Zombie games as well and some zombies are hard to shake and are more diverse in their choices as compared to the Dead Island zombies.
Better AI: Check
Better Voiceacting: Check
Better Plot: Check
PARKOUR!?: CHECK
HARDCORE PARKOUR!!?: HARDCORE CHECK!!
What Dead Island Should Have Been: CHECKMATE!!!

Really excellent sequel to the original Dead Island series. The game is flat out gorgeous. There have been some glitches on surfaces, but overall it runs smoothly, even when in multiplayer. The coop is great. Too many people trying to be the zombie currently. It can make nights last forever, but you earn huge exp for it. Also it's easy to win as the survivors if you keep you cool. I have won 7 of 8 matches with just two people.
Gameplay mechanics function pretty closely to the Dead Island series in terms of combat. There are no specializations with characters anymore however and just a universal skill tree. The movement is really one of the high points for myself. It is a HUGE world and you are free to roam wherever you please. It's not like some sandbox games where it's "open" but 3/4 of the map is blocked off and you can't access it or you have only certain routes you can take to locations. This is truly a game where you can go anywhere you can reach.
The sound is used very well in the game. You hear them approaching, the screams in the distance, and the dread of rushing volatiles or hunters really gets you going. The in game chat is the low point currently as there is no controls over adjusting volume or push to talk. The sound does help with the appropriate dread you should feel.
Lastly, that previously mentioned dread is what I think was really missing from the Dead Island series. I was never really scared or anxious the whole time I played them. You will panic the first nightfall. You will forget how to climb when you are cornered. It will be awesome.

Enemy Unknown (Base Game):
The game is frustrating if you don't understand what you should be doing with your base, so I recommend reading at least a little bit about that beforehand, or at least paying a lot of attention to what happens to you in game. The first several months of the game are most crucial; once you get past that, the game becomes much better and relies more on your decision making versus RNG. RNG still plays a huge role (I have missed a shot I desperately needed with a 97% chance to hit) and you'll have to get acquainted with Lady Luck fairly quickly. The game is really entertainnig, and the last sequences of the campaign are a blast. Multiplayer is a bit lacking, but I would buy this for the single-player and not the multiplayer. Going above normal difficulty is begging to be probed. Vigrously. Playing harder difficulties with Second Wave options definitely breathe fresh air into the game though, and I would recommend trying it as soon as you beat the game on Normal.
Enemy Within (Expansion):
EW adds a hefty load to the game. MEC Troopers, gene-modded soliders, and new enemies add a whole new level of awesome to the experience. On top of that, there are new weapons, and numerous Foundry upgrades. EXALT are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but killing EXALT soldiers gives you their weapons, which are nice if you haven't upgraded to laser tech early game (which really shouldn't happen in the first place). EXALT will be a pain in your side. Covert Ops will suck in a teeth-grinding kind of way. Other new enemies like Mechtoids will make you beg for mercy. However, as always, the fun of this game lies in the frustration. I think I've restarted a new game 3-4 times already as I've tried to ascend difficulties on EW.
Long War (Mod):
The Long War mod for XCOM: Enemy Within (easily found on NexusMods or with a quick Google search) overhauls the game. Being true to its name, the game takes much longer to complete. I've spent about 5-8 hours on my current playthrough and I'm barely past the third month. To really get a full scope of the changes, you'd have to look up the features list for Long War (which you can find here:
). In short, the game is much harder, slower (in a good way), and fights are way more about tactical positioning and decision-making. Overall, it makes XCOM a much more enjoyable and robust game.

DRAGONFALL analysis:
Pros:
- Great story
- Immersive setting
- Interesting characters
- Nice, strategic, turn-based combat
Cons:
- The game does not explain anything to you. For example, there are these ley lines things on the ground, that somehow improve magical abilities. However, the game does not explain this to you, and nor does it say HOW your magic is improved. This is just an example, because you have to pretty much figure everything out by yourself here.
- The NPCs don't cover every role/class possible (like in games such as Dragon Age). This is actually not a big deal, but I started the game as a Shaman (summoner/support mage), only to find that the game already provides you with one, but not with a damage-oriented mage. You can hire some mercenaries to fill those roles by paying cash, but I don't think this solves the problem.
- The items/spells systems are not clear and have some pretty big flaws, and as I stated before, nothing is explained to you.
Two examples: 1) You can by spells/armor for yourself, but not for your companions, but no one tells you that. At the same time, you can buy consumables for them. 2) If you equip an ally with a consumable before a mission, the item will be lost after the quest, even if you didn't used it.
Even if its flaws, I must reccommend this game for anyone who's fond of turn-based strategy games (it plays a bit similar to XCOM) or who likes a game with great story. Just be sure to read a guide or something before playing.

Right... So where do I begin... The game left me with quite a mixture of feelings...
Let's clear the negative bits first. The game is more linear than most linear FPS's this days (and the RPG being more linear than most FPS's says a lot). There is almost no chance to explore or approach the mission in any variety of ways. The game practically forces you from point A to point B in a most direct and unforgiving way. There is simply nothing to do in between of those points. No exploration, no looting, no chatting with random NPC - nothing.
Another major let down of this game are dialogs. While generaly well written, multiple choice answers make no sense. As no matter what you reply will be, the conversations take the same course. You can flatter other NPC to high sky or you can tell them to kiss your *** - makes no difference whatsoever in majority of cases.
So to cut the long story short - the game is hugely let down by its linearity. Its ultimately linear in every imaginable way - from converasations to how the missions go.
But let's "knock it off with those negative waves" and be positive for a bit.
First and foremost the game's atmosphere is absolutely marvellous. Considering the simplicity of graphics, sound and setting the game does absolutely fantastic job in recreating a world that, despite its linearity, is still interesting to be in. Many games, while being much more graphically advanced and running on much higher budget have tried and failed to deliver the same.
The atmosphere somewhat reminds me of the first Deus Ex, only with magic, elves and orks thrown in. Same dark, run-down, but strangely attractive urban-setting of the near future. You really feel comfy, entering the pub after roaming the slums, you really want to ask bartender for a pint (shame that game won't let you) and chat with the bouncer, while you at it.
The plot is fairly strong. Somewhat predictable, but still has a few unexpected twists and provides a good story.
Other than that - game has a lot of potential to expand on what it has already achieved, to fix its downfalls and to become a classic in its own right. Developers have already done the most important thing - creating an interesting and immersive world. Now its only a question of expanding on dialogues, exploration, more side quests and making the game-world bigger and more detailed.
So I would still recommend this game and "Dragonfall" is already on my wishlist (although not at the top). If you aren't fully convinced - just wait for big sale and buy it then. It probably wouldnt be ultimate purchase of the year, but still - few coins well spent :)

I've been playing through the Arkham Series and I have to say this one has been the most exciting off the bat.
* The graphics are groundbreaking, the facial expressions immersive and the rain looks very realistic over the cowl and other objects. I couldn't help but to switch costumes every 20 minutes just to see how they'd look on this beautiful engine in action. definitely a step up.
* The environment (as in the city) is fantastically fleshed out besides the awkward futuristic industrial section that disrupts the vibe set by the rest of Gotham City. (Thankfully we don't spend much time there) outside of that you've got as close to an accurate Gotham as we may ever see. All the landmarks you may recognize are present out and within the boundaries if you're looking, Even Arkham asylum, Wayne Manor and Ace chemical.
* The combat is mostly the same though I'd say there are a handful of different combos and finishing options. The Bat is at the top of his game here, moving as fast as one straight outta hell you can often subdue multiple foes carrying guns because of how much range he's given when jumping from foe to foe. Personally I found this game out of the rest to 'av been the easiest on a Hard difficulty solely because of how fast he is in combat. Doesn't take much away from the experience as you are still challenged, but most mistakes don't essentially mean death like the previous games.
* The story in Arkham Knight is pretty theatrical, giving off much more meaning to it's (main) plot points than the previous games. This is the final chapter in the Arkham series and the game does a good job in driving that home with the character interactions/duologue, stakes, cutscenes and overall demeanor of batman. (If that makes sense) Rocksteady did a great job capturing the "feel" of batman in so many moments I felt it was an experience which held it's place against the comic books and far surpassed the movies.
Many of the things I felt were out of place was in ways how batman treated the villains and anti-heros with such callous and lack of empathy (sort of like in origins he couldn't care less about crippling a police officer; albeit corrupt ones) in many stories and in the animated series he wasn't so black and white about justice.
An example I'd like to point out is how he throws a man who committed a victimless crime for a good hearted reason in the same cell (no walls between) with ♥♥♥♥ing super villians. literally people willing to kill him for fun and Batman is without a word on the mention of this. So the writing isn't so great on the side plots.
The boss battles are a farcry from their peak in Arkham City. Most are forgettable where as 6 years later I still remember the ones from Asylum.
Each and every boss fight goes one of three ways:
You're often preforming small investigations (I mean 1 minute) in one spot then wandering around (the whole city) until you find the next, rinse repeat until you find the villian and bring them in.
You reach a weapon cache or area in need of securing, beat the thugs in a brawl or a series of silent takedowns, rinse and repeat.
Or one of the infamous seemingly endless tank battles where you motor around in the batmobile's tank mode and mind numbingly take aim and spam the right trigger (M1)
It's nothing notable and is one of the most visible complaints for Arkham Knight. There was so much potential for Arkham Knight bosses and each one is more disappointing than the next leading up to what may be one of the worst anybody could ever expect for the amount of progress needed to reach them.
**Shutters**
Anyway,  Despite it's unforeseen shortcomings in hardware comparability, Side quests and side boss battles, Arkham Knight is one of the best batman experiences available and I'd say it's a must play for any batfan because of it's accessibility and pick up and play nature. I'd give Arkham Knight 8 Arkham cities out of 10. Pick it up for $20 OR lower you'd be looney not to HAHAHAHAHAHAHHAHA

A Metroid-vania, 4 dimensional puzzler that sounds great on the surface, but ends up just leading to subpar experience.
I had high hopes going into this game, and still believe it is a game that most people should try, just for the sheer insanity of it. I really liked a lot of the early puzzles where they were based on thinking on your feet and observing the world around you. However, a puzzle game would be remiss if it didn't add some new twist as the game progressed to keep the mechanics interesting.
This extension comes in the form of a gun, that lets you collect and place blocks in the environment. And early on, this skill is cool and adds to the gameplay. But this is where you start to see a shift in the game. What was once again about dealing with these insane rules of engagement, quickly devolves into something whose mechanics feel surprisingly similar to Portal.
However, the gun brings me to my biggest complaint about the game, which is it's Metroid-vania, run into a puzzle now but you may not be able to solve it attitude. It led to sections of the game where I would beat my head against the wall thinking that I could solve it, or that I had all of the powers I could get and then there must be a way to solve the puzzle with what I had. But instead I was just wasting my own time on a puzzle I wasn't equipped for.
I did love the mind-bending puzzles, when they were around and the aesthetic of the entire game is visually stunning. This game does end up being ultimately competent and I would suggest it to anyone who really loves puzzle games, but for the casual observer I would suggest maybe playing the first couple of minutes at a friend’s house.

This game is a unique strategy game that is very fun, but unforgiving.  This is one of the best turn-based strategy games i have ever played.  There is an erie vibe to the aliens for the first half of the game because you know nothing about them, or how good new enemies are.  After a while though, you start using the aliens weaponry against them and that is when the game changes from trying to survive to fighting back and being a force to be reckoned with.  The gameplay alows you to use a squad to take out the aliens (usually just staight forward, but there are some protecting civilians missions and disabling bombs that mix it up) and what XCOM does well, is get you emotionally invested in these soldiers, and when one dies (exspetially your lead soldier) it hurts you emotionally and in the game.  It hurts you in the game because if your main squad dies on a mission and you are trying to train a rookie squad, the aliens don't hold back and will keep attacking you with the dificulty they had with your better squad.  It is also almost impossible to make every country happy and you will have to decide wich ones are more important to you.  These aren't bad things of course unless you don't like challenge.  It can also be unforgiving if you make a bad move like have one of your guys sprint out of cover, because your guys can easily die unless you have really good armor.  Some of the bad things are that if you don't know how important somethings are at the begining like statilites, you may have to start a new game because you are so umprepared later on.  The camera angles can also screw you up like if there are more than one floor, it sometimes is hard to choose the floor you want to move to because it keeps switching the view.  To sum it up, this is a great turn-based game that is challenging, but not too much so it is not fun.

I don't think I've ever beaten a roguelike. This one proves to be no exception. I hope that doesn't hurt my review. I hope you guys don't think less of me because I can't get my ship up. To sector 7.
Anywho. Your character is a space ship. The crew is more inventory than anything else. You can even buy them at shops. It's like playing captain in Star Trek assuming that your crew listens to you. And assuming that Star Trek ships died every episode and you'd get a new ship to watch, instead of the same crew every time.
This certainly is a strong contender in the strategy/roguelike genre. The music is solid, especially if you like retro or 8-bit styled music. The graphics are not super duper shiny, but if you're coming from Nethack, you expected worse. And don't get me wrong, these graphics really reinforce their purpose. Shinier would probably have felt out of place in the genre.
Now then, if you're considering buying this, I'm sure you've already found out that the battle in this game is an interesting kind of real time. It's kind of the same real time that Final Fantasy 12 was. The game can go on and on if you leave it, but you can only act once meters have filled and you can pause while telling your crew what to do. For the record, I really liked Final Fantasy 12. And by extension I enjoy this game too.
If you're looking for a strategy game that will kill you, but can be overcome, this is the place to find it. It's got DF style "fun" (read: dieing often) in droves. And if you like that, then this game will suit you well.

Killing Floor 2 is the Sequel to Killing Floor (duh), an amazing zombie game where you fight off waves of undead creatures. Not more not less.
KF2 is basically a better version of the first part, though it is still in Early Access it is already playable and even has more different classes than the first part.
Gameplay is simple, you pick a class, a map and a character. Then you have to survive multiple waves of enemies, each wave harder than the one before. Between these waves you buy weapons, ammo and armor to keep up with the growing number of enemies. There are a couple of different creatures, all with unique abilities and different weaknesses.
Pros:
+Good graphics.
+Great soundtracks.
+New and old classes.
+Customizable weapons and characters.
+Awesomely designed maps.
+Server Browser.
+A ton of achievements
Cons
-No new enemies except 1 new boss. (Most enemies received small changes)
-Gameplay only interesting if you like these types of games, otherwise repetitive and without long time motivation.
-Lobbies with AFK players.
-In game purchases that are way too expensive and only give optical enchantments (on top of DLC content)
I am definetly a fan of Killing Floor, though I cannot play the game for more than 2 hours in a row as the gameplay i somewhat repetitive. Keep in mind that the only thing you do is surviving waves after waves. There are a lot of different classes and weapons though so you have a lot to experiment.
Must buy for fans of the first part !

Shadowrun Returns lives somewhere between a point-and-click adventure and a tactical RPG like XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but the lack of voice acting and completely linear plotline makes everything seem unfinished. However, once you accept the forced march through story, it's actually pretty well-written and the combat is fun. Just expect everything to be a dime short of a dollar--this game has all the hallmarks of a project that ran out of money too soon. However, since this game is modular and easily modded
, it may improve over time.
The first story module that comes with the game, Dead Man's Switch, is not quite as interesting as the first DLC module: Dragonfall.
TL;DR: If you enjoy turn-based, three-quarter RPGs such as Fallout 2 and Baldur's Gate 2, you may enjoy this one, especially if it's in the $5-10 range.

It's simply awesome. Sure there's a little lag here and there, but it's still a beautiful game that runs well, which was really all I wanted from the start.

Enemy Unknown (Base Game):
The game is frustrating if you don't understand what you should be doing with your base, so I recommend reading at least a little bit about that beforehand, or at least paying a lot of attention to what happens to you in game. The first several months of the game are most crucial; once you get past that, the game becomes much better and relies more on your decision making versus RNG. RNG still plays a huge role (I have missed a shot I desperately needed with a 97% chance to hit) and you'll have to get acquainted with Lady Luck fairly quickly. The game is really entertainnig, and the last sequences of the campaign are a blast. Multiplayer is a bit lacking, but I would buy this for the single-player and not the multiplayer. Going above normal difficulty is begging to be probed. Vigrously. Playing harder difficulties with Second Wave options definitely breathe fresh air into the game though, and I would recommend trying it as soon as you beat the game on Normal.
Enemy Within (Expansion):
EW adds a hefty load to the game. MEC Troopers, gene-modded soliders, and new enemies add a whole new level of awesome to the experience. On top of that, there are new weapons, and numerous Foundry upgrades. EXALT are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but killing EXALT soldiers gives you their weapons, which are nice if you haven't upgraded to laser tech early game (which really shouldn't happen in the first place). EXALT will be a pain in your side. Covert Ops will suck in a teeth-grinding kind of way. Other new enemies like Mechtoids will make you beg for mercy. However, as always, the fun of this game lies in the frustration. I think I've restarted a new game 3-4 times already as I've tried to ascend difficulties on EW.
Long War (Mod):
The Long War mod for XCOM: Enemy Within (easily found on NexusMods or with a quick Google search) overhauls the game. Being true to its name, the game takes much longer to complete. I've spent about 5-8 hours on my current playthrough and I'm barely past the third month. To really get a full scope of the changes, you'd have to look up the features list for Long War (which you can find here:
). In short, the game is much harder, slower (in a good way), and fights are way more about tactical positioning and decision-making. Overall, it makes XCOM a much more enjoyable and robust game.

This game is a unique strategy game that is very fun, but unforgiving.  This is one of the best turn-based strategy games i have ever played.  There is an erie vibe to the aliens for the first half of the game because you know nothing about them, or how good new enemies are.  After a while though, you start using the aliens weaponry against them and that is when the game changes from trying to survive to fighting back and being a force to be reckoned with.  The gameplay alows you to use a squad to take out the aliens (usually just staight forward, but there are some protecting civilians missions and disabling bombs that mix it up) and what XCOM does well, is get you emotionally invested in these soldiers, and when one dies (exspetially your lead soldier) it hurts you emotionally and in the game.  It hurts you in the game because if your main squad dies on a mission and you are trying to train a rookie squad, the aliens don't hold back and will keep attacking you with the dificulty they had with your better squad.  It is also almost impossible to make every country happy and you will have to decide wich ones are more important to you.  These aren't bad things of course unless you don't like challenge.  It can also be unforgiving if you make a bad move like have one of your guys sprint out of cover, because your guys can easily die unless you have really good armor.  Some of the bad things are that if you don't know how important somethings are at the begining like statilites, you may have to start a new game because you are so umprepared later on.  The camera angles can also screw you up like if there are more than one floor, it sometimes is hard to choose the floor you want to move to because it keeps switching the view.  To sum it up, this is a great turn-based game that is challenging, but not too much so it is not fun.

If you enjoy drop in-and-out 4 player campaign done correctly, this is the game for you and your friends.
Pros:
-Coop works great, functions great.  None of that, "You are too far ahead, you can't play" Or "You're 3 levels higher, now your friend can't even deal damage to zombies!" (Borderlands and Dead Island)
-Combat is fun, and looks amazing.  You hit a zombie in the shoulder, no more shoulder.  It's accurate as hell. (the damage)
-The running and moving throughout the environment is just insanely fun.  You learn different areas of the town, your own personal routes, build momentum and really feel like a badass with the parkour system.
Eh:
-The skill system is done well, because to upgrade agility, you need to run around or use agility skills (which is a system I love)((same with power and surviver))  the reason I rank it in between, they could've added more skills for us, but being a console game, they're limited to "Only one attack button, so hold to do this attack, so now we can't give you multiple attack unlocks!"
-The performance is shoddy.  It's playable for me, and I'm usually very picky.  On my rig I get 35-50 FPS with settings low. (still looks great though)
-There is bugs, but we haven't seen anything game breaking.  Minor♥♥♥♥♥♥like rarely a zombie is inside the safezone, or glitches through a fence from knockback, but overall they're minor and nothing truely ruining the game.
-Competitions are SUPER FUN, but they come up randomly (which is OK) but when you initiate it, because it's a console game and we have like 8 buttons to work with, you have to hit your medkit button, which consumes a medkit, FREEZES YOU IN PLACE, and anybody else in the game has 10 seconds to reply, then another 5 second countdown.  Meanwhile the world moves on, so enemies get closer to stealing the air drop, zombies get closer to you (they don't attack) and it just feels broke as hell that it freezes your character.
Cons:
-All in all, it's a console port.  The menus are smooth, but still rather annoyingly designed to be navigated by a controller, not a mouse.  So moving inventory is annoying.  Kind of on par with Skyrim, it just doesn't feel good at all and it takes way longer than it should.
-I don't like games where you get no choice in things.  The main character starts to act more reasonable a few hours in, but it'd be a lot more fun if you could decide fates here and there.  It's hard to get into when your character goes from being a saint to the grim reaper then back to being a saint again.
Maybe more to come, overall I highly recommend the game, if you enjoyed Dead Island, Borderlands, Assassin's Creen, any game like that with friends, it's all the same blueprint.   Main story, side quests, upgrades, kill♥♥♥♥♥♥

Funded this game back when the kickstarter campaign was around. Spent $10, and would gladly spend $20+ on it. Granted, I am a long-time shadowrun fan, but it's a great game for rpg fans.
While the graphics may not be the greatest, and the original story was pretty good at best (the Dragonfall DLC definitely makes up for it, it's another game in itself), what really makes up for it is all the user generated content that is coming out.
A reboot of the snes title was the first project I saw pop up, and have been following since.
Shadowrun Unlimited, is more of a non-linear style of game. I'm only a couple of hours into it, but there is so much more to it than the original game (more cyberware, more programs to be used in cyberspace, etc.), and it has much more replayability (random missions) than the original game.
That's just a couple of mods that I've been keeping an eye on, and there's plenty more where those came from.
If you like turn-based strategy, with both mystical (magic, dwarves, elves, etc.) and futuristic elements, it's most definitely worth picking up.

Definitley recommended if you're overdue for a dose of the 1980's!

Killing Floor 2 is the Sequel to Killing Floor (duh), an amazing zombie game where you fight off waves of undead creatures. Not more not less.
KF2 is basically a better version of the first part, though it is still in Early Access it is already playable and even has more different classes than the first part.
Gameplay is simple, you pick a class, a map and a character. Then you have to survive multiple waves of enemies, each wave harder than the one before. Between these waves you buy weapons, ammo and armor to keep up with the growing number of enemies. There are a couple of different creatures, all with unique abilities and different weaknesses.
Pros:
+Good graphics.
+Great soundtracks.
+New and old classes.
+Customizable weapons and characters.
+Awesomely designed maps.
+Server Browser.
+A ton of achievements
Cons
-No new enemies except 1 new boss. (Most enemies received small changes)
-Gameplay only interesting if you like these types of games, otherwise repetitive and without long time motivation.
-Lobbies with AFK players.
-In game purchases that are way too expensive and only give optical enchantments (on top of DLC content)
I am definetly a fan of Killing Floor, though I cannot play the game for more than 2 hours in a row as the gameplay i somewhat repetitive. Keep in mind that the only thing you do is surviving waves after waves. There are a lot of different classes and weapons though so you have a lot to experiment.
Must buy for fans of the first part !

Shadowrun Returns is a game I find hard to give excessive praise, but it's a game that I also find hard to dislike. When it comes down to it, it's a completely solid game, even if it's shallow. Nevertheless, I enjoyed it and feel fully satisfied with the experience, and I didn't have any trouble playing all the way through. There are certainly some notable flaws, however.
Let's start with the story, since this game relies heavily on it's writing to motivate the player. The writing and characterization is good, I felt very absorbed in the universe, but the story itself is fairly lacking. It's a shame as well, it starts out great. You got a murder mystery with a lot of interesting faces dying to be talked to, with a few twists and turns here and there. The problem is that it just doesn't developed. It feels extremely rushed. The characters are lovable and relatable to the very end, but I started skipping through dialogue that dealt with the actual plot about 2/3rds through the game. It escalates in a comical direction, with an extremely weak and one-dimensional villian. It's extremely predictable, and just plain boring. The last stretch is so typical and lackluster that I had little to no investment in the actual plight, I just wanted to see if the characters would drop some more interesting backstory about themselves. It gave me closure, but it's not memorable at all. It's just too bad, the beginning was really good, but the plot started going so fast in such a linear direction that it forgot to flesh itself out, leaving some questions unanswered and plot points underdeveloped. It got the job done, but I was hoping for more.
Where the game really shines are the characters and their own personal issues. Almost all the staple characters have their own personal motives and vendettas, and I was interested in all their stories. I enjoyed going back to base and talking to every single one of them that were willing to open their mouths. The game does a fantastic job of setting up this belonging feeling, that you're part of this organization of runners. Although, as I stated before, as the game escalates it leaves behind this deep characterization in order to fawn over its own hilariously absurd and out-of-place world-threatening dilemma.
The combat is serviceable. It's ultimately shallow and linear, there isn't a lot of variation or depth, and there are some balance issues. But it's still fun, you get to characterize some characters simply by their fighting styles. It's too easy as well, but not game-ruiningly so. It's fun, if you really like X-COM-like turn based combat, you'll probably enjoy it if you can stand it being a tad shallow.
The game is overall fun, I would recommend it. It doesn't really have any offending flaws, it just doesn't quite reach the large potential it could've. It's not particularly memorable, but it's enjoyable. I would wait for a sale, but when the price is suitable to you, I'd say to go for it just to get immersed in the world.

The Good: Perfected combat and stealth system, wonderful story that has all the best parts of Batman combined, better structured world and side missions, wonderful visuals, the Batmobile is a great addition
The Bad: Terrible PC optimization that involves complicated tweaking, Batmobile tank battles are tiresome
The Batman Arkham games are some of the greatest things to grace the video game industry in the past decade. With the most advance combat system since God of War; and not to mention the best super hero video games series ever made; Arkham Knight continues this trend. While Origins was a bit of a snag, I don't count it as part of the Arkham trilogy. Arkham Knight is another masterpiece that any Batman fan will love.
Scarecrow and the new Arkham Knight are the main villains in this game, but don't worry, there's plenty of Joker as well despite being dead. Joker is a manifestation in Bruce's mind and he constantly appears everywhere putting his two sense into everything Batman does; it's great to hear him again. Arkham Knight is also probably the best structured Arkham game yet. Instead of a hodge podge of little repetitive missions everywhere the game has a Most Wanted mission wheel. Known Batman villains are to be stopped and captured through missions branches that are a blast. Firefly, Penguin, Two Face, and various other villains have their own little sub-plot. This brings Arkham Knight to a meaty and well balanced missions structure that the game desperately needed. The only other side things you can perform are AR missions that include fight and Batmobile challenges and Riddler trophies. Oh yeah, I said Batmobile.
It's finally here! The one and only Batmobile. It plays just like you think, controls like you think, and is as bad♥♥♥♥♥as you think. The Batmobile can transform into a tank allowing you to engage in battles with enemy tanks, but the best use of the Batmobile are puzzles. Sadly, the tank battles are probably the worst thing in the game. While they work, they are the same thing over and over and over again; nothing changes. Enemy tanks will have a white line go across the screen showing the trajectory of their shot. This allows you to dodge enemy missiles and shots. That's great and all, but why does combat have to be this slow? Towards the end the battles just get bigger with 50+ tanks in one area, that's not exactly fun in my book. While the tank battles aren't very frequent, they are happening often enough for you to sigh and wish it was over. As for the puzzle solving, the Batmobile fits better here. Using the power wench to crawl down sides of buildings, using the wench to power things up, ejecting out of the Batmobile to glide into tunnel. All of this feels just like in the movies and comics; no disappointment there.
Combat has been perfected in Arkham Knight with added moves to make an extremely complex fight system that is so simple to learn. Outside of the counter system that we are all used to, knew knock-out moves are introduced. Using your gadgets it much easier as the button combos for them are easier to remember. LT for Batarang, LT+B for electric shock to enemies with taser sticks, LT+Y for Batclaw, RT+RT for Freeze Blast. Very easy to remember and the controls pop up on screen to help you out when the option is available. Same goes for knock out moves, as well as fighting heavy enemies. These guys have their own system all to themselves. Do a fast punch combo, parry a guy behind you, a red exclamation pops up at a guy with a taser stick, LT+B, he's down, continue pummeling the heavy, three more counters, then knock the heavy out. All of this is one big combo and it's so fluid and fast and one of my favorite fighting systems I have ever used.
The second combat system to Arkham is the stealth part. This has been expanded exponentially in Arkham Knight. There are more gadgets introduced which allow more ways to take down opponents. The stealth areas are much larger and allow for multiple ways of taking people down. We're used to stealth take downs in various ways from hanging, grates, and gliding behind people. Multi-level grate combat is introduced as well as enemies being able to destroy grates so you can no longer use them. Using a voice synthesizer allows you to give commands to enemies and set up traps with your electric gun or disruptor. The disruptor allows you to sabotage weapons and drones to knock out enemies (yeah, can't say kill since Batman doesn't do that). The stealth combat is fantastic and so much fun and allows for strategy over beating everyone up.
Outside of these knew gameplay elements is the story. Arkham Knight has a long and well told story that you actually care about. There are some great moments in the game that really get you hooked and the ending is satisfying. I really felt the strengths and weaknesses of Batman come out through the story several times as well as the other characters. My favorite part of the game is the ending with Scarecrow, but I can't give it away except it's a first person shooter sequence. WHAT?! Play it to find out!
Let's talk about visuals. I know that the entire world knows how terribly optimized the game was for PC, however if you have a powerful rig it is very playable. Not perfect, but enough to not be really noticeable. This requires tweaks (there a tool available on the Steam forums) to the game settings to get it to work. Out of the box the game won't run very well at all. There are some nice new effects like RainWorks, Interactive Smoke and Fog, and various other effects. They look amazing and Arkham Knight is one of the most detailed and good looking games in a long time. However, a game should ship working and this is just unacceptable. Most people don't know how to tweak a PC game and will get frustrated and demand their money back (which happened and suspended the sales on Steam). The other issue is you need a very new and powerful system to get the game to  run well. I tried and a GTX 670 and while I got 60 FPS when I was above the city it dropped below 30 on the ground. Interactive Smoke and Fog dropped the game to 5  FPS, however on a GTX 970 there were few issues. The frame rate will vary constantly. You will jump between 60 and 30 a lot, but the tweaks available make it less noticeable. Anyone running a GPU older than a year will have issues for sure and should play the game on a console for now.
As it stand, Arkham Knight is a fantastic game and the pinnacle of the Batman video game franchise and super hero games in general. Taking all of what made the series great and optimizing and compiling the best of what everyone loves. More villains, more story, more Batman. That's what we came to see and we got what we want.
~Score: 9/10

South Park creators, Trey Parker and Matt Stone, have struck gold again with this amazing video game adaptation of their popular animated series. Not only is it the best video game based on an animated series, but it does hold its ground as a consistent RPG, with its intense turn-based combat system, vast areas to explore and creative customization. This game is one that I recommend wholeheartedly to South Park fans everywhere.

First of all... I feel like the one thing that ruined this game for me was 3rd person view. UGH.
Is it scary? Well... not really... it mostly relies on some jump scares.. creatures suddenly showing up. You get over it fast. Since you have a weapon, there really isn't any reason to be scared, right??
Time: This game was pretty short. Finished in under 18 hours on Normal.
Controlling: Keyboard and mouse. I'm not entirely sold on the set up of game play. I'm a lazy gamer. I like one button clicks. Not hold "left mouse button down, focus on object, press Ctrl" to do whatever
Bugs: not really any... pretty smooth... except for maybe the character 'catching' on walls and stuff.. but that's the curse of 3rd person view. Camera view was sometimes bloody terrible.
Motionsickness: yes, somewhat/frequently. A lof of the time just running down the halls and having to constantly move the camera view in order to see anything.
Story: ... I'm still not sure what happened. :D I kind of floated through it not really paying attention. A major flaw in this game I would say is the ridiculous amount of gear and gear upgrades you can get. I pretty much spent all my money on ONLY the Plasma Cutter and saving money for the Suits. Upgrading the gear was very far and few between mostly because of the amount of Power Nodes you can get. You can NOT max everything out... you have to really focus on a couple things. For me, Plasma Cutter DMG and Suit HP.
Perhaps in more difficulty levels you can continue to max items out? I don't know. Not gonna check.
I generally had fun killing stuff in this game. I LOVE the GPS system of this game (a little indicator line that tells you exatly where you need to go), but the map feature sucked butt.
I already played Dead Space 3... and that was more fun than DS1.
Anway, regardless of this somewhat negative review, I still recommend playing this game. It was entertaining despite the minor flaws that go against the grain of my typical play style.
