This game, this game is one of the few titles I can name that truly inspires my mind to delve depths unimaginable the setting is superb, the lore rich and thick and let's not forget the beautiful controls and gameplay all in all I would say this title is one of my absolute favorites, but let's talk about why.
First off the setting is one of the, if not the most beautifully crafted settings to grace the games industry the world feels alive and full of character and emotion as though it is dripping pure atmosphere and spawning true intrigue this is because it is built off of an amazing title already being part of the deep and wonderful world of Shadowrun making it one of the best modern iterations of a classic game series I have ever had the pleasure to step into.
Now let's saunter on over to the lore of the game, which is built upon the original Pen and Paper title and the superb yet confusing NES and Genesis title, not to spoil anything too major but the entire world has been changed massively by an event called the awakening and yea, you know what just go read up on everything else.
The gameplay is another area I want to cover as the game plays like an Turn Based Roleplaying Game, now the game comes with one preinstalled mission which is actually quite huge but there are a lot of player made missions on sites like NexusMods and even on the workshop itself add on the beautiful levelling system which stops you becoming extremely over powered early and you have fantastic gameplay.
But I don't think the game is one hundred percent perfect, the preinstalled story called Dead Mans Switch, unfortunately feels undercooked and doesn't pull off the gritty superb story I expected in short your friend is killed and he hires you post death to find and kill the drek that killed him, I'm not gonna spoil anything but I thought the end villain was weak and uninteresting when they could've done something great with an established character from the beginning.
I also shouldn't forget the DLC Dragonfall which in and of itself adds much more to the world and is it's own excellent piece of content adding new characters and more awesome story development.

I can't feel comfortable recommending a game that not only released in a virtually unplayable state, but the publishers didn't even offer any sort of apology for the people who paid them money and didn't opt for a refund (or in some cases, couldn't get a refund due to the place of purchase having a "no refunds" policy unless you pay them money first - thanks, EB!)
that said, I did actually enjoy the game. when I finally got to play the non-slideshow version.
it had a satisfying conclusion to the story, and it was actually quite pretty when it was finally working properly. driving the batmobile is a ton of fun, and I actually enjoyed the tank sequences.
the problem with the tank sequences, in my mind, isn't that there's too many of them - it's that they're used in replacement of traditional boss fights. the boss fights in Arkham Asylum and Arkham City - and even AC Origins - were some of the most memorable sequences. who doesn't remember the showdown with Mr. Freeze, or escaping the clutches of Killer Croc in the water system below the Asylum? those squences helped make those games great! but having no final boss at the end of the third game in the trilogy? that should never have been green lit. I know you get to fight Riddler in a boss fight after the final showdown, but you don't *have* to, and that's the problem. even if it had been batman on foot versus the tank, that could have been amazing, but instead we got another in a long string of tank battles.
it's a good game on its own, but compared to the first 2 games, the ending felt like a let down.
I would have given it an 11/13 had it not been broken at launch, had a bad ending, and if it didn't seem like the publishers didn't care about their most loyal fans, but because of all that I have to give it a 4/9

Over time, you will able to identify the identical obstacles each of 6 levels throw at you which will help you survive if you make the correct reactions.  There are 6 levels in this game.    Naturally, each level has higher difficulty until the last level that is the hardest.   The problem I find is that this game is really oriented toward audience with good twitches/reactions.   Those that doesn't react quick with their fingers on keyboard or mouse will likely find this game rather frustrating instead of fun challenging.  I find myself not reacting fast enough in many cases.  There were times I did find it frustrating and I was very happy I finally beat this game in the end.

~~~This game was reviewed on a GTX 1070, 32GB DDR4 RAM @ 2400MHz, i7 6820HK @ 3.8GHz~~~
---
Oh, how this game loves you... and hates you, too.
Oh, how at times its gameplay is masterful with such refined adeptness, but then so repetitively boring and frustrating. Oh, how the story is so intricate, nuanced, and deliciously brooding and yet full of cliche teen-angst and predictable-ness with ample clout for eye-rolling. Oh, how the visuals cascade your eyes with splendor, until the damn game crashes on you,... again.
I really love this game; I really hate this game, too. It's a crazy and yet totally sane dichotemy.
No spoilers ahead, but a few points to illustrate the above preamble.
1) Vehicle combat just blows. Sure, it's fine for about 30 minutes, but becomes such a chore late in the game, it completely detracts from the brilliance of being Batman. Did I mention being Batman is brilliant? Yes, it most certainly is. Unfortunately, this brilliance is marred by You being the Batmobile as much as You being the Batman. Point: the Batman is awesome; the Batmobile sucks.
2) The Arkham Knight, while a new character (sort-of) in the Batman cannon, is a lame♥♥♥♥♥villain, especially so when the plot finally culminates to his reveal. Even considering this is a video game based on a comic, the amazingly ludicrous lengths this character goes to annihilate the Batman (and where did he even get the money to invest in an ENTIRE army seemingly the size of North Korea's?), is borderline comical, especially once the 'reveal' happens. Color me critical, but I just can't look past the melodramatic teen-ansty-ness of the Arkham Knight. But! Minding this aside, the story is quite entertaining, with concise and to the point cutscenes that continually drive the momentum of the story (until the Arkham Knights talks...some more). It's as if the game appreciates your curiosity and intellect to piece together and predict the direction of the story to only slap you in the face with another bantering, banal commentary by the Arkham Knight. Point: the story is great; the Arkham Knight pretty much sucks.
3) This game is gorgeous. Like (and I usually don't start sentences with 'like') it's absolutely stunning. The character animations from lip-syncing to body-movement and fluidity of combat are simply phenominal (2015/2016 standards). Even though the game takes place at night, the city streets are dazingly detailed and there are so many nuanced atmospheric effects on screen, it's a relentless avalanche of visual-splendor. And yet, even after the debauched luanch over a year ago, the game crashes, and regularly. Sure, when it's running, it runs well, but I experienced a crash every 20 or so minutes of gameplay - far, FAR too often. Point: it's visually stunning; it also crashes A LOT!
So, how in the Gotham (notice I replaced 'world' with Gotham, because I'm clever) does this game fair? Well, despite its clear shortcomings, it's still oh-so-good... until it's oh-so-bad.
I can so recommend this game, until I don't want to anymore! I'm flummoxed. Perhaps you will be, too, or won't?!?

Deadspace is a sci-fi scare-fest + adventure. Think Doom3 with a bit more story. Love or hate EA, this is a very very well crafted game even if you are playing it in 2015. The production quality is great, very few bugs (more on the few later) and overall does a great job keeping me at the edge of my seat. Deadspace uses all the tried and tested scary movie tricks such as audio spikes, lighting, flashes-of-monsters and shadows to great effect. This game tries to scare the #$%^ out of players and most would be lying if they managed their first playthough without getting caught out at least once.
The weapons and upgrade system work for the game. They tried really hard to not put any UI on the screen. Some players will hate it because that means there are no UI for health bar, stasis energy or crosshair. These are merged with the character model. Even inventory menus and maps come up as part of the character's holographic display. I find this method pretty immersive but yes at some camera angle, it does not work at all. Sometimes when combat gets hectic, you will have a hard time finding out how much health Issac (your character) still has.
One very important thing for steam players to know is that the Deadspace on steam has the difficulty bug that plagued this game's original release. No matter what difficulty you started your game in, it will revert to Medium difficulty. Some say it's due to the Continue feature, but trust me, i'd tried everything including editing the binary save but no matter what you do, it will go back to Medium. This could be a deal breaker for some, but I could live with it.
BTW I played this with Steamlink and SteamController. Do not use Steamlink if you can't connect your PC to your Steamlink with a LAN cable. Steamlink don't work so well over WiFi.

I saw that this game was on sale for Halloween.  Being a big fan of Halloween and enjoying the occasionally spooky game, I thought I'd buy this one.  I have played a little bit of the first Killing Floor game, but I didn't get into it.  I have, however, played a LOT of the Left 4 Dead games on PC and Xbox and I was pleasantly reminded of those old gaming experiences with this new game.
This is a fantastic "I want something easy to get into" game.  Solo play is fun and rewarding, multiplayer is fun but less predictable.  You can learn the controls easily but there is a LOT of content to explore with the numerous perks and loadout customizations.  I consider myself a casual gamer (I'm not min-maxing or strategizing much; for me, games are meant to be entertaining and fun first and foremost) and I'm not a competitive/intense person in general, but this game is thrilling and made me feel engaged in a way that other games haven't.
Pros:
-Controls are intuitive, easy to learn
-Great perk diversity
-Efficient gameplay (Not a lot of filler/wasted time)
-Customization options for game settings (number of waves, difficulty, etc.) and for build
-Solo is very playable and rewarding
Cons:
-Significant problems with matchmaking and being put into empty servers (Solution: Look through server list and join on that you like yourself)
P.S. For an early access game, KF2 is in great shape and will surely only get better as the devs continue their work!

Oh, how this game loves you... and hates you, too.
Oh, how at times its gameplay is masterful with such refined adeptness, but then so repetitively boring and frustrating. Oh, how the story is so intricate, nuanced, and deliciously brooding and yet full of cliche teen-angst and predictable-ness with ample clout for eye-rolling. Oh, how the visuals cascade your eyes with splendor, until the damn game crashes on you,... again.
I really love this game; I really hate this game, too. It's a crazy and yet totally sane dichotemy.
No spoilers ahead, but a few points to illustrate the above preamble.
1) Vehicle combat just blows. Sure, it's fine for about 30 minutes, but becomes such a chore late in the game, it completely detracts from the brilliance of being Batman. Did I mention being Batman is brilliant? Yes, it most certainly is. Unfortunately, this brilliance is marred by You being the Batmobile as much as You being the Batman. Point: the Batman is awesome; the Batmobile sucks.
2) The Arkham Knight, while a new character (sort-of) in the Batman cannon, is a lame♥♥♥♥♥villain, especially so when the plot finally culminates to his reveal. Even considering this is a video game based on a comic, the amazingly ludicrous lengths this character goes to annihilate the Batman (and where did he even get the money to invest in an ENTIRE army seemingly the size of North Korea's?), is borderline comical, especially once the 'reveal' happens. Color me critical, but I just can't look past the melodramatic teen-ansty-ness of the Arkham Knight. But! Minding this aside, the story is quite entertaining, with concise and to the point cutscenes that continually drive the momentum of the story (until the Arkham Knights talks...some more). It's as if the game appreciates your curiosity and intellect to piece together and predict the direction of the story to only slap you in the face with another bantering, banal commentary by the Arkham Knight. Point: the story is great; the Arkham Knight pretty much sucks.
3) This game is gorgeous. Like (and I usually don't start sentences with 'like') it's absolutely stunning. The character animations from lip-syncing to body-movement and fluidity of combat are simply phenominal (2015/2016 standards). Even though the game takes place at night, the city streets are dazingly detailed and there are so many nuanced atmospheric effects on screen, it's a relentless avalanche of visual-splendor. And yet, even after the debauched luanch over a year ago, the game crashes, and regularly. Sure, when it's running, it runs well, but I experienced a crash every 20 or so minutes of gameplay - far, FAR too often. Point: it's visually stunning; it also crashes A LOT!
So, how in the Gotham (notice I replaced 'world' with Gotham, because I'm clever) does this game fair? Well, despite its clear shortcomings, it's still oh-so-good... until it's oh-so-bad.
I can so recommend this game, until I don't want to anymore! I'm flummoxed. Perhaps you will be, too, or won't?!?

与えられる宇宙は小さく、そして逃げることを強いられる。
6種のクルー候補は能力の差異を保持しながら、運命共同体となる他ない。
宇宙船は特に戦闘に置いて的確なマネジメントを欲していて、
相手のバリアを貫通する攻撃を求めている。
船内に火がついたら減圧するか、人員を投入して消化作業にあたらせる必要があり、
設備が損傷したらクルーかドローンに直させなければならない。
もしそれがクリティカルな設備に複数起きてしまったら、例えば酸素なしでの
生存は不可能なように、緊急性の順序を学び対応しなければならない。
熟練したクルーを失うことは特に大きな損失だ。
もし戦闘に長けた種族が不意に乗り込んできたら、テレポーターで敵船に

困難は常にダメージとチャンスを孕み、過程は準備に過ぎない。
失敗こそがゲームの本懐で、成功は喪失と感じてしまうことに気付く。

Highly reccomended, especially if you remember the paper n' pencil, SNES or Genesis games.  Turn based combat, but the use of cover makes for good strategy.  AI tends to target the player, and it's one of those 'if the player goes down you lose, regardless if someone could save said player' which is a stupid bit of design that's been accepted as industry standard.
WARNING:  This is NOT a hand-holder, you CAN screw your build, and grinding is NOT an option.  Cash is scarce.  You must build practically, specializing in three areas:  Offence, primary role (this may be the same thing) and Survivability.  Think Fallout 1 & 2:  You can't do everything.  Thankfully, most of the time you can hire the help to do it for you.
There's a few bugs here and there, and the system could use a bit of polish.  Firearms specialists feel a bit overpowered compared to mages, but make no mistake:  magic is invaluable and you'll always want at least one magic user of some sort.  Hires in Dead Man's Switch seem to have been built before the system was tested.
Note that you won't likely to be able to recreate any characters from the paper and pencil game; the system just isn't the same.  Street Sam's can't have Wired Reflexes AND Dermal Plating for example, and the Wired Reflexes don't give extra AP passively like they did in previous editions.  Drain is replaced with cooldown (although casting from hitpoints remains an option).
Once you get the hang of the system however, it's well worth it.  Strong builds are rewarding, and certain builds allow soloing runs on Normal, but you'll never get so powerful you can afford to get cocky.
Fans of the console adaptions will be pleased, as there's plenty of shout-outs.  Highly replayable as well, due to the number of ways to solve situations depending on your build.
ADDITIONAL EDIT:  I cannot recommend the Dragonfall DLC highly enough!  It includes several improvments in game design and having experience from the first game shows.  While Dead Man's Switch is definitely a love letter to the SNES/Genesis games, Dragonfall adds more depth to the characters and feels more like a true RPG with the ability to talk to a regular set of runners inbetween runs.  It is also a vastly more satisfying experience and well worth its price because it's basically a separate game entirely.

If ever you played the original X-Com game, you'll remember that whilst being an amazingly fun piece of software to waste a good few hours on each session, the interface looked like♥♥♥♥♥and handled horribly.
X-Com: Enemy Unkown has taken this problem in hand and totally re-invented the interface, making gameplay a much smoother experience than it was before.
For the uninitiated - the idea behind the X-Com series is that aliens have invaded, and it's your job to lead a rag-tag team of scientists, soldiers and engineers (an organisation dubbed "X-Com") to defeat the aliens in a combination turn-based strategy and base-building game, training troops, fighting battles, building up your bases and researching new technologies along the way.
It was characterised by a combination of two things - firstly, the amazing amounts of detail and atmosphere that went into your team; individually named soldiers with (relatively) unique appearances, individual weapons customisation etc. made it feel like you were running a real operation staffed by real people, and watching all your little chumps gain XP, level up and (frequently) die permanently really made the experience a joy to behold.
The second thing that characterised X-Com was that it was very hard. Since gaining new materials and XP relied on fighting aliens in battle, the fact that encounters were all randomly generated often meant that, whilst the game did have an escalation element (only wheeling out the big lads in later levels), you could be left high and dry with inexperienced soldiers wielding pop guns against gigantic alien killing machines with laser rifles for nipples and plasma cannons for teeth. (Read: It could get very frustrating at times).
In 2012, however, Firaxis brought the series back to life - new 3D graphics, a re-designed interface and access to a wider array of weaponry and equipment loadouts, as well as special perks for levelled-up soldiers to really add that element of uniqueness and character to your team.
As well as being a much more highly-polished version of the original, Enemy Unkown retains the wonderful character and world-building elements of the first X-Com game; the turn-based battles are brilliant fun to play, combining both challenge and detail as well as showing off some truly intuitive games design in the process, and controlling your personal favourite squad of berks gets really absorbing when you've tweaked the moustaches and voices of each chap to make a really characterful squad.
The base-building is also a well engineered element of the game, as it is very quick and easy to operate, and doesn't play more of a part than it needs to, thus preventing things getting dull, and the same goes for scientific research and weapons engineering - the ability to just leave projects ticking over in the background whilst you go out to kick aliens in the teeth before coming back to base with looted alien alloys to make more laser guns with really does prove a most intuitive and entertaining cycle to be a part of.
The game isn't without a couple of faults, however.
The pain of random encounters is still prevalent, albeit not to as significant a degree as before, but you can still be left high and dry by a lack of encounters and end up trying to fight off huge alien bruisers with little more than a starting squad of crappy guys.
The other chief problem is that as the alien forces escalate relatively quickly, training new troops becomes somewhat irrelevant; if your A-Team is out in the field, you can survive maybe one guy getting turned into patè - perhaps two at a pinch, but in reality if your top squad gets significantly weakened you might as well just hit the restart button, as trying to train up a new squad of chumps fresh out of the barracks in a late-game scenario is damn-near impossible.
Despite this, however, X-Com: Enemy Unkown is a fantastic piece of game design; thoroughly absorbing, a joy to play and just generally an awesome time-sink, it's guaranteed to provide many happy hours of alien genocide.
Well worth a look if you're into sci-fi, turn-based strategy or micro-management.

As a species, humans have learned much about the many rules of Geometry. We make definitions, we draw pictures, we run experiments, we crunch numbers. Imagine if Geometry, by the same token, wished to learn about us humans, diverse and seemingly upredictable as we are. This game is that journey. Whereas we experimented with fragments of Geometry, like triangles, like circles, Geometry experiments of our species, like you, like me. When we conjectured rules about Geometry, we drew a picture, did some math, and tested it's consistency. When Geometry conjectures rules about humanity, it crafts a puzzle, does some math, and tests your consistency. Over time, using these experiments, we were able to prove many things about the Truths of Geometry, given some basic assumptions. Brainbending, and seemingly always to have some kind of overarching moral statement that is forever just beyond one's grasp, I am left wondering what it was that Geometry was proving about Humanity with this game, or what were it's basic assupions about us.

I wanted a game in which "running away" was the most legit method of dealing with a shambling hoard of flesh eating monsters.  I wanted a game where "but I can REACH that roof" was a fine method of escape.  I wanted a game where I was rewarded for intelligent behavior in a crisis, not reckless.
Behold:  Dying Light - a game that in less that 30 minutes did what my parents were unable to do for years (when I was younger and stupider):  enforce a GOD DAMNED CURFEW.
"XP is doubled at night!"  Yeah, I'll bet it is.  The game could seriously offer to rain down free AK-47s at night and I would still hoof my way back to a safehouse, crawl to my little soiled mattress, and hit the 'F' key to skip ahead to the morning every time.
This game is fun.  It has the right combination of survivalishness, FPSness, and Mirror's Edge.  You can fight the zombies - and are given tons of tools for doing so.  However, fighting the zombies is not your job.  Your job is to find crap, fix crap, and live to tell about it.  You'll have to skull thump a zombie here and there.  And there.  And again.  And AGAIN- STAY DOWN YOU CR- sorry, distracted.  But the real meat of the game is avoiding them.  The game is also not too cruel in your failing - if you do find yourself around a bunch of zombies, getting away isn't a trial.
... unless it is night.  At night, the SCARY zombies come out.  They're faster than you.  They leap higher than you.  I think some of them shoot lasers.  I'm not sure.  I think you can fight them too - again, I'm not sure.  I tried and one of them ate my face.  Then I tried running and another one ate my face.  Lots of face-eating.  You have to learn to distract, use your tools wisely, activate traps, and run your♥♥♥♥♥over to a safezone ASAP.  You're both forced to learn an area and think quickly.
Overall, it is pretty fun.  And pretty.  I haven't played for more than a few hours, but I still enjoy it.  So far I'm only venturing into single player - and let me tell you now, the story mode is... interesting.  Give it time.  Let it stupidly handicap you for an hour or so until you get your freedom.  Then?  Run.  Frolic.  LIVE!
Just be back before dark.

This game is probably one of the funniest and coolest RPGs I've ever played. I think before someone decides to buy it, however, there should be an understanding of what this game is and what it isn't.
First what it is:
1) This is a game that was made in collaboration with Matt and Trey and the quality of their work shows. The visuals are fantastic and it looks as if you were watching an episode of South Park. Exploring South Park is great because they included many of the landmarks that we've grown to love from the show and you can interact with almost every building. I would strongly suggest that you open as many doors as you can as there can be some uh...interesting surprises.
2) If you are a constant watcher of South Park and have seen most of the episodes, this game will be a treat in many different ways. I have found myself constantly having fun exploring every inch of South Park because there are a ton of references to earlier episodes. Some are subtle, like Cartman's CD's Faith Plus One which can be found in the drawer of his room, and others are very apparent such as the mouse with Mr. Garrison's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attached to his back. You can really tell how much the developers worked to get as much South Park memorabilia as possible. All this allows the game to become extremely interesting and does not make exploring a chore.
3) This is a game that you just need to go into expecting to have fun and not take anything too serious. The game mechanics and quests are relatively simple and I have not felt any frustration with this game (except the quest where you have to find Mr. Hanky's little nuggets). Every time I play this game I get nothing but enjoyment from the quality of the writing to amount of customization that the game gives you. This is a very nice thing about The Stick of Truth; the amount of customization that is allowed is phenomenal and much more than I expected. I started out with my character having dark hair and a suit. Now he has red hair and a flaming red beard with a bird nesting in it. The weapons look great and I have yet to find a generic looking item. Many times, in other games, you find items that look exactly the same and it is only when you find a rarer item that the items look unique. That's not the story with this game. Every time I get a new item I have a blast checking it out and seeing how it looks as it's always a funny item or something that is totally unique to South Park. You can also modify your "weapons" (a stick, crutches, an alien probing machine) by adding something like runes to them that give them higher stats.
What the game is not:
1) Don't come into this game expecting a traditional RPG like the older Final Fantasy games or other notable JRPGs. It seems that many people expected this to be a somewhat serious RPG that would play like others before it. That is definitely not this. As mentioned before, this is a lighthearted RPG that focuses more on providing an authentic South Park experience rather than being the next Skyrim or Final Fantasy.
2) This is not a lengthy game that will take 50+ hours to complete. I finished this game in about 20 hours but that is because I did every side quest and tried to find all Chinpokomon. If you only do the main story line then the game will be much shorter. I strongly suggest that you do as many side quests as possible because not only are they super fun, but you get the chance to get additional characters which you can summon in fights (except boss fights) such as Jesus Christ, Mr. Hanky, Mr. Slave, Tuong Lu Kim, etc.
3) This is not a fantasy game like traditional RPGs which will emerge you in a world of magic. One of the most humorous things about this game is that you will be constantly reminded by both the kids and adults of South Park that you are playing a game. When you are learning the controls at first, Cartman admits that you must take turns attacking to which Clyde replies, "that's lame," resulting in Cartman acknowledging that it's lame but that's what the rules are. There are other times when you are walking around South Park and adults will say, "you know you're never gonna get laid dressing up like that," or some kids will say, "you're not playing that stupid game too are you?" I've heard several people complain that this somehow hurts the immersion but it really shouldn't, as this is South Park and it wouldn't feel like it if it was too serious.
Overall I really enjoyed this game. It's finally a game which does justice to South Park and which fans of the show will truly enjoy. That being said, if you don't really like South Park or have only seen a few episodes, this might be a little more difficult to enjoy as you might not understand many of the references and hidden objects that pop out. If you're on the fence about it, just watch a few videos and check out the game play and see if it's something you can see yourself enjoying

So i've played all of the Arkham games and I must say, half of the game is just so disappointing, and the other half is really good and a great improvement from the past games.
Pros:
+ Has the same Arkham feel and formula, but it improves and adds upon it:
Everything feels 100% exactly the same, which is a good thing mind you! The combat, the flying, the skill tree, the gadgets. All is there, all controls and feels the same, etc.
There's some new gadgets, not a lot, and none too interesting, but still additions nonetheless. You can grapnel boost higher, smash through windows, throw batarangs mid-flight, and most importantly, there's many more moves and combos you can pull off. If you can master all the different moves and combos, you can pull off some really stylish looking hits, which makes playing as Batman feel even more badass and even more like Batman.
The animations are also very smooth most of the time. Yes, Batman can still magically roll 15 feet within a second to punch another enemy, but most of the time, every counter, ever double takedown, hell, even triple takedowns look so natural and seamlessly happen during combat.
+ Graphics:
I usually don't factor graphics into my opinion on a game, but the graphics in this game are so insane that i'd actually consider it a selling point. The rains effects are really good. The way you can see each individual drop hit your head and your cape, the way it looks on the ground, and the way it hits the side of building looks really really good.
The shaders, the lighting, and the level of detail on every character is just insane. And don't even get me started on the water. Just look at the ocean. The waves are huge and move so realistically. Best looking water in a game ever, and yes, i'd say this is the second best looking game (unmodded) next to Battlefront EVER.
+ Gotham City is 4x times larger:
The map is much bigger. Gotham City is finally of respectable size. It could've had maybe one more island in there to really seal the deal, but it's still a major improvement over City.
Arkham City was too small and felt "bordered" if you get me. Blackgate being in the center ruined it because it just created an invisible wall that ruined traversal. It just felt very claustrophobic, all the buildings were short, there wasn't anything to see, and the buildings were too densely packed .
This however, has three and a half islands, all well sized, spread openly with no obstructions (besides neighboring buildings), and most importantly, has a lot of iconic Batman landmarks like Falcone Shipping, Wayne Tower, Ace Chemicals, Lex Corp, etc. These said buildings are really high which makes Gotham City feel like a proper Gotham City.
Now onto the negatives of the game...
Cons:
- Long, drawn out, and terrible story:
The story is the same crap. Most of Gotham has conveniently evacuated, big bad villains have taken over, yata yata. That's all fine and dandy I guess, but just pointing out that it's nothing original.
As far as it being drawn out, well, it is. It goes on for about 20 hours which is too long in my opinion. Especially considering there's a fair amount of filler in the story (more on this later.)
Basically, the Arkham Knight is some "new" (not really) "mysterious" (not really) villain who knows who Batman is and wants to kill him. Not gonna spoil who he is, but it's VERY easy to tell who he is if you've read the comics, especially Death in the family (which is not canon to Arkham Knight, but similar backstories with a certain someone. Not trying to spoil it if I can help it!)
- Batmobile is overused to the point where it's almost a joke:
*In my opinion, the overuse of the Batmobile does NOT make the game unplayable like people say, nor is it AS overused as you might think, but it is still VERY overused. Just not every other mission or anything like that*
To add to my disclaimer, it is overused way too much. It's an awesome and welcomed addition to the Arkham games, but I feel like doubling it up as a tank ruined the game too much. There are way too many moments where Batman or a civilian is stuck in a rut, and the Batmobile acts as a Deus Ex machina to save the day.
Getting shot by tanks? Have no fear, Batmobile is here! Here's some mindless tank battles with unmanned tanks. Need to get past an obstruction? Have no fear, Batmobile is here! Here's a tow cable that will conveniently tear the wall down, or solve some puzzle.
It feels like the game is parodying itself. I find it hilarious.
Also, the Deathstroke boss fight is a god damn tank battle. I have to spoil this because you can't get your hopes up for a boss fight against one of the coolest Batman villains unfortunately. Shame, because the Deathstroke boss fight in Origins was the best boss fight in any of the Arkham Games.
Overall, the tank battles are filler and copouts for actual well designed boss fights.
- Side quests take the Ubisoft route:
What I mean by this is they took the lazy route to the side quests and just copy and pasted the same exact objective for each side quest 15-20 times over. There's those Farcry inspired outposts, (which are poorly designed for both predator and open fights), more filler cannon fodder tank battles to engage in to clean up Gotham, etc.
Even the side quests with actual villains are the same thing. For the Firefly missions, all you do is put out a fire, chase Firefly, take him down, and he gets away. Same exact thing for Man bat. See him flying, go after him, take him down, inject him with whatever, and he flies away. I know the side quests in Arkham City were all the same formular to a degree, but this is just more of that lazy game design in this game.
- They somehow managed to make the Joker return, and it feels SO ham fisted:
Don't get me wrong, I love the joker, I think Mark Hamill does a great job voice acting him (this game included), but it's poorly executed, and very intrusive to the main story.
It's poorly executed because he shows up around every corner. even during important moments that have nothing to do with him. He just never shuts up, It's distracting, and while he's well voice acted like I said, Rocksteady have found a way to make me despise him. Might be because he's in all four of the Arkham games?
Maybe some verbal interaction between Batman and Joker would've been nice, but no. He's just there and Batman is a mute.  If Batman talked to him, this could've given them the opportunity to at least give a little exposition on the Arkhamverse lore.
Joker was great in Asylum and City, but he DIED at the end of City. We need to move on from him now.
- Arkham Knight is poorly voice acted:
Despite being voiced by Troy Baker, he just sounds like some hacker nerd with an inferiority complex. I liked the way he was voiced during the scene where Batman reveals the Arkham Knight's identity, but that's just one several minute long cutscene.
Conclusion:
All in all, I think it's pretty good. Many improvements, but also, there are some major things that ruin the game. It had the potential to be the best Arkham game, but it failed. I will still recommend it because it's a nice improvement from the previous games, and it's not bad to the point where an Arkham fan should skip playing it.
It is definitely worth getting in 2016.
It's $29.99 now, $14.99 if you can get it on sale. You will get your money's worth. As far as optimization is concerned, it's definitely gotten better, but there's still stutters and wonky framerate fluctuations. This sounds very damage controlling of me to say, but it looks better than the PS4 version, so it's fine in my opinion, especially considering the amazing graphics and the low price.
Strong 7/10, definitely buy if you love the Arkham games and need your Batman fix, but it's a letdown nonetheless. Cheap price should make it a LITTLE more acceptable.

At its core,
is a casual, story-driven RPG. More so than any other modern RPG, this game is driven on writing rather than any gameplay mechanics. And since this is South Park we're talking about, the writing consists of much shock humor and repeated WTF moments. In fact, I've come to accept that the game is so defined by its writing that any attempt at gameplay analysis is ultimately moot.

Early on in my first playthrough, I thought I had discovered the optimal configuration of weapons, equipment and patches that would allow me to break the game wide open. Then I realized this was NOT
and such efforts were ultimately in vain. This is not a challenging game, even at Hardcore difficulty. The greatest mistake I made was searching the internet for that twelfth Timmy express flag and learning more than I wanted about the story. Whenever you read ahead, you lose the most important thing this game has to offer.

There is little point in guides and walkthroughs in the first place. I suspect that
made it easy for you specifically so you don't feel the compulsion to search out secrets on the internet in the first place. On a second playthrough and for achievement purposes, sure! But it's not entirely inaccurate to call
an extended interactive episode of South Park where you are the hero. Except that it prompts the question: who pays 40 bucks for an interactive movie? This is strictly a Steam Sale purchase; put it on your wishlist, avoid all spoilers and wait.

So, is it funny? Well YMMV but on the whole I'd pretty much say yes. You don't have to be a South Park aficionado to appreciate the game and this is coming from someone who hates the politics of the series. The in-jokes are mostly relegated to the articles of vendor trash you pick up across your journey and without giving anything away, the humor mostly comes from trope lampshading, many instances of WTF, a dedicated fart button and boss fight music.

I really,
wish you could do more with the combat system. There's a majority of enemy encounters that can be eliminated through clever interaction with the environment... but that just feels like cheating yourself out of more gaming content! You never have more than one party member at a time and can't even modify their stats/equipment, making for an extremely single character-centric RPG. Some people might have no patience for party management but this game is lacking in substance already, so any opportunity for customization would be welcome.

I'd still recommend purchasing this game (20 bucks seems like a fair price) and experiencing it for yourself rather than following a Let's Play. There's plenty to discover in your small secluded mountain town and it's obvious that the developers spent a lot of time stuffing the whole place with secrets. South Park's distinctive "cutout" animation style and bright colors lends well to RPGs, making it easy to pick out which object you can interact with and the radial battle menu makes for clean, intuitive battles. Shallow as it is,
makes for an accessible RPG.
Just don't do like I did and buy the DLC. It's all level 2 equipment which you quickly outgrow into irrelevance. Speaking of which, I think it's relevant to say that the "treasure location" panel on the world map is bugged, just so you don't go wasting 20 minutes searching for nonexistent items. Apart from all that, you're fine.

With the performance issues resolved, I can finally play this.
Of the Arkham trilogy (Origins doesn't count), Arkham Knight seems to be the Return of the Jedi.  That sounds rather harsh (and I liked Jedi), but following up Asylum and City, it had a lot to live up to - and while it ended up pretty damn good in my eyes, I don't think it reached the heights of the first two games.
Knight's big(ger than City's) open world and the Batmobile were the main attractions for the game, and both are factors in the game's excellence and faults.  The game tries to do everything Asylum and City did, add yet even more, and, to their credit, did not try to make any of it shallow.  It accomplishes this very well, but, in a way, all the things seem to get in the way of each other.  Too many gadgets, most of them dumped on you from the start.  Too many fight tech, causing me to forget about some when I don't use them for a good while in the game.  The Batmobile takes a good while to get used to, as it handles very uniquely (I can't even think of another game to compare it to).
All the chaos of the streets of Gotham thrown at Batman seems to reflect the amount things the game itself throws at you from the beginning.  This runs counter to how perfectly Asylum flowed, and how City followed up.  Where those games were solid, Knight seems a little shaky.  Thankfully, not too shaky.
There's some dumb Call of Duty-esque non-gameplay, pseudo-interactive sections here and there - especially at the beginning - but that is only a tiny bit of a 50+ hour game, luckily.
Overall, I highly recommend.  My criticisms of the game feel like nitpicks, because of the two Rocksteady Batman games it follows, but that doesn't stop it from being an excellent game, and end to this series.

As a species, humans have learned much about the many rules of Geometry. We make definitions, we draw pictures, we run experiments, we crunch numbers. Imagine if Geometry, by the same token, wished to learn about us humans, diverse and seemingly upredictable as we are. This game is that journey. Whereas we experimented with fragments of Geometry, like triangles, like circles, Geometry experiments of our species, like you, like me. When we conjectured rules about Geometry, we drew a picture, did some math, and tested it's consistency. When Geometry conjectures rules about humanity, it crafts a puzzle, does some math, and tests your consistency. Over time, using these experiments, we were able to prove many things about the Truths of Geometry, given some basic assumptions. Brainbending, and seemingly always to have some kind of overarching moral statement that is forever just beyond one's grasp, I am left wondering what it was that Geometry was proving about Humanity with this game, or what were it's basic assupions about us.

This was the first "major" kickstarter campaign I funded that came to fruition, and the first one where I can honestly say "money well invested".
For it's limited budget and short development time, the game delivers exactly what it intended to. Solid, old school roleplaying in a well-loved setting. It catches the atmosphere and the "feel" of the universe just perfectly IMO. The graphic style and looks are superb for me.
The initial campaign is short, but very well done. It has a wonderful "detective noir" flair in the first act, many references for old shadowrun players and readers, and some pretty interesting battles, none of which feel like filler material just there to increase game time. The second act is a bit more linear, but still well written and with some very satisfying runs.
The tactical turn-based combat is interesting, though not perfect yet, but it beats most modern RPG hackfests hands down. The interface is a bit too "tablet style" for my taste, as is the inventory system.
The intitial save game system was bad, no doubt about that. But that has been corrected with the latest patch and Dragonfall expansion.
The original campaign is pretty short (about 12 hours for a thorough playthrough), but I take quality over quantity any time. And as a Kickstarter backer I got Dragonfall for free, and that campaign is simply excellent!
All in all, I'd rate it an 8/10. More than worth the price on both the main game and the Dragonfall expansion. Extremely cheap if you consider all the user-made content available.

This game is probably one of the funniest and coolest RPGs I've ever played. I think before someone decides to buy it, however, there should be an understanding of what this game is and what it isn't.
First what it is:
1) This is a game that was made in collaboration with Matt and Trey and the quality of their work shows. The visuals are fantastic and it looks as if you were watching an episode of South Park. Exploring South Park is great because they included many of the landmarks that we've grown to love from the show and you can interact with almost every building. I would strongly suggest that you open as many doors as you can as there can be some uh...interesting surprises.
2) If you are a constant watcher of South Park and have seen most of the episodes, this game will be a treat in many different ways. I have found myself constantly having fun exploring every inch of South Park because there are a ton of references to earlier episodes. Some are subtle, like Cartman's CD's Faith Plus One which can be found in the drawer of his room, and others are very apparent such as the mouse with Mr. Garrison's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attached to his back. You can really tell how much the developers worked to get as much South Park memorabilia as possible. All this allows the game to become extremely interesting and does not make exploring a chore.
3) This is a game that you just need to go into expecting to have fun and not take anything too serious. The game mechanics and quests are relatively simple and I have not felt any frustration with this game (except the quest where you have to find Mr. Hanky's little nuggets). Every time I play this game I get nothing but enjoyment from the quality of the writing to amount of customization that the game gives you. This is a very nice thing about The Stick of Truth; the amount of customization that is allowed is phenomenal and much more than I expected. I started out with my character having dark hair and a suit. Now he has red hair and a flaming red beard with a bird nesting in it. The weapons look great and I have yet to find a generic looking item. Many times, in other games, you find items that look exactly the same and it is only when you find a rarer item that the items look unique. That's not the story with this game. Every time I get a new item I have a blast checking it out and seeing how it looks as it's always a funny item or something that is totally unique to South Park. You can also modify your "weapons" (a stick, crutches, an alien probing machine) by adding something like runes to them that give them higher stats.
What the game is not:
1) Don't come into this game expecting a traditional RPG like the older Final Fantasy games or other notable JRPGs. It seems that many people expected this to be a somewhat serious RPG that would play like others before it. That is definitely not this. As mentioned before, this is a lighthearted RPG that focuses more on providing an authentic South Park experience rather than being the next Skyrim or Final Fantasy.
2) This is not a lengthy game that will take 50+ hours to complete. I finished this game in about 20 hours but that is because I did every side quest and tried to find all Chinpokomon. If you only do the main story line then the game will be much shorter. I strongly suggest that you do as many side quests as possible because not only are they super fun, but you get the chance to get additional characters which you can summon in fights (except boss fights) such as Jesus Christ, Mr. Hanky, Mr. Slave, Tuong Lu Kim, etc.
3) This is not a fantasy game like traditional RPGs which will emerge you in a world of magic. One of the most humorous things about this game is that you will be constantly reminded by both the kids and adults of South Park that you are playing a game. When you are learning the controls at first, Cartman admits that you must take turns attacking to which Clyde replies, "that's lame," resulting in Cartman acknowledging that it's lame but that's what the rules are. There are other times when you are walking around South Park and adults will say, "you know you're never gonna get laid dressing up like that," or some kids will say, "you're not playing that stupid game too are you?" I've heard several people complain that this somehow hurts the immersion but it really shouldn't, as this is South Park and it wouldn't feel like it if it was too serious.
Overall I really enjoyed this game. It's finally a game which does justice to South Park and which fans of the show will truly enjoy. That being said, if you don't really like South Park or have only seen a few episodes, this might be a little more difficult to enjoy as you might not understand many of the references and hidden objects that pop out. If you're on the fence about it, just watch a few videos and check out the game play and see if it's something you can see yourself enjoying

A wonderful RPG, even if the campaign in the base game does it's best to try to convince you otherwise. While many of the major technical and design flaws have been excised, the base campaign is still plagued by level and story design that feels like it's just stringing you along from one too-long fight to the next. It doesn't help that your words, skills, and actions also have very little effect on either the conversation or the campaign level. It's not bad per-say, but I didn't feel terribly invested in the story or characters.
The DLC expansion "Dragonfall" however is excellent and is everything that the base campaign should have been. It's significantly better designed, with far stronger writing, level design, and campaign structure. In the first hour, I had a far better sense of who my character was, where I was in the world, and was invested in narrative. The world feels much more vibrant and dynamic (even though there's quite a bit of illusion of false choice as is typical of the genre) than the base game.
I very highly reccomend that you purchase dragonfall along with the base game. In my opinion, the $30 price of entry for both is a better value than $15 for just the base game. The difference in quality between the two campaigns is stark, and it's very likely you'll bore yourself about a third of the way through the base game and never think to pick up the DLC if you don't buy both and you'd miss out on a great RPG.
It's also worth noting that the game has workshop support and is very friendly for creating user-made content including adventures and campaigns ala the original Neverwinter Nights. While I have not tried any of these yet, the content available looks quite promising.

At its core,
is a casual, story-driven RPG. More so than any other modern RPG, this game is driven on writing rather than any gameplay mechanics. And since this is South Park we're talking about, the writing consists of much shock humor and repeated WTF moments. In fact, I've come to accept that the game is so defined by its writing that any attempt at gameplay analysis is ultimately moot.

Early on in my first playthrough, I thought I had discovered the optimal configuration of weapons, equipment and patches that would allow me to break the game wide open. Then I realized this was NOT
and such efforts were ultimately in vain. This is not a challenging game, even at Hardcore difficulty. The greatest mistake I made was searching the internet for that twelfth Timmy express flag and learning more than I wanted about the story. Whenever you read ahead, you lose the most important thing this game has to offer.

There is little point in guides and walkthroughs in the first place. I suspect that
made it easy for you specifically so you don't feel the compulsion to search out secrets on the internet in the first place. On a second playthrough and for achievement purposes, sure! But it's not entirely inaccurate to call
an extended interactive episode of South Park where you are the hero. Except that it prompts the question: who pays 40 bucks for an interactive movie? This is strictly a Steam Sale purchase; put it on your wishlist, avoid all spoilers and wait.

So, is it funny? Well YMMV but on the whole I'd pretty much say yes. You don't have to be a South Park aficionado to appreciate the game and this is coming from someone who hates the politics of the series. The in-jokes are mostly relegated to the articles of vendor trash you pick up across your journey and without giving anything away, the humor mostly comes from trope lampshading, many instances of WTF, a dedicated fart button and boss fight music.

I really,
wish you could do more with the combat system. There's a majority of enemy encounters that can be eliminated through clever interaction with the environment... but that just feels like cheating yourself out of more gaming content! You never have more than one party member at a time and can't even modify their stats/equipment, making for an extremely single character-centric RPG. Some people might have no patience for party management but this game is lacking in substance already, so any opportunity for customization would be welcome.

I'd still recommend purchasing this game (20 bucks seems like a fair price) and experiencing it for yourself rather than following a Let's Play. There's plenty to discover in your small secluded mountain town and it's obvious that the developers spent a lot of time stuffing the whole place with secrets. South Park's distinctive "cutout" animation style and bright colors lends well to RPGs, making it easy to pick out which object you can interact with and the radial battle menu makes for clean, intuitive battles. Shallow as it is,
makes for an accessible RPG.
Just don't do like I did and buy the DLC. It's all level 2 equipment which you quickly outgrow into irrelevance. Speaking of which, I think it's relevant to say that the "treasure location" panel on the world map is bugged, just so you don't go wasting 20 minutes searching for nonexistent items. Apart from all that, you're fine.

A cool RPG looking back to the good old days of legendary isometric games like Fallout 1 & 2 - but Shadowrun Returns suffer from modern stupification in aspects of linearity and complexity. Another game that would go from 7/10 to 9/10 by dropping all the mobile device/console porting crap and instead focusing on making a solid complex game for players that use a keyboard and mouse input... The interface is quite clunky but does it's job kind of ok, but simple things like the lack of a proper inventory management on quests and weird vendor buy/sell dialogue makes me MAD!
The main story module "Dead mans switch" is extremely linear and side quests are few. As an RPG heavily focused on combat it still has a solid story and memorable characters, all dialogue being text based makes for a huge variety in dialogue options that is sadly not always used to create a more complex story. Things like the stat based etiquette system works nicely but could really be more developed and used often. Although personally I prefer Arkham City over Knight, Knight has gotten a lot better since its very rocky PC release.
Note: I condensed the two categories into the top 3 for each.
The Good:
- The map is at least 4x as large as City
- Rocksteady took cues from their partner, WB Games (Arkham Origins) in adding some new combat features and special takedown moves, as well as many other things
- The story is much deeper than any of the previous Arkham games, and it actually gets to the point where you start feeling emotional for Batman/Bruce Wayne.
The Bad:
- Mindless Bat-Tank sections where you just repeatedly launch missiles at incoming drones
- Capped FPS, but you can go as high as 90fps
- Meaningless Batmobile chase scenes as filler content
Overall, I'd say to pick this game up on a sale, but only if you've played either of the previous games. Arkham Knight contains story spoilers for both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City.

I will attempt to keep this as concise as possible while still being
1: The graphics look older than many games and yet it can be surprisingly good looking on some maps (e.g. Volter Manor) and graphics matter less as it is fairly fast paced and you are not likely to be closely examining the wall textutures although the rather prolific blood textures can look a noticeably poor at times.
2: The maps are complex and varied, while still being surprisingly easy to navigate.
3: The matchmaking system as of now doesn't work but the server browser has decent filtering options and well populated server meaning it is not too difficult to find a game.
4: The enemies are visibly different and varied in their attacks with even the lesser mobs being able to kill you if they catch you off guard.
5: The gameplay is more akin to counter strike global offensive than left 4 dead. The goal is to survive the waves of various zombies that are sent against you If at least one of you survives them all you win if all of you die you lose. This allows for tense, fast paced combat while needing some strategy to survive.
6: The classes are determined by levellable perks that you are free to change at any time. As of yet i have not had time to play them all but some are definetly more fun than others and a common problem with the ones I've had a chance to play is that weapons seem to empty fast and you spend alot of time desperatly trying not to die while reloading.
Overall Killing Floor 2 is an intriguing game that only needs a little polish to turn it into the next Co-op masterpiece. It's not perfect, The matchmaking is not yet functional and it has a few balancing issues but is still a strong contender for the next Left 4 Dead!

This game has been one of my favorite games for years now, because it has such perfect atmosphere and sound. Horror video games today in my opinion just do not really "pop" anymore. Games filled with jump scares at every corner becomes a bore, because everything is expected after awhile.
Now, Dead Space on the other hand is a gem, it provides horror through both suspense, gruesome imagery and of course the wonderful sound provided. Things like scratching, or roaring from necromorphs always used to terrify me when I began playing this in my early teens. I used to have trouble playing this if it wasn't morning time, or if there weren't enough light on  in my living room. I don't see many games today that are as interesting as Dead Space or any of the games made after it (I wish Dead Space 3 was on here). The Dead Space universe is very insightful and interesting, and I have always loved the main protagonist //especially in the later games.
The game is rather gory. If you can't handle things like that, I would recommend you not torture yourself, since Isaac has several different disturbing ways of dying in this game.
Now for the most important part, I find this game incredibly fun. Playing in the dark with friends at your side during this game is probably the most fun from this game i can remember having- especially if your friends don't know about Dead Space and some of the scares that come with it :).
The shooting is exceptional, and most of the guns are fun to use, though I usually just use the Plasma Cutter and the Line Gun. Also, new outfits can be used, with better rig and protection, so it is fun to try and save up for a new look. I highly recommend getting the third game if you enjoy Dead Space, even though it is not on steam. It is a multiplayer game, and it is certainly worth wasting hundreds of hours on with friends. It isn't as scary as this one is... but the multiplayer aspects make up for it.
I definitely recommend using a controller for this game, I feel that a mouse will not provide the sensitivity that a controller could, since i first played this game on xbox and i was already used to the controls and all. /:
Also... try not to give up on the most frustrating part of the game, AKA the asteroid mini game of hell. It is pretty ridiculous.

If you're a fan of the show, then the game's a safe purchase. It captures the look and feel of the show perfectly and plays like an extended episode, with cameos from a lot of its best characters.
It plays like a JRPG, with turned based battles that start out simple but hide a deceptive amount of depth. While some of the sidequests feel a little repetitive and can drag on, the story keeps you going forward. There's also some replay value to the game, with 4 different character classes, a good amount of character customization options, the choice of your in-game buddy (which you can change on the fly) and branching paths for some of the missions.
But best of all, the game is genuinely funny. Constantly. Its writing (and voice work) are top notch, and the jokes are consistently great and true to the show's atmosphere.
It's South Park successfully distilled into a game, and it's well worth your time (and money).

Turn-based cyberpunk fun.
Fantastic writing, great art (the player and NPC portraits are full of character and style), and flexible character development (mix magic and hacking, summoning and swordplay, or any other interesting combination of skills that seems cool to you). Do yourself a favor and play it on Hard or Very Hard to get the most enjoyment out of the strategic combat system. The main drawback is the linearity of the base campaign (Dead Man's Switch), but the story is enteraining enough that it's a minor complaint, imo.
Environments are interactive in various ways depending on your skills -- for example, leylines and sources of elemental spirits can be tapped by casters, and various terrain can be used as cover during combat to raise defenses.
The DLC campaign, Dragonfall, greatly builds on every enjoyable aspect of the base game as well as broadening the scope of the world. More sidequests, more interesting characters, more player choices, and more gritty Shadowrun atmosphere and story (along with several different endings).
There is also an extensive library of player-designed campaigns, made via the built-in content creator tools, after you finish the two official ones. Or you can try your hand making scenarios of your own. Totally worth the price, though I'd highly recommend getting Dragonfall too, since the base game feels rather short and linear on it's own.

Shadowrun Returns: Wow! what went wrong? First off even though this is marketed for the PC it is not a PC game. It is a tablet game that will run on a PC. The obvious flaws of which range from the horribly cumbersome UI to the constant loading of small maps meant to save RAM. Perhaps this could be overcome by an entertaining story, or indepth RPG system. Unfortunately Shadowrun Returns contains nether. The story is bland and generic, the characters dull, and the so called dialog options for the user seem result in the exact same outcome. This coupled with the fact that there is so much story in the campaign that one would spend more time clicking though unimportant text boxes rather than taking part in action makes makes the game feel full of filler material. Lets face it writing is cheaper than programming and the creators highly exploited this fact. Speaking of action: think XCOM with Down's Syndrome. No real thought to it, its just there. Don't expect strategy, just put up with it so you can read some more text. The supposed payoff is the leveling system. Being this is a tablet game there is a generic number line which you can add generic points to generic skills in order to do the same thing you could do before, but slightly better. Nothing innovative, nothing entertaining, nothing worth paying for. The most amazing thing about Shadowrun Returns is that that it was released ten years after its genesis predecessor and is somehow still a huge step backwards. This becomes even more amazing when you consider the highly sucessful kickstarter campaign it had and it was still released with a high price tag. Bravo Harebrained Schemes! <Begin slow clap> I say again: Bravo! You really got us good. Not only did you scam a bunch of long time Shadowrun fans, but you managed to significantly bruise kickstarters reputation with the gaming community. I am actually quite impressed that you pulled it off so easily. Enjoy spending all that money.

Linear BEV solo(offline) RPG.  With that said, worth about 12 hours of entertainment if you're into the genre.  Be you a street tough cyberer'd Samurai dicing up thugs with your sword, or an elite decker hacking the matrix to make your Nuyen.  Nostalgic fans will enjoy a shadowrun leveling system with a few new tweaks.
There may be a few flaws.  There's little replay value in the campaign, as the storyline pushes you through with almost no sandboxing.  The game gives you freedom to pick your shadowrunners, yet seems to lack a certain feel of customization and increasing gains like most other RPG types.  No real stopping to grind out some shadowruns for Mr. Johnsons as in previous video game incarnations.  Some obvious bugs and crashes, but nothing to get too worked up over.
All in all, a pretty decent reboot.  (P.S. the deluxe version doesn't include an additional campaign - just some soundtracks & PDF text)

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a fantastic turn based strategy game that balances depth and complexity with intuitive and understandable systems. Each class feels important and useful, and the process for upgrading your squad's gear makes you feel accomplished and awesome.
The difficulty levels are well implemented, allowing strategy newbies to easily get the feel for the game on the lower two difficulties before tackling the challenging Classic and Impossible difficulties.
There are a few hitches here and there, between some awkward camera management for multi-level structures and accidental door breaches due to some oddities in the UI, but overall the game plays like a charm.

This game is freaking awesome. A cyberpunk game with the same story telling potential as Dragon Age? Turne-Based combat that isn't a complete drag on the action? An excellent digital rendition of the Shadowrun system? All present and accounted for.

“Faster than light” is one of the oddest examples of an indie game. With its major success on
, it has made itself into a game that should turn some heads. You are the unlucky star captain of a spaceship, in charge with the mission of delivering an important message to the front line, all while the rebel fleet is chasing you. You system hop from one planet to another, while encountering random events that will most likely end in your painful death. The game is one of the most difficult games you could pick up, you will die, you’ll die and die and die and DIE…but for some reason, it’s ok.  The game features a permanent death system, which makes any loss on your team almost a devastating experience. But while this game may be difficult, you will feel yourself drawn into playing another new game in the hopes of doing better the next time. FTL should be game to consider, and for the price that steam has it at, you have no excuse.

Players step into the boots of Isaac Clarke, a systems engineer that's part of the dispatched maintenance crew. Outside of fixing the communications issues, Isaac has a number of reasons for arriving on the Ishimura -- he has a number of friends that are stationed on the ship, including someone very special to him that sends an urgent holovid with a few cryptic messages before she disappears. Unfortunately for Isaac and his crew, shortly after they arrive on board the crippled vessel, all hell breaks loose. Their craft is destroyed, leaving them stranded on the Ishimura. The crew is attacked by nightmarish creatures known as Necromorphs, who kill most of Isaac's team and separate him from the surviving members. Even worse, the ship and its systems have started to be corrupted or are failing thanks to the Necromorphic infestation. It's up to Isaac to wander the halls, search for any friends or survivors that are still alive, and fix as many problems as he can until he can find a way to escape the ship, which can take you 12 or more hours to complete.
- Jeff Haynes

Great South Park humor,  a surprisingly epic story, and excellent and engaging gameplay. I'm thoroughly enjoying every minute. This might net me strange looks, but I LOVE the UI design in the menus (inventory, quests, etc) - it's simple but effective and has a great feel to it.
The two biggest complaints I've seen are the length and the difficulty. The length is naturally very dependent on how you play the game. I've been taking my time and enjoying myself and I expect I'll be in the 25-30 hour range for the first playthrough. Personally I feel the 4 different classes offer some replayability, and I'm definitely enjoying the game enough to want to give it another go when I'm finished.
As many avid gamers will point out, the game isn't particularly difficult even on Hardcore difficulty. It's clear the game was designed to be managable for casuals, and dedicated players who collect all the gear and think about their character setup will find combat rather easy. This can be a little frustrating but there's plenty you can do to make things more challenging. I want my character to have a very specific look, so I'm using ♥♥♥♥♥♥ equipment that looks the way I want but doesn't give me much in terms of stats or bonuses. Not only does this let me control the appearance of my character better, it helps level the playing field and makes the game more challenging. I also recommend forgoing the use of consumables in combat, as they can easily unbalance things in your favor.
If you're at all interested in this, I very highly recommend giving it a go. I think the retail price is a little steep but $30 is definitely worth it and anything lower is a steal.

My review compares Killing Floor 2 to Left 4 Dead 2 as those are the two leading titles in zombie fps and I imagine many people who are interested in Killing Floor 2 came here as a result of playing Left 4 Dead 2 and other similar zombie and or fps titles.
I break PVE FPS games down into 4 basic categories of rating -
Enemies - (Quality and realism of design)
Weapons - (Quality and realism of design)
Gameplay - (Overall control, range of available abilities and different strategies for gameplay)
Storyline - (Effective implimentation of stories and scenarios that develop and progress in a way that does not lose the players interest)
You could argue Killing Floor 2 is better in 3/4 categories: enemies, weapons and gameplay are all superior to that of Left 4 Dead 2.  Killing Floor has more weapons and they're more realistic and detailed.  Killing Floor has more realistic looking zombies that are more cringe worthy and gross as well as more overall gore and blood without being tacky about it. Finally, the play style of Killing Floor can range from as simple as Left 4 Dead to very complicated with a requirement for refined strategy to stay alive.  With fast reflexes and some FPS experience you can play Left 4 Dead on its hardest difficulty without much need to learn or adapt, on the hardest difficulty of Killing Floor it doesn't matter what your skills are you have to learn and refine a strategy to staying alive which often means working in cooperation with and relying on teammates who also must know the strategies and be good at FPS. This gameplay aspect is a big + for Killing Floor as it adds a scaling difficulty to the game which entices people to grind play the game and build groups etc for end game/high skill content. Left 4 dead is majorly void of that dynamic.
Left 4 Dead only wins in the storyline category with their campaign style scenarios built into the levels you really get an unmatched feeling of being in a zombie apocolypse.
After playing over 48 hours of this goddamn game, I have still yet to beat the final level. 10/10 would recommend.

Now, to the nitty gritty.
FTL : Faster Than Light is a roguelike in space. If you don't know what a roguelike is, it's a truly random adventure. Nothing is constant, and every new game is a reset algorithm where nothing is guaranteed.
Well, one thing is guaranteed.
You. Will. Die. (Seriously.)
This game is unforgiving with its random generation. You could lose crew members to spiders, asteroids, or diseases. And it's gonna suck.
But when you get a new crew member from liberating a slaver ship, then it's gonna ROCK.
And yes, there is luck involved. It's a roguelike, so that's always a factor. People have won the war eight nor nine times.
I only did it once. I still love this game.
Get it, just so you can see for yourself.

text:
Step 1: Find game with better soundtrack
Step 2: Come to terms with your failure
There is one thing I know for sure: each of us will fail, at something, at some point. The question is: what will we do about it?
All successful people I know attribute part of their success to failure. Though it’s usually painful, we learn from failure. I know that my own failures, and there have been many, have planted the seeds for future success and constant humility I carry with me like a small talisman.
Failure forces you to become resilient. We’ve all heard of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance; they are the steps one follows to get through grief. I came to realize that one could have a plan of action for coming to terms with failure — a roadmap to help find your way out of despair and build resilience to make you stronger for certain other failures that await.
I began as an investment manager in the late 1980’s fresh out of Wharton. Having had consistent success since then, it is hard to believe that the heady days of early 1998 would set the stage for a stunning and swift near collapse of my firm and career.
Things couldn’t have been going better. My firm was coming off a hot streak of several years. We were growing and making good money for our clients, and therefore good money for ourselves. We had just negotiated the sale of half our business for an enormous sum, meaning I would have officially “made it” at 33 years old. That is until the summer of 1998.
A tornado hit the financial markets as Russia defaulted on their debt and the collapse of Long Term Capital Management seemed to bring Wall Street to its knees. (A crisis, when compared to the crisis of 2008, could best be described as adorable.)
Our funds quickly headed south and we weren’t well positioned to save them. We made many mistakes; some due to hubris, some due to poor judgment, some due to poor efforts keeping investors informed.
When the deal to sell half the firm was terminated by the buyer in the fall of 1998, our business was in shambles. Adding salt to the wound, the market rallied strongly in the end of ’98, making our relatively poor performance that much worse. My failure thoroughly in place, and my ego and self-esteem in tatters, I waited for the dust to settle. The stage was set. I could either be resilient or decide to be washed up at 33.
Opting to be courageous, I devised a step-by-step plan to find my way back after a really big moment of underachieving. I’ve found that deliberate planning helps me get to a place where I can have the objectivity to learn from a debacle.
And really, if you can’t learn anything from failing, what good is it anyway?
Here are my steps:
1.    Allow yourself a very short, defined moment of wallowing in the failure. Maybe you give in and permit yourself one weekend of binge TV watching, laying on the couch and eating crap. Do not, however, let this step drag on.
2.    Get back in the game, even if you have to play hurt.  Fake that you’re ok. It’s completely acceptable to know you are faking your resilience at this point.  You can’t expect immediate results, but you can act confidently knowing one-day things will be ok.
3.    Recalibrate what’s important. Here’s a moment to reassess what your priorities are and revise how you’ve been spending your time, if necessary. If you’ve lost a really important promotion, a long sought after election, or an end to a relationship, you’re going to feel pain for a really long time. The bigger and more unique the failure, the harder it will be to imagine that you could ever feel better. Very often a big failure leaves you with more time on your hands than you thought you would have. Finding solace in a new interest or self-improvement you’ve always meant to try should be high on your priority list.
4.    Re-visit. This is an important step that is both immediate and serves the long term.  On the heels of your great catastrophe, write yourself a letter and be sure to include everything you’re thinking; every pain, every embarrassment, every feeling of loss or shame. Put the letter away. Take it out six months later and evaluate how much these intense feelings of hurt have subsided. Time heals wounds, fades lines in the sand, and opens never-before considered perspectives.
5.    Change up your routine to help you find a new normal. However, keep some semblance of order. Make your bed everyday…literally.
These steps have helped me more than once. I’m lending them to you because fortunately for the moment I’m not using them (though I’m sure I will again).
The goal, forever and always, is to be in a position to learn from failure, for that is its gift. It will lead you to future successes and ultimately help shed the fear that failure often brings.
