I'm impressed with how much I enjoy this game. It's relentlessly satisfying. These differences struck me as compared to KF1:
1. Wow, it's almost surreal to be playing such a
Killing Floor. It's gorgeous. I'm so used to KF being a fun-to-play mod for Unreal Tournament circa probably 2003 or something.
2. I'd swear that despite having 10 times the graphics, it runs
on my rig than old KF did.
3. Did I just cut that Husk completely in half with this four-inch knife?!
4. Wow, I should almost definitely not have survived all that abuse I just took.
5. Looks like there isn't really a guaranteed strategy vs. Scrakes and Fleshpounds anymore.
That last one is the biggest one. KF1 engendered a much more cerebral team tactics sort of gameplay where someone would spot a big zed, call it out and hope his team had the correct reaction ready for it - explosives for Fleshpounds, sharpshooter for Scrakes, what have you. In KF2 these monsters don't appear to have these glaring vulnerabilities, nor the same kind of devastating strength for that matter, so the team response to seeing one now seems to be "everybody shoot the ♥♥♥♥er." I'd hesitate to say I hate this change, because while it was satisfying to be on a well-greased team that operated by the numbers in KF1, there's also an obvious flaw in
that from random♥♥♥♥♥players. So KF2 is more of a team shooter than a squad shooter, to put it in an obtuse Zeory way. Considering I still like to think of Killing Floor as mainly an excuse to commit slow-motion ultraviolence against everything, I don't really mind the shift.
And ultraviolence there is. High-impact, highly cinematic slash-and-burn is the name of the game here. One of my biggest issues with KF1 is that it was very unsatisfying to score any sort of shot other than a direct headshot, as there was practically no visual and literally no audial feedback on body shots. In the sequel, everything you connect with gives you an appropriately weighty response, and the chunks you blow off the ragdolling dead♥♥♥♥♥♥are amazingly dynamic.
Honestly aside from the tactical shift I described, I can barely imagine there's anything to dislike about KF2 if you even somewhat liked KF1. It looks better, it plays better (no more "my shotgun looked up at me and swore that Scrake did not have a head"), there are more perks with a better EXP system and more bonuses, you can actually aim dual handguns now... It's a hell of a time.

South Park fans; For certain! The more you have watched of the show, the better, to get more of the references. However, it isn't essential to have watched all of the show to still enjoy the scenarios, story, and humor.
Non-South park fans; I would generally not recommend it simply because it is that faithful to south park, so if you do not like south park you likely won't like this. However, there is always a chance that this could serve like a different way to gain a taste for the show.

Here's hoping for a sequel or expansion!

If you're a fan of South Park the show, then chances are you'll be a fan of the game.  I was wary at first because I loathe turn-based RPG games, but in true South Park fashion the game parodies the mechanics to make it fun to play and challenging (at least to non-TBRPG players).    You play the new kid in town who finds himself caught in a power struggle over The Stick of Truth between the Cartman-led humans and the Kyle-led Elves.  Naturally, there's more to the Stick of Truth than either of these two sides realize, and soon you find yourself the only one who can save the town of South Park from an unforseen darkness!  The whole town is there for the player to explore and fart on when not doing the story missions.  The developers took the time to include as many main and side characters in the show's lore as the game could hold I think, and really helps with the feeling that you are IN South Park.  The only drawbacks are the story campaign is almost too short, sometimes the keyboard controls are not instantly intuitive, and mission objectives can be VERY vague leaving one to wonder, "what the hell am I suppossed to do??"
Pros:  Excellent production design: Visuals, sound effects all straight fromt he show itself.  Voice acting is top-notch to go along with the great writing.  Main and side quests vary and are fun to play through.  Lots of options for different types of play: Warrior, Mage, Jew, etc.
Cons: A bit on the short side, limited replayability unless you want to explore all the different character classes, keyboard controls for certain powers can be confusing, vague mission objectives at times.
Again, fans of the show should enjoy it since it's about as close to playing an episode of South Park as one can get.

Picked this up on offer this Bank Holiday weekend and have really enjoyed it. I have yet to explore the additional content (which looks really good) so this refers only to the main campaign 'Dead Man's Switch'. I enjoyed the Shadowrun universe, the characters were almost consistently interesting, the dialogue options fun and there was enough variety on offer to warrant two or three play-throughs (well, almost three, more on that later). In fact, this game has inspired me to learn more about Shadowrun - a marketing success, for sure!
Character creation allows for a lot of customisation, either from one of the standard templates or free-form (the latter allows some creative combinations once you've got the hang of the gameplay mechancis). While there is a lot of replayability in character classes (you'll have a different experience as an Adept than as a Decker, for instance) it struck me that my playthrough as a decker (who can hack into the 'Matrix' and fight additional combat scenarios within computer programmes) allowed greater access to content and secrets. A shame as I did feel the game was sort of pushing me to play as a decker, and while this is an interesting and challenging character class, it limits your access to combat and magic specialisations.
My main criticisms are that even a year after release I kept encountering bugs - including a major game-breaking bug that meant I could not finish a level. In short, it simply would not end combat or allow me to initiate dialogue at one point, even when the combat was over and dialogue bubbles were above people's heads. This was a pain and recurred again even after a level restart. Other criticisms were niggling and broke the immersion rather than the game - playing as a troll, for instance, didn't change dialogue options to a playthrough as a human or as an elf - which was a shame (bar one person calling me a racist name) and I'd loved to have used the in-game mechanic of building your own gang to go on more than just main plot missions. A couple of side missions could have helped me diversify my character build, get some better equipment and feel more prepared to take on the end of game boss on the hardest difficulty.
The game itself is focused on a single short story (took me about 8 hours the first time, 5-6 after that) which felt more like an introduction to the universe than a standalone game, which is an odd design decision, but it did mean I finished the game eager for more - rather than with a 'more traditional rpg' like Baldur's Gate where I tend to get fed up well before the finale. While this focus meant a satisfying resolution to the compelling storyline, it also meant there were no side missions, no additional content and limited opportunities for exploration. While additional content looks to rectify this, most involve creating new characters, so those I created for Dead Man's Switch won't be coming with me.
tl;dr - Great, immersive, colourful and engaging game that I'd rate 3.5-4/5. This score would be higher if the game was longer, featured greater variety outside combat, had opportunities for exploration and a few more side missions and didn't have game breaking bugs this long after release!

The first section of this review is regarding the Dragonfall DLC campaign, as of originally writing this review, I had not touched the original Dead Man's Swtich campaign, so keep that in mind when reading. Theres a second section that covers Dead Man's Switch.
To start, it's a good game. A really good one. It feels like a CRPG from over a decade ago, and I say that in the best way possible. It honestly feels like it could have been made by Troika, and I say that in both a good and bad way.
What do I mean by "both a good an a bad way"? Well, the game has some good writing, genuinely interesting characters, and a sold cobat system. The game is also buggy, but not so much that it's game breaking.
When speaking of a the combat system, we're looking at a very XCOM esque sort of feel complete with grid-based movement and overwatch for helping to keep areas locked down. You'll likely often find yourself moving your characters from cover to cover while pushing forward and taking down enemies. The combat system works on a cooldown system for abilities, in which once an ability is used, it cannot be reused for X number of turns. All in all, the game actually offers satisfying tactical RPG experience complete with guns, magic, and swords.
In terms of the bugs well, here's a few examples. At one point in the game I had a set of side objecties. Those objectives disappeared from my mission log, which from my expericne, shouldn't happen, but fortunately that did not prevent me from completing those side objectives and getting the payout from them. At another point in the game, a character I was talking to repeated dialogue from earlier on in the game when I spoke to her. It seemed clear that that piece of dialogue should not have been spoken, as it completely went against the more recent gdialogue I had just had with her (as in, literally seconds before). Also, not really a bug, but movement can be finickey if you want to move a charater to a tile behind another character, since the game will generally select the other character rather than move the one you wanted to move.
Writing is... pretty subjective obviously, but I enjoyed it quite a bit. I really liked all of the characters, I found converstations interesting, I liked learning about the past of my companions, and I liked watching them grow as I continued to run with them. The chararacter aren't exactly super dynamic, as there'll never be huge changes  in their personality, but still, as you converse with them, you can tell they're growing, which is actually more than I can say for quite a few other titles in the genre. The game also offers a number of superficial choices, in that you can't actually alter the course of the story, but it will still give you feedback about the effects of your decisions in terms of the world around you, so while it doesn't change the storyline, it still feels like it has an impact. Aside from that, doing things one way over another may provide more karma (experience) or money.
In any case, I bought the game on sale, so betwen the original title plus the Dragonfall DLC, I ended up spending around 15 USD, and it was most certainly worth that and more. That said, $30
be a little steep if you're
interested in Dragonfall, as it's not actually all that long (longer than the original campaign from what I'm told, and just better all around), but then again, it might not be, because it really is good.
I'll add to this review after running Dead Man's Switch I suppose, but bottom line is: Dragonfall is a fantastic campaign that's well worth paying for and playing.
I might as well start by saying that yeah, it's pretty much worse than Dragonfall in every way possible, but still decent.
The writing is Dead Man's Switch is far less compelling to be frank. The characters aren't as interesting, they never really appear to gorw, and you don't really interact with them, or even the world very much. It's a very much guided experience that sort of just shuffles you from level to level as the story unfolds. I feel that my most major problem with the storyline is that I find it pretty much impossible to make a connection to any of the characters since you don't really get to interact with them much.
Honestly, I'd say that if you're going to get Shadowrun Returns, get it for Dragonfall and think of Dead Man's Switch as an extra campaign despite the fact that Dragonfall is DLC which you'll have to pay for. Dead Man's Switch is nothing to really write home about, so if you get the game, you should really get the DLC. If you're more interested in the user-generated content or the combat system, the base game still has that going for it of course.

It provides a challenge, but it's so addictive that you just want to come back and torture yourself some more! The concept is ridiculously simple - guide your triangle through an oncoming barrage of walls that are (usually) hexagonal in shape. If you survive for 60 seconds, you beat the level. One minute doesn't seem like a long time, but on Super Hexagon, fractions of a second can seem like an eternity, especially if you die when your time is between 59 and 60 seconds (this happened to me on several occasions)!

Stick of Truth's a surprisingly engrossing RPG, and a good entry point to the genre for South Park fans.
It's clearly a console game, with limited options and no modding ability, fairly low difficulty level, and plays very well on a gamepad. And it's not particularly long for an RPG - you can get through the meat of it in around 16 hours without rushing.
However, it's great fun. You can explore the entire town of South Park, sifting through shops and houses for items, and as you progress through the main story, you'll unlock new abilities that allow you to reach new areas of familiar locations. Levelling happens very frequently, via two separate systems - one skill tree is unlocked by amassing 'friends' on South Park's pseudo-Facebook (accomplished by completing quests or exploring), and the other is unlocked by gaining XP from combat.
Combat happens very often, whether you're just wandering round the town or engaging in quests. It's turn-based, with you controlling an ally (such as Kenny or Butters) as well as your own character. There are several different damage types, which can multiply each other (for example, if you set an enemy on fire, then farting on them will cause much more damage). Weapons range from throwable tampons to ninja stars to Cartman's "respect-mah-authoritah" truncheon, and you can modify all of them to have additional properties.
Player customisation is epic. There is a VAST range of outfits, ranging from SWAT uniforms to Crab People cosplay, all of which give you different perks, and can be customised with different colours and abilities. You can find glue-on facial hair, makeup, wigs, and get a nosejob at Tom's Rhinoplasty to look like David Hasslehoff. And though you can only select a boy (for story reasons), you can get a makeover to pull off a very convincing lady-boy.
Graphics are... South Park. The whole thing's totally seemless, with your character appearing in cutscenes with full outfit customisation, and it does feel like a really long episode of the show. Particularly given that the voices are all accurate (most of them being performed by Trey Parker and Matt Stone anyway, who were intimately involved in the game's development).
Writing's a little bit hit-and-miss. Though you can thoroughly explore the town, meet most of the show's characters and perform sidequests for them, most of these off-piste sections aren't particularly funny, and are more fan service than anything else.
The focus of the writing is very clearly in the main story. It's funny, imaginative and shocking, and doesn't *require* you to have a knowledge of the show (though it helps). It doesn't have the rapid-fire succession of inspired random weirdness that made the show great originally, or the cutting satire that's kept it so successful in recent years, but it does have a gargantuan helping of the body humour (toiletry and sexing, basically) that's always been a South Park staple.
Let's put it this way. If you like the idea of slapping Nazi zombie cows with large pink vibrators, or of harnessing the aromatic powers of your colon to subdue gun-toting SWAT agents, stop reading and hit the 'buy' button.

"Welcome to Vice City, 1986. . . ."
Introduction
Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. In a sense this is the game turned the franchise from a cult classic, to a game that everyone wanted. Since while in GTA, and GTA II, it was a top based shooter. There was no real story line, and general it was a cult game series. GTA III, it gave you a silent hero based in 2001. You suddenly were able to shoot in a 3-D environment, and had an actual story line. Well here in Vice City, they've take the formula that worked, and added more to it, so let's do it!
Story 10/10
The idea is you're Thomas Vercetti, a man who has just done 15 years in jail for "the family", your sent down south to buy some cocaine and get it back north. Well the deal goes south, and now you owe the 'family' a load of money, and you need the cocaine. As you investigate what happened, and you get your revenge. You'll see how Tommy changes in Vice City, from a hired gun, to something more. What I like about this story line, is that it's believable. Based on what I've found of the era (mid-80's), and the character profile we get of Tommy. Since if someone were thrown into his situation, with his connections. What he becomes is plausible, pending him getting arrested or killed. As a note here to the writers, they could've gone with some very immature humour, but when it does go funny, its done with a sense of class almost.
Graphics 9/10
I know some people are going to be screaming at me over this, since I gave the graphics a 9 rating over a 10. This game is 12 years old, and yes its aged well. I've seen modem games with worse graphics, at a higher price.Each gun, each car, even key people look unique.
However, the problem is there are gaps where you see 'blue', and sometimes the details that separate two cars is so small you need to be the developer to see it. The other problem is running though trees, half the time Tommy is hidden from you. Which means you can't see him, and you see a 'blue' outline around the leafs.
Sound & Music 11/10
This is not a joke people. I am giving this game a 11/10 for music and sound. Since this is audio perfection. One of the reasons why I bought this game was for the in game radio. Besides the fashion, the radio music & chatter help set the mood for the game. You get an idea of what it was like to be in the 1980's. Where the cold war wasn't over yet, or how rap music was brand new. This is where you're going to get the real bang for your gaming dollar. Since I admit it, there are times I just load up the game, slap on a station as I do something else on my PC.
Besides the music, you can listen to how a gun fires and you've got a good idea of what's being fired at you. Maybe you can't tell the difference between two Semi-automatics. However, if someone close to you is firing a pistol, and the guy next to him is using a shot gun. You can tell the difference, and when you're outgunned, that kind of information is handy.
Game play 8/10
I've got a few complains about the actual game engine per say. Sometimes the game lags for a few seconds when swapping radio stations, or exiting a vehicle. Other times, you can't see a 'target' circle on someone you're simpering, and when you pop off the shot it works. Who can forget that when firing from a vehicle, how there is no targeting circle. Its all guess and check. With the exception of when you're being driven by someone else.
Now the beautiful part of this engine is how you've got to account for something moving. Most games if you're moving, you aim, you fire, you hit. In This game, you need to account for the motion of yourself, or the target, and sometimes both. The controls that are used are used in almost every game so the learning curve is not a long one.

Highly recommended if you're willing to put up with a wonky port. Vsync locks the game to 30 fps, but running over 60 fps results in gamebreaking bugs. You might be able to fix that by forcing Vsync in your video card control panel, but I have a 144Hz monitor and it didn't work for me, even when I set my monitor to 60Hz.
Also, there is awful negative mouse acceleration that makes playing this game with M+K really difficult. Some people have reported that locking to 60 fps fixes that too, but as with the bugs it didn't work for me. So, I ended up playing this game in "console mode" at 30 fps with a controller. That was actually OK, as good frame pacing and tactfully implemented motion blur make 30 fps totally fine in this game, and the shooting is not awful with a controller since it's relatively short-range and imprecise.
Anyway, if you're not familiar with Dead Space, it's a survival-action horror-ish game where you have to dismember your enemies by cutting off their limbs rather than shooting them in the head or the body. The combat is excellent and very weighty and visceral. You have to cut, stomp, and bludgeon your enemies to death with engineering tools rather than shoot them run-and-gun style like in many shooter games. You also get to scavenge for ammo, health packs, and power nodes to help upgrade your armor and ammo. It's got a resource management component, but I didn't find that keeping my ammo well-stocked was all that hard.
It takes place on a mining starship where the crew have all been infected with an alien parasite that transforms them into the limb-swinging monsters you have to fight. There's a lot more backstory, of course, but to reveal it would be to spoil the fun of uncovering what happened. You learn about the story from clues in the environment itself, rather it's text notes or messages scrawled in blood on the wall. There aren't too many jumpscares - the game is more gory than scary.
The level design is linear but gives you just enough freedom to make you feel like you're in a real place and not a corridor. It's clearly dated graphically, but the design aesthetic of the game is consistent and compelling - this is a game world that's fun to look at and explore, even though it's full of gore.
Overall, definitely worth a look if you're one of the 2 people who haven't played it yet, but be aware of the PC port issues before buying.

Stick of Truth's a surprisingly engrossing RPG, and a good entry point to the genre for South Park fans.
It's clearly a console game, with limited options and no modding ability, fairly low difficulty level, and plays very well on a gamepad. And it's not particularly long for an RPG - you can get through the meat of it in around 16 hours without rushing.
However, it's great fun. You can explore the entire town of South Park, sifting through shops and houses for items, and as you progress through the main story, you'll unlock new abilities that allow you to reach new areas of familiar locations. Levelling happens very frequently, via two separate systems - one skill tree is unlocked by amassing 'friends' on South Park's pseudo-Facebook (accomplished by completing quests or exploring), and the other is unlocked by gaining XP from combat.
Combat happens very often, whether you're just wandering round the town or engaging in quests. It's turn-based, with you controlling an ally (such as Kenny or Butters) as well as your own character. There are several different damage types, which can multiply each other (for example, if you set an enemy on fire, then farting on them will cause much more damage). Weapons range from throwable tampons to ninja stars to Cartman's "respect-mah-authoritah" truncheon, and you can modify all of them to have additional properties.
Player customisation is epic. There is a VAST range of outfits, ranging from SWAT uniforms to Crab People cosplay, all of which give you different perks, and can be customised with different colours and abilities. You can find glue-on facial hair, makeup, wigs, and get a nosejob at Tom's Rhinoplasty to look like David Hasslehoff. And though you can only select a boy (for story reasons), you can get a makeover to pull off a very convincing lady-boy.
Graphics are... South Park. The whole thing's totally seemless, with your character appearing in cutscenes with full outfit customisation, and it does feel like a really long episode of the show. Particularly given that the voices are all accurate (most of them being performed by Trey Parker and Matt Stone anyway, who were intimately involved in the game's development).
Writing's a little bit hit-and-miss. Though you can thoroughly explore the town, meet most of the show's characters and perform sidequests for them, most of these off-piste sections aren't particularly funny, and are more fan service than anything else.
The focus of the writing is very clearly in the main story. It's funny, imaginative and shocking, and doesn't *require* you to have a knowledge of the show (though it helps). It doesn't have the rapid-fire succession of inspired random weirdness that made the show great originally, or the cutting satire that's kept it so successful in recent years, but it does have a gargantuan helping of the body humour (toiletry and sexing, basically) that's always been a South Park staple.
Let's put it this way. If you like the idea of slapping Nazi zombie cows with large pink vibrators, or of harnessing the aromatic powers of your colon to subdue gun-toting SWAT agents, stop reading and hit the 'buy' button.

TL;DR
A definite buy for anyone who loves intense FPS action. Honestly I've never been into the zombie scene and still aren't, but that doesn't mean I didn't have fun with this one.
The game is based around 6 players working together to survive a number of waves of Z.E.D.s, the in game name for zombies. The shooting mechanics are fairly simple, wiht different guns have different bullet velocities. Not to mention with the difficult recoil, the game encourages tapping or bursting over full out spraying, but you can if theres an emergency.
The gun play is enjoyable, with the bonus addition of ZED Time, a slo mo perk that activates when you kill a zombie at close range.
The melee combat is honestly one of my favorite parts of this game, heavily reminding me of the combat system from Chivalry. You have heavy and light attacks that are affected by what way your character moves, a block, and a bash, which usually results ina thrust. Using this you can easily use the Beserker class to smash open zombie heads for an entire game, a very pleasing task.
Overall a good buy, especially for the beta. All kits are evenly balanced, with all contributing if played right. And if you buy the game now to November 6th, you recieve access to 4 exclusive Horzine Combat suits and Pistols in white, green, blue, and red.

I'm not sure why this game has had so many bad reviews; I really enjoyed it.
Shadowrun Returns is based on the old pen and paper role playing game Shadowrun. Set in a world where magic has "returned" to the Earth along with races that we are all familiar with in Fantasy stories. Magic and technology, spells and hacking all blend into this mishmash of Cyberpunk and Fantasy, and for the most part it works pretty well.
The mechanics of the game will be familiar with anyone who has enjoyed games such as Fallout 1 & 2 or any X-Com games. The game has turn based combat and a deep class system, wherein you level, spend points (known as Karma) and find more powerful weapons, clothing and spells.
The campaign that comes with the game: "Dead man's switch" is quite enjoyable, if a little short, however this game has steam workshop and plenty of mods to try out once you are done.
A few negative things do crop up in this game, however. First and most obvious from the get-go, the graphics are horrendous; they are actually not that far beyond the Super Nintendo game and that was made in 1993... but graphics aren't everything right? What about the fact that you cannot export your character that you so lovingly built up in the campaign into other mods? Unless you basically hack the game, that is. And just like any game with "dice rolls" this game is seriously suspect when it comes to calculating chance.
All in all good game. It needs to have more accessibility so that you can export characters into different adventures, but you will still get alot out of it.

Highly recommended if you're willing to put up with a wonky port. Vsync locks the game to 30 fps, but running over 60 fps results in gamebreaking bugs. You might be able to fix that by forcing Vsync in your video card control panel, but I have a 144Hz monitor and it didn't work for me, even when I set my monitor to 60Hz.
Also, there is awful negative mouse acceleration that makes playing this game with M+K really difficult. Some people have reported that locking to 60 fps fixes that too, but as with the bugs it didn't work for me. So, I ended up playing this game in "console mode" at 30 fps with a controller. That was actually OK, as good frame pacing and tactfully implemented motion blur make 30 fps totally fine in this game, and the shooting is not awful with a controller since it's relatively short-range and imprecise.
Anyway, if you're not familiar with Dead Space, it's a survival-action horror-ish game where you have to dismember your enemies by cutting off their limbs rather than shooting them in the head or the body. The combat is excellent and very weighty and visceral. You have to cut, stomp, and bludgeon your enemies to death with engineering tools rather than shoot them run-and-gun style like in many shooter games. You also get to scavenge for ammo, health packs, and power nodes to help upgrade your armor and ammo. It's got a resource management component, but I didn't find that keeping my ammo well-stocked was all that hard.
It takes place on a mining starship where the crew have all been infected with an alien parasite that transforms them into the limb-swinging monsters you have to fight. There's a lot more backstory, of course, but to reveal it would be to spoil the fun of uncovering what happened. You learn about the story from clues in the environment itself, rather it's text notes or messages scrawled in blood on the wall. There aren't too many jumpscares - the game is more gory than scary.
The level design is linear but gives you just enough freedom to make you feel like you're in a real place and not a corridor. It's clearly dated graphically, but the design aesthetic of the game is consistent and compelling - this is a game world that's fun to look at and explore, even though it's full of gore.
Overall, definitely worth a look if you're one of the 2 people who haven't played it yet, but be aware of the PC port issues before buying.

Tommy Vercetti, a loyal former member of the Forelli Family, has just been released in 1986, serving 15 years for killing 11 men in the Harwood District of Liberty City in early 1971, earning him the nickname The Harwood Butcher.[3] Tommy's old boss, Sonny Forelli, fears that Tommy's presence in Liberty City will heighten tensions between the other Liberty City families and bring unwanted attention to his organisation's criminal activities.[4]
To prevent this from happening, Sonny ostensibly promotes Tommy to a capo and sends him to Vice City under the guardianship of a crooked lawyer and Sonny's contact Ken Rosenberg to act as their buyer for a series of cocaine deals for Sonny, whose interest is to expand his family activities down the South and to overrun the Liberty drug market with the high-end cocaine from Vice City, hoping to create a monopoly on the Liberty City drug ring to establish the Forelli Crime Family on the top.[5]
Soon, Tommy and his bodyguards are awaited at the Escobar International Airport by Ken, who gives them an info about the deal and takes them to the docks, where they are awaited by the Vance Crime Family, prominent drug kingpins of Vice City led by Victor Vance, who arrive in the chopper with Diaz. As they settle the deal, they are ambushed by several armed and masked men, who kill Victor and Tommy's bodyguards. Tommy narrowly escapes with Ken from the docks, and as a result, he ultimately loses both Forelli's money and the cocaine in the process. Ken drives to his office, while Tommy returns to his hotel.[6]
When Tommy informs Sonny of the ambush, Sonny loses his temper and threatens Tommy with the consequences of attempting to cheat the Mafia. Tommy promises to retrieve the money and the cocaine and kill whoever was responsible for the ambush.[7] Towards this end, Tommy meets up again with Ken at his office, who leads Tommy to retired Colonel and mid-level drug dealer named Juan Garcia Cortez, who was Victor Vance's contact and who organised the deal between the Vances and the Forellis. Cortez expresses regret about Tommy's bad deal and promises that his own lines of inquiry are being made to find out who masterminded the ambush plot. Tommy also meets Cortez's daughter Mercedes, who becomes Tommy's confidante shortly thereafter.
While Tommy waits for the outcome of Cortez's investigation, he meets cocky 21-year old British record producer Kent Paul, real estate mogul Avery Carrington, and a mysterious man, who introduces himself as Lance Vance, younger brother of Victor and the underboss of the now-defunct Vance Crime Family, who wants revenge for the death of his brother and also wants the Vance Crime Family back on the map.[8]
As time passes, Tommy befriends Cortez and begins to do regular work for him as an errand boy and hitman. On one such job, Tommy is called in with Lance to protect the deal of a drug baron named Ricardo Diaz during a deal with the Cubans, looking to buy some high-end cocaine. During the deal, Diaz is ambushed by a gang of Haitians, but Tommy is able to kill them and save the deal, as well as Diaz's life. Consequently, Diaz begins hiring Tommy for his own agenda. Tommy takes this work because it pays well, in spite of his distaste for Diaz. On another errand for Cortez, he plans to meet a French courier to retrieve missile chips stolen from the French government. The deal is ambushed by several French agents and Tommy later kills the courier, who fled the ambush with the chips, retrieving the items.
Tommy learns from Cortez that Cortez's own lieutenant, Gonzalez, was partially responsible for the ambush on Tommy's cocaine deal since he is the only person besides Cortez to know about the deal, and Cortez asks Tommy to kill Gonzalez as a favour, since he was a man who he did distrust and was working behind his back. Afterwards, Cortez voices his suspicion that Diaz might have been behind the ambush. Tommy initially continues the status quo to prepare for his attack, but his hand is forced when Lance attempts to take revenge by himself and fails, forcing Tommy to rush across the city and rescue him from the junkyard in which he is held. With the die cast, the two move quickly to raid Diaz's mansion and execute Diaz. With Diaz dead, and Colonel Cortez fleeing the country to escape the French, the established drug empires in Vice City quickly crumble and Tommy and Lance personally take over, becoming Vice City's drug kingpins.
Tommy becomes the head of his own organisation, the Vercetti Crime Family, distancing himself from the Forelli Family and Liberty City and more interested in personally controlling Vice City than being Forelli's puppet. But the more powerful and rich Tommy gets, the more Lance begins to exhibit paranoia and sociopathic behaviours, to the point that he begins to abuse his own bodyguards and constantly calls Tommy in states of hysteria, losing his mind over being just a powerless second-in-command as he was under his brother for the past 2 years. Tommy begins to suspect that Lance is up to something.
Tommy makes alliance with Umberto Robina's Cubans against Auntie Poulet's Haitians, even though he is at the same time hypnotised by Poulet's voodoo into helping the Haitians as well. However, Tommy and Poulet part ways Tommy and the Cubans sneak explosives into the Haitian drug factory disguised in Haitian gang cars and blow it up, effectively ending the conflict and putting the Haitians out of business, enabling the Cubans to take over Little Havana. Umberto then becomes Tommy's partner. He also becomes friends with Big Mitch Baker, a leader of the biker gang and a Vietnam veteran, with both the bikers and the Cubans becoming protectors of Vercetti family business.
As his drug business expands, Tommy buys assets in nearly bankrupt companies such as a car lot named Sunshine Autos, a cab depot Kaufmann Cabs, a popular night club called The Malibu, a local boathouse, a print shop, Print Works, an ice-cream company, and an adult film company, all of which he turns back into competitive businesses. He also becomes a personal bodyguard to glam metal band Love Fist, and pulls a major bank heist. He starts to control almost all the assets and ties of Vice City: Sunshine Autos as a chop shop, Kaufmann Cabs for money laundering, The Malibu Club for dispatching drugs, the ice-cream company for the production of drugs and the film company to control the underground movie scene.
Eventually, the Forelli family discovers that Tommy has gained control over entire Vice City and without having sent a single dime back to them. Sonny is enraged that Tommy has become independent and is hustling him, and sends collectors consisting of high-ranking Forelli members to force money out of Tommy's assets. Tommy disposes of them, but after they injure the elderly operator of his print shop of counterfeit money, he decides to cut Sonny and the Forelli family out of his business, severing his ties with the Forelli family.
An angered Sonny arrives in Vice City with a small army of mafiosi, intent on taking their tribute by force. Sonny and his henchmen soon arrive at the Vercetti Estate. Just as Tommy attempts to give them their tribute in counterfeit money, Sonny reveals he is the one who set Tommy up fifteen years before, sending him to kill the eleven men who were expecting him since he was feeling that Tommy would himself take over Sonny's business. Lance then exposes himself as a traitor, revealing Tommy's attempt to fool Sonny, and also admitting to informing Sonny about Tommy's activities in Vice City. Lance explains that he did it because Tommy started to disown him and didn't treat him equally, and wanted him dead so he could rebuild the Vance Crime Family and the fortune he had with his brother. An enraged Tommy starts a gunfight.

Having a lot of fun thus far. As far as gameplay, I find it a satisfying balance of survival/evasion, and actual zombie killing. If you want to blow away hordes of zombies with massive guns this may not be for you.
Performance on the other hand is spotty at best as I see the game consume far more system resources for the visuals it produces. Don't get me wrong, the games looks nice, but it doesn't look drastically better if at all than a Crysis 3 or FarCry 4 and taxes my system much more. My system auto detected at the highest playable settings with view distance at 50%. View distance seems to do nothing from 50-100% after playing with it besides lower fps, so I settled for about 70%...whatever. I have a i7-4770, factory overclocked Gigabyte 780 Ti 3GB, 16GB DDR3 RAM, Samsung 840 Pro 256GB install drive. Currently playing at 1920x1080 with settings as stated and indoors I see a constant 60fps with vsync on. Outside I typically get between 40 and 60fps seeing dips as low as 32fps or so. No matter where I am in the game vram usage is between 2400MB and the full 3072MB or whatever it comes out to be that my card has. This was by no means a scientific observation, just me watching MSI Afterburner. I hope as the game matures with patches and nVidia releases new drivers performance will be better as I would like to turn off the games post process AA and try the supported DSR and scale to my 1080 monitor.
Other stuff one may be concerned with and that I have been reading about are crashes. I have had the game crash only once after about 2 hrs of play. Nothing frequent like some report.
Will update when I get a chance to play with some other people as it looks like there are some fun multiplayer modes.

Antichamber is an experiment in non-linear, abstract puzzle solving.
If you've played Portal, it is easy to describe and understand the design of this game by stating that it is the opposite of Portal.  Portal has a consistent rule-set that fits in with the universe we already live in.  Physics behave properly and in a mechanical fashion, doing one thing will lead to another.  Antichamber is not like.
From the very start Antichamber requires you to throw out what you understand about the world and relearn how things are.  To some, this might not be fun or make sense, as I've seen many reviews state that this game is overrated and not fun.  These people are attempting to force the game to fit their understanding of the world and their expectations of reality, and this will just not work.
Antichamber has a ruleset that you can learn and follow to progress rather easily, but it is internally consistent and not something that you would have experienced before.  Despite this, some of the puzzles within the game will immediately make sense, and others will require abstract thinking.
There are small flaws within the game, and according to some, it isn't finished (see Pink Cube discussions), but this easily one of the best puzzle games I've ever played.

XCOM: Enemy unknown and the following exapansion, Enemy within, are extremely entertaining to play. It's a rare game that doesn't shy away from difficulty and challenge while able to mixing these elements with fun and frustration. (at the time of writing this revies, I already finished Classic/Ironman on Enemy within and the review will reflect this)
The game put you in charge of XCOM, a paramilitary organization that fight the alien invasion. You have to manage your base, manage panic level of your supporting countries, and train your troops through combat against these extraterrestrial invaders. The game basically divided into two phase, Geoscope and TBS combat.
The Geoscope is rather bland but essential to the progress of your gamr and overall victory. You can't increase monthly funding without building sattelite. You can't build sattelite without building an uplink. You can't build an uplink without energy. Essentially, the game require planning and knowlwdge of previous failure to minimize the loss of time and resource. Moreover, your troops will die without weapon and armor upgrade which directly tied to the Geoscope as well.
The real fun (and frustration) is the TBS gameplay against the alien. Eliminating aliens means more money, more resource, and less panic. Your men recieve EXP point which increase their rank and unlock new perks and statistical increase. However, you will lose some of your men and perhaps some battles. You will see 90% hit chance shot miss three times in a row.
You will learn that you are your own greatest enemy. Hubris means death. It's a part of playing XCOM.
However, Enemy unknown suffered from slow pace combat due to overwatch trapping is the way to minimizre your loss. All player has to do is scout ahead, spot the alien, pull the scout back, put everyone on overwatch. The alien will charge at you (or not) and got shot to death.
The game also suffer from strange pacing. You will see greatest difficulty during the first two or three months but the rest of the game will be a breeze. The game gets easier the longer you play. While I understand that it's a part of the narrative, it's still feel 'not right'.
Enemy within isn't an actual DLC but an integrated expansion into the original game. 2K tackle the combat pacing with addition of MELD, a substance that allow you to turn your troop into cybernetic mechanized warrior (MEC) or genetically modified soldier. MELD urge player to hasten the pace and take some risk since it will self destruct after a while. A great addition to the game. MEC trooper can use flamethrower, puch alien in the face, shoot grenade, etc. But they also unable to take cover due to the gigantic size, cost considerable amount of MELD to create, and require your soldiers to take surgery that irreversibly turn them into a cyborg.
Genetic modification is less graphical but difinitely more creepy. Soldier undergone the gene modification will recieve power to jump to an extreme heigth, regenerate health, camoflague - at the cost of planting alien DNA within their body.
Not that these customizations not good (they are awesome!!) but it is still creepy. Especially considering Dr.Shen's reaction when the XCOM encounter Floater for the first time.
Enemy within also counter the sniper tactic from enemy unknown with Seeker, a matrix-ish octopus robot that cloak and strangle a lone trooper. Making it harder and riskier to leave your sniper alone in the rear and even harder to get MELD.
Alien also has an answer to your MEC trooper, the Mectoid. A sectoid grafted in a collosal exoskeleton that shoot plasma cannon with uncanny accuracy. Sectopod also recieve damage reduction from all source, forcing player to consider some debuff/buff perks instaed of pure damaging.
Enemy within also add another human faction, EXALT. Another paramilitary organization that use alien technology to fight the alien with earth-dominating purpose. They view XCOM as a threat and will sabotage your reaserch, steal your funding, and increase pani level. XCOM can respond by sending a lone agent to perform covert operation and a few days later, you have to send a team to extract your agent. Adding EXALT make the game more complex and a require a bit more juggling to cycle your troop between fighting the alien and fighting the EXALT.
Two sub-campaigns, Operation progeny and Slingshot, are rather hard to play since they add more problem during the first two months of the game. But the rewards are substantial, earlier access to advanced weaponry and guarantee Psionic soldier are definitely worth the endeavor.
Second wave options serve the game in term of replayability. These options can be added during the beginning of the game to add more chaos and difficulty to the game. Enemy within add a few more options. notably the training roulette. However, the greatest option of this game is Ironman mode which autosave the game for you after every move, essentially make all things permanent.
Overall, the game is great for strategy fans and Enemy within DLC is difinitely worth the price tag. A 9/10 for me.

DMS is pretty linear and has a relatively barebones story, but gives room for roleplaying. I played a decker, however, and it's really unfortunate that decker skills are pretty much useless in it.
Dragonfall is much better, with more options to end each quest, well-written characters with their own backstories who stick with you throughout the game (this might not sound like much, but it's what DMS was sorely lacking), and chances for all character classes to shine (my decker/rigger actually did awesome stuff!.
I VERY highly recommend this.

Problems ranging from audio and graphic glitches ... screen/game freezing .. to mouse controls not working properly. The gangster story, all the vehicles there for you to use, cool missions and side-missions, adult humor. To this day I remember all the little details about it. Yes, the combat was and still is clunky but who cares when it is fun. An added bonus is that you do not have to deal with RGSC in this game. The game is awesome and is missing just a bit more polish to be as good as the sequel - San Andreas. But just like SA it suffers from licensing and how Rockstar treats digital distribution of games. Because you DO NOT OWN IT when you buy it here, you just borrow it. They might change the game when they wish and as recent events have shown they can remove stuff. Songs, options, fixes and in this way also all of the mods made throughout the years. Sometimes they swap it with a mobile port entirely. Vice City already had stuff removed and this will go on in the future. So as time goes your copy of the game on Steam gets worse and worse ... while old disk copies and even pirated versions remain the best quality available. THIS is why I do not recommend buying it here.

When you buy this you're not just buying the box, but a community of game designers with dozens of excellent campaigns and stories to experience. Shadowrun is about immersing yourself in the dark world of a cyberpunk future. It relies heavily on storytelling and it does an excellent job. Expect a wonderful original story, a tool to craft your own, and an opportunity to be part of a community of brilliant writers who make even more campaigns for you to enjoy. With Shadowrun, what you're getting is a community.

Turn Based strategy games are, for the most part, fairly easy going. Sure, there's still a good chance of things going wrong, but making one error doesn't necessarily mean the end of the world.
This isn't the case in XCOM, where even the tiniest mistake could mean you lose half your squad in a single turn, or worse. There's very much a sense of surviving by your finger tips, at least for the first third of the game. The enemy isn't going to wait for you to build up your base or get that power armor. They're constantly escalating the scale and magnitude of attacks, forcing you to adapt as they do. And just when you think you've found your groove, they'll throw something new at you that will force you to re-evaluate your strategies.
That said, the difficulty curve is a bit weird. The first half of the game is a frenzy of balancing costs, research, and panic as you struggle to fufill your duties to the nations of the world as well as training soldiers into an effective fighting machine. But once you've armed your colonels with the best weapons and arms money can buy, that sense of urgency dissapates as your forces now possesses the means of curbstomping even the most tenacious of aliens in the blink of an eye. The only real threat by this point are the Sectopods and Ethereals, but they're relatively rare. The ending's also fairly anticlimatic, raising more questions about the Ethereals and their motivations rather than answering the ones we already had.
Aside for that, XCOM:EU is a riviting game that does an excellent job of putting you in the mindset of commander, forcing you to make the tough calls as you struggle to fend off the alien hordes.

I decided to have another run through of this gem over Halloween - I've owned various copies on various platforms over the years but figured it might as well refresh my memory from my first playthrough back in 2008.
For a horror fan, this game is a must. The atmosphere this title manages to evoke is amongst some of the best I've ever come across in my 20-year gaming career. If you're a fan of The Thing, Event Horizon, Alien, anything along those lines, you will *relish* the game's mixture of music, storytelling and pace. The fact that I've just finished my god-knows-how-many-th run through here in 2015 having thoroughly enjoyed every minute really underlines how well the devs did.
The game does like it's share of jump scares but I found it didn't overdo them - rather than go down Doom 3's route of continuously letting loose horrors from hidden cabinets, half the time the game lets your own head do it's work for you - you'll glimpse things rushing down corridors, you'll hear whispers in the dark without any clear source, every so often something will clang and crash. It's classic horror stuff of messing with your head to make the reveal all the better. The game drip-feeds it's story by way of audio logs, footage, and gradual exposition across what used to be a place where it's crew worked and lived, as you slowly learn what the f*** happened on this doomed ship, and the excellent voice acting really pushes the script in the right direction.
Technically, it's a fairly standard third-person shooter - much of the ruckus about how your character is an average blue-collar Parker-from-Alien engineer thrown into a nightmarish ghost ship crawling with horrific entities is fairly thin, as your 'improvised engineering tools' can be turned into shockingly devastating instruments of destruction (quite what a miner needs a giant particle cannon for is explained as, um, shooting rocks... yeah, makes you wonder how fast and ferocious rocks are in the future) but none of that is really important - expect a gameplay pace sitting somewhere between Mass Effect 1 and Gears of War with *very* rough narrative outline and atmosphere similar to System Shock 2. Intially playing like a Survival Horror, padding down corridors with a palpable feeling that you are only alive by sheer luck with precious little kit, the game steadily becomes more and more action-packed with Isaac the Engineer undergoing some serious nerd rage, upgrading his contraptions to fight ever more gross and numerous monsters that take leaves out of pretty much every sci-fi horror of the last 20 years.
But don't play this for the simple gameplay, as entertaining as it is. Play it to enjoy a truly awesome sci-fi horror and wish that the gaming industry produced half as much as this stuff as it did CoD clones.
Then play it's sequel. Like me. :D

I haven't seen many AMD system spec reviews on here so I thought i'd write my own.

First Impressions were...surprisingly alright with this hardware. For those complaining of a "Sh!tt3 console port!" it is far from it. That said, it is also far from a flawless console port;
The devs clearly made an effort to create the game to natively support eyefinity, so already, you can see that they did put some thought into PC.
It is true what they say that the game uses 1 core at 90-100%, while the rest *ARE* technically used, it is almost negligible, since they hover at about 30-40%.
The game does not "natively" support Crossfire...at least...not yet. Of course, it is possible to override by selecting "enable crossfire for games that don't support it in CCC" but this helps in some sections, while dropping frames in others. Interesting.
Again, we can see here that the engine CAN take advantage of two GPU's...just not optimized yet.
For all of this hardware, and everything maxed out, sans draw distance, and the
Nvidia options off, I get 30 FPS outside and inside. Keep in mind that these are relatively constant frames, as mentioned before, there are frame drops here and there, and if this was resolved, while not perfect, 30fps hold, is playable.
Overall, i'm impressed with what I've seen so far. Some of the best Zombie AI I have seen yet; they react, to every sound you make. I love it. When the sun goes down, you genuinely feel afraid, and vulnerable. Awesome way they implemented that. Even if Day/night cycles are somewhat scripted.
The facial animation could have been better. They certainly don't use Rockstar's facial animation tech that's for sure. But..it's...alright.
I do recommend this game. It is SO UNBELIEVABLY RARE to see a new "AAA" game to come out these days that's playable. I'm looking at you, Ubisoft. But this one, while certainly not free from it's own bugs, i'm impressed.
Gameplay itself is good. Story is fun and interesting (to me at least). Mechanics work GOOD.
With bugs, I give this...
8/10, would copy Skyrim's lockpicking again.

No game launches without its issues.  Dying light is no exception.  It became apparent almost immediately there was some FPS issues with the game, which after a day users quickly resolved was due to view distance issues.  Now you can adjust this FPS issue by making your view distance less, but this still doesn't mean that it should be fixed.  The most disappointing part of the game is that COOP seems to not work on PC.  The host or the players always seems to crash which makes playing with friends almost impossible, however the "Be the Horde" mode seems to work just fine.
Other than those two major issues, there are some minors ones.  The film grain, constant blurring around the edges, and the blur streams as you move are always present unless you make some changes to the core files in your game.  These should be options the player can toggle, not a requirement.  After playing the game for a few hours, my eyes get strained because of these effects.  Thanks to some clever users though, you can at least remove the film grain/noise from the game, which makes the game look significantly more pleasing, especially at night time.
Other then these quarks, the game itself is endless fun.  It never gets old kicking zombies off buildings and into spikes.  Parkour anywhere, as fast as you can find the next spot to jump or climb too.  Its quite fun and I personally look forward to when COOP is working to give the game my full blessing.

This is one of the best games I've ever had the privilege to play. Sure, it can seem obtusely difficult at times, but when you mess up and die it's never the game's fault. You really feel like it's you that made the mistake. The exoctic alien planet you traverse throughout the game has been beautifully modeled with retro graphics, and the soundtrack is one that I would place very highly on a top 10. I would even go as far as to say It's even better than some other  popular roguelike platformers out there, such as Rogue Legacy and Spelunky. It could be that the gameplay is based more around combat, or that the difficulty increasing over time mechanic is unique to this game. You have to find a balance between slowing down to get money (or muney), tracking down items, and rushing to find the teleporter.  All of these make for an extremely polished and addictive experience, and the game doesn't take much processign power to deliver gameplay constantly at a silky-smooth 60 FPS. With several classes to unlock, artifacts to find, over 100 different items, and unlimited replayability due to random elements, this is probably the best 10 bucks you'll ever spend.

The very first thing I can say about Enemy Unknown is that it is the most challenging game I have ever played. Now don't get me wrong, I don't mean that as something negative. I love XCOM and it's ability to make you think about every move you're about to make.
I think half the reason I bought XCOM was the fact that you can customize each operative you send out in a mission. Having a squad full of your friends or original characters really adds to the depth of combat. You live and die through every one of your soldier sent out into battle (in my case, mostly die).
Aside from the fun of forming your own team to take down alien baddies, I genuinely enjoyed the combat. Even on the easier difficulty, the game had me trying to think two steps ahead. What kind of enemies will I encounter? Should I split up my squad to cover more ground or keep everyone close in case we run into a lot of trouble with a Cyberdisc or Berserker or Sectopod? This is the most evil game on the face of the planet, disguised in simplicity. When you begin, a game of Super Hexagon will typically last five to ten seconds on hard. After what feels like hours of your feeble triangle being squished by incoming shapes and new high scores achieved by mere tenths of a second, you will begin to gain skill. Finally, with a triumphal score of one minute, you will beat the hard level. And then realize that hard was actually the easiest level, and it goes on to harder and hardest and hardestest.
When I'm in the zone, this game is fantastic. Beating this game was one of the biggest achievements in my gaming history. However, this game also had times where I was so mad I wanted to just bash my computer with a hammer. If you want to give this game a try, there's a free version online. It's a bit different and only has the easiest difficulty, but it'll give you a taste of what this game is like.

Enemy Unknown has its flaws and suffers from a tiny bit of "consolization" in terms of scope, depth, and interface, but it's still quite an accomplishment. After years and years of disasterous attempts to bring the X-com game style back into the limelight, this is most definitely the most successful. Though I personally don't think all of the changes to the original formula were good ones, XCOM stands on its own as a great game on its own merits.
Enemy Within gets an even higher recommendation from me! It's a glorious example of Fraxis' ability to make "classic" expansion packs, while everyone else is lost in a sea of DLC. Instead of adding another world or story or anything, Enemy Within just makes the game more... everything. The additional game mechanics serve to further set it apart from any pre-established formula, while the rest is simply hundreds of little details that desperately needed a boost, such as map variety (the maps are numerous enough now that their presculpted nature is actually a joy), equipment variety (the game puts more "toys" in to give a better feeling of choice and playstyle), and soldier personalization (both in terms of abilities and appearance).
My favorite thing of all, though, is a simple option (that I highly recommend!) at the beginning of the game which allows you to randomize the available abilities characters get to choose from. This is AWESOME and they clearly put a lot of thought into making it balanced, allowing interesting combinations without giving game-breaking overpowered situations or taking away vital skills that define the class types. It really gives each character more personality as you begin to use them for what you know they can do, not just their class types, and you don't need to rank a soldier up very far to begin defining a unique role. A few example of this that I've done, all with characters with only four or five abilities:
- A sniper who gets massive bonuses if she's on a rooftop and has supressive fire abilites
- A heavy weapons guy who acts as my team's best medic (usually a support role)
- A grenadier support character who can carry multiple, more powerful grenades in addition to extra smoke grenades
So, overall, I'd recommend the game! But now that Enemy Within is out, I can't imagine wanting to play without it.

As someone who is not a fan of horror games, Dying Light walks a well balanced line bordering on action adventure and zombie slaying goodness.  During the day you are playing a game of "the street is lava," parkouring through the rooftops only making a quick dash onto the street to scavenge supplies or make a more direct path to your destination while avoiding zombies. Any interaction results in a fluid combat experience that only escalates as your character levels up.
Night brings many more challenges as your visibility is sharply reduced and the abundance and difficulty of zombies exponentially increased. You will need to move much more slowly and avoid detection by the larger zombies which will trigger a chase if they spot you. If this happens, run, dont fight, just run to the nearest safe house.
Early on, focus on leveling up your agility class as running and avoiding zombie hordes is your main tool of survival.
Overall the gameplay is fun, fast and fluid. Crafting is nice but can get repetitive with the same items being scattered all over the world.  Graphics look nice but can be enhanced by removing the grainy look through some script modification. The game is not too well optimized for PC at launch (mainly for AMD users) but turning down your draw distance can help combat some of those FPS jumps. If you have an Nvidia setup (like myself) you should be well off for a smoother gaming experience.
Overall I give Dying Light a 8/10 mainly due to some repetitiveness in item scavenging and distortion of how under powered  you are early on compared to late game but it is definitely a title worth checking out.

Alright, let me start this off by saying that this is an absolutely fantastic game. Great, lets adress why the developer doesn't deserve your money.
Ok, so I love the Dead Island games. It had a short story that was alright, but the gameplay was good enough to make up for what the story didn't quite deliver on. Now, you might ask me, WTF are you talking about? This is Dying Light, not Dead Island. And you would be right, except I would be, too. I'm sad to say that this is a re-release of Dead Island. The quests are very much the same, the storyline has changed, but the progression is way too similar.
If this was the only thing that Techland recycled I would be like, "cool, whatever." Except it wasn't. Animations, textures, side quests, character and enemy abilities are all very similar. Basically more half of the game code from Dead Island feels exactly the same in Dying Light.
So, this leads me to conclude that if you have already played Dead Island, this game won't give you anything you haven't already experienced. So don't buy it.
Inevitable counter-argument: This game is better than Dead Island. It is more complete, and if you enjoyed Dead Island, you will probably enjoy this too, even if you might feel like you are paying money for two copies of the same game. Also parkour, and flykicking zombies. It's pretty badass.
I'm just sad that developers can get away with re-releasing a game where the only thing they changed is the cover. But other developers do this too, think CoD series. I guess I wouldn't have a problem with this if they were upfront about this game actually being the next Dead Island.

Half-Life 2 культовыя вселенная получившая более 30 наград по всему миру, именно Half-Life 2 произвёла вторую революцию в жанре Action. Да что я говорю, у меня с тех времён наклейка наград на мониторах.
Проснитесь и пойте, мистер Фримен... Что меня удивило с самого начала, даже в 2015 эта игра выглядит ну очень привлекательно! Начиная от графики и заканчивая физикой.  Да сейчас я не помню такого замечательного искусственного интеллекта, который бы всегда поворачивался к тебе лицом и отпихивал рукой, подойди ты вплотную. Что касается самого мира... Чёрт, я всегда мечтал побывать в мире "1984" Джорджа Оруэлла, откуда и были взяты большинство деталей тоталитарного режима Сити-17. Хотя внешний вид всё же больше напоминает Россию 70-х, чему свидетельствуют Волги на улицах. Но самое главное, что первое впечатление не просто затягивает в игру, а удивляет спустя почти 10 лет после выхода!
G-Man'е: Сама игра проста и разнообразна одновременно. С одной стороны у нас абсолютно линейное прохождение, с другой - большие локации, создающие иллюзию свободного мира. Ну а с гоночными средствами, разнообразными монстрами и 11 видами оружия, перед нами получается целая вселенная, прикрепленная своей историей и мистикой, которая заключается не только в таинственном G-Man'е, но и многими вопросами, возникающими во время игры. Ответа на большинство я, кстати, так и не получил, но буду надеяться, что два последующих эпизода хоть как-то мне их разъяснят.
Но что я оценил больше всего - в игре нет ничего лишнего. Ничего. Каждый солдат на своём месте, каждый монстр нужен миру. Любой твой спутник важен, любое их действие логично. Здесь даже логично объясняется, почему ты не можешь идти дальше, и причина не кроется в том, что только Прайс ты не умеешь поворачивать ручку двери! У нас есть герой (Гордон), красивая и умная помощница (Аликс), лучший друг (Барни), враг (доктор "Большой Брат" Бринн), предатель (Джудит), проблема (тоталитаризм), её олицетворение (Цитадель), а также загадка (G-Man). Этой игре не нужен сценарий, ей не нужна экранизация - она и есть фильм.
В завершении "Half-Life 2"  меня не покидало ощущение, что я вновь прохожу игру 2003 года, за исключением вида от первого лица. Если же говорить только о серии Half-Life, разница такая же, как у тех же частей Hitman & Max Payne. "Half-Life 2" получает честные 10/10. Честно, я мог бы написать очень большую рецензию, но думаю этого хватит. Episode One, Episode Two...

Antichamber is a delightfully challenging first-person brain-tease. Calling it a puzzle game feels misleading, It doesn't merely *contain* puzzles; the entire game is the puzzle, and a viscous one at that.
After throwing you headlong into a bizarre and confusing environment to explore, the game gradually introduces you to new concepts and mechanics. However, it never shies away from introducing you to puzzles, gates, and dead-ends that you are not yet prepared or equipped to solve. Part of the game is learning how to overcome these obstacles. Another part is simply remembering where those obstacles are -- and how to return to them -- once you have the means to overcome them.
Antichamber is one of the most enjoyably maddening games ever. You will be stumped and confused. The game expects and wants you to be stumped and confused, and will do almost nothing to help you. It's not bad design, but rather the entire point and intent of the design. It's at once incredibly devious and incredibly rewarding.
I highly recommend it.

Yes! This is a game-changing puzzler that breaks alot of the rules and forces you to forget them, and make up your own. Many puzzles have multiple solution types, and you can get to some locations through multiple different paths. Many paths feature very different types of puzzles so even if a single puzzle has you horribly stumped, you can still find another route sometimes. The manipulation of blocks, and the various extra abilities each new upgraded gun has will provide new challenges and challenge your thinking all over again. Some of the puzzles aren't even linear! Forget regular 3-d space, this is like being in a hypercube, or something even MORE complicated then that. The ending is a bit odd, but the variety of puzzles and the strange-ness of the environment and various elements combine together into a very wonderful journey that I have relived again, and again, because of the beauty of it.
No performance problems at all, nice storyline, will exploit it further as soon as the cold seasons starts :-)

I didn't play the game at launch because of all the problems regarding the PC port and I must say that the waiting has paid off with this title. One year later, after numerous patches, the game has fixed most of the performance issues and bugs. Best graphics in a Batman game so far deliver a breathtaking Gotham City that you get to explore at good frame rates. However, I noticed some frame drops in the Batmobile and I see that a lot of people are complaining about the same problem. In 50h of gameplay it crashed once for me, but I was very satisfied with the overall performance.
The story is awesome and as far as I can tell you should play Arkham Origins, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City in this order if you want to fully understand and enjoy it. Skip Blackgate - that game is bad. Without going into very much detail: you'll get to fight against most adversaries from the Batman universe and sometimes your assistans will join to help.
The Batmobile is a big part of the game and integrates vehicle combat as a new gameplay element. Most of the time you will use it as a tank to destroy drones and it gets repetitive, but sometimes you'll also need it to pass certain puzzles or transport captured villains to your headquarters: the GCPD building.
Combat on foot is similar to the previous games - part melee encounters, part stealth sectors where enemies have fire weapons. A new  takedown system and gadgets have been added to Batman's repertoire.
Gotham City is your stage once again, but this time you'll encounter more elements from the open-world genre. These come in the form of various optional missions such as liberating towers, taking out drones or disarming land mines. You can treat them as time fillers or new opportunities to test your moves and gadgets. On the other hand, the villain optional missions are more fun and make a better part of the story with mini-boss battles and cut-scenes at the end. All optional missions reward the player with Wayne Tech points needed for upgrading your suit, gadgets and Batmobile.

Antichamber was one of the biggest let-downs for me this year. A classic case of me falling for professional reviewers, really. I heard people talking about how amazed they were by this game, playing it at PAX while it was still in development. How mind bending and innovative, how hard or near impossible to grasp it was.
But it isn't. It's a very clumsily put together puzzle game that seems to try its best to confuse you.
You're thrown into a big maze like level, full of bare, same-looking corridors. There's a bunch of pictures and text, giving the impression to be some kind of bizzare super self reflected, meta level commentary on the game itself and/or life in general; or maybe it isn't and that's just what I'm seeing/reading, but in any case it's there to confuse you. And I think the game does this with evil intent, using this confusion to obscure its biggest flaw: that there is no game.
The graphics are horrible, the sound design is non existant (there's practically no music in the game & almost no ambient sounds), the puzzle design is terrible as it is mostly a bunch of old portal tricks (not the game Portal, but portal level loading technology as used by all 3D games since the 90s) and the level design, as I already stated, is just a big huge winding corridor.
If you like puzzle games and play this game for the first time after having read a very negative opinion like this one, going at the game with very low expectations, I can see how it might surprise you and you'll like it.
But if you have any hopes that this could be a good game, another Braid or what have you, you'll probably be sorely disappointed - I was.
If you think about playing this, wait for a sale. Don't spend more than 5 bucks on it, it's not worth it.

*I think this game is a masterpiece among roguelike games, with a neat gameplay, beautiful art, and insanely great soundtrack.
Basically you have to get through a few stages, where on each stage you have to find the teleporter, kill the boss and proceed to the next one. Meanwhile you fight off monsters that get more powerful over time, and earn money to unlock chests and other containers that contain useful items. The more items you want, the more time it will take you. So, you can either quickly run through stages with fewer items and lower difficulty, or you can search the whole level and open every container - and have insane difficulty on 2nd or 3rd stage already.
There are quite a few characters to pick for a run, but they need to be unlocked.
Every level also contains a unique artifact that affects gameplay. Once discovered, can be activated at the beginning of a run.

TechLand's new release, Dying Light, seems to be at first another dead island. it features the same style of game ideaology.
Saying that, it seems that they have introduced new elements to the game, it is fun, true to play, and even challanging in certain occasions, however, i have many problems with this game.
the first of which is glitches, bugs, and things that should no happen, zombies stuck in walls, being stuck on a wall, weird parkour interactions that sometimes sent you in weird and not always wonderful places, however that said it is not overtly common for a game so early in the release, so some hope can still be held for this point.  (anyone noticed how people have 'flooded' hair?)
Secondly, it is the storyline, it is nice and some aspects are new, but some of them seems to be following Call of Duty's poor choice of "rinse and repeat". a lot of the story line bare too many similarities with zombie cliches and famous TV shows, games and movies. additionally, a lot of the mutant zombies, or special zombies, bear a lot of similarities with Left for Dead, (it seems they even have a refence to this game, "left 4 bread") such as the bomber (boomers in l4d), i could continue making similarities but i find no point in doing so.
Additionally, the map is very well map, that compliments to developpers, however, the one issue i have with it is the fact you spend almost the entirety of the latter half of the game in the sewers, i mean it is a zombie game and crawling through sewers is almost a necessity, but they could tone it down a bit, they are other ways to travel in the world thens sewers you know? i mean, make a scene about driving a car, or hiking through the woods over the mountain, i don't know, just not as many sewers next time ok?
Now, onto more serious stuff to point out.
I have always used CTRL as crouch since i was old enough to reach the keyboard,  but this game uses C, which i have no issues with on it's own, however, this couple with the usual shift (sprint) meant the crouching is almost impossible to do unless you entirely rebind your keys. this could have been easily solved by allow us to bind multiple keys to one actions.
Also, the control and general movement in this game is poor, compared to other free-runner games, it is almost laughingly annoying and perhaps slow, even at maximum aligility, it feels like you either pulling super-human stunts/parkour moves (such as jumping of massive heights into about 3 feet of garbage and walking out of it alive, intanct), or that you are so slow you'd loose in a race to a 100y.o granny with a broken walker.
Alright, enough bagging this game out. here's a few pros:
The graphics are nice, the lightning effects are night with fires and various lights are also pretty cool and make me want to run around at night with my light of just to admire the effects.
The gruesome nature of this game has been well done, and this is a necessity for a game of this genre, yet i cannot help but feel it was still somehow underdone, as if they could of done more, should of done more, but didn't for some reason i do not know. but still this is definitly a plus.
the weapons, modifications and such: i mean who doesn't like going around setting fire to zombies or electrifying them with a sparkingly electric machete? 'nough said.
the co-op and multiplayer is also a nice aspect, something which i have not done in vaste amounts, but it is stilll a nice feature to have.
i await to see if anything will be done in any future updates.
The game is enjoyable, and more so with friends.

If your looking for a review on GTA Vice City you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
