I didn't play the game at launch because of all the problems regarding the PC port and I must say that the waiting has paid off with this title. One year later, after numerous patches, the game has fixed most of the performance issues and bugs. Best graphics in a Batman game so far deliver a breathtaking Gotham City that you get to explore at good frame rates. However, I noticed some frame drops in the Batmobile and I see that a lot of people are complaining about the same problem. In 50h of gameplay it crashed once for me, but I was very satisfied with the overall performance.
The story is awesome and as far as I can tell you should play Arkham Origins, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City in this order if you want to fully understand and enjoy it. Skip Blackgate - that game is bad. Without going into very much detail: you'll get to fight against most adversaries from the Batman universe and sometimes your assistans will join to help.
The Batmobile is a big part of the game and integrates vehicle combat as a new gameplay element. Most of the time you will use it as a tank to destroy drones and it gets repetitive, but sometimes you'll also need it to pass certain puzzles or transport captured villains to your headquarters: the GCPD building.
Combat on foot is similar to the previous games - part melee encounters, part stealth sectors where enemies have fire weapons. A new  takedown system and gadgets have been added to Batman's repertoire.
Gotham City is your stage once again, but this time you'll encounter more elements from the open-world genre. These come in the form of various optional missions such as liberating towers, taking out drones or disarming land mines. You can treat them as time fillers or new opportunities to test your moves and gadgets. On the other hand, the villain optional missions are more fun and make a better part of the story with mini-boss battles and cut-scenes at the end. All optional missions reward the player with Wayne Tech points needed for upgrading your suit, gadgets and Batmobile.

Antichamber was one of the biggest let-downs for me this year. A classic case of me falling for professional reviewers, really. I heard people talking about how amazed they were by this game, playing it at PAX while it was still in development. How mind bending and innovative, how hard or near impossible to grasp it was.
But it isn't. It's a very clumsily put together puzzle game that seems to try its best to confuse you.
You're thrown into a big maze like level, full of bare, same-looking corridors. There's a bunch of pictures and text, giving the impression to be some kind of bizzare super self reflected, meta level commentary on the game itself and/or life in general; or maybe it isn't and that's just what I'm seeing/reading, but in any case it's there to confuse you. And I think the game does this with evil intent, using this confusion to obscure its biggest flaw: that there is no game.
The graphics are horrible, the sound design is non existant (there's practically no music in the game & almost no ambient sounds), the puzzle design is terrible as it is mostly a bunch of old portal tricks (not the game Portal, but portal level loading technology as used by all 3D games since the 90s) and the level design, as I already stated, is just a big huge winding corridor.
If you like puzzle games and play this game for the first time after having read a very negative opinion like this one, going at the game with very low expectations, I can see how it might surprise you and you'll like it.
But if you have any hopes that this could be a good game, another Braid or what have you, you'll probably be sorely disappointed - I was.
If you think about playing this, wait for a sale. Don't spend more than 5 bucks on it, it's not worth it.

*I think this game is a masterpiece among roguelike games, with a neat gameplay, beautiful art, and insanely great soundtrack.
Basically you have to get through a few stages, where on each stage you have to find the teleporter, kill the boss and proceed to the next one. Meanwhile you fight off monsters that get more powerful over time, and earn money to unlock chests and other containers that contain useful items. The more items you want, the more time it will take you. So, you can either quickly run through stages with fewer items and lower difficulty, or you can search the whole level and open every container - and have insane difficulty on 2nd or 3rd stage already.
There are quite a few characters to pick for a run, but they need to be unlocked.
Every level also contains a unique artifact that affects gameplay. Once discovered, can be activated at the beginning of a run.

A great puzzle shooter for those of you who would like a brain fuzz.
The style this game goes for is very minimalistic, which helps from a whole aesthetics point of view and it also means the whole environment is very purposefully designed to give very subtle hints through the use of highlights.
Its puzzles are not frustrating to solve, and rather than having one set answer to one linear course of puzzles, there are usually multiple ways to reach the next goal in line.
I see it being compared to the Portal series, which I have to admit Portal is still superior to this, generally speaking. The puzzles and variables for this game are very well crafted, but as a whole experience, the minimalist style does make the game bland outside of the puzzles, so the game is, quite unfortunately, a one time play through with next to zero replay value.
Again, a great puzzle shooter. Its price point is a bit high, but would definitely recommend the game on sale.

I remember that I played KF1 from a free weekend and instantly fell in love w/ it, then I decided to buy KF1 until I saw KF2 available for early access, so I've bought this game in full price last April 2015 and here are my thoughts
PROS:
-core gameplay is still present from KF1

-devs are listening to the community's demands

CONS

-Objective mode is not present(yet)

A very enjoyable game. Xcom Enemy Unknown and Within is a great tactical game that can give you a marvelous experience. You should purchase the expansions as it adds a variety of maps and new mechanics that do nothing but enhance the game. In the vanilla Enemy Unknown I would often come across the same map several times in the same playthrough and I got bored quickly of the fact that enemy ships were always in the same spot. It does sometimes crash randomly on you which is a problem as it can come at the worst time. The enemy variety is great as it makes you fight a number of different aliens that range from soldiers, to aliens that can turn your squad into zombies. Xcom is great at delivering some brilliant moments of master level victory to crushing defeat. You could be fighting aliens and salvaging their ship while whiping the floor with them, only to have your elite soldiers turn to zombies or even mind controlled and stolen from you. It was hard to hit Enter and make my sniper shoot a laser through my heavy's skull. The game comes with many variations to spice up your game such as a second wave option that makes each soldier's skill tree different instead of class dependant. I've loved this game for a long time and would easily recommend it to anyone who wants a tactical single player game. I have't touched the multiplayer.

Half-Life 2 культовыя вселенная получившая более 30 наград по всему миру, именно Half-Life 2 произвёла вторую революцию в жанре Action. Да что я говорю, у меня с тех времён наклейка наград на мониторах.
Проснитесь и пойте, мистер Фримен... Что меня удивило с самого начала, даже в 2015 эта игра выглядит ну очень привлекательно! Начиная от графики и заканчивая физикой.  Да сейчас я не помню такого замечательного искусственного интеллекта, который бы всегда поворачивался к тебе лицом и отпихивал рукой, подойди ты вплотную. Что касается самого мира... Чёрт, я всегда мечтал побывать в мире "1984" Джорджа Оруэлла, откуда и были взяты большинство деталей тоталитарного режима Сити-17. Хотя внешний вид всё же больше напоминает Россию 70-х, чему свидетельствуют Волги на улицах. Но самое главное, что первое впечатление не просто затягивает в игру, а удивляет спустя почти 10 лет после выхода!
G-Man'е: Сама игра проста и разнообразна одновременно. С одной стороны у нас абсолютно линейное прохождение, с другой - большие локации, создающие иллюзию свободного мира. Ну а с гоночными средствами, разнообразными монстрами и 11 видами оружия, перед нами получается целая вселенная, прикрепленная своей историей и мистикой, которая заключается не только в таинственном G-Man'е, но и многими вопросами, возникающими во время игры. Ответа на большинство я, кстати, так и не получил, но буду надеяться, что два последующих эпизода хоть как-то мне их разъяснят.
Но что я оценил больше всего - в игре нет ничего лишнего. Ничего. Каждый солдат на своём месте, каждый монстр нужен миру. Любой твой спутник важен, любое их действие логично. Здесь даже логично объясняется, почему ты не можешь идти дальше, и причина не кроется в том, что только Прайс ты не умеешь поворачивать ручку двери! У нас есть герой (Гордон), красивая и умная помощница (Аликс), лучший друг (Барни), враг (доктор "Большой Брат" Бринн), предатель (Джудит), проблема (тоталитаризм), её олицетворение (Цитадель), а также загадка (G-Man). Этой игре не нужен сценарий, ей не нужна экранизация - она и есть фильм.
В завершении "Half-Life 2"  меня не покидало ощущение, что я вновь прохожу игру 2003 года, за исключением вида от первого лица. Если же говорить только о серии Half-Life, разница такая же, как у тех же частей Hitman & Max Payne. "Half-Life 2" получает честные 10/10. Честно, я мог бы написать очень большую рецензию, но думаю этого хватит. Episode One, Episode Two...

I've played the original Dead Space at least 5 times through, xbox 360 version I just purchased a steam copy so I may update this later. This truely is a masterpiece horror game that captures the same wonder and experience we feel watching classic horror movies, In away it's like strolling into the world of Alien one a single ship infected by madness.
So far the gameplay handles about the same, a heavy combat styled horror with no short supply of monsters to mutilate. I do recommend playing on the hardest difficulty because one thing the original dead space seemed to lack was a proper challenge, though the unlockable Impossible mode is definitely worth a replay. The story is in short a spiral into insanity over the next three games that does not disappoint, and the original will always hold a special place for me as it's honestly the most horrorific. You spend just about the entire game acting alone looking at your companions on the otherside of glass or a deep trench never really in touch with them. You're always looking over your shoulder plasma cutter at the ready to rip apart necromorphs as they stalk you and attack in herds.
With a bit of skill I'm sure you can survive the night, oh and do play it in the dark the best horror deserves a proper setting! Remember kids; conserve ammo, health, and stasis!

On the other hand, the simple addition of EXALT does nicely shake up the game and the extra council missions are incredibly fun to do. The MEC class is a fantastic addition that is definitely satisfying to use and offers new strategic options, the Meld resource is a good extra goal to chase after, and the numerous extra research, foundry and of course gene mods are certainly a welcome addition that only serve to make this already highly enjoyable game that much better.

Arkham knight is my second favorite entry in the arkham series, just behind city, it features the epic conclusion to rocksteady's trilogy and some truly incredible story moments. Cons:
-Overused batmobile at end of the story
-batmobile stealth
-lack of boss fights
-occasional glitches
Overall this is probably my favorite game of last year and I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the previous entries in the arkham franchise especially if you want to see the conclusion of what happens after arkham city. Highly Recommended.

I came into this game with next to no real opinion about it. My thoughts were mostly "Let's see what this was all about" after grabbing it for stupidly cheap from the horror sales at Halloween. I knew it was horror (or meant to be) and felt like giving it a shot.
This game really surprised me, because after starting the game I played the campaign from start to finish over the space of 2 days, and I utterly loved every minute of it. Ok, over no point during the game was I actively frightened. Some mild jumps now and then from enemies popping up or suddenly being behind me. What got me was an active sense of everything being -creepy- as all balls. Everywhere. Add in that the sense of isolation throughout the majority of the game really helps with the atmosphere as well.
The weapon selection is comfortably varied, the dismemberment mechanics for defeating your enemies is really nicely worked, the upgrade system is nice, everything with the gameplay worked really nicely.
The plot is reasonably simple, but very well executed. Also a personal fave horror theme of mine, being the more "Eldritch" based plotline. You're not meant to understand the evil at work here, and if you were to try you would be driven to insanity.
I have very few complaints with the game. Some of the chapters/areas of the ship feel a bit same-y in terms of visuals, given the nature of the Ship you're on, and one or two of the fights with an invincible enemy aren't scary or terrifying so much as frustrating. Thankfully there aren't many of those situations in the game.
A highly enjoyable series, and well worth getting if it's on a deal again.

When it was released in 2007 I remember Dead Space being one of the best horror games I had played since the Silent Hill 2/Fatal Frame CB-era. Going back how does it hold up today? A bit on the good, a bit on the bad it seems.
First off know that if you like horror games and have never picked up the series then there’s really no reason not to play the game. Despite some of its shortcomings it’s still a deeply immersive experience. Though I think the series as a whole gets lauded as “thah scuriest games evurh!” far too often (as you’ll eventually become used to its brand of trying to scare you and begin predicting where the next enemy is coming from) that doesn’t change the fact that the environments are excellently crafted, deeply foreboding, and the gameplay is fun if not perfect.
In fact while I believe the later games certainly improved on the mechanics, and I eventually grew to like Isaacs voice (he’s silent in this one), I think overall this game creates a far better atmosphere. You rarely if ever feel safe, the graphics while aged still look nice, and unlike the later entries unless you’re playing on the easiest difficulty or two (or are a horror god) you’ll be rationing supplies to an extent. Additionally while some dislike it I quite liked the fact that except for a few rare occasions almost all communication with others is done via radio, true it isn’t as cinematic as later entries, but it gives the distinct impression that only you can save yourself and no help is coming. It’s true that thanks to an upgrade system most people do feel rather powerful by the end, but you have to work toward that and in the early to middle game it’s true survival horror.
As for the bad, well as I said later games improved on the mechanics and that’s because some of the mechanics are broken. The big mechanic of “shoot the limbs” is completely missed by the inclusion of weapons that can do just as much damage shooting for the core (it can be fun to play through with only the base weapon and it is perfectly effective, but isn’t required and if you’re just breezing through can totally be skipped). The Zero-G sections are awe inspiringly painful to play, you’ll get the hang of it but because you have no control and can only jump from point-to-point it isn’t fun. And the physics are all over the place as well as the hit-boxes at times, especially where stomping or some of the more concentrated weapons are concerned.
There’s also a small factor that never really bothered me but I see brought up all the time so it’s worth mentioning. This game truly is “fetch quest, the FPS”. Though the underlying plotline, the history, and the environment of the ship itself are all very interesting the actual activities you’re asked to complete aren’t. EVERYTHING is broken and because the other survivors are a bunch of sissy pants you literally get to fix a starship as a one-man engineering crew. The fact that the other elements are so strong glossed over this for me, but lots of people note it and I can’t deny its truth.
In short the game is still a classic. Some of it hasn’t aged as well as other parts but like great horror games from the very start of gaming chances are you’ll easily forgive those things in light of the overwhelming positives.

There are no words for how much I could recommend Shadowrun Returns. It brings back the excellent feel of old isometric view strategy RPGs like Fallout and Wasteland in a modern day, with the Sixth World taking you in and shaping you into a runner. Dead Man's Switch, the base campaign that comes with Shadowrun Returns is a good entrypoint into the Shadowrun world if you have never experienced it before. Unfortunately it lacks in a bit of my favorite aspect, Decking, but it makes up for it in an exciting, well paced story.
The expansion, Dragonfall, takes what SR started in Dead Man's Switch and runs with it even further than it went before. Instead of being in the ever used area of Seattle (one that was used in both 16-bit consoles as well as DMS), it takes you to Germany to face off against an Elder Dragon.
The best feature of SR is the Steam Workshop. The community has taken Shadowrun Returns and made their own campaigns, their own weapons, skills, anything you can possibly imagine being in the Sixth World. Just, go check it out.

Do you like games that screw with your head? Do you like wondering around for hours feeling like a rat in a maze? Do you just want a new kind of "puzzle game"? Then this is the game for you.
Antichamber is a game that throws you into a maze like a blind puppy. You are left to wonder around, confused and completely alone. Every turn you make is just another step in no direction. While you can beat the game in only 5 minutes, the real fun is how deep into the game can you get before getting extremely confused? I mean, I haven't even finished the game yet myself, but I have had so much fun. Oh, and do NOT use a walkthrough. Even though the game is a maze, it is only one maze. It doesn't change. If you use a walkthrough, you just basically wasted the $20/$10/$6.66/Whatever you paid for it. There really isn't much else to say about the game without ruining it. It's got simply yet beautiful visuals, and the "puzzles" are very immersive. Most parts of the maze don't care only about where you where. There are times where it depend son where you are looking, or HOW you are walking.
If you want some brain bending, buy this. If you just want a game to waste a good 5-15 hours on, then buy this. It will not disappoint. 8.5/10

This is a review for the game in its current state, August 2016.
This is the weakest and most irritating of the Arkham games, but is still a good game. Someone on the development team apparently thought that when I bought this game, what I really intended to buy was World of Tanks: Batman Edition. Someone else apparently thought I mean to buy The Dukes of Gotham 2015. Thankfully, though, there were still some clear minds in the room who knew that I bought exactly what I intended to buy; another Batman game. It was those rightminded individuals who made this game worth playing.
The biggest problem with this game is being forced to use the Batmobile about 50% of the time. The drone tanks, after the first couple of battles, are just annoying and repetitive. Fighting battles against them is something I just wanted to get past, rather than something I enjoyed. One or two of the more difficult battles that had to be repeated were downright irritating. I'm glad to have the batmobile in the game and it is without a doubt the most badass Batmobile that has ever been dreamed up by anyone, but the way it was implemented was poor. It was way overused and the drone enemies you fight in it are boring and repetitive.
Chase scenes in the Batmobile are equally boring and repetive. You just drive around chasing enemies and destroying the entire city in the process. You'll knock down telephone poles, trees, park benches, taxis...you name it. By the time I've caught the bad guys I wonder if it's even worth saving Gotham anymore after I completely laid waste to the city by chasing them. You do this over and over and over again.
Thankfully there is also some good old Arkham gameplay, including flying through the city, the incredible combat system and some Batman detective work. The voice acting is absolutely outstanding as usual. The Joker is phenomenal. It's almost worth the price of admission just to listen to Mark Hamill's Joker. I can't say a bad word about any of the voice actors. They were all excellent.
If you're a huge Batman fan and a huge fan of the Arkham series (like I am), I'd say $30 is a fair price. There is plenty of content and the game is fun when it actually lets you play Batman. However, I do not recommend any of the DLC. All of the DLC stories are 30 minutes or less. I especially do not recommend the Batgirl DLC. It's just as short as the others but for some reason it's $6.99 instead of $1.99. It's also riddled with bugs. Although I have to admit it has the best dialogue of any of the DLC.

Anime (Japanese: アニメ?, [anime] ( listen)), also informally romanized as animé, are Japanese animated productions featuring hand-drawn or computer animation. In Japan, the word refers to all animation, being a shortened form of the rōmaji animēshon ("animation").[1] Outside Japan, the meaning of the word anime can vary slightly; definitions include animation from Japan or, alternatively, a Japanese-disseminated animation style often characterized by colorful graphics, vibrant characters and fantastical themes.[2][3] Arguably, the stylization approach to the meaning may open up the possibility of anime produced in countries other than Japan.[4][5][6] For simplicity, many Westerners strictly view anime as an animation product from Japan.[3] Some scholars suggest defining anime as specifically or quintessentially Japanese may be related to a new form of orientalism.[7]
The earliest commercial Japanese animation dates to 1917, and production of anime works in Japan has since continued to increase steadily. The characteristic anime art style emerged in the 1960s with the works of Osamu Tezuka and spread internationally in the late twentieth century, developing a large domestic and international audience. Anime is distributed theatrically, by television broadcasts, directly to home media, and over the internet. It is classified into numerous genres targeting diverse broad and niche audiences.
Anime is a diverse art form with distinctive production methods and techniques that have been adapted over time in response to emergent technologies. The production of anime focuses less on the animation of movement and more on the realism of settings as well as the use of camera effects, including panning, zooming, and angle shots. Diverse art styles are used and character proportions and features can be quite varied, including characteristically large emotive or realistically sized eyes.
The anime industry consists of over 430 production studios including major names like Studio Ghibli, Gainax, and Toei Animation. Despite comprising only a fraction of Japan's domestic film market, anime makes up a majority of Japanese DVD sales. It has also seen international success after the rise of English-dubbed programming. This rise in international popularly has resulted in non-Japanese productions using the anime art style, but these works are usually described as anime-influenced animation rather than anime proper.

Dead Space is pretty cool, I guess.
Set in the distant future of 2002, you play as Isaac Clarke, a man with two dads: Isaac Newton and Arthur Clarke. Unlike many Sci-Fi protagonists, Isaac is a space Engineer, which is like a normal Engineer but in space. And if EA promotional content is anything to go by, Isaac is also a golfer, a skateboarder, a mercenary, a world famous pugilist, and probably a really good kisser.
One day, Isaac and friends go to fix a bunch of broken stuff aboard the USG Ishimura, a ship that's literally named "Rock Village". Unfortunately it does the opposite of make villages out of rocks and instead cracks planets open to eat the sweet sweet planet juice hiding inside. Ooh baby.  Unfortunately, someone opened the space zombie can and now there are space zombies everywhere.
On the bright side, even though Isaac majored in engineering, he also apparently minored in being a unkillable death god from the 4th dimension because Isaac's right hook hits with about enough force to send the moon out of orbit and crashing into the planet below. When this game was still coming out back in 2008, the developers boasted that Isaac was at a disadvantage because he was an engineer and not a space marine. But Isaac still opens up more cans of Whoop A than the entire Earth military combined. It must be all that pent up space sexual frustration. Because he's in space.
The most unique aspect is that, outside of maybe one or two weapons, Isaac remains in his field of expertise in terms of equipment. But then again, his first weapon is called a plasma cutter. As in a tool that cuts things with plasma. Why don't you just give him a asteroid chainsaw while you're at it?
Actually, do that, that would be awesome.
But outside of developer words, Isaac is a huge faker. Sure he screams at everything and runs like a girl. But at the same time the guy can quick draw and open fire like the best of them.  But lets stop talking about that hunk of murder for a moment and talk about the Ishimura itself.
The Ishimura is the largest and oldest ship of it's class. Roughly 1.6 Km in length if the wiki is to be believed. When you're inside it's dark, dingy, Event Horizon inspired interior, you can actually kind of believe that people lived in there. Outside of the workbench and the machine that sells you murder tools for money. There are constant reminders that the Ishimura at one point, had it's own ecosystem and community. The ship seems to have everything from accommodations, recreational areas, movie theaters, video games, posters of products, vending machines, and even a restaurant. My favorite was the Zero-G basketball. Get dunked on, son.
The Necromorphs, Daughter Space's antagonists, are gross little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Originally the inhabitants of the USG Stonetown, the necromorphs now hunt through the halls, killing anything that doesn't look like them as well as spreading this weird mossy flesh stuff that looks like the stuff I find on my toilet seat.
But now that everyone is dead, outside of a few induviduals, as well as all of the angry space zombies onboard, is the Ishimura scary? Well, outside of the atmoshpere, no, not really. If anything the game is like a reverse horror story about alien lifeforms doing their best to try and stop an angry man covered in metal bits, jacked up on blue milk and packing more heat than the Detroit police department.
Is Dad Space a good horror game? No. Is it fun? Yes, I would say so. The weapons are crunchy and fun to use, the enemies have enough variety to make you switch up your strategies, and there's enough bread crumbs and rewards for exploration to get you into finding audio logs and picking up space money to buy space stuff.
I'm not saying that Dude Space would be scarier if Isaac was defenseless. I happen to not enjoy horror games where you run away a bunch very fun because I'm already very good at running away from my problems. I'm just saying that maybe they should have turned it down a bit, maybe even gave Isaac less equipment but more evasion options, such as hiding or sweet slide tackles. Not even half way through the game I had to start putting health items away because my aim is as perfect as I am handsome and I was losing space for ammo in favor of the blue milk boxes.
But should you play Father Area?
It's a fun game, just not a scary one. I did not find myself pooping my pants or screaming really loudly for YouTube money. But I did find an appeal in going from room to room exterminating the space Vampires. It's almost like a natural selection thing.
Man eat planet.
Space zombies eat man.
Immortal war god eat space zombie.

Shadowrun Returns runs very well on Linux, does not crash suddenly, graphics render well, I've had no problems running it.
I wouldn't call the writing in this game "spectacular”, but certainly you can tell they cared about the story and the dialogues. Although your choices in dialogues don't really alter the game very much, and sometimes not even the NPC's response, the game text is not a default, vague writing just to fill in dialogues. There is a common universe and plot going around and it's not a common sci-fi cliche. There is some depth to the story and that is noticeable, but it is not very developed: the writing and dialogues don't alter the outcome of the game very much.
If you are crazy about graphics, I wouldn't exactly recommended, but if you like graphics as in Bastion, you might be satisfied. Textures are mostly still, and you move through a fixed-camera map which you can pan with the mouse. Graphics are pretty, they don't look outdated at all, but they are not intended to be realistic.
In this default campaign, trying to let as little spoilers as possible, you will try to discover something. This process is full of dialogues and there is a story behind it, but when it boils down to it, you are just following what the game directs you to do. You don't actually understand what you are getting from dialogues and put the pieces together: the pieces are put together for you. If you are looking for a game that makes you think, probably not the best choice. This is an action game.
Shadowrun Returns provides you with a fair amount of character customization as you gain "karma", the game's word for experience. Doing many things, from picking things from the ground to killing enemies, will earn you karma. You can spend that to increase your stats and earn skills in the process. The race you pick is crucial to this, and that's good: races are not a mere aesthetic choice, rather, they set the limit for how much you will be able to invest in a certain stat.
Overall, if you like turn-based combat, don't care too much for cartoonish graphics and likes reading the dialogues and understanding the story, give it a try during sales, as it's the case right now. I wouldn't buy it for the original price tag, but the game is nice and very enjoyable, certainly worth my time.

This ain't your nephew's Dragon Age 2 or Witcher. Instead of going for needless voice-overs and cheesy cutscenes, this game aims purely for great dialogue - in written form. For the uninformed, dialogue in written form is a tradition which had been going on for many, many centuries.
What you're getting here is an Old School western RPG, very reminiscent of the first two Fallout games. It shares two of their biggest strengths - great writing and interesting setting. The biggest detriment is that the gameplay here follows an extremely linear plot. That wouldn't be so bad, if the game also didn't feel so short. It's absolutely adequate for the price you're paying, but you can't help but feel like there's something missing when you arrive at the end. However, that may just be, again, because of the very, very good writing.
Despite the fact that barely any dialogue choices and actions has a greater impact on the story, this game inspires one to play through it again with different characters and mindsets - just to read all the NPCs' reactions to all the dialogue choices. I can't stress that point enough. Some people notice the difference between 'okay' writing and great writing, and some think of AAA titles as high art.
DRAGONFALL DLC:
Dragonfall, in two words: Pretty amazing. For me, what really makes Dragonfall stand out in comparison with the original campaign, is the difference in plot structure.
For one thing, the game is much less linear. There are several missions to do in the middle section of the game; these can be done in any order you want, and it's entirely possible to skip one (maybe even two) of those missions.
Another major improvement is the fact that companions stick with you and are there to talk to after every mission. There are more than enough of these permanent companions hanging around that you never have the need fore hired companions. The original campaign had a great variety of interesting characters who would accompany you for a mission or two; here, they stick around and have new dialogue after every major mission. There's character development, and in the end, there's even closure.
Which brings me to the ending. Bluntly put, it's really, really good - enough to be a major point in this review. While the original campaign left you no choice in the end and the feeling of closure was kinda missing, Dragonfall delivers both in the end, and it does so very, very excellently, too. You are not only given a very meaningful choice which has the potency to shape the future of the setting, but the consequences of that choice are also portrayed adequately. After the end of the game, you are given one more chance to talk to every NPC of the main hub, every one of your companions and even new NPCs, depending on your choice. There's closure for every character and your choice is possibly being questioned in some of the best dialogue of the game.
But, lastly, the best thing about this DLC is that it delivers more of the old. Shadowrun shines when you get to interact with strong characters and are given absolutely free reign - the first Harlequin dialogue from the original campaign comes to mind - and there is much of that, here.

This is a review for the game in its current state, August 2016.
This is the weakest and most irritating of the Arkham games, but is still a good game. Someone on the development team apparently thought that when I bought this game, what I really intended to buy was World of Tanks: Batman Edition. Someone else apparently thought I mean to buy The Dukes of Gotham 2015. Thankfully, though, there were still some clear minds in the room who knew that I bought exactly what I intended to buy; another Batman game. It was those rightminded individuals who made this game worth playing.
The biggest problem with this game is being forced to use the Batmobile about 50% of the time. The drone tanks, after the first couple of battles, are just annoying and repetitive. Fighting battles against them is something I just wanted to get past, rather than something I enjoyed. One or two of the more difficult battles that had to be repeated were downright irritating. I'm glad to have the batmobile in the game and it is without a doubt the most badass Batmobile that has ever been dreamed up by anyone, but the way it was implemented was poor. It was way overused and the drone enemies you fight in it are boring and repetitive.
Chase scenes in the Batmobile are equally boring and repetive. You just drive around chasing enemies and destroying the entire city in the process. You'll knock down telephone poles, trees, park benches, taxis...you name it. By the time I've caught the bad guys I wonder if it's even worth saving Gotham anymore after I completely laid waste to the city by chasing them. You do this over and over and over again.
Thankfully there is also some good old Arkham gameplay, including flying through the city, the incredible combat system and some Batman detective work. The voice acting is absolutely outstanding as usual. The Joker is phenomenal. It's almost worth the price of admission just to listen to Mark Hamill's Joker. I can't say a bad word about any of the voice actors. They were all excellent.
If you're a huge Batman fan and a huge fan of the Arkham series (like I am), I'd say $30 is a fair price. There is plenty of content and the game is fun when it actually lets you play Batman. However, I do not recommend any of the DLC. All of the DLC stories are 30 minutes or less. I especially do not recommend the Batgirl DLC. It's just as short as the others but for some reason it's $6.99 instead of $1.99. It's also riddled with bugs. Although I have to admit it has the best dialogue of any of the DLC.

I will freely admit I love this game. The gameplay is solid, the aesthetics are fantastic, and there's a steep challenge and a wealth of loot/unlockables to find. It's well-crafted and executed, design-wise.
It's unfortunate, then, that this game is an absolute shoddy mess when it comes to the technical side of things.
PROS:
-Fun gameplay
-High degree of challenge
-Great aesthetics
-Expert sound and music design
-Loads of loot and unlockables
CONS:
-Game-ruining bugs far more frequent than they should be
-Some of the worst menu design I've ever seen
First of all, there's a bug that occurs rarely but shouldn't occur at all, where you spawn on a stage and simply fall through every platform. This respawns you at your starting point, but since the floors for some reason do not work, you'll just keep falling. This instantly ends a run as it renders the game unplayable.
There are times, especially on higher difficulties, where you will get a LOT of things going on at once. Problem is, the game can't handle it. Massive slowdown is not infrequent, and it's entirely possible for the game to crash entirely. I have lost an HOUR LONG run because there was too much going on onscreen and the game crashed. If you're going to make a heavy action game with enemies constantly spawning, you need to program the game to handle that- something the designers here certainly did not accomplish.
More minor complaints include the worst menu interface I've ever dealt with in a game. The pause menu can only be exited by actually moving the mouse and clicking resume. This wouldn't be so bad except the gameplay makes no use of the mouse- you have to take your hands off the keyboard to click resume, which can delay you and mess you up if you paused during an action-heavy moment. Seriously? Is it that hard to program the escape button to exit the menu the same way it entered it?
Also, menus are navigated entirely by clicking- which would be fine, if not for the fact that the button sizes are so small.  And you'd think there would be a key to return you to the previous menu- nope, you have to click back, since hitting escape just opens the pause menu over the regular menu. It's a 100% keyboard-based game but the menus use only the mouse. The menus in the game are a complete disaster as a result. Like I said, minor complaint, but worth noting.
All in all, I can't recommend this game in its current state. It is, quite frankly, broken. Yes, you will have some great runs, but the fact that such game-breaking bugs exist is absolutely inexcusable for a retail game. Don't buy- wait until these issues are sorted out.

I have to begin with admitting that I haven't actually finished Antichamber, but I don't really think it matters (unless there's some earth-shattering finale I've missed). I took a few days off from playing it, and when I returned, I just felt like I'd lost the thread a bit and I couldn't get back into it. I might pick it up again one day, but I've been distracted by Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon for now.
I was quite wary of playing another 'Portal-style' first-person puzzle game, as I'd been disappointed by some other FPP I'd played (I forget which), but the look of Antichamber, it's glowing reviews, and a half-price offer on Steam persuaded me to give it a try. And I have to say it's completely unlike any other game I've played, and any comparisons to Portal fade away in seconds. The simplicity of the controls lull you into a false sense of security, because things are certainly not what they seem.
I'm not sure how to describe the kinds of puzzles you encounter, because figuring them out feels like you're somehow allowing your conscience mind to take back seat and allowing cognitive instincts and your subconscious to take over. I know that sounds a bit wanky, but I honestly can't think of any other way of explaining the way the puzzles are presented to you and how you have to approach them. Yes, they take place in a physical environment, but nothing, absolutely nothing is explained to you. It's all one, rather-steep, ambiguous, learning curve. No hints, no companion to guide you, no story to indicate what your ultimate goal is. All you get is a set of black plaques containing proverbs which relate to the puzzle you've just solved.
Echoing the principles of quantum mechanics, the way you perceive the puzzles in Antichamber can alter how they behave. A large part of the initial approach to the game is simple trial and error, but once you pick up the basic principles you start to alter your approach accordingly. It's only when you get your hands on a device that allows you to manipulate small cubes (it doesn't sound very exciting, does it?) that you start to feel like you're playing a proper game, rather than a set of random puzzles.
It's a good job the all-white environment and the background ambient music is very soothing, because some of the puzzles would probably have you throwing your mouse at the screen in frustration. But despite feeling like just giving up sometimes, I never once felt angry or frustrated at the puzzles. I'm a firm believer that any puzzles in a game should contain just enough clues to allow you to solve them, and the biggest part of solving the puzzles is finding the clues, or recognising what IS a clue. I remember a couple of times in the old Tomb Raider games I'd spend hours running around in circles because the clue to the next step of the game was either far too discreet, relied on you stumbling across something by accident, or utterly non-existent. I also feel that games, even puzzle games, have become far too spoon-fed in recent years, and it's refreshing to play a game that contains no cut-scenes, no tutorials, and even very few configuration settings. You switch the game on, and you play. It's a principle that I wish was applied to all games, not just puzzlers. Allowing the player to learn as they play has become a forgotten art, and constant reminders about what buttons you need to press to perform an action have become a seemingly ubiquitous annoyance. I digress.
Although I described a trial and error approach to the puzzles, it never feels like you're running around in circles. If you've missed a clue, you just have to take a moment and reevaluate your surroundings and adjust your approach. The multiple patch approach also offers the chance to try something different and return to a particularly troubling puzzle at a later point. Many puzzles actually require you to return to them later in the game, you just have to learn which are which!
A excellent game, and a beacon to all developers who should have the balls to try something different.

X-COM: Enemy Unknown is a remake of the classic game by Microprose X-COM (or UFO). In this game the player takes control of the commander of an organization responsible for countering an invasion of planet Earth by hostile alien forces. The commander must command his forces in battle, recover and reverse engineer alien technology and balance his attention between the nations of the world, who when dissatisfied with his performance will withdraw their support and cut their funding.
While this game doesn't deliver jaw-dropping visuals it pretty much outshines most recent games in terms of gameplay, both in the tactical combat sequences and the geoscape game phases. The tactical combat system is easy to learn and can be mastered with a bit of thought, although due to its limitations and the design of gameplay mechanics it will undoubtedly cause many players to wind up yelling at their screens in frustration during moments such as when soldiers somehow manage to miss shots at point plank range or panic when their buddies receive fleshwounds.
Similarly, the geoscape game in which the player constructs his base of operations, conducts research and manufactures equipment is a treat. Pretty much everything in store during this game phase is simple and intuitive.
The story of the game isn't exactly its strong point and the voice acting of several characters (such as the Fraulein doctor) can be considered cheesy. I'd like to edit my original review of this game. My opinion of it hasn't changed, I still think it's a fantastic game that feels like a blend of several other game aspects done brilliantly. I'm altering my review as I have been able to read through the Core Rulebook of the Shadowrun RolePlaying Game system (5th Edition)
Many of the game mechanics found in the tabletop system are present in the game as it is here, such as ettiquettes, scoping out a job and figuring out the best approach, multiple ways of handling every job and so on, as well as the action point system that is used in the combat aspects and Decking. The changes between the Tabletop version and this game are very minor, and have only been done so that it translates comfortably to the format of a computer game. These changes, I welcome. I have encountered no changes to setting, backstory for the world, main mechanics, or generally anything which detracts from either tabletop or PC experience. That may sound really minor, but realistically that's something that's insanely hard to get right.
Hats off to the developers for this game, it is truely fantastic

Ah, one of Valve's most popular masterpiece, Half-Life 2
It's easy to understand why people would say this is the best game of all time, from the implemention of physics, to the story, which is simple but never bore me
Let's talk about it in parts
Story: 9.5/10
Like I said before, the story is simple, filled by surprises, interesting and memorable characters, and a little fun time. All in all, it's not a great story with complex political stuff or such. But the story will make you feel you are the mighty Gordon Freeman, that the one people talk in this game is YOU, not a character in a fictional world. And I think Valve should have a credit for making the player feels like they are the main character. I have never feel this important in a game, feeling like it's my world, where I have part in it, to protect it. It's not perfect of course, as it's not the end of the adventure.
Graphic: 8.5/10
Outdated is the first word comes to mind of course, remembering this game is 10 years old. Sure, close ups are really really bad, but the panorama this game has still manage to catch my breath at times. There are times where I stand at a high place, and stop for a while, only to admire how beauty the view is. Valve has really made a beautiful world in this game. As for enemies, friends, and other creatures in this game, I'll just say they did great job not to make it look very outdated.
Sound: 9/10
In an action game, we don't usually listen to music in game, as we are distracted by the fast enemies coming and be killed, not for this one. At least for me, the music is really great, fit with the atmosphere, and still keep our focus in the game. At times the music will make us feel vulnerable, at other times it makes us powerful. For sound effect and other stuff, it's at least very believeable, quite close to the real sound though there're times where it sound a little different. I really like the gun's sound though.
Level design: 10/10
You know what will come, but you'll still be surprised when it comes. That's the easy version of level design in Half-Life 2. Valve who's made their name famous from Half-Life, took their recipe of level design further and perfected it, then implement it in Half-Life 2. The one word t describe is fun. It's just fun defending yourslf from enemies, and never it is a boredom. There's surprises in the way.
Oh believe me, there're a LOT of surprises, and Valve sure love their zombies
Technical: 8/10
It may be my computer, but it took about 5-10 seconds to load between levels
Final verdict: 9/10
A masterpiece
Lots of fun
A believeable world
Story that's just.... play it yourself
And a genius level design

This is the Arkham game that Gotham deserves; but not the one it needs, right now.
I am going to split my review into two parts and talk about the particulars of the game.
Starting off with the good side of the game, I have to give it kudos for the story and the feeling of the Batman. The tagline 'Be the Batman' was not misleading. This is probably the most complex game that will really allow you to live and breathe the Batman (behind the safety of your monitor). The new additions to the combat and predator environments are just what was missing for that complete experience. The 'Fear Takedown' is something that was something I felt was necessary back in Arckham City - just that quick reaction that we all praise Batman for. Also the engine is just mesmerizing. You can enjoy an incredibly detailed city and character.
As I've said, the additions are great. Not too many but enough to really freshen up the Arkham feeling. Batman feels more powerful and his punches seem like they hit harder. The stealth system has also seen a very nice and smart make-over. You can now perform stealth takedown when standing above or further away from the enemy - Batman will make the necessary movement to reach the target. Also a nice (optional) system will take the world into extreme slow motion when you're spotted, before you're fired upon - so you can react.
The Batmobile turns the game from a 'two type' action sequence into a 'three type' action sequence and pretty much takes up one third of the game time; however the Batmobile itself feels right at home and has a very badass effect whenever it gets you out of a jam.
To avoid spoilers this whole section will be covered.
The wide variety of AR challenges and the possibility to play them which each of the characters adds a lot of entertaining more hours to the game time.
While most DLCs are basically AR Challenges or suits and skins, the "Season of Infamy" expansion is the best story extension you will ever find in a video game - if nothing else interests you, take that one.
Now to switch on the negatives of this game; fair warning, I will try to be as picky as it gets so that everyone finds what they're looking for...
While the additions to combat are astonishing and quite entertaining, using them when attempting to free flow can be quite annoying. Sometimes a certain combo will be broken due to the game not performing a move properly (such as the combat pick-up).
The targeting system of the game is also FUBAR in the sense that mid-combat you will click to perform a standard attack on a foe and Batman will pick that single one shield guy in the crowd and break your combo. This is even more frustrating when attempting those purist AR challenges or achievements (on a personal note I rage quit 3-4 times for a week to get those, due to poor game reaction). Other minor bugs include cutting your reaction time to zero - to elaborate, say you decide to perform an attack: you click and after you did an enemy pops the threat warning to attack you, and there is nothing more you can do about it. This has happened to me time and time again on those AR challenges with 6+ shield guys, where they would insta-hit you just as you hit the ground after a dodge. Also, some foes tend to teleport three or four meters and hit you, from off screen; again, giving you no time to react.
The frustration can really be heavy if you are an OCD perfectionist player.
Afore mentioned frustration of completing extensive AR challenges would be enough on its own. However, the game provides only that (as most of the story expansions are DLCs). The showcase of Batsuits and Skins really does nothing to improve the experience. Don't even get me started on the Artwork.
Expanding the story, some DLCs like "A matter of family" and the others, included in the "Arkham Stories" section of the menu are good. Not great. However most expansions include AR challenges and skins. It could not be more pointless. I have to pay to look differently for absolutely no reason? (since the in game suit is pretty much the best looking - don't start screaming. I love the Christian Bale Batman, for instance, but without his mouth/chin it just doesn't have the right feeling to it; so do the rest)
An extra category to the cons, because there is nothing good about it. From my experience, your system performance is really up to luck. Similar systems with different producers might operate differently. And while the game has FPS capping options, you'd be a God to get above 90FPS. And even if you would, once you call in the Batmobile you will be instantly transported to 6FPS Land, Population you; so have fun.
In my opinion, this is a game worth buying, with season pass, on any big Steam Sale. It is a solid game, quite enjoyable. But if you feel it's getting on your nerves, you need to put it down for a while, before picking it back up.
My rant into the cons of this game is as true as I've experienced it and I wasn't alone. Like most reviews I had to present the bad side. It's a poorly optimized game - after all it was withdrawn from Steam for many months after release. But if you liked the others, you'll love this one. And it is a tribute to the franchise.
Have fun, all!

Firaxis has their turn-based strategy gameplay down to a science.  After years of honing their skills with the broad strokes of the Civilization series, the team has now scaled down to focus on the intricacies of battle   The core experience is divided into two parts: the turn-based squad level tactical game; and the metagame of equipment upgrades, skill trees, scientific research, and managing panic levels around the world.
First, let's talk about the story.  It is standard videogame science fiction.  Creepy aliens abduct people, secret government ops fight back while upgrading their equipment with alien technology.  It does just fine and, most importantly, stays out of your way and allows you to "create your own stories" with the squad members you train.  I have never played the classic XCOM game, but brutal difficulty is a mechanic here.  Ideally, you play Ironman mode(where the game autosaves every decision, so soldier death is permanent).  I have yet to make it all the way through an Ironman game myself!  Regardless, name your squadmates after your friends or characters from movies and you end up caring when your maxed-out Colonel Starbuck gets their face ripped off by some fast moving critter with spikes for legs.
Now the metagame.  You'll spend roughly a 1/3 of your time in the headquarters menus.  Everything is presented with a fairly clean interface and it gives you a number of options on how you might want to proceed.  Do I research alien armor alloys so my soldiers last longer?  Or do I focus on weapon technology and build laser shotguns?  Don't forget about saving some of that hard earned cash to increase satellite coverage!  It all feels compelling and definitely is rewarding to step onto the battlefield with that newly engineered plasma sniper rifle.  That being said, the game does demand that you prioritize certain research and building tasks in order to advance the story missions.  It also becomes apparent after a couple playthroughs how essential some of the upgrades are, breaking just a bit of that illusion that you can play absolutely any way you want.  The Second Wave options menu and Enemy Within DLC do expand on this area quite a bit though and provide some wonderful extra options.
Finally, the tactics game.  Superb!  There is a fantastic balance between depth and accessibility.  Engagements play out like intricate, four dimensional games of Rock-Paper-Scissors; constantly balancing unit cover, sight lines, suppressing fire, and reloading becomes imperative.  Remember, it's turn-based.  So a lot of the fun is in anticipating enemy attack patterns, taking the time to think, and methodically moving your squad to maintain support for each other.  All the information you need is readily available and the different skill sets of each squad member are easy to apply to battlefield conditions.  It's wonderful...until it seems to defy itself.  The AI in this game will occasionally make you RAGE.  Untimely misses, logic defying lines of site, and inability to modify which tiles are enroute to a location will drive even the most sedate players nuts.  That, and the camera control can be utterly obnoxious.
None of the issues with this game have ever made me not want to pick it back up again.  The strategy is engaging and you feel a direct influence from your research and engineering decisions.  It is an absolute keeper and would be of special interest to any thinking man's game collection.

Was only suppose to play half an hour or so and then go watch a movie before bed, ended up playing 5 hours straight and ruining my next day at work.
The game itself certainly is impressive, the main narrative is interesting and the side missions are surprisingly rich compared to other games. With surprising plots and twists that really keeps it interesting. This could however could also be down to random encounters (such as airdrops) that can turn a lazy stroll down the street to a gazelle race through the city or hide and seek that will have you scurrying around on all fours while waiting for whatever is hunting you to turn their backs.
The main Zombies “biters” are little better then a nuisance if you are paying attention, the only time I have had real issues is when I ran smack into a hoard while being chased by “virals” which are infected living that can give you a run for your money, very 28 days later like. That and there are a lot spoiler zombies that will have you worried (Volatile) when the sun goes down.
Had a very “Fun” moment where 2 people had joined my game just as it was getting Dark, we were pretty much playing Sandbox. Running around and bullying the “biters” laughing and comparing different ways of killing them and the few “virals” that interrupted us. (Coop makes it a lot easier as you can gang up on more powerful zombies and watch each other’s backs)
This changed big-time however as the sun went down, we went from hunting to being hunted real fast. Trying to keep it together as a group when a hoard of virals are hot on your heals is both terrifying and hilarious at the same time, we ended up chased into an apartment complex which turned out to be a dead end. But thanks to great teamwork we actually held out till morning by holding a small apartment with one entrance, one person would heal and repair his weapons while lending an occasional kick while the two others held the Volatiles at bay with UV lights and everything from leg furniture to screwdrivers and wrenches.
Most heart racing experience I have had in gaming for a very long-time, our elation at surviving however went south when we realised the battered and retreating Volatiles had been replaced by a hoard of zombies “biters” that swarmed the building we were in. Seeing your team being dragged down one at the time by a wall of dead flesh, before being pulled out of your corner and devoured was surprisingly enjoyable.
Only real thing I can put my finger on is optimization, the game doesn’t seem to be 100% optimized and if you have AMD graphic card you might encounter some FPS drops that shouldn’t happen. Hopefully this will be addressed in patches.

Half-Life is one of my favourite games of all time. And I came into the sequel with such high hopes after how great the original was, and the sheer amount of amazing reception this game got. However, I was disapointed. Don't get me wrong, I love the living crap out of this game..... buuuuuuuuuuuut it didn't get the same experience out of Half-Life 2 as I did with Half-Life 1.
Visually, this game was a revolution. This game was the best looking game on the market at the time and it still look good today! However, I do prefere the darker, scarier art style of HL1 but that is personal preference! Just looking at the amazing visuals today is just amazing. The level of detail and amount of options is amazing considering this game came out 10 years ago!
Gameplay is one of the best features of this game. Although linear (even more than HL1) the game is fantastic. The physics in the game is just mind blowing! The game utilises physics superbly. The Game is packed with puzzels, challenges and intense fire fights through out the game. This game is a game where you want to find achievements because there are tonnes of easter eggs to find in the game. The game has extraorinary gameplay is fun to play with the physics.
Story wise it was disapointing. I'm not saying it was bad or anything, I'm just saying it's not as good as the original. I found there was more atmosphere and I prefered the survival-horror Sci-fi setting rather than the "City 17" Rebellion. I prefered Gordon Freeman as a man trying to survive than... well Jesus!He is portrayed like Jesus in this game!!!! The game trys to be Half-Life 1 in some ways (the opening train ride for instance) but it doesn't deliver the same effect as the original! The characters that where "Supposed" to be in Half-Life 1 because they weren't called Barney or Eli in the first game and they weren't properly developed in the first game. If so I would of connecte with the characters more. I connected more with characters like Alyx and D0G because they were new characters and they were developed propely. But the ending is crap and leaves me wondering. Even worse, they resolve it in DLC! WHAT THE HELL VALVE! YOU DON'T DO THIS!!!!!
Then there is the lack of Deathmatch. WHAT THE HELL! Deathmatch was one of my favourite parts of Half-Life 1. There were so many gamemodes and maps that were actually very fun. Now I have to pay more money. It's only five bucks but I am not paying five extra bucks for the complete collection!
So all together I am paying 31 dollars for the complete experience that I would expect out of the game! No No NO! And now I realise where this money hungry trend is coming from Activision And EA!
All round it's a great game. Although the Original had a better atmosphere and story! There no doubt about it that the gameplay has improved over the original. A great story and with revoultionary graphics! Shame I have to pay 31 dollars for the entire expierence!

To this day, I still remember playing this game all those years ago on my commodore 64. It still sits on the shelf above my computer, complete with the box, manual and all 11 floppy disks, as a tribute to how great this game is. So, Half life 2, where to begin?
When this game came out in 1988, it made a huge impact on the game industry, because at the time the idea of creating a first person shooter was absurd. Even the original half life wasn't in first person, and that came out on the vic-20. Now, before I say anything else, let me just get this out of the way. This game is old and it shows. Although the developers have done a fantastic job of making it run nice and smooth on modern computers, completely eliminating the constant disk swapping present in the original version, there are still many things that might make the younger gamers hesitant about purchasing this. But enough about that, let's get to the game itself.
This game practically invented the first person shooter genre. Now, anyone familiar with BASIC programming and the commodore 64 can see where I'm going when I say the commodore 64 was a slow system. Like, really slow. Every time you move, the graphics on screen have to be redrawn, which usually takes a second or two. The game is drastically simplified in that the game, instead of featuring open, free roaming environments, works on a grid based, tile-walk system, similar to pokemon or the old bard's tale games. Over the course of the game, you level up, and can choose to increase either your health, stamina or magika, which really allows the player to take the time to craft the kind of characters they want.
Now on to combat. There are three guns in the game, the pistol, the shotgun, and the SMG. It's up to you to discover their individual strengths and weaknesses in order to get through the loading screens in one piece. Just remember: Ammo is a precious resource, and must be used only when you truly need it.
Concerning the story, it is definately one of the most finely crafted tales ever woven. Beautiful writing. Unfortunately though, you'll still have to download the paragraph book from the half life website, because when the game was first released, they didn't have the data storage to include all that text in the game.
In conclusion: This game is still a classic, and holds up even today. It is truly sad that the new generations will turn the other cheek at this game and walk away, but in my humble and biased opinion, I give it a buy.

Or sometimes you pull it together. You manage to fight off the space pirates but now you're sitting here with just the one crew member who didnt suffocate, and by elimination looks like he's become your new pilot.

Despite being one of the most anticipated video games of 2015, Batman: Arkham Knight had a bar that needed to be kept at some standart, after the release of Batman: Arkham City. Unfortunately, just after the poor release on PC, reputation of Rocksteady’s Batman franchise has crashed to shreds. But the port wasn’t the only problem. Devs have put so many cool features in previous titles, it is clear that they were so busy with upping their “game” they actually managed to fail at some point. This is my personal opinion obviously but I think the mechanics isn’t where Rocksteady has failed. It is the plot.
Arkham Knight persona was the last thing Arkham Franchise needed when devs decided to bring
on the table. They could have worked on couple of things, yes but recreating, hell, just only rewriting the origins has taken so much from character, what is left of it was just whimpy annoying robot guy who has anger management issues.
As for the “No Joker” card, we all have been expected this coming but this much? Wow. Even tho I call bs about all the infecteds behaviours, gotta say, I liked the whole deal. Nice touch. Again, I shouldn’t say this but, wasn’t it too much of Joker?

Was only suppose to play half an hour or so and then go watch a movie before bed, ended up playing 5 hours straight and ruining my next day at work.
The game itself certainly is impressive, the main narrative is interesting and the side missions are surprisingly rich compared to other games. With surprising plots and twists that really keeps it interesting. This could however could also be down to random encounters (such as airdrops) that can turn a lazy stroll down the street to a gazelle race through the city or hide and seek that will have you scurrying around on all fours while waiting for whatever is hunting you to turn their backs.
The main Zombies “biters” are little better then a nuisance if you are paying attention, the only time I have had real issues is when I ran smack into a hoard while being chased by “virals” which are infected living that can give you a run for your money, very 28 days later like. That and there are a lot spoiler zombies that will have you worried (Volatile) when the sun goes down.
Had a very “Fun” moment where 2 people had joined my game just as it was getting Dark, we were pretty much playing Sandbox. Running around and bullying the “biters” laughing and comparing different ways of killing them and the few “virals” that interrupted us. (Coop makes it a lot easier as you can gang up on more powerful zombies and watch each other’s backs)
This changed big-time however as the sun went down, we went from hunting to being hunted real fast. Trying to keep it together as a group when a hoard of virals are hot on your heals is both terrifying and hilarious at the same time, we ended up chased into an apartment complex which turned out to be a dead end. But thanks to great teamwork we actually held out till morning by holding a small apartment with one entrance, one person would heal and repair his weapons while lending an occasional kick while the two others held the Volatiles at bay with UV lights and everything from leg furniture to screwdrivers and wrenches.
Most heart racing experience I have had in gaming for a very long-time, our elation at surviving however went south when we realised the battered and retreating Volatiles had been replaced by a hoard of zombies “biters” that swarmed the building we were in. Seeing your team being dragged down one at the time by a wall of dead flesh, before being pulled out of your corner and devoured was surprisingly enjoyable.
Only real thing I can put my finger on is optimization, the game doesn’t seem to be 100% optimized and if you have AMD graphic card you might encounter some FPS drops that shouldn’t happen. Hopefully this will be addressed in patches.

NOTE: This is a shortened review without screenshots.For my full review, please visit
It’s often said that licensed games usually don’t carry a lot of quality. Unfortunately, we live in an age where many good video games have such huge budgets that developers and publishers aren’t willing to take a risk on a new franchise, instead churning out poorly-made games based on franchises and preying on the fans of the franchise.
This is not one of those cases. Though it had a somewhat tumultuous development cycle, the end product is a fantastic representation of everything that’s great about the South Park series. If you’re a fan of the series, or at least its style of humour, this is a no-brainer. For others that have never been impressed with the juvenile and tasteless jokes ubiquitous throughout the South Park universe, I’d recommend that you avoid this title. This isn’t because the gameplay can’t hold a candle on its own – It can, and it was a fun romp in its own right. It’s more that the developers spent so much effort on building the perfect South Park game and added as many of their well-renowned politically incorrect humour that it becomes unavoidable if it isn’t your thing.
The game begins with you, (“D-bag”) and your parents moving into South Park, Colorado. You’re then tasked with making friends in the new town, which isn't easy given that your protagonist is mysteriously silent throughout the game. Before long, you’ll find yourself involved in a real-life role playing game with the other kids in South Park. There are two factions – The humans, led by Cartman, and the elves, led by Kyle. Both factions fight over a stick – the titular Stick of Truth, which supposedly possesses the power to control the universe. Throughout your journey, you’ll encounter numerous (and often ridiculous) obstacles and hazards and meet a tonne of infamous characters from the South Park franchise and an even greater number of references to events that have occurred in the TV show.
Fans of the series who have seen the South Park episode “The Return of the Fellowship of the Ring to the Two Towers” will find the setting very familiar. As in the episode, the characters don costumes representing their class and/or position (including a cross-dressing princess Kenny) and are deeply engrossed in their roles, but they do occasionally have to break out of character in order to satisfy their real-life commitments, which more often than not involves the parents telling them that it’s time for bed.
The game itself resembles other turn-based, quick time event (QTE)-heavy RPGs such as
and the dreaded
. Battles aren’t random, but rather are usually initiated by walking into an enemy. During each battle, you’re given a party of up to two characters (your main character and a character that you can choose and switch between). Each character has its own unique set of attacks and abilities. For each action that you choose, there’s an associated QTE action that you have to perform perfectly in order to maximise the effect. This often includes pressing a certain button at some point in time, mashing another button, spinning the left control stick or some combination of the above. Unlike in
where the timing of these was very lenient and forgiving even if you happened to miss it,
requires you to be on your toes. The window of opportunity for pressing these buttons is fairly strict, and the consequences of missing button sequence can lead to severe consequences. For example, one of Kenny’s special abilities involves him calling a horde of rats. Once the rats appear, you’re required to rapidly and repeatedly pull your left control stick to the left and right. If you succeed, the rats swarm your enemies for significant amount of damage. Should you fail however, the rats will literally eat Kenny alive. When it’s your opponents turn to attack, you’re once again given a small window to press a button in order to defend their attack, which results in reduced damage or prevention of a negative status effect. Overall, actively pressing buttons at the correct time matters in this game, which adds a level of intensity to every battle. It’s a fantastic combat system that forces the player to be actively involved, rather than continuously mashing a single button and hoping for the best.
Whist outside of battles, your character is freely able to roam around South Park, gathering quests and looking for loot (equipment, potions, cosmetic items or junk to sell), collectables (i.e. Chinpokomon) and even more friends to add to Facebook, which helps to unlock perks which will assist you in battle. Completing side quests usually rewards you with equipment, friends or even “summons” that you can call to battle when things get rough. The Mr. Slave summon ability literally causes him to violently shove an enemy up his butt for impressive, but disturbing results.
The game also gives you access to certain abilities that you can use to solve simple puzzles that are strewn across the game. Whilst some of these puzzles have to be solved in order to progress, many of these merely offer you an easier way to deal with enemies without actually fighting them in battle. If there’s a rock sitting on a ledge above your enemy, you can shoot it with a slingshot and have it drop on your enemies, which avoids the necessity of combat entirely. There are many more examples of manipulating the environment in order to gain an advantage or avoid combat entirely, but I'd hate to spoil the fun of discovering these for yourself. Overall, it’s a very refreshing and unique mechanic that’s highly welcome in a game where things may otherwise get stale.
Visually, the game beautifully replicates the aesthetic that the show is famous for. It’s not mindblowing by any stretch of the imagination, but it’s just the way any fan of the show would want it to look.
More importantly, the developers, in conjunction with the creators of South Park, have done a wonderful job replicating the world of South Park.  Every building in town can be entered and interacted with. The game is chock-full of characters and/or references to characters or events from the series. The voice-acting is on-point, with the original voice actors of the show providing the voices of the characters. Characters have context-sensitive remarks. If Cartman is in your party and you walk into Kyle’s house, you bet he’ll mutter something about Jews and/or make a derogatory remark regarding Kyle’s mother. Ultimately, the game does a tremendous job at making you feel like you’re a part of the world that is South Park, and fans of the show really couldn’t ask for anything more than that. With that said, if you’re not a fan of the show or think it’s too vulgar, please turn away now. This game pulled no punches in vulgarity, and even as a long-time fan of the show, there are certain segments that I think are a little bit too disturbing or distasteful. Your mileage may vary.
After numerous delays, I’m happy to say South Park: The Stick of Truth is a tremendous title that successfully replicates both the humour and personality of the show, whilst providing a refined, tightly-controlled and satisfying combat system to boot. Whilst it's a solid game in its own right, your enjoyment of the overall experience will be very heavily influenced by just how much the humour that the show is famous for actually appeals to you. As a result, I wouldn't recommend this to anyone that hates the show, but would recommend it without questin to anyone that is a fan.

Looks can be deceiving, but this game is more addictive and larger in scope than it appears.  Despite its complex nuances, FTL is very simple to pick up and play, and the tutorial it comes with does the job.  (Watching gameplay videos on Youtube helps, too.)  If you enjoy Sci-Fi games with some RPG elements and tabletop board games, then this is the game for you.  Totally beats Solitaire.  FTL is like a board game in the sense that there is no save feature, choices/consequences are permanent, and each playthrough is totally random like the roll of the dice or drawing cards.  Your choices in the path you take, what ship upgrades you get, how you manage your crew, whether or not you should pursue a distress signal, etc. can all heavily influence your gameplay.  Best of all, this game is wonderfully challenging (you are meant to completely fail on some of your attempts!) and has a great retro soundtrack with excellent ambience.  Totally worth the ten bucks and has surprisingly superb replay value.
