Killing Floor 2 is an excellent game and Tripwire has come a long way from the original Killing Floor. The graphics are extremely polished, the gameplay is more exciting and challenging than the original Killing Floor, and the devs are constantly updating the game. Reading the other reviews, alot of people are complaining about two main things: Update Progress and Microtransactions. I'd like to address both of these problems.
1)
First off, the devs DO update Killing Floor 2. Many people complain that the devs do not update on a frequent basis, however one must remember "Quality over Quantity". I would rather have a game be polished and have exciting gameplay and take a while to be released than have a game that was made rather quickly due to fans urging the devs to make the game ASAP. As Shigeru Miyamoto said,
2)
Killing Floor 2 does indeed have microtransactions. However, these
affect gameplay whatsoever! Unlike the original Killing Floor, which had microtransactions/DLCs that had different weapons that had different mechanics than the weapons from the base game, Killing Floor 2's microtransactions only affect the game
. It has no affect on the game whatsoever. No one is pushing the players to buy any microtransactions and nor are they missing out on anything.
All in all, Killing Floor 2 is an amazing game. The gameplay is much more hardcore and intense than Killing Floor 1 (It's also MUCH more chaotic. Try playing with a full squad on Hell On Earth.), the music and sound effects enhance the gameplay, the graphics are amazing and the perks are much more balanced compared to the ones in Killing Floor 1. 10/10 would play again.
UPDATE
I wrote this review over a year ago and I stand by it. Tripwire, after all these years, STILL continue to update it. Currently there are 10 perks that have been fleshed out and constantly get newer guns. I wholeheartily think that you should get this game if you're a fan of blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up.

I've now played 3 out of 4 Batman Arkham games and I can say without a doubt that this one is the most fun so far.
It got off to a rough start with performance issues and unpromising gameplay but as you progress you become increasingly immersed in the innovative world of the Knight's Gotham. Everything about this game felt fresh and new. The gameplay, while similar to past games, remained exciting and interesting and flowed much smoother than past games.
The new Batmobile mechanic is super fun too. Learning to use each aspect of the vehicle became a fun and interesting challenge, even while the tank levels became slightly stale.
The tank levels are easily the most difficult part about this game and provided a small amount of frustration on normal, compared to the teeth-grinding frustration of the gargoyle-stealth levels in past games. However, rather than just discouraging the player, these challenges that Arkham Knight provides are fun and competitive.
One failure of Batman Arkham Knight is the boss battles. There's only one or two fun and interesting battles, the rest are rather uncreative or easy. You won't be getting another Deathstroke fight in this game.
Graphics-wise, this game blew me away. I played on maxed settings and the atmosphere and realism it provided brought the game to a whole new level. It gave Gotham character while maintaining the gritty and dark feel of the past games.
The biggest problem with this game in my opinion is the story. It's a rather overused plot structure and overly melodramatic at times. The actual Arkham Knight part of the story was interesting and the side quests could be enjoyed if you didn't try to play them all (they become repetitive). Towards the end the story took a few interesting turns but ultimately ended in a confusing and convoluted manner, creating a Batman inconsistent with his own character.
Despite its flaws, it definitely worth picking up if you're new to the franchise or a veteran of the Arkham games.

If you enjoy horde mode in other games (COD Zombie mode etc.) then Killing Floor 2 is a great pickup. If that can be allowed to happen with the second game here, then I think this game will thrive as long as the first one has and continues to.
Cosmetics in this game are great for personality etc, but having the "CSGO" crate and looting system is just unimaginative, and a quick way for the devs to grab a quick buck. I do however like the idea of using the Community Marketplace to buy and sell the cosmetics you find, and value being based on the total number of such items on the marketplace. All in all I don't hate the system I just think it could have been designed much better than an existing system in a different game.
Overall the game is well worth the money and has so much potential. With continued development I think it could be a game that last for many years.

Either way, it's a rather enjoyable game, especially with the Enemy Within expansion, which added some much needed content and map diversity. Definitely worth a buy if you're in the market for a turn-based strategy game and can overlook a few small flaws.
As an overall rating, I'd give XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion a solid 8.5/10.

Game runs well, I'm not one to record specs, but, compared to the other, console version of this game I tried, it has less framerate drops, and looks smoother overall.
My main issue is with the controls. Sure, the K+M controls run well enough, but, just moving around and/or aiming was enough to make my head uneasy (not that I was scared) in less than 10 minutes... controller HEAVILY recommended.
As for the game itself, not bad. The story is interesting, and, the atmosphere is excellent, making for some unnerving tension... at times. My main issue with the game is that, once the tension wears off, the uneffective jump scares kick in, which make me go "meh", rather than, "goodness, that was shocking!"... I don't know, maybe it gets better in the later bits, but, I've managed to get farther on a console, and, there was less tension than previously. As for the design of the monsters (like, the necromorphs), they're actually pretty amazing, and I've never seen anything really like them. Going back to the whole jump scare tangent for a second, all the scares started to wear off after the first level for me. In the first level, I'd see a ton of vents and monsters pop up, and, for some time, I'd be (at the very least) a little shocked. Now? I see a ton of vents, and then picture well over 100 monsters, with a paper taped to their head that reads "am I scary yet?"...  no. Again, maybe I'm being too harsh considering I'm not even half-way through this game yet.
All in all, do I recommend Dead Space (from what I've played thus far)? Yes, but, really only for the atmosphere and story. But, do I recommend the PC version? Maybe. The K+M controlls, while not exactly awful, don't work the greatest, BUT, it does run FAR better than any console version I know of... or, maybe that's just me.

Shadowrun Returns is an top-down isometric RPG game, set in the universe of the Shadowrun pen & paper role-playing game.
You take direct control of your central character, followed by the companions you choose or forced to by the game. Combat mode is activated when you encounter aggressive NPCs. Combat options include using cover, summoning creatures to fight for you, healing and boosting your team, spells, melee weapons and gun play. You have direct control of your own team. Interaction with the world and team is highly limited when out of combat unfortunately.
When you start a game, you pick your character's gender, race (human, elf, ork, dwarf or troll) and either pick a pre-designed class or build your own. The character creation and progression system is highly flexible, you are given points which you allocate to certain abilities, enhancing them or giving you more options. You earn more of these by progressing through the plot or doing side quests in game. Throughout the game, you can also learn new spells, buy new weapons or invest in implants (at the expense of your ability to cast spells).
The default campaign that comes with the game is short, linear, and filled with plenty of good and interesting characters that aren't fully fleshed out. Good plot, but missed opportunity. User generated campaigns are hit and miss, but some surpassing the default campaign.
Graphics look beautiful, and really delivers the cyberpunk look and feel. Music and sound effects are good, but with only a limited selection, you end up hearing the same few tracks and sounds often.
TL:DR: good for scratching that old-school isometric RPG itch, some good strategic choices to make in the game. The default campaign is fine, but limited, might want to check out the user made stuff, or DLC.

Shadowrun Returns is a classic RPG combined with modern gameplay elements but it's focus clearly lies on storytelling and immersion. It aims to create a believable world based around the popular Shadowrun pen&paper ruleset and in that it succeeds. It took me around 16h to complete the main campaign most of which was reading dialogues similar in structure to that of games like Baldur's Gate or Planescape Torment. On pure gameplay and mechanics it lacks however although you will love the combat system if you liked X-Com: Enemy Unknown.
But if you really want a good game buy this and get the DLC "Dragonfall". It beats the maingame astronomically. While the maingame focuses purely on the main character Dragonfall introduces persistent team members for the first time that develop relationships between them and yourself over time. They even managed to create a richer and more dense story around the awakening of the Dragons with lots of plot twists and filled with morale decisions where there is simply no clear right or wrong. And when you are finished with both campaignsthere is always the workshop to come back to where you'll find a huge number of player created adventures. Shadowrun Returns has the potential to keep you engaged for several years as, so far, the devs are constantly working on new content for the game but even more so the community. Currently a number of the best modders for the game are working together on a massive scale campaign. So even if the next piece of DLC is not that great, there is still something to be looking forward to.
In short words this game is best described as a mixture of Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment, X-Com and Fallout. That all combined with it's active modding community easily makes Shadowrun Returns the best "C"RPG of this time.
It's on sale until the May 5th, so grab it. It's a steal.

This could however could also be down to random encounters (such as airdrops) that can turn a lazy stroll down the street to a gazelle race through the city or hide and seek that will have you scurrying around on all fours while waiting for whatever is hunting you to turn their backs.
The main Zombies “biters” are little better then a nuisance if you are paying attention, the only time I have had real issues is when I ran smack into a hoard while being chased by “virals” which are infected living that can give you a run for your money, very 28 days later like. That and there are a lot spoiler zombies that will have you worried (Volatile) when the sun goes down.
Had a very “Fun” moment where 2 people had joined my game just as it was getting Dark, we were pretty much playing Sandbox. Running around and bullying the “biters” laughing and comparing different ways of killing them and the few “virals” that interrupted us. (Coop makes it a lot easier as you can gang up on more powerful zombies and watch each other’s backs)
This changed big-time however as the sun went down, we went from hunting to being hunted real fast. Trying to keep it together as a group when a hoard of virals are hot on your heals is both terrifying and hilarious at the same time, we ended up chased into an apartment complex which turned out to be a dead end. But thanks to great teamwork we actually held out till morning by holding a small apartment with one entrance, one person would heal and repair his weapons while lending an occasional kick while the two others held the Volatiles at bay with UV lights and everything from leg furniture to screwdrivers and wrenches.
Most heart racing experience I have had in gaming for a very long-time, our elation at surviving however went south when we realised the battered and retreating Volatiles had been replaced by a hoard of zombies “biters” that swarmed the building we were in. Seeing your team being dragged down one at the time by a wall of dead flesh, before being pulled out of your corner and devoured was surprisingly enjoyable.
Only real thing I can put my finger on is optimization, the game doesn’t seem to be 100% optimized and if you have AMD graphic card you might encounter some FPS drops that shouldn’t happen. Hopefully this will be addressed in patches.

Killing Floor 2 is an excellent game and Tripwire has come a long way from the original Killing Floor. The graphics are extremely polished, the gameplay is more exciting and challenging than the original Killing Floor, and the devs are constantly updating the game. Reading the other reviews, alot of people are complaining about two main things: Update Progress and Microtransactions. I'd like to address both of these problems.
1)
First off, the devs DO update Killing Floor 2. Many people complain that the devs do not update on a frequent basis, however one must remember "Quality over Quantity". I would rather have a game be polished and have exciting gameplay and take a while to be released than have a game that was made rather quickly due to fans urging the devs to make the game ASAP. As Shigeru Miyamoto said,
2)
Killing Floor 2 does indeed have microtransactions. However, these
affect gameplay whatsoever! Unlike the original Killing Floor, which had microtransactions/DLCs that had different weapons that had different mechanics than the weapons from the base game, Killing Floor 2's microtransactions only affect the game
. It has no affect on the game whatsoever. No one is pushing the players to buy any microtransactions and nor are they missing out on anything.
All in all, Killing Floor 2 is an amazing game. The gameplay is much more hardcore and intense than Killing Floor 1 (It's also MUCH more chaotic. Try playing with a full squad on Hell On Earth.), the music and sound effects enhance the gameplay, the graphics are amazing and the perks are much more balanced compared to the ones in Killing Floor 1. 10/10 would play again.
UPDATE
I wrote this review over a year ago and I stand by it. Tripwire, after all these years, STILL continue to update it. Currently there are 10 perks that have been fleshed out and constantly get newer guns. I wholeheartily think that you should get this game if you're a fan of blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up.

Half-Life 2 is a game that no fan of first-person shooters should miss. The game is primarily an adventure in which you "fight the power" and begin an uprising against a totalitarian and unfeeling alien government that has enslaved the vast majority of the human race into carrying out its various biddings. From whacking cyborg policemen with a crowbar in the first level to manually controlling laser-guided rockets in mid-air to drop two gunships from the sky while your vast army of giant bugs terrorizes the super soldiers residing in the local prison facility, your journey will make you feel as though you're accomplishing a lot.
Valve did a great job of designing HL2's levels around rewarding exploration, as well as giving players little resting periods between hectic gunfights to solve physics-related puzzles in order to advance or claim extra goodies in the form of health or ammunition. As for story, the game has more of it than meets the eye; look around and you might find newspaper clippings telling of a "Seven Hour War"; listen carefully to Dr. Breen (the "puppet antagonist") and you might discover why there are no children to be seen in the entire game. Lastly, without giving anything away, I'd like to add that the game's final level STILL, to this day, leaves a lasting impression on me; it is most definitely one hell of a ride.
I think the only glaring flaw this game has is its rather vague and abrupt cliffhanger ending (cue Episodes 1 and 2). There are, of course, other smaller issues, like the occasional enemy standing still and accepting your bullets to their face with glee, or the frustrating vehicle controls (yes, there are driving segments, and they don't end quickly). I also wish the game gave the player more opportunities to approach a group of enemies stealthily, as their spidey-senses usually kick in once you've entered the same acre as them.
In conclusion, I give Half-Life 2 nine damn cats out of ten. It is truly a treat.

This game is beautiful, charming and funny all at the same time. It challenges everything that you think you know about first-person worlds, which will make you wriggle with delight at various points in the game. There is no dialogue, story, characters or music, but there are still emotions that flood through your brain.
Imagine you have stepped into a hallway with two doors leading out. A red door to the left and a blue door leading right. You, being a systematic kind of fellow walk to the left first, but that just leads you back to the junction with the red and blue doors. You try the right door but it still sends you back again. The real joy comes from feeling dismayed and walking back the way you came in, only to find yourself in a new setting that you have never seen before. Moments like this are priceless, and the game has a great many of them. More than once you may think that you found some sort of glitch that got you past a chamber, but these are built right into the game and you feel like a complete pro every time.
Have a little try, and keep an open mind. There is no such thing as a dead end.

If you like Puzzles--I highly, highly reccomend this game. It's absoultely amazing.
The puzzles are self-contained, in that with the exception of a few metroidvania-esque elements, everything you need to solve the puzzle is right there, as well as being univseral--no puzzle is unique, learning from one puzzle can help you in all other puzzles.
The game has no concept of failure--there is no wrong route, only different routes. This does not make the game EASY--it took me 8 hours to play through my first time, as compared to 2 hours for my first playthrough of Portal. In fact, the game is very difficult, but in a good way.
Rather than a lot of puzzle games, where you solve the puzzle, and then tediously carry out the solutions--think sliding block puzzles, for example, mentally working out the solution is only half the challenge--in antichamber, it takes less than a minute to solve any puzzle once you have worked out the solution in your head. The challenge is figuring out the rules of the puzzle, not implementing them.
Though the game may seem haphazard at first, it's very well put together. While almost no assumptions you may have about how physics works apply to the game, the games physics system is both consistent (applies everywhere) and complete (nothing feels unexplained). As mentioned in the previous paragraph, the challenge is in learning how the game works.
Seriously, this game is amazing, and I really reccommend it.

I bought this game specifically to "invade" other player's games with the pre-order Night Hunter. I am extremely dissapointed with what it turned out to be.
1. Calling it an "invasion" of other games is just a slimey lie. The pre-order was marketed as if you're invading a player's campaign or open world, but in reality it's just a cheap PvP versus mode with little-to-no satisfaction. It's literally just a matchmaking mechanism and 90% of the time it seems like it doesnt even work because players either dodge the match or it simply fails to connect. OR the matches don't exist. Take your pick, you can waste a good 15 to 60 minutes just trying to "invade" a game and it may not even go anywhwere if the human players just up and quit with no explanation. Probably has something to do with the poor quality of the multiplayer game and less about players quitting intentionally.
2. The goal of this fake "game invasion" is for the humans to destroy a certain amount of nests. Your job as the night hunter is to kill them a certain amount of times before they can desroy the nests. That's all there is to it and it's pretty lame. If you bought this to "Be The Zombie", you might as well get Evolve instead because you'll likely have better functionality and more depth. The only thing I like is the fact that the Night Hunter has a skill tree, but this glorified versus mode is so lacking and unplayable due to connectivity issues, what's the point?
3. Even though you're called a "Night Hunter" as if you're some kind of stealthy zombie, you're not stealthy at all because the Human Players can SEE YOU ON THEIR RADAR for a pretty far distance away. It's gotta be the most absurd feature in the Night Hunter mode. In other words, it's pretty much impossible to really even sneak up on anyone. They'll ALWAYS know you're there if they know how to use a basic FPS radar, which kind of kills some of the hunting fun.
I can't possibly recommend this game after having such a huge "Be The Zombie" letdown. I feel deceived that the developers weren't upfront about the gameplay and advertised all of this crap about invading other player's games when in reality it's just a crappy versus match making mode that players can choose to turn on or off. There is lack of free-roaming and depth to such a cliche versus mode.
But regardless of everything else, the worst part is that it's just so difficult to even get a game working in Be The Zombie mode. Like I said, playing as the Night Hunter was my only reason for getting this, yet it's near unplayable due to unresolved connection problems.

Two things can be said about the X-COM universe: the aliens are always evil and it’s grand daddy to turn-based tactical strategy games.
For many older players, the mere whisper of X-COM: UFO Defense is enough for them to wet their pants without a shred of embarrassment. Well, XCOM: Enemy Unknown has changed the series besides losing the hyphen in X-COM. Graphical enhancement comes to mind. And a bit of gameplay freedom lost in favor of streamlined design, as fans of the original would probably point out. Be prepared for little grey men, psionics, UFOs, and pretty much every beloved sci-fi staple in existence.
Let’s be realistic: compared to most strategy games, XCOM: EU has a flexible, dynamic campaign that is a wonder to the genre. When compared to the original, maybe not so much, but today we aren’t reviewing that game. So this game works primarily by a milestone campaign. You must reach certain milestones to progress, but in-between you are free to play as you see fit. You can choose to help certain nations out, or not. Take a pick of missions for a choice of reward. Spend your cash on soldiers or ships. Still, those milestones must be reached or you are unable to go on. You race to stay one step of the alien invasion and falling behind means a slow death by lack of funding. No funding means you can’t keep fighting the good fight. So the ability to make plenty of choices is there, but the game isn’t completely freeform.
Developer Firaxis Games spared no expense on bringing XCOM to the modern era. The graphics are as good as can be expected for a squad tactical game. Aliens burst into viscera with a satisfying punch. Lasers (of course there are lasers!) and explosions feel as good as any action game. The animation prowess going into the Thin Man give him an exceptional amount of character. Slow motion camera work often captures the action in grisly detail. However, the responsiveness of the controls are questionable, most notably with the jetpack and grapple. Soldiers are also known to fire off in a different direction and still hit their target. The game isn’t perfect, but being turn-based does tone down many of the problems into mere annoyances. Except certain areas are not as random as they should be (looking at you, UFO assaults); that’s a problem that doesn’t go away.
Let’s talk about the most important part of all tactical games — the combat. XCOM is fairly action-packed, as far as turn-based gaming goes. Your soldiers can move in leaps and bounds across the map, relying on each using two actions per turn. The selection of gadgets are interesting and diverse, ranging from grappling hooks to alien grenades. There’s even a mechanized unit that can replace a squad member. The class system by itself is a bit shallow and constricting. However when combining various equipment, psionics, gadgets, and other squad members, XCOM’s freedom gives you room to exercise your tactical genius. Just not too much room, especially since most weapons are class restrictive.
Surprisingly, XCOM: EU has a ranked multiplayer mode. While co-op might have been a better direction, the competitive (1v1) system is well-designed and doesn’t feel like just a tacked on bullet point. And the multiplayer aspect is much needed, as the game has slim DLC options and a lack of modding tools. Ouch.
Overall, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a worthy addition to both the series and the strategy genre. Make no mistake (if you do, a rampaging Muton will surely cut you down), XCOM’s limited, streamlined strategy is a cornerstone of its design and it shows.
Side note: If you’re playing the game for the first time, I don’t recommend choosing any difficulty higher than Normal. Trust me!

It is true, however, that the game is an ultimate hodgepodge of gameplay mechanics burrowed from dozens of predecessors with not that many new ideas, but the end result is worth it.
Also the game fully supports Dualshock 4 (Playstation 4 controller) with the correct button prompts without any additional software requirements (no need to emulate Xbox controller, for instance).

I've been a massive fan of the original Killing Floor since 2011, and it has since been my favourite game. Of course, when Killing Floor 2 came out, I went ahead and got it on day 1.
KF2 has gone through many ups and downs, and for a long while, I really felt iffy about this game. But now, it really feels like it's taking off as a terrific game, and I really do feel like I am playing a proper Killing Floor sequel. And on top of the game being really fun, the developers are very active on /r/killingfloor, and while there was a point a few months ago when they were ignoring some popular complaints, they have since been taking into account every tiny complaint, suggestion, and bug findings that people have been posting on there.
Something that people still seem salty about is the in-game store. But I do not see the big deal in it, since it's all purely cosmetic, and does not add anything to the game. Some say that adding this slows down the process of actually making the game. For a while, this definitely did seem like the case. But now, it really feels like their priority is back to focusing on making the game amazing, and making sure everyone is enjoying it as much as possible.
So I say buy it, for sure. Even the full price is worth it, but of course you can wait for a sale and snag it at a discount. And while you're at it, I would also still suggest the original Killing Floor, which comes with the deluxe edition. That would be cheaper than getting each game seperately, and as a bonus, you get some nice extras and cosmetics for KF2.

I'm not really sure why I'm so addicted to this game. I played for over two hours and died dozens of times before I even beat the first level. Game is beyond hard. But it is constantly teasing you with the promise of more power ups. You are basically trying to collect as many life-preserving, alien-killing items you can before you are overwhelmed by the randomly spawning enemies of increasing number and difficulty. And just when you think you may have enough to escape through a porthole, the creatures unleash an unfathomable assault and you realize your existence is meaningless. This is underscored by the fact that your avatar is barely visible onscreen, surrounded by a vast, indifferent world.
The game is so much fun I don't care that I keep dying. And by the time I finally beat a level for the first time it felt like a miracle. Then I was killed almost instantly by the most basic enemies I found in the next world. This game will not hold your hand, and it will mock you when you die, and you will happily come back for more.
The graphics are rendered in beautiful pixelated minimalism. I was at first confused by the size of everything. Why are the figures so small? Because the game wants you to realize you are small. And the rest of the screen will eventually be full of the instruments of your doom. It's an incredible creative choice.
The music is also amazing. Each level essentially has one song that plays on repeat. But I didn't mind the repetition because the compositions are so dynamic and exciting. I will be seeking out the soundtrack posthaste.
This is one of the best games I've played in recent memory.
EDIT: I should have mentioned that so far I have only played the game solo. I can't comment on the multi-player, or whether the difficulty changes significantly with more players involved. For now I enjoy the isolation of playing alone, but it is brutal.
Together with Enemy Within this game is a top-notch turnbased strategy game and definitely worth the money, but maybe waiting for a sale does not hurt your pockets that much.

If you're a Shadowrun fan, or at least have some experience with the old SNES and/or Genesis games (the 2006 Xbox one doesn't count), this is worth picking up. Shadowrun Returns plays like XCOM with more RPG elements and without the punishing difficulty that is a hallmark of that series. The story is full of references and inside jokes that will render fans of the series nostalgic, but even if you're new to the series, important concepts and characters are explained at least adequately enough for the story to make sense. My one complaint is that the story, which is fairly short, is extremely linear and offers virtually no sidequesting. However, this game is meant to be just one "campaign" in the Shadowrun setting, and the real replay value lies in the editor, which allows players to create their own adventures and share them with the world. Despite its linearity and lack of meaningful choices for the player to make, I say buying it is justified by its low price tag. I hope this game helps give the Shadowrun setting more publicity, because it's definitely unique and worth investigating.

Antichamber is a very cognitive experience, an almost perfect example of the thoughtful puzzler, abstracted away from even a framing narrative.  It's a novelty that I exulted in, one of the most beautiful states of mind that I've recently had the chance to enjoy.  You play this game by leaving all external cues behind, and you learn to move through the not-a-world by applying internally consistent rules.  Yet, for all that abstraction, it offers graceful pointers, where the lessons learned are themselves collectibles.  It is a game about the game, which is not like other games...  I love it so much;  11 hours and an absolute joy to return to.  This.... this is what finely crafted thought looks like, when it is turned into a shared world for others: Abstract Art  that I can really walk through.  It creates a monument of inquisitive perception in the mind of the player.

Two things can be said about the X-COM universe: the aliens are always evil and it’s grand daddy to turn-based tactical strategy games.
For many older players, the mere whisper of X-COM: UFO Defense is enough for them to wet their pants without a shred of embarrassment. Well, XCOM: Enemy Unknown has changed the series besides losing the hyphen in X-COM. Graphical enhancement comes to mind. And a bit of gameplay freedom lost in favor of streamlined design, as fans of the original would probably point out. Be prepared for little grey men, psionics, UFOs, and pretty much every beloved sci-fi staple in existence.
Let’s be realistic: compared to most strategy games, XCOM: EU has a flexible, dynamic campaign that is a wonder to the genre. When compared to the original, maybe not so much, but today we aren’t reviewing that game. So this game works primarily by a milestone campaign. You must reach certain milestones to progress, but in-between you are free to play as you see fit. You can choose to help certain nations out, or not. Take a pick of missions for a choice of reward. Spend your cash on soldiers or ships. Still, those milestones must be reached or you are unable to go on. You race to stay one step of the alien invasion and falling behind means a slow death by lack of funding. No funding means you can’t keep fighting the good fight. So the ability to make plenty of choices is there, but the game isn’t completely freeform.
Developer Firaxis Games spared no expense on bringing XCOM to the modern era. The graphics are as good as can be expected for a squad tactical game. Aliens burst into viscera with a satisfying punch. Lasers (of course there are lasers!) and explosions feel as good as any action game. The animation prowess going into the Thin Man give him an exceptional amount of character. Slow motion camera work often captures the action in grisly detail. However, the responsiveness of the controls are questionable, most notably with the jetpack and grapple. Soldiers are also known to fire off in a different direction and still hit their target. The game isn’t perfect, but being turn-based does tone down many of the problems into mere annoyances. Except certain areas are not as random as they should be (looking at you, UFO assaults); that’s a problem that doesn’t go away.
Let’s talk about the most important part of all tactical games — the combat. XCOM is fairly action-packed, as far as turn-based gaming goes. Your soldiers can move in leaps and bounds across the map, relying on each using two actions per turn. The selection of gadgets are interesting and diverse, ranging from grappling hooks to alien grenades. There’s even a mechanized unit that can replace a squad member. The class system by itself is a bit shallow and constricting. However when combining various equipment, psionics, gadgets, and other squad members, XCOM’s freedom gives you room to exercise your tactical genius. Just not too much room, especially since most weapons are class restrictive.
Surprisingly, XCOM: EU has a ranked multiplayer mode. While co-op might have been a better direction, the competitive (1v1) system is well-designed and doesn’t feel like just a tacked on bullet point. And the multiplayer aspect is much needed, as the game has slim DLC options and a lack of modding tools. Ouch.
Overall, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a worthy addition to both the series and the strategy genre. Make no mistake (if you do, a rampaging Muton will surely cut you down), XCOM’s limited, streamlined strategy is a cornerstone of its design and it shows.
Side note: If you’re playing the game for the first time, I don’t recommend choosing any difficulty higher than Normal. Trust me!

Thought it was gonna be exactly like Dead Island, ended up being an improvement imo.
It's not perfect so if you wanna see what I have bad to say about the game, skip to the cons.
It's a great experience if you actually get into it, if you like killing zombies and parkouring, you should feel right at home, in this new enviroment. So here's a serious review.
Before I start, alot of people with AMD cards report bad fps, so be aware of that.
Actually check the system requirements before purchasing, so you don't end up complaining about hardware problems.
- Pros/Features-
+Decent story, there are still ridiculous and bizarre side quests. There are some really colorful characters in this game. But honestly, if you have a sense of humor you'll get a good laugh out of some parts of the storyline.
+Parkour, allows you to navigate the enviroment in a very different way, viral zombies can parkour as well and are pretty decent at it.
+Survival senses (Spider senses?) If you press the Q button, your survival senses kick in and will basically show little markings on lootable objects/items that you can pick up or interact with.
Some people may find this a turn off, but honestly, there is ALOT of looting in this game, when your running from zombies, or low on time, it's helpful. It also shows the waypoint, so it's easy to figure out where your supposed to go without checking the map constantly. Overall it's a nice feature, and extremely helpful.
+Crafting is very simple, create shurikens, medkits, molotovs, even beneficial boosters which are created with herbs. (Such as improved night vision, or damage resistance) As well as blueprints which let you modify weapons you already have, and add pretty devasating effects. Very similar to dead Island with the blueprints, except there are alot more. Some even let you put multiple elemental effects on a single weapon.
+Weapon mechanics work well. Different weapons have different amounts of upgrade slots. You can add things like "Crusader" or "Juggernaut" to your weapon to increase handling/durability etc. on top of this you can upgrade with blueprints you find such as fire, electricity, and toxic. similar to Dead Island, but a step up with the new upgrades. You can also repair your weapons using tool parts that you loot. Eventually the weapon will break, but it's nice that you can repair and delay the inevitible.
You can also dismantle weapons which gives you 1 or a couple repair parts.
+Control over the combat. With the skill tree upgrades you can unlock the ability to dodge, unlock new weapon moves. Grapple opponets, dropkick them. You can also kick zombies/humans into spikes in the enviroment, and even use traps found in the open world such as electric fences, car bombs, and more.
+The player can also hold up to 4 different equipments at a time (Shurikens, grenades, molotovs, UV light, etc.)
+3 different skill trees, level up independently (Agility, Power, and Survival.) Everytime you level one of these up you can pick a skill which gives access to new crafting items, unlocks new moves such as the dropkick, or increases speed and whatknot. There's quite alot of upgrades.
Power is increased by fighting enemies, you unlock combat moves for weapons among other things.
Agility is increased by doing parkour, jumping, etc. Unlocks moves like the dropkick, also increases stats.
And survival is increased by doing quests and recovering airdrop packages. These give alot of upgrades like making crafting more effective, learning new crafts, and also unlocking moves. When you die you also lose survival points, which makes it more intense.
Overall the skill system is really good in my opinion, they can each go up to level 25.
+Looting feels good, honestly I think they nailed the RPG feeling of just getting tons of loot.
You can go in alot of the buildings, picklock chests. Most of these buildings have locked doors, so you have to look around and find different entrances such as going through a roof door, or lifting up the garage door.
The human enemies will drop melee weapons, if their using them, as well as throwing items.
And even the special zombies have some weapons you can pick up which include the concrete rebars and sledgehammer.
+Special zombies are actually pretty interesting. It basically has the suicider from Dead Island still, but their are spitters which lob poisonous exploding bile (extremely annoying) And concrete rebar wielding zombies which are like 3 times the size of a normal zombie. Even the hazmat zombies are cool, they sound grim, and explode on death.
Night zombies, are brutal...and yeah I stay away from them.
(Very much a stepup from Dead Island with some of these zombie variants imo.)
+Guns are a HUGE improvement from Dead Island. They handle better, and actually kill the targets instead of them just soaking up bullets. Exception to this is some of the special zombies, which depending on the type can take alot more bullets.
The guns are somewhat overpowered because of the availability of ammunition, but they cause major noise which usually attracts alot of zombies.
+Human combat is intense, most of the enemies wield different weapons, can throw knives, and will dodge accordingly, they can even block items such as throwing knives unless you time them correctly. The gunplay here is also improved, they die quite easily from bullets, but if they are wielding guns they can kill the player just as quickly if given the opportunity.
This is my experience with the game, I came into it expecting a mediocre game and ended up getting an awesome open world experience. If you like killing zombies, parkouring, crafting, making awesome weapons, exploring an open world, just buy the game and play it. Develop your own opinion.
- Cons -
-Experienced quite a few crashes throughout my gameplay. A couple during cutscenes, and alot over the course of just traveling/doing missions. Nothing game breaking though, thankfully the autosave works out. Still, it's annoying having to reboot the game.
-No manual save (This is a big deal to me) I really hate when games leave you with an autosave feature and no manual save. Haven't had any huge problems with it yet, but it would be nice to be able to manually save.
-Some people report AMD card problems.
- No vehicles, but parkour is more fun in my opinion, didn't really have a problem with no vehicles.
-"Resize buffer failed" Not sure what this means, but this has crashed my game about 5 times over 13 hours. Thankfully the game autosaves, and I haven't lost any of my loot to it yet. Still it's extremely annoying and needs to be fixed.
-Most of the time when I load my save my character says "OH♥♥♥♥♥♥" I don't really consider this a con, but it's pretty entertaining.

Since I haven't finished the game, this is more of an impression than a full review. But as to why anyone would want to sit through this game is beyond me, since it's about as boring and generic as you can get. The approach to "horror" here revolves almost entirely around jump scares - and this would maybe be fine if the game weren't trying so hard to be "scary," but as is, it just becomes annoying. With the over the top dismemberment and enemy design, the mediocre attempts at "horror" become so extreme that they lose all potency and just become funny instead.
So, as a horror game, Dead Space is a failure. And as a shooter, it's competent, but the game takes place almost exclusively in dimly lit generic corridors, so it gets boring pretty quickly. The game also has some technical issues on the PC. For example, on my system, switching on VSync introduces a massive amount of input lag and make the game unplayable. Playing a game with VSync off is usually not such a big deal, but since the game is primarily illuminated by flickering lights, screen tear is a pretty big issue.
Honestly, if you're interested in this game and haven't played System Shock 2, go play that instead. It's a much more compelling experience and infinitely more terrifying.

Plays like the illegitimate love-child of Half-life and System Shock at first. It manages to be creepy and reasonably well-paced for the first half, but soon becomes a dull assortment of switch quests, twitch-muscle timing, and wave on wave of enemy killing.
For a game that initially makes combat more interesting and tricky than the norm, it's sad that Dead Space goes down the route of spamming critters on the player by the end. You can forget tactics and planning out your attack strategy by the final third, it becomes just a super tedious shooting gallery.
It's so sad: you finish level 6 thinking this is a good game, but by level 12 you're thinking it's dull, boring and repetitive.
I'd only recommend picking it up on sale.

I will begin by saying that the drawbacks for the game are that if you are looking for an encompassing story, sprawling maps, and unequaled cooperative-focused gameplay like Left 4 Dead, this game is similar but not quite that. To elaborate, the maps are smaller, and while teamwork is important, it is not as essential or salient as it is in Left 4 Dead. This game does, however, surpass the aforementioned Left 4 Dead in the feeling that it gives you when you kill hordes of ♥♥♥♥♥es. I have never played a shooter that gives you a more satisfying feeling with every pull of the trigger. This is especially so when using weapons like the shotguns or the grenade launcher: when you hit an enemy, your target reacts, crumples, and/or explodes in such a way that you FEEL powerful. As a related aside, I find aspects like the entrance of the scrake (a type of enemy), who walks onto the field, points at you, and crosses his neck with his finger to make the animosity and rivalry of the situation have a personal feeling to it. Finally, if you are not a hard rock/metal fan, then the game's soundtrack will be a moot point. If you are a metal connoisseur like me however, you will be elated by the exceptional pairing of tracks like "Bitter End" by Fit for a King that literally make my lip and nose curdle (see also: Doom 2 guy when you hold the trigger down long enough) with the thrill of prejudicially destroying swarms of enemies coming at me. For these reasons I would highly recommend Killing Floor 2.﻿

I'm not really sure why I'm so addicted to this game. I played for over two hours and died dozens of times before I even beat the first level. Game is beyond hard. But it is constantly teasing you with the promise of more power ups. You are basically trying to collect as many life-preserving, alien-killing items you can before you are overwhelmed by the randomly spawning enemies of increasing number and difficulty. And just when you think you may have enough to escape through a porthole, the creatures unleash an unfathomable assault and you realize your existence is meaningless. This is underscored by the fact that your avatar is barely visible onscreen, surrounded by a vast, indifferent world.
The game is so much fun I don't care that I keep dying. And by the time I finally beat a level for the first time it felt like a miracle. Then I was killed almost instantly by the most basic enemies I found in the next world. This game will not hold your hand, and it will mock you when you die, and you will happily come back for more.
The graphics are rendered in beautiful pixelated minimalism. I was at first confused by the size of everything. Why are the figures so small? Because the game wants you to realize you are small. And the rest of the screen will eventually be full of the instruments of your doom. It's an incredible creative choice.
The music is also amazing. Each level essentially has one song that plays on repeat. But I didn't mind the repetition because the compositions are so dynamic and exciting. I will be seeking out the soundtrack posthaste.
This is one of the best games I've played in recent memory.
EDIT: I should have mentioned that so far I have only played the game solo. I can't comment on the multi-player, or whether the difficulty changes significantly with more players involved. For now I enjoy the isolation of playing alone, but it is brutal.

It's really damn good. My opinion is pretty biased though, because I grew up playing Fallout 1 and 2 and other turn-based strategy games with RPG elements.
Now, I can't say Shadowrun Returns is excellent in every aspect and it has flaws. Probably the main disappointment about the game is the fact that it's incredibly linear. I think there is only a couple of side-levels and everything else is pretty much traversing through areas from point a to b while killing enemies or talking to people and exploring. All 3 of these aspects are also dumbed down (I can't compare to the original Shadowrun because I haven't played it but the closest that it gets to is Fallout 1/2 for me, actually thinking of it, it's more like Fallout: Tactics).
The fighting system is very close to the X-COM one and you've got AP, HP, 2-3 weapon slots and special abilities. Special abilities are presented in a wide variety though: you've got all sorts of♥♥♥♥♥♥- from being a shaman who summons stuff to a decker who can hack computers and transfer himself into cyberspace.
Dialogues and social interactions aren't voiced (obviously) and suffer from being linear too. Most of the time you'll find yourself looking at 3 options and they all mean the same but the NPC reacts differently to each one. There are also some special charisma/etiquette-based options that pop-up every now and then, too.
Exploring is stripped to its bare minumum as you've got levels filled with NPCs and sometimes promps would show up telling that there's something lying in a room: either a quest item or equipment.
I've just covered all of the negative things. That's it. Everything else that's in the game provides a really cool experience: let it be the soundtrack of the game, its story or its world. It also has workshop support! Final verdict: if you see this game below 10$ and even just a tiny bit interested - go ahead and check it out.

First off, this is a good game, it has solid mechanics and it is fun to play but there are problems (Disclaimer: I am a complete fan of the original)
Having said that, it is a pale shadow of the mighty first game from which it takes its name (And even X-COM: Apocalypse) and it appears to be a syndrome that a lot of remakes suffer. The problem could be called "Streamlining" (Total War Rome 2 has this problem as well).
1st is the research tree which is significantly smaller than the original. There is only one advanced Interceptor and very few weapons for it to research. The squad sizes are also very small (4-6) compared to the original so when you lose someone experienced it hurts a lot! (Losing 1 or 2 people in a mission early on can cripple your chances of completing it.) The maps are smaller and the mechanics of engaging enemies (Small groups that get their own "!" animation when you come across them) is disappointing.
Base building has been made much less interesting since in the original your base could be invaded (and you could have multiple bases). The X-COM: Enemy Within expansion does actually have a base defense mission but it is scripted, happens once, and how you built your base does not come into it.
Which brings me to my main problem with the new X-COM. I do not feel like the Commander of X-COM. In the original there were no scripted events, it was all organic gameplay. I made the decisions, I hired the scientists, bought the ammo, kitted out the soldiers in details and planned ahead and I was fighting for the Earth. This may sound dull but it added to the immersion.
In the new X-COM the game plays out with 3 main characters and I feel incidental to the whole thing. I could just go put some slippers on and let them do it. You are hand-held and guided through every part of the game, constantly being told what to do, what you should do and what to expect by the "main" characters.
This game is also much shorter in terms of the time taken to complete it. I just finished a game having shot down a mere 6 UFOs. In the original I would barely be seeing more than their initial scouts at this point. The ending is also very abrupt and jarring.
So yes, this is a good game overall, it has some of the hallmarks of the original but overall it is a hollow shell compared to it, even with the expansion (Which I HIGHLY recommend). I am hoping that some of the X-COM indie games like Xenonauts (
and early access on Steam ) can give me my real X-COM old-school fix.

Thought it was gonna be exactly like Dead Island, ended up being an improvement imo.
It's not perfect so if you wanna see what I have bad to say about the game, skip to the cons.
It's a great experience if you actually get into it, if you like killing zombies and parkouring, you should feel right at home, in this new enviroment. So here's a serious review.
Before I start, alot of people with AMD cards report bad fps, so be aware of that.
Actually check the system requirements before purchasing, so you don't end up complaining about hardware problems.
- Pros/Features-
+Decent story, there are still ridiculous and bizarre side quests. There are some really colorful characters in this game. But honestly, if you have a sense of humor you'll get a good laugh out of some parts of the storyline.
+Parkour, allows you to navigate the enviroment in a very different way, viral zombies can parkour as well and are pretty decent at it.
+Survival senses (Spider senses?) If you press the Q button, your survival senses kick in and will basically show little markings on lootable objects/items that you can pick up or interact with.
Some people may find this a turn off, but honestly, there is ALOT of looting in this game, when your running from zombies, or low on time, it's helpful. It also shows the waypoint, so it's easy to figure out where your supposed to go without checking the map constantly. Overall it's a nice feature, and extremely helpful.
+Crafting is very simple, create shurikens, medkits, molotovs, even beneficial boosters which are created with herbs. (Such as improved night vision, or damage resistance) As well as blueprints which let you modify weapons you already have, and add pretty devasating effects. Very similar to dead Island with the blueprints, except there are alot more. Some even let you put multiple elemental effects on a single weapon.
+Weapon mechanics work well. Different weapons have different amounts of upgrade slots. You can add things like "Crusader" or "Juggernaut" to your weapon to increase handling/durability etc. on top of this you can upgrade with blueprints you find such as fire, electricity, and toxic. similar to Dead Island, but a step up with the new upgrades. You can also repair your weapons using tool parts that you loot. Eventually the weapon will break, but it's nice that you can repair and delay the inevitible.
You can also dismantle weapons which gives you 1 or a couple repair parts.
+Control over the combat. With the skill tree upgrades you can unlock the ability to dodge, unlock new weapon moves. Grapple opponets, dropkick them. You can also kick zombies/humans into spikes in the enviroment, and even use traps found in the open world such as electric fences, car bombs, and more.
+The player can also hold up to 4 different equipments at a time (Shurikens, grenades, molotovs, UV light, etc.)
+3 different skill trees, level up independently (Agility, Power, and Survival.) Everytime you level one of these up you can pick a skill which gives access to new crafting items, unlocks new moves such as the dropkick, or increases speed and whatknot. There's quite alot of upgrades.
Power is increased by fighting enemies, you unlock combat moves for weapons among other things.
Agility is increased by doing parkour, jumping, etc. Unlocks moves like the dropkick, also increases stats.
And survival is increased by doing quests and recovering airdrop packages. These give alot of upgrades like making crafting more effective, learning new crafts, and also unlocking moves. When you die you also lose survival points, which makes it more intense.
Overall the skill system is really good in my opinion, they can each go up to level 25.
+Looting feels good, honestly I think they nailed the RPG feeling of just getting tons of loot.
You can go in alot of the buildings, picklock chests. Most of these buildings have locked doors, so you have to look around and find different entrances such as going through a roof door, or lifting up the garage door.
The human enemies will drop melee weapons, if their using them, as well as throwing items.
And even the special zombies have some weapons you can pick up which include the concrete rebars and sledgehammer.
+Special zombies are actually pretty interesting. It basically has the suicider from Dead Island still, but their are spitters which lob poisonous exploding bile (extremely annoying) And concrete rebar wielding zombies which are like 3 times the size of a normal zombie. Even the hazmat zombies are cool, they sound grim, and explode on death.
Night zombies, are brutal...and yeah I stay away from them.
(Very much a stepup from Dead Island with some of these zombie variants imo.)
+Guns are a HUGE improvement from Dead Island. They handle better, and actually kill the targets instead of them just soaking up bullets. Exception to this is some of the special zombies, which depending on the type can take alot more bullets.
The guns are somewhat overpowered because of the availability of ammunition, but they cause major noise which usually attracts alot of zombies.
+Human combat is intense, most of the enemies wield different weapons, can throw knives, and will dodge accordingly, they can even block items such as throwing knives unless you time them correctly. The gunplay here is also improved, they die quite easily from bullets, but if they are wielding guns they can kill the player just as quickly if given the opportunity.
This is my experience with the game, I came into it expecting a mediocre game and ended up getting an awesome open world experience. If you like killing zombies, parkouring, crafting, making awesome weapons, exploring an open world, just buy the game and play it. Develop your own opinion.
- Cons -
-Experienced quite a few crashes throughout my gameplay. A couple during cutscenes, and alot over the course of just traveling/doing missions. Nothing game breaking though, thankfully the autosave works out. Still, it's annoying having to reboot the game.
-No manual save (This is a big deal to me) I really hate when games leave you with an autosave feature and no manual save. Haven't had any huge problems with it yet, but it would be nice to be able to manually save.
-Some people report AMD card problems.
- No vehicles, but parkour is more fun in my opinion, didn't really have a problem with no vehicles.
-"Resize buffer failed" Not sure what this means, but this has crashed my game about 5 times over 13 hours. Thankfully the game autosaves, and I haven't lost any of my loot to it yet. Still it's extremely annoying and needs to be fixed.
-Most of the time when I load my save my character says "OH♥♥♥♥♥♥" I don't really consider this a con, but it's pretty entertaining.

I can't think of any, i've been playing for quite a while and haven't run across any game breaking bugs. I'll add more cons if I do find some though.

My initial review of this game was rather negative, but I've decided to rewrite it now that many of the things I complained about in my first review have been addressed.
First off, the biggest thing: Perk skill trees have been given a much needed overhaul! Not only have skill descriptions been 'defluffed', but skills in general are much more useful. I'm still a little disappointed that they're mostly percentage based, passive buffs, but the new skills allow more customization and give a nice buff to perks that desperately needed it.
On top of that, the drop system has been rebalanced to drop skins and items much more frequently than before. It was always rather disappointing to get to the end of a match and be given a USB or supply crate that you have to pay extra to open for your efforts. The new system is much more rewarding and is just generally a more pleasant end user experience.
In addition, game flow has been improved greatly. I no longer find myself constantly inundated with hordes of zeds as long as my team and I are competent. The game in general feels closer to Killing Floor 1, while still feeling different enough. Bosses have been improved as well - Hans Volter is no longer a boring, annoying slog that wipes your team if you so much as give him an inch, and the Patriarch is a much bigger threat. There are still some things I'm not totally happy with - I still think waves are too short in general, and I'm still not sure how I feel about the scrake and fleshpound announcing their presence with a loud roar, but these things I've mentioned are a welcome step in the right direction.
Killing Floor 2 still has some ways to go before it really stands up to the original, but I'm very happy with the direction Tripwire has taken with the game and the fact that they're listening to and implementing community suggestions. I'm very much looking forward to KF2's future.

Since I haven't finished the game, this is more of an impression than a full review. But as to why anyone would want to sit through this game is beyond me, since it's about as boring and generic as you can get. The approach to "horror" here revolves almost entirely around jump scares - and this would maybe be fine if the game weren't trying so hard to be "scary," but as is, it just becomes annoying. With the over the top dismemberment and enemy design, the mediocre attempts at "horror" become so extreme that they lose all potency and just become funny instead.
So, as a horror game, Dead Space is a failure. And as a shooter, it's competent, but the game takes place almost exclusively in dimly lit generic corridors, so it gets boring pretty quickly. The game also has some technical issues on the PC. For example, on my system, switching on VSync introduces a massive amount of input lag and make the game unplayable. Playing a game with VSync off is usually not such a big deal, but since the game is primarily illuminated by flickering lights, screen tear is a pretty big issue.
Honestly, if you're interested in this game and haven't played System Shock 2, go play that instead. It's a much more compelling experience and infinitely more terrifying.

UPDATE: AMD users are reporting serious issues running the game. If you run an  AMD system then I'd wait and check forum posts for any patch updates.
First of all realise this, we have ourselves a AAA game that doesn't have game breaking bugs upon release (apart from AMD users of course at present) not requiring a 5gb patch download to fix them so kudas to Techland devs for a stand up job on that part.
So the first thing people are going to be thinking is "another zombie game?". Well it's like this, people complain about there being too many zombie games and how zombie games are out, as a developer myself I hear this a lot yet people continue to make them, why? Simply because gamers like yourself if you are taking the time to check out reviews keep buying them so they are most defintely still in at the moment.
To break it down think about a next gen Dead Island and the game is generally simular, just better. It's a lot more dark and serious with no comedy bits as a AAA zombie game should be. Oh and parkour takes a big role as well, so if you played mirrors edge and/or assasins creed then you may just feel at home on that part.
The graphics are decent, don't really have any major complaints or anything. The game play itself is smooth and runs at a steady 60 fps (win 8.1 64bit, 16GB, 980 GTX, Intel i7). I've heard reports of some people having some fps drops but generally it's to levels only an extremist would comlain about.
Co-Op plays seems popular but that it's early days yet, Be a Zombie mode was empty though.
Decent talent tree set up, a lot more involved than that of Far Cry 4 (and most FPS games for thatm matter). It's a good game getting positive reviews, the only problem is that when it comes to types of Zombie games I don't even think the consumer knows what they want, which makes it harder for studios to deliver however with Dying Light they made a very good attempt at least, time will tell if it will go all the way.
Oh, don't underestimate zombies as the game can be tough at times regardless.

The Shadowrun franchise has seen several video game adaptations, but until last year's Shadowrun Returns, none of them managed to capture both the atmosphere of the sci-fi/fantasy hybrid universe and the flexibility that tabletop games typically allow. With the Dragonfall expansion, Harebrained Schemes has buffed out many of Returns' blemishes, making it the closest any video game has come to embracing the unabridged spirit of this classic cyberpunk setting.
Shadowrun is a mishmash of dystopian science-fiction themes and standard high-fantasy tropes. The game takes place in an alternate future following an event known as the Awakening, which reintroduced magic into an otherwise ordinary world. With that catastrophe, dragons of unimaginable power have been released, humans have been torn and split into different metatypes (that is, dwarves, elves, orks, and trolls), people can hack computers with their brains, and a precious few individuals have learned to tap their soul and fuel magic of all sorts. The eponymous Dragonfall refers to the defeat of one of the toughest and most genocidal dragons unshackled by the Awakening: Feuerschwinge.

AC is a game that will stretch your thought processes, arouse your curiosity, make you learn and above all else reward you when you put all those skills into practice. It will also most likely test your patience, punish you for not thinking outside the box and at times make you want to throw your PC out the window.
AC is a FPS puzzle game close to the likes of portal but much more imaginative, you will find yourself in interactive connected world, actions you take will close or open routes and you are the rat in the maze. You will start looking closely at things and they might not seem what they first appear to be and sometimes just the action of looking at something might have unintended side effects.
It is beautiful in its simplicity and yet there is a lot of depth to that simplicity that if you don’t pick up on will hold you back, some of the subtle parts really reward your curiosity and willingness to keep trying.
You can’t die in this game, and often what you see as a failure to start with is actually a new approach to what you desire. You reveal the map as you go through corridors and rooms but as helpful as this is you also need to build a map in your own mind as a linear map does not reflect the reality you will find.
There is no complete linear path from the start and you can wander to many different locations, you quickly start to realise a section that you are not ready for but you try and gleam some clue that could help you in your current state, it is nice that as you roam you almost get a sneaky peak at what is to come. It can also make the start quite challenging as you get disorientated and try to find what to do.
When I first got the game, I played for an hour, scratched my head put it down and did not have much drive to pick it back up again, about six weeks later it was there looking at me in my Steam list and I thought you know what I will give it another go. A day and half later and two solid four hour sessions and I had completed the game and was now upset the ride had ended.
I was happy with 8-9 hours of game time to complete to complete it especially with finding most of the secret sections along the way. AC makes you feel part of a secret world that the game designer made, it is almost like a sci-fi movie that you are playing a character in somebodies mind. Many of the secret sections you find are bits where the designer has shown you early concepts and you can see the years that the game must have taken to create.
After finishing I was on Youtube and forums seeing how other people completed it and resolved many of the challenges in the game, I was surprised but not shocked when I saw a video showing someone complete the game in less than five minutes! As I said it does not have a linear path and this proves the point. The game is not about speed but how you go about the journey of the game and your own development in it.

After the start of the game wandering around like an idiot you find near the end how you have learned and things that were so alien and unnatural become second nature.
One of things I like about this game is that most of the challenges are thought exercises and once worked out you go through the motions to complete the challenge, unlike say times in Portal where you map out what to do in your head and then spend 15 minutes trying to time a portal correctly.
Considering the many different aspects, the lack of a linear path and the ability to try and test so much out I only found two bugs, one was a simple restart of the game and it was resolved. One was a lot more infuriating as it was on one of the harder parts and a rare puzzle that required a bit of timing and skill to achieve. I had worked out how to do it and attempted it multiple times but it did not work, I then spent even longer trying to think even further outside the box until I eventually googled it and found it was quite a common bug, again a restart resolved the issue but the time lost was annoying.
Overall I would say this game takes you on a wonderful journey, for me it was anger and annoyance that transitioned into intrigue and what felt like an expanding of my ability to view things in different ways.

A pleasant enough game if you don't mind such absolute randomness that the sense of challenge is ruined. Even on easy difficulty the game is notorious for absurd surprise attacks and seemingly arbitrary changes to the established rules.
The constant pressure of being pursued leaves you with never a moment to explore, regroup, or restock. This would be fine were it not made possible by the use of one impossible sci-fi trope (warping about willy-nilly from star to star) while countless others are omitted. This makes a novel premise for a story, but it's exhausting in a game where dying means starting over from the beginning.
It's this last element which makes me smirk a bit at this game's marketing as a roguelike. There's no going back up the steps, hurriedly reading a scroll, stopping back in town, or spotting a hopeless situation down the hallway and finding an alternate route. A good roguelike can do without some of these things, but leaving out every one of them except permadeath and bad luck launches this game out of that category entirely, and lands it squarely in the realm of Oregon Trail and the most obnoxious Choose Your Own Adventure fare.

In a nutshell: a solid little old-school CRPG, somewhat reminiscent of the original Fallout - at least in terms of tactical combat, story, NPC characterisation, and exploration.
Firstly, the upsides. The story is genuinely quite intriguing. There are twists and turns, and you may not be quite sure who to trust for some time. The NPCs you meet are richly portrayed with good writing, interesting quirks, and in-game portraits. The Shadowrun theme (Lord of the Rings meets Cyberpunk, with a heavy dose of Blade Runner noir) is well done and evocative.
Combat is turn-based, with a surprising amount of tactical options. Mages can take advantage of ley-lines, shamans summon elemental spirits from foci, riggers enable their drones, deckers hack into the matrix, and so forth. Any particular combat may play out quite differently depending on your party composition. There is a decent amount of gear available to find and purchase, and a wide variety of skills to customize your character.
The maps are old-school isometric, richly detailed although sadly not very interactive. Most are fairly small, and there are few "hot points" to manipulate. However, this is not significantly different from classic games like Baldurs Gate, Fallout or Planescape Torment. Like the original Fallout, there are often alternatives to shooting your way through an encounter: either through decking into the matrix, diplomacy and bribery, stealth, etc.
The downsides? The game is a little on the short side (8-12 hours), and it is absolutely linear. There is some minimal exploration in each map, and a few optional side-missions... but otherwise, you're on a railroad. There is no voice-acting or video cutscenes, which younger players may find less acceptable. There is minimal replay potential given the linearity of the story, although a dedicated player may enjoy trying a different PC and party build to see how they handle the set encounters.
So... is it a recommend? Yes - if you enjoyed the original Fallout, Arcanum, Baldurs Gate, or similar. The story and NPC characterization is worth the budget price, and outweigh the negatives. Moreover, the game is supported with a design toolkit (there are already custom modules available in the workshop), and it's an excellent introduction to the world of Shadowrun.
That latter point is important, because there's already a stand-alone sequel - Shadowrun Dragonfall. And Dragonfall is even better than the original (quite good) campaign. Dragonfall is far less linear, longer, more equipment choices, better NPC companions, and an even more intriguing story. It also features more replayability, with multiple endings depending on PC choice.
Overall, I give Shadowrun Returns a 7/10 (recommended for old-school gamers), and the Dragonfall sequel an 8/10.

Ever played Final Fantasy Tactics? This is waaay better! Manage your soldiers, assign new abilities as they increase in rank, build their weapons and shoot some aliens! No two matches feel the same, as the AI offers new challenges every time: as soon as you begin to feel comfortable there comes along a new species, forcing you to rethink your approach. What's better is that there is no single way to play the game, but you have to adapt to your base layout and to your soldiers' classes. Immersive game world, very detailed but not hard on your computer specs, so it's always very smooth. Beyond base management, research and engineering the battlefield is the game's strong point, and I guarantee you'll think the AI cheats when your colonel misses a 95% shot, and you'll swear and shout at the screen whenever your squad faces unforeseen annihilation; you will cry like a baby girl when you meet the Sectopod! Yeah, it's that immersive.
Also consider getting the Enemy Within DLC, it expands the game adding maps and features like genetic mods and freakin' MECHS! Worth having but pricey, maybe wait for a sale as the base game is fine as it is, and that's saying A LOT in these days.

I Originally Wrote a Review a few days after this game was released on steam and i said to wait for it to get better. It has been over a year and i have decided i should write a more proper review.
The Game itself has been fixed for 90% or more of people which I really like. I had some issues with fps drop and a couple crashes when this game first came out but even then i still loved the game itself. Having upgraded my pc since then and recently played this again. I can give a detailed review.
Batman Arkham Knight, despite the shaky launch. Is a dream come true for any Batman fans out there. The amount of fun and adventure had in this world is truly wonderful to grasp and a must play for any who have played the previous games. I would even argue to call this the best of the Arkham games in my opinion, though in general Arkham City was probably the best. It does have its cons, but despite this the game lives up to all expectations.
Pros:
Gameplay:
Like all Arkham Games, you really feel like the Batman. All the correct steps have been taken to make this game fun and enjoyable as Batman. The Gadgets, the Batmobile, the endless gliding. Is enjoyable in all aspects.
The Batmobile:
Perhaps Batman's greatest weapon, the batmobile grants the players access to a deadly arsenal whilst also getting a tool handy in navigating the city. Freeroam mode is fun as you can constantly roam through the city at high speeds going over ramps and breaking through certain objects to places you wish to go is simply music to one's ears. The Combat mode is also fun as you can really enjoy yourself blasting tanks to shreds and using handy tools to make the environment work for you. The Batmobile definitely brought a fun element to this game.
Story:
Without spoiling, though i suspect at the making of this review most of you will already know how it end. The Story is beautiful. Perhaps the best story in all the Arkham Games, perhaps with the exception of Arkham City but either way is still amazing. Certain moments and easter eggs really can make you emotional and the mind-boggling plot twists can sometimes even keep the best of us confused. Simply put, like the rest of the Arkham Games, Arkham City delivers a story that keeps you satisfied till the very end.
Open World:
The Open World in this game is pretty massive, nowhere near as big as say Fallout 4 or The Witcher 3 or even GTA, but bigger then any Arkham Game to date. Traversing the city has never been so fun. Though sadly there isn't much depth to the freeroam other than to complete the missions. Even so, it is fun none the less.
Variety:
The variety in this game probably is greater then any other Arkham Game. The amount of gadgets and characters and overall gameplay is so traverse, the amount of takedowns and fight scenarios and even individual story plots is truly inspiring. Every character has unique weapons and abilities. Every gadget has its use. And every takedown has its rhythm.
DLC:
Though the DLC does cost money, I can guarantee you, you will not mind the extra cost. The DLC in this game brings extra stories for a player to complete and every one of them is amazing to play, every skin gives its own feel and effect. I don't want to sound like a 'sellout', but I am implying that the DLC for this game is great:
Cons:
The Batmobile:
"What? You said it was a pro!" I did. However, the batmobile was overused and made certain sequences boring and simply made fights seem like you did it 5 minutes beforehand. It even ruins certain aspects of the game.
Boss Fights:
Not all Boss Fights are bad but the ones that had the best potential were dumbed down and ruined my experience. Deathstroke for example, a person who is a considerable match for Batman in skill.... You don't even fight him 1 on 1. It's a tank battle. If you were excited about Deathstroke, i would advise Arkham Origins. Even the Arkham Knight boss fight doesn't feel very fun. Don't get me wrong, some of the fights are a blast... but the most interesting ones were made boring.
Conclusion:
Batman Arkham Knight had perhaps the shakiest start to a launch then any other game of its calliber. But after a year of waiting, It's the game everyone dreamed of, the console port was always an option but the PC fans were never satisfied. I can safely say it was worth the wait and any who wish to buy the game in future. Just know it is worth it.
Score: 9.3/10

Out of all the fancy games I've gotten here on steam, this is the most I've played. I'm relatively new to the scene here, and many of my game preferences tend towards the old school pixelated feel. Risk of Rain is my first roguelike game, and I hated it at first. I was getting nowhere in this game!
But patience was employed and I acquired a feel. Once I got a new character I was hooked. The strategic value skyrocketed as I struggled then gleefully adapted to the play style of each character. To date, my favorite of the lot is Engineer, though I do enjoy playing the Loader.
Perseverance is key, and one eventually strikes a balance between mining the enemies for xp and coinage and getting the hell out of the stage.
