This game is very fast paced and keeps you interacting with everything constantly. The play style is very much like a mix of Dead Island and Mirror's Edge. You're constantly climbing walls and jumping on roof tops while running for your life from hoards of zombies. At night, super zombies roam looking for you, which makes the nights the best and hardest part of the game. The missions are fun, easy to track and easy to find. During the day the zombies are pretty much Dead Island zombies. During the nights everything go crazy and you're running into walls if you don't have your flashlight on. I think that the zombies seem more realistic because they will jump you if they hear you or see you. Night is not to be taken lightly.
When you do die your survival points do go down, making survival much more important.  You can choose to sleep through the night or to brave the dark which rewards you with double experience.
Like Dead Island there is a "skill tree" system that is pretty similar. You also can upgrade your weapons by combining items that you salvage. The thing that makes it not Dead Island is the parkour, the night attacks and the overall speed of the game.
I give it a 8 out of 10. It's fun, fast paced and exciting.

First of all I loved, still do love KF1. It was an awesome experience to play it. Also it had that sarcastic funny style. And yes, I may be basing my review in comparing it to the first game, but as someone who was expecting a sequel and not a new game it's inevitable.
Based on that even though the game isn't bad, I am giving it a negative review. Killing Floor 2 so far has showed me that it isn't really the sequel of that amazing exciting game we played before. Even though it is a pretty good game.
A couple of motives:
1) They have done something horrible to the character voices and dialogues; instead of the funny and witty remarks and voice commands of KF1 we are stuck with annoying and unfunny, the worst part is that you can't silence them completely.
2) For some reason almost all the official maps lack (clearly on purpose) an area to hold appropriately, instead we have almost only open areas that tend to chaos. Sure, they don't want to make it easy but they make it difficult annoying and tedious, not difficult fun and rewarding. Consequently kiting is just plain annoying with those random "all over the place" respawns; you end up completely surrounded with little chance to escape and do a "thin ice pirouette" with few team members alive or as last man standing. Which was a common thing to see in HoE KF1 and it really added excitement to the game. Well, unless you are playing as a Berserker of course.
3) The achievements are generally very mechanic, dull and uninteresting.
4) Overall the game lacks atmosphere, it gets dull and boring quickly.
I don't mind the Inventory system, the item drops add replay value to the game I guess.
Conclusion:
If I consider this game as a totally different game that isn't a continuation of another, then it's a good game. If I consider it as a sequel of a game that is one of my favorites ever, then it's really meh. It's like TW tried to make a serious game, and it ended up bland. I have really tried to like the game half as much as I liked KF1 but I just can't.
It's aite.

Roughly ten years after its original release, Half-Life 2 holds up fantastically. Fun shooting that tosses you into a variety of different situations with a large arsenal of weapons means the gameplay alone is enjoyable, but Half-Life 2 is made unforgettable by its cold, bleak atmosphere that ranges from oppressive to ominously empty and its mysterious universe, which the game forces you to examine all the little details around you to get a full grasp of.
Despite being graphically dated, featuring fairly blurry texture work, Half-Life actually stands out and looks much better than many other games from the era, arguably even ones that were used as graphical benchmarks like Doom 3 and Far Cry. Despite having a realistic graphical style, Half-Life 2 features incredibly strong art direction and some of the best environmental design in an FPS I've ever seen. I came out of this replay very impressed with the art team's work.

I've decided to change my review. If you want to see the original review I'll paste it below the new one. First off let me say the game is an improvement on the original in almost every way and if you liked that one, you will love this one. Second, I still enjoy this game despite leaving a bad review for it, but I'm changing it to a "no" because I can't fully support this game while it's using its current business practices. Third, this game has microtransactions. It's early access and it has microtransactions. This game is $29.99, is unfinished, and has the gal to ask you for MORE money in the form of cosmetics, loot boxes, crafting supplies, and keys to unlock your loot boxes. How is this allowed? You expect me to support what you're doing while not making it abundantly clear that you're locking away items behind a paywall? I can't and will not get behind that without saying something about it. You might be thinking to yourself "oh it's only skins for your gun, it doesn't actually have an effect on the gameplay!" and you'd be right to say so, but the thing is it's still in early access. "Oh you're being silly, the devs want more money to help develop the game!" so why did they decide to spend so much time on creating these useless skins instead of adding a meaningful update to the core game? So far TWI has made good updates, and I applaud them for that, but it doesn't change the fact that they're still trying to milk everything they can from you in a game that isn't even finished yet. I can't support any sort of game that does this unless all the content that you can get from microtransactions can also be unlocked via normal gameplay ala Halo 5. So far the only games with "good" microtransactions follow Halo 5's formula which is: all DLC is free, game is constantly updated, and anything you can pay for you can unlock through normal gameplay without having to craft (and trade items TO CRAFT). Everything in the game needs to be able to be unlocked simply by playing it. If TWI wants my recommendation, and a good chunk of their fan's at that, then they'll need to find an alternative to this "zedconomy" they've created.

This review is made after all patching has been made.
(NOTE: SSD Is not neccessary, am running on normal HDD with 7200rpm on 2TB WD Black with ZERO hiccups)
Let me start off by saying the game could be unstable on certain systems. But let me assure you this. At first before all the patches, yes..i couldn't agree more that the game was really unoptimized and has lotsa graphical glitches. After patches, it gets better but still isn't that well optimized.
So what i did is upgrade to 16GB DDR3 RAM, and it fixes some of the performance issues, but still can't use gameworks with 780ti due to video memory limitations. Then i upgraded to GTX 1070, and i couldn't be more happier that i don't have any major problems with the performance even with Gameworks Enabled.
i have both the PS4 and PC version. Theres still some rain features that doesn't look as detailed as the PS4 version especially on Batman's suit, but its still there on the PC version, except it isn't as much as the PS4 version. But overall graphics are awesome on PC especially if u are playing on 4K @ 30fps. Seriously it looks amazing.
On 1080p the other hand, am able to run the game at 60fps constantly with all gameworks features enabled, but the graphics could look a little muddy because of the limitations of the Anti Aliasing.  One disappointment on the graphic side is the usage of Fog and smoke. In the past arkham games, there are a lot of areas that uses smoke and fog and even papers. But not in arkham knight. there isn't really much to see here with smoke and fog. Also i believe after several patches, the devs lowered down the amount of smoke coming out from the Batmobile tyres whics is a disappointment as well. Also some areas where there used to be lotsa smoke density gets lowered down too...thats a shame..
Sound is Superb. All the details could be heard clearly and 5.1 is awesome especially if u have a good soundcard and speakers.
Controls, depending on your taste but i recommend an xbox one controller, except during the tank battles, keyboard and mouse works very well!
Overall, i recommend the game on PC especially if u have a good rig. But on AMD i couldn't guarantee the same. I purchased all the DLCs on PC because i think it's cheaper than the PS4, unless u wanna play the scarecrow nightmare, which is just basically Race, then get the PS4 version.
I just hope WB wont make a mess anymore on the PC version of future games. Pls get Monolith to port the games for PC if possible. Apart from that, Batman Arkham Knight on PC is still a great choice.

This game is a wonderful addition to anyone's horror library. The third person over-the-shoulder gameplay style is similar to that of Resident Evil 4 and 5, leaving Isaac as a relatively slow but powerful tank with the ability to run when he needs to escape certain death.  It is a game that will make you question what the "right" decision is as you unravel more of the games dark story which is driven by conspiracy, betrayal, and mental insanity.  I definitely recommend it to lovers of survival horror games, as well as those who enjoy third person shooters and would like something different than your average run 'n gun.

Risk of Rain is an platform indie game with many rogue-like elements. You unlock new characters and items, to help you through the game. The game is very fun and challenging, but if you want to make it to the end, you need to play smart and use your time wisely.


There's not much to say about the story in this game, the description text explains that "You are the sole survivor of a space train wreck", however that is not the case if you're playing multiplayer; then you can have *four* survivors, but I digress.

There is a lot to say about the game play. Firstly, the controls are pretty simple, you have several attacks (all of which are different based on the character you're playing), you move to the left, right, and jump.
There are numerous unlockables throughout the game, new characters and items. There are actually unlockables that you can only get with certain characters, so that keeps you playing and trying out new things.
The game advertises itself as "full of rogue elements" and to a degree it's quite right, but there are some consistent factors: the first level is always the same, time continues to tick... the longer you play = the harder the game gets.

There are 15 achievements for this game. I suspect the reason I haven't written the review for this great game yet, because I... shamefully... haven't been able to unlock the last 3 achievements I need. (at this time: 4/16/15)
There are only a few easy achievements that you unlock just by playing it, most achievements you will need to do something very specific. Be it, find a new character to unlock, or use a specific item on another specific item/NPC.

Risk of Rain goes for $9.99, I personally waited for a sale (much to the frustration of my real life friends who wanted to play it with me)... but in the end that's a fair price for this game, based on how much time I've spent playing it.

I've mused to myself in the past thinking "I wonder if these older indie games will age differently then console or ROM games". It seems like many indie games age well because they have unique-addictive-artistic-theme's to them.

One final note: this game shines when it comes to multiplayer, playing on your own gets old, playing with friends feels like you're playing a classic arcade game with friends.

Roughly ten years after its original release, Half-Life 2 holds up fantastically. Fun shooting that tosses you into a variety of different situations with a large arsenal of weapons means the gameplay alone is enjoyable, but Half-Life 2 is made unforgettable by its cold, bleak atmosphere that ranges from oppressive to ominously empty and its mysterious universe, which the game forces you to examine all the little details around you to get a full grasp of.
Despite being graphically dated, featuring fairly blurry texture work, Half-Life actually stands out and looks much better than many other games from the era, arguably even ones that were used as graphical benchmarks like Doom 3 and Far Cry. Despite having a realistic graphical style, Half-Life 2 features incredibly strong art direction and some of the best environmental design in an FPS I've ever seen. I came out of this replay very impressed with the art team's work.

I never quite got into the original XCom as did others; I enjoyed the game but never to the point where I wanted to, say, write fanfic about it. It was a fun, but flawed, classic with as many good points as bad. Still, I was as excited as the next grognard when I heard that Firaxis was rebooting the series. My opinion of this newest title, however, is similar to that of the original: it is a classic, albeit somewhat flawed, game.
Despite the moans of many, I find the removal of action-points an acceptable compromise towards making the game more accessible and less tedious than the original. The game moves more quickly now, advancing to those memorable firefights at a more rapid pace. But the game feels suspiciously hollow, with numerous missing features. Customization is shallow, the maps and missions are repetitive, and the aliens feel toothless lacking the ability to assault the XCom base. These gaps seem purposeful, probably to be filled in with DLC. The end result is a game which offers an often memorable experience but not one which drags me back to play it more than once.

X-Com...just the title evokes memories of an old DOS 386, watching my squad getting cut down by Sectoids, zombified by Chrysalis, throwing the grenade...and having it bounce to my feet.  For those who have followed the series, the story is pretty much a re-hash for the first game.
The Good:  I enjoyed the updated interface, the fact that your squad would automatically go into cover, the simplied Action Point (AP) system, and the way they kept a good feel of the original game.
The Bad:  I miss the base micro-management.  I miss the Base Assaults and the Base Defends.  I miss the little things that were taken out to make this a more streamlined game (not to say that it's a bad thing).
The Ugly:  The worst part of the game is the cover scheme.  Now, it's great that your guys go into cover automatically, simplifying the AP system.  But, JFC...watching your guy shoot straight through a wall (or be shot straight through a wall) without damage TO the wall is...disconcerting.
All in all, this is a great game.  I've enjoyed playing this as much as I enjoyed the first game.  Whereas it doesn't hold the fun and charm of the third game, but...it's a good nod to the original.
As a side note:  The DLC Expansion, "The Enemy Within" does add in some fun of both the first game and the third game.  I won't spoil anything, I think that is something everybody needs to learn, themselves.  But if you're a fan of TBS games, a fan of actual strategy games...this is definitely one to pick up.

So excluding the atrocious PC port Dead Space is a fantastic and immersive horror experience. Now I got to be frank with you, I pretty much spoiled Dead Space when I saw a let's play from like 3-5 years ago yet my memory was very vague when I played this game. To tell you what's going on in the story I recommend you play it for yourself because duh spoilers, that plus other people who give reviews will tell tend to explain the story, mine is more of the experience.
Besides spoiling the game for myself I have also played Dead Space 2 and completed it (On the Xbox 360) and have got to say that the experience was very unique compared to if I played Dead Space 1 first and then 2. You know that feeling when you look at a picture of a famous monument and actually went there? Or go and experience that one place that's so talked about and then actually visit it? Well that's what Dead Space 1 was like when I played it, so much of the trilogy's plot all revolves around the events of what happened on the USG Ishimura and the planet Aegis 7 along with the developement of the main protagonist Isaac Clarke, that plus the event's of the USG Ishimura acts as a catalyst for pretty much the entire 3 game's story.
As a survival horror game Dead Space does it pretty well even though the gameplay mechanics are straight up Resident Evil 4 just with new stuff that you can do. Now yes as much of the Dead Space community has stated Dead Space 1 is a lot more scarier than is Dead Space 2 for many reasons. Now I'm pretty tough when it comes to scary games yet Dead Space still tends to frighten me compared to the jump scare infested and cinematic sequel that was Dead Space 2. The game kept my heart at an above than normal pulse in certain parts and some parts have truly made my heart race.
The Immersion in Dead Space is incredible with the sound design being spot on along with the game's mechanics and setting working together to make the immersive experience amazing, here's how it works: Dead Space's indicators is all attached to the character's body such as the character's "RIG" stating the player's health along with the Stasis meter being on the character's RIG aswell, The game's mechanics such as the Stasis ability and Kinesis ability are all integrated uses in the game's setting, story, and lore, not some thing tacked on for just gameplay purposes. For example the use of stasis and kinesis are actual tools used by the USG Ishimura's crew along with the weapons of the game being mechanical power tools used on the ship (excluding the Pulse Rifle of course). The sound design is spot on and it all makes sense and adds to the game, you will hear distant screams of unlucky survivors and necromophs alike that will make you wonder if there were any other survivors still on the ship through out your journey, you will hear clanks and sounds in the vents and in the distance that make you tense thinking that a necromorph can come out of any vent at any time possible.
Dead Space's story is very interesting and many of the concept's of the game are ones that I have never seen in anything before, sure the game take's influences from franchises such as Alien along with how the premise of the game has already been done by titles such as System Shock 2. Besides that I think the game is very original for its time and I think anyone should do some research on the lore because the setting of Dead Space with planet cracking, the Marker, necromorphs and the Church of Unitology is one that I find interesting.
The port for Dead Space on PC is atrocious, not for the fact that it has issues but by the fact that it's bugs are absolutely pathetic, like really, some of the bugs in this game make Call of Duty: Ghost's PC port look good, I mean here's a list of the bugs that I've encountered:
1. The game doesn't even try to run on AMD alone

4. Player model/Isaac Clarke tends to spaz out when you sprint on some parts of the ground
5. Finicky mouse controls with horribly low sensitivity even on the highest setting
6. Some wierd thing that happens to a tram door that gets stuck mid animation that causes you from passing
7. Characters that die tend to spaz out when they go from static character to ragdoll (hilarious and somewhat immersive breaking)
8. (MY ABSOLUTE HATED) So there will be parts where you will have to float in space and there is a slight chance that your character make freeze via clipping into geometry and just die as if Isaac sufficated from I don't know, polygons? This happened to me like 3 times and 2 were by the end of the game
But hey that doesn't mean it's a bad game! So go out and buy it and have a good ol' time!

Batman:Arkham Knight is pretty cool, I guess.
Back in the distant past of 2014, I decided to write a bunch of stupid words in a row and it somehow made a review for a game called Batman: Arkham Asylum. This somehow entertained a bunch of people and two years later I'm still writing stupid words and somehow making video game reviews out of them.
But now we're going back to where it all began with Batman: Arkham Asylum 4. I mean Arkham Knight.
You play as Bruce Wayne, a man who still has the world's deadest parents. On his spare time, Bruce likes to use his money to dress up like a bat and beat up people less fortunate than him while also adopting children who also have dead parents so he can train them to beat up people for him. So with his team of other amazingly fit men in costumes and one girl in a wheelchair, Bruce uses his training, gadgets, and beautiful body to beat up the scum of Gotham city.
Arkham Knight apparently had a rough start, though I kind of missed out on because I played the game roughly a year after it came out. It's still kind of sluggish, but I wouldn't call it unplayable.
"But Dirk, you handsome devil with a heart of gold." You say. "I already know all that and read about it and watched reviews that covered all these problems. How is the game itself?"
You are very flattering to me.
To get the graphics and all that fun stuff out of the way, I played this game on a 650 ti I put together myself after a journey that involved an angry wizard and a smelly man named Herbert. It ran...Alright, I guess. I had to turn down some settings and put the game at 30 fps, but it never dipped below that, so it was alright for me personally.
The night before Halloween, Scarecrow: one of Batman's most sinister villains, threatens to cover the people of Gotham in his signature spooky gas. Only this spooky gas is EXTRA SPOOKY. Though it would probably make Halloween super rad, you probably don't want to be hit by the spooky toxins, so the people of Gotham evacuate, leaving only a handful of police men, the criminals of Gotham, and Bruce. I mean Batman.
Now with all the bystanders gone, Gotham essentially becomes your playground as you glide, swing, drive, and punch your way to

To me, Akrham Knight felt like a mixed bag, considering it's larger than both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, there's a lot of ground to cover and a lot of things to do. The thing is, all those things feel a bit weaker than they did in the last two games. For example, the Riddler missions are probably the weakest they've ever been. It doesn't help that Eddie decides to repeat the same few lines over and over until you finally punch him into a prison cell. Also, why race tracks, Eddie? Why?
I should also bring up the Batmobile, something iconic to the Batman series but hasn't really been of any use until this game. It controls alright and it's kind of fun to use sometimes, but I wish there wasn't so much of a focus on it in some missions. Like Eddie. Screw you, Eddie.
I feel like combat is a general improvement over the first two games, and Origins too, I guess. You have a few more moves that make fights a bit flashier as well as some tag team moves with buddies that show up every now and then. But at the same time, enemies kind of go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with what they do with you. Between normal mooks, large mooks, medics, electric mooks, mooks with knives, mooks with shields, mooks with stun batons, nukes, jet planes, and Gary Busey trying to eat your teeth, it can get overwhelming at times. Especially so when Bruce decides to PUNCH THE GUY WITH THE STUN BATON AND SHOCK HIMSELF INSTEAD OF THE MOOK WHO'S HEALING ANOTHER MOOK, BRUCE YOU MASOCHISTIC RAT ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Arabic Knight also has some pretty sketchy design and story choices. Like
. Also the Arkham Knights, one of the big villains of the game. His real identity isn't even a spoiler. Because that guy you guessed, that's him. I won't say because someone will get mad, but yeah, you're right.
The last fight with the Arkham knight as well as the fight with
are also pretty lame. I was expecting amazing one on one duels, fist to fist, mano a mano, instead we have tank combat because we gotta show off that neat Batmobile.
I also kind of find it funny that Arkham knight likes to kind of throw away a lot of plot things from Arkham origin, with a few only getting quick mentions. Maybe Rocksteady agreed with me on the design and story decision Origin went on and how they strayed a little too far away from the Arkham universe in favor of the Nolan universe. Which is kind of crummy in comparison.
But should you play Spiderman: New York day?
I'm not the biggest fan of Batman, but he's still in my top 20's at least. Bringing back the voice work like Kevin Conroy as Batman and all the attention they put into the universe itself shows that Rocksteady has a pretty big hardon for Batman himself, which is nice to see in a developer. Arkham popularized the punch+counter two button system and they still do it the best. Is it a game everyone will like? Probably not. But if you're a Arkham fan or a Batman fan, you can't really go wrong. I wouldn't buy it at full price though, maybe wait for a sale.

Waited for quite a while to catch this one on sale, gotta say I was a bit disappointed. The general game and mechanics are really fun, all the characters I've played so far feel really unique. The different characters feel particularly nice whenever you play with friends and put together a team. The music is pretty nice, but I was stuck on the first level long enough to get sick of the song and turn on my own music(This never happened with Wings of Vi, where I was definitely stuck listening to certain tracks for 10x as long)
My biggest problem with the game is that it seems riddled with arbitrary difficulty. All of the enemy animation reads (that I have experienced by reaching level 6) are fine, and can be learned with a little time and effort. The problem is, they are just far too tanky for it to be reasonable, this leads to some really terrible cheesing tactics. For example, standing on the other side of a platform gap and nuking a large crowd. I hate to have to cheese things in general, but it's almost like the game is built around cheesing large groups of enemies, they are just far too tanky for the amount of damage you put out, even with a stellar powerup lineup. No, I haven't unlocked all of the powerups yet, but I doubt that will change the level of vitality that these enemies possess. You either stand out of range and spam the shoot key, or you jump into a crowd and risk getting your health chunked away (this situation is especially true in later levels) When you eventually end up having to cheese it, it just feels cheap, it's honestly one of the most disappointing aspects of the game, to me. I'm a huge fan of difficulty, I've worked through tough titles such as Spelunky, 1001 Spikes, and Wings of Vi, and this game just doesn't present an enjoyable difficulty where you can learn little nuances in the mechanics to further your skills. It's all about blasting a huge crowd of enemies that should have been dead 30 shots ago.
(This is my first review, so if it's♥♥♥♥♥ sorry)
tl;dr - Mechanics are fun, but the enemy balancing seems poorly done to the point of ruining the experience for me. Don't buy at full price, but if you have friends to play with, catch it on sale.
Edit: Also, about half of my hours on this game are AFK. When I close the game, steam doesn't realize it's closed, so to fully close out of it I have to shut steam down. It's weird

I never quite got into the original XCom as did others; I enjoyed the game but never to the point where I wanted to, say, write fanfic about it. It was a fun, but flawed, classic with as many good points as bad. Still, I was as excited as the next grognard when I heard that Firaxis was rebooting the series. My opinion of this newest title, however, is similar to that of the original: it is a classic, albeit somewhat flawed, game.
Despite the moans of many, I find the removal of action-points an acceptable compromise towards making the game more accessible and less tedious than the original. The game moves more quickly now, advancing to those memorable firefights at a more rapid pace. But the game feels suspiciously hollow, with numerous missing features. Customization is shallow, the maps and missions are repetitive, and the aliens feel toothless lacking the ability to assault the XCom base. These gaps seem purposeful, probably to be filled in with DLC. The end result is a game which offers an often memorable experience but not one which drags me back to play it more than once.

X-Com...just the title evokes memories of an old DOS 386, watching my squad getting cut down by Sectoids, zombified by Chrysalis, throwing the grenade...and having it bounce to my feet.  For those who have followed the series, the story is pretty much a re-hash for the first game.
The Good:  I enjoyed the updated interface, the fact that your squad would automatically go into cover, the simplied Action Point (AP) system, and the way they kept a good feel of the original game.
The Bad:  I miss the base micro-management.  I miss the Base Assaults and the Base Defends.  I miss the little things that were taken out to make this a more streamlined game (not to say that it's a bad thing).
The Ugly:  The worst part of the game is the cover scheme.  Now, it's great that your guys go into cover automatically, simplifying the AP system.  But, JFC...watching your guy shoot straight through a wall (or be shot straight through a wall) without damage TO the wall is...disconcerting.
All in all, this is a great game.  I've enjoyed playing this as much as I enjoyed the first game.  Whereas it doesn't hold the fun and charm of the third game, but...it's a good nod to the original.
As a side note:  The DLC Expansion, "The Enemy Within" does add in some fun of both the first game and the third game.  I won't spoil anything, I think that is something everybody needs to learn, themselves.  But if you're a fan of TBS games, a fan of actual strategy games...this is definitely one to pick up.

Whether I'm running amok with a chainsaw on the beach, racing cars down crowded city streets or seeing how long I can last on a crime spree until the police finally overwhelm me, GTA: Vice City remains not only my favourite in the entire series, but also my all-time favourite game full stop. As far as I'm concerned, if you only ever play one GTA game in your entire life, it should absolutely be this one.

Very good game that looks and plays very well after 7 years have passed. The horror element is pretty constant while not going stale. The only bad thing about the game I've heard is the controls, but I got used to them very quickly and found that to be a nonissue. My favorite thing about this game is the amount of ways that you can die, which made death a bit less frustrating and a bit more fun. The game also has a pretty novel fighting system, where it often makes sense to dismember enemies before killing them which I haven't seen to the same extent in any other games. Very recommended.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a brilliant hilarious game,
That brings the crude humour of South Park and mixes it with solid Turn Based Combat.
One of the funnest gaming experiences I had in 2014.
+Hilarious story, with loads of references to the show that fans of south park will love.
+Good amount of customization.
+Loads of unique levels and areas keep the gaming feeling fresh.
+Lots of favourite characters from the show voiced by the real actors.
=Combat is solid, however as the game progresses I feel like you become hugely over powered by the end.
-For an RPG, the game is very short. Completed it in a litte over 12 hours.
-Would of liked to have seen more sidequests to give it more longevity.
All in all, this is a very solid game that fans of the show should not miss. However if you are not a fan of the show or do not enjoy crude humour then this game is not for you, as it is around every corner.

Shadowrun Returns marks a return to the Shadowrun universe in video game form after a really long hiatus. And it is indeed a brilliant return. The gameplay itself isn't much to shout about. If you've played games like XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you'd already figure it out although XCOM's gameplay was still more refined than the one in Shadowrun Returns.
This, being a Kickstarter-funded game, there's no voice-acting, just text-based dialogue. Text-based, but very well-written. In fact, the story is the game's strongest point. A cyberpunk conspiracy with all sorts of twists and turns while also showing off the different types of creatures or people who populate the world.
As of now, the main game's price has been reduced a few dollars, so I see no reason why you shouldn't purchase it. Don't expect a revolution in gameplay and you'll definitely enjoy this game as it is.

I will have this review split into 2 sections. One on the game itself and the other on the current state of the PC versions.
So the final part in the Batman Arkham series and I can honestly say its an amazing way to end a very loved series. The game is a true love letter to anybody that is familar with the Dark Knight and has some references from some of his most memorable moments in history.
Gameplay: This Arkham game has the most in depth combat system with everything you've known from the previous games and adds a lot more. To be honest it has gotten more difficult since it has more enemy varieties that keeps you on your toes to not mess up your combo. Same goes for the stealth sections which adds more features so you can experiment how you can take down your enemies. The Batmobile has be a mixed bag for everybody, IMO its fun. For the first few missions the Batmobile does feel like its been shoved in there especially the Riddler challenges but its still fun to use and you can also upgrade it. Whats new with the AR challenges is they include challenges for the Batmobile which can be racing tracks or combat and they aren't as good as the rest of the challenges IMO. The open-world aspect of the game has the most collectibles and side missions than the previous games.
Story: Being the final part in the Arkham series, the story is amazing and has a really good and honestly a sad ending... But the story is told really well and references some of Batman's greatest moments from his comic books and is shown off very well. After like 20% through the main story you will come across a bit of a shocking twist with someone making a comeback... which I won't spoil! I would say this has the best story out of the whole series, just passing Arkham City and you will be amazed by the ending.
Conclusion: Batman Arkham Knight is a great ending to one of the best video game series of all time and your a big fan of anything related to Batman you will have an amazing experience with this game. Combat is a lot of fun as well as the Batmobile which may be different for a some people but regardless I had an amazing time with this game.

An alternate story arc to the long running series: X-Com.  The game Is a fresh reprisal to the series with a new art direction and Turn Based Combat system.
PROS
-------
+ The Game has replay value.
+ The Art style is a fresh start from what we've seen in past X Com titles.
+ The Turn Based Strategy is a new feature to the genre.
+ Customizing your soldiers is fun, from their armor color to their hair style.
+ The aniamted cutscenes from the story line to the combat is worth watching.
+ Squad experience and abilites add a new level of strategy.
+ Variety of aliens too keep fighting interesting.
CONS
-------
- Managing resources gets to be a hassal.
- Keeping the nations happy is more of a chore .
- manufacturing Satelites and other much needed items take to long.
- Story feels meaningless and lacks something outside of (aliens invade we must defend).
- No Co-Op Mode.
Neutral Feelings
-------------------
+/- Some folks may not enjoy the turn based combat
+/- Cannot manufacture ammunition for weapons like previous titles
+/- Story doesn't expand beyond the concept of "Aliens attack and abduct humans."  There's nothing too explain WHY or even expand upon the reason for this.
+/- Not many mission variations.  We see typical UFO Crash/Landings to investigate.  Abduction Alerts and rescue the civilians.  But there's nothing else too add variety.  There are some alternate missions in the DLC and recent Expansion, but not enough too break the monotony.
My Thoughts
--------------
The game is a Welcome addition to the long going series and great for gamers not familiar with the series.
It is gratifying too see the iconic Grey Alien appear in the game, as it's been an unsung spokeman for the series.  Likewise goes for the classic UFO, if only with a new shiney look.
Closing Thoughts
------------------
The Game is a must have for anyone who enjoys: XCOM Seres, Science Fiction games, Turn Based Games, and squad management.
The use of cover for your squad adds a new level of strategy for the game.  This along with using high ground to your advantage adds to the strategy.
The Replay value for this game is very high.  As your base will vary each time, missions appear at new intervals, no one mission is ever the same.
Though there are a few elements that are difficult too achieve, such as keeping the nations happy and secure and building new gear with lack of funds and resources.  This does not ruin the fun factor of the game.
It's great too see cinematics of in game with teh characters at the base and on the field (such as spotting new aliens and takign the kill shot).  But it would have been good too see more from the base npcs and watching your air craft engage in epic dog fights with a UFO.
Personal Score
-----------------
9.0 / 10

I honestly don’t know if I should recommend this. Was it entertaining? Yes, but mostly because it felt like playing Arkham City again. It’s another Batman game: better than the average action title, but nowhere near as good as its predecessors. Arkham Knight gets so much wrong. Firstly, the story is really two stories that have no business intersecting one another. The game kicks off with Scarecrow threatening to release a cloud of fear toxin over Gotham. Scarecrow could have been an amazing antagonist. Imagine the entire city transformed into a gallery of Batman’s worst nightmares: a surreal hell-scape that would have fit perfectly with the game’s Halloween setting. But all Scarecrow does is say, “You’ll lose, Batman” on TV screens. The fear gas does less than it did in Arkham Asylum. 80% of the story focuses on the new Arkham Knight villain. (If you can’t figure out who the Knight is in the first hour, you should probably question your knowledge of Batman. Yet, somehow Batman himself is perplexed the entire game.) The Arkham Knight leads the story in a terrible direction that feels more like exploring a dystopian cyberpunk world than playing as Batman. He fills Gotham with tanks, drones, and soldiers – far removed from supervillains and detective work. Batman spends most of his time in the Batmobile (also a tank). It’s overused to the point of nauseam. I hate the Batmobile. I hate its slippery controls, how slowly it moves, and how long and tedious its combat feels. Not to mention it kills people. The game tries to gloss over it by giving the tank “dummy” rounds and creating a ridiculous shock field that only zaps enemies when you run them over. But they are absolutely dying, especially when you ram into cars until they’re mangled soup cans. The first game in the series offered Batman a handful of gadgets, but designed the world around using them. Arkham Knight gives him dozens of gadgets and doesn’t have any level design at all. Every patch of Gotham looks like every other patch. It’s ugly, monotone, and lacks any recognizable landmarks. Even the combat feels bloated. Enemies are specialized to such an extent that beating them becomes a chore. Big enemies, electric enemies, ninja enemies, electric ninja enemies, enemies with shields, enemies with electric shields, enemies who heal other enemies and make them electric, enemies with guns, enemies with bigger guns, enemies that require beat-downs, enemies that require shocks, enemies that require the Batarang, enemies with quick-time events. It becomes so ridiculous, the game provides tutorials until the last hour of play. Everything is supersized until you’re gliding from one waypoint to another in a gigantic, empty world. When the story does get some room to breathe, it’s amazing. Some of the villains are even creepy. But they’re treated as afterthoughts. And don’t get me started on the DLC. I really wanted to play as Harley Quinn. In fact, for three games, all I’ve wanted to do is play as Harley Quinn. Know how long her missions are? 20 minutes. I’m betting some players will rush through them in ten. I paid real money for 20 minutes of gameplay? She has THREE fights in her entire story! The other DLC missions are just as bad. Batgirl’s is glitchy and short; no one cares about Red Hood, and all the characters are just dumbed-down versions of Batman. Do not waste your money on the DLC. Oh, and as a final note, yes, the game is finally playable. Barely. My GTX 900 series card runs it at about 40 frames-per-second. It eats up a staggering amount of processing power – so much that my computer will lag for five minutes after closing the program. It’s the worst-optimized game I’ve ever played. Nothing about Arkham Knight compares to its predecessors. Only buy it if you’re really desperate for some Batman action.

This is a great turn based strategy and tactics game. There is a long term economic strategy component that adds a great amount of tension and critical decision making throughout the game. Do I build satellites to make more money later, or guns and armor to make my soldiers more durable now?
Missions are great, they feel like a cross between Final Fantasy Tactics and the first 2 Fallout games. Losing soldiers hurts and is permanent and losing the mission increases panic and may cause a country to drop out of the XCOM initiative costing you their monthly financial support.
The game encourages you to be cautiously aggressive. The need to be agressive is really amped up in the Enemy Within expansion as there is a new resource only collectable in missions, this resource is time limited and can be destroyed by weapon fire.
The expansion Enemy Within also adds 1 new class, and a new path to upgrade your soldiers, and a number of non-weapon & armor forge-based upgrades. Most of these are quality of life upgrades like unlocking two item slots for all soldiers, but really add some depth to decision making on where to spend resources.
Overall the expansion adds some new missions and new faction to duke it out with as well as some cool features and mechanics.
All in all I give this game a 9/10 with the expansion.

To combat the spacebeasts you're provided with a myriad of weapons, of which you can carry up to 4 at any given time. You can switch them out at HUBs though I only found 3 of them satisfying to use. Along with the weapons you get a couple of cool abilities which work well in harmony. Despite the pointless CQC, I found targeting limbs and blowing stuff up very fun. You also get some cool looping level design which works well in this environment and an interesting story.
From a technical side it isn't the most proficient game out there. Cadavers tend to randomly bug out and just writhe around uncontrollably which will likely scare you more than the scripted scares. More importantly some game breaking bugs exist where the only cure may be to restart the game so save often and on multiple save files! As Nevermore didn't once say it's a Dead Love in a Dead Space. *Hey! South Park fans who didn't play this game! We don't take kindly to your kinds around here!*
Are you a South Park fan? Then don't wait for anything, buy this game and play it! It's that simple. I watched all 18 seasons just so I wouldn't miss anything and it really helped. If you are not a South Park fan, the decision is not that simple.
The game is one giant stream of references to the TV Show, full of characters (duh), songs (playing in a radio) and even the loot. You know what you'll find in Cartman's mom bedroom. You will laugh a lot. And I mean a LOT.
The story starts with another LARP played by kids of South Park but few hours later other "forces" come into play and it quickly becomes a crazy mash of nearly everything (sadly, some things are missing) that's ever been in the show. It's one hell of a ride from start to finish.
From the mechanics point of view it's a weird mix of basic mechanics which you can (and often have to) combine and that makes the game quite complex.
The character progression is the most basic thing you can imagine. You choose from four different classes at the beginning of the game: The fighter, thief, mage and jew. Yes, jew. Every level you can invest one point into your class specific abilities which are progressively unlocking with your growing levels. At the end of the game, you'll have most of the abilities maxed out.
Then there are your perks, which are passive bonuses. Every time you reach a threshold of facebook friends (yes, really) you gain one perk. You can use them to complement your specific play style, or whatever you like.
Item progression is very good. You constantly find new items with all kinds of different bonuses. You can use melee and ranged weapons and three parts of an armour. Most of them are modifiable to further adjust your play style.
Abilities, perks and items are all in the spirit of South Park, of course.
The combat system looks like the same old boring JRPG thing where every turn you choose one attack from a menu for each and every one of your characters and then watch the enemies do the same, right? Wrong.
Obsidian managed to make the combat fun and enjoyable with one simple thing. "Quick time events" or something like that. Each attack, block or ability can be executed effectively if you manage to press the right button(s) at the right time. It's much more engaging and if you manage to pull it off, it feels *so* powerful. But even with this great addition, it still gets repetitive near the end. However, it's a great achievement for JRPG style combat!
The cause of repetitive combat is the small number of abilities. At the beginning of the game you have two of them and with the rising levels you end up with five. Most of the time it's completely fine, but once you find the correct order of using them it becomes boring a little bit.
In addition to abilities and basic melee and ranged attack, every character has a special ability. You can summon unique characters after you've done some quests for them. Butters is a paladin, so he can heal you. I won't spoil the other characters, but all of them have something funny prepared for you.
You are a ... (I won't spoil it!) so you will have one more ace in the hole, and that's magic. And by magic I mean farts, of course. They can be very powerful if you execute them right.
Because abilities cost you action points, magic cost you mana, and enemy attack surprisingly cost you health, you can use consumable at the start of each round.
Exploring the beautiful town of South Park is a big part of the game. You can run around by foot, or if you find fast travel points, by something that will make you laugh. At first there will be places where you want to go because of loot or whatnot but you can't find the way in there. That's because you didn't get one of many crazy weird "powers" yet. As the story progresses you'll be able to teleport, shrink, destroy barriers and ask your buddies to do something specific for you. On many occasions you will have to use some combination of them. This brings new complexity into the adventuring part of the game and it's great fun. One small issue is the controls. It was clearly made for controllers and on the keyboard it's annoying to "scroll" through them like a slave when they could be bound to some keys. The other problem is that the game doesn't tell you why you can't do something and when you'll be able to.
South Park: The Stick of Truth is an approachable game made for everyone. At the same time it brings complexity with rich possibilities of interaction with the game world. It's the funniest game I've ever played, but that's because of the gigantic amount of references to something I understand. I don't know if someone who doesn't watch South Park would find it funny. But from the mechanics point of view it's somewhat original RPG with not very complex mechanics and really enjoyable combat system. The only trouble I remember experiencing is clunky controls and user interface.
It's a great game.

By FAR one of the best puzzle games I have ever played. I would highly, highly recommend this game. At first glance a lot of the puzzles appear to be cheep tricks but they grow to be rather fun and most importantly, intellectually stimulating (what puzzle games are supposed to do).
One of my favorite aspects of this game is that the puzzles can be solved in a plethora of ways. Where as in most puzzle games, each puzzle only has one solution: the developers intended solution. Which may be quite obscure and therefore difficult to disconcern (which DOES NOT make for a good puzzle game).
Here however, there are many ways to solve a puzzle here and the skills you learn along the way are being constantly tested and reapplied in a perfect balance that neither sees intense reptition (of practicing skills) nore far reaches (i.e. learning algebra I then being expecting to jump straight into calculus).
Futhermore, theres a very limited factor of aggravation- most puzzle games like to have a few puzzles that require you to do something very precise within a very limited window and when you fail, require you do to the whole puzzle over again. While there is SOME of that here, the amount that you have to redo is significantly shorter than most other puzzle games (as youll see when you learn to properly wield the transport system).
My ONLY complaint about this game is that you need a pair of sunglasses to play it, really guys, turn down the brightness which you cannot do in game. The options you can configure in game are quite limited (mostly resolution), you have to go into the config files to manually rebind keys and lower the intense brightness (EVERYTHING is vibrant, VIBRANT colors, usually pure white).
While not being stone set linear like most puzzle games, there are multiple paths to take especially if you cannot figure out a particular puzzle, but ultimately you have to have completed a central goal (the weapon portrayed in some of the SS's) to progress on to additional paths. So its not entirely free lance- carve your own path but, its close. As such It has very limited replayability, especially as most of the puzzles revolve around learning a central key hidden method (quite satisfying when you find them on your own).
Now its not the mind f*** that all the reviewers claim it to be. However its very fun to explore, and can be sort hard to follow spacially, but you'll get it rather quick off the bat.
I *HIGHLY* recommend this for puzzle game lovers.

While a fun play through and introduction to the universe, it is necessary to buy the dragonfall campaign to truly see what this framework is capable of.

Side quests are few and far between, you have no control over how your npc companions (depending upon the campaign by harebrained) level up, and a general lack of freedom in what should be a more open world experience. However, the game is primarily designed for being a tool that players use to build their own campaigns. Sadly though, this shouldn't have to be a substitute for harebrain's lack of campaign building talent.
The game also needs co-op, just hear me out. This is turn based game, based upon a pen a paper rpg, with focus on building a single character for a player with full stats/"classes", with tools to build your own campaigns and maps. While entertaining to experience in single player, and as cool as the build your own rpg framework is, it missed its calling. This is a tool that could be expanded to actually run a pen and paper campaigns! There are things like
but lets be honest, the visual tools and dice support are lacking for odd ball rpgs like Shadowrun (huge lack of cyberpunk visuals like tiles/characters/creatures and a lot of custom equation building required to get it running properly). Adding networking/co-op would allow a savvy dm to build their own maps/campaigns and run a pnp rpg with visual support and a set rule framework for combat! (seriously, the art direction is gorgeous and no need to worry about that "one player" cheating their stats or rule loop holes).
Overall, for the price ($30 if you buy all the dev built campaigns) it's worth the money. The 2 campaign  stories are fun, the lenghts of the stories are good, the changes in Dragonfall are proof that harebrained is listening to the community to improve upon their stories, tool upgrades, and improving rpg elements in their own work. There are a few bugs/optimizations that need to be sorted out but, I also need to upgrade my pc (really badly) so I'd like to hear how those with beefier rigs hold up. (I'm pretty sure the issues I ran into were due to the HD graphics straining my rig at high resolutions).

I've always wanted a really great sequel to the child-heroics, and bizarre mundanity of Earthbound. Nintendo will never give us that, but Trey & Matt did a hell of a job with creating a fluid, open world South Park rpg that blends some of the best characteristics from Earthbound with some of the best writing the SP creators are capable of producing.
Clocking in at under 20hrs. on the hardest setting, the game isn't terribly long for an rpg, but there isn't much in the way of grinding levels, and there are only a few sidequest collections. While I would've loved a 40hr. South Park rpg, the main storyline takes up most of the game time, and it rarely lags in quality or pacing. I rarely get to pay this compliment to an open world rpg, regardless of how big or small that open world is.
Don't forget to bring a towel and use a controller. The gameplay seems to have been designed for a controller, and not a wealth of shortcut keys, like typical crpgs.

This is how I imagine a great Star-Trek game would have been. You control a starship and command a crew, each of which you can assign to fulfill different roles. There is a huge variety of tactics available in FTL; everything from boarding enemy ships to destroying the enemy's oxygen supply to suffocate the crew. The random events throughout the game will entice you to step outside the conventional boundaries of your play style in a risk versus reward fashion.
Death is permaneant in FTL, so once you die you must start over from the beginning. This element gives your decisions weight and makes you invested in the world. Each wound to your ship's health/hull carries over unless you are lucky enough to stumble upon repair shops. There's no backtracking in FTL because the premise of the game is to avoid a fleet of rebel forces pursuing you ever-slowly across the galactic map. Once the rebel fleet passes over a certain point, you cannot return to that point, and you must push forward.
FTL is a great strategy game that involves a lot of entertaining thought and suspense. I wouldn't be able to do it justice in a review, and Youtube videos often don't highlight what's truly fun about the game. However, I can reccommend it from my own personal expierence. If you're into strategy, then this is one of those games you'll just have to see for yourself.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a shining example of how a series can be freshened up, but still be as good as the classics. Many games have changed their core principles in order to earn an extra buck with a different audience, but XCOM keeps it real.
The XCOM games have always delivered a unique experience where players manage resources outside of the battlefield, but also successfully carry out demanding missions on the ground. These situations keep you invovled, and you are always struggling to fight the imminent apocalypse. Keeping track of your pool of soldiers, the amount of money you have, ongoing research and development projects, panic levels, and aircraft never gets old.
While XCOM has a fantastic turn-based strategy system for the actual combat, just as much of the strategy is in keeping the XCOM Project funded by different nations throughout the world; Put one nation's needs above another, and you'll be losing their support. In addition to that, you have the ability to increase the resources gathered monthly by launching satellites above certain nations. You protect these satellites with the aircraft you keep in the hangar, which can be equipped with a variety of weapons.
The game does have it's shortcomings, however. Enemies may randomly spawn during a mission, and I'm left wondering about some of their design choices. For example, the unmanned weapons platform that can replace a soldier in your squad is criminally inaccurate, and it lacks the ability to use cover. The UFO vs. XCOM aircraft system is weak, and the skill tree decisions you make when a soldier is promoted are generally unbalanced, making one choice better than the other.
In the end, XCOM delivers a great turn-based strategy experience on the field and  strong-yet-flawed project management off the field.

Though not without its flaws, Risk of Rain is never-the-less a solid game. The gameplay is easy to pick up but difficult to master, and a good range of characters cater to different play styles. I believe that I've got my money's worth out of Risk of Rain, and I highly recommend it.

Antichamber is difficult to explain. It's a game that forces you to question everything about its world and take nothing for granted. Any preconceived notion you have about how a game should work will only hinder your progress - Antichamber has its own rules, and even those rules are subject to change. It's rare that a game makes me think about its mechanics in such depth - Portal and Fez are two others that come to mind - but Antichamber makes you analyze and puzzle harder than those games.
Did you see that movie Cube or its sequel? Antichamber is kind of like that, but you can't die. There's no failure in this game - just delay and redirection as you try to make sense of its reality. It's like being caught in an M. C. Escher drawing, and it's wonderful.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a shining example of how a series can be freshened up, but still be as good as the classics. Many games have changed their core principles in order to earn an extra buck with a different audience, but XCOM keeps it real.
The XCOM games have always delivered a unique experience where players manage resources outside of the battlefield, but also successfully carry out demanding missions on the ground. These situations keep you invovled, and you are always struggling to fight the imminent apocalypse. Keeping track of your pool of soldiers, the amount of money you have, ongoing research and development projects, panic levels, and aircraft never gets old.
While XCOM has a fantastic turn-based strategy system for the actual combat, just as much of the strategy is in keeping the XCOM Project funded by different nations throughout the world; Put one nation's needs above another, and you'll be losing their support. In addition to that, you have the ability to increase the resources gathered monthly by launching satellites above certain nations. You protect these satellites with the aircraft you keep in the hangar, which can be equipped with a variety of weapons.
The game does have it's shortcomings, however. Enemies may randomly spawn during a mission, and I'm left wondering about some of their design choices. For example, the unmanned weapons platform that can replace a soldier in your squad is criminally inaccurate, and it lacks the ability to use cover. The UFO vs. XCOM aircraft system is weak, and the skill tree decisions you make when a soldier is promoted are generally unbalanced, making one choice better than the other.
In the end, XCOM delivers a great turn-based strategy experience on the field and  strong-yet-flawed project management off the field.

I really loved my time with Risk of Rain.
As with many games of this sort, it started out feeling really hard, and it got easier the longer I played.  It's a platformer where you shoot at the enemies spawning all over the place until they overwhelm you or you beat the game.  The difficulty ramps up over time, so in theory, you're balancing on a fence between slowing down to become more powerful and speeding up to keep the enemies more managable.
In practice, the player power curve continues to climb, while the game difficulty hits a peak.  If you can survive long enough , the game actually becomes trivial.  It's crazy fun, though, thumping a game that was casually slapping you down only a number of hours before.
For me, there is only one downside to Risk of Rain, and it's that the game's internal achievement system doesn't always work.  Spending a while to get an achievement only to have it not recognized (repeatedly) gets really old and takes some of the replayability out of this game for me.  I've had fun.  And now I'm done.  Totally worth the $.

In XCOM: Enemy Unknown players are tasked with running a military base who's sole purpose is to defend the Earth from alien attacks. The base view is presented in an ant farm style, which allows you to explore the structure of your base as though it is a living system. Unfortunately in this iteration of XCOM satellite uplinks/nexus are so vital to your success (especially on harder difficulties) that you are forced into a fairly standard base makeup. If you don't focus on getting your satellites up, you will almost certainly lose.
The main focus of the game is the battles, which on the whole are interesting and tense. Cover is vital during tactical battles, and if you do not use appropriate cover on harder difficulties you will quickly lose your valuable soldiers as often times taking one hit means death. Forcing yourself to use Iron Man difficulty or otherwise not reloading your saves is almost certainly the most interesting to play the game and means that losing a soldier is permanent. But it's this chance of permanent loss that brings so much tension and excitement to the battles. There is nothing like the joy of nailing an alien on a 25% chance shot and save a squad member's life, or the sting that comes from missing a 97% shot you thought for sure was in the bag. Soldiers rank up from battles and learn more and more abilities as they do. Successfully completing missions and killing aliens you can recover their technology in order to research it and further improve your soldiers. The visual upgrades your soldiers get from new equipment is probably one of the most appealing aspects of the game. Seeing a loved soldier move up from standard gear to become a future soldier with glowing guns and sleek armor is fantastic.
Unfortunately in the battles the AI opponents do not follow the same rules as the player units until they are 'activated' by coming into field of view of your soldiers. Until they activate they are essentailly one 'unit' and will teleport around the battlefield (outside of your view usually) into positions of varying believability. For instance one time I cleared a building by killing all the sectoids within, and then my soliders heard a sound coming from the neighbouring building. As I stacked my soldiers up on the doors and prepared to breach the building they suddenly heard sounds behind them. I sent them back to the first building only to find more sectoids had teleported onto the ones that I just killed, and were no longer in the building my soldiers heard them in only two turns ago. Another case of this is when my rookie soldiers began to panic and hunker down, I once had a group of sectoids teleport in the middle of my soliders! They quickly took cover on every side of my soldiers and were flanking from so many angles that there was no chance success at all.
Another way in which the game 'cheats' is during some missions (usually 'council' missions like escorting VIPs or defusing bombs) aliens will simply drop in from the sky. They'll either drop in out of view, behind you, in perfect sniping positions, at your flank, at all of your flanks... in other words, pretty much anywhere. There is a pattern to when they drop in, but there is no warning, or rather the warning comes as they are dropping on top of you which kind of renders it useless.
While there are certainly some problems and questionable decisions in this reboot, overall it is a very worthy successor to the original. XCOM: Enemy Unknown kind of screws up the base building by railroading you into satellite focus, and the tactical battles by cheating the rules your soldiers are forced to follow. On the other hand they enhance the experience by allowing your soldiers to learn interesting abilities when they rank up, including some interesting equipment and enemy types, and just making the game much shinier and easier to play.
Overall it is clearly one of the most solid strategy games on Steam despite it's flaws. It is one of my favourites in my collection and I'm sure that will only be reinforced by Enemy Within.

XCOM:Enemy Unknown has quickly become one of my favorite turn-based strategy games in a while. It is incredibly fun and rewarding to build up a base as you see fit and equip soldiers with all kinds of weapons and armor as you give them orders in battle against alien invaders. The ability to customize your soldiers' names and appearances was a nice touch that can help make the game seem more personal or can be used to make it more silly. You are given a reasonable amount of freedom to deal with the alien threat however you choose. Do you choose to focus on researching armor for your soldiers first? Or do you want to focus on your interceptors? Maybe you want to spend your money on another satellite and forego building that Laser Rifle for the time being. The choice is yours. The recent expansion, XCOM: Enemy Within, added a number of new and extremely fun features including base invasions, mechanized soldiers, and genetically modified soldiers. These add a new level of depth that make the game even more fun. The replayability of the single player of this game is endless due to the various difficulties, Ironman Mode, and a number of modifiers Firaxis has included to alter the game slightly. That being said, the game isn't without flaws. There are a number of minor bugs specifically UI related. At times it is difficult to tell where your cursor is, especially on stages where there a number of different levels to the stage (like the roof of a building), which can lead to some frustrating situations when your soldiers end up going someplace you didn't want them to (especially in Ironman mode!). The RNG can be frustrating and feel unfair at times, but, hey, that's the nature of RNG, isn't it? Overall, the game is absolutely terrific and is a must-buy for anyone into sci-fi and/or turn-based strategy games! 9/10.

Cyberpunk is a genre as much built on the atmosphere as it is on the technology. Everyone has that formative memory of the giant advertisements and smog-belching smokestacks in Blade Runner, Some games make the mistake of keeping the slums out of the cyberpunk, but Shadowrun Returns has the formula down just right: "high tech, low life." The game is a fun return to an earlier era for me, given my experience with the tabletop game - but the experience is fluid and accurate, reminding me of so many times spent around a table being suspicious about your Fixer or the latest contact you made.
The gameplay can be somewhat halting and awkward at times - a concession to make in order to accommodate the system itself, of course - but it doesn't diminish the enjoyment of this authentic cyberpunk game. Combat is strategic, if somewhat sparse on detail, and emphasises the differences in roles within the party itself. The decking is sadly quite anaemic compared to the tabletop world, a blue-gridlines re-creation of the combat systems, with Agents standing in for Spirits, and spells replaced with Decker attacks. Nonetheless, it rounds out the flavour of the game well.
If you're looking for an engaging Cyberpunk story, with a dash of magic and plenty of political intrigue and conspiracy, I highly recommend Shadowrun Returns.

One of the best games I've ever played.  The depth of micromanagement and tactics possible in such a simple format is incredible, and the game is as far as I can tell bug-free.  One of the few games in my vast collection that I cared enough about to get every single achievement.  Many have complained about the oppressiveness of the random number generator, and there is no question the game can be brutal, but if you take the time to learn the game mechanics, there are many deadly situations which are avoidable, and there are many strategies available to improve your chances in various ways.
The game seems so simple on the surface, but this is deception.  Many of the game's mechanics are emergent and overlap with eachother in surprising and unexpected ways, which can be confusing in the beginning.  Things will happen and you won't understand why, or you will think you understand what happened and it was lame, but actually you missed something important.  Emergent problem-solving and micro-management is a major part of FTL, and a critical path to success.
Here's an example: what is the best way to deal with a fire on your ship?  That's easy!  Vent the room into space!  Well, what if your oxygen system is also offline?  Venting will use up a bunch of your ship's critical remaining atmosphere, and your crew probably need oxygen to survive long enough to repair.  Ok, so sent a crew member to manually put out the fire.  What if your crew are injured and won't survive being on fire long enough to put it out?  Send them to the healing room first!  What if there are boarders who are attacking another critical system on your ship?  What if there is an ion storm while all this is going on?  And don't forget about the enemy ship attacking you!
It turns out that these sorts of complex situations (and there are a pile of them) can potentially be dealt with in many ways.  Maybe you have a System Repair Drone, so it can put out the fire AND fix your oxygen room while you deal with the boarders.  Maybe you have the Fire Suppression augment.  Maybe you can shoot the room with a Healing Burst bomb to heal your crew so they can live long enough to put out the fire.  Maybe your crew are Rockmen so they are immune to fire, or maybe they are Lanius so they are immune to the vacuum of space.  Maybe you have upgraded blast doors so the fire can't spread out of the room and will eventually burn itself out.   Maybe the fire is in the Medbay, so as long as you get there fast before the room becomes disabled, your crew will get healed faster than they will take damage putting out the fire.  Or maybe you can just put all your crew in the Medbay and vent the rest, probably making it easier to kill the boarders while simultaneously helping put out the fire and heal your crew.  It will be a little tricky to repair the oxygen room with no oxygen in it, but you can deal with that after the fire's out!  Maybe you have a Clone Bay instead of the Medbay, so letting your crew die putting out the fire is fine, cuz they will respawn.  Maybe you don't have any of that, and desperately throw all your crew into the room at once and put it out just in time before they die.  Or maybe, you just say screw it and ignore the fire for now because you have other more important issues to deal with.  Knowing that all these things can happen makes it so much more delicious to weigh whether to spend your limited resources on a particular thing in the store that may mitigate them.
The number of complex problems and adventures in solving them that you can have in this little spaceship simulator are extensive.  If you put the time in, victory is super rewarding.

Dead Space shamelessly rips off of far greater games, and oftentimes fails to live up to the games it so desperately tries to imitate. That being said, Dead Space is redeemed by its fantastic combat, pacing, and production values. Overall, Dead Space is a solid title that deserves to be bought when on sale.
The major negatives that drag Dead Space down are all tied to its derivative nature. Dead Space attempts to have non-linear metroidvania-style level design, most likely due to classics such as System Shock 2.  Unfortunately, Dead Space does a generally poor job at it. In System Shock 2, the levels were built open for a reason; the Von Braun was built to imitate a lived in space. People who have played System Shock 2 will clearly remember how the decks were divided into sleeping quarters, marketplaces, cargo bays, and other sections that fit together in a plausible way. Dead Space's levels, however, are extremely hublike and repetitive in nature. The areas have no sense of practicality at all, often being a string of bland metal hallways, connecting rooms that are filled with decorative and pointless machinery. Speaking of which, the game's is graphically strong, but aesthetically lacking.  It really feels like the designers based the ship's design off the grungiest parts of Alien and Event Horizon, and the monsters off of the goriest segments of The Thing. The unfortunate part is the lack of discipline involved; the designers simply spammed these incredibly derivative visual designs over everything, but seemed to forget that the goriest parts of The Thing were only scary because they happened sparingly and unexpectedly, and the darker segments of Alien and Event Horizon were only atmospherically suffocating because of the way they contrasted against otherwise sterile environments. And of course, the combat itself does suffer slightly, as it sometimes leans too heavily on classic survival horror titles such as Resident Evil. It can arbitrarily try to make itself clunky, which isn't effective at raising tension, and is only frustrating when paired with the mouse and keyboard.
The amazing thing about Dead Space's core mechanics is how they manage to redeem the rest of the experience. Blasting limbs off of enemies is viscerally satisfying, and the major drawbacks of the game feel extraneous to the core experience, which is, once again, fantastic. There aren't that many types of enemy, but each and every one requres a different set of tactics to take down, meaning that the player will constantly have to adapt to mixed hordes of undead. While the game is not nearly as scary as, say, Amnesia or Silent Hill, there is always the tension that comes with being startled or overwhelmed by enemies, and the extra shot of adrenaline is definitely welcome.
Overall, Dead Space is a solid 6/10, and deserves to be picked up on sale, along with the vastly superior sequel that refined and nearly perfected the formula.
