A classic example of atmospheric horror that will, surely, stand the test of time and remain as one of the best horror games,  and one of the best sci-fi games, I've ever played. I have a lot to talk about for this one kiddies, so grab some popcorn or something. I won't spoil anything for you either, so don't worry about that, if you haven't beaten the game yet
SOUND:
____
First and foremost: One of the most important pieces of any horror game is effective sound design. I didn't notice it as much on my first playthrough, sadly, because I only played in Stereo, but I went back recently and replayed the whole game in Surround Sound, high volume, with headphones, and oh boy, did I have a lot of pants to replace. Players aren't going to jump if a group of Necormorphs ambush them while the Betty Hill theme is playing in the background, likewise, the whispers you can hear throughout the ship wouldn't be as effective if they were accompanied by a vuvuzuela. In that sense, this game exceeds all expectations. They use just the right sound, every click, inhuman gurgle, and automated announcement falls so perfectly into place that you'll surely be looking over your shoulder.
Again, to experience this, play at high volume with surround sound headphones. I guarantee you, the difference in fear is like night and day. On my first playthrough with just stereo, that I did years ago, I didn't even flinch once at any scares, on my most recent playthrough, with surround sound, I cried at least five times.
The soundtrack is scary enough that even listening to it out of the game makes me feel like I should be on edge, looking over my shoulder. Beautiful composition, that fits perfectly with the world established by the game.
The sound aspect of Dead Space scores a 10/10 from me. Suberb job, every audio-design student should play this at least once to see how much of an effect using sound correctly can have on a person's experience. It's the difference between confidently strolling down a corridor and hesitantly walking down it, moving your legs oddly as your legs are soaked in fear-urine.
____
GRAPHICS:
___
By graphics, I don't mean 'oh look how high-definition this texture is!", I feel like people put too high of a value on that. A game can have 1080p textures and still look like digital vomit. No, what I mean is how appealing a game looks, the over-all design and how it flows together, immersing you.
Dead Space's graphics are as good as the sound: They make you paranoid, even. The subtle way the gray hallways seem to endlessly blur together, mixed with the scratching of something following you, will make most people, myself included, feel intensely claustrophobic.
It's beautiful how every texture, every object, seems to flow into eachother, all of them playing into the theme that 'I really, REALLY shouldn't be here". From the uncanny way the monsters still retain 'just' enough of their human appearance, to the way certain vents blend into the floor so you can't tell a monster may pop out, to the way the lighting may be just dim enough you dread the idea something may pop out, Dead Space has got you covered.
The Ishimura feels like a real ship, every deck feels just unique enough, yet consistent enough you can tell it's part of the same ship. It serves to further create an atmosphere of tension and loneliness.
Dead Space's graphics get a 10/10.
____
GAMEPLAY:
____
Dead Space's gameplay is superb, but not a 'perfect' experience by any means. There are both pros and cons to the resource management. While at times it can correctly make situations more tense, at other times it just raises my blood pressure and makes me want to punch my monitor.
It's a mixed bag as far as resource management goes, while the combat remains fairly standard. It's a point, click, you're dead kind of deal, with very little variation between the best ways to dispatch monsters.
There isn't much to say about the gameplay, it's average. 7/10.
___
STORY (No Spoilers: Don't worry)
___
I'm going to be vague here to avoid spoiling anything, but the story of Dead Space is an emotional rollercoaster, and I craved more, and more as time went on. I was truly interested in fully understanding what went on on the Ishimura, and learning all I could about the crew who manned her. Furthermore, seeing how the characters interacted actually played out quite nicely, and their treatment of eachother was rather realistic. I myself have seen work environments where people act like that in real life, so it was refreshing to see actual human-like characters.
The mystery, suspense, and all out dread is flawless. It has an odd balance where not knowing what's happening is horrifying, but understanding exactly what's happening is JUST AS SCARY. It's a weird trait that I don't see too often in horror games anymore. Most of the time, when you learn the mechanics behind the monsters in a horror game, their motives, their origins, it removes some fear, it grounds them into a Earthly point of view where you can try to understand. But in Dead Space, it's like the more you understand the more otherworldly your situation truly seems. It'll keep you on the edge of your seat. This is a game where you HAVE to read all the text logs and listen to the audio-logs, or else you'll miss a big chunk of the experience, and believe me when I say all of the video/audio/text logs are written well enough that they're juicy and will leave you pondering them.
Dead Space has one of my favorite game universes of all time, and for that the story gets a 10/10.
___
OVERALL:
___
Overall, Dead Space is a stellar (Heh, see what I did there?) example of a truly genius execution of the decades old concept of being stranded in space with monsters all around. May Dead Space long live as an example to both the sci-fi and horror game developer and player communities as an example of when things are done right.
For decades to come, I imagine Dead Space will still stand as one of the best horror games ever made, and THE best horror game franchise that EA's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t marketing ever ruined.

This game has so much love dumped into it day in and day out. The developers are passionate and I've never had more respect for a game developer. Killing Floor 2 is everything Left 4 Dead claims to be and it isn't finished yet. To start, the beauty of shooting, slicing, stabbing, bludgeoning, burning, freezing, electrocuting, and blowing up the zeds is a gaming marvel to experience. The 'gib' animations and diversity for every attack is incredible even after 150 hours I still find myself seeing zeds die in brutal/funny above all satisfying ways. Every word I used are literal features in the game and provide buckets of gorey action filled violence that feel stimulating when you add in gaining xp towards whatever class you're playing. The max level for every class is 25 but personally I think for an aesthetic purpose they should remove the cap so you could just keep leveling up but unless you play one class only it takes a very respectable amount of time to level up and gives off that "grind" feel even if the game itself is very linear it's a nice reward for playing. Along the rewards for xp like new perks, at the end of each game you have a chance to be dropped crates/weapon skins similar to csgo. The game has a micro-economy with really awesome items like character cosmetics, weapon skins or a rare variation of either. The characters are all very cool, diverse, silly, have a bit of dialogue, maybe even a lot but at times i wish they'd add in more voice lines because "looks like a friday night kebab... just" gets old after a while. The boss battles are very linear, straight forward, and what I like is strategy can be applied to it, but the style of game being a violent shoot everything game you still have that option. Battles are hard, but winning them is satisfactory and the developers constantly are working on how to improve things. This is an internet opinion but I made all the points I could from my perspective. If you like violent nonstop action full of swearing, blood, bullets, and death get it. It's a game that should be regarded how L4D is, and once they roll out objective mode (in the works at the time of this review?) it'll be the go to 'zombie' shooter.

The new XCOM is missing some of the things that made the original SO awesome. That's true. But, after an initial moment of Disappoint, I've come to recognise it's a really fantastic game—a very, very worthy reboot that is the "Batman Begins" of the XCOM story...even if that does sadly bring with it the XCOM version of "the Batman voice".
It's clear Firaxis asked the question at every turn: "How can we streamline this?" Yes, in some cases, this has resulted in lowering the bar of the tactical and strategic games—there's no escaping that (most evident in the scale of the tactical maps and the way the game channels you toward the action); but it's also resulted in a much faster, arguably more engaging game that I can see appealing to a broader community than just the hardcore strategy fans (like me) who loved the intricate challenge of the original game. I can even see the FPS action-set, they who usually play games like Call of Duty of Counter-Strike only, enjoying XCOM a lot—the appeal is that strong. 
As an aside, if you're a fan of tabletop games like Warhammer 40,000, I think you'll love XCOM's approach to the tactical game, as it has much in common with WH40K—especially once you hit the multiplayer with the army-building.
Subjective Assessment: 9/10

To this day, Dead Space is still one of the most entertaining survival-horror games I've ever played.
You start your carnage-fueled journey on a misson to report the findings of a deep space mining ship called the USG Ishimura (aka, HELL INCARANATE). You play as Isaac Clarke, an everyday ship systems engineer, as a seemingly-routine repair mission becomes a struggle for survival. Clarke originally chose the mission to make contact with his girlfriend who is also stationed on the damaged vessel. However, the least I say about her, the better. The plot closely resembles classic sci-fi horror movies and has a very errie, claustrophobic feeling to it; making all the more intense compared to your average cinematic game.
One of the best ways to sum up why this game is miles ahead of it's (past and even current) competition is the way Isaac uses his weaponary. The game is centered on a mining vessel in outer space and obviously that means not a lot of guns are gonna be on the ship. So, because of this, many weapons are "improvised heavy-tools" like Isaac's weapon of choice, the 211-V Plasma Cutter, a tool designed to be used in mining operations and surgical applicaions. But, in many ways, this actually makes you a very formable opponent.
The varible creatures you encounter in the game, called Necromorphs, are mutated and reanimated corpses, reshaped into horrific new forms. Think a zombie crossed with xenomorph and the alien from The Thing. YEAH...... but, worry not. They have a weakness, coming back to your weaonary. The only quick and effective way to kill the creatures is to literally chop them to pieces by removing the head, arms, legs, and other appendages until the creature is destroyed. Do I have your attention now?
I know this review is actually kind of short and disjointed but this is ONLY because telling more will only ruin your experience. I sank at least 40+ hours completing trophies and new game plus modes on the PS3. This is great game for completionists. Trust me, if you've been looking for a fun, scary game to really leave a mark; this is it. So grab some friends, pop some popcorn and give it a try!!!

If you're a fan of the old-school turn-based games, you'll enjoy this one.  If you're a fan of coorporate run futuristic dystopias, you'll enjoy this game.  If you're a fan of the table-top game that this is based on, you'll enjoy this game.
The strongest point of this game is it's story.  The writing is fantastic and the world is immersive.  Walking into this world knowing almost nothing about it, the game gives you plenty of story to build off of.  Each of the characters feel like people and even the slang used in the game that's unique to the world is easy to understand, even for someone who has never came into contact with it before.
The artwork for the game is superb.  The game combines 3-D and 2-D elements in the form of painted portraits for most NPCs and the 3-D element of game play.  The world itself isn't very interactable, but it isn't necessary.
The game play can get very static very fast, especially with combat.  Once you figure out that the AI is going to react certain ways and the trick to not getting your face blown off, it can get dull quickly.  It's absolutely worth finishing the game, however, as the story is fantastic.
If you're a fan of Baulder's Gate, this game will remind you of it in its play style.

It's been a while since I last played a classic, turn-based RPG - and when I say a while, I mean the likes of Forgotten Isles. So picking up this game was quite refreshing for me since most titles nowadays are all high energy ball-busting action. It would also be right to say that I don't have past references to any other Shadowrun titles, so my impressions here are purely stand-alone.
Putting it simply - I'm quite impressed. Let me get to some of the simple points that make this title a gem:
Writing: The narrative is well written albeit some "street" language that sometimes sticks out badly. The sights and sounds (as though these were not enough) of apocalyptic Seattle is well supported by transition build ups and some witty dialogue.
Role-playing Mechanics: The game mechanics builds its own simple character customization. You only really get to build your main protagonist via a simple characteristics points system. You simply have to progress through the story to earn your points and design a character from a set number of characteristics. The game builds on several archetypes but does not restrict a player into any cookie-cutter format. (Check out the Nephilim Network to get some quirky combination inspirations.)
Setting: Explore an apocalyptic Seattle teeming with classic RPG lore races, armed to the teeth with Guns, Cybernetics and Magic. Timelessness is often a great appeal to any story, and this title just has the right mix.
Art and Music: While being somewhat leaning towards cartoon-like, the world of Shadowrun Returns is beautifully crafted. The city sprawls are rich in detail. On the one hand you will be running around streets blaring with neon signs and shop fronts. But on another, you get to traverse dark alleys, dimly lit halls of medical facilities and cult complexes to uncover the mystery that drives the campaign. This is supported by pulses of techno music transitioning into eerie fantasy sequences.
Of course the game is not without its faults. While dialogue and the story telling are well written, character focus seems to be lacking since most often than not you will be running around the sprawl with game-generated Shadow Runners. True, there are some key NPCs that you get to interact with but the times can be very short and too far in between for such a short campaign.
Inventory system may need a bit of a re-work but nothing too major to murder the experience.
I've read some concerns about saving games but I've hardly found it an issue - so maybe they have fixed this one already. My only suggestion really right now is you might want to try starting a game at a much higher difficulty level. I'm currently running with a Decker at the moment in Normal setting, and it seems like a cake walk - what more if you go for the more heavy hitting classes?
By no means is the game perfect - it has a few rough edges but it definitely delivers the merchandise well. If you feel like slowing down a bit, go out of the usual, this read & click title might do the thing for you.

A quick note - I've only played Dragonfall, and have not yet touched the original campaign.
This was a really well-done narrative game, with a surprisingly fun tactical component, reminiscent of x-com (and the upcoming Wasteland 2).  While linear, the game did a stellar job of making it not feel linear.  The narrative was rather strong, and kept me interested the entirety of the way through.  The author's of the game clearly knew the setting well (as one would hope with the creator of the setting being on the team), and knew what elements worked well and wouldn't work well in the world.
There are some caveots: there were some bugs which cropped up periodically, that if I hadn't been regularly saving would have forced me to restart the mission.  (On the other hand, at least this game would let you restart the mission without too much fuss).  There were some instances of some items dissapearing permanently if I didn't pick them up.  Another big issue is the lack of ability to change my party member's gear, or to even control them outside of combat.
Overall, this is one of the strongest narrative games I have played in a long while.  Even some annoyances (and the inability to give weapons I find to party members is a big one for me) were unable to dissuade me from finishing the game.  I can't stop talking about this game to my friends, and perhaps you won't be able to either.

Trading with them is like striking a deal with Rick Harrison from Pawn Stars: you can't win. They will denounce you for no reason, but just five turns later they want to be friends. They propose to ban one of your luxury recources in the next World Congress session, and a few turns later they want to trade for the exact thing they want to ban. Get it when it's on sale (which is pretty often nowadays), it really is worth the money

This has been the most interesting gaming experience I've had for a while, mixing exploration with puzzle solving perfectly in the midst of an eerily tranquil atmosphere. The difficulty is pitched perfectly with challenges that feel rewarding to solve, with hints that are cryptic, but not so obscure that they aren't unhelpful. I found most puzzles that seemed "unsolvable" were resolved after stepping back and returning later with a new approach. Remembering what you have learnt before, but finding new ways to approach things is key here. It's a fantastic experience to encourage you to look at anything from a new perspective and genuinely feels rewarding to find a solution.
Definitely not for the impatient, but certainly a great experience for those who like exploration and challenging puzzles.

I didn't play the original Shadowrun back in the early nineties, so the game gets no retro love in this review. Shadowrun returns is a average cyberpunk and magic theme RPG. The main defect in the game is the vacuity of the gameworld comprised of the different interconnected areas. The game basically gives you only plot items to interact and the city locations are small.
True to the "pocket world" RPG approach the plot is your average RPG pipeline stuff. Shadowrun Returns was a pretty entertaining game, but Dragonfall takes it to another level. There are combat systems out there in the world of turn-based strategy games which are more sophisticated or "deeper" than Shadowrun 4.0's ruleset (as implemented here, anyway), but very few, if any, that are written as well as Dragonfall. In keeping with the original game, the combat is designed to be fast and exciting, but streamlined so that it doesn't get in the way of storytelling. Combat also isn't the end-all, be-all of accomplishing goals in Dragonfall. There are plenty of ways to deck or leverage your way out of a situation without entering combat mode, and they are just as satisfying--this isn't Warhammer 40K or Battletech, after all. Rather, it's a table-top RPG campaign that someone digitized, and it's pretty awesome.

I wanted to make this review short and sweet, but it's hard to stop writing, even when excluding facts that could potentially contaminate an exceptionally well thought-out gaming experience. There's just so much to say. Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure here.
Before I really get into the review, you should know the background of how this game was reviewed. Valve did not want to send out copies of their game (for fairly obvious reasons) before it was released to the public. In order to play the game, I, and several of my colleagues throughout the industry, took a trip up to Seattle to visit Valve in order to have some private time with the title. I was given a little room to myself where I could close the door, turn off the lights, click my little red slippers, and pretend that I was sitting at home. It worked for the most part, largely because I was so engrossed with the game that when I came out of my trance I often had to take a moment to get my bearings. Obviously, Valve was happy to bring me into a controlled environment for ideal playing conditions.
The system that I played the game on had these specs:
•ASUS P4C800-E dlx motherboard
•Intel P4 3.2GHz CPU
•2.0GB DDR400 dual-channel RAM
•Radeon 9800PRO 128MB video
•Creative Audigy 2 ZS sound
•Western Digital 160GB SATA HD
Obviously, since we were only allowed to play the game at Valve, this is the only system that we've had the chance to play with. That said, at 1280 resolution, the game ran flawlessly, even in the most extreme environments with tons of geometry and lots of objects moving around, both with and without AI. The Source engine is an impressive piece of software from the outside looking in. There's a large chance my brain would melt like Velveeta in a microwave should someone try to explain its inner workings.
Video Review The long-awaited release of Half-Life 2 is finally here. Valve has spent years perfecting this sequel to one of the most respected first-person shooters ever. Has the wait been worth it? Tune into this in-depth video review, which includes tons of sweet new direct-feed. What are you waiting for? Download this while you read the rest of the text review.

What's particularly impressive about the game running so well is that it does so without compromising any part of gameplay or design. Environments are complex, colorful, and highly detailed; AI is certainly impressive in that NPCs work as teams, flank, react to sound and movement, and then engage with lifelike aggression. But like I said, we're going to have to wait and see what the game runs like on a more standard system after it's released. Therefore, you can look for an additional supplement to this review about how the game runs on lower-end systems after we've had the chance to check.

The other problem with reviewing the game up at Valve is the simple fact that we couldn't test out Steam and how well the product registration system necessary to playing Half-Life 2works. I'm not exceedingly happy about the forced registration even if it is understandable in today's climate of highly pirated games, though I can't say I believe this will stop ultra-determined hackers from cracking the game regardless.
Still, no matter what you think of Valve's business policies, Half-Life 2 is a "must buy" game. If you're a fan of the series, that was already obvious. Heck, if you're a PC gamer chances are you're going to get it at some point anyway. But if you're new or skeptical of the genre and want to see a prime example of the power and excitement of a first-person shooter, this is it. And it begins with the continuation of a story. Wake Up and Smell the Ashes...
Last time we left Gordon Freeman, the unlikely scientist-hero from the first Half-Life, he was traveling. Yes, just traveling. The mystery was where he was traveling to and why all of the incidents at Black Mesa had happened (not to mention why the game was rife with so many horrific jumping puzzles towards the end). Half-Life 2 begins with Gordon arriving via train with the G-Man teasing his mind with sickly whispers of warning. The last stop of the arriving train is City 17, a bastion of the alien Combine forces, yet another mystery themselves.
For the rest of the story, you'll have to play the game yourself. I'm absolutely dedicated to getting through this review with your chance at an untarnished gaming experience intact. That means no spoilers. Suffice to say, there are lots of twists to curl your brain along the way, some a bit more predictable than others, but all welcome and interesting.
While the writing and plot points will act as fly paper to your attention, the real winner here is the way the story is presented. Through the eyes of Gordon Freeman, you'll experience roughly 17-20 hours of consciousness which tests your senses and captures your mind. The simplicity and style with which this story is presented are perhaps the most graceful maneuvers of the many that Valve has carried out. From the moment you take your first steps off of that train and into the station at City 17, you'll begin to be tutored in the ways of this bizarre eastern European city. Public service announcements, private conversations, and the actions of characters around you, whether part of the Combine or simply waylaid citizens, create a stifling and threatening feeling that City 17 has become some sort of elaborate prison preaching the chance for freedom and opportunity without choice or desire.
While I was ultimately left a little bit frustrated by the open-endedness, the journey to get to the end of the story was assuredly interesting and opened up the doors to many more possibilities. It's easy to start speculating about this or that, just don't let it drive you nuts. The deeper you get, the darker and more intriguing it becomes until you get to the end... which you'll have to see for yourself.

This frightening vision of the future is only made stronger by a stunning visual style that manages to express artistic vision while coming as close to reality as I've seen in my decades of playing video games. One of the most stunning moments comes with the first steps out from the train station and into the city proper. It's the wild realization of a fantastic dream. The Combine citadel looms on the horizon as a testament to their power, authority, and technological capabilities. It's both impressive and oppressive at the same time, serving its purpose with more presence than an army of a Combine soldiers and Striders ever could.
Light plays a significant role in the beauty of Half-Life 2, not only because of its quality, but because of the way that it tracks the passage of time. Each passing level brings the sun down a bit more until you're encased in an eerie canopy of unease at just the right moment in the game. Shadowrun: Returns and its Expansion/DLC Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a turn-based tactical RPG game created by a studio called Harebrained Schemes out of Seattle, WA. The base game Shadowrun: Returns was released on Steam on July 25th, 2013, and the DLC Shadowrun: Dragonfall was released on February 27th, 2014.
For those not familiar with the Shadowrun universe, it is based on a cyber-punk futuristic planet Earth. It is the 2050’s. The world is run by enormous, greedy corporations who will stop at nothing to acquire power. The twist is that a few decades earlier (around our current modern-day) magic returned to our world. With it came elves, dwarves, trolls, ogres, and other magical creatures.
Shadowrunners are for-hire mercenaries who will do just about any job as long as there is money to be made. Whether it is stealing secrets from a corporate rival, working as security to protect those secrets, or taking out individuals that stand in their way of power, they are hired by big corporations to do their “dirty work”. They work in the seedy underbelly of this corporate society and live and survive in the shadows.
I discovered Shadowrun when I was browsing around Steam looking for something new to play. Dragonfall was pretty highly recommended, and after reading up a bit on it I thought it sounded like something I would enjoy. I started it up and decided to start from the beginning and play through the original campaign. I was immediately sucked in to the story. I just had to keep playing, if for no reason other than to find out how the story turned out!
The story for each of the campaigns is probably the best feature of the game. I don’t think I’ve been this captivated by a video game’s story since Final Fantasy VII! Even though there are no video cut scenes and no voice overs, the story is told VERY well.
The story is progressed by speaking with various NPCs in the game world. When you speak to them you are given a number of choices as to how you want to respond in the conversation. There are a few places in the game where the dialogue options you choose will change the sequence of events to complete the mission. There isn’t a LOT of these places, but they are there. Also some dialogue options may not be available to you because of certain conditions. For example, if your Strength stat is high you may be able to bully that gang leader into giving you the key you need to progress. But, if you lack strength and are more intelligent, you may have to use brains over brawn to get what you need. There is also a feature called “Etiquette”. The game describes etiquette as “knowing how to behave in various social situations”. In-game this means you will get certain dialogue options based on what etiquette you choose when you create your character. In the example above, if my character has the “Gang” etiquette I may have a dialogue option when talking to the gang leader that will open up different options for completing the mission.
Character progression is pretty straight-forward. When you create your character there are a few class archetypes that you can choose from. This gives you a basic set of skills to start from. As you progress you will acquire more skill points that you can spend on any skill you want. If you want to spend your skill points to be a shotgun-wielding mage you can, or if you want to specialize in being an uber “Decker” (Shadowrun’s version of a computer hacker) you can do that too. While skill points come pretty easy, it’s still a good idea to specialize in one or two areas. The campaign isn’t long enough for you to get enough skill points to max out everything.
The skills were all pretty well explained right in game. All of your teammates and other Shadowrunners that you can hire all have their own set of skills and abilities. So if you are a shotgun-wielding mage you can hire a teammate that has the hacking skills you need for a mission. I kind of like this system. It lets you build your character however you like and then you can complement your skills with those of the shadowrunners you run with.
From the very beginning I felt like the game environment and the atmosphere were very well done. I felt like I was running around in the movie Blade Runner! Everything was futuristic, yet familiar. The characters I interacted with and their portraits definitely captured the cyberpunk feel. Each character you encounter has their own personality and they are very unique. I thought the music was great too, even if there wasn’t a lot of variety. I thought it fit well with the theme of the game.
The tactical combat style is what attracted me to the game in the first place. I found the combat to be a lot of fun, and in some places it was VERY challenging. For most missions you have your player character and three other Shadowrunners to make up your team.
When you are walking around the map everything is in real time. But, as soon as combat starts, it switches to turn-based tactical mode. Every member of your team has a set number of “Action Points” (AP) that you can spend each turn. Firing your weapon or using a special ability may cost an AP point. Moving to a different location with better cover may cost another. Casting that healing spell or reloading your rifle will cost another. This is where the tactical part comes in. You have to decide what you want each member of your team to do each round. Do you want to focus fire and finish off one enemy at a time, or do you spread out and burn them all down at once? You also have to be careful that you don’t leave yourself pinned down somewhere without enough AP to use that medkit to keep you alive in the fight. Once you spend all your AP for that turn, the computer will play the turn of your enemies. Once they are done it is your turn to spend your AP again. Add in that each weapon type has a different range and friendly-fire can be hazardous to your teammates, it makes combat VERY interesting.
The Good, The Bad, and the Ugly
As a whole I very much enjoyed Shadworun: Returns and Shadowrun: Dragonfall. The story lines for BOTH campaigns are among the best I’ve ever seen in a video game. The first campaign is a BIT slow to start but it’s only so at the beginning. Combat is a lot of fun and can be pretty challenging at times. There were a few missions I had to play through a couple of different times with different strategies before I was victorious.
I really enjoyed the skill system as well. It was easy to understand and easy to use. I didn’t feel like I needed to go online and read hundreds of forum posts to learn what the best build for my character would be. I could just pick a couple of skills I wanted to learn that were fun for me and go with it and be successful.
The only bad worth mentioning is the length of the campaigns. My total play time on Steam is 48 hours, and that was running all the way through both campaigns. I’m sure I’m a lot slower that a lot of other people. However, considering the inexpensive price of the game and the fact that there is a lot of player generated content on the Steam Workshop, there is a lot of replayability here. Hopefully they will also be releasing more DLC in the future.
About the only “ugly” I can say about the game is a couple of buggy missions I encountered. In one mission there was an event that didn’t trigger properly and I was unable to continue because a door would not unlock. I had to replay that mission one or two times before it finally triggered properly and I could advance.
Also, some earlier reviews criticized Shadowrun: Returns’ save system. At release you could only save at certain checkpoints. This is no longer the case. I’m not sure if it was with the release of Dragonfall or if it was before that, but they changed the game so you can now save anywhere.

Played the main campaign awhile ago and liked it well enough.  About 10 hours of gameplay.  I never played the tabletop version and so I'm no expert as to how closely the game remained tied to the specifics of that world, but the environment felt genuine and created a very interesting and captivating setting for the story.
Main campaign is alright.  Game's not retail price and it shows.  UI and movement/cover systems are a little wonky.  Tactical combat system is a bit simplistic, as are the items and inventory management.  Everything feels just a bit... insubstantial.  Still, as I said before, the environment is interesting.  Decent music reminiscent of the old top-down Fallout games.  Game suffers from some bugs, primarily related to transition triggers (I.E. When something becomes searchable, or when an NPC shifts from neutral to enemy due to an event, things tend to go a bit off-kilter at times).  Also the original campaign suffers from a lack of a save system in favor of an uncontrollable checkpoint system that can result in some frustrating losses of progress.  You can see why they went this route -- trying to get you to just roll with the punches and accept imperfect outcomes -- but for perfectionists like me, that tends to be more irritating than provocative.
Regarding the Dragonfall DLC, there are some significant improvements.  NPC characters are developed with greater depth and are generally more interesting and likeable.  Story feels more complex as well, and all of the little nuggets of Shadowrun lore strewn about are a welcome help to the immersion factor.  It is DLC though, meaning that most of the fundamental annoyances (transition trigger bugs, lag when controlling friendly NPCs not originally part of the party, Slightly sticky UI design, simplistic combat/inventory management and tactical combat system) are all still present.  Still, neither the main game nor the DLC are full retail price, so one gets what one pays for.  They did put in a quicksave function which, while not perfectly implemented, does get the job done.  Being able to save at will reduces the amount of progress you lose on the occasional progress-ending bug you may encounter.
DLC is about 18-20 hours gameplay (granted I did a few things over for better outcomes).  The niggling complaints above aside, I really enjoyed it.  Good story, good NPC characters, good immersion level, and decent length for the cost.
I guess my biggest complaint is that this isn't a AAA full retail title.  I would have liked to see a cleaner UI, a more complex tactical combat system, and a longer campaign.  The story was so well-written and the base environment so rich and interesting that I would have happily paid more for the opportunity to spend more time there.  Looking forward to any future DLC they may release.

At the time of this writing, Hairbrained Studios have only released "Dead Man's Switch" and "Dragonfall", with the latter a significantly stronger module than the former. Both are heavily combat-based, and while careful positioning and action choices can tilt battles in your favor, the RNG can make sure that even if you do everything right, your team can still be wiped in a couple rounds due to keyboard-smashing bad luck (in this respect, the combat is very similar to X-COM: Enemy Unknown). But if you're getting an RPG like this, you're hopefully getting it knowing that luck is part of the game.
It's all very good fun, particularly on harder difficulties. Agonizing over how to build your character, whom to take on a mission, and how to position them each round should please old-school turn-based RPG purists. The story arcs and character depth are not really fantastic, but the game is built on going out and completing runs (usually by shooting/stabbing/blowing things up, with only occassional decking responsibilities).
Definite recommend, particularly if you've played the pencil-and-paper version.

X-Com Enemy Unknown is a rare type of game that only come's around once in awhile. It is gripping, crafty, and terrifying. An engrossing, deep turnbased combat game, married neatly with a real time strategic base mechanic makes this one of the standout titles of 2012.

X-Com is a successor of the classic X-com titles from the mid to late 90's. While this new title has been developed by a differrent company, Firaxis, they have managed to preserve what was so enthralling about X-Com and the alien threat. With a new engine,powered by Unreal Engine 3, Firaxis brought X-Com to a new generation with slick graphics and fresh gameplay.

X-Com has two main layers. The first is the "meat" of the game, which is the tactical combat. Players are tasked with squads between 4 to 6 elite soldiers, each with varying skills and abilities that are unlocked as they get kills and survive more missions. A range of custumizable options are in the game, such as changing their appearance or names, and choosing different skills as they become available. On the battlefield players are faced with the ever imposing alien threat, which is intelligent and ruthless. The aliens have many different species, which act as the classes. From the lowly sectoid to the fearsome muton, players will be constantly challenged with ever increasing numbers and powers. All the aliens feel very distinct, and the ai does avery good job of keeping players on their toes. They will use any advantage they can get,be it suppression and flanking, or simply ganging up on one man, and will remorselessly destroy the unprepared squad. Thankfully X-Com has a few tricks of their own. As players progress, new armour and weapons become available, such as the S.H.I.V, a mobile weapons platform that replaces a soldier in the field and can act as agressive mobile cover, or the skelton suit, which allows soldiers to use a grapple hook to reach elevated positions. Perfect for getting that sniper in for the kill. Late game will players will see even more advanced alien technologies be adapted for your soldiers use, and even delve in to phsycic abilities.

The second layer of X-Com is the base management. This is where players are tasked with monitering global panic, issuing promotions to vetrans, researching alien technologies, and contructing a fortified base from which to launch operations. It is here that all new weapons and tactics become available, so it is crucial to manage X-Com's limited resources wisely, as one mistake could leave you  without the proper weapons or technology to survive the increaing alien menace. As permadeath is in the game, players must strive to keep their soldiers equipped with the latest and greatest if they hope to achieve victory. Missions will occur at random and vary from seek and destroy, a timed bomb diffusal in which the player must find and diffuse bombs scattered around the map before an alotted amount of turns, to Vip escorts. Each mission takes place on a randomly chosen map, so no two playthroughs are the same.
X-Com Enemy Unknown is a a fantastic title that will challenge and entertain, and I highly recommend to all types of gamers.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown manages to flawlessly meld base-building with turn-based tactics, to keep you playing "one more mission" all through the night. Masterfully presents you with tough choices such as "Which country do you save from the big bad aliens?" and "Should I shoot these aliens with a rocket or fall back to a better position for next turn" and presents you with just enough information to figure out which one has the highest chance of success. While some people seem to dislike the fact that some core mechanics of the game are essentially random, I feel that this randomness is required: the art of XCOM is figuring out how to game the odds in your favor, and to deal with those cases where (inevitably) they turn against you.
Not everything is explained perfectly in the tutorial, but the basic concepts are simple to grasp through play. This makes the game fairly easy to pick up, and higher difficulty settings present a challenge even for veteran players. My only minor criticism is that the difficulty curve is a bit less than ideal: the game actually gets slightly easier towards the end. That said, you will know this is an awesome game when you spend 5 minutes planning your next turn, and then throwing your keyboard at the wall because that 95% shot misses.

This game captures the spirit of South Park really well, and perhaps more surprisingly, has legitimately interesting and fun mechanics. The combat is fun, out of combat is fun, the story is fun, and, of course, the characters are fun. It's entertaining enough that you can play while someone watches and they won't get bored (my girl sat through the whole damn thing). It's not very long though, which isn't so much a hit against it, as it was just the right length to pick up and beat in a weekend (along with all the side quests).
I will also say that it's not very challenging however. The pacing promises that you will always have more abilities than you'll really know what to do with, money and items come easily, and if you pay enough attention to the mechanics to have a specific build, you will steamroll most encounters (although the enemy variety may muck you up if you're too focused around one subset of mechanics).
If I had to gripe about anything, it would be the inventory which felt clunky, and was organized alphabetically rather than say by level (the name of an item doesn't really provide as much context as the level requirements).
Totally worth the sale price. Eagerly awaiting the sequel (or DLC xpac).

Shadowrun Returns is a game for those who enjoy old-school RPG's. Dragonfall DLC is a must have.
The games strengths are in good writing, rich world history and all in all beautiful artwork.
The world is beautifully detailed whether you're in the streets of Redmond Barrens, a luxurious corporate headquarter or busy market hub in Germany. I might not be the biggest fan of the "cartoony" style the designers went ahead with but all in all it works.
The portrait artwork is also beautifully done.
Dialogue and text is descriptive and good all through the games, lack of voice is the proper way to do an rpg when you have good writers.
While there are many things in the game that could have been done better, far better even, I cannot think of any major  flaws or issues in design.
Base game delivers an okay story and gameplay although it's lacking in many ways I still managed to get some 12 hours of gameplay from it and did not feel bad about getting the game but I did feel like it could have been done better and certainly it could have been bigger.
Dragonfall DLC is a whole different story however. In fact, I would say that Dragonfall is -the- reason to buy Shadowrun Returns.
Dragonfall provides you with a more classic Shadowrun feel, the storyline is excellent, the permanent companions have personalities and plenty of dialogue in and out of missions and even the local npc's are always worth talking to.
Dragonfall features more of the actual Shadowrun gigs, the game is full of choices to make, plot twists to uncover and provides far richer experience for all types of characters as all types of skills have more uses.
The Dragonfall DLC provided me with additional 18-20 hours of gameplay, far more than the base game does.
Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall dlc's only major problem is that it leaves me wanting for more. So much more.. I want a bigger game with more content!
Harebrained Schemes has a great basis set up, hopefully they will continue in the path of Dragonfall as it is obviously doing so many things right.

Shadowrun Returns is, as its name suggests a game based off of another. So for the fans of the SNES title "Shadowrun", this release was a hopeful return to one of the classics. The game had big shoes to fill due to its name alone. So the question was always going to be how well it met the high expectations placed on it.
The game captures the look and feel of the SNES Shadowrun extremely well. No one seems to shoot at you through windows anymore, and random enemy generation is gone, but neither of these make the game look or feel off the mark. The audio is also pretty well placed, and while the voice acting isn't the greatest, it doesn't feel out of place either.
So why am I not recommending the game, if it's done so well to capture the feel of the original? It is because that it doesn't go deeper than that. The introduction to the game is a little slow, with proper care being taken to introduce you to the characters. This gives you a reason to care about them, so it isn't a bad thing on its own. What is a bad thing is that if you play it long enough you become aware that this wasn't an introduction; it's how the game plays. Huge amounts of text, peppered with small and unsatisfying battles are the meat and potatoes of this.
So we've established that the game is highly story driven at the expense of combat, which isn't what I was looking for in a Shadowrun sequel, but isn't necessarily bad depending on how the story is told. The story however, doesn't manage to land on anything I cared about, so what ended up happening is I got a lot of text thrown my way, and I didn't really care about any of it.
The combat, when you get to it, is also different than you would expect it to be. It is no longer free form, but grid based, like Final Fantasy Tactics or XCOM. The combat controls are done well enough, but the battles themselves are so lacking in difficulty that it would be difficult to lose them, regardless of what you did. Grid based combat systems need to be challenging enough to require thinking and tactics, or they don't work. The grid based combat system in Shadowrun Returns does not work in this way, and oddly extends beyond combat. When you are exploring a zone that might have fights in it, you often start in the grid for seemingly no reason. XCOM does this too, but it just feels awkward here.
My overall impression is that Shadowrun Returns was really close to getting it right, and fell short. The majority of my play time on the game due to how close it came.  It really felt like I should be enjoying it like I enjoyed the original. For me, it never really stopped feeling like a slow build up to something that never comes.

Shadowrun Returns is my first venture into this universe, and after a ten hour campaign, I'm completely obsessed. If you are also new, but a little wary about dropping the money for this title, allow me to explain a little about the game...
SR is an isometric-style Rpg, set in a future-fantasy universe, where elves and dwarves wield shotguns and cast spells. Starting up the default campaign, Dead Man Switch, you create a character. Race, class and appearance are all up to you. Then, the developer, Harebrained Schemes drops you into a well-written and thoughtfully crafted story, presented in a text-based format - no voice acting here, and I think it's better for it, but that's personal preference. Dialog options are different depending on how you build your character and elicit different responses from NPCs, with charisma allowing you to sweet-talk, and etiquettes let you rub elbows with the many groups that populate Seattle.
You play a Shadowrunner, a type of mercenary, doing the dirty-work of multi-billion dollar corporations and aristocrats for cash. Gameplay is very reminiscent of the recent Xcom: Enemy Unknown. If you didn't like that, chances are you won't like this. Every turn, each combatant is given a certain number of moves, from moving to shooting and using items. It's very tactical and you could wind up dead if you don't think before you click. Several jobs you undertake have you bringing other Runners on to watch your back and take a cut of the pay, so you're almost never alone.
I found no hick-ups in the gameplay during my play-through. The specials and items are balanced well, meaning death is often the fault of the player's ill preparation. The game is fair, which is about all a gamer could ask for. Also available are game editors, allowing anyone to write their own stories and scenarios for others to enjoy. I haven't been able to try any out because there currently seems to be a bug that causes the ugc to be downloaded to the wrong files, making them difficult to locate.
Shadowrun Returns is a gem that I'm glad was funded. It's not for everyone, but if it sounds like it's up your alley, I urge you to pick it up.

Dying Light is Dead Island done right.
At first glance you will see many similarities between this game and dead island, such as the loot, the crafting, the weapons, but it takes that formula and cranks it up a notch.
There is a huge map, complete with fantastic visuals, to get around by mostly using parkour, running up walls and sprinting from rooftop to rooftop.  The large map means a lot of places to explore to find loot and weapons, as well as blueprints that will allow you to craft some amazing and bizarre weapons.  There is a full day and night cycle, day time being a relative breeze with slow ambling zombies that are easy to take down.  Night is dangerous, volatile infected are extremely fast and strong and hunt you down in packs, making sneaking at night essential.
The story is quite interesting, and can even be played with up to 4 friends, you can also invade your friends game as a powerful zombie and hunt them down.  There are also plenty of side quests that help you get money, loot, and skill points.  There are 3 different skill trees to improve by surviving, fighting, and using your parkour skills, each with a decent amount of skills to upgrade.
If your at all interested in these types of zombie games then I would say to definately give Dying Light a go.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a great, modern version of a cult-classic from the '90s. The earth is getting attacked by an alien invasion. The nations of the world found the XCOM to deal with the invaders - and you are the commander.
The gameplay is divided into two parts - the strategic base building game, were you deal with developing new weapons, deciding what countries to protect with satelite surveillance or shooting down UFOs. The other part is the tactic mode - you send a squad of 4-6 elite soldiers to deal with the invaders. Turn based you move carefully, kill some invaders and try to take prisoners for further interrogation. Your soldiers progress in an RPG like manner in four classes: Storm, Heavy, Support and Snipers. Be carefull who you move first - one wrong move can kill a soldier you invested hours in.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a game of decissions - do you buy a laser weapon or the better armor? When multiple cities get attacked at once - you have to decide which to defend, risking the other city and nation to get lost on you forever.
You are the only chance for earth to repel the invasion. Use it - and have fun in a game I already spend 50 hours in.

I love this game. The aesthetics are all around very pleasing. Even though it's in 8-bit graphics, the sound helps make it feel like you're stuck in a sci-fi adventure on an unknown and hostile planet. The difficulty of "normal" is not for the faint of heart, and for the most part you'll be screaming and yelling each time you die. But not because the game isn't fair (mostly), but because you feel like you haven't quite mastered skill sets of the 12 characters or quite picked up on which items work better together initially.
With each new playthrough you feel as though you get better and better, and you start to learn the mechanics of the game and how to use the terrain and its' features to your benefit. You start to wonder if you should use the statue one more time in hopes that it will give you a item but at a risk of not getting anything, or take a little extra time to search a little more for another chest, but at the expense of time, in which the game gets harder as time goes on.
This game is not without its faults though. Some of the platforming, particularly the rope climbing sections, are fustratingly difficult to pull off. Some gaps look as though they should be cleared with ease, but you are always 1 pixel short from making that successful jump. I appreciate the more difficult enemies with color pallete swaps, but I would also like to see a directory of what the colors mean or maybe have a tooltip above the health that describes the type of enemy you are hitting. This is isn't all of the faults, but the biggest at the moment and I'm sure most of the faults can be updated via with a patch.
Overall, this game is worth your time and money. It's hard, yet, addicting nature of that "one more run" to see how far you get taunts you in the back of your mind.

I wanted to make this review short and sweet, but it's hard to stop writing, even when excluding facts that could potentially contaminate an exceptionally well thought-out gaming experience. There's just so much to say. Half-Life 2 is, simply put, the best single-player shooter ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Half-Life 2 compared to other single player shooters. What Valve has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there is an excellent shooter here. Half-Life 2 doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of first-person shooters to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure here.
Before I really get into the review, you should know the background of how this game was reviewed. Valve did not want to send out copies of their game (for fairly obvious reasons) before it was released to the public. In order to play the game, I, and several of my colleagues throughout the industry, took a trip up to Seattle to visit Valve in order to have some private time with the title. I was given a little room to myself where I could close the door, turn off the lights, click my little red slippers, and pretend that I was sitting at home. It worked for the most part, largely because I was so engrossed with the game that when I came out of my trance I often had to take a moment to get my bearings. Obviously, Valve was happy to bring me into a controlled environment for ideal playing conditions.
The system that I played the game on had these specs:
•ASUS P4C800-E dlx motherboard
•Intel P4 3.2GHz CPU
•2.0GB DDR400 dual-channel RAM
•Radeon 9800PRO 128MB video
•Creative Audigy 2 ZS sound
•Western Digital 160GB SATA HD
Obviously, since we were only allowed to play the game at Valve, this is the only system that we've had the chance to play with. That said, at 1280 resolution, the game ran flawlessly, even in the most extreme environments with tons of geometry and lots of objects moving around, both with and without AI. The Source engine is an impressive piece of software from the outside looking in. There's a large chance my brain would melt like Velveeta in a microwave should someone try to explain its inner workings.
Video Review The long-awaited release of Half-Life 2 is finally here. Valve has spent years perfecting this sequel to one of the most respected first-person shooters ever. Has the wait been worth it? Tune into this in-depth video review, which includes tons of sweet new direct-feed. What are you waiting for? Download this while you read the rest of the text review.

What's particularly impressive about the game running so well is that it does so without compromising any part of gameplay or design. Environments are complex, colorful, and highly detailed; AI is certainly impressive in that NPCs work as teams, flank, react to sound and movement, and then engage with lifelike aggression. But like I said, we're going to have to wait and see what the game runs like on a more standard system after it's released. Therefore, you can look for an additional supplement to this review about how the game runs on lower-end systems after we've had the chance to check.

The other problem with reviewing the game up at Valve is the simple fact that we couldn't test out Steam and how well the product registration system necessary to playing Half-Life 2works. I'm not exceedingly happy about the forced registration even if it is understandable in today's climate of highly pirated games, though I can't say I believe this will stop ultra-determined hackers from cracking the game regardless.
Still, no matter what you think of Valve's business policies, Half-Life 2 is a "must buy" game. If you're a fan of the series, that was already obvious. Heck, if you're a PC gamer chances are you're going to get it at some point anyway. But if you're new or skeptical of the genre and want to see a prime example of the power and excitement of a first-person shooter, this is it. And it begins with the continuation of a story. Wake Up and Smell the Ashes...
Last time we left Gordon Freeman, the unlikely scientist-hero from the first Half-Life, he was traveling. Yes, just traveling. The mystery was where he was traveling to and why all of the incidents at Black Mesa had happened (not to mention why the game was rife with so many horrific jumping puzzles towards the end). Half-Life 2 begins with Gordon arriving via train with the G-Man teasing his mind with sickly whispers of warning. The last stop of the arriving train is City 17, a bastion of the alien Combine forces, yet another mystery themselves.
For the rest of the story, you'll have to play the game yourself. I'm absolutely dedicated to getting through this review with your chance at an untarnished gaming experience intact. That means no spoilers. Suffice to say, there are lots of twists to curl your brain along the way, some a bit more predictable than others, but all welcome and interesting.
While the writing and plot points will act as fly paper to your attention, the real winner here is the way the story is presented. Through the eyes of Gordon Freeman, you'll experience roughly 17-20 hours of consciousness which tests your senses and captures your mind. The simplicity and style with which this story is presented are perhaps the most graceful maneuvers of the many that Valve has carried out. From the moment you take your first steps off of that train and into the station at City 17, you'll begin to be tutored in the ways of this bizarre eastern European city. Public service announcements, private conversations, and the actions of characters around you, whether part of the Combine or simply waylaid citizens, create a stifling and threatening feeling that City 17 has become some sort of elaborate prison preaching the chance for freedom and opportunity without choice or desire.
While I was ultimately left a little bit frustrated by the open-endedness, the journey to get to the end of the story was assuredly interesting and opened up the doors to many more possibilities. It's easy to start speculating about this or that, just don't let it drive you nuts. The deeper you get, the darker and more intriguing it becomes until you get to the end... which you'll have to see for yourself.

This frightening vision of the future is only made stronger by a stunning visual style that manages to express artistic vision while coming as close to reality as I've seen in my decades of playing video games. One of the most stunning moments comes with the first steps out from the train station and into the city proper. It's the wild realization of a fantastic dream. The Combine citadel looms on the horizon as a testament to their power, authority, and technological capabilities. It's both impressive and oppressive at the same time, serving its purpose with more presence than an army of a Combine soldiers and Striders ever could.
Light plays a significant role in the beauty of Half-Life 2, not only because of its quality, but because of the way that it tracks the passage of time. Each passing level brings the sun down a bit more until you're encased in an eerie canopy of unease at just the right moment in the game. At first, I was sceptical about this game. Indie 2D platformer with roguelike elements and pixel artsy visuals - how original is that, am I right? Still, I was kind of drawn to it.
I got it as a gift from a stranger some time ago, and it was basically just sitting in my library ever since. Recently, I've been looking for something new to play and I've decided to give it a go. I learned very quickly how wrong I was…
Storywise, there's not that much to talk about:  Your character somehow survived the explosion of the space cargo ship. You crash landed on an unknown planet, which is bad enough by itself. Unfortunately, the whole place is swarming with all sorts of strange, deadly creatures. As you can probably imagine, none of them is what you'd call "friendly". You need to get out of this place…
Leaving the planet is not as easy as one would hope. There are 6 (somewhat) randomly generated levels, each harder than the previous one. To get to the next level, you need to find a teleporter, activate it and then survive another 90 seconds, during which you fight the boss and waves of enemies. Only after killing everything, you can progress to the next level and repeat the same procedure.
Other than your 4 basic combat skills, there are many different passive and active items to be found  These can be bought with the money you've earned by slaughtering
native inhabitants. However, it takes a while to get those $$$, which is unlucky, because the game is getting tougher over time. That means you have to decide pretty soon whether to grind for a few minutes and become as OP as you possibly can, or just try to speedrun the whole thing with only a few items. It's your call.
Even with multiple attacks, controls and the whole combat model is really easy to get into. I've played with a controller most of the time, but it's absolutely fine with keyboard too.  It feels nice and fluid. Chaining attacks is fun, but it also requires a bit of a planning to pull off, so it's not just downright brainless button mashing. Also, difficulty increasing over time is a nice little mechanic and takes the game to a whole new level (heh). Same goes for collecting and stacking different items. All in all, the game actually requires quite a bit of tactical thinking.
Next, I love the amount of content they've put into the game. There are about 100 items total and it takes a while to unlock and find all of them. More than that, you can unlock 11 additional characters. All of them have their unique skill set, allowing for different playstyles, meaning very different experience. Thanks to this, and randomly generated levels, the replayability of this game is insane.
Besides, there are diary logs, describing some of the monsters you've encountered, and also "shipping details" for all of the items you've found so far. These add more little details to the story and enviroment, making you more invested into the universe you still know nothing about. Moreover, the atmosphere is just wonderful. Pixel art style is spot on and the soundtrack by Chris Christodoulou is just stellar (I'm done with puns now, I promise…).
While it can start to get a little bit ridiculous after 20 minutes or so, I enjoy that. Not being able to see your character through the mix of enemies, health bars, damage values, effects and particles may be stressfull for some…but making it out alive is veeery satisfying, cathartic even. When thing go wrong (and the frequently do), I always feel like I know exactly how I screwed up, despite all of the chaos and randomness. Don't get me wrong, this game is REALLY HARD and will kill you again and again and again… but it still feels more fair than any other rogue-like I've played.
On the other hand, beating this game for the first time was one of the most rewarding gaming experiences I think I've ever had…
There are only a few little problems, but I feel like I should mention them anyway.
First, the Steam overlay doesn't work at all with this game, which surprised me. That means no screenshots on Steam. Obviously, you can still use the OS's built-in print screen function, but it's a shame that you can't share it with you friends that easily and basically support the game more. Not sure what to think about that. Also, full controller support and Big Picture mode support would be swell.
That's pretty much it, nothing else to complain about.
Risk of Rain is rock hard, yet fair and fun to play. It combines several interesting mechanics in a very cool way, and the amount of content and replayability is amazing. The world of RoR is eerie, strange and beautiful at the same time, thanks to it's visual style and great soundtrack.
If you're a fan of rogue-likes, or hard games in general, you should just buy this game right away - it is definitely worth of both your time and your money. If you are short-tempered however, I would advice you to reconsider.

If video games were likened to human beings, Killing Floor 2 would be like the girlfriend / boyfriend who decided that just being fun and charming wasn't good enough for you, and decided to hit the gym to get super fit, all the while ditching the cargo pants and stained sweatpants for something a lot more flattering.
This game is an improvement over the original in almost every way.  Explosive gunplay, beautiful graphics, snappy controls--it's all there.  The new perk levelling system is also fun, and is an improvement over the original in that it provides inherent benefits in the form of Perk Talents to each perk, and not just being thrown free perk weapons upon spawning.  These can be changed on the fly between waves, allowing players to change their playing styles even within the same perk depending on the needs of the team.  For instance, a medic focused on healing and team buffs may decide to switch to a more of a combat role without changing perks if it occurs to him that the team doesn't need as much healing as originally thought.
Communications between TWI and the fan base has also improved dramatically after a period of near silence, even if there was never any doubt that TWI intend to support KF2 as long as they can (as evidenced by the stellar track record with KF1).
If KF2 continues to go the way it has been going as of late, I can see myself playing this game for years to come, and I don't see myself being alone in thinking this way.

Now here's a strange one!  First, let me state the obvious.  Antichamber is a VERY indie game.  I'm talkin SO EXTREMELY INDIE that it requires the use of CAPITAL LETTERS for EMPHASIS.  Just warning you that If you aren't ready to try something you've never experienced before, then steer clear until you are, because as I said, Antichamber is a bit of a strange one.
Antichamber is less of a game and more of an experiment in first-person gameplay.  Think of it as a puzzle game like Portal, but without the interesting characters or story.  That may sound like an objectively negative critique, but it's more a comment on the nature of the beast rather than how likeable it is.  The puzzles, however, are stunningly deep.  Often they spit in the face of player intuition and videogame conventions, yielding an experience that you genuinely feel like you accomplished something when you plans succeed.
The biggest thing holding back this game is the lack of context.  Without characters or a plot, I found the game rather dull, which I suppose is consistent to the nature of experiment-em-ups like this.  There is no reason to see this game through to the end other than for the experience of it.  No tangible destination, no tantalizing goal, just more puzzles.  I found myself getting absorbed in the activity of solving the puzzles, but with no real motivation to pick the game back up afterwards.
There is genius at work here, but without context, it just seems like the developer is enjoying screwing with my head (which they probably are).  A story, perhaps even a mind-boggling one, would have helped this game become more memorable to me.

Antichamber is a thoroughly mind-melting first-person puzzle game that utilizes non-euclidian geometry as most of the puzzle elements. Now there's a sentence that doesn't apply to most games.
The visuals are very simple; the hallways are mostly white, with only black lines to indicate where corners are. Colors are very important in this game; they can help you orient yourself as the world changes around you (did I mention that you can be walking down a hallway, get to the end, turn around, and see a completely different hallway behind you?). The color of your gun also determines what its powers are. There are several sections of the game, each requiring a different gun to solve its puzzles.
Speaking of puzzles, they are a doozy. Because the game does not rely on traditional notions of geometry, they can really do whatever they want. I don't want to spoil any of the puzzles, but don't feel discouraged if you can't solve one the first time you try. Sometimes there is a tool or technique that you have to get in a different chamber first. And even if you get completely stuck, you can just hit Esc at any time and go to the Antichamber.
The antichamber serves as a main menu. The game's options and controls are all plastered over one wall, a map of all of the chambers you have been to (you can travel to any one of them from the antichamber) a view of what claims to be the exit, and a big chalkboard of the lessons you have learned.
Those lessons are my favorite thing about the game. They are often placed just before or after a puzzle, and they contain a life lesson that pertains to that particular puzzle.
I've played about three hours of the game, and I have discovered two different colors of the gun, and I think there are two more. I'm kind of stuck though, and I might have to bite the bullet and look at some walkthroughs.
I would say that a reasonable price for this game is $10, so you should definitely wait until it is on sale to pick it up.

Shadowrun was a game that came out back in 1989.  The first video game was 1993 for the SNES system.  The last video game being produced was in 2007.  There are plans for a Shadowrun online, but no release date yet.  For now, we have this game to enjoy.
The game plays with elements of other games merged together.  Character creation is similar to the Baulder's Gate franchise.  You have choices of different races (Human, Elf, Dwarf, Troll and Ork), a bunch of different professions (street samauri, mage, etc), and tons of weapons and skills.
Leveling and skills are similar to early Mass Effect, where you put points into the skill and with more points abilities are unlocked.
Combat is similar to the more recent XCom: Enemy Unknown system.  You have cover (partial and full), Action Points, overwatch, etc.  Mix in guns with sword and sorcery and you have a deep combat system.  Although movement and cover are like XCom, the tactics remind me of Baldur's Gate.  You need to use the right spells at the right time.  Area spells, and shotgun sprays for that matter, can hit your party.  Combat is turn-based.
There is an editor for the game to create user content.  The game will play chapters in the characters career, so loading user content is just another job for the shadowrunner to do.  The editor is complex, so learning it takes time, but it is detailed enough to create some great content.  There is some great content out there and will help keep the game fresh.
Overall, I love the game.  I love turn-based RPGs, I loved the new XCom, and I love the shadowrun setting.  If you do as well, then you should be playing this game instead of reading this review!!

Addicting but frustratingly flawed. How far you move is variable, and any given keypress might move you futher than, or not as far, as you intended. This inconsistency is prohibitive.
Also, the game is intentionally visually confusing, but it succeeds too well. I frequently believe I should have lost, but did not, and vice versa.
I am frequently unable to tell at which exact pixel my unit is located, and unable to move it in a reliable manner. This is a recipe for terrible. As a player of bullet hell games, I'm no stranger to moving small objects through obstacles within a distance of one pixel... This game could have been designed better.
That aside, the starting levels are always possible to beat- there is no "chance" or "luck", you win or lose on your skills alone, and I blame myself for more failures than I blame the game's design.
However, I'm convinced that the later levels can and do generate sequences where you are physically unable to win given the established mechanics, and they introduce an element of chance in a game that is supposed to rely on skill, which I'm sure is one of the seven deadly sins. For example, the "camera" might angle around so you cannot see where the next turn is, as it often does in all levels, but the later levels move faster while the unit you control is always restricted to the same speed. Juvenile. Simply juvenile. There were at least 10 different instances while I was playing this game where my jaw dropped at the level of depravity The Stick of Truth splashed onto the screen. Normally, I'd roll my eyes, but... admittedly? I actually kind of liked what turned out to be a surprisingly satisfying RPG.
As most people have said, if you're a fan of the show, you're going to like this game. Me, though? I've only really been tolerant of it, never really an actual fan. Too much of that deplorable, in-your-face gross out factor they tend to tout just doesn't get me laughing, but there's something about the way this game incorporates the concept of a roleplaying game with an episode of South Park that I really have to applaud.
To me, the humor isn't really the strongest suit of this game. To give you any idea of what you're in for, your 'right click' button (often reserved for important actions in other games) is 'fart'. Now to give them credit, the writers will occasionally pull out a surprisingly good joke, but most of what I liked about the story was the wit and playfully ironic jabs toward one of my favorite genres. The story is interesting, with its share of funny moments, but where the game really seems to shine is just how incredibly similar to the show the entire game looks and feels, and how the RPG elements are woven into the tapestry of gameplay. The voice actors, as you can imagine, do a fantastic job, and the music is actually pretty clever in itself.
The game does lose me on a few points though. It's locked at 30 FPS, and when the whole screen is scrolling left and right, you -are- going to see some jittering. There are also quite a few 'busy' quests that felt like they purely existed to waste time, and while there are some clever elements to combat, it does get kind of boring at times. Oh, and if you're an achievement hunter, prepare to play this game a few times. There are a number of pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥prerequisites.
Long story short, if anyone out there is just kind of tolerant of the show and not a huge fan, sort of sitting on the fence? I'd say get it when it's on sale. Fans of RPGs will find something to enjoy, as will fans of juvenile humor.
