Killing Floor 2 - my all-time-favourite Zombie Game! :)
KF2 is a wave based Zombie Survival Game that offers lot's of variety in terms of "classes", weapons, enemies, maps and difficulty. You will have to survive from 4 to 10 waves, depending on your preferences, of challenging, annoying and downright deadly enemies. Once you completed that you will face a boss - either the iconic "Patriarch", known from the original Killing FLoor, or Hans Volter, an evil german Scientist whith a weakness for Gas, Grenades and Machineguns... i mean, what did you expect?
Getting into some details.
Currently we have 9 classes. Each one with different abilities, weapons and playstyles.
Berserker, a Meele focussed tank Perk who is very effective in taking out the big guys. Commando, a Assault Rifle wielding class who's efficient in popping a lot of heads. Support, the brawler. Shotguns and ammo/armor drops are his thing. Field Medic, i mean
Demolitionist, the explosive master. The newly implemented M16 + Grenadelauncher adds a huge possible variety to this class. Firebug, the maniac. Molotovs, flamethrowers and sci-fi weapons are his stuff. Gunslinger, this guy loves dual-wielded pistols. Sharpshooter, the precision class. Crossbows, Sniper-Rifles and Railguns - just your usual things. SWAT, master of SMG's and the #1 Spray-and-pray-perk.
Each class gains passive bonuses like realod speed, weapon damage and  health with each level and is allowed to pick an ability every 5 levels. These can be switched (even mid-game) and are the key to surviving as a team.
The weapons do have a huge variety. Shotguns, SMG's, AR's, Explosives, RPG's, Railguns, Crossbows, Katanas, Flamethrowers [...]. Each weapon can be used by every class - however, they only unlock their full potential when being used by the specific perk.
The weapons can be bought with "dosh" that you earn by killing Zed's, healing, wielding doors [...].
Info: When dying you will only drop your
. Keep that in mind when playing.
Not going to spoil much here... just know that the good old Killing Floor Classics are all here and are even more demanding than in the first game! Sirens, Bloats, Scrakes [...].
The bosses number currently only 2... Hans and the Patriarch. Both bring a lot of abilities and wepaons into the fight and really do pack a punch - but they also offer a variety of tactics to use against them. healing that can be stopped, invisibility that you can detect [...].
Both are fun to challenge and hard to beat!
Like in a lot of other games, Killing Floor 2 offers microtransactions. Firstly, you can buy a few packs and items in the ingame store. These now rotate, so its possible to find entirely new stuff you never saw before. Next, you drop items in Game. (24 hours = 1 drop possible). These consist of crates, usb keys and lower tier items, but have a slight chance to drop crate keys / usb keys as well. USB keys offer weapon skins, while crates offer cosmetics. Both optional, both okay.
With the latest update of the shop, the possibility of crate / usb items being sold there, the market price might drop for a lot of things. A good thing - for the majority of players.
The versus-mode, not yet tested by mself, is a mode where human players can take over ever the survivors, or the zombies. It is popular in certain parts of the community and defenitely a good addition to the game.
Depsite the price of 27€ the game does have Microtransactions - but that doesnt make it a bad game. It offers hundreds of hours of fun and variety, plus the possibility of challenging yourself over and over again. The higher difficulties really do make the game more interesting! The only small downside that exists, is the fact that a lot of players boost their perks on level servers and thus it now is not possible anymore to "detect" a good player by his perk lvl. Sad thing, but nothing to worry about if you have a few other friends to play with.

If you’re unfamiliar with the Shadowrun universe, it’s set in future earth and incorporates both cyberpunk and fantasy elements. Before now, Shadowrun has been a very popular tabletop game, an action RPG on the Sega Genesis and even a team-based multiplayer FPS.
Thanks to Kickstarter, Shadowrun has returned as a traditional isometric-style RPG that plays very similar to the old Fallout games, with combat that feels like it’s out of the XCOM games.
Character creation involves choosing your class and race, in the Shadowrun universe you can be a Human, Elf, Troll, Orc or Dwarf, each of which have their own unique restrictions and perks associated with them, for example, Trolls and Orcs tend to make terrible Deckers or Riggers because of the high intelligence required, however they start with more HP and are better at strength-based abilities.
Your class choice has a huge impact on how you will be playing the game in combat situations. The classes include;
- Street Samurai, master of weapons, both melee and ranged.
- Mage, master of magic and magical support.
- Decker, master of the matrix (cyberspace).
- Shaman, master of the spirits, summoning and magical support.
- Rigger, master of mechanical drones and engineering.
- Physical Adept, master of unarmed and chi magic.
Regardless of which class you choose at the start of the game, you can always later specialize in a different field of skills, your class mostly just affects your starting stats and gear.
Gameplay outside of combat is in real time, you control your character by clicking where you want to move or what you want to interact with, if you have companions they will automatically follow you.
During combat, the game becomes turn based. Each character in the fight has a certain number of action points they can use during their turn. For example if you have 3 AP you could choose to run to cover, fire a burst of bullets with your SMG and then cast a heal spell on one of your friends.
Rather than having a leveling and experience points system, Shadowrun Returns simply rewards players with karma points for completing tasks which they can spend on leveling up their skills.
Although Shadowrun Returns is an RPG, it doesn’t quite incorporate all of the elements of freedom that most RPGs have. For example, you cannot go back to areas you have already been or choose what order to do certain tasks in. The main campaign follows quite closely to the story with very few side missions.
While on an actual mission you are given a fair amount of freedom in regards to how you accomplish your tasks… will you open the door by jacking into the matrix, battling security programs and finding the door controls, will you fight your way in meatspace to the door switch, leaving a trail of destruction in your wake… or will you simply get your break down the door because you’re a giant troll with ridiculous strength?
The game has a lovely soundtrack with a real cyberpunk feel to it. There is no voice acting though, so if you aren’t a big fan of reading dialogue you may find that off-putting.
I found the story to be absolutely amazing! It was probably the best story I’ve experienced in an RPG thus far. My only issue is that it ended after 10 hours of gameplay and I felt like I had not fully developed my character yet and that there was still a lot of things I wanted to try. But I suppose 10 hours of gameplay isn’t bad considering the game comes with a built in module/map editor and there are loads of modules on the Steam Workshop.
If you’re looking for a more freedom-based experience with this game, I recommend getting the module ‘Shadowrun Unlimited’ from the Workshop.
Overall, I really liked this game, it has just about everything I look for in an RPG. It lacks a bit of freedom in the main campaign, but makes up for it with modding tools and DLCs.

Shadowrun Returns is set in a fantastic, cyberpunk, distopian earth, where mega-coorporations are running the show, drug dealers roam the streets, and mercenary adventurers, called "shadowrunners" take on dangerous work for the highest bidder. On top of everything else, magic has returned to the world, which puts a novel spin on the whole cyberpunk setup.
This game has a brilliant atmosphere, captivating from the start, pulling you into the dirty streets of a blade-runner-ish seattle, and putting you into the skin of a shadow runner. Shadowrun returns features a great story, with lots of twists and reminds me of the Torment due to its emphasis on dialogue, rather than battles. On the downside it's very linear, with only a couple of occasional options for side-quests. But this is not necessarily that bad, because it focuses on the plot and tells the story without infinite distractions and pointless errants.

In front of you is a hallway. You'll want walk slowly at one point, because at a certain point the hallway will transform into a room you've probably been to before if you don't jump, and that area in itself has a confusing layout, with invisible floors, rooms that  only allow access if you aren't looking at them as you enter, and areas that only exist if you enter them from the right doorway, not to mention many, many odd block puzzles.
Antichamber probably gets a lot of comparisons to Portal, and for good reason. Both are puzzle games who rely on novel elements of level design and the ability to manipulate the environment to create what could be seen as a larger puzzle as a whole.
However, Antichamber, focuses entirely on the latter. There is no antagonist, no threat of danger. The worst thing that may happen is you accidently boxing yourself in somewhere, and even that is an incredibly minor inconvenience due to your ability to return to any room you have visited from the main menu, which seconds as a sort of universal hub room.
Also unique to this game is its sense of exploration. Antichamber is the best example I can think of as a puzzle-focused first-person Metroidvania-style game, where your only limitation in exploration are which tools you have collected. Oftentimes you will find yourself delightfully lost, as you rush forward only to find yourself back where you began. Antichamber is not about completing the labyrinth, it's about exploring it. Also, there's no David Bowie, pretty fantasy settings, or quirky puppets. But the ability to manipulate reality is a nice consolation prize.

Dying Light is Dead Island done right.
At first glance you will see many similarities between this game and dead island, such as the loot, the crafting, the weapons, but it takes that formula and cranks it up a notch.
There is a huge map, complete with fantastic visuals, to get around by mostly using parkour, running up walls and sprinting from rooftop to rooftop.  The large map means a lot of places to explore to find loot and weapons, as well as blueprints that will allow you to craft some amazing and bizarre weapons.  There is a full day and night cycle, day time being a relative breeze with slow ambling zombies that are easy to take down.  Night is dangerous, volatile infected are extremely fast and strong and hunt you down in packs, making sneaking at night essential.
The story is quite interesting, and can even be played with up to 4 friends, you can also invade your friends game as a powerful zombie and hunt them down.  There are also plenty of side quests that help you get money, loot, and skill points.  There are 3 different skill trees to improve by surviving, fighting, and using your parkour skills, each with a decent amount of skills to upgrade.
If your at all interested in these types of zombie games then I would say to definately give Dying Light a go.

It might sound weird to call a game "important," but Antichamber really pushes the envelope in terms of how a game can change the way you think - both about games and about yourself.  Every time I think I've mastered an element of gameplay, I turn a corner and go *right* back to feeling like a rat in a maze.  The greatest moments are when I am forced to deliberately drop what I think I know, start from scratch, and see everything with new eyes.
If you think of games as art, then this is a masterpiece of minimalism, speaking volumes with a paucity of elements.  If you don't think of games as art, then this will change your mind about that.  If you think games can't be art, then just play this anyway and see what you think.

"Aliens", "The Thing" and "Event Horizon" had a baby.
This is where it all began. Forget the second and third games in the series, the first entry is it's own unique entry in the series before going completely off the rails by the third installment. What differentiates it is that the original game despite the gross-out horror and violent gore is that it is more story-driven than it's successors. The entire game plays out like a science-fiction horror film in deep space, richly establishing it's own universe and characters well before the other shoe drops, our woe-begotten protagonist and two others with him finding themselves stranded on a failing derelict ship that they had been searching for and finding no crew aboard but blood all over the place..then finding out that they're less alone than they thought and quickly having to fix the ailing ship to save themselves while defending themselves from terrifying nightmarish creatures. It sounds like a cheesy 80s thriller when I describe it that way but it's so much more than that and considering it often goes on sale for like 5 bucks these days you're certainly in for a treat.

Night is Coming.
Take Farcry and smash it together with Mirrors Edge and throw in a post-apocalyptic world where nearly everything wants to eat your face off and ladies & gentlemen you have Dying Light.
TL;DR
I'm not sure if my play time has updated yet but I've clocked around 13 hours so far I think and oh my. I wasnt expecting it to be this good so soon. No bugs (yet) smooth 60 FPS on max graphics settings, which are gorgeous. Free running WILL feel clunky the first 10 minutes you do it then once you get the hang of it it is so much fun and it's all in first person which makes it that much more beautiful. There are multiple skill trees and perks too take and a wonderful, user friendly crafting menu that will give you a real incentive to go out and loot everything and anything you can find to help you survive the city.
The zombies are not OP nor are they too dumb as there are so many variations on the different types of zombies. You might be having fun smashing a few of the slow walkers up when suddenly you get ambushed by 3 runner zombies because you made too much noise. Or you may be looting a few stores and one zombie notices you and then all his friends are coming toward you. The AI is simply brilliant.
And that brings us too the night. When the hunters come out. These zombies ARE OP and if you try and fight them head on, chances are, You. Will. Die. Even running away is simply not good enough to evade the hunters you have to utilise all your free running skill and cunning and "juke" them across the rooftops, balconys, cars, anything to escape. Sure you can head to a safe zone and sleep through the night but with risk comes reward. If you stay out at night you're gathering extra loot to stay alive and also earning bonus experience towards your skill perks.
I have honestly not felt more on edge and intense in any game for a long, long time. The feeling of being out alone with no safe zone near by when the warning for night is issued is butt clenchingly scary. Better gather alot of gauze  and string because you're going to need to craft yourself a new pair of pants.

If video games were likened to human beings, Killing Floor 2 would be like the girlfriend / boyfriend who decided that just being fun and charming wasn't good enough for you, and decided to hit the gym to get super fit, all the while ditching the cargo pants and stained sweatpants for something a lot more flattering.
This game is an improvement over the original in almost every way.  Explosive gunplay, beautiful graphics, snappy controls--it's all there.  The new perk levelling system is also fun, and is an improvement over the original in that it provides inherent benefits in the form of Perk Talents to each perk, and not just being thrown free perk weapons upon spawning.  These can be changed on the fly between waves, allowing players to change their playing styles even within the same perk depending on the needs of the team.  For instance, a medic focused on healing and team buffs may decide to switch to a more of a combat role without changing perks if it occurs to him that the team doesn't need as much healing as originally thought.
Communications between TWI and the fan base has also improved dramatically after a period of near silence, even if there was never any doubt that TWI intend to support KF2 as long as they can (as evidenced by the stellar track record with KF1).
If KF2 continues to go the way it has been going as of late, I can see myself playing this game for years to come, and I don't see myself being alone in thinking this way.

I grew up on Valve shooters. Counter-Strike, Day of Defeat, Half Life 2. Playing this again brings back so many memories. While the multiplayer games have *not* aged well, the Half Life series of games remains a solid gaming experience.
The puzzles feel fresh even though the mechanics have now existed for a long time in gaming. Perhaps the best part of the game is the story though. The story helps you to make sense of the chaos around you in the game and appreciate the slow moments where Gordon Freeman, the MIT graduate and physist-extraordinaire gets to do what he does best, solve physics based puzzles.
A nice mental stretch from the dull monotony of the typical roided-beefcake of an action hero, Gordon and his story here in Half-Life remain sincere even after more than a decade. When you make a game like this, you can be sure it will last and remain a stalwart example of why video games can convey such amazing stories and lessons.

In front of you is a hallway. You'll want walk slowly at one point, because at a certain point the hallway will transform into a room you've probably been to before if you don't jump, and that area in itself has a confusing layout, with invisible floors, rooms that  only allow access if you aren't looking at them as you enter, and areas that only exist if you enter them from the right doorway, not to mention many, many odd block puzzles.
Antichamber probably gets a lot of comparisons to Portal, and for good reason. Both are puzzle games who rely on novel elements of level design and the ability to manipulate the environment to create what could be seen as a larger puzzle as a whole.
However, Antichamber, focuses entirely on the latter. There is no antagonist, no threat of danger. The worst thing that may happen is you accidently boxing yourself in somewhere, and even that is an incredibly minor inconvenience due to your ability to return to any room you have visited from the main menu, which seconds as a sort of universal hub room.
Also unique to this game is its sense of exploration. Antichamber is the best example I can think of as a puzzle-focused first-person Metroidvania-style game, where your only limitation in exploration are which tools you have collected. Oftentimes you will find yourself delightfully lost, as you rush forward only to find yourself back where you began. Antichamber is not about completing the labyrinth, it's about exploring it. Also, there's no David Bowie, pretty fantasy settings, or quirky puppets. But the ability to manipulate reality is a nice consolation prize.

It might sound weird to call a game "important," but Antichamber really pushes the envelope in terms of how a game can change the way you think - both about games and about yourself.  Every time I think I've mastered an element of gameplay, I turn a corner and go *right* back to feeling like a rat in a maze.  The greatest moments are when I am forced to deliberately drop what I think I know, start from scratch, and see everything with new eyes.
If you think of games as art, then this is a masterpiece of minimalism, speaking volumes with a paucity of elements.  If you don't think of games as art, then this will change your mind about that.  If you think games can't be art, then just play this anyway and see what you think.

Since Dying Lights initial announcement many years ago, I have always been looking forward to this game. As a big fan of the dead island series, I knew that I would love this game when it finally came out. After a few years followed with one or two delays, I can happily say this game was worth the wait.
Whilst it's launch was a little choppy in some areas, mainly regarding the multiplayer in my personal experience, for the most part it has been very smooth and it's fair to say that it has had a much more sucessful launch than that of other games recently. It only took me 5 minutes of tweaking a few settings to get a performance that I considered acceptable to play with, with my system just over recommended specs I certainly have smooth performance, with the exception of a few FPS drops here and there and a little video stuttering, however it doesn't really remain much of an issue.
If you were a fan of the dead island franchise as well as Mirrors Edge, chances are you will quickly fall in love with this game, it's combining the two as well as adding more content. It may look like very similar gameplay to that of Dead Island, however I felt that when playing the fluency of the parkour system, the setting, the plot and the story, characters and overall content just made the game feel so much more dynamic and direct with the player. In addition, the day/night cycle is incredible. Firstly, ignore anyone that says it's fixed. It's not, the cycle is 100% dynamic, some quests (the prologue) just set it to night or such to introduce the setting. But once your out of the prologue, it's 100% dynamic. Me and my friend at first thought night was just sort of a little gimicky selling point, it was only until we were on  a mission collecting chocolates for some guy that we were warned night was coming, and when it did we were gone pretty quickly.
Do not take the night cycle as a gimick, it's very unique, works very well and adds so much more the game. You don't have to play through it, you can skip it (sleep). However, i advise you try playing through night, through it's encoruagement of double xp and the changes you are forced to undertake to simply survive. You cannot go all out, you will fail and die almost every time. You must plan around the infected to achieve anything, stay hidden, use UV wisely and such. It feels like an entirly different game at times during the night.
Overall, well I don't think I have enjoyed the launch of a game so much in the past 2 or 3 so years, with the last being Far Cry 3. This game is simply fantastic and I cannot wait to see what they have planned for the future. With a few issues for me perosnally here and there (that is just my experience, not to be conflicted with that of others) Techland have pulled this off very well. I recommend you buy this, 100%. Worth it's money. Great game. So much fun whatever you end up doing, plenty of funny and shocking moments. Hilarious and addictive with friends.

This is my first review.  I rely so much on the reviews of others when playing games that I really feel I owe it to my fellow gamers to write reviews as well.  I've found that reviews are the absolutely best way of telling a good game from a bad one.
OK, Dead Space.  Yep, it's definitely a console, but it's a good console game, at least, generally speaking.  The game plays well and is polished and free of flaws.  The graphics are superb, and the game is actually kind of unique.  It's sort of like a first person shooter (it's third person), but it breaks off in some new and interesting ways: the style of aiming (via a laser site projected from the "weapons"), the unique ways that enemies must be defeated, and the fact that your weapons aren't really weapons at all but really the game world's version of industrial tools.  Second, the plot may seem a little stale at first (it definitely shares a lot in common as regards plot with many of the classic space horror games such as the Doom series), but there are a couple of interesting twists.  I found myself getting interested in the story before the end.  Finally, the game is pretty challenging and requires dexterity and brains to complete, especially on the hard and impossible difficulties.
And, the bad.  Most of the bad come from standard console tropes.  First, you have to save into game slots from save stations (keep in mind that consoles charge their players for save game slots in the form of proprietary memory sticks).  As a result, you are often in a situation where you have to play through the same complicated sequence over and over again, doing mundane tasks before a difficult battle.  Second, the layout of the game is predictable and repetitive with some areas being kind of safe locations where the save spots and stores are located.  Third, the save spots and stores break the immersion of the game as they are unbelievable in the context in the world and clearly included just because this is a game.  I prefer a horror game such as this at least take itself seriously.
Overall, this game was a lot of fun to play, and I think I might go back and replay it at some point:)

I played Shadowrun with a great group of friends back in the late eighties.  We were fortunate to have an awesome GM that could really develop a great and exciting story.  As I played through Shadowrun Returns and the DLC, Showdowrun: Dragonfall, I kept thinking back to the old days of paper, dice, beer and game sessions that would last well into the early morning hours.  Shadowrun Returns captures exactly what it was like in the old pen and paper days, minus the friends, unfortunately.  The world is rich and refreshingly different from other game settings.
Combat can be exicting, but not very deep.  The are many character archetypes to play, but development of a character's skillset is sparse.  Those with little knowelege of the Shadowrun setting may also find themselves lost as to what is going on with the story.  The first adventure, The Dead Man's Switch, was a little slow for me to get into.  However, for those familar with the Seattle area will enjoy some of the local references and themes.  The second adventure, Dragonfall (a seperate DLC), was realy good and grabbed me right away.  It improved on many of the game mechanics, had more interesting characters, and had a more interesting story.
Overall, the game was very good.  It isn't very expensive and provides many hours of play.  Shadowrun Returns has that old pen and paper feel to it, which I enjoy very much.  Give it a try, especially if it is on sale.

A pure, uncensored South Park experience - take that for what it's worth.  Those with a sense of humor who laugh at jokes because they're funny and don't back away because it's politically incorrect, will adore this game.  Those who are squemish, who say "You can't joke about that!", or who think some things should be off limits, steer clear.
For those with an adult attitude, this game is hilarious, witty and charming.  The jokes are pure South Park all the way through, and you'll be chuckling through it all.  As funny as South Park is on Comedy Central, it's still holding a lot back, which is what makes this game so much fun - it's uncensored, unbound, pure South Park, the way the creators, Matt and Trey, intended it to be.  Nothing is off limits, and you'll be laughing all the harder for it.
Beneath the humor is a solid RPG experience too; everything from spells, potions, PP and HP management, armor, weapons, etc.  It's all here, it's balanced, and it's a thoroughly enjoyable experience for the gamer.  Exploring, finishing all quests and beating the game took me about 19 hrs, though you could probably see and do everything in 15.
I recommend this game wholeheartedly, and can't wait for a sequel!!

Shadowrun. I picked up the Pen and Paper RPG when I was younger. Sadly it took years before finding a group to play it. Luckly around my University years I found a decent group of people and we are gaming since than. I am an hardcore fan so probably my Review could be a bit biased. Frist of all I strongly suggest to read a bit before gaming. Just the "Primer" which is a small guide\introduction to the World of Shadowrun available from the site Shadowrun Universe (official site for all things related to Shadowrun). Once you have the Primer you can have a good idea of what to expect from the Setting. I know that at a frist glance it looks strange maybe even too much but trust me it is awesome. The more you will dig the better it will get, specially if you start to read the various RPG manuals and novels. If you liked the setting buy this game. The basic Campaign included in Shadowrun Returns is a classic. If you never rped or played Shadowrun (I am mostly referring to SNES and GENESIS Games) this is a wonderfull start. The narration is set in 2050s which is a very cool period for Shadowrun (keep in mind that in the current RP Setting the time is around 2075) and it is based on some of the hottest plots of that period. The game is a basic Turn Based Combat with RP elements in the form of dialogues where the various options depends on which skill you have. Back when it was just published the Game lacked few things like save anywhere option. Luckly this was fixed up in the 1st DLC Dragonfall. Dragonfall is even better than the basic game. The Devs listened to us Players and fixed few things and I dare to say even took inspiration from some of UGC - User generated Content (More of this later). Dragonfall can look a bit boring at the start with the logic of "Do a Run, get back and run again" (Run is a work, a mission in Shadowrun) but the Narration, the Plot goes always up till its end. In Dragonfall I was not impressed by the first Runs but nearby the end I could not stop to see how this Story was going to end. The only negative side of both Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall is that you can not manage your NPCs. You can select who can help you in a Run but you do not have any kind of control on their Skills and how they improve. Probably this will be fixed in future DLCs. If the basic game and the DLC are not enough there are UGCs. Shadowrun Community is very active and Devs select from time to time some UCG to play just to show up how much it is good. There are a lot of good Artist out there who are working on big UCG like remakes of SNES and Genesis Shadowrun Games. I strongly suggest to take a loot at "Shadowrun Unlimited". I hope all of this makes sense. In any case, if you start to play and dig into the Shadows of Shadowrun remember: "Shoot straight, conserve your ammo and never make a deal with a Dragon".

In Shadowrun Returns, you play the part of a Shadowrunner named... well, you choose your own name, gender and race... and you embark on a journey to hunt down and bring to justice the Emerald City Ripper - murderer of your old friend Sam Watts.
As with most RPGs, there is a fair bit of text to battle through, however, in Shadowrun Returns, this is more of a plus point than a negative. The story is so wonderfully written and each and every character encounter is like reading a from a thoroughly enrapturing novel. The dialogue is beautifully tailored for each character's unique personality and often you'll uncover side missions which can bring in precious Nuyen (the game's currency), and/or increased character attributes such as karma, for helping out a damsel in distress.
The game is played from an overhead, isometric view, unlike the direct top-down Sega Genesis iteration. The backdrops are gorgeously painted, as are the character portraits that pop up upon engaging with the locals.
Movement couldn't be simpler. Simply tap to where you want to go and your character will walk or run to said position, comrades (if applicable) faithfully in tow.
The battle system is also fairly easy to get the hang of. You have a set amount of moves, or Action Points, each turn. These AP can be used for moving, attacking, casting spells and using items such as med-packs, should you or one of your team require a bit of patching up. It's a turn-based strategy affair that works brilliantly... no unwanted, random battles here!
What I really love about Shadowrun Returns is the mixture of real world (the game takes place in Seattle) and fantasy. The game combines technology and conventional weapons with magic and the traditional fantasy character races such as elves, dwarves and trolls.
As well as character races, there are six classes available; Mages, Street Samurai, Decker, Rigger, Shaman and Physical Adept.  Mages utilise magic, Street Samurai are the warriors of the bunch, Deckers are like futuristic super-hackers, Riggers control drones that aid in combat and/or healing, Shaman "see dead people" and can also talk them into lending a hand in battle and Physical Adepts are able to use magic spells to increase their performance and attributes, as well as unleash a few cans of the old whup♥♥♥♥♥
If you're after a game that has an involving storyline, excellent control system, intriguing and engaging characters and is something that you can pick up and play, despite having no prior experience with the RPG genre, I highly recommend Shadowrun Returns. It's almost more of a character driven, point and click adventure with the added depth of an RPG thrown in for good measure.

Fantastic game. The whole way through, the experience feels like watching a really good South Park episode or South Park movie, and the game is a *really* solid RPG, to boot.
But the game isn't without its flaws. I want to spend a few paragraphs on some criticisms of the game, and then we'll talk about what makes the game awesome.
The game feels heavily "consolized." Loading screens are far more frequent than they should be and the controls often don't make much sense. Throughout the game your character will be taught "magic spells" from various NPCs. Each time you learn a spell, you are taught a series of controls to use that spell. However, these spells can be used both in and out of combat, and in both situations the controls are different from one another—and in neither situation is the spell invoked the same way the game inititally taught you!
Your out-of-combat utilities (like firing a ranged weapon at something in the environment or sending a buddy to perform a task) are equally awkward to select and use.
Now, here I should note that I played with a controller attached to a PC. I started the game with a keyboard/mouse but changed very, very early on to give my normal gaming posture a rest (I play games a lot with the keyboard/mouse), and also because South Park: The Stick of Truth seemed to be tailored more toward a controller. Perhaps the controls are better with a keyboard/mouse, but using a controller felt awkward in many parts of the game. But not in combat. In combat the controls felt great. More on that later, though.
On top of that, the game's humor can be off-putting in some parts. This isn't a real criticism so much as it is a warning—it IS South Park, after all! The show has a reputation of making comedy material out of even the most sensitive of topics, and this game also doesn't hold back. I like to think of myself as a fairly easy-going guy and I try not to take many things too seriously, but there were parts in this game that I felt myself somewhat rushing through or avoiding just to get away from an uncomfortable topic.
There's a lot of back-and-forth running around the map in this game, and loading screens are absolutely everywhere. The loading screens are a real slowdown.
So let's see. The loading screens, the really iffy controls in much of the game, and the warning about how the game remains very South Park in its humor are all the things I wanted to make sure to mention. So, now we can talk about the stuff that makes this game a fantastic one!
While moving on the map and navigating menus is often awkward with the game's controls, combat is something the game gets very, very right. As I mentioned earlier, this game is a very solid RPG, and The Stick of Truth's turn-based combat is airtight. This isn't your typical "select an ability and watch what happens" kind of turn-based combat. Here, you'll select an ability, and then you'll influence the outcome of the ability with some simple, but fun controls.
For example, Butters the Paladin has a "Hammer of Justice" ability. To use it, you select it and then choose a target. The game then has you rotate the left control stick in circles to make Butters spin (think Olympic discus tossing), and at just the right instant, press the A button. Succeed, and you'll deal bonus damage to the enemy! If you mess up, Butters will still deal damage, but not as much. Again, this is coming from the perspective of using a gamepad to control the game; I'm sure this is different for a mouse/keyboard, but the principle is the same.
Combat is filled with awesome stuff like this. When you are attacked, most of the time you are given the chance to block some of the enemy's damage by pressing A at just the right time. Some enemy attacks strike multiple times, requiring multiple well-timed blocks! Different enemy attacks have different timings as well, so you'll always need to be on your guard.
These combat mechanics make even turn-based combat a very active affair. The action is fast and challenging, so you'll need to be spot on with your controls. Thankfully, controls in combat are responsive and intuitive, and anytime there's some ambiguity about what to do in battle, there are useful tooltips and pop-ups to remind you of how to use an ability.
While combat is great fun, the game also very often presents you with multiple ways of dealing with foes. Sometimes you can distract them and sneak by. Other times you can use the environment to defeat your foes without having to confront them. Keen awareness of your surroundings and appropriate use of your abilities out of combat can speed up your progress and yield satisfying results.
It should be noted that if you sneak by enemies, you probably won't get experience for dealing with them. But in the cases where you can use the environment to defeat them, you'll be awarded experience as if you had battled them!
There are many quests to accomplish throughout the game, and a few side quests can be completed as you progress. As far as questing is concerned, it's your typical RPG fare—pick up a quest, complete the objectives, turn the quest in. The game does nothing to revolutionize questing, but it handles questing very well.
The story-based quests, however, are always greatly satisfying to accomplish because you are awarded not only with experience and often loot/money, but also with story exposition done in only the way South Park can. It really does feel like you're earning a little piece of a South Park episode or South Park movie when you complete a story quest.
The writing in the game is spot on. You'll get to watch the South Park characters you're so familiar with do the things they do, in the way they do them, while interacting with one another and with your character. I found the story largely fun and interesting.
I was often quite pleased with the developers' efforts to include as many South Park characters as they could in the game. This could not have been an easy task to accomplish, but the game is solid through-and-through with the show's characters, and because the show has been running so long, these characters bring with them their histories, backdrops, and references that the South Park fan should thoroughly enjoy.
Character customization is very in-depth for a game with such a simplistic visual style. You'll begin the game by choosing a class, and then customizing your looks. As the game progresses, you will find, like, a bajillion different ways to customize your charcter's costume ("gear"), hair, facial features, makeup, and accessories. You'll even find "strap-ons" (for weapons) and "patches" (for armor) that let you add significant bonuses to your gear, letting you really specialize or round out your character and playstyle.
I did make a warning above about the game's humor, but for South Park fans, that (most of the time) means you're in for more of what you enjoy about the show. There were plenty of times I found myself actually laughing out loud at the characters' antics; or at the writing; or at the timing of a joke; or just at South Park being South Park. It's a funny game.
There is also a difficulty slider bar. Early in the game I cranked the difficulty to max and didn't look back, and for me, it was quite rewarding. The window of opportunity to block enemy attacks seemed drastically smaller, necessitating more precise timing, and enemies often didn't go down without a fight. I had to stay on top of my gear choices and customize appropriately. Which buddy to bring into battle with me was also a serious consideration, and more than once I had to stock up on potions.
Overall, it's just a really solid RPG, and I'd strongly recommend it to any South Park fan. I could go on about it, but I feel I've covered most of the relevant aspects of the game, and apparently Steam has a character limit for reviews. :)

While it may be a far cry from San Andreas or Modern GTA games in terms of content, I'd say this one is my personal favorite for its atmosphere, characters, setting, soundtrack, easter eggs, and nostalgic value. With 1980's charm pouring out of its♥♥♥♥♥ it makes of a unique entry in the series, being riddled with several nods and references to events, and Movies/TV shows (notably Miami Vice and Scarface). The gameplay is your run-in-the-mill post-GTA III formula a.k.a a free-roam sandbox. You go on missions to kill people while protecting and optionally developing your own dirty business that will eventually pay for itself to eventually achieve vengeance. While the story is linear, being a sandbox game, you have plenty of freedom. In addition, you have several sidequests, such as Vigilante and Ambulance mission, or item collecting, with worthwhile rewards, like increased Max Health or Missile-Firing Choppers. The game supports both Keyboard+Mouse and Gamepad modes, which puts this game ahead of its time in this particular aspect.
The cons are fairly simple fixes. Being a pre-HD era game, the game isn't optimized for Widescreen monitors, and while there is an in-game option for Widescreen, it steches the HUD and just crops the top and bottom. This can be fixed either by playing it in 4:3, or via simple mods for true, uncropped/unstretched Widescreen. Another issue that may affect most modern rigs is that you may have trouble getting the game to run. This again can be fixed through simple tweaks.
If you're gonna get into the GTA games and don't mind playing something that's only a decade old, this entry is definitely one that shouldn't be overlooked.
DO NOT buy this whatever you heard about it.

My first foray into the Shadowrun world was many years ago, on the SNES.
Back then, being young and still in my "Honeymoon Period" of gaming, the game meant alot to me. The atmosphere, the music, the style, the story....
Shadowrun Returns has surprised me.
While I hoped the game would be good, I also expected it to be rather NOT good.
However, I'm very much enjoying this game.
While the graphics are acceptable to look at, and although the lack of a rotating camera is kind of a disappointment, the game and story has been quite engaging.
I enjoy the turn-based combat, positioning my team and managing their remaining moves, spending them on "moving, or attacking or healing" and the story has been fun, despite me not quite getting that ol' atmospheric feeling I got from Shadowrun on the SNES, all those years ago, but that's not to say the game doesn't have it's own charm, to make up for that.
My only complaint really, apart from the lack of a rotating camera, is that the game-system that determines "points of interaction" seems underdeveloped. It is certainly adequate, to take part in the interactive story of the game and the combat supplies the "necessaries" for it to feel like a fun game, I just feel like, after searching for clues in games like Fallout 3, or The Elder Scrolls series, that the system in Shadowrun seems rather obvious, forced and "on rails".
This is not a problem however as, like I said... The story is fun and it's engaging being part of it... And the combat is enjoyable.
The bottom line is... I feel that Shadowrun Returns is perfectly reasonable as a game. I'd recommend it... I just wanted so much more. It's lacking that "Next Gen" aspect that I was hoping for - something truly groundbreaking, or at least incorporating the ideas in modern games that work.
Shadowrun is a good game. The engine is adequate... But I hope for far better to come, from future games in the Shadowrun Universe.
That being said, I look forward to experiencing Player-Made missions in Shadowrun Returns. I think that, as a tool for telling an interactive story, it's going to be pretty decent.
While it takes some of your own imagination to really appreciate the game.... If you can manage to give that, then I expect some enjoyable stories to be woven with this engine.
So my overall rating would be GOOD, not great (and certainly not what I hoped)... But a steadfast source of enjoyment nonetheless.

Alright, so I have never played an XCOM game before, or even a game of it's genre, but I got instantly hooked. There is nothing quite like it. Missions are full of nail-biting suspense; your soldier's lives are decided by your tactical and management skills.

The campaign is there, but it is a tiny part of the whole XCOM experience. There's cinematics, but they're more in the background. The real meat of the game is through various missions, whether Story-specific ones, or Alien Abduction/Crash Site and Terror Missions. Character customization is actually well done, and trying to create a custom squad, with different names and nationalities is a blast.  Just... don't expect them to live long...
An awesome all-around package that's meant to be played multiple times, XCOM is for any fan of tactical turn based combat. Like I said before, I had never played a single XCOM before, but I'm wishing I did because the game is like no other.

Lay out a strategy and keep your fingers crossed, you're in for a bumpy ride.

FTL is one of those games that just defies classification. At it's core it's an RTS: you order your crew around your ship, fighting off boarders and putting out fires (literally). So what is FTL, really? It's damn fun.

XCOM:Enemy Unknown is one of my personal favorite games. The gameplay is diverse and impressive and you can find yourself immersed after playing the game for only a few hours. Firaxis has managed to create a game almost infinitely replayable, and they've managed to create a game that you'll WANT to play an infinite amount of times. The graphics on this game are also very impressive, if your computer can handle them. Textures are very detailed and the sound design is top notch. Ambient noises, such as the aliens chilling sound effects, resonate as you try to take your unit safely across the map. The single player campaign by itself is deeply immersive and fun, but you can also team up with 3 other friends for some co-op action. The melee combat is visceral and intensely satisfying, you'll go out of your way to bash zambi skulls in when you're not incinerating them, impaling them, electrifying them, or blowing them up with a variety of weapon upgrades and traps.
There's also a pretty deep three pronged skill tree where you can develop either your survival, parkour, or melee combat skills. The agility tree is particularily interesting giving you a much wider selection of acrobatic maneuvers to help you navigate Harran or run circles around zombies.
I've barely gotten into the meat of the game, but even at this point I would highly recommend this title.

First off: teleporting zeds is gone, and only happens when they are unable to get out of a spot. the medic is actually a fun class, but is heavily overrelied on just like the first game unless you force your team to go without one.  Coordination with a lot of public games leaves a lot to be desired, but when you get that one set of people that communicates and understands when to flee from an area is when the game starts shining again.  The perk leveling outright is far easier in this game and less irritating in the first game, which literally encouraged you only really doing one thing to contribute to the team.  In KF2, this has been redone so that just by striking it you gain exp as if you're the killer of it.  Your kill count no longer becomes something to work for in this game unlike the first game which was all it ever encouraged.
Sprinting despite what a lot of KF1 people might have you beleive is more of a breathing room thing that was sorely needed rather than to be hated. why should a situation fall apart just because, that one spider took your attention too long or, if your medic is dead, your bezerker is dead...why should your team now be entirely screwed because you can't beat the fleshpound to the door for 2 vital seconds to get everyone reorganized?  trust me its not a bad thing to add things to make the game more enjoyable.  Also with the new perk choices what seems like a silly idea becomes more of a matter of preferance and playstyle.  Don't like only being the rpg weilding Demo?  Grap the level 5 Shock Trooper perk skill for that very helpful 20% reload and stumble power increase...nothing says entertainment more than a flying skrake or Fleshpound suddenly vulnerable for hammering.
Yes some things changed overall as well: medic no long gets overpowered armor...oh well.  Support welder no longer welds quickly...ohwell, they can repair a broken down door they have with this new system of theirs for it.  A demo can trap a door so it explodes when broken.  Knowing your role is still more important...even more so now...than being the top on the leader board.  No more having a commando need to chase down stalkers for their level...things like that are a thing of the past with the exp system as it is now. you even get exp for 'spotting' them even if you don't kill it...why not?   There's still room for skill as a bezerker, especially with the parry system.  If it can't keep wailing on you it can't destroy you.  Sharpshooter is as it was from the first game, but Gunslinger is the perk separating the handgun proficiency from the main part of it.  not too keen on that one but hey...at least they separate themselves with differing choices in perk skills.
Most quit at the badly done damage update before they fixed it, not bothering to see if they changed it going back to killing floor 1 and staying there.  That's fine.  I've played both enough to know...I think I'll prefer this one more. also conviniently all the funny things stated about content difference? silly.  They both have their ups and downs, but the arguements are stale and overdone to death...if you feel like getting your feet wet in Zed blood again and Killing Floor 1 didn't have that chemestry for you and your friends, give this one a shot.

Dead Space was one of the first survival horror games I ever had the joy of playing. My friend gave it to me for a night and told me to play it on the Xbox 360, I was expecting an average horror experience, a few jumpscares here and there, nothing special. What I got was truly overwhelming and forced me to exit the games numerous times.
I had to go out and buy this game, I HAD to, and so I did. It quite literally took me around a month to complete; not because it is a truly long game, because I couldn't continuously play it without taking a breather to relax myself. This game puts you on edge, you never know what to expect and you never know when it is going to happen. Throughout my first playthrough I was constantly checking my surroundings, ensuring that I was safe, although when I turned around a necromorph was staring me directly in the face I was on the xbox 360 dashboard quicker than I could've shot the thing.
Although, even after exiting the games countless times, I did not want to stop playing, it's something about Dead Space which made me want to just keep playing, keep discovering the secrets of the USS Ishimura, and keep discovering the eery and isolated atmosphere that Dead Space provides so brilliantly.
Overall, I would give this game a solid 10/10, and the only thing I could complain about is that there is no character development for Isaac (main character) whatsoever, as he doesn't have a voice! You quite literally just hear him moan in pain for 11 hours of gameplay. It still doesn't stop Dead Space from being one of the most solid and enjoyable games I've ever had the joy of playing, and would highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of survival horror games.
Oh yeah, a small precaution for future reference:
After playing Dead Space, every time you hear 'twinkle twinkle, little star' you'll most likely cower in fear.

A pure, uncensored South Park experience - take that for what it's worth.  Those with a sense of humor who laugh at jokes because they're funny and don't back away because it's politically incorrect, will adore this game.  Those who are squemish, who say "You can't joke about that!", or who think some things should be off limits, steer clear.
For those with an adult attitude, this game is hilarious, witty and charming.  The jokes are pure South Park all the way through, and you'll be chuckling through it all.  As funny as South Park is on Comedy Central, it's still holding a lot back, which is what makes this game so much fun - it's uncensored, unbound, pure South Park, the way the creators, Matt and Trey, intended it to be.  Nothing is off limits, and you'll be laughing all the harder for it.
Beneath the humor is a solid RPG experience too; everything from spells, potions, PP and HP management, armor, weapons, etc.  It's all here, it's balanced, and it's a thoroughly enjoyable experience for the gamer.  Exploring, finishing all quests and beating the game took me about 19 hrs, though you could probably see and do everything in 15.
I recommend this game wholeheartedly, and can't wait for a sequel!!

Fantastic game. The whole way through, the experience feels like watching a really good South Park episode or South Park movie, and the game is a *really* solid RPG, to boot.
But the game isn't without its flaws. I want to spend a few paragraphs on some criticisms of the game, and then we'll talk about what makes the game awesome.
The game feels heavily "consolized." Loading screens are far more frequent than they should be and the controls often don't make much sense. Throughout the game your character will be taught "magic spells" from various NPCs. Each time you learn a spell, you are taught a series of controls to use that spell. However, these spells can be used both in and out of combat, and in both situations the controls are different from one another—and in neither situation is the spell invoked the same way the game inititally taught you!
Your out-of-combat utilities (like firing a ranged weapon at something in the environment or sending a buddy to perform a task) are equally awkward to select and use.
Now, here I should note that I played with a controller attached to a PC. I started the game with a keyboard/mouse but changed very, very early on to give my normal gaming posture a rest (I play games a lot with the keyboard/mouse), and also because South Park: The Stick of Truth seemed to be tailored more toward a controller. Perhaps the controls are better with a keyboard/mouse, but using a controller felt awkward in many parts of the game. But not in combat. In combat the controls felt great. More on that later, though.
On top of that, the game's humor can be off-putting in some parts. This isn't a real criticism so much as it is a warning—it IS South Park, after all! The show has a reputation of making comedy material out of even the most sensitive of topics, and this game also doesn't hold back. I like to think of myself as a fairly easy-going guy and I try not to take many things too seriously, but there were parts in this game that I felt myself somewhat rushing through or avoiding just to get away from an uncomfortable topic.
There's a lot of back-and-forth running around the map in this game, and loading screens are absolutely everywhere. The loading screens are a real slowdown.
So let's see. The loading screens, the really iffy controls in much of the game, and the warning about how the game remains very South Park in its humor are all the things I wanted to make sure to mention. So, now we can talk about the stuff that makes this game a fantastic one!
While moving on the map and navigating menus is often awkward with the game's controls, combat is something the game gets very, very right. As I mentioned earlier, this game is a very solid RPG, and The Stick of Truth's turn-based combat is airtight. This isn't your typical "select an ability and watch what happens" kind of turn-based combat. Here, you'll select an ability, and then you'll influence the outcome of the ability with some simple, but fun controls.
For example, Butters the Paladin has a "Hammer of Justice" ability. To use it, you select it and then choose a target. The game then has you rotate the left control stick in circles to make Butters spin (think Olympic discus tossing), and at just the right instant, press the A button. Succeed, and you'll deal bonus damage to the enemy! If you mess up, Butters will still deal damage, but not as much. Again, this is coming from the perspective of using a gamepad to control the game; I'm sure this is different for a mouse/keyboard, but the principle is the same.
Combat is filled with awesome stuff like this. When you are attacked, most of the time you are given the chance to block some of the enemy's damage by pressing A at just the right time. Some enemy attacks strike multiple times, requiring multiple well-timed blocks! Different enemy attacks have different timings as well, so you'll always need to be on your guard.
These combat mechanics make even turn-based combat a very active affair. The action is fast and challenging, so you'll need to be spot on with your controls. Thankfully, controls in combat are responsive and intuitive, and anytime there's some ambiguity about what to do in battle, there are useful tooltips and pop-ups to remind you of how to use an ability.
While combat is great fun, the game also very often presents you with multiple ways of dealing with foes. Sometimes you can distract them and sneak by. Other times you can use the environment to defeat your foes without having to confront them. Keen awareness of your surroundings and appropriate use of your abilities out of combat can speed up your progress and yield satisfying results.
It should be noted that if you sneak by enemies, you probably won't get experience for dealing with them. But in the cases where you can use the environment to defeat them, you'll be awarded experience as if you had battled them!
There are many quests to accomplish throughout the game, and a few side quests can be completed as you progress. As far as questing is concerned, it's your typical RPG fare—pick up a quest, complete the objectives, turn the quest in. The game does nothing to revolutionize questing, but it handles questing very well.
The story-based quests, however, are always greatly satisfying to accomplish because you are awarded not only with experience and often loot/money, but also with story exposition done in only the way South Park can. It really does feel like you're earning a little piece of a South Park episode or South Park movie when you complete a story quest.
The writing in the game is spot on. You'll get to watch the South Park characters you're so familiar with do the things they do, in the way they do them, while interacting with one another and with your character. I found the story largely fun and interesting.
I was often quite pleased with the developers' efforts to include as many South Park characters as they could in the game. This could not have been an easy task to accomplish, but the game is solid through-and-through with the show's characters, and because the show has been running so long, these characters bring with them their histories, backdrops, and references that the South Park fan should thoroughly enjoy.
Character customization is very in-depth for a game with such a simplistic visual style. You'll begin the game by choosing a class, and then customizing your looks. As the game progresses, you will find, like, a bajillion different ways to customize your charcter's costume ("gear"), hair, facial features, makeup, and accessories. You'll even find "strap-ons" (for weapons) and "patches" (for armor) that let you add significant bonuses to your gear, letting you really specialize or round out your character and playstyle.
I did make a warning above about the game's humor, but for South Park fans, that (most of the time) means you're in for more of what you enjoy about the show. There were plenty of times I found myself actually laughing out loud at the characters' antics; or at the writing; or at the timing of a joke; or just at South Park being South Park. It's a funny game.
There is also a difficulty slider bar. Early in the game I cranked the difficulty to max and didn't look back, and for me, it was quite rewarding. The window of opportunity to block enemy attacks seemed drastically smaller, necessitating more precise timing, and enemies often didn't go down without a fight. I had to stay on top of my gear choices and customize appropriately. Which buddy to bring into battle with me was also a serious consideration, and more than once I had to stock up on potions.
Overall, it's just a really solid RPG, and I'd strongly recommend it to any South Park fan. I could go on about it, but I feel I've covered most of the relevant aspects of the game, and apparently Steam has a character limit for reviews. :)

To start, coming into this I thought this was going to be just a revamped version of the Sega Genesis Shadowrun title. Keep that in mind if you have not played the Sega Genesis version because this review and my feelings concerning this installment are based on comparisons between the two games. But here are the reasons why I think this new PC version is WAY worse than
it's console predecessor:
1. The word "linear" begins in no way to describe the disgustingly linear nature of this game. You don't really get any side jobs from Johnsons, there are two open areas in the whole game instead of the 4 or 5 from the Genesis tiltle. Furthermore there are no shops, gang hideouts, corporate buildings or abandoned buildings where the supernatural baddies were found in the Sega version. In the latter version you were able to endlessly grind by doing any matter of small job like courier work, matrix runs, larceny and even ones where you'd get paid to go into abandoned buildings and get paid a flat rate per ghoul head you come back with. NONE of that awesome content that made that game more appealing.
2. No random encounters. All the battles are staged and preset. In the Sega game if you get a run to steal something from a corporate HQ you could employ stealth, deck into the matrix while in the building to glean info on the location of your target.
If you didn't trip alarms you could go in the building and come back out without anyone being the wiser. None of that in this new game. Every encounter is scripted with the same number of enemies everytime. You cannot grind levels at all in this game and pretty much have to pick 2 skills to excel at or have a mundane "Jack of All Trades" character who is OK at everything but good or great at nothing. The original plot from the Genesis version was very twisty and turny giving the illusion that there were side storylines going on but there really weren't.
3. Alot of reviews I read about this game really tout the writing of this storyline. I say to these people "Read the story from the Genesis version". It was awesome. It spans four different "suburbs" of Seattle. There are WAY more players in the plot as far as NPC's, everyone has their finger in this pie as far as NPC organizations including all three major corporations, Lonestar, and even a local tribe of native americans, the plot actually climaxes in a tribal land environment which, if memory serves was a 5th open area location you could navigate. There are 2 open areas in this new game with no open doors into other locations other than the cantina where ALL of your vendors, johnsons, and NPC quest givers reside. Main quest NPCs, Johnsons, and Vendors were all scattered over the 4 city locations in the game along with all the different corporate HQ buildings, Lonestar HQ, a prison facility, hotels to rest up and heal. The list never ends.
4. Shadowrunners in this new game are only available for hire when you are anticipating a run. In the Sega version you could hire anyone that you had the cash to hire AND you could opt to hire them just for one job OR until they die. The price to hire a shadowrunner who died on a previous "botched run" will charge you more money if you desire their services again. It was MUCH better. I will say that the newer game has a better selection of shadowrunners though as the original game had characters already at certain high scale clubs or down and dirty dive bars situated in the 4 urban locations of the game. But only being able to use shadowrunners while you're on main story missions is lame. Your not actually going on shadowruns at all. You're on a quest following leads that you are prompted to find.
5. I beat this game in like 4 or 5 hours total gameplay. I am glad I got this game at a discount and I will not be buying the DLC.
There is one more thing I did like better about this version, though it is not a saving grace by any means. You can create your own character from any race you want and there is a much wider variety of character classes to choose from. In the first game you could only be human because the character whose murder you are solving was your brother, your brother was human. Lame. In this one the person whose murder you are solving was your good friend and long time partner in running the shadows so you can be any race you want for that reason. That was a sizeable improvement but not a good trade off for the free roaming you could do in the first game. Also, there is more strategy needed in the battles you have in the new game. If you choose a Decker you better hire some big orc or troll samurais or adepts to absorb bullets for you or frustration may get the better of you. I abandoned my original elf decker build for a troll samurai because of how badly I was getting squished (on Easy difficulty).
Not the worst game I spent $15 on but it definitely inhabits the bottom of the barrel with the worst of 'em.

This game is the perfect end to the Arkham series. The main story was well written, but the ending scheme is too much for players that don't pursue the "platinum" status on games.

The game has the right amount of references to the comics, making the experience even greater to long term fans of the Dark Knight. The endings schemes was the Achilles heel of the game for me. Dying light is the lovechild of Dead Island and Mirror's Edge, with a sprinkle of Left 4 Dead within it's Be the Zombie Mode.
The single player campaign by itself is deeply immersive and fun, but you can also team up with 3 other friends for some co-op action. The melee combat is visceral and intensely satisfying, you'll go out of your way to bash zambi skulls in when you're not incinerating them, impaling them, electrifying them, or blowing them up with a variety of weapon upgrades and traps.
There's also a pretty deep three pronged skill tree where you can develop either your survival, parkour, or melee combat skills. The agility tree is particularily interesting giving you a much wider selection of acrobatic maneuvers to help you navigate Harran or run circles around zombies.
I've barely gotten into the meat of the game, but even at this point I would highly recommend this title.

Although this is certainly not the scariest game I have ever played, it did provide a few good jump scares, an eerie atmosphere, and a constent sense of dread. If you are looking for a violent, gory, horror type of gameplay, Dead Space knocks it out of the park. If you are looking for something that will keep you up at night jumping at your own shadow, then you better should look elsewhere for games such as Outlast or Alient Isolation.
Dead Space takes you through several different types of environments which keeps most of the experiences fresh. Unfortunately, you will end up revisiting several areas and looking at the interior of a ship does become bland after several hours. That being said, the graphics are fantastic considering how old this game is.
Much of the weaponry is very fun to use. Not all of the weapons is simply a point and click (although most are). Using secondary fire options and the nature of the guns takes a bit of getting used to but can have very satisfying, gory results. You will likely find your favorite 2, maybe 3, weapons and you will use and upgrade those throughout the game. As a result, weapon variety leaves a bit to be desired.
The difficulty was decent, but I haven't tried the insane mode just yet. You will likely die a couple times through a particular playthrough if you are an experienced gamer with third person shooters.
Overall, this game was fantastic. There are some areas for improvement (hopefully they were fixed in Dead Space 2) but will definitely entertain you for many hours and has a lot of room for replayability. Definitely a game worth picking up, especially if it is on sale.

Dead Space relies very heavily on jumpscares and shocking imagery for it's horror. Don't get me wrong, it can certainly get quite tense every now and again, but it never really starts to feel like a 'Survival Horror' game as the game is fairly generous with both ammunition and health. Unless you're playing on higher difficulties you're probably not going to find the game all too challenging to be honest.
That being said, Dead Space ironically excels at one of the aspects often done poorly in horror titles: It's combat. Almost every weapon in your arsenal is viable in any situation, giving you some very refreshing freedom to find a playstyle that suits you. The violence and gore is definitely also satisfying for those of us that enjoy watching limbs come flying off. The voiceacting is solid and the soundwork in general is very tight.
You are very rarely (if ever) bored while playing Dead Space as you'll find yourself utterly immersed in it's great combat almost all the time, except for when the game gives you a break, typically in the form of exposition-sequences or fairly decent puzzles. While you don't have to be a math student to get over these hurdles they can definitely throw a spanner in the works every now and again.
7/10 - Complete with a compelling story with a few surprising twists along the way I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes gore, violence and a character that controls like a tank. The only real downsides to this game I can think of off the top of my head is perhaps the slight lack of challenge, the unreasonably confusing map, and the fact that it has some severe issues with Mous/Keyboard controls. A gamepad is strongly recommended for this title.

I know I don't have much playtime in the game, but I've been getting really into this game the past few days after being told of the rebalances. I'm just going to have a list of what I think are pros and con.
Pros:
1.) The perk level system in this game feels far better than KF. I found it a bit easier to level up perks that took a while in KF 1.
2.) I think multiple bosses is an amazing idea and adds a little bit more fun when you reach the boss wave.
3.) Versus seems like it would be fun to have, though I would have preferred the KFO mode from the first game. For those that don't know, KFO was Objective based and felt like a mini-campaign.
4.) The new perks that are out right now are really fun to play with.
5.) The options you get every 5 levels for your perks offers a bit of variety to each perk and it can be fun to try some of the other perk skills out.
6.) This one is a bit mixed from what I saw, but I don't really mind the skins that much. The only thing I bought in-game was the box armour for $4 and I love it to death. That and some of the skins do look pretty good, as well as some of the cosmetics I've seen on others.
7.) The double EXP weekend + increased drop rate on items is also something I think is nice to have to help those that want to level through normal gameplay.
8.) The new voices for everyone is really fun to listen too and can be funny, at times.
9.) The lock-on feature for the medic guns is awesome and helps newer players, as well as experienced ones, be much more reliable as a medic.
10.) The game feels really balanced in its current state, but the SWAT is a little too powerful on versus mode. However, I like to blame the poor balancing for versus instead of the perk itself.
11.) Some of the new weapons are really fun and my current favourite is the Pulverizer melee for the Beserker.
12.) You can now create a lobby and make lobbies public, friends only, and private.
Cons:
1.) The versus mode NEEDS a rebalancing. Patriarch is broken as hell with how much damage he does with his melee, berserkers with the movement speed perk skill can outrun Patriarch until his health drains and makes the game last longer than it needs to be, the smaller zeds are somehow much stronger than the Fleshpound and the Scrake, they need to add the other difficulties or make the versus game able to have both medium(7 rounds) and/or long(10 rounds).
3.) The matchmaking option is kind of dumb with how it keep reconnecting me to the same server and, if the server has a custom map that's failing to download, you'll be forced to look through the server browser.
4.) Hans Volter is a bit underwhelming in the games I've played on Suicidal. I see his shield melt by my teammates and it takes the challenge away from the boss wave. The good news is this isn't a common occurrence.
5.) The kick system is either bugged or needs to make it based on majority because I've seen good players get kicked when the voting was 2 votes for yes and 4 votes for no. I rarely see the vote kick poll started, but I've seen this happen twice and I think it's a kind of ridiculous. This can be even worse on versus where the zeds can vote and force the human team to keep a troll, AFK player, or a stubborn medic that refuses to heal so he can get kills to level his perk up.
6.) The start up time is pretty awful. I'm not sure if everyone deals with this, but it takes way too long to start the game up.
7.) Every major update, as far as I know, has reset the settings of the game and require you to fix them every single time.
8.) The "Survivalist" perk doesn't seem very well thought out. Mid way through the skill choices you're stuck with either a medic grenade or a moly and neither of those are better than regular grenades in most situations. They could have had a heavy weapons guy or throwing weapons expert, martial artist(as originally intended), or just add new weapons instead of making a perk that seemed great on paper, but terrible when in play.
This one won't be listed as a con since it's not really important, but I'd love it if the weapon inspection was a bit slower or maybe gave you a key to bind that lets you look at the skin or gun itself. I like the amount of detail on the guns, but it's hard to see with how fast the animations are.
That's a semi-small list of things I think about the game and I hope it helped. This is the first actual review I've ever done so feel free to give me advice or list off a few things you think need to be added. I can update this to include more info and make it better for those that read it.

I was a big fan of the Paper & Pencil RPG since its first edition for its unique and immersive world of cyberpunk-meets-fantasy.  I just finished playing both pre-made campaigns (yes, you can also write & share your own campaigns) called "Dead Man's Switch" in the original game and "DragonFall" in the DLC update.  They fully deliver the atmosphere of the shadowrunner experience in these campaigns, and both storylines play out like good novels - I *highly* recommend playing this game, especially with the DLC update to allow mid-scenario game saves.
It is generally a turn-based combat system where you have several "classes" but you are free to hybridize.  The archetypes include an offensive-spell-wielding Mage, a spirit-summoning Shaman, a computer-hacking Decker, a drone-controlling Rigger, a Chi/martial-artist Physical Adept, and of course the cyberware-laiden Street Samurai.  You also have a choice of playing a human, a dwarf, an elf, an ork or a troll - each with advantages and limitations.  Scenarios are written with multiple ways of success, but choosing a well-suited team for each mission is still critical.  I personally played a human detective-type character who was generally a Physical Adept but with a more diverse skillset, and made sure I had at least a spellcaster and Decker on my runs to cover my bases when possible.  The character generation system is not as detailed as the RPG but you will find the balance and flavor of the development makes the same kind of characters with most of the possible character concepts reconstitutable if you wanted to relive your gaming heydays.
All dialog is text-based, so you only need speakers to listen to the theme music and sound effects.  I am a Linux user, and being able to play this game without a reboot was a *big* plus for me (but I still need Win 7 to make my own campaigns).  The storyline really flows, and I often found myself spending hours non-stop trying to unravel secrets and plan out a larger strategy.  Expect a game to take 50 hours or more to complete - I did Dragonfall in just under 60 hours on Easy without any redos of battles.
One big drawback - this is Single Player only.  No co-op or competitive play.
One word of caution - you play street-savvy shadowrunners (i.e. black-ops for hire) so it is a gritty world with lots of moral grey zones, foul language, blood-spilling violence and innuendo.  This is supposed to be a dystopian future of the mid 21st century, so be ready for some hard-luck stories and tough choices between jepardizing your pay or your conscience, with no hope of making a dent in the struggle between the urban poor and the ultra-rich puppet-master megacorps.  Also, be careful with your choices - they will impact later game play.  Fun times! :D
Take a gander at the game, and review some Let's Play videos to see if you'd get into a game like this.  Personally, it was well worth the price.  Thanks for reading.
