Batman: Arkham Knight, a game that manages to accomplish many feats, despite the hurdles it faced due to its (not so steady as a rock) launch.
As a rather well-seasoned reader of the Batman comic books and graphic novels, an experience such as this and the other games in the Arkham series is most welcome. Having been waiting for this game in particular for years, since the tremendously thrilling and rather daring ending to Arkham City, which is still one of my favourite games, as I continue to cherish its brilliance. After the long years of waiting for this epic conclusion, I can't for a second say that I was disappointed.
The game itself - As a game, a playable experience, Batman: Arkham Knight takes the player, playing as Batman/Bruce Wayne himself on a journey mostly unlike every other adventure he's ever been on. The level design is incredible, pitting you against your foes in imaginative ways, still, the levels are usually as open as you'd like them to be. The city of Gotham has never been depicted in such a beautiful manner, with it constantly being reshaped to keep the game looking fresh as well as giving you other things to adjust to and different sights to behold. The combat that Rocksteady has become famous for, which has often been said to set the bar for combat systems in such third-person adventure games, continues to improve. It feels faster and more fluid than ever before and makes you feel invulnerable once you master the technique of beating Gotham's scum in every way one could imagine, whilst also punishing you, should you become overconfident and forget your basics. The Batmobile is drivable, as you should know if you've already made your way to this review. It is a welcomed addition, due to its genuine Batman feel and empowers the player with the power of what is essentially a high-speed tank. However, personally, the game seems to overuse the batmobile at some points in ways that don't quite seem believable even in the world of Bamtan, for instance: Riddler's race tracks replacing most of his logic puzzles.
The story - Personally, I believe this to be one of the best stories within a game that I've ever witnessed, with the twists and turns that keep it exciting, brutalising Bruce's memories to draw sympathy from the player, immersing them in the want to defeat the villains at hand. The story follows Batman as he tries to stop the Scarecrow from releasinga new, more potent and disastrous version of his infamous fear toxin. As he closes in on the scarecrow and his evil plans, the evil-doer's brand new henchman steps in, in all his mystique. Obviously with a vendetta against the Bat of Gotham, the mysterious new Arkham Knight maintains a sense of urgency throughout the game, as you attempt to uncover the terror that lies beneath his mask. This offers an interesting and exciting section to the main campaign,at times seeming strong enough to support its own subplot.
Graphics - Depending on what device you play Batman: Arkham Knight, you can see huge differences in the level of detail some of these world-renowned developes have gone to. It was a true shame that the launch of the game was completely undermined on PC by the apparently appalling port from consoles.However, having played and completed the game on both the Xbox One and PC (post-patch), I can honestly say that it was worth the wait. The game's beauty hides in the darker details of the characters and the city itself. And if you get the final DLC 'Season of Infamy', the beard gracing Jervis Tetch's face forced my jaw down in awe.
DLC - Sadly, this is the main gripe that I have with the game, although it doesn't spoil the game itself. The vast majority of the dowloadable content is utter tripe, if you really crave more of the side characters, such as Batgirl, Robin, Nightwing and so on, then the first few DLC packs are just for you. Hoever, they are around twenty minutes in length and are as shallow as that 17 year-old blonde girl in high school that everyone liked a little more than made sense. They offer no closure to the stories within the campaign itself and aren't satisfying in the slightest and feel more like a chore than an enjoyable extension of the game. However, the final downloadable content pack called 'Season of Infamy' is the complete opposite, as it offers closure to several characters, such as Mad Hatter, Killer Croc, Mr. Freeze and the tie-up I had really been waiting for since Arkham City: Ra's Al Ghul.
Conclusion - In my opinion, as this entire review is, Batman: Arkham Knight is a gaming masterpiece, its story fulfills the perfect setting to highlight the experience that a developer such as Rocksteady can immerse a player in, providing a gratifying conclusion to the Arkham series. As a game and an overall experience, Arkham Knight delivers on every level.
As this review was written a year and six days after its release, I feel like it is more of an attempt at thanking the hard-working developers at the Rocksteady. And so, thank you for reading, and if anyone at Rocksteady is reading, thank you so much for creating some of the most enjoyable content to me.
If you genuinely wanted a review to see if it's worth buying, I'd say so, whether or not you're a big fan of the Dark Knight. By now, it's pretty cheap , and if you want more, definitely invest in the 'Season of Infamy' as it was a satisfying closure to the masterfully created series,

Easily one of the most entertaining games I have played. I'm not much for the Roguelike/Roguelite series and games which are similar, however I easily spent Eight hours playing with friends, repeatedly trying over and over. I took a break around 12AM EST and found myself playing it again around 2AM until around 6AM. This is a very easy game to lose track of time in, however the difficulty continually spikes whilst playing, which.. Is actually quite fun to work around.
From my gameplay experience with this game, it has promoted teamwork with item combinations between my friends and I, and I have just enjoyed every moment of it.
Pros:
- Easy to understand item system.
- A multitude of classes and characters to choose from, to figure out your own personal playstyle.
- Easy to set-up online multiplayer (Currently only usable in a Beta release).
- One of the most amazing soundtracks I have heard in gaming. After Eight hours, I still want to hear more.
- Up to Six player Cooperative.
- Continually scaling difficulty, which promotes teamwork and makes player develop new strategies.
- Item Collection, and Monster Journals. Each menu option tells you more about the items you use, and the monsters you fight.
- Intuitive Combat System unlike other Roguelike/Roguelite games.
- Combat Focused instead of Platforming Focused unlike most other Roguelikes/Roguelites
Cons:
- Port Forwarding is required for this game, and some ISP's may block the native Port this game uses. (Try using 7777).
- Game Crashes are somewhat present, and if such happens whilst gaming, your data is lost.
- Lag prevalent regardless of Ping of players joining a server.
Regardless of the Cons, I definitely would recommend this game for you. I can easily see myself playing this game for upwards of Fifty hours. The game is even on sale currently (4/5/2015) for 2.49.

Having heard all the hubbub about this game, I decided to give it a try. So the main hook is that it's Resi 4 IN SPACE...WITH SPACE ZOMBIES...AND AN EVIL FUTURE CULT...IN SPAAAAAACE! But in all honesty, the game has enough of an identity to be a loving tribute to its inspirations, the most obvious being films like Event Horizon, The Thing, and more obviously, Aliens. Resource management was something of a breath of fresh air for this modern gamer that had me counting every shot and wailing in frustration when I had to improvise with the crappy TK system. HOWEVER, I ended up feeling more frustrated than scared. While the visuals certainly sell me on this bleak future and the gameplay has all the makings of a hearkening back to old-school survival horror, the actual attempts at horror are far too predictable. The narrative is too familiar, too well-tread to really throw any surprises at the player. It's all gross-out horror all the time, with blood spewing from every orifice and Isaac flaying bodies or being flayed in overlong, ridiculously silly death animations that stop being scary the tenth time you see them. Of course there's an evil space cult that worships an evil alien rock that causes people to commit suicide. Of course the protagonist is slowing going crazy. And of course the government is evil in the future. True, its world alludes to its inspirations, but the game sometimes feels like it's trying way too hard to scare us. In fact, the scariest part of this game is how teeth-grindingly annoying it can get. Personally, when you fight the controls while trying to fight the enemies, that's not "a geniune survival horror experience". That's just frustrating. This is a bit tangential, but Silent Hill never quite had this problem, to cite a more traditional approach to the genre. You had the option to run right past the enemies because the game acknowledged that the combat was poor. In this game, combat is a main focus and it gets extremely chaotic and frustrating on the later levels. What should be a tense and twitchy fight for survival ends up being a dreary, tedious slog of memorizing where enemies jump out at you so you don't have to restart for the umpteeth time. And watch out for the necros in the 11th chapter that more really fast. I guarentee that you will want to chew a leather sandwich with nails while fighting them. Despite my gripes, this game is still a great ride despite running out of steam towards the end. Try it out for those wanting to see a major studio take a chance with a horror-themed property before AAA studios declared horror dead (which it isn't and will never be). Just don't expect anything really special in terms of a narrative if you are also a connoisseur of sci-fi horror. And play on normal difficulty setting for the least amount of frustration, unless you're a masochist like me and play on the second-to-hardest difficulty and die. A LOT.

Batman: Arkham Knight, a game that manages to accomplish many feats, despite the hurdles it faced due to its (not so steady as a rock) launch.
As a rather well-seasoned reader of the Batman comic books and graphic novels, an experience such as this and the other games in the Arkham series is most welcome. Having been waiting for this game in particular for years, since the tremendously thrilling and rather daring ending to Arkham City, which is still one of my favourite games, as I continue to cherish its brilliance. After the long years of waiting for this epic conclusion, I can't for a second say that I was disappointed.
The game itself - As a game, a playable experience, Batman: Arkham Knight takes the player, playing as Batman/Bruce Wayne himself on a journey mostly unlike every other adventure he's ever been on. The level design is incredible, pitting you against your foes in imaginative ways, still, the levels are usually as open as you'd like them to be. The city of Gotham has never been depicted in such a beautiful manner, with it constantly being reshaped to keep the game looking fresh as well as giving you other things to adjust to and different sights to behold. The combat that Rocksteady has become famous for, which has often been said to set the bar for combat systems in such third-person adventure games, continues to improve. It feels faster and more fluid than ever before and makes you feel invulnerable once you master the technique of beating Gotham's scum in every way one could imagine, whilst also punishing you, should you become overconfident and forget your basics. The Batmobile is drivable, as you should know if you've already made your way to this review. It is a welcomed addition, due to its genuine Batman feel and empowers the player with the power of what is essentially a high-speed tank. However, personally, the game seems to overuse the batmobile at some points in ways that don't quite seem believable even in the world of Bamtan, for instance: Riddler's race tracks replacing most of his logic puzzles.
The story - Personally, I believe this to be one of the best stories within a game that I've ever witnessed, with the twists and turns that keep it exciting, brutalising Bruce's memories to draw sympathy from the player, immersing them in the want to defeat the villains at hand. The story follows Batman as he tries to stop the Scarecrow from releasinga new, more potent and disastrous version of his infamous fear toxin. As he closes in on the scarecrow and his evil plans, the evil-doer's brand new henchman steps in, in all his mystique. Obviously with a vendetta against the Bat of Gotham, the mysterious new Arkham Knight maintains a sense of urgency throughout the game, as you attempt to uncover the terror that lies beneath his mask. This offers an interesting and exciting section to the main campaign,at times seeming strong enough to support its own subplot.
Graphics - Depending on what device you play Batman: Arkham Knight, you can see huge differences in the level of detail some of these world-renowned developes have gone to. It was a true shame that the launch of the game was completely undermined on PC by the apparently appalling port from consoles.However, having played and completed the game on both the Xbox One and PC (post-patch), I can honestly say that it was worth the wait. The game's beauty hides in the darker details of the characters and the city itself. And if you get the final DLC 'Season of Infamy', the beard gracing Jervis Tetch's face forced my jaw down in awe.
DLC - Sadly, this is the main gripe that I have with the game, although it doesn't spoil the game itself. The vast majority of the dowloadable content is utter tripe, if you really crave more of the side characters, such as Batgirl, Robin, Nightwing and so on, then the first few DLC packs are just for you. Hoever, they are around twenty minutes in length and are as shallow as that 17 year-old blonde girl in high school that everyone liked a little more than made sense. They offer no closure to the stories within the campaign itself and aren't satisfying in the slightest and feel more like a chore than an enjoyable extension of the game. However, the final downloadable content pack called 'Season of Infamy' is the complete opposite, as it offers closure to several characters, such as Mad Hatter, Killer Croc, Mr. Freeze and the tie-up I had really been waiting for since Arkham City: Ra's Al Ghul.
Conclusion - In my opinion, as this entire review is, Batman: Arkham Knight is a gaming masterpiece, its story fulfills the perfect setting to highlight the experience that a developer such as Rocksteady can immerse a player in, providing a gratifying conclusion to the Arkham series. As a game and an overall experience, Arkham Knight delivers on every level.
As this review was written a year and six days after its release, I feel like it is more of an attempt at thanking the hard-working developers at the Rocksteady. And so, thank you for reading, and if anyone at Rocksteady is reading, thank you so much for creating some of the most enjoyable content to me.
If you genuinely wanted a review to see if it's worth buying, I'd say so, whether or not you're a big fan of the Dark Knight. By now, it's pretty cheap , and if you want more, definitely invest in the 'Season of Infamy' as it was a satisfying closure to the masterfully created series,

Your soldiers can die and your supporters can abandon the cause. You can change their names, their hair, face, race, armor, colors, ect. But not their sex, so no sexy army of alien killing women for you unless you throw all the men out the nearest airlock.
You can turn some of your soldiers into biological marvels or cybernetic titans that literally punch aliens in the face and gun them down with a giant minigun, among other later upgrades. Eventually some can even tap into their psychic potential, to mind-control aliens and so on.
Assuming you have everything, there are generally three stories running between each other. There is of course the base 'save earth' story, the ' badass triad guy with intel' and the 'crazy humans determined to fight the system, man.'
At this point I haven't played beyond 10 hours but having seen a playthrough of the base game, I feel I can say its at the very least a must buy during a Steam sale.

Right off the bat I can say this... taking Ridley Scott's Alien, Paul W.S. Anderson's Event Horizon and John Carpenter's The Thing....Slamming them together into one survival horror Sci-Fi game was BRILLIANT!!!
Now I will admit that this game was a little bit lacking in subtle undertones in the horror department and was relying more on jump scares  but not all games can be like the early Silent Hill games. However all that is made up by the environment of USG Ishimure and how claustrophobic you feel in its lonely dark corridors.
The combat focus of not relying on head shots but instead dismemberment was a very nice touch. This gear shift in tactics makes your choice of weapons to carry very important. In a game like Resident Evil 4 a fully automatic weapon aimed at the head of a zombie will have the same result as a magnum but in Dead Space your fully automatic Pulse Rifle is almost useless against a necromorph and you'll just end up waste ammo. Using "tools" were by far the best weapons in the whole game such as the Plasma Cutter or the Ripper which adds to the " your a engineer on a mining ship" motif.
The story of Issac Clark does seem a bit dull at times but what more do you want from a guy that doesn't talk and only grunts while swinging his arms about or stomping his feet. Now the universe that the game takes place in is outstanding in my opinion since a lot of Sci-Fi aspect are very true. For instance the idea of "planet cracking" for resources isn't far from the truth. Some day in the future we will find ourselves mining the stars for ore and metals. These little things in the background of the plot makes the nerd in me giddy. The use of Anti-gravity tech and a "stasis module" brings another level of depth to the game play mechanics in the areas of puzzles and combat. By using the Stasis on rushing enemies you can slow them down for a brief moment to tear them apart with your weapon in hand, while the Anti-gravity will allow you to alter parts of the environment around to navigate through obstacles and ferry important items.
Even after playing through the game years back I still do enjoy coming back to it ever now and then with a big smile on my face.  So if you like a gore filled Sci-Fi nightmare where you find yourself being spooked by the sounds of tapping on metal or pipes blowing off steam at just the right time where it makes you stain your desk chair with brown goo then pick up a copy of this game, Dim the lights, put on a beef pair of headphones and maybe scotchgard your chair in case you get a bit jumpy from things going BOO!

This is a great turn-based RPG and also kind of an interactive episode of South Park. If you like the show, then you are going to like (and understand) the jokes, the characters and the art style. Given that they have struggled for a long time to achieve this game, I believe they were successful in translating the show into a game language and, at the same time, in maintaining its identity.
Overall, the game mechanics are fun and engaging, and keep you at the same time alert and entertained during the combats. I encountered minor issues with quick-time events during the execution of some special abilities. Mostly they were due to the fact that the background and the characters are so colorful that at times it was difficult to notice before timeout that a button press was being requested.
The game also has some minor bugs related to ocasional skin loading and update of the amount of treasure in some areas of the map. However, these bugs do not get much in the way of the playing experience.
The major complaint I have about this game is the replayability factor. You become so emerged in the South Park universe that, once the main quest is over, you get the urge to freely explore the town and get more of the sensation that you are part of that world. However, there is very little left to do once the main story is over, since the town sort of reboots and even some of the side quests become unavailable. Although this is understandable, since the game is not meant to be a South Park sandbox or even a true open-world game, the idea is very attractive, so if you are a fan you can't help but feel a bit of disappointment at the end of the game.
Aside from that, I highly recommend the game for fans of the show who also like (or don't mind playing) RPGs. It is a really fun and engaging experience, and I sincerely hope there is a sequel on the way.

This review touches on both the base campaign that comes with Shadowrun Returns and its newest DLC: Dragonfall.
Dead Man's Switch, the original campaign that comes with Shadowrun Returns, was a fun, if not flawed RPG experience. Although the story was compelling, certain conceits associated with the relatively small budget and kickstarter origins hampered the overall experience. This included a somewhat linear story, few side quests, a lack of a proper save-game system, coupled with a combat system that clearly favored certain classes over others.
With the most recent patch and the new official campaign, Dragonfall, Harebrained Studios appear to have eliminated most of the criticism inherent to the original experience. In many ways, Dragonfall is the game longtime fans of the Shadowrun license were looking for when Shadowrun Returns was released. This time around, the excellent writing, complex characters,  and intriguing atmosphere are matched with rebalanced combat, great side quests,  and an overall stronger RPG experience. This also includes a much needed "save-anywhere" feature.Plus the new setting, Berlin, is much more compelling the classic "sprawl" locale which is  common to this genre. In short, Dragonfall improves on Dead Man's Switch in nearly every way and is a must have for fans of classic RPGs, Sci-Fi, and turn-based combat alike. Highly recommended.

I frantically attempt to vent atmosphere in my ship to combat the fires that are slowly raging out of control. Just as my oxygen content drops to lethal levels, an enemy missile destroys my oxygen generator. I watch in complete helplessness as my crew dwindles one by one, the last one gasping his last before I see the game over screen. Again.
Faster Than Light is a difficult roguelike that for all the tiems you'll die, is strangely enchanting. It's definitely a balancing act. Do you attempt to save the space station from giant man eating spiders, or do you leave the station to it's fate to drift across the empty void? Do you take the pirates bribery, or do you say "Nay!" and open fire? There's a lot of content packed into this tiny game, and decisions can either benefit you or cost you dearly. And no, "friendly" controlled space is no safer than enemy controlled space; I can vouch for that.
If you want a difficult yet utterly charming game that you're destined to die in, you can't do much better than FTL, and at 10 bucks, you'll definitely get your money's worth.

A crowning achievement of strategy, one of the best if not THE BEST strategy game I've ever played. Seriously, it even made me change my mind about turn based combat. It is unfourtunately not without it's flaws.
As tense as it makes the game, the difficulty does get kind of silly, especially when the Aliens are able to turn your guys into zombies and throw floating machine gun things at you. This is happening just as you figured out you can research something other than second hand nerf guns.
Speaking of weapons, everything other than the before-mentioned nerf guns both look and sound really cool. The laser sniper even does the Mass Effect folding gun thing. The aliens however start with plasma weapons and eventually go all the way up to the floating machine gun things I mentioned earlier.
The alien types are all nicely varied, different strategies and weapons have to be employed to beat each one, even if they do get a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t later on in the game.
And now you can play it with giant robots and super soldiers I honestly don't know what could make this game better, maybe some way of rewarding soldiers who actually hit somet- oh wait, you can. The medals system is a cool way to provide passive buffs to soldiers without the need for gene therapy and can be transferred on to the Super Soldiers and Giant robots.
I do have a few complaints with this new DLC though, Normal has been "balanced" I didn't even finish the base game, partly because it was so hard and partly because there were only like five maps in total that got really boring after a while. But now I'm about a quarter of the way into the game and I still haven't suffered a single loss, granted I am playing on normal whereas in the base game my manorexia wouldn't let me play on anything other than classic, which I've heard has been made harder, well the balances are probably for the best then.
On the subject of harder difficulties, there's a new alien type that cloaks and strangles your soldiers, at this point they aren't anything other than a nuisance, because if you have everyone close together then you can just get him on overwatch as he goes to strangle the soldier. Unless he's gone for a sniper or someone that is for some reason completely isolated from the rest of the squad.
The DLC also fixes a ridiculous amount of bugs and adds general polish to the game, soldiers can now speak in the language of their country, so we don't get Russians speaking fluent English in an American accent anymore, there are more customization options for the troops and soldiers on overwatch tend not to shoot through walls anymore.
Overall, the base game and the DLC are absolutely brilliant, I would reccomend buying them both together and starting with the DLC though as that brings so many balances and fixes to the table it's not really worth it to play the base game anymore.

Half-Life 2 is extremely well-made and passionately executed. So often the game makes you chuckle in disbelief, press the "F9" (load last save) key because you feel you *must* see that breathtaking sequence again and in overall it makes you replay it time and time again. This game is, in simple words, an astounding accomplishment.
Exceptionally well thought-out storyline and immersive experience; we see everything from Gordon's eyes. Half-Life is unique in the sense that you are not the intended game's protagonist, the game's protagonist is YOU. Everything is left up to your own interpretation, understanding and words. There's so much to say about the saga of Half-Life (because yes, the Episodes as well as the first game and its two expansions, OF and BS, are just as fantastic), but words are weak to convey justice to such a magnificent game. In my opinion, it is simply the best first-person shooter of all time. The most well thought-out and influential, at least. Even though the typical "dystopia-alien invasion" storyline is quite common these days, Valve found a way to make it unique. I believe what makes Half-Life stand out from everything else is that Valve grabbed a storyline which is now common and sometimes hackneyed and made it BELIEVABLE. They made it feel REALISTIC and BELIEVABLE to the player, and crafted a wonderful, unusual protagonist which was given somewhat of a story but the rest is filled by you; this protagonist makes this absurd world of aliens, torture, blood, fear and dystopia work, no matter how unrealistic it may seem.
Half-Life, the entire franchise, has haunted me for a long time. The story is as rich and big in complexity as it is in enigma, so many questions are conveyed and yet left unanswered. I love the game, I'm in complete love with Gordon Freeman and the other characters (specially Barney) and with how well all the chapters in this game were made. Ravenholm is capable to fetch a perception of sadness and fear, the rebellion and the uprising elude feelings of both hope and doom, questions of *what* is going to happen arise and more disappointment appears because there are *no* definite answers, at all. Valve keeps throwing stuff at you and you don't ever have enough time to process it. And when you sit down to think about it, too many answers are possible. Valve takes the whole "open to interpretation" notion at a whole new level.
I'd recommend this game to everyone, and if you don't have this game in your Steam library, I'M JUDGING YOU REAL HARD HERE. No, but it's a must-play, even if it isn't your type of game. Even with how exceptional the game is, however, many people may not and do not enjoy it, not only because it might not be "their cup of tea", but because Half-Life 2 is a game which requires patience (not as much as the first, though!), and it may not be a good game to someone who plays games to slouch or relax a bit, or to play for a short while. It's pretty intense and hectic. However, I'd still recommend it nonetheless.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn based strategy game.
As far as many of you know this game is a remake of the original X-Com games, and therefore there are two possibilities. One is that the game is bad and the second that the game is great, so the question is on which side is XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
The story : well what can be said about the story ? you take role as the commander of the XCOM project that it is the last line of defense of the earth against the unknown ( Aliens )  enemy, your role is to lead you soldiers to victory, expand your base, make difficult choices, and of course to defend earth by any cost. The story itself is just a side bonus I guess. You won't really follow it and to be truthfully the game could be without storyline.
Gameplay : This is where the fun begins, the gameplay is all about : researching the aliens, creating new technology and weapons, lead soldiers to victory by turn based tactics mechanics, carefully making decisions and the most important thing the difficulty of the game can be changed by the player, but it is recommend to play Ironman mode which doesn't allow you to load you last saves in order to experience the real meaning of making decisions.
Bugs : There are a few "bugs" that will make the game to be a little awkward, the camera angle will make you see a wall when in reality you should see you soldier fire at an enemy, there will be sometimes a problem when trying to lead the soldier to the second or third floor. Other than that everything is okay.
Sound : There isn't too much to say about the sound except that it is exactly how it should be
Graphcis : What can be said about the graphics ? especially of a game that came out in 2012, I can only think of one word "Good"
AI\Difficulty : This is one of the strong points that XCOM has, The AI is far from being stupid ( like in most FPS games nowadays ) and there are times when you will be utterly destroyed by them ( If you play at the more higher difficulty when you have no experience, like me ). The difficulty of the game is impressive, you may be asking yourself "what can be so impressive by the difficulty level ?" well let me answer you to that, the game accepts both casual\biggener or new to the franchise and accepts to the hardcore and experienced gamers to the X-com game. You can add some "mods" in order to make the game more challenging or easier it only depends on you
Summary : XCOM Enemy Unknown is one of the best 2012 games, its challenging, fun, interesting and has infinite replayability. The game accepts both casual and hardcore gamers and is my personal recommendation to people who want to try strategy game ( when they didn't played even one ).
Overall I give this game a 9\10.

I didn't go into this one expecting much, regardless of my time put into Dead Island, I could never bring myself to finish it, it just felt.. well, wrong. Dying Light soon changed that expectation as I was jumping from rooftop to rooftop, electric shiv in hand, being chased by a group of particularly nasty Virals.
Gameplay wise, the addition of Parkour to what is fast becoming a stale theme adds a whole new dynamic, and against some of the nasties you come up against you're going to need it. It's entirely possible to stealth past hordes of the undead, only picking off the odd one or two who are blocking your goal, or even luring them away using the ingame crafting system.
The skill system adds a good amount of character progression and customization, offering three different trees which all level up individually.
The melee combat has a nice flow to it, transitioning from swipes and swings to crushing downwards blows, and each weapon has it's own handling style. Whether a sturdy length of pipe or a chunk of concrete and rebar pried from one of Harran's larger undead beasties, the results are satisfying, with all the right gruesome in all the right places.
Graphically, everything set to high is netting me a Frame Rate of around 55 FPS, which, reading some of the other views is not as common as everyone would like, hopefully this will be rectified in a future patch. I generally expect a lower quality in open world games due to the amount going on at once, but I was truely surprised by what I was met with. Highly detailed environments and some great character design, though finding 5/7 zombies in a small pack all wearing the same shirt is a little strange, we'll just pin it down to a local football match and carry on shall we?
If I had any major gripes so far, they'd probably be focused around the co-op aspects. It's mentioned there are 7 runners left, so why do we all play as the main character from the Single Player campaign?
I've had some noticable issues around the cutscenes while playing with friends too, occasionally one of them will jump a few lines ahead of the dialogue from the NPC, causing the cutscene to end early and leave others wondering what happened. Hopefully things like this could be straightened out in the future, they're certainly not game breaking, but can detract from the experience.
Overall, I've been pleasantly surprised by Techland's latest entry to their zombie stab-em-up, and look forward to playing it more when I don't have to be in work in a few hours. With a few patches and a tidy up here and there, it looks like we could be off to an amazing start to 2015.

Although Antichamber's graphics may seem simplistic and boring, the gameplay more than makes up for it. The gameplay engine immerses you in a non-euclidian space where nothing acts the way you expect, and the skills you learn scale on themselves from the very beginning to the end of the game. There is always a logical explanation of why something happens in Antichamber, but it is never what you first assume. This wonderful game is a must-have for inquisitive minds or puzzle-fiddlers.

This is a great turn-based RPG and also kind of an interactive episode of South Park. If you like the show, then you are going to like (and understand) the jokes, the characters and the art style. Given that they have struggled for a long time to achieve this game, I believe they were successful in translating the show into a game language and, at the same time, in maintaining its identity.
Overall, the game mechanics are fun and engaging, and keep you at the same time alert and entertained during the combats. I encountered minor issues with quick-time events during the execution of some special abilities. Mostly they were due to the fact that the background and the characters are so colorful that at times it was difficult to notice before timeout that a button press was being requested.
The game also has some minor bugs related to ocasional skin loading and update of the amount of treasure in some areas of the map. However, these bugs do not get much in the way of the playing experience.
The major complaint I have about this game is the replayability factor. You become so emerged in the South Park universe that, once the main quest is over, you get the urge to freely explore the town and get more of the sensation that you are part of that world. However, there is very little left to do once the main story is over, since the town sort of reboots and even some of the side quests become unavailable. Although this is understandable, since the game is not meant to be a South Park sandbox or even a true open-world game, the idea is very attractive, so if you are a fan you can't help but feel a bit of disappointment at the end of the game.
Aside from that, I highly recommend the game for fans of the show who also like (or don't mind playing) RPGs. It is a really fun and engaging experience, and I sincerely hope there is a sequel on the way.

Antichamber has blossomed from an Unreal Tournament 2004 project into a deceptively minimalistic puzzle game. It is an excellent addition to any gaming library thanks to its challenging puzzles and its psychological manipulation of common expectations.
While the basic cell-shaded graphics may be down to the game's budget, Antichamber pulls them off brilliantly. Bright primary colours blanket areas where other games might use high quality textures, and interesting particle effects stand out as a visual cue rather than as something to be expected. This adds to the game's poignant art style, as well as making it run smoothly on less capable computers.
Antichamber's gameplay mechanics switch between bending the fabric of reality and rule-oriented cube placement. Many puzzles' currencies are doled out as these collectable cubes, with different colours representing possible hints towards a solution. Other puzzles involving movement, physics, and even view orientation are welcome additions that are interspersed regularly. The pacing flows nicely between areas, and each puzzle is unique enough to stay fresh. Rooms that seem inaccessible earlier on will eventually be attainable once new techniques of manipulating cubes are discovered. While this does make for a lot of back-tracking, Antichamber's theme revolves around revisiting the impossible.
Aside from teaching the basics of how to utilize its tools, the game leaves interaction with its cubed building-blocks up to the player. The imposed experiential learning leads to many “Eureka!” moments during Antichamber's journey. The game balances them perfectly with some of the more difficult challenges; each solution is just enough of an ego boost to keep spirits high before perplexing players with a new situation. Even the more stupefying tasks never seem arduous, in part because of their basic elegance but also thanks to the omnipresent musical atmosphere.
Excellent sound effects are probably the main reason why Antichamber maintains such a calm ambiance. Whether splashing through a shallow pond or standing on a windy mountaintop, the sounds of nature are always present and never get tedious. This contrast between the game's claustrophobic interiors and its superb outdoor soundscape is very mentally stimulating and adds to Antichamber's aloofness. Thankfully, the oddly juxtaposed soundtrack avoids over-complicating itself, which keeps the focus on exploring and solving puzzles.
Depending on how thoroughly it's completed, expect this journey to last between eight to twelve hours. Although certain puzzles are inevitably stumping, pulling through them is what makes Antichamber so satisfying to play. Its engrossing atmosphere and frequent instances of disbelief combine to form one of this generation's most appealing puzzle games.

The game isn't all bad but for me, it was a disapointement.
+ The artwork looks good enough...
- Except for the animation.  They're cheap and clunky and different skill will just use the same animation.  It's very unsatisfying.
+ The environement are attractive...
- But they quickly become repetitive.
+ The story is interesting.  The main plot give you a decent enough reason to go on an adventure.
- The narration is not that great.  The writting and dialogue is just correct.  And there is a lot of it.   It wouldn't be too much if it was better.  Also, the conversation choice you make doesn't matter.  You can just randomly pick any dialogue option and skip through the dialogue as fast as you can.  It won't impede your progression in any way.  There is only one or two situation where you actually have to read and remember some elements of the conversation to solve  a puzzle but it's really basic, you don't have to think and they're gonna point you exactly what information you need.  Or you can just try to solve the puzzle randomly, there is no failure state.
- The story is extremely linear.  There is no real side quests and no exploration. You can even really decide where you go in the world.  You're at this point in the game?  Well, you can stay in this current location or it this waypoint to be teleported to your next location.
+ You can create your character and you a have a decent amount of option.
- Some character builds are pretty much useless.   The deckers are one of the things that make the world of shadowrun special.  In this game, there is no point playing one.  You can't solve the game mainly by decking and everytime decking will be needed a decker will be provided.
+ Turn-based "tactical" combats. Those are fun!
- Unfortunately, not in this game.  The first few combats are fun but they quickly become boring and repetitive.  Startegy is not really required and once you got one, it's gonna fit every combat and situation.  Just stick to it.
- Gears and skill lack variety and is not satisfying.  When the bigger gun or the stronger sword become available you just buy it.  You won't really see a difference, the feels is gonna be the same and, I guess, at this point in the game, the enemies just got a little stronger so... it takes pretty much the same amount of hits to kill someone.  The spells and skill aren't impressive nor satisfying.  As I said earlier, differents sklls doesn't even have a different animation... from your regular attack!
+ Melee character can move and attack on the same action point (if the target is not to far away).
- You can't decide exactly where you character move around the target.  It doesn't matter that much since there is no flanking or rearing mechanic but, if an other  character want to use a grenade or a shotgun, your melee character can end up stoping right in the blast radius.  And there is friendly fire.
+/- There is friendly fire.  Usually I like friendly fire but, because of the previous point, I'm not sure if in this case this is a positive.
+ You can hire a team and control it.  (I'm really trying to be positive here)
- The character you hire are mostly blank, personality-less nobody.  You look ast the stats, does it complement what you're looking for?  Yes?  Hire. They won't talk and, once again, the choice you make here won't affect the strory (or even the gameplay) down the line.  There is one character you can take on your team that has some story importance and some dialogue line but, don't be fooled, she won't have any dialogue line during the mission.  Also, she sometime ask you to pick her on your team for when you're about to do some other missions; do it or don't, it really doesn't make a difference.   The won't mention it in the dialogue later.  So, I guess, if her stats fit your team...  There is also some other characters with personality that are gonna be asigned to your team for some specific mission wheter you like or not but you won't be able to hire them outside those missions.
- You can't turn the camera.  And sometime, mobs, teamate or other crap get in the way or where you would want to click.   It  can make it hard to attack/heal/buff one specific target or to move to a specific spot.
+ The music is good.
- Soudn effects, not so much.  There is also no voice acting.   This is not such a big deal to me but may be this game could have been saved by really decent performance.
+ There is a campaing editor.  I haven't played with it or try any user designed content.  After the official campaign I just had enough.
I could say more but those are the main points that I liked and that annoyed me.  I hope it will help you make a informed decision as to wheter you buy this game or not.

I frantically attempt to vent atmosphere in my ship to combat the fires that are slowly raging out of control. Just as my oxygen content drops to lethal levels, an enemy missile destroys my oxygen generator. I watch in complete helplessness as my crew dwindles one by one, the last one gasping his last before I see the game over screen. Again.
Faster Than Light is a difficult roguelike that for all the tiems you'll die, is strangely enchanting. It's definitely a balancing act. Do you attempt to save the space station from giant man eating spiders, or do you leave the station to it's fate to drift across the empty void? Do you take the pirates bribery, or do you say "Nay!" and open fire? There's a lot of content packed into this tiny game, and decisions can either benefit you or cost you dearly. And no, "friendly" controlled space is no safer than enemy controlled space; I can vouch for that.
If you want a difficult yet utterly charming game that you're destined to die in, you can't do much better than FTL, and at 10 bucks, you'll definitely get your money's worth.

On top of the story, the games is a sandbox world where random events, airdrops (free airdrops, take that H1Z1), 150 collectibles and notes to be found, 3 skill trees to max out, etc will keep you busy for a long time.
During the day, running around the city, scavenging everything you can find, avoiding or killing zombies, hunting airdrops, hunting other scavengers can be done at a normal pace. But once the night comes, I sart to rush things because beeing out there will be a challenge. A challenge that pays off. Everything you do grants you double xp in fighting and agility. So there seems to be a scaling in the game to keep the tension of roaming the streets up.
I only experienced one bug during my 10 hours of play. The sound. At some point, the sound would become metallic. Like it is a bit distorted. Not only the voices, but also the fx. It does kill the immersion, but will not last long. Afther a while everything goes back to normal.
And now, back to the game.

I usually don't like these open world games since I find them to be bland and repetitive, but I'm really enjoying this game so far.  It doesn't really do anything outstanding, but the combination of all the mechanics really come together for an enjoyable experience.  The combat is weighty and satisfying.  The parkour, while starting out slow, picks up once you unlock more perks and becomes enjoyable, almost like a less in-depth Mirror's Edge.  The crafting, while basic, will have you scavenging for blueprints and materials to craft certain items.  The only thing that I really don't care for is the story.  I would have preferred if this game didn't try to take itself too seriously and instead had fun with itself, almost like Dead Rising.  It's difficult to pull off a serious Zombie story these days when The Walking Dead exists.  I think most people won't be playing this game for the story though, so the uninteresting story isn't a huge deal.  Another complaint I have is that the game throws you into the open world fairly early and bombards you with a ton of zombies.  Maybe this was done on purpose, but in an open world game, I don't want to struggle with encounters early on since that will just discourage me from engaging in combat at all.  It does give you a fair amount of tools to deal with the hordes of zombies, so that's good.
Overall, from what I played, the game is fun and I can see it getting better as you unlock more perks and blueprints.  If you are jumping into this game expecting a 10/10 masterpiece, then you will be disappointed.  The game doesn't do anything exceptionally well.  If you buy this game expecting a fun world to run around in and kill zombies, then you'll like it.  It improves significantly on Dead Island and isn't a choppy, buggy mess.  I would say it's worth the $60 price tag just because of how much fun you can have with the game.
Performance wise, it runs fairly well.  I haven't run into any major frame rate drops or performance issues.  I'm using a GTX 650 and it's running well on Medium settings.  I've heard that some people with AMD cards are having issues, but I believe that the game is optimized for Nvidia cards, so that's probably why.

TL;DR: Play as Isaac Clarke, the unluckiest son of a ♥♥♥♥♥(literally) engineer in video gaming history ever. Be haunted by a mysterious artefact that is somehow the key to stopping aliens(but still wants to kill you because plot holes).
Dead Space is supposedly a survival horror TPS game. While I personally don't think this game as a good horror game, it at least attempts(and sometimes succeeds), which is much more better then Dead Space 3(that game didn't even try).
This is what the game is about: you are part of a repair team, heading towards the USG Ishmura, the biggest 'Planet Cracker' in the universe. It sent out a distress call and lost connection, so you, as the engineer(you're accompanied by Kendra, a hacker, and Zach Hammond, a security officer, and his team), is to fix up Ishmura(and your ship as well, the USG Kelion) and find the source of the call. Of course, everything goes south when in the first 30 minutes, you become haunted by the 'Necromorphs', mysterious, grotesque and dangerous humanoid creatures that quickly panics the entire team. Now, since you're the only one able to do anything(because game protagonist logic), you have to find out what the ♥♥♥♥ happened here.
The game is kinda like what everyone calls it: Resident Evil in space. After all, the developers based the gameplay off of Resident Evil because they didn't have much time for development. Though there are very unique gameplay features in Dead Space.
The game doesn't have a HUD(Heads Up Display). Your health is represented by your RIG, the Resource Integration Gear. Everyone has one of these in the future- it a computer device(looks like a mechanical spine) that you attach on your back. Since this is a TPS, you can see your RIG most of the time, and as your health goes down, the bar on your RIG gets low(like how health bars get low), and it changes color to blue to yellow to red.
This game also has a inventory and a store system, so you press tab to see your inventory. When you press tab, your suit(you wear a engineering/or a mining suit that makes you look like a
) will display a hologram inventory screen in front of you. It fits in with the SF feel of the game, and is much more immersive then a generic HUD. Your ammo will also be displayed when you aim, much like Halo, though your number of clips is not displayed, so you have to check your inventory.
You will find money inside crates and corpses of Necromorphs, which can be used at the store to buy ammo, health packs, etc. You will also find schematics for new items so you can just install it at the store and buy it. New suit schematic are important as they increase your armor and inventory size. You will also find 'Power Nodes' to open 'Node Rooms', which has very good things like much needed ammo on higher difficulties, and most important of all, new schematics(there are only one schematic for one item, so if you miss that schematic, it's gone for good).
You can also go to the Bench and upgrade your RIG(armor, health, air, etc), weapons, your Stasis Module which slows down enemies and objects, and your Kinesis Module which picks up heavy objects without a use of ammo- very important in higher difficulties. You upgrade them with Power Nodes, so be careful- you never know if you'll find a Node Room right after you spend all of your Nodes on upgrades.
There are also good variety of weapons, though the first free weapon you get, the Plasma Cutter, is very versatile and is good at everything(it's basically the best weapon in the game. you never want to sell it) As you can see from the name, it cuts things. It's a tool for cutting rocks, but in this game, it's used to cut off limbs. Why? Because headshots or bodyshots doesn't work for these monsters. You have to make them useless by cutting off their limbs. They don't die just from headshots(though they do lose their vision), and their torso is made out of ♥♥♥♥ing metal or something.
So we know the gameplay is at least something, so move on to the story- it actually has a very deep world(that you get to know more about in the second game), and the story intrigues you right from the start. The atmosphere and the story in general is heavily inspired by a 1997 movie 'Event Horizon'. The box cover for the game(a hand floating in space) is a homage to a scene in the movie, actually.(the more you know) It has that general feel of 'what the ♥♥♥♥ happened here' like in Half-Life or Bioshock(this game probably did the best job on that), and finding out the mystery by checking out all of the text logs is pretty fun. The dispute between Kendra and Zach(Kendra says 'let's get the ♥♥♥♥ out of here', while Zach says 'We still have a mission') also seemed to be pretty good, though it stops right after Kendra disappears, then she comes back then Zach disappears.
Oh, and Isaac- you just gotta ♥♥♥♥ing feel for him. He doesn't talk(he does in the later games), but he just does all of these things, and everytime he screams of fear(his 'AHHHHRG!!' is very memorable in some death scenes), you can't but say "dude... this is ♥♥♥♥ed up.". And oh yeah, the death scenes in this game is notorious for being grotesque(much like the rest of the game), and it's true. It's the only thing all of the fans have praised throughout the series(the later games adds even more).
Let's take a look at some of the other miscellaneous things though- the graphics are not dated. It's good enough, and the gore is like I said, great(though I don't know if it's a good thing or not). The soundtrack is very similar to Half-Life's case. It's mostly ambient tracks, which makes the atmosphere a lot better, but lot less memorable.
So we narrowed down Dead Space, and is it a good game? Yes, it is. It's a great game in fact- and you can tell from all of what I said earlier. Though it still has its cons.
The controls. The game's notorious for having terrible mouse controls, while it gets better in the later games, and gets better in this game as well if you tweak some of the files, the fact that they haven't released a official patch on Steam makes me feel pain inside. The difficulty is also a problem. If you get used to it(and you will), it's really really easy. If you watch

, he plays it on Medium and does not die a single time(and he's known to suck at bideo gems). The boss fights are especially bad- you just shoot at the yellow balls and poof, you win. Every. ♥♥♥♥ing. Boss.
Also, the 'survival horror' part is very subjective- the game does a good job of jumpscares in fact. They pop out of the vents and sometimes sneaks up on you, etc. They even play dead sometimes. But all of the monster spawns are scripted, so if you know where they'll spawn(or if you played 70 ♥♥♥♥ing hours like me), it's not that scary at all anymore. The atmosphere still might still spook you, though many people have said that they are not even scared of that anymore. Dead Space 2 and 3 leaves the whole 'closed down environment' atmosphere behind(well, maybe not Dead Space 3), but Dead Space 2 has other things to scare you(spoilers!).
Except for that, there isn't much to say. I give Dead Space a 8/10, it's a great game. The execution is near perfect, though the minor gameplay issues and the bugs ruins it a bit. The storyline is still great though, and since it is even more expanded in the later games, I highly recommend you to buy Dead Space 2 and 3 as well. In my opinion(that I will explain in the Dead Space 2 review), Dead Space 2 is gamelay-wise better, and while Dead Space 3 was a huge disappointment, it's still a good game and you should try it out.

I've played this game three times I think.
I love the little philosophies in it - none of them are that political tripe and are brilliantly straight forward and time-tested, I'm just going to go ahead and say that.
Now, just a warning, many parts of the game are incomplete. There's a room that was never finished, the pink blocks don't do anything, and many rooms and secrets are underutilized. I don't know why that is, but maybe, it could be considered retroactively as a distraction, even if they were meant to be something before. The end goal has to do with that black non-Euclidean "cube."
The gameplay itself is flawless and straightforward. The puzzles, however, are simply not always decipherable even after several location resets, and this is a good thing - it gives it tons of replay value. It also chains these lil ♥♥♥♥ers. Puzzles branch off into different puzzles, and much of it depends on where you start, because that will determine how many placeable cubes you can harvest. Some areas will also change if you've completed them before (but not that much).
I have one big piece of advice for you: Learn to sequence break, and love it. (Hardcore
players, of both 2D and 3D games, know what I'm talking about). If you like to play by your own rules, learn to break those. At times, you can use either method, but other times, you will be sorely stuck with one or the other. Some puzzles absolutely require you to pull some wild stunts, and some require gratuitous patience and good timing.
Regardless, it's dual-nature makes it an A+ puzzle game, outclassing most in it's genre. While it's mechanics cannot be compared to other games because of their differences,
use of said mechanics is something else.
It's a damn shame it wasn't finished. I wonder if there will ever be a second one.

--Dragonfall a major improvement, but probably not worth the price--
The original 2013 release of SR:R with the "Dead Man's Switch" campaign was much hyped but fans, backers and eager well-wishers were left disappointed by the story and fairly difficult to master content editor.  The UGC community mostly languished.  With the 2014 release of Dragonfall, SRR's second DLC/Expansion/Content Pack/whatever moves both the game itself and editor forward significantly, making this a much more worthy purchase.
When compared against similar offerings, though, SR:R struggles to shine at its price-point.  On the one hand, fans of squad turn-based action are probably going to find Shadowrun's system and environments a little underwheming in comparison to XCom:EU, which I think is the current front-runner in that arena.  SR:R includes a solid cover/LOS system, a decent mix of abilities for your squads, and some well scripted encounters.  Where Shadowrun falters is not just a limited 2-d engine (XCom's 3d is not only visually impressive it also provides easier to interface tactics and planning), but in a lack of obvious synergies between teammates.  While you will overall find youself needing a well balanced team, you never get the sense that the team is a cohesive unit aside from an occasional accuracy buff from one character to another.  Shadowrun also struggles to let you manage your team (inventory, power selection) beyond your own Player-Character. Finally, SR:R is docked a few points for some frustrating engine issues- mostly slow menus and frustrating click-tracking.
On the other hand, held up against role-playing games, Shadowrun's story modules are short and fairly linear.  With Dragonfall overall content is up to ~30 hours between the two stories, and neither of the stories are unenjoyable, but both feel much more linear than about anything on the market- from the various Spiderweb games (Avadon, etc) to Bioware offerings.  Dragonfall definitely improves the game's offerings in terms of characterization, team member story and sense of moral choice.
What makes Shadowrun stand out, though, is the setting.  Shadowrun's unique blend of grim-banal cyberpunk and high-fantasy have long made it a fan favorite, and there's almost nothing like it on the market still.  Both stories do a great job in introducing and immersing players into that world.
As of now, I recommend this game as enjoyable, but might not suggest buying at the $30/$35 regular Steam pricing, unless you're already a Shadowrun fan.  The price may be worth it if Dragonfall reinvigorates the UGC community to release a few more high-ranking modules of their own, though.  Otherwise, wait for a sale of some sort.

This recommendation comes from sort of an interesting place. I love Paper Mario and I love Earthbound. I do not really like South Park all that much, though this game has kind of made me appreciate it a bit more. I really wanted to play this game for a while, and when it went on the steam sale I had to pick it up just because I had a big RPG itch that needed scratching. I wasn't disappointed. I completed the 11-12 hour game in about two days, being completely hooked. The game is filled with humor poking fun at video games and culture in general. Graphically speaking it looks identical to the TV show and your character fits in extremely well, while being a silent protagonist(which leads to some very funny jokes). I can't believe how much I laughed at a game based off a show I never really cared for. This game is a MUST buy for RPG fans even if you don't like South Park I'd say. Unless you're TOTALLY against the idea of South Park.
Alright Pros and Cons time.
Pros:
+Looks visually identical to the TV show
+Hilarious
+Really fun timed battle system
+Does not hold back on the rudness and crudeness of the show(may be a con to some, though I felt it was MOSTLY a strength)
+Tons of collectables and interactions
+Feels like an entire season of South Park starring you
+have to add another pro saying again how hilarious the game is
Cons:
-Some flickering graphical bugs that were easily fixed by restarting the game, but still something to look out for
-Incredibly easy, I only died once in my whole playthrough
-Only able to use one other party member
-Maximum level is only 15 as far as I can tell (in general I think the combat system is great, but the damage and levels and party members should be revamped if they ever do a sequel)
TL;DR
Even if you aren't a South Park fan, or even dislike it, there is still a lot to like here. Try it out!

South Park is one of those shows where either you love it or hate it and if you love it, then you will adore this game. It blends a decent turn-based RPG with the hard-hitting humor that made South Park famous.
The gameplay is solid if a little bit simplified. The character creation is pretty well-made and the four classes (fighter, mage, thief, and jew) help to foster that replayability factor. Each companion character (Cartman, Stan, Kyle, Kenny, Butters, and Jimmy) brings his signature one-liners and varied movesets that make picking your partner a form of strategy. It doesn't take too long to learn which characters you like tagging along and what kinds of weapons and armors help to make your character strong. It's a simple game really. It doesn't take long to master. What makes it so memorable is how you can interact with various characters from the series and A LOT of characters make cameo appearances.
My only two complaints about this game are that it is short (by RPG standards) and the ending sucked. This game cries out for a sequel (and I really hope one is in the works). In every game that is usually on the right bumper, for this game they messed up the most basic part of a video game being able to play it, that alone relegates it to the bargain bin since it may take years for them to fix.

I've played this game three times I think.
I love the little philosophies in it - none of them are that political tripe and are brilliantly straight forward and time-tested, I'm just going to go ahead and say that.
Now, just a warning, many parts of the game are incomplete. There's a room that was never finished, the pink blocks don't do anything, and many rooms and secrets are underutilized. I don't know why that is, but maybe, it could be considered retroactively as a distraction, even if they were meant to be something before. The end goal has to do with that black non-Euclidean "cube."
The gameplay itself is flawless and straightforward. The puzzles, however, are simply not always decipherable even after several location resets, and this is a good thing - it gives it tons of replay value. It also chains these lil ♥♥♥♥ers. Puzzles branch off into different puzzles, and much of it depends on where you start, because that will determine how many placeable cubes you can harvest. Some areas will also change if you've completed them before (but not that much).
I have one big piece of advice for you: Learn to sequence break, and love it. (Hardcore
players, of both 2D and 3D games, know what I'm talking about). If you like to play by your own rules, learn to break those. At times, you can use either method, but other times, you will be sorely stuck with one or the other. Some puzzles absolutely require you to pull some wild stunts, and some require gratuitous patience and good timing.
Regardless, it's dual-nature makes it an A+ puzzle game, outclassing most in it's genre. While it's mechanics cannot be compared to other games because of their differences,
use of said mechanics is something else.
It's a damn shame it wasn't finished. I wonder if there will ever be a second one.

GTA Vice City, a game created by Rockstar North (Edinburgh, Scotland), which was released a year after the release of GTA III, on October 2002 for the PS2, and later ported to PC in May 2003.
This time around, the game was based in Vice City, which resembles Miami.
You are playing as Tony, a member of the Forelli Family, which is based in Liberty City. The Don decided to expand its borders, so they give you huge ton of money and send you to Vice City to make a deal. Unfortunately, you get ambushed. All the money is lost and now you have to find a way to pay them back.
GTA Vice City solved all the issues that the 3rd one had.
, songs in radio stations and weapons. They even added flyable helicopters and a plane to the game.
The solved the issues with gangs being hostile towards you. For those that don't remember, 5 out of 7 gangs would be hostile towards you by the end of the game in GTA 3. It became really annoying considering that some gangs had shotguns which could blow up your car in 2 shots. Well, in Vice City, there would be only 1 gang that would be hostile to you.
The plot itself is also very enjoyable, unlike GTA 3. It has a very cool feel to it, as if i am in some Al Pacino movie. Just watch a few minutes of it and you may understand why.
They added more game mechanics. You could damage cars with melee weapons, shoot the tires (the cops would even have spiked strips during chases), and now you are able to shoot through windows of a car, giving you the ability to kill the driver.
They added the ability to wear outfits (some areas, like the police station can only be accessed with such uniforms).
They added motorcycles.
They added assets and safehouses which can be bought. Assets would have a set of missions that if you complete, you would get profit from. Safehouses would allows you to save your game and store additional cars in the garage. GTA III had only 3 safehouses, which are unlocked as you progress through the story. Well in Vice City, you get 9.
They also added a few helicopters, and a plane that was actually flyable this time.
The amount of weapons increased, usually each weapon tier would give you a choice of about 3 weapons. But the biggest change was the addition of melee weapons. Unlike GTA III, where you only had a baseball bat, in Vice City you get to play with katanas, chainsaws, screwdrivers, machetes, golf clubs and so on.
Unlike GTA 3, Vice City featured a full map that you could view, and icons were visible throughout the whole game.
They added the ability to crouch. Most of the time i see some one playing older GTAs, most of them never use that mechanic. Well, let me clear some things out for you. Most objects in GTA, even cars, are made that way, so that when the player crouches, it fully covers him. But when you are starting the firing animation, your character will rise a bit above his cover. So in a way, this is kind of like the Gears of War cover system.
Now most people don't understand the importance of this mechanic. If you played GTA III, you probably know that there weren't a lot of shootouts. Most of the game, you are using your cars for your missions. Well, the crouching mechanic changed that, making at least 50% of game involve shootouts.
If you really planning on completing every mission in the game, you need to learn to take cover.
Well, this is probably the only game that is set in the 80's period. The songs in the radio, the cars, the city itself - the game is just so good at capturing the feel of the 80s. This is definitely a gem.
As always, the PC port suffers with the same issues as in GTA III. Mouse problems and FPS locked to 30. Most glitches can be fixed with SilentPatch, which i suggest you install before playing.
Other than that, this is the 2nd game of the GTA III era, which are all connected. And chronologically, plot wise, they are set in this order:
1986 - Vice City
1992 - San Andreas
2001 - GTA III

Brilliantly written from start to finish, this game was clearly created by people with a great love for the Shadowrun universe. Characters have a great deal of depth to them, the plot is interesting, the world feels real. It's an absorbing experience.
That being said, It plays awkwardly. The game is always pushing you along its linear path, this isn't necessarily a problem as the plot is usually gripping enough to keep you enticed but people expecting a roaming RPG full of side-quests are going to be a bit jarred.
Combat takes place on an X-Com style grid, it's serviceable enough but it feels very clunky. Clunkiness is one of the games problems in general, even when not in combat actions take just a few moments too long. It feels frustratingly slow at times.
However, Shadowrun Returns is still a great game. There are some very friendly modding tools and a healthy number of mods available to keep you playing well beyond the 13 hour long campaign. Well worth it for any fan of cyberpunk.

A surprisingly difficult yet addictive game.  Great in short bursts.  As many of the other reviews jokingly go on about, you *will* be hearing the phrases "Begin" and "Game over" a lot (though usually not necessarily in that order...).  At first I couldn't even survive 5 seconds; now I still rarely break 20 seconds.  After putting a total of about one hour in here and there according to Steam's count, my longest/maximum run is still only about 30 seconds.
Edit 09/21/2015: Okay, since originally posting this review, I have put a fair amount of playing here and there into Super Hexagon, to the point where I can often break 25 seconds, and even 35, 45, 50, or even 60 seconds (which effectively "beats" the level... my highest time I believe was in the low to mid 80s)... but only on the Hexagon difficulty level, which is effectively the "easy mode" (if such a thing really even exists in the first place) of this game.
In the end my original observations still stand; it is an excellent game... it has that classic arcade style, hard as hell difficulty level, reach for the high score feel to it from the days I was growing up that are long gone.  For that reason I can keep coming back to it for a few quick games, just like with similarly simple-yet-addictive games when I was a kid, and play for some good old-fashioned fun.  It's gaming from simpler times... brought back to the new millennium.

I wake up, on an alien planet, where I can't see any signs of life. I can't remember much, only that the ship I was on blew up. I look around, and spot a random container. It must have survived the crash. I walk towards it, but suddenly the ground begins to shake. I stumble and fall, afraid that the ground beneath me is about to fall, but something else happens. In front of me, the dirt rises, forming a small hill. How curious, I wondered, and then I noticed the beast under the dirt, fully burrowed out of the ground, and it seems to glare at me. It's a giant crablike creature, and begins to crawl towards me. I struggle to raise my gun, and shoot it, but the creature seems unfazed. I walk backwards, putting more and more bullets into it, until the beast finally falls. I walk towards the thing to inspect it, when I suddenly feel a sharp pain on my shoulder, as I feel a hundred knifes sink into it. When the blades are removed, I spin around, and I find out that those were the teeth of a vicious bipedal reptile hell bent on murdering me. I jump back as it prepares another strike, and start to feel painful electricity running through me. It appears I've stepped on a floating jellyfish. I stumble backwards and fall off a cliff. After I painfully land, I look upwards, and see a thousand eyes upon me, all of them belonging to dangerous creatures. I know right then and there, that these are my last moments, and there isn't even anyone to say goodbye to. I close my eyes, preparing for my death, as I sense all the beasts moving towards me. The pain I feel as I am being ripped apart is indescribable. Then all senses, all feelings, are gone.
Then I respawn.

After just finishing this game I can concur that this is a great title to have.  If you are a horror buff, a lot of the stuff in this first game isn't very new (given that it's old that isn't surprising), but it does manage to deliver well.  Things legit creep you out in certain locations, and you can feel yourself slowly starting to get chipped at inside with each new chapter and each new monsters that get in your way.  But then some things can surprise you and kind of break the terror in an almost comedic sort of way (Chapter 7 Bench anyone?).
If you are a Sci-fi buff, this game has science fiction in shovelfuls.  You actually feel like you are on a mining ship and the level of detail they put in it makes it something you'd expect to find on an episode of Battlestar Galactica or Star Trek.  It once again makes me wish that we didn't stop at the end of the Space Race and kept going; just imagining being aboard a ship like the USG Ishimura and going on a mining run into deep space gets me all tingly...
The nice part is that the devs of Dead Space are from the old school of game design; a sad laugh given the state EA is now.  Secrets can be found wherever a trained eye can find them, and some of the most worthwhile secrets are easily missed if you're too focused on something else.  Even though this is nothing compared to games back in the day, it would be nice if more developers added this much detail in a single player game like this.
If you've never had interest in the games before, or if you are looking for something to try but don't want to purchase anything brand new, I recommend this game.  This is a nice little horror title that gets the blood racing for a bit but an equally nice sci-fi title that gets the imagination going.  Altman be praised!

**TO ALL WHO ARE HAVING MOUSE ISSUES WITH THIS GAME**
1. Run the game.
2. Start Task Manager (Ctrl+Alt+Delete).
3. Highlight the game then right click.
4. Click "Go To Process".
(should take you to the "Processes" page with GTA already highlighted)
5. Right click the game and click on "Set Affinity".
6. Then it's going to ask you "Which Processors Are Allowed To Run?".
with the options to check on or off:
_<All Processors>
_CPU 0
_CPU 1
_CPU 2
_CPU 3
7. Check <All Processors> off and only check on one CPU, doesn't matter which one, but I always just go with the first one: CPU 0.
8. Click "OK" when chosen, close the Task Manager and click back on the game and all should be well.
9. None of this will work if the game isn't already running before you open the Task Manager.
**Note: This is the fix for Windows XP, Vista & 7, I do not own 8, but I would assume it's very similar, if not.. there's always YouTube lol**

The Good:  Excellent voice acting, hillarious in a genuinely funny way, Authentic to the series stories, locations and characters.  The premise of a city-wide LARP game is a clever mechanic and they use it to lampshade RPG conventions as well as lampoon gaming tropes.  Tons of "wink and nod" moments to fans make this feel like you are living inside a South Park episode.  I would classify it as one of the best licensed games of all time, with writing by the actual writers and voice acting by the actual voice actors of the series, it's a top-notch South Park product and an excellent game at once.  The exploration system makes exploring the semi-open world easy and intuitive by highlighting interactive objects for you and training you into new mechanics slowly
The Bad:  Like all JRPG-style fighters battles can get repetitive, though the interactive system and amount of tactical choice helps.  The balance is a little wonky, some classes feel flat-out easier than others.  Equipment balance is likewise off with certain tactics and item combinations (like bleed damage/fire damage debuff combos) trivializing the game's combat content entirely.  There is a lot of back-tracking as you get new abilities at five different points that unlock new options for getting around the overworld.  For completionists, a lot of optional items and side-content is totally missable and can't be backtracked to.
What I'd pay for it:  I would have bought this for full AAA retail price (60 bucks US or so) easily.  If there is a sequel I'd pre-order and consider a delux edition purchase
The DLC:  Adds some items to the early-game only, definitely not "pay to win" DLC in any form but doesn't add a ton except a little more tactical flexibility to the very early game.  I would KILL for some actual mission-adding DLC, but sadly it's not in the cards.
Buy this if you like:  The T.V. show.  JRPGs, Comedy games, obscene humor, parody.
P.s.-- Obsidian game without a single bug.  I think that might be a sign of the apocalypse or something.

3) The music. Oh the music of this game is one of the best I have heard in many games. Not saying its THE BEST music ever but the music serves its purpose and dies that effectiely. It really gives you a place in the game and is surprisingly immersive for a strategy game.
