I wake up, on an alien planet, where I can't see any signs of life. I can't remember much, only that the ship I was on blew up. I look around, and spot a random container. It must have survived the crash. I walk towards it, but suddenly the ground begins to shake. I stumble and fall, afraid that the ground beneath me is about to fall, but something else happens. In front of me, the dirt rises, forming a small hill. How curious, I wondered, and then I noticed the beast under the dirt, fully burrowed out of the ground, and it seems to glare at me. It's a giant crablike creature, and begins to crawl towards me. I struggle to raise my gun, and shoot it, but the creature seems unfazed. I walk backwards, putting more and more bullets into it, until the beast finally falls. I walk towards the thing to inspect it, when I suddenly feel a sharp pain on my shoulder, as I feel a hundred knifes sink into it. When the blades are removed, I spin around, and I find out that those were the teeth of a vicious bipedal reptile hell bent on murdering me. I jump back as it prepares another strike, and start to feel painful electricity running through me. It appears I've stepped on a floating jellyfish. I stumble backwards and fall off a cliff. After I painfully land, I look upwards, and see a thousand eyes upon me, all of them belonging to dangerous creatures. I know right then and there, that these are my last moments, and there isn't even anyone to say goodbye to. I close my eyes, preparing for my death, as I sense all the beasts moving towards me. The pain I feel as I am being ripped apart is indescribable. Then all senses, all feelings, are gone.
Then I respawn.

Way back in 1989, FASA Corporation, publisher of role-playing games, wargames and board games, released the first version of
, a science fantasy tabletop role-playing game. It was cross-genre, taking elements from both cyberpunk and urban fantasy and putting the player in a world where humans co-exist with elves, dwarfs, trolls and other exotic races, where magic and cyberware are common and the Matrix is accessed by deckers, jacking into the network with cyberdecks connected directly to their brains.
I was introduced to Shadowrun while attending middle school by some older friends of mine with long hair and/or glasses who were heavily into tabletop role-playing games. Over the years we tried many different games, like
and the
system, but Shadowrun was always the one we returned to and the game that gathered most players. Shadowrun has continued to thrive since its release as one of the most popular tabletop role-playing games and in July 2013, Shadowrun Fifth Edition was released.
The Shadowrun universe has spawned a massive amount of properties, including action figure games, two magazines, over 50 novels and four more or less successful video games. The latest video game installment, Kickstarter-backed
, was just recently released and this is my quick and dirty review.
I have to admit that I don't remember all the details of the Shadowrun rules, it's been over 15 years since I last sat down to play, but from what I can tell, Shadowrun Returns is true to the core rulebook. The game takes its rules from the second and third edition of the rulebook and everything from character creation to the available items feel familiar. All races and classes, from Street Samurai to Shaman are there, all the different types of magic are available, deckers can enter the Matrix, and riggers can control drones. The only thing I haven't seen is the astral space, so I'm not sure if it's in the game, but players familiar with the Shadowrun universe will immediately feel at home nonetheless.
Shadowrun Returns features isometric graphics, and you move your character around and interact with people and objects in real time. But as soon as the drek hits the fan and the weapons come out, the game switches to a turn-based model. Your team can consist of up to four characters, including yourself, and they all have a number of move points determined by each character's attributes. The combat, both in the real world and in the Matrix, is fairly simple, but in my opinion just as complex as it needs to be.
The game comes bundled with one campaign set in Seattle, and a single campaign might not seem like much, but it will keep you entertained for 8 to 10 hours. There's also a Berlin campaign in development by the gamer's creators, Harebrained Schemes, but it's not scheduled for release until October. The campaign will be free for Kickstarter backers, but the rest of us have to get it as a paid DLC. That said, Shadowrun Returns comes with a level editor with virtually endless potential. And the game editor is the real strength of Shadowrun Returns: It's a framework that enables game masters to create their own campaigns and share them with the community.
One of the great things about the tabletop version of Shadowrun was that it was very social, but if you were hoping for the same experience with Shadowrun Returns you will be disappointed. The game only supports singleplayer at the moment, but multiplayer might be implemented in the future. Multiplayer would be a sweet treat, but I'm not sure how it would be solved in practice. Who is the main character on a multiplayer run? Who will control the NPC team members? Thankfully, I'm not a game designer, so I'll leave these challenges for Harebrained Schemes to solve themselves.
Since the game is just released, there are a few bugs here and there, but nothing major. Harebrained Schemes is also working closely with the players to find and remove bugs from the game and very recently released the first game patch. It contains both balancing changes and bug fixes the game needed. If there's one major issue I'd like to point out, it's the design decision to only save the game when the player moves from one area to another as opposed to letting the players save when real life needs their attention. It can be pretty damn tedious to replay parts of the game because you had to abort a run.
Despite these few shortcomings Shadowrun Returns is a great game. If you ever played the tabletop version and enjoyed it, you owe it to yourself to buy and play Shadowrun Returns. The base campaign that comes bundled with the game is perhaps a bit linear, but complex and intriguing enough to keep you entertained from start to end. There is also massive potential in the game editor. I'm very excited to see what kind of campaigns the community will create and share.
Maybe even my old game master will sit down and re-create his epic campaign from back in the days? That would be downright wiz.

Dead Space, A survival horror game by Visceral Games, released on October 20th, 2008. Does this game still hold up 7 years after its release? Or does it fall into that over-flowing "Just another horror game" bucket?
You take on the role of Isaac Clarke, a engineer who was sent on a mission with a few others to check on a interstellar mining ship called the "USG Ishimura" after it has gone dark. Very early in the game you find out that Isaac's love interest named Nicole was a member on the Ishimura. It is obvious that nothing goes to plan, since a game called "Dead Space" surely won't be about an engineer walking in and fixing a wire then walking out with a big smile on his face.
What I love about this game is that it brings back the horror that we all know and love, even on normal difficulty I ran into parts where Necromorphs were swarming and I barely had any ammo remaining. Another great aspect that I liked was the fact that Isaac is a silent protagonist, and you almost never get to see his face. This helps get attached to him early in the game, and also creates a connection to the people Isaac and you will come across. These are just a few things that made this game such a joy to play. Voice acting is superb, there aren't any cheap jumpscares with screams louder than a Metallica concert and even if there was a few jumpscares, they were always worth it and were never just filler. Ishimura was an amazing place to set such a game, it really felt as if I was stuck in the ship, small signs of escaping gave me such a desperate feeling. The gameplay feels smooth and new, making you have to aim your shots when a raging necromorph comes running at you like you were a Playstation 4 during Black Friday.
For a person that barely enjoys horror games and misses those times where horror was about the tension more than the scare, not about having Slenderman creep up behind you and poke you in the♥♥♥♥♥with a loud jumpscare (Pretty much every horror game). Visceral Games made a masterpiece that some people need to remember, horror didn't end with Resident Evil 4. I recommend this game to anyone that is even slightly interested in psychological horror games, or even horror games in general. Just don't forget to aim for the limbs. ;)

South Park не знает удержу в своем стремлении стать ультимативной скатологической комедией. Вырезанные на консолях в Европе и Австралии семь сцен выглядят попыткой прикрыться фиговым листом. Оставшегося все равно хватает, чтобы не один раз показать стремление перейти любые допустимые границы. Лишь намеренно примитивный внешний вид спасает обложку от рейтинга «Только для взрослых». Audio:  For a game driven by activities and interactions with NPC's the audio is all over from sounding like whispers to exploding your ear drums leaving you playing while riding the remote like a movie.  Seems no attention was payed to this aspect at all which normally is never a complaint.
Controls:  For a game about parkour they out the jump button in the worst spot on the right bumper instead of the left trigger or the A button.  This is the first time in gaming history ever played a game where such a commonly used feature is delegated to such an odd spot.  The left trigger is for using equipment or a button for survivor sense, for a parkour game priority shoulda been given to the left trigger for jump instead of using equipment, it feels clunky and playing the game is the most important part, graphics, sound, an ambient world, none of it matters when the basic concept of playing the game is broken.
Equipment is bound to the left trigger, equipment can be thrown objects or ya know equipment.  In every game that is usually on the right bumper, for this game they messed up the most basic part of a video game being able to play it, that alone relegates it to the bargain bin since it may take years for them to fix.
Parkour:  broken due to the poor controls, if they were going for a free run experience without removing your thumb from the controller duck would be on the bumper instead of on the b button which means removing your thumb.
Dead zone:  there is a slider for this but it seems broken or doesnt seem to make much of a diff leaving users slipping and sliding all over like its club penguin all over again.
Devs have been absent from the steam community on the forums for weeks.   Sadly they seem to have abandoned the community or worse maybe the game itself.
Parkour part 2:  It sucks pretty bad, alot of jumps require perfect precision, but this isnt mirrors edge, its a poor mans version of mirrors edge that requires pixel perfect precision to grab onto object or your character just hits them and falls to their death.  If your character is shimmying you cant look down to see if there is land below you, this leaves countless times players will just plunge to their death.  Its just idiotic design, do a chin up and notice your head tilts down its called a neck, for some reason the character in this game doesnt have one.
Parkour 3:  There is no way to climb down unlike other games where pushing towards an object as you fall grabs it in this game there is no way to do this.  Time after time your player will climb somewhere high with no way to get down.  Just hurl yourself off to your death since there is no way down off of alot of places.
Parkour 4:  Parkour is a fancy word for walking.... its just fancy walking, the wordy "parkour" itself causes pain to hear people use since it implies their doing something other than just fancy walking, its not impressive, quantum physics, or calculating derivatives is impressive but fancy walking is dead last on anyones bucket list.
Many jumps are so precise with their distance that being one bit off means absolute failure.  Meaning some dev sat there and made them as annoying or difficult as possible for no reason, this is evident right in the tutorail which goes on for probably 30-50 minutes the longest tutorial in history just to show players where the jump button is.
Menuitis:  Game suffers from ridiculous menus and button prompts.  There are load zones, and unless you press a button it wont finish loading.  Worst part is if you die you need to play a button mini game before it lets you play the game again, pressing X to skip a hint then A to load, how about just load the game and skip all these dumb button prompts.  Stuff like this is pleb tier, imagine if Resident Evil everytime you opened a door you had to jump through button hoops to get to the other side, that is what this game is which means Resident Evil from 29 years ago is better designed than this game.  Going through a load zone or dying shouldnt be a mini game, the game should be playing the game, which seems to be the last thing on anyones mind who made it.  For some reason in multiplayer this doesnt exist.

This game is defnitely "What you see is what you get". And what I saw before playing this was pure unadulterated style. Every gun you use has power to it. The physics make every kill gruesome. It is the perfect horde mode game. But it isn't a mindless horde mode game - Tripwire has made every enemy have it's own attack pattern and this makes the game challenging and fresh each and every round.
This game is also about teamwork believe it or not. You choose from a selection of perks that all need to come together in order to achieve victory. You've got your standard medic class that supplies heals, you've got a crowd control Firebug that burns enemies to a crisp, Demolition can wipe waves in one solid explosion - and guess what? They're all fun to play.
The GORE IS OUTRAGEOUS. Coupled with the Slo-mo, watching your bullets carve a zeds skull into chunks is one of the most visceral and stylish things I've seen in a game. And it's exceedingly important in a game like this where your objective is to kill. The bullets have force and you can even start to feel bad for the zeds after a while. Sometimes, they don't even die right away and start seizing up - I'll put a bullet or two into them so they can go to zed heaven.
The fleX fluids and gibs definitely add to the mayhem, but the fluids need to be optimized. The GTX 1060 that I'm running drops frames like crazy and unfortunately I had to turn it off, but research showed me that even the GTX 1080 suffered the same issue. The fleX gibs works wonderfully - guts sticking and hanging from the ceiling really made me feel like a badass.
This game is fun. It's pure fun. And that's what is most important to any game, in my opinion. If you like killing zombies with guns, this is the perfect reflection of that attitude.

Caution: play at your own risk; incidents of time mysteriously vanishing reported.

Antichamber is a puzzle game based around warped reality (walk through a door, turn around, the door now leads somewhere else) and moving coloured blocks to trigger switches. If you intend to play this game, the most important characteristic you need is patience. For the first half of the game I spent alot of time confused, sometimes even frustrated. I often complain about games that are too hand holdy, but I felt that Antichamber was too far on the opposite end of the scale, giving almost no indication of what I was supposed to be doing. The non linear progression didnt help, because I was often unsure if I was supposed to solve a particular puzzle now or come back later with new equipment. However the second half of the game became much clearer, and I did start to have fun. I got to the end in under 8 hours, without using any external help, so I guess the game must have done enough to teach me the rules, even if I didnt notice it was happening. Best to pick it up on sale.

This game is awesome. I highly recommend it. It has somewhat of a similar feel to Portal - it's a first-person, geometry-breaking puzzle game. It will mess with your head, in a good way, and challenge your accustomed ideas about how to play games.

Antichamber is a first-person puzzle game that loves to trick the player with rule changes, visual sleights, false walls and impossible spaces as well as some testing logic problems.
You start the game in a black-walled chamber with the controls printed on the wall next to a clock ticking down from 90 minutes. From here you enter the game's maze, where a staircase can lead to its own foot, walls and floors can vanish when you touch them, a set of rooms can be both horizontally and vertically adjacent to each other and pressing your face against a window can change where you are standing.
The puzzles are well designed and for the most part - difficult.
Antichamber is not a linear game. You will often find yourself bouncing off several puzzles simultaneously in different parts of the maze.
In my opinion is Antichamber a must have for every first-person puzzle game fan.

The combat is what brings it down for me. Sure it has more moves which is a really good thing, but what Rocksteady did was to change the base mechanic from BAC (Batman Arkham City) and BAO (Batman Arkham Origins) where you were in total control of the direction you fought. In BAK (this game) your character is changing direction automatically and all you have to do is press hit and counter buttons and your character flies left, right, forward and back punching out enemies automatically.
In the previous games your character hit in the direction you looked which was awesome. Full control and tight fighting. I have no idea why they changed this and it drags down the score a lot for me since i basically wanted the game for the fighting challenges. Previous titles if you hit in a direction and no enemy was there you kept hitting air while an enemy could come and smack you from behind. Not in this game. Your char will automatically hit backwards and take care of the enemy. The way they make it harder is by having much more harder enemies that require stun/jump over/gadgets. However you find yourself very often hit an enemy you didnt want to hit. You look at an enemy and think you will hit him but nope - the game decides that you should hit someone else in another direction... I mean?!
I had hopes that there was an option to change it back to non-auto direction fighting (standrad fighting mechanic option) but there is none. You are stuck with this. So if you loved the fighting in the previous games you might not like this combat. Sure its the same on the surface with more bells and whistles and many seem to be ok with it, but if you enjoyed having full control of who you hit then prepare to be let down. Personally i loved having full control. Its what made the fighting so good.
It is a cool game overall so if you can live with not feeling equally skilled in combat and you want to play the final Batman game then get it. :)

In a small American town in the early 1960s, Scotty Smalls is the new boy in the neighborhood, seeking desperately to fit in. He would be welcomed on the local sandlot baseball team that practice every day, which only has eight players. Smalls however, can't play baseball; on his first visit to the sandlot he finds himself in the outfield with a fly ball descending toward him which bounces off his glove, causing the other boys except "Benny the Jet" Rodriguez, the team's leader, to burst out laughing. Smalls, humiliated, leaves.
Smalls asks his stepfather to teach him to play, and while his stepdad agrees, Scott cannot successfully catch or throw the ball. Benny soon teaches him what he needs to know, and with Benny's support, he gets a place on the team.
Meanwhile, behind a wall at the end of the sandlot is a backyard inhabited by "the Beast", a English Mastiff, a dog so large and savage that it has become a neighborhood legend. One day the boys' last ball lands in the backyard of the Beast. My first 30 hours into the game. Be advised it might be long, but if you read on it'll get very exciting
-Chose to lead the US, thinking it was the most OP country, starting with the   ancient era with a large map and lots of AI empires and city states
-Establised Washington DC as capital and first settlement
-Focused on doing basic stuff in the early stages, farming, building mines etc.
-Created a small defense force, and a scout unit to explore into unknown territories and find new resources
-Met with the Polynesian, The Shoshone, and Brazillian Empire, established friendly contact (only contact that we made ourselves)
-Slowly beginning to strengthen my economy through trade.
-Suddenly we were discovered by the Songholians and the Mongolians
-Their leaders, Askia of the Songholians and Genghis Khan of Mongol, showed friendly intentions and wanted us to work together
-I accepted (Big mistake people)
-America expanded and our friendliness spread over towards other empires and city states
-America became famous for destroying barbarians and for its coal and silver
-Sweden came into the picture, and did not like my alliance with Polynesia and Songhol
-They started to annex 2 of Polynesia's settlements, Honolulu and Samoa
-Of course, being friendly as ever, the US retalliate
-We rekt the Swedes and reclaimed both cities plus annexing one of Sweden's settlements, Sigtuna.
-We gave back Samoa to the Polynesians, but made Honolulu our own for its seaport
-We conquered the city state, Panama City, because they did not want to share their crabs
-Meanwhile Sweden was the first to make contact with every empire, making them the absolute power of the World Congress with the most delegates
-Songhol did not like Sweden either, and we both made a research agreement so we could make it to the Industrial Era faster
-We made hostile relations with Sweden, causing most of the European empires (England, the Celts, Greece, and Denmark) to boycott us
-Achieved the first gun powered unit before anyone else, the Minutemen, and have cannon units and later on artillery
-Became the most superpowered nation at that time and forced the Europeans to negotiate a peace treaty
-Made it to the modern era. (This is where it gets interesting)
-Recieved intel from the Celts and Shoshones that Songhol was planning to backstab me.
-I took it as fake intel, Songhol was a great ally why would they attack me?
-While I was (litterally) not looking, they have achieved the atomic era first and their military was more advanced than mine
-They declared that I was not to be trusted and became hostile
-I learned later on (after the Cold War) that because I chose "Freedom", as an Ideology, and not "Order", we were considered traitors
-Began the Cold War between US and Songhol-Mongol-Shoshone alliance
-The US started building its army, causing a Great Depression
-Sweden offered help, I accpeted and we became allies.
-Songhol made to "Nuclear Power State" first and game concluded that I lost.
-But for the sake of American Spirit, I did not quit the session and continued
-Sweden's port city was attacked by Songhol subs and aircraft carriers carrying planes and an atomic bomb
-US with it's "meh" modern navy with no nuclear power, made a suprise attack on the fleet, destroying the nuclear ship, their subs, and a few troop carriers
-Started engaging their borders without help. Sweden was also being attacked by Denmark because of land complications
-Prayed to God, and then pushed my troops towards the border
-The Songhols deployed their infantry plus Bazooka units, attack helicopters, and bombers
-We hold the border and because we had P-51 Mustangs and B-17 Bombers, plus AA guns, the only country that has AA guns at the time
-We took down alot of their units not because we were advanced, but by sheer numbers and awesome strategy
-They lost 3/4 of their army, their nuclear bomb, their entire Navy, and the US still held their ground without taking any of their land, with only losing an artillery unit
-They negotiated a peace treaty
-We became best buds (but still keeping an eye on each other)
10/10 best history simulator ever. Would go on Cold War with the Songhols again

My specs:
I5 4690k and a gtx 970 on windows 10. Game installed on a SSD.
Performance:

Game:
Wow this was a great finish to the story after 4 batman games. Basically every chump in Gotham has teamed up to literally exhaust the batman along with a massive army of drones, tanks, and various ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, dead and alive. It was really intense to see batman get pushed to his breaking point and almost giving in as things got desperate.
Theres plenty of things to do across 3 sections of the city, you can go to them any time but can only take the batmobile after finishing certains missions. Theres also LONG side quests that are really cool. The map is huge and takes a few minutes real time to get across even when driving, but its still pretty dense. Theres lots of ramps and hidden shortcuts for the batmobile and its fun to drive. Same engine, so it feels like Mad Max's driving mechanics. That classic arcade, drift for miles, fun. A lot of the functions from the other games are still in but theyve expanded the options of your gadgets and suits to give you a lot broader approach to do things how you want.
Cons:
Your custom batsuits dont show up on the cutscenes, for obvious reasons.
The batmobile gets airtime easily, so small hops can make you lose control easily in a chase. I worked around this by a quick right click to turn into a tank to catch my traction
If you use a keyboard and mouse its easy to attack the wrong target if your cameras not perfectly centered on them due to the limitations of WASD
Theres an extended Outro cinematic after 100% completion. Youll probably have most of this done already, but it includes the few hundred riddler puzzles. I just watched it on youtube (dont spoil it for yourself though, its worth it to beat the game first)
The Chris Nolan and Rick Snyder batmobiles dont have a tank mode, but they have guns on them like in the movies.

Great source material, execution has some flaws but overall a fun game.  A bit oversimplified IMO but that also makes it a friendly, unintimidating introduction to the genre.
The combat mechanics are a bit simplistic, especially for ranged weapons--I can't figure out why none of the newer squad based tactical RPGs like this have copied the excellent
'spend action points to improve aim' model, which is very flexible and intuitive.  If you haven't played that game, go buy it now, it's one of the all-time best in the genre and has aged extremely well.  The magic and drone aspects of Shadowrun combat are well implemented, so props to the developers for integrating everything so well.
The story held my interest, though (spoilers)
The writing itself is god-awful at times.  It could have used another couple proofreads (it's/its, comma usage) and stylistically it reads like decent internet fan fiction with some crap parts.  If you're going to do a text-heavy game like this, you'd better make damn sure you have the writing chops to do it.  Hire some damn writers, Bioware and Black Isle didn't seem to have this problem way back in the 1990s.
Still, a fun ride overall, and the developers did a great job of capturing the universe.  I recommend playing it on 'Very Hard' which puts you on even footing with the enemy but plays more like you would expect 'Normal' or 'Hard' to.  Choose 'Hard' if you're new to this sort of game.

The first installment in the Dead Space series is set in the year 2508 and begins when a mining starship, the
, sends out a distress signal during a mining operation on the planet Aegis VII. In this game, players step into the role of
― a ship systems engineer whose journey starts on a seemingly routine mission to fix the communication systems on the planet cracker.
It is not long until he realizes that he stepped into a living nightmare of vicious alien creatures and a dead silence ship where he must constantly fight to get out alive.
The story in Dead Space is one of its strongest points. Most of it is told via video, audio and text diaries you find scattered around the ship. Another strong point is the atmosphere, a lot of it due to brilliant sound effects. It's a very impressive looking game overall, though sometimes you will feel like you are going through the same corridors over and over again. The combat is also good. Some sections may look a bit repetitive, however, the strategic dismemberment and the stomping are just extremely fun and satisfying.

If you enjoy tactical turn based combat and compelling storylines this game is for you.
Pros:
-Great writing
-Fun turn based tactical combat
-Greater than average ability to feel like your character's skills and the choices for specialization matter
-Unique setting that if you're not familiar with may definetly be worth losing 30-40 hours in
-Great RPG giving a mix of storytelling and classic character building
-Player generated content that adds replayability
Cons:
-Lots of writing (do not play if reading text makes you bored)
-No multiplayer (I sincerely hope they add in co-op multiplayer in future DLC, but I understand why it is not currently a part of the game as they have focused on creating an immersive single player environment with compelling companions, but as anyone who has played tabletop RPG's in the past knows, a large part of the fun of these games is being able to run around with your friends attempting to complete the various tasks of a shadowrunner)
Other Points of Interest:
-I strongly recommend not playing Dragonfall until you have completed Dead Man's Switch (the original campaign) Not only is dead man's switch a better intro to the universe + mechanics, but after playing Dragonfall you will not want to go through Dead man's switch because it will feel like a tracked, clunky version of Dragonfall
-If you're not really sure if you're interested in the gameplay go look up the Shadowrun Universe, because a large part of what makes this game great is how well they portrayed it, and if off the bat you don't like things like the idea of decking, the implementation of magic, or the way that orks, trolls, elves, and dwarves came into existence, chances are that you will continue to be annoyed by whatever annoyed you in a text based RPG.

After going dark for many years, the XCOM franchise returns with a revamped and redisnged tactical strategy with XCOM: Enemy Unknown. A truly knuckle-biting fight against the alien threat is what you will find, due to punishing difficulty, risk versus reward, and permadeath. But part of what makes this XCOM different from those in the past is the emphasis on a tight knit squad; losing soldiers in UFO Defense was to be expected, but losing one, two, even more soldiers in Enemy Unknown is crushing. In the opinion of this player, that is for the better.
Among a more intimate focus on your soldiers, XCOM: Enemy Unknown simplifies a lot of the (honestly) more tedious elements of the past. Painful amounts of micro-managing your Rookies and Meatshields is gone, with a simplified loadout that makes getting into the action a lot easier--not at the sacrifice of depth however. Tailoring builds and loadouts to the various classes can shape the way you play, and it's definitely not a loss to simplify things. A simplified ammo and move system are the other most prominent changes, along with a cap of 6 operatives on a mission, but again, the change in focus to closer squad-based tactics makes this acceptable.
The managing aspect of the game is however, a bit lacking, but arguably focuses on harder choices. Gone are the times of buying scientists and engineers; mission rewards and monthly gains are the only way to speed up the XCOM R&D department. This is good--amassing stacks of cash was far too easy in UFO Defense. What IS lacking however, is the aspect of multiple bases and increasing XCOM coverage. This missing aspect may speed the game up, but the progression of becoming a legitimate threat to the xenos was awesome, to say the least.
Mechanically, the game is very solid. You are often, especially in the early game, at the whim of the RNG, but ranking up your soldiers shows the very tight and fierce mechanics behind eleminating the enemy and getting everyone back alive.
Longevitiy wise, the game will take you quite a long time to finish a run-through, assuming you haven't played before. Expect a solid run-through to take place in the range of anywhere 'tween 10 and 15 hours for your first time.
Difficulty wise, Classic with the Ironman modifier (prevents save-scumming) is the best way to go. I'll be frank-- XCOM: Enemy Unknown will definitely eat your lunch at some point. It'll eat your lunch, kick you in the teeth and expect you to buy it another meal. The game is unforgiving, especially within the first few hours of gameplay. This period of time forms a weird inverse bell-curve, where the beginning and end are harder than the middle.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is not without faults however. While maps are diverse and interesting for various tactics in handling the situation, gone are the totally randomlly maps that UFO Defense threw at you. This is certainly a feautre missed, and the maps eventually get old, especially on subsequent playthroughs. Other imperfections include glitchy enemy detection, a now very rare (but once game-breaking) teleportation of enemy patrols, resulting in almost certainly total-party kills. Other technical goofs include animations being wonky when soldiers pop out from cover to shoot aliums. Often it'll be nice and procedural, but often it'll be buggy and your soldiers (and aliums) will glitch through walls to squeeze off some shots.
Minor technical issues aside and some over-lookable design differencing, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a great way to re-introduce the squad-focused turn-based strategy game to a new era. Older players may dismiss the game, and that's fine, considering it's a different game-- but FNGs and other players open to a riveting and nerve-wracking strategy game with lots or replay value and tough-calls to make will find a game that is unpassable by a self-respecting gamer of any breed.
Remember, we will be watching.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

When your engines are on fire, your shield system is disabled, and the nefarious alien boarders have you cornered in your own med bay, you will find yourself cursing that you didn't upgrade your blast doors instead of purchasing that Hull Laser. Ignore the old bad reviews--there's nothing really wrong with this game.
If you don't know what Killing Floor is about, it's a game in which you and 5 other players hold your ground for 10 consecutive and increasingly difficult waves of Zeds (half-zombie failed genetic experiments) and, if you survive them all, a Boss comes alone on one last wave (2 bosses available ATM, not sure if more are coming.)
It may sound dumb--I'm usually not really into wave-games myself--but this one is good. Popping Zeds' heads off, burning and exploding them is just plain fun--which makes tha game playable even after you've leveled all your perks to lvl 25 (max) which, as some other reviews mentioned, takes about 300 hours (with the current perks; at least one more is coming as far as I know.)
Now, if you've played KF1, you know how the game goes. Compared to it, KF2 is better in every aspect (KF1 is unplayable after you've tasted KF2.) Seven out of the 9 currently available perks are the same as in KF1, and their weapons as well. This sucks a little bit because it's nothing new but, on the other hand, you'll already be familiar with how each of these perks work.
Every 5 levels you get unlocks two new skills for you to use when playing with the perk you leveled. You choose 1 from the 2 available lvl 5/10/15/20/25 skills to use and can change them any time you want (other than during waves.) Basically there are two main ways to play each perk, but you can also choose the skills however you want.
The maps are pretty well done, but only half of them or so are actually made by Tripwire. It seems they got lazy and decided to make independent/community maps official (I wonder if Tripwire pays these guys.) Still, these are good as well and there must be some 10-15 maps currently available (I'm not exactly sure how many, I forgot to count.)
Getting the Achievements is quite a challenge (and thus fun) since managing to beat most levels on Hell on Earth (hardest difficulty) is pretty tough, even with a good team.
Updates come quite often but the vast majority of them, in truth, are nothing but rebalances of the game (often disbalancing it) and minor bug fixes. The addition of actual content is much rarer but either I got lucky or Tripwire has been ramping up their efforts because I got the game right after the Sharpshooter Perk came out and some 3 months later the SWAT Perk and a new (community) map were "already" released as well. Anyway, even as it is, the game is already 100% playable and perfectly enjoyable.
The Store is also worth mentioning--you can buy (for real money) aesthetic items. That usually pisses me off, but it's actually not so bad. Once every 48 hours, after finishing a game, you'll either receive a basic/crap item or a supply crate/USB drive. The latter ones require a paid key to open and, other than buying items from other players from the Steam Market, paying to open them is the only way you can get the decent stuff--and that means gambling, which means you'll probably get something crappy anyway (but still "exclusive," different from the common drops.) The plus side is that you can sell the "crap stuff" you get and sometimes (rarely) you'll drop (for free) something worth a dolar or two. (Btw, some of the rarest stuff--from crates/USBs--gets sold for up to a couple hundred dolars in the Market.)
So... yeah, I definitely recommend buying KF2. It's already a complete game and worth hundreds of hours of fun as it is. Any content they add from now on is a plus, and there's at least a few more things to come which should make the game even better in time.

I waited on the berlin expansion to review this game, and I definitely recommend it now.
The original campaign, Dead Man's Switch, had a handful of problems at launch that had kept people from being as upbeat about it as they could, but many of those have also been fixed as of the expansion (Weapon balance, save system, bugs). Dead man's switch is a pretty cool campaign, and has a lot of nostalgic throwbacks to the SNES game. It's very Shadowrun Seattle (Megacorps, historic figures, gang control), and a bit short and linear, but still cool. I would give it a 8/10 or so.
The Berlin expansion is the most hooked I've been by an RPG in a really long time. The writing is fantastic, the characters are cool, and the world is really fun. The combat isn't quite as polished as say, XCOM, but it's passable and doesn't detract in any way. The flux state (prior to the invasion and second Berlin wall going up) is well depicted, and you become very invested in the stories of everyone living in your block of the anarchists haven.
There's much more freedom to approach things differently in the Berlin expansion, and you can take on side missions from the Berlin hub in the order you want, or even skip one or two if you want. It's also a bit longer than Dead man's switch, and features some new weapons. I would give Dragonfall a 9/10, easily.

TLDR Overall (9 out of 10 so far). If you liked Dead Island but wanted more grit, tension (man, the nights in this game), freedom in movement, variety in gameplay, satisfying combat and levelling, an actual penalty for death (and thus reason to want to stay alive) and exploration (a deeper thinking man's Parkour Dead Rising Island you could say) then this should definitely be for you.
Well, this game had a very odd and worrying release with delays, push forward's, date changes (feeling for those peeps having to wait an extra month) and late review copies among other things. You'd be forgiven for starting to think this was going to be another UbiGate' incident.
Thankfully, this is not the case, aside from some odd syrup like frame stuttering (if you have a 2GB graphics card, put the Texture Quality setting to medium as it relates to the caching of the texture memory rather than the texture quality itself according to Nvidia and my eyes agree) when on high texture setting (other settings such as nvidia hdbo+ or draw distance may need to be tweaked / turned off to fix it totally). Aside from that the game works flawless (it's been a little while for me to have release of this quality since all the ubisoft unpaid QA and hassle).
The game itself does have a nice (once you get used to it and trust your dude's gonna grab) parkour / jumping and climbing system, the melee doesn't incorporate the stick (I'm on a xbox gamepad) for its manual attack (got all auto aim/helpers off) but it still feels manual, beefy, brutal and satisfying (slow-mo killcams for the win again). The visuals are sweet but the stylized / grittiness sometimes hides it somewhat (some people might feel the grain filter is a little strong at first much like Mass Effect except in that game you could turn it off) but not to a level that it should be a problem for most.
I was worried about the game losing Dead Islands crafting, looting and discovery aspect as the gameplay shown before release didn't really show any of these aspects but rest assure, it's there if not even more so. There are 3 skill trees which seem nicely filled with sweet stuff, levelling is mostly done Skyrim style (monkey do, monkey learn, monkey gain), there is story documents, blueprints and loot a plenty to be found in locked chests (lockpicking is a feature but it's lockpicking materials are a plenty), baskets, bins, cupboards, fridges etc and the crafting is still as deep as DI but you no longer need a workbench to get it going. Interestingly items have a repair limit thus far, I don't know if something on the skill tree will remove or increase that but it's worth noting should you plan to get too attached to early to your newly crafted and modded Electric Water pipe!
You have a survival instincts scanner system (similar to Dragon Age Inquisition) which lets you see where there are interactables / items to use and find within your general vicinity (it's important too because thus far I don't see any indicator helpers on the main or mini-map of items or POI, perhaps it's an upgrade or NPC shark info, don't know) and its important you're not shy about using / spamming it after having a blind look around yourself because it can be the difference between missing a blueprint or not.
Also a special mention / thank you to Techland for bothering to actually let you players bypass cutscenes / dialogue / intros etc should they need to (I'm looking at you Far Cry 4).

I play a lot of different games.  Most of them I get into and drop after playing for 4-5 days.  This is the one game that I continuously go back to.  I've played KF1 since release, and KF2 brings me the greatest joy you can only achieve through mowing down zeds in the most gruesome ways possible.
I'm excited for the full release of this game, and hope for the special events to make a return to the game (like the Christmas and Halloween zed events).
Pros:
-Gory.  So very, very gory.
-9 different perk classes, with a 10th and final being released in November
-Difficulty scale much larger than KF1.  The scale in KF1 just involved faster movement, more hp, more damage, etc from zeds at higher difficulties, but Suicidal and HoE in KF2 also have alpha zeds and different animations for zeds along with those buffs.
-In conjunction with the last point, difficulty at higher levels require teamwork.  If you're the kind of person who runs off and does his own thing apart from the group, you probably won't last long in a HoE 6 man game.
-Community maps.  Currently the game has 11 maps, and TWI releases more every so often, but if those get stale you can play maps made by the community.
-TWI I believe is a great studio in my opinion.  I've heard contrary statements from other players, but from what I've seen in KF1, the constantly release new content and updates for free regularly, and I hope they continue this practice in KF2.
Cons:
-If you're playing this in early access, perks and zeds get buffed/nerfed every update, but that comes with the territory of EA.
-Player vs Zed pvp mode needs some definite balancing.  I've played a handful of matches and it seems the odds are strongly stacked in favor of zeds.  The only game I saw players win was when the person playing Patriarch was awful.
-Not necessarily on the con list, but microtransactions and a weaponskin/costume drop system are in this game.  I don't consider it a con, because it is purely cosmetic and you don't have to buy or farm any of the items, but I've seen other people complain.

My first 30 hours into the game. Be advised it might be long, but if you read on it'll get very exciting
-Chose to lead the US, thinking it was the most OP country, starting with the   ancient era with a large map and lots of AI empires and city states

-Focused on doing basic stuff in the early stages, farming, building mines etc.

-Slowly beginning to strengthen my economy through trade.
-Suddenly we were discovered by the Songholians and the Mongolians
-Their leaders, Askia of the Songholians and Genghis Khan of Mongol, showed friendly intentions and wanted us to work together
-I accepted (Big mistake people)

-America became famous for destroying barbarians and for its coal and silver
-Sweden came into the picture, and did not like my alliance with Polynesia and Songhol
-They started to annex 2 of Polynesia's settlements, Honolulu and Samoa

-We rekt the Swedes and reclaimed both cities plus annexing one of Sweden's settlements, Sigtuna.
-We gave back Samoa to the Polynesians, but made Honolulu our own for its seaport
-We conquered the city state, Panama City, because they did not want to share their crabs
-Meanwhile Sweden was the first to make contact with every empire, making them the absolute power of the World Congress with the most delegates
-Songhol did not like Sweden either, and we both made a research agreement so we could make it to the Industrial Era faster
-We made hostile relations with Sweden, causing most of the European empires (England, the Celts, Greece, and Denmark) to boycott us
-Achieved the first gun powered unit before anyone else, the Minutemen, and have cannon units and later on artillery
-Became the most superpowered nation at that time and forced the Europeans to negotiate a peace treaty
-Made it to the modern era. (This is where it gets interesting)
-Recieved intel from the Celts and Shoshones that Songhol was planning to backstab me.
-I took it as fake intel, Songhol was a great ally why would they attack me?
-While I was (litterally) not looking, they have achieved the atomic era first and their military was more advanced than mine
-They declared that I was not to be trusted and became hostile
-I learned later on (after the Cold War) that because I chose "Freedom", as an Ideology, and not "Order", we were considered traitors
-Began the Cold War between US and Songhol-Mongol-Shoshone alliance
-The US started building its army, causing a Great Depression
-Sweden offered help, I accpeted and we became allies.
-Songhol made to "Nuclear Power State" first and game concluded that I lost.
-But for the sake of American Spirit, I did not quit the session and continued
-Sweden's port city was attacked by Songhol subs and aircraft carriers carrying planes and an atomic bomb
-US with it's "meh" modern navy with no nuclear power, made a suprise attack on the fleet, destroying the nuclear ship, their subs, and a few troop carriers
-Started engaging their borders without help. Sweden was also being attacked by Denmark because of land complications
-Prayed to God, and then pushed my troops towards the border
-The Songhols deployed their infantry plus Bazooka units, attack helicopters, and bombers
-We hold the border and because we had P-51 Mustangs and B-17 Bombers, plus AA guns, the only country that has AA guns at the time
-We took down alot of their units not because we were advanced, but by sheer numbers and awesome strategy
-They lost 3/4 of their army, their nuclear bomb, their entire Navy, and the US still held their ground without taking any of their land, with only losing an artillery unit
-They negotiated a peace treaty
-We became best buds (but still keeping an eye on each other)

So Dying Light is one of those zombie games. Zombies in 2015? Why are zombies even still a thing? Thats a great question! I have no idea...
Now being how Techland also made Dead Island the combat and skill progression is almost exactly the same.  Techland has refined the combat but has kept the same brutal, bloody, chunky combat.  Heads explode in a shower of brain and bone. There are critical attacks which damage and break bones, you see this through a detailed x-ray view of the damage. There are three different skill trees and three different ways to upgrade them. There is the Survival Skill tree which is your crafting and passive boots tree. you gain Survival levels by liberating safe zones and progressing through the story and side missions. There is also the Agility tree which you gain levels by--what else? Parkouring. As you run and jump your way across rooftops, dirty, bloody streets and around arms and hungry teeth the levels you make allow you to run faster, gain more moves to escape and to fight.  The Power tree is the last skill tree and is pretty self explanatory. The more you hit things the better you hit things.
In Dead Island the Island feels dead. The said Island is crawling with zombies who are dead. The characters are also Dead, the story is very, VERY dead. Which is sad because I liked Dead Island for all of its flaws but things like that make it very hard to play the game. In Dying Light the characters are actually pretty well made regardless of Techlands facial animations which seem to have a very limited and undetailed range of emotions. (I sometimes confuse the zombies with the humans because they both share the same crazy eyes and long distance stare. But it really isn't that bad. The zombies are covered in blood, the humans are not.) The voice acting on all the side characters as well as your own main character are great. Very good in fact. There is a nice feature which I wish games did more often is when you start up the game your main character has a first person objective reminder almost like reading a diary or a journal. In fact that could be one of the main elements as your character is dropped into the infected city of Haram to locate a renegade faction leader and you periodically check in with your superiors to debrief. The opening monologues are often phrased like that.
Techland has not had a good track record when it comes to making good characters or story and the story in this one, seems like it could be pretty predictable.  There are two factions warring for survival against the zombies and themselves. There are 'Rais' men whom are the characteristic bandits and there is the Tower, a collection of 'runners' and scouts who find supplies and equipment as well as the precious Antizin, a suppresant of symptoms for those who are bitten by a zombie. The supplies themselves are being dropped by an international task force called the GRE which has locked off the city of Haram by land, air and sea as well as jamming all radio frequencies in and out of the infected city. Your main character is a GRE agent whose task is to kill the leader of one of the two factions, whomever he is.  His identity is a secret and your character has to blend in among the Towers populace, liberating Safe Zones, completing tasks for the survivors and main story quests in order to figure out who is who. Now these are not called 'tasks' anymore as they were in Dead Island, they are 'Quests'. I don't know why I made that point but I guess I did.
The city of Haram is beautifully designed, it feels like a real city under quarantine and under siege of mindless flesh eaters... but are they so mindless. What happens when night falls? Is it really so safe? No. No it is not.
This is where Dying Light makes it's distinction among other zombie games. After night falls the city comes alive with swarms of fast, rabid zombies whom you stand no chance of fighting. You have to run. The game also changes after night, It becomes a real true survival horror game where as in the day time it is a happy-go-lucky zombie splattering free-running adventure!
This concludes my Dying Light 'review'. Now seeing how I preordered this game at -15% and was sort of expecting this level of execution by Techland I am quite happy with my purchase if not for the dubious launch and preorder bonuses that plagues the industry so. I expect to get my $45 out of this game for a long time.
Oh and did I mention that you can invade other players world a-la Dark Souls as a lean mean killing machine zombie? Just one extra feature that I'm sure someone will like.

When your engines are on fire, your shield system is disabled, and the nefarious alien boarders have you cornered in your own med bay, you will find yourself cursing that you didn't upgrade your blast doors instead of purchasing that Hull Laser. This game is as addicting as it is sadistically merciless, and will keep you begging for just one more bloody turn!

This is a review based on the first 2 hours of gameplay - played through the entire initial prologue (fairly extensive and lengthy). Coming from an FPS veteran who cut his teeth on Wolfenstein 3D and has played almost every FPS since, I can unreservedly recommend this. If you enjoyed Dead Island, this is a very similar, albeit FAR superior game. This doesn't have nearly the same comic-book feel to it, and the graphics are impressive.
Pros:
Free-running/parkour - this is done very well - not frustrating and clunky like Assassin's Creed, and it's also not a "can't miss" QTE either. You're not a superhuman, and it IS possible to miss ledges/grabs/balances - however, this is largely due to player skill, not any form of bug. The free-running/mantling aspect is handled fluidly, and lends a sense that your body actually has some weight to it - it takes some skill, it's not just a matter of "look at the grapple point, press a button, automatically teleport there with an animation". Very life-like.
Graphics - high resolution, well put together. Not quite on the level of the new Frostbite engine, but very good - no complaints here.
Gameplay - if you liked Dead Island, you'll like this. Very similar. Crafting weapons, primarily melee-based, gather supplies/blueprints, special Giant Zombies etc.. Like another reviewer mentioned, the difference here is they focus more on the horde-mechanic, as opposed to a lot of individual encounters. Thus far, they definitely incentivize the free-running, think smart aspect as opposed to blithely wading into an encounter with your trusty rusty pipe.
Cons - The buildings and locales are all very similar. This could be because I'm primarily still in the early portion of the game, however I did enough side-exploring to see what the city offered. Not a lot of variants that I could see - mostly a favela-looking jungle of shanties. Not necessarily a bad thing, but also won't blow you away with variety.
9/10 - Simply put, if you liked Dead Island and want something slightly less comic-bookish, this is the game for you. It's basically Dead Island with free-running, but much, much better put together and less clumsy.
For anyone ever wanting to fly faster than light - and have fun doing it!

I'd been craving the old-school SR like the ones on Genesis and SNES which I played when I was hardly into my teens, and everything in the KS pitch sold me that this would bring it back to those days.  When SRR finally released and I played through it, I came out satisfied.  It has a solid and deep story, good combat (which has since been balanced and improved), fairly simple puzzles, and yes..it had some flaws like no manual saves (again, resolved since then), but it didn't really bug me that much.  Most of all, they made choice matter.
And then along comes Shadowrun: Dragonfall.
Dragonfall absolutely oozes greatness.  There's insane depth of characters and the world, down to the smallest details, even in conversations with side characters like Simmy Kim and reading the Shadowland BBS.  It's a very rare thing where a game captures me so well that I sit and read every single piece of text I come across (and there's so much to read in this series).  I especially appreciated the design in this DLC of having the quest hub, but more importantly, there were so many more rich side quests throughout the campaign than in the base game.  They also upped the design on the puzzle elements a bit which I appreciated (the original campaign's were generally way too straightforward).  But enough of a wall of text, let's break things down:
Aside from the depth of lore in this world, the story of this campaign alone was so great.  Just when you     think you've got things figured out, something throws you for a loop.  You face lots of decisions that test your morals, many of which mostly seem to test just how close to "the line" you're willing to step, or if it's even a question for you.
This time around, you've got a dedicated crew.  Sure, you could hire runners to go along with you, but the crew is where it's at.  They've got deep stories and I loved every bit of exploring them.  The SRR Dead Man Switch campaign had people occasionally joining you, like Coyote, but those companions pale in comparison to the attention given to the crew of Dragonfall.  I cared about my crew.  Hell, I felt bad that I always had to leave one member behind on my runs having only room for a team of 4.  I felt like I was neglecting them most of the game and that they were going to confront me about it at some point.
I played on hard difficulty, and essentially did the same rifle-focused street samurai build I did in SRR.  I found it much more balanced, and there were several missions with some real tension as the fights raged on.  The Matrix served a good purpose as well; it felt much more key to this campaign than the first.
They already established this with SRR, they just painted a whole new world for Dragonfall's Berlin setting, and it's gorgeous.
So that's it in a nutshell.

Ignore the old bad reviews--there's nothing really wrong with this game.
If you don't know what Killing Floor is about, it's a game in which you and 5 other players hold your ground for 10 consecutive and increasingly difficult waves of Zeds (half-zombie failed genetic experiments) and, if you survive them all, a Boss comes alone on one last wave (2 bosses available ATM, not sure if more are coming.)
It may sound dumb--I'm usually not really into wave-games myself--but this one is good. Popping Zeds' heads off, burning and exploding them is just plain fun--which makes tha game playable even after you've leveled all your perks to lvl 25 (max) which, as some other reviews mentioned, takes about 300 hours (with the current perks; at least one more is coming as far as I know.)
Now, if you've played KF1, you know how the game goes. Compared to it, KF2 is better in every aspect (KF1 is unplayable after you've tasted KF2.) Seven out of the 9 currently available perks are the same as in KF1, and their weapons as well. This sucks a little bit because it's nothing new but, on the other hand, you'll already be familiar with how each of these perks work.
Every 5 levels you get unlocks two new skills for you to use when playing with the perk you leveled. You choose 1 from the 2 available lvl 5/10/15/20/25 skills to use and can change them any time you want (other than during waves.) Basically there are two main ways to play each perk, but you can also choose the skills however you want.
The maps are pretty well done, but only half of them or so are actually made by Tripwire. It seems they got lazy and decided to make independent/community maps official (I wonder if Tripwire pays these guys.) Still, these are good as well and there must be some 10-15 maps currently available (I'm not exactly sure how many, I forgot to count.)
Getting the Achievements is quite a challenge (and thus fun) since managing to beat most levels on Hell on Earth (hardest difficulty) is pretty tough, even with a good team.
Updates come quite often but the vast majority of them, in truth, are nothing but rebalances of the game (often disbalancing it) and minor bug fixes. The addition of actual content is much rarer but either I got lucky or Tripwire has been ramping up their efforts because I got the game right after the Sharpshooter Perk came out and some 3 months later the SWAT Perk and a new (community) map were "already" released as well. Anyway, even as it is, the game is already 100% playable and perfectly enjoyable.
The Store is also worth mentioning--you can buy (for real money) aesthetic items. That usually pisses me off, but it's actually not so bad. Once every 48 hours, after finishing a game, you'll either receive a basic/crap item or a supply crate/USB drive. The latter ones require a paid key to open and, other than buying items from other players from the Steam Market, paying to open them is the only way you can get the decent stuff--and that means gambling, which means you'll probably get something crappy anyway (but still "exclusive," different from the common drops.) The plus side is that you can sell the "crap stuff" you get and sometimes (rarely) you'll drop (for free) something worth a dolar or two. (Btw, some of the rarest stuff--from crates/USBs--gets sold for up to a couple hundred dolars in the Market.)
So... yeah, I definitely recommend buying KF2. It's already a complete game and worth hundreds of hours of fun as it is. Any content they add from now on is a plus, and there's at least a few more things to come which should make the game even better in time.

I play a lot of different games.  Most of them I get into and drop after playing for 4-5 days.  This is the one game that I continuously go back to.  I've played KF1 since release, and KF2 brings me the greatest joy you can only achieve through mowing down zeds in the most gruesome ways possible.
I'm excited for the full release of this game, and hope for the special events to make a return to the game (like the Christmas and Halloween zed events).
Pros:
-Gory.  So very, very gory.
-9 different perk classes, with a 10th and final being released in November
-Difficulty scale much larger than KF1.  The scale in KF1 just involved faster movement, more hp, more damage, etc from zeds at higher difficulties, but Suicidal and HoE in KF2 also have alpha zeds and different animations for zeds along with those buffs.
-In conjunction with the last point, difficulty at higher levels require teamwork.  If you're the kind of person who runs off and does his own thing apart from the group, you probably won't last long in a HoE 6 man game.
-Community maps.  Currently the game has 11 maps, and TWI releases more every so often, but if those get stale you can play maps made by the community.
-TWI I believe is a great studio in my opinion.  I've heard contrary statements from other players, but from what I've seen in KF1, the constantly release new content and updates for free regularly, and I hope they continue this practice in KF2.
Cons:
-If you're playing this in early access, perks and zeds get buffed/nerfed every update, but that comes with the territory of EA.
-Player vs Zed pvp mode needs some definite balancing.  I've played a handful of matches and it seems the odds are strongly stacked in favor of zeds.  The only game I saw players win was when the person playing Patriarch was awful.
-Not necessarily on the con list, but microtransactions and a weaponskin/costume drop system are in this game.  I don't consider it a con, because it is purely cosmetic and you don't have to buy or farm any of the items, but I've seen other people complain.

Okay, I finally have to write a little something after playing the Dragonfall DLC.
First off, to quickly go over Shadowrun Returns:
Let me preface this by saying I am a kickstarter backer.  Back when SRR popped up on Kickstarter, I immediately jumped on board.  I'd been craving the old-school SR like the ones on Genesis and SNES which I played when I was hardly into my teens, and everything in the KS pitch sold me that this would bring it back to those days.  When SRR finally released and I played through it, I came out satisfied.  It has a solid and deep story, good combat (which has since been balanced and improved), fairly simple puzzles, and yes..it had some flaws like no manual saves (again, resolved since then), but it didn't really bug me that much.  Most of all, they made choice matter.
And then along comes Shadowrun: Dragonfall.
Dragonfall absolutely oozes greatness.  There's insane depth of characters and the world, down to the smallest details, even in conversations with side characters like Simmy Kim and reading the Shadowland BBS.  It's a very rare thing where a game captures me so well that I sit and read every single piece of text I come across (and there's so much to read in this series).  I especially appreciated the design in this DLC of having the quest hub, but more importantly, there were so many more rich side quests throughout the campaign than in the base game.  They also upped the design on the puzzle elements a bit which I appreciated (the original campaign's were generally way too straightforward).  But enough of a wall of text, let's break things down:
Aside from the depth of lore in this world, the story of this campaign alone was so great.  Just when you     think you've got things figured out, something throws you for a loop.  You face lots of decisions that test your morals, many of which mostly seem to test just how close to "the line" you're willing to step, or if it's even a question for you.
This time around, you've got a dedicated crew.  Sure, you could hire runners to go along with you, but the crew is where it's at.  They've got deep stories and I loved every bit of exploring them.  The SRR Dead Man Switch campaign had people occasionally joining you, like Coyote, but those companions pale in comparison to the attention given to the crew of Dragonfall.  I cared about my crew.  Hell, I felt bad that I always had to leave one member behind on my runs having only room for a team of 4.  I felt like I was neglecting them most of the game and that they were going to confront me about it at some point.
I played on hard difficulty, and essentially did the same rifle-focused street samurai build I did in SRR.  I found it much more balanced, and there were several missions with some real tension as the fights raged on.  The Matrix served a good purpose as well; it felt much more key to this campaign than the first.
They already established this with SRR, they just painted a whole new world for Dragonfall's Berlin setting, and it's gorgeous.
So that's it in a nutshell.

I never played the original Shadowrun (SNES and Sega Genesis, apparently), but after playing Shadowrun Returns, I'm going to find it.
Shadowrun Returns is one of the few games in the "RPG" category that is, in fact, a Role-Playing Game. Unlike Dungeon Siege, Diablo, BioWare Game or Final Fantasy, Shadowrun actually requires you to interact with NPCs and the manner of those interactions actually impacts the game. Imagine that. So many games claim that NPC interactions affect outcomes, but this is the first game I've played in a while (not including the Elder Scrolls/Fallout 3 sub-genre) in which that's actually true.
Dead Man's Switch (the original campaign) has a little bit of important dialogue, but Dragonfall (the first DLC campaign) is LOADED with character development and NPCs that actually behave differently depending on how you treat them.
But the beauty of Shadowrun Returns isn't the official campaigns. It's the editor, and the integration with Steam Workshop. I've not actually used the editor yet, but judging from the vast range of quality in the user-created content, it must be pretty easy to use. On the one hand, that means a LOT of just pure garbage content. On the other hand, it means that learning how to use the editor isn't a stumbling block for somebody who's got a great story to tell.
So while the original campaign is really quite good (I mean really, really good. It's one of the few campaigns of any game that I'm perfectly happy replaying several times in a row), Dragonfall really showcases what the game's engine is capable of.
If you've ever played the old Fallout games (Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout Tactics), this is a lot like those. If you haven't played those, think of it as turn-based, squad-based Diablo, with almost no emphasis on gear. There is an equipment treadmill, but it's not very involved. More along the lines of Mass Effect 2.
There are three or four pistols (for example), and you buy the most expensive one you can afford. So while there IS a reason to make more money and get the better stuff, it's not the need that it is in other games (Diablo, for example). Sorry to keep making the comparison to Diablo, but that's the other game I've been playing most recently.
Shadowrun Returns is also one of the few games I've played that knows how to use a touchscreen. Most games work "well enough," but SR has a touchscreen mode that makes it function beautifully. And by "beautifully," I mean that the PC version plays just as well on my Dell touchscreen as the Android version plays on my Samsung Note 2.
I don't know if anyone but me cares about that, but with the increasing prevalence of Windows 8, I figure it's worth mentioning.
I know I'm making a big deal about Dragonfall, and I mean to. It's an excellent campaign, and is actually (in my opinion) worth the price of a full expansion pack, as opposed to the increasingly-common 2-dollar DLC. But I suppose I should really talk more about Dead Man's Switch. It's an engaging mystery with great characters. It doesn't have the meaningful dialogues and character developmnet of Dragonfall, but I was immediately taken with both Dresden and Kluwe. They're not "important" characters, but the fact that placeholder roles are filled with well-fleshed and well-written characters is just indicative of the attention to detail paid by the devs. It's a well-polished introduction to the world of Shadowrun.

Dying Light is a game filled with zombies and parkour. This game is great but there are some pros and cons to this game, just like most triple A titles. This is one of my first serious reviews due I believe I need to warn people about what they are buying here and some of the current issues.

-AMD systems be warned the performance is not great when you get past the tutorial. I found myself dropping frames randomly and the parkour and at night time it can be quite difficult getting around at 20-25 fps. So until we get a patch for AMD think carefully about buying this game.(Now most AMD performance issues have been fixed after patch 1.4.0)
- The lip sync with the characters is not great for this title and is quite easy to notice. Some may think this is not a huge issue but I like to get immersed in my games and this sort of broke immersion for me.
- The eyes on some of the characters are bit all over the place and sometimes put me off from looking at them. Again this sort of broke immersion for me.
- This game has really interesting characters and keeps you intrested in the story (So far).
- The graphics are stunning and truly live up todays standards and beyond.
- The crafting system and skill trees and are well organised, balanced and contain a variety of player choices.
- The parkour system is really good and does not feel glitchy and broken like Assassins creed has felt for a very long time.
- The mechanics of how the game works and how it sort of forces you to hide and run at night instead of stand there and fight all the unique zombies the game has to offer.
- Bad performance for AMD users (Fixed after 1.4.0)
- Bad lip sync and strange eyes on some of the characters
- The story is good and the characters feel realistic and well designed
- The parkour makes this game so unique from Dead Island and makes the game feel a lot different
- The night and day cycle in the game seems so far very good and uses the play styles well
- Crafting system is well designed and the skill tree is not rushed
AMD users this is a serious issue about performance and is the main issue stoping me from playing it and should be considered as a main factor to considering wether to buy this game at its current price tag. Overall I would rate this about a 8/10(UPDATE so 9/10) for a good story and really improved on the features that went so wrong in their previous games, but the performance for AMD users is really irritaiting.
Thanks for reading my review and if you buy this game, enjoy!

I never played Shadowrun when it was on the NES or whatever else it was on. I joined the world with Shadowrun Returns and I have to say its a good place to start. It opens up a lot of doors, and even some windows, to a whole new world of science and magic. The controls feel clunky sometimes, but its by no means game breaking. Its turn table based combat, good guys go first more often then not, and then the bad guys.
You get to make your own character from various races and classes. You don't have to stick to class you pick at creation though. You can be a mage with some intense decking skills, or a rigger who knows some summoning. They don't force you to stick to a class. Just be careful, as the game often hints 'A Jack of all trades is a master of none.'
You play as a Shadowrunner, a gun for hire in the streets. You've fallen on some hard times and seem to be thinking more about your future then your past, till you get a call from a old contact. A guy you used to run with, Sam. He's been killed recently and set up a 'dead mans switch' in his brain to send you a message when he finally kicks the bucket. Well, someone kicked his bucket for him and you need to travel to Seattle and find out who did it. There are some serious twists and turns as you dig deeper into this world, trying to uncover who did it.
Dragonfall is leap and bounds ahead of Dead mans Switch. The graphics feel tighter, but there is no real change. Some of the sounds and combat has been tweaked a bit and the save anywhere anytime button is a lifesaver. The supporting characters feel a lot more real, and can be interacted with anytime. They have backgrounds and lives, and aren't afarid to give you a piece of their minds if they think your doing something wrong.
In the newest 'dlc' you get a whole new campgain, set up for a new character but thanks to some dedicated players you can import your character over to this save file to run the DLC. Your out on a run with long time friend Monica and her crew in Berlin. Its a simple job, a smash and grab type. However things aren't always as they seem... Monica ends up dead and you and the crew end up fleeing for your lives. With Monica dead there is a seat to be filled in the community where she lived, and her crew wants revenge. Will you be the vengeful angel and the savior all in one package?
