If you like progression, and leveling up, you will at least get 300 hours out of it. If you like a lot of variaton, this game kinda lacks of it. After maxing out all the perks, you're kinda ''done'' with the weapons, maps and perks, or at least, I am. There is too little amount of weapons (and therefor playstyle) and a lack of maps that brings down the addiction to this game after a while.
The new perk, survivalist, I call it cheap, easy and uninspired. I also think it's not the best co-op perk you can pick, since your teammates are kinda in the dark what task you are going to take on you.
There are still some annoying bugs ingame like zeds clipping and zeds that walks past an obstacle and instead walk past it walk(/glitch) half over it, which make you just miss that damn headshot.
Versus mode, the game mode I like the most after leveling all perks that is, still needs a lot of work. The balance isn't still right. It's better, but not right. Some perks are a bit too strong for this mode, like beserker, demo and medic. Some zeds got a bit too much off a health and damage buff, other zeds (like sc and fp) are underpowerd. The spawning control is still ridicilous, still the problem that your team might get usseless zeds for 4 waves, while the other team gets sirens and tons of crawlers and bloats from wave 2 on already, and some extra sc and fp spawns just for the fun of it. Patty is way to easy to play with. I think the health can maybe be lowerd a bit further, and the damage output also needs to turned down a bit. Yea, Patty should be strong. But the zed team keeps getting zed spawns untill the last human is alive. That is just too much, even with a good and high level team. Patty should be nerfed a little bit, but also be harder to control. Make his turning speed slower, his starting speed slower, make it so that it actually needs a little bit of practice and tactic before you can wipe out the human squad without that much of an effort, please.
The dropping system is awfull, if you ask me. Yea sometimes you get somethin sweet, like a gunskin (I like that, as long as it's free and just cosmetic), but I/most players(or all?) still get 90% crates and USB's, things no one really wants. In the meantime your inventory stocks up with a shtload with those things, while on the market you can barerly sell them. This make the dropsystem just an annoying add-on.
If you like this kind of games, co-op FPS, with a (for now simplistic) game mode that offers the PVP-genre, I can recommend this game. You will get your money out of it.
But for the longer therm, this game really needs a whole lot more weapons, maps, and better balance over all.
Original -EA- review;
What can I say about Killing Floor 2.. Nothing but love honestly. Never played the original Killing Floor, noticed this game (KF2) was in a free weekend a year ago, played it, bought it, and played it a whole lot more.
I think 300 hours was for leveling up all perks to level 25. So yeah, enough time you can spent ingame if you look at it that way.
The game isn't perfect. I like the perks, I like the guns, I like the maps. But I would like to see some more weapon choices and a lot more (official) maps. I've noticed that once I reached all my perks to level 25, the guns and maps weren't special enough anymore to keep me luring in. You can play with a different perk, but everytime you play with that perk you kinda handle it the same way, as in the same order to buy guns and which ones you actually use. So more gun variation could help to play differently within a perk itself. And for the maps, after playing them so many times, you can almost dream where the zeds spawn and where to find ammo and armor. Would be nice if the spawn points for both zeds and ammo/armor can variate a bit more, and it would be even greater if there would be a whole lot more of maps. Some more achievements would help too. I'm not an achievement hunter or something, but in a game like this I like to see achievements like a "Killed 100 bloats", "Killed 500 bloats", "Killed 1000 bloats" achievements (for every zed). Would help to find some challenging within the game itself too, after you're basicly done progressing with the perks.
If I'm correct, theres still coming a (free) perk, a couple more weapons and some maps. So most points I think this game lacks off will get some more in it.
None the less, this game is great. Has it flaws, but with a good team around you, you definitely will be having fun and get your money out of it.

TLDR Overall (9 out of 10 so far). If you liked Dead Island but wanted more grit, tension (man, the nights in this game), freedom in movement, variety in gameplay, satisfying combat and levelling, an actual penalty for death (and thus reason to want to stay alive) and exploration (a deeper thinking man's Parkour Dead Rising Island you could say) then this should definitely be for you.
Well, this game had a very odd and worrying release with delays, push forward's, date changes (feeling for those peeps having to wait an extra month) and late review copies among other things. You'd be forgiven for starting to think this was going to be another UbiGate' incident.
Thankfully, this is not the case, aside from some odd syrup like frame stuttering (if you have a 2GB graphics card, put the Texture Quality setting to medium as it relates to the caching of the texture memory rather than the texture quality itself according to Nvidia and my eyes agree) when on high texture setting (other settings such as nvidia hdbo+ or draw distance may need to be tweaked / turned off to fix it totally). Aside from that the game works flawless (it's been a little while for me to have release of this quality since all the ubisoft unpaid QA and hassle).
The game itself does have a nice (once you get used to it and trust your dude's gonna grab) parkour / jumping and climbing system, the melee doesn't incorporate the stick (I'm on a xbox gamepad) for its manual attack (got all auto aim/helpers off) but it still feels manual, beefy, brutal and satisfying (slow-mo killcams for the win again). The visuals are sweet but the stylized / grittiness sometimes hides it somewhat (some people might feel the grain filter is a little strong at first much like Mass Effect except in that game you could turn it off) but not to a level that it should be a problem for most.
I was worried about the game losing Dead Islands crafting, looting and discovery aspect as the gameplay shown before release didn't really show any of these aspects but rest assure, it's there if not even more so. There are 3 skill trees which seem nicely filled with sweet stuff, levelling is mostly done Skyrim style (monkey do, monkey learn, monkey gain), there is story documents, blueprints and loot a plenty to be found in locked chests (lockpicking is a feature but it's lockpicking materials are a plenty), baskets, bins, cupboards, fridges etc and the crafting is still as deep as DI but you no longer need a workbench to get it going. Interestingly items have a repair limit thus far, I don't know if something on the skill tree will remove or increase that but it's worth noting should you plan to get too attached to early to your newly crafted and modded Electric Water pipe!
You have a survival instincts scanner system (similar to Dragon Age Inquisition) which lets you see where there are interactables / items to use and find within your general vicinity (it's important too because thus far I don't see any indicator helpers on the main or mini-map of items or POI, perhaps it's an upgrade or NPC shark info, don't know) and its important you're not shy about using / spamming it after having a blind look around yourself because it can be the difference between missing a blueprint or not.
Also a special mention / thank you to Techland for bothering to actually let you players bypass cutscenes / dialogue / intros etc should they need to (I'm looking at you Far Cry 4).

-- This recommendation is for Dragonfall --
Set in Berlin, Dragonfall is unrelated to the previous campaign, Dead Man's Switch, but the developers have taken the fans' points of criticism to heart and worked on them. The campaign is no longer so linear and railroaded (though you shouldn't expect loads of side-quests, it's still not that kind of game), and gives you more choices during your Runs. The companions are more fleshed out, and even though shotgunning badass Coyote is gone, there are four new party members, with their own backstories, strengths, and weaknesses. You can still hire 'generic' Runners if so inclined, but they don't have as much personality.
If you liked the original Shadowrun Returns, pick this one up without a second of hesitation. If you prefer backflips, explosions, killcams or any of that other shiny stuff, don't bother. This game is old-style, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
-- Original recommendation for Shadowrun Returns: --
I see so few people on my friendslist own this game, and I wonder why. Shadowrun Returns is exactly the kind of game we complain is no longer being made. Finally we get another turn-based Role-playing/Strategy game, and it pleases me greatly to say that Shadowrun Returns is a very impressive effort to put the genre back on the map.
Don't get me wrong, the game is no huge-budget production, so don't expect cutting-edge graphics or cool combos or flashy action scenes. What you CAN expect is great writing, diverse characters, some solid good old turn-based gameplay, plenty of character customization options, a wonderfully crafted world and an overall experience that keeps calling you to turn your computer back on and play some more.
Like I said, the game isn't without its imperfections, but if you look for quality over packaging, you'll be able to overlook those flaws with ease. I would have loved some more exploration and dialogue options, and a greater number of side quests, and the game gives you very little information about how to play it (tooltips aren't always bad, Harebrained Schemes) but as it is now, it's a very respectable and worthy effort to both breathe life into an old and underappreeciated game genre, AND in a setting that was forgotten by, or even unknown to, people who weren't around for the SNES or Pen-and-Paper era.
If you like solid, oldschool gaming, you'll do yourself a great injustice if you pass this one up, so show the industry that games shouldn't all be Call of Duty or Skyrim.

The original game felt a little unfinished but Dragonfall is an absolute corker. Haven't enjoyed a story in an RPG in ages. Massive, massive props to HBS for not resting on their laurels and going all out to improve just about every area of the game.

* The enviromental takedowns don't always trigger pressing Space+Left Mouse Button and actually made the fight with Professor Pyg impossible. The only way to do it was to swap to the joypad for that.

Wow, the Dragonfall campaign really changed my opinion on this game. I didn't really enjoy Dead Man's Switch (the original campaign), it felt forced, linear, barren and dull. All that coupled with the game's inherent limitations and plenty of bugs, left a bad taste in my mouth. I do enjoy tactical combat and "old-school" RPGs, but I was about to give up on Shadowrun Returns.
Then came Dragonfall. Still pretty much linear (though you notice it less this time around), still riddled with bugs (take old bugs out, put new bugs in, the development process kinda goes that way) and still with more or less the same annoying game limitations... yet it manages to outshine all these drawbacks with a helluva good story, enjoyable NPCs and character interaction, ambiguous moral choices that you can actually care about, challenging and entertaining combat and several new ways to do old things, including new tech and spells, plenty of skill checks (which also meant that no matter how good you got, you were never going to get the full information on everything, which is a good thing in my opinion). It's a huge leap up from Dead Man's Switch and has redeemed Shadowrun Returns in my eyes. Highly Recommended.
I hope SR continues to give us content comparable in quality to Dragonfall, so that we can all put that Dead Man's Switch nonsense behind us. l found out bitterly what this game couldn't do when I played through Dead Man's Switch. But I just now found out what this game CAN do after I played through Dragonfall. And that is: BE ENTERTAINING!

Review for DMS (Dead Man´s Switch) & DF (DragonFall) Campaigns
When Shadowrun Returns DMS came out, i liked it, but wasn´t really happy.
The writing, atmosphere and graphics were nice and fitting, you really could delve into the Shadowrun universe and have fun.
What was not so nice, were the lack of good/real party members and the unability to customize them. Also the story itself was pretty straightforward, with few optional decisions possible.
What was horrible was the lack of a proper saving system.
With DF Harebrained Schemes finally delivered the save system. So the horrible part is gone. They also tried to deliver some optional questing and a bit more interesting&permanent team members. B for effort, but for a truly good rpg the customization/inventory management of your party is still lacking, also the characters of the fix team members could still use some makeover, at least personal quests.
The story once again is fitting, and the whole game has a bit more variety, without changing much of the base gameplay.
So, to make this short, if you like Shadowrun and haven´t bought this game yet - do it! ;)
If you like rpgs/cyberpunk, you now can give it at least a try.

Shadowrun Returns is a decent romp through a cyberpunk world.  It does a good job of making the world seem much larger than it is at first, and personally I really liked the characters, missions and story.  Since the cyberpunk community is rather small as far as selection goes, this is a no-brainer for anyone hoping to get some good PnP-lite action in.  The stories are told well enough and with community mods, you'll have plenty to dive into if you really like it.  So for the price is isn't a bad deal.
If that seems like a general compliment, it is.  The game itself is a bit too simplistic for its own good, and fails to standout beyond its initial premise and art style.  This is a game with roots in the pen and paper role-playing world making it impossible to not ask 'where is the rest of it'?  Whether your character uses throwing knives, magic spells or a shotgun the gameplay is identical.  Levelling feels arbitrary because the skills are almost identical for any 'specialty' and there seems to be little reason to really diversify your party.  It's that mentality which does the most damage.  Character customization is highly limited outside of some nice details such as cyberware that becomes visible on your character, and weapons are as bog standard as you can get and don't even seem to have unique models.
It's an average budget RPG with decent replayability and a fantastic setting.  The biggest mistake here was not trying for anything better.  Instead of a unique game in a unique setting, we got one that would be right at home on your cellphone next to Candy Crush.  It isn't a bad game, which explains the recommendation, but there's too many oversights or just plain missed opportunities to stand out that keep this game from being much more than a casual enjoyment.

It's basically Dead Island but way less boring and tedious.
So you start out knowing nothing about the world you've been dropped into other than what the opening sequence gives you before you get to the main menu (Unless you skip those like me, heh) Then it's a pretty cliche begining for a zombie game
Survivor (You)
Dropped into Zombie world (Or island in this case?)
Meets bad guys that aren't zombies
Meets good guys that aren't zombies
Zombies get set off by noise
We have the basic formula which I'm not a big fan of, but we also have some new elements that you may like:
Parkour
gives our zombie game a different feel, a different pace. This allows you to go where ever the hell you want any time you want. During the day you can just run around with a wrench and beat zombies to death, but once night rolls around, like I said before the zombies go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This new aspect will become your best friend
Crafting
It's not "new" but components are not found easily. You will find yourself holding a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of useless material such as duct tape. (I know I did) The crafting System works almost exactly like Dead Island. Hell this entire game IS dead island in this area. mods are really fun too.
Combat
It's not boring, nor is it the best combat in the world. It's fast paced for the most part but when your weapons get damaged (Yes durability is a problem) it takes about 5 seconds to repair them; not forgiving in a fast pace combat environment. Sound of combat (guns, melee hitting things) attract more zombies, but what I do like is the ability to use this to your advantage. No spoilers but you will find that sound is your best friend and worst enemy. Also there are only like 5 guns in the game
Now on to how the game looks.
Graphics
Despite the endless threads about the game stuttering which I think Nvidia may release a patch for soon this week, the game itself is beautiful at max settings, it may be a good example of what a good game should be.
Animations
The animations of viewmodels is beautiful, a big plus is the fact that I can see my legs. But other characters REEK of Motion Capture, its almost painful to look at them if you've had past mocap experience. The lipsync sucks as every game does in the door, so its not a plus or a negative.
Models
Everything is seems high poly and looks pretty nice. Nothing much to say about that
Story
(Spoilers since the game is very story driven)
Very anticlimactic, has its twists, but in the end the final "boss" felt more like a TWD fight than an action RPG. Disappointing

Dying Light is incredibly fun. It easily could have been a contender for GOTY 2014 had it come out last 2014. Beautiful graphics, exciting gameplay, rewarding parkour system. This is everything that I had wanted Dead Island to be, even without the parkour element. Everything about this game screams polish and you can clearly see the amount of thought and detail that went into every crevice of this game.
They've taken interesting ideas from other games including Farcry, Mirror's Edge, Assassin's Creed, etc and spun them all into an amazing story-driven Zombie Survival game.
The zombies work as they should, with many different varities for you to avoid or hunt. Some are slow and stupid, while other freshly infected are fast, smart, and climb just as well as you can. There are also zombies that spit acid bombs, suicidal fat zombies that run at you and explode into blood and guts for crazy damage. There are even giant zombies with armor and sledgehammer type weapons that are more difficult to take down.
The guns in this game work MUCH better when compared to the original Dead Island series, they actually feel and sound like guns, are very accurate depending on the type of gun you are wielding. But they also don't feel overpowered, because the noise attracts the fast running zombies if you continue to fire them off and it becomes very easy to become overwhelmed by hordes if you dont play smart.
About mid-way through the game the story gets CRAZY and intense. I won't post any spoilers, but when you transition areas from The Slums to Sector 0, it becomes almost an entirely new game and reinvigorates the atmosphere with beautiful scenery and even more parkour fun. Rooftop to rooftop, sliding and jumping whilst dodging or killing zombies and humans with guns. It's insanely entertaining.
There is also a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of gathering/crafting to be done in this game.. From crazy modified weapons, to medkits and molotovs, DIY grenades, flares, firecrackers and thrown weapons like knives, axes, etc. The list goes on and on. You have to find the blueprints either through quests or hidden around the world to create some of the better and more satisfying weapons in the game.
+ Immersive Graphics
+ Exciting Gameplay/Crafting
+ Smooth Movement and Parkour
+ Interesting story/sidequests, the characters have tons of personality
+ The atmosphere of the game is dark and gritty, easy to get lost in
+ Fluid Combat System
+ Lots of Gore
+ Tons of hidden areas to explore
+ Not a buggy mess like Dead Island was
+ New Game Plus
- Flares are a little OP
- All of the best gear is sold at the merchants
- Some people are having trouble getting decent framerates, depending on hardware
- Day/Night Cycle can be controlled by certain storyline and quests, not always entirely dynamic. (This is only true for early game)
I'm hearing a few complaints about poor optimization, but I'm not seeing that at all, personally. I get about 100 FPS indoors and 60-80 FPS outdoors, with everything Maxed at 1080.

With the upcoming release of the final product, Killing Floor 2 is certainly in my opinion a step up from the first installment. KF2 features roughly the same enemies as its predecessor with a few additions and tweaks and adds more perks (classes) to the game.
Now if you're not familiar with the genre, KF2 is standard cooperative Players-vs-Enviroment first person shooter in which you and up to 5 teammates (6 total) will attempt to survive against a horde of enemy zombies, aptly named Zeds, for some times. The enemies will spawn in waves (4 or 7 or 10). Each wave will have a variable amount of Zeds, different types and in the mid-late game, much stronger unique type of Zeds will spawn.
Each perk comes with a its own arsenal of weapons and bonuses and you can freely switch between them per wave. Each perk has a maximum rank of 25 levels and you'll gain a choice between two different types passives for your perk every 5 levels. There's a total of 9 perks to choose from, so leveling them all up to 25 is a very time consuming process.
There's 4 degrees of difficulty in the game, Normal/Hard/Suicidal/Hell on Earth. Each difficulty will offer an increase in the total amount of Zed spawns, increase in their HP/resistances and the number of "champion" Zed spawns. Between each wave you're given rougly a minute to visit a random resupply station in the map to upgrade your gear. While you gain more exp at higher difficulties, there's a learning curve regarding the mechanics of the game and new players should not attempt anything above Hard until they're more experienced with their perks and their game knowledge.
At the end of each wave, you'll get a boss, either the Patriarch or Dr. Hans Volter, each with own unique array of abilities. Killing the boss is a team effort and there's not much room for mistakes. With the Zedconomy update, the game features micro-transactions and skin/cosmetic item drops. None of these offer a competitive advantage and they're purely for show.
Furthermore there's a PvP mode in which players take control of Zeds and fight against other players, similar to the Left 4 Dead 2 PvP mode.
Alternatively you can play the game offline, you vs the waves of Zeds if you're looking for a more solo experience, although the game truly shines when cooperating with other members in your team.
The game surely has its drawbacks however. There's a stiffness in the gameplay which is apparent from the places you can move/jump. Obviously I won't expect Dying Light type of parkour, but the game feels very restrictive about where you jump. This might sound like a pet peeve and in truth it might be, but when running to escape Zombies I believe using the environment is a great way to improve your game experience. Unfortunately KF2 is very stingy in this regard. Jumps that seem possible are not, you might get stuck in a few places so basically learning where you can and cannot go is one of the first things you need to master in order to succeed in higher difficulties.
Champion Zeds, the Scrake and the Fleshpound are relentless and there's not really an aggro system. In higher difficulties, if they focus you and your team is all over the place, you're nearly guaranteed to die. The game will very very rarely forgive errors by the players. That's not necessarily a bad aspect of the game, but when you consider that you cannot outrun "enraged" champions or any of the Bosses, then it will get a little bit annoying. A few tweaks and balances regarding bosses and their mechanics is still needed to be on the table however that does not mean it's extremely hard to win. Good skill and cooperation from a mid-high level team will make the game seem easy at times even on Hard/Suicidal difficulties. What I'm trying to say is that balancing this game for everyone is indeed a very arduous job for the developers but we're seeing a few steps into that direction.
The game updates with free (for now) contents, including new maps, new perks (don't know if any more are going to be added in the future but I do hope so) on a semi regular basis, hopefully the rate will increase when the game finally leaves early access.
There's a few bugs here and there but nothing too serious (will note at the current time of this review, online matchmaking is broken and entering any game is only done via server browsing) that will have a detriment on your overall game experience.
All in all, fans of coop FPS (Left 4 Dead, Vermintide, etc.) will enjoy this game. You won't be blown away by the graphics or the gameplay, the game's pretty solid and the retail price is quite decent for the amount of time you'll spent playing this game. A good recommendation for fans of the genre and a good starting game for people just getting into gaming in general.

To me the first campaign of Shadowrun Returns "Dead Mans Switch" was only okay. Dragonfall on the other hand moves clearly away from just being okay and moves to great!
The first improvement is that the story is more straight as in dead mans switch. Dead mans switch had one plot twist after another plot twist and in the end it all went a bit absurd. Drahonfall however is more straight but also far from boring. It is actually nice knowing what is actually going and. Yet Dragonfall also has some nice twists, but they work pretty well in the story.
Gameplay wise Dragonfall corrects some of the mistakes made in the first campaign. Finally there is a nice and interesting hub you can roam around in. You can find and to talk so nice little characters and of course get some side quests. It also probably did improve the experience of the hub, that a good friend of mine is actually living at the real moritzplatz in berlin.
The fights in the game feel more challenging, since the AI is a bit more agressive compared to the first installment. Also little visits in the matrix (that were not too popular by some players) are now mostly optional. Speaking of options, you now have a lot more options in how you want to play the game. It might be wise to invest some karma into skills that are not actually skills related to battle. You will find quite some different opportunities how you want to handle a lot of situations. You might talk your way out of a fight or find a route around it etc.
Graphic wise Dragonfall is still no Crysis but I have made my peace with how the game looks. However I would really like to see more animation in the game in general. May it be character animations or stuff in the gameworld, we could really use more of it.
The biggest strength of the game are most likely the characters in your runner crew. They raise some good old memories from times like Baldurs Gate and Planescape. Against trends set by devs like Bioware, the characters in your crew or not just wanking material and so you talk to them not only because you want to see a silly softcore scene with them. In fact you just talk to those characters because they are interesting and you want to hear what they have to say about certain situations and how they became the characters that they are in the game. Thankfully the characters to get the space they deserve and they can just be what they are and not what the player wants them to be,
Dragonfall was a great experience and it is one of the games when you are sad when it is over. I do hope we will get another campaign like Dragonfall in the near future.

This game surpassed my expectations both positively and negatively. As amazingly fun and satisfying as it is, it is also one of the most rage inducing games I have ever played recently
Pros: Things I loved
-Satisfying sound effects (oohh glorious gore)
-Intelligent Human AI, for example if you pull out a gun they will surrender if they have only melee weapons. However, if they have strength in numbers they will not give in, they will simply keep their distance and throw knives and♥♥♥♥♥♥at you from cover and roof tops
-Great parkour mechanics, not clunky or faulty in the slightest
-A truly immersive story, it not only has emotion but suspense as well as a dynamic protagonist as well.
-Weapon customization and rarity is very balanced
-Night time is challenging, you truly are the prey at night. Fighting back against Night Virals is almost useless. Night is very dramatic, anxiety inducing, horrific, and exhillirating. But they still sweeten the pot with double XP if you're up to the challenge after dark.
-Wonderful and properly implemented environmental kills
Cons: Now for the rage inducing part
-Despite the wonderful AI for humans. They are extremely overpowered. Not only are they pretty much unaffected by kicks (one of your most useful abilities), they also seem to have superhuman reflexes and health as well. Also they tend to throw knives with almost 100% accuracy, seemingly from angles that not even Captain America himself could throw♥♥♥♥♥♥from and hit his (moving) target.
-Zombies grapple you every five seconds, and medkits are rare. Though they can be quickly countered it happens way too often. However it is something you must be smart about as this game is not about plunging through hordes of infected. It encourages you to keep your distance however the main issue is it's used a little too frequently, and it is also a very clunky mechanic. If a zombie attempts to grapple you, kicking it a split second too late (even if the kick lands successfully) the hitboxes be like "Nah he got you first." The main dodge and throw thing you do is ineffective because of this. 60% of the time it will register the zombie grappling you regardless if you press the series of buttons first.
-The game tends to kick you while you're down a lot. You lose XP when you die, and if you're broke and have no equipment it adds insult to injury with constant death as well. A lot of the game depends on how well equipped you are, and if you're not well equipped enough not only do you die a lot, it's very hard to climb out of that pit of chronic death once you're already ♥♥♥♥ed as it is, it's not very helpful when you're losing XP non stop at the same time. Especially at night.
-The game tends to bs you into instant death a lot. It's very aggravating especially the fact that every flammable object tends to explode for seemingly no reason a lot of the time.
Summary: Great game, the combat mechanics need improvement for specific things.

"Risk of Rain" is all about replayability; unlocking stuff and doing achievement challenges. You weigh the risk of staying longer in an area to collect more powerups against the ever more powerful spawning monsters. The game is on a timer, ticking down to an inevitable conclusion, either you beat the game or you die. There are no extra lives, no timer reset and (supposedly) no point of pause and rest.
A successful playthrough is fairly short, with most ending at about 25-30 minutes from beginning to end. You'll die alot, though. Most of the time, in fact, especially with just the starting items and character. If you get upset easily at dying in a hugely promising run due to unfair randomization, then this is not an enjoyable game. It's very much like "Spelunky" and "Sword of the Stars: the pit" in this regard, so if you like those games then you'll also like Risk of Rain.
One huge point in the game's favour is the variance between games, making it feel worthwile to keep playing after beating it the first time around. There aren't tons of enemies to encounter and the couple of semi-randomized stages will be cycled through in a couple of playthroughs. However, the amount of items to collect, the artifacts that alter the game in various ways and the vast difference between playable characters keeps the game fresh for hours upon hours.
This leads into the game's big strike against it, which paradoxically is its many unlocks.
Almost everything in the game needs unlocking, from every artifact, to just about every character and item. This might not sound like such a big deal at first, and I'm sure the developers would claim it prolongs the life of the game, but in reality it takes far too long to get to the fun parts.
A lot of the unlocks can only be done in succession, meaning you have to do one unlock in one playthrough before the next becomes available for unlocking, and these chains can go dozens of playthroughs deep. Also, most unlocks are based and dependant on randomization, which realistically means you're doing several playthroughs just for everything to click.
If you have to endure dozens of hours of grinding for the chance at experience the game in its entirety, I feel it detracts from the overall gaming experience. Once you've overcome that hurdle and gotten everything unlocked, however, it's great fun to try different item builds on different characters, challenge yourself with artifacts and higher difficulties. I've played over 40 hours, roughly half of which was doing achievements and the rest enjoying the game. I'll definately return to this one from time to time.
If it's on sale, you should absolutely pick it up! If you're partial to roguelikes, "Risk of Rain" is a fairly safe purchase.

Dying Light is fun, fast paced, and visually beautiful. I am running the game on an AMD platform using an old GFX card and it still is running at 60fps. I am only a little ways in but here are some quick bullet points.
- Combat is much more fluid than Dead Island. Sure you feel like you are swinging wildly sometimes but I love the frantic nature of combat. This isn't a zombie killing simulator as much as its a zombie survival.
-Visuals are impressive, I have the game running on lowest settings and it still looks good (game being played on an ASUS 6850). I will be running the game on its highest once my new GPU fan arrives today (XFX 7970 fan was garbage). The game hates multi monitor setups though. This needs a patch but is a mild annoyance. Unplugged my hdmi cable for my second monitor and was good to go.
-A lot of people have complained about the quests and that they revolve around go from A to B. I see that but the fun is in the journey and I really am enjoying going from A to B. Parkour system is fluid with some minor hiccups every now and then.
-The contrast of going out at night versus day is incredible. Truly feels like two seperate experiences.
-The cutscenes have way too much movement in them, creates for some motion sickness. I had to look away during the opening, was Jason Bourne x100.
-As of this writing, there seems to be no other people out and about like me. You are supposed to be one of many runners, yet I have seen noone. This creates an environment that makes me feel alone (not sure if good or bad)

It's so frustrating writing a review with so many factors to consider, as there is a character limit to a review and there's only so much attention that the ADHD-ridden mass of "gamers" are willing to give to a review. Let's start with the game.
Is KF2 better than KF1? It's hard to explain, but although KF1's got more content, KF2 in the end does not have the weight of ten tons of DLC that KF1 has. The gameplay feels smooth and polished, almost in detriment to the quirky joy of watching the comparably stiff knife-slashing animations from KF1 as you cut a Crawler being turned into the effortless and more natural-looking slicing and dicing that you dish out. It loses that "game" feeling as it delves more into streamlined animations and it goes further into a feeling of uncomfortability like what you get seeing a certain kind of doll that trespasses into the forbidden Uncanny Valley. Neither real nor game, the pleasure you feel cutting through Zeds with glorious nippon steel is slightly sullied with a tinge of "it's almost too smooth" on the aftertaste. There's nothing that can be done about this, of course. The guns, the armor, the fundamentals remain similar though different enough to be qualified as a sequel whilst retaining familiarity enough to keep oldies from KF1 able to play.
However, there is a line that's crossed as well in the department of content. Although you'd argue that it's Early Access, it's been some time since they've gotten started with the whole business and from what you can read in other insightful negative reviews, it's been a rollercoaster that I was lucky enough not to fall in before. It lacks sorely in weapon diversity, especially compared to KF1 (although, again, the DLC is atrocious). The difficulties offer more a way of scaling with your level rather than presenting further challenge, although I've yet to pass over Hard and there are apparently new Zeds in the way of "blue dragon is now red dragon, run in fear" with some extra quirks here and there that add a bit of a variety compared to the old Clot-Crawler-Gorefast-Stalker-Bloat-Siren-Husk-Scrake-Fleshpound progression that you've come to love in KF1. All in all, it feels different yet suffers from a lack of content to a degree that the difference in feeling doesn't help it enough. Further modifiers, increased weapon diversity, increased class diversity, etc. would probably help it further, but one cannot tell developers how to make their game.
Most obvious ones are the addition of Sprinting, the changes to the gradual gains from leveling Perks as well as the addition of a simplistic A-or-B Perk Trees AND the new perks, and the addition of some "new" Zeds and new weapons.
Sprinting makes you sprint, simple. No meter or anything, sprint forever. It's not all that amazing and I prefer the old rushing towards the trader with knife in hand, hobbling like a man that's about to brown his pants. Sprinting doesn't feel like it adds anything to the game, rather feels like change for the sake of change.
Gradual gains are incredibly reduced, since there are now 25 levels. Instead, every 5 levels you get to choose which nifty bonus you want to the Perk; you can choose things like A: 35% more damage, B: 100% increased mag capacity. However, the choices seem skewed to the favor of a single side. You will often see choices of Do more damage -or- Reload slightly quicker or equivalent. In the end, most Perk trees always seem to lean to a certain set of choices that are obviously better than the other.
The new perks tend to rest on the side of "It's basically X class but with Y kinds of weapons." Gunslinger is a Sharpshooter, and SWAT is a Commando. Differences are that Sharpshooter no longer uses dual-wielded weapons, instead those go to the Gunslinger, and that SWAT uses submachine guns instead of assault rifles. They both serve similar purposes, but achieve the results through slightly different means. Gunslinger, at least, has the benefit of a high ROF and manageable recoil and accuracy with the perk tree, whilst SWAT seems a bit on the less-interesting-though-not-necessarily-weak side.
The "new" Zeds are either reskins with nifty tricks, or reskins with nifty tricks. The two "new" types of Clots are Cysts and Slashers. Cysts are like dumb Clots that trip if they miss you, and Slashers are annoying little ♥♥♥♥ers that won't let you shoot them. Other than that are some yet-to-be-known-to-me variants that only appear in Suicidal and HOE Difficulties. Nothing spectacular have I seen so far, but the small bit of added variety in Zeds is like a little teaser for what could be accomplished if the devs took it further and added in some more new Zeds.
The new weapons are all nicely animated, including the old ones, but in the end I've yet to look and see and thus feel a weapon that makes me think "I love this gun." The effortless and smooth cutting, slicing, and shooting of the various Zeds sort of works against this purpose. It makes every weapon feel great, and since every weapon is great, no weapons are great. The AA12 chews through Zeds as easy as the starting Shotgun, though with increased ROF. There are some exceptions, but for the most part it's nothing all that special.
Microtransactions, in an Early Access game? A crate drop system that's worse than any other game that utilizes that horrid ♥♥♥♥ing system? Un-♥♥♥♥ing-forgiveable. Attempting to justify this merely broadcasts ignorant submissive-consumerism and that you don't realize that customers as a collective should be working to change these sorts of things rather than mindlessly submit, starved for a game that's even subpar. Not calling for a violent rebellion, just that you understand what the Hell you're doing trying to defend something that is so vehemently anti-consumer.
Although I'd like to go into all of the♥♥♥♥♥♥Tripwire's done in the past, I've wonderfully forgotten most of it, though I could swear it was something along stealing Community assets and ♥♥♥♥ing with modders that were trying to help add content into games where they instead took them and pushed their own♥♥♥♥♥♥in, selling off the equivalent of cheap knockoffs compared to the modders' dedicated works, but then there's a whole world of♥♥♥♥♥♥down there that I'd prefer not to remember vividly. Point being, they have ♥♥♥♥ed over their RO2 community before and with how they were treating KF2 for a while, it's safe to assume even now that they will destroy everything good that has only just truly started surfacing in KF2.
My advice is to stick clear of this until it gets more content and a bit of polish and it may be something worth buying. Right now, though, it's nothing too special. It's a smooth and shiny FPS based around warding off waves of monsters. You get the same in KF1, just without the smooth and shiny. Rest assured when I've racked up the hours on this bad boy, it's because I have nothing else I feel any desire to play, and so it falls to this. And remember who you're giving your money to. I may have signed up for a train wreck in progress, but you don't have to do the same. Do research aside from Steam reviews. Your money doesn't just disappear into a black hole. Somebody has your money at the end of the transaction. There are no actions without consequence.

Rather simplistic but fun RPG in the world of Shadowrun. It's simplistic because you can't change anything in the story, there is no branching you can't take different directions. There are no side quests. It's also rather short.
Yet i'd say that it's easily worth playing, because what Harebrain does well is imagining the world, creating a story in that world, putting interesting characters in that story, writing fascinating background stories for the characters, etc. etc.. And these are all here and very well done.
The combat is turn based and it works quite well, although it gets a bit boring at the endgame, where ther's basically no talking involved just shotting through dozens of baddies. The leveling system is plain, but gets the job done, you can create very divers characters from the shaman through the decker (hacker) there are lots of variations.
...and then there's the Dragonfall campaign:
They listened to their fans and vastly improved upon the original campaign. The writing, the characters (my companions here are the most memorable video game characters since I don't even know when), the story, hell even the gameplay is a lot better.
There is a central hub now, where you can take side quests, make donations, buy stuff or just converse with random residents. Almost every main mission involves at least one serious choice too.
Everything that was missing from the original campaign is right here in an almost perfect package. Definitely one of the best DLCs I've ever played.
One important warning though: There's lots of reading involved in both campaigns, so if you want non-stop action this is not for you!

Realistic review of this game for anyone reading these. If you can't stand reading walls of text stop here.
1: The game has a great story telling element if your not just a hack and slash gamer. Lots of reading so be prepared for it and if your not the reading type, ignore this game.
2: Very well designed characters and plots. Every character has their own unique personalities, but some feel a bit cliche.
3: Very linear plot. Don't plan on doing side quests. Or anything not involving the straight and narrow path before you.
4: Game comes with an editor. Editor isn't the same one that the makers use, so don't expect it to do half the stuff you see in game. (Hairebrain you would do well to update this on the extreme if you want to have a continued following for a good long while. Gradual expansions will get you money, but keeping interest seems to be a little more important especially when it took me a wopping 13 hours to beat this game on hard difficulty.)
5: As noted above, plan for 10-13 hours of gameplay if you actually spend the time reading everything and enjoy the game for what it is. Murder mystery with plot and intrigue. Fun stuff.
6: This game has about zero replayability, pending expansions or other spin offs entirely. So if you play it through, I suggest doing it on a harder difficulty for the simple fact, your gonna do it once. Might as well make it challenging.
Overall I'd give this game a 7/10. Wasn't the best game I've ever played, but it was definitely a throwback to when thought was actually put into games instead of people cramming first person shooters down our throats. Well done developers and team and goodluck on more games in the future. Keep it coming. Update that editor big time too.

Just as a heads up to potential buyers, if you do not like to fiddle with computer tech stuff, don't try this game. As I write this, I've been stuck for about an hour with one problem after another: Laggy mouse (turn off vsync), mouse sensitivity too low in-game, and normal in menues, and a fabulous Show Stopper Game Destroying bug right at the start of the game, where you are actually stuck and cannot continue the game. An invisible wall prevents you from moving forward. The solution? Well, I googled it, and after a good long while (the official fix on steam did nothing), I found a tip that said to turn on Fraps (!) to lower the framerates. And it worked....!
This is 2015, and the game intro screen says the game is from 2008. They have had seven years to fix these annoying and game breaking bugs, and haven't done it. Shame on you EA. My already low opinion of them has become even lower.
As for the game content, I expect that to be good. I will continue playing the game. But any immersion will be completely ruined due to the crappy interface. Would I recommend the game? Well, the short answer is "no". The long answer can be found above: Don't buy the game unless you are willing to try and overcome these technical problems.
After playthrough:
After overcoming the initial problems, I discovered that there were more problems later on, linked to vsync, and turning it on and off. And having a mouse where sensitivity could be increased helped against the low mouse speed. The game content? It is excellent, a high quality game experience. For example:
- No unnecessary running
- Lots of shortcuts after completing an objective
- No "stupid" deaths, like falling off a ledge
- Checkpoints before difficult fights
- Creepy atmosphere, good plot
All in all, you can tell that this is a well-thought out game. That people have really worked with the details. It is a little strange to play an FPS game where you can neither duck or jump, but in a way it is relaxing. You know if you can't reach someplace, you're not meant to go there. No invisible walls (except the bugs) to prevent creative players from going where they are not supposed to.
Last impression... well, I downloaded and started playing Dead Space 2 just now, and all the issues were fixed. It makes me wonder why they didn't fix this game as well. It's a shame, since it's such a nice game in all aspects except that.

By this day almost everyone knows how disasterous the release of the PC port of Arkham Knight was, so if you're reading this review your questions most certainly are:
My answers are:
and
.
I'll begin by saying that I played it on a GTX 960m (mobile card) which certainly isn't the most powerful on the market. Compared to Arkham City - which by this day is one of the most well optimized games I played, better than Arkham Asylum even if it came out 2 years later - this game chugs a lot of VRAM and various ressources; after lowering a bit the resolution and disabling some effects I managed to get it working somewhere between 45 and 60fps. The frame rate drops especially in the batmobile sections and if you're flying over a very crowded area, but it always stays perfectly playable.
Other than that, the only recurring issue I found is the sound cutting randomly in some sections, but it always comes back in a few seconds. The game crashed on me only once and a second time I had to restart it because I triggered a cutscene with the batmobile in a tight section and it didn't let me play anymore.
And how is it, gameplay-wise? Well it's great, to put it simply. Its sheer amount of content is baffling compared to the previous titles: tons of subquests with different objectives, countless AR challenges that give you points, an introduction of new enemy units like the medics or the machine gun soldiers that add to the challenge, and of course everything with the batmobile. I found all the tank battles very funny even if sometimes of a frustrating difficulty - in general, this game is much tougher than the previous ones as the enemies have much more weapons to counter your tactics. The hand to hand combats are indisputably the best in the series for the amount of moves and variations you can do and the general smoothness of the flow.
There's hardly a moment when driving around in Gotham to continue the main story you won't find something new to do, could it be a mine to defuse or an enemy checkpoint to destroy, and when you don't dear Alfred will notify you regularly of the new missions available.
The only thing I didn't like about AK is how the game throws you into the mayhem from the get-go, it makes the whole atmosphere much more tense than in previous titles where you felt you could put a lot of time into exploration. As a result, even the ever tedious hunt for the Riddler's trophies becomes more stressful; but you can always finish the last quests after ending the regular game as usual.
In the end I totally recommend to play this title if you have a powerful PC, but only after Arkham Asylum and Arkham City (the latter still being imho the best in the series) because AK takes for granted many things regarding controls and strategies that you've learned in the previous titles.

"Risk of Rain" is all about replayability; unlocking stuff and doing achievement challenges. You weigh the risk of staying longer in an area to collect more powerups against the ever more powerful spawning monsters. The game is on a timer, ticking down to an inevitable conclusion, either you beat the game or you die. There are no extra lives, no timer reset and (supposedly) no point of pause and rest.
A successful playthrough is fairly short, with most ending at about 25-30 minutes from beginning to end. You'll die alot, though. Most of the time, in fact, especially with just the starting items and character. If you get upset easily at dying in a hugely promising run due to unfair randomization, then this is not an enjoyable game. It's very much like "Spelunky" and "Sword of the Stars: the pit" in this regard, so if you like those games then you'll also like Risk of Rain.
One huge point in the game's favour is the variance between games, making it feel worthwile to keep playing after beating it the first time around. There aren't tons of enemies to encounter and the couple of semi-randomized stages will be cycled through in a couple of playthroughs. However, the amount of items to collect, the artifacts that alter the game in various ways and the vast difference between playable characters keeps the game fresh for hours upon hours.
This leads into the game's big strike against it, which paradoxically is its many unlocks.
Almost everything in the game needs unlocking, from every artifact, to just about every character and item. This might not sound like such a big deal at first, and I'm sure the developers would claim it prolongs the life of the game, but in reality it takes far too long to get to the fun parts.
A lot of the unlocks can only be done in succession, meaning you have to do one unlock in one playthrough before the next becomes available for unlocking, and these chains can go dozens of playthroughs deep. Also, most unlocks are based and dependant on randomization, which realistically means you're doing several playthroughs just for everything to click.
If you have to endure dozens of hours of grinding for the chance at experience the game in its entirety, I feel it detracts from the overall gaming experience. Once you've overcome that hurdle and gotten everything unlocked, however, it's great fun to try different item builds on different characters, challenge yourself with artifacts and higher difficulties. I've played over 40 hours, roughly half of which was doing achievements and the rest enjoying the game. I'll definately return to this one from time to time.
If it's on sale, you should absolutely pick it up! If you're partial to roguelikes, "Risk of Rain" is a fairly safe purchase.

One of EA's only enjoyable titles, credit to Visceral.
With regards to setting, this game nails (no pun intended) the spooky, scary atmosphere to make you feel on edge without relying on jump scares (although there are a few) or other cheap methods. Repeatedly walking through the corridors of a seemingly abandoned mining ship constantly fills you with paranoia, making you wonder if there is a necromorph waiting for you around the corner or is it just a box of goodies that you can stomp. The small accents and details given to the environment such as the bloodstains and scrawled writing on the walls, the eerily empty hospital and beds, and the large ship systems, really complete the setting.
Game play wise, most of the time you will be plodding along fixing the numerous ship systems that inevitably screw up, and along the way using makeshift engineering/mining tools to slay the hordes of necromorphs that try to murder you. Due to this, the games atmosphere is frequently broken by a reasonably stressful gunfight that ultimately becomes hilariously fun. This change of pace is welcome, and I found myself utilizing my flamethrower to crazily burn down multiple enemies. Ammo conservation is however a big factor as ammo can become very hard to find past the halfway point and due to the enemies becoming harder and more frequent,  this can easily turn fun to plain tedious. There were some areas near the endgame where I had not been conserving my ammo and med kits too well, and fights involved would take many, many deaths to pass without running out of ammo or med-kits. Although, I did have my faithful stomp with me if I struggled too much, and there were many times when I entertained myself by going on a glitchy stomping frenzy. The boss fights are also a highlight, as they are unique enough in order to be excused of their lack of frequency (I say that, but there were still a reasonable number) and are very enjoyable. The final boss though, oh man is it epic.
Overall the game is a relatively good length, but there are extra difficulty modes that I didn't try (I played on normal) that can prolong the experience. This game is a horror classic and I highly recommend it, even though I'm not big on horror.

This is a review of the Dragonfall DLC Campaign, not the original game.
To sum everything up in a single statement, Dragonfall is a vast improvement over everything in the original campaign.
The story is much less linear and includes a job system which allows you to pick and choose which missions you want to send your Shadowrunners on. Between missions you return to a hub town where you can stock up on new equipment, magic or cybernetic implants. There is an auction system which rewards players who go out of their way to hack or find extra information. This information can be sold at an online auction for extra money. It is also possible to donate information to an anarchist group who uses it against the mega corporations of the world. There are also many more opportunities to take advantage of the stats of your character, while high charisma and int builds still have the most options it is also possible to use your other stats in many situations, such as using strength to intimidate, or quickness to make fast reactions and avoid perils.
The DLC campaign is easily as long as the original, if not longer, and is better in almost every single way. I really hope the devs will continue to release more DLC of this caliber.

By this day almost everyone knows how disasterous the release of the PC port of Arkham Knight was, so if you're reading this review your questions most certainly are:
My answers are:
and
.
I'll begin by saying that I played it on a GTX 960m (mobile card) which certainly isn't the most powerful on the market. Compared to Arkham City - which by this day is one of the most well optimized games I played, better than Arkham Asylum even if it came out 2 years later - this game chugs a lot of VRAM and various ressources; after lowering a bit the resolution and disabling some effects I managed to get it working somewhere between 45 and 60fps. The frame rate drops especially in the batmobile sections and if you're flying over a very crowded area, but it always stays perfectly playable.
Other than that, the only recurring issue I found is the sound cutting randomly in some sections, but it always comes back in a few seconds. The game crashed on me only once and a second time I had to restart it because I triggered a cutscene with the batmobile in a tight section and it didn't let me play anymore.
And how is it, gameplay-wise? Well it's great, to put it simply. Its sheer amount of content is baffling compared to the previous titles: tons of subquests with different objectives, countless AR challenges that give you points, an introduction of new enemy units like the medics or the machine gun soldiers that add to the challenge, and of course everything with the batmobile. I found all the tank battles very funny even if sometimes of a frustrating difficulty - in general, this game is much tougher than the previous ones as the enemies have much more weapons to counter your tactics. The hand to hand combats are indisputably the best in the series for the amount of moves and variations you can do and the general smoothness of the flow.
There's hardly a moment when driving around in Gotham to continue the main story you won't find something new to do, could it be a mine to defuse or an enemy checkpoint to destroy, and when you don't dear Alfred will notify you regularly of the new missions available.
The only thing I didn't like about AK is how the game throws you into the mayhem from the get-go, it makes the whole atmosphere much more tense than in previous titles where you felt you could put a lot of time into exploration. As a result, even the ever tedious hunt for the Riddler's trophies becomes more stressful; but you can always finish the last quests after ending the regular game as usual.
In the end I totally recommend to play this title if you have a powerful PC, but only after Arkham Asylum and Arkham City (the latter still being imho the best in the series) because AK takes for granted many things regarding controls and strategies that you've learned in the previous titles.

Gameplay - enjoyable; if you played the older Batmans you'll feel right at home. Same as in older games yet different - as has always been the case with every new Batman game. There is quite enough of side-missions, lots of things to do - maybe even too much for its own good. I'd often find myself doing one branch of side-missions, mission after mission, which got repetitive and I got bored while the main storyline with interesting variable missions just sat there. The main storyline is long enough.
Story - not bad but meh, could be better. Nothing I can say about it unless I put spoilers here, but it's definitely the darkest yet.
Graphics/audio - great.
Technical side/optimization - much better than when it first came out (that was an unplayable mess) but it's still not perfect per se; framedrops are there sometimes (mainly if you have 2GB or less VRAM) and I'd definitely welcome more graphics settings. But it is perfectly playable and that's all you can ask for. It requires sufficient hardware power though, please don't be one of those people who buy it, discover it is unplayable on their 1GB GPUs or 740s (or mobile 660Ms) and then write a bad review and bash the game about it. Nowhere does this game claim it will run on inadequate hardware. It is what it is, take it or leave it. Take a good look at the minimum requirements and rest assured that they're not kidding, it is the true utter minimum. Recommended requirements is kind of a meh-tier rig to be playing this game on, expect meh-tier (but perfectly playable) results; nothing more, nothing less. Think twice before buying if you don't meet the requirements.

I was so looking forward to this game. Ever since I first read/heard about it. Finally picked it and DS2 on the cheap from Steam. Started off promising and by started off I mean the intro was pretty decent. Short, simple. And then I found out that there's no first person view and the 3rd person view is... inaccurate. Like... floaty. Move the mouse and you kinda sort point in the direction you want... which might be OK if you weren't using a pinpoint precise weapon against wiggly, sometimes even dodging enemies whom you need to shoot in their tiny limbs... Also the "aim before you can fire your weapon" thing is definitely NOT intuitive. I can't count the number of times an enemy jumped out from 5 feet away and I hit trigger, only to swing wildly at thin air, doing nothing but moving myself within range of the enemies sharp, pointy bits. But the "comfortable" camera angle for moving around means when you do aim, you point at the ground, so when an enemy appears you have to aim and then adjust, which might be OK if the mouse-aim controls were a little more precise. Having just come out of Skyrim and a replay of Bioshock 1, these "floaty" controls are just ... terrible. I've tinkered with the sensitivity and turned down graphics options and such thinking perhaps it's just a lag thing, but no, it seems the game is designed that way. This is all just first impression, an hour of play on my lunch break. It's not so horrible that I won't give it another try later. But... unless the controls suddenly snap into high gear, I'm not going to get my hopes up.

The battles in this game can really test your hardware, as in the impact resistance of your keyboard and mouse. Victory is sweetest asphyxiating assaulting marauders or teleporting rock men and giant mantids with the aid of a death dealing boarding drone to purge an enemy vessel. Each ship you send out is either going to be victorious or be torn apart, only saves are to pick up from one run. Luck finding parts in encounters can be a maddening factor at times, but the victories are nail biting and will leave you pumping your fist damning your enemies to the cold vacuum of space.
Combat is very strategic with regards to timing your weapons, targeting specific areas of enemies, and keeping your crew alive by any means. Sometimes this means sending someone in to repair the O2 while the airlock is opened to bleed fires out. Seconds matter and thankfully you can pause anytime to assign actions, which is critical. Well worth the 10 for fun. Replay may suffer after unlocking ships or winning

This game turned out to be a pleasant surprise, as I was getting a severely bad taste in my mouth due to the absence of early review copies being sent out and the general preorder brigading that has been going on lately. I bought a copy for myself and a friend mostly on a whim, and so far I've been having a blast. Point-by-point review to follow:
Pros:
+Graphics are extremely well done and the game runs quite well on my 970 (see one exception below)
+Combat system is quite nuanced, even if it seems simple at first glance. It is very much a risk-reward system, with stamina  levels being quite well-balanced and even nail-biting at times.
+Story so far has been enjoyable, although I've been getting pulled away by the innumerable side quests that become available with each progression of the plot.
+Crafting system gives you a sense of accomplishment when you manage to get the parts for that badass weapon you've been eyeing, while the limited repairs force you to continue scavenging for backup weapons at all times.
+Loading sequences are quite short, even though I have this loaded on a conventional 7200RPM HDD.
+Skill trees are infuriatingly well-balanced, insofar as I have had trouble deciding what skill to get pretty much every level, with the ever-elusive grappling hook taunting me from afar.
+Parkour allows for speedy travel while still maintaining an air of danger. Narrow ledges do not clip you to them, so if you accidentally walk off, you're toast, and the addition of destructible roofs and awnings that draw volatiles (freerunning zombies and the ilk, all of which are pretty much terrifying) forces you to stay on your toes at all times.
Cons:
-Online multiplayer, while fun, gets a bit...weird at times. Zombies will phase through walls when you're not looking at them, overrunning a previously secure area with zombies that have no right being there. Can probably be hotfixed with relative ease, so I'll see what happens with this in the coming weeks.
-Perhaps it's due to the fact that I have this game loaded on an HDD instead of my SSD (no more space, unfortunately), but the first 2 seconds or so of cutscenes usually freeze up for me, making a rather jarring transition between game and cutscene.
Overall, a great game, even though it was riddled with speculation about review embargos and such. Worth the buy at full price, especially if you're a sandbox fan like I am.

The Dragonfall expansion single-handedly did justice to Shadowrun Returns. The Dragonfall campaign build brings a much more involving and intricate storyline, choices, side-missions and memorable NPC companions, resulting in longer gameplay and satisfaction compared to the 12-hour long original.
There were certain tweaks to the mechanics of the core game, it seems. For example, there will no longer be extra action points garnered from cybernetics, but this is compensated for via game balancing. There are new portraits to choose from (though still quite limited visual customization) but no changes to the skill trees. Games can be saved at almost every point of the game now, not just at savepoints, so that's another step forward. There are new music scores with this campaign, and they all set the mood satisfactorily for the throughout the gameplay. I still find the beats from the original campaign more to my liking, but that's personal opinion.
Some issues inherent in the original was still present in this one. Missing sprites, limitations to allocating picked-up items to teammates outside of combat and the occassional AP bug can still be encountered. However, I would not personally hold this against the expansion as this one is does seem like the developer's turn of churning out an AAA campaign using the same builder tools made available to the community.
I grew up playing and loving role-playing games that were akin to reading sci-fi fantasy book sets. After Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Arcanum and Neverwinter Nights, I am relieved to be able to add Shadowrun Returns into my collection of RPG games worth the ages. To enjoy this one, you'll have to read, children, and dig into your storeroom for that old thing called an 'active imagination'. If Shadowrun Returns left you feeling wanting, then Dragonfall will bring you past dessert.

For the sake of building credibility, I have completed the story to the 120% mark which includes the main story, all sidequests, and all Riddler trophies and riddles. For this review, I would like to comment on these three items as they are the largest components of the game.*
*I have not completed all of the AR challenges (which are in abundance as usual) and I have also not gone through New Game Plus, but these things are not exactly critical to looking at this game in relation to the rest of the series.
- Main Story -
So I remember playing Arkham Asylum many years ago. There were many moments in that game that were absolutely, without-a-doubt, stunning to the point that they could be considered hallmarks of gaming storytelling. I loved it so much as everything felt absolutely perfect. If I were to rank the rest of the series in order of how much I enjoyed the game's story, Arkham Knight would be a close second. My ranking can be almost entirely attributed to the role Joker plays in this game. While he is poised as an annoying companion that follows you around everywhere you go, he has the most personality of any character in the entire series. You grow to love him and hate him all at the same time. The role he plays makes this game that enjoyable.
The other characters are sort of there and, if you are a fan of Batman as a whole or just the Arkham series, you will get more than enough enjoyment out of connecting with them. You will find yourself connecting with some over others depending on your personality, but I believe that is just a testament as to how much care Rocksteady put into writing their lines and roles.
Both Predator and regular combat scenarios are familiar, however, there are some new twists thrown in. The more brutish figures have gotten a face-lift with new weapons being added to their existence. Those can be very annoying as they already have extra health and attributes, but they can be overcome. (The one big issue with these guys is when you get to Predator scenarios in which you have multiple walking around with chain guns. You will quickly find out that they are extremely powerful to a fault, leading them to feel a bit cheap.) The other new individual that honestly makes me want to put my fist through a wall is the medic. These SOBs not only hit like a normal enemy, but they can revive fallen enemies in both combat types. If that was not enough to worry about, they can also charge their companions with electric fields that surround their bodies. If you even touch those people, you will be shocked, lose your streak, and start falling into a pit of attacks that cannot be dodged as you may not see through the lense flair. The medic is probably the most annoying thing about this new campaign. Other than that, however, same as previous Arkham entries.
The Batmobile is new to this game and, I swear to you, it will cause you to either hate this game as a whole or force you to change your pants because you love it that much. I am closer to the latter extreme as the sound of the engine blasting through the streets is enough to make me forget that I spend so much time driving around in this game. With the new mode of transportation also comes new combat sections in which the Batmobile becomes a Battank(?). This is another situation in which your mileage may vary: you will either love it or hate it. It is quite easy to master and, again, I found it to be rather enjoyable.
If I had the chance to talk to the developers and get them to change one thing, I would make them change the way the gadgets are selected. Veterans of the series will recognize that it is no longer a simple directional press on the D-pad because that button now houses other menus that track your progress. These menus could easily have been made into tabs found when pressing "Back", leaving the gadgets to have their own designated buttons set. Be forwarned, you will hit the wrong menu many times in learning which direction to press and you will still make mistakes.
Overall, this game is worth buying on the main campaign alone. If it were missing all of its side missions, I would still be pleased with how everything is put together and I would play it again without a problem.
- Sidequests -
Sidequests in this game are worth their own game. The diversity of villains from previous Batman games and lore is more than enough to satisfy one's desire to deviate from fighting Scarecrow. Some people you will want to fight more than Scarecrow if you love the villain that much and I found myself doing so on my first playthrough. They have differing tasks that make each quest feel special and you feel rewarded when you see them locked up in GCPD (a feature that I absolutely adore).
My one qualm is that there are some villains chosen here that I wish would have been made DLC rather than villians that shipped with the base copy. I will not name a specific character given the mystery surrounding him, but I hated that I had never heard of him, yet he was put ahead of Mr. Freeze who was added as DLC. Very annoying to say the least, but at this point, the complete edition of the game is cheap enough to make it so that you do not miss out.
- Riddler Trophies and Riddles -
This is honestly the most disappointing category compared to the previous two. The first Arkham game, while flooded with hundreds of trophies and riddles, felt like there was serious care put into making them a big component of the game that was rewarding in the end. Arkham City made them a little more complicated and required some challenges to be finished in order to access them (I was not a fan of this, but it was not that bad). I swear to God, this game amplified the annoying components of City and minimized the amount of fun riddles from Asylum. There are no Secrets Maps from Asylum and they replaced it with the annoying Riddler Informants that only give you a few locations. You will spend and exponentially longer time trying to find all of the riddles in this game as compared to others. The sheer size of the map and the newfound vertical depth make it even harder to find these little buggers and you will grow angrier with time.
Now some will argue that they are optional and, while it is true, they are required in order to reach the completion mark (and they are attached to a sidequest). The way they feel forced on you really takes any leftover enjoyment from the collection process that was already weakened by the increased world challenges associated with them. I hated having to get all of these trophies and I hope that no game tries to do anything like this ever again.
- Final Thoughts and Considerations -
The PC version of this game had a rocky launch and I feel like that has prevented people from truly experiencing a great conclusion to the Arkham franchise. If you have not played any of the games in the series, play the first two (and maybe Origins) before this game. You will feel a great sense of reward after finishing the journey that is this series and you will understand why I am so passionate about this game's value. Easily a must-own in my opinion and I urge everyone to at least play through the main campaigns of not only this game, but the entire series.

Risk of Rain is a game somewhat comparable to The Binding of Isaac in that you collect mostly passive items and activated ones to kill things while finding your way to the next stage, and the only thing you can get out of a failed run are more unlocked items and characters you may have earned. It also features online co-op as well as local play.
Without the use of the in-game artifacts you can discover during gameplay, the game feels slow as ♥♥♥♥ as you and your friends will most likely end up kiting enemies all the time. However, the Glass artifact makes the players' damage output actually tolerable and lowers starting health enough for a fair compromise, and therefore makes the game much more enjoyable by making both the player and every enemy able to die much faster.
By default players have to improvise by finding randomized items because enemies get (slightly) tougher every passing minute on the game clock, and money found from containers and dead enemies is required to open chests containing these, though it may also be spent on reactivating any heal/attack drones around that might be of use or trying your luck at shrines. For such an important mechanic of the base game's gameplay, it is interesting that
Command allows players to cherrypick items they want (even supposedly locked items!), and chests/shrines/drones can be removed in favor for enemies having a chance of dropping items with Sacrifice, and Honor can force most enemies to spawn as Elites...that have a bigger chance of dropping items if a certain item is picked up. The result is that a large chunk of randomization can be exchanged for consistency if one so desires, with players spending less time finding items and rushing find the teleporter out.
Perhaps the biggest problem I have is that the game certainly wasn't balanced around Glass, especially with Honor activated. This means the first two or so levels have a chance to spawn an elite version of a boss that now spews electricity, called the Overloading Magma Worm, which very easily insta-kills players using a character without any real means of dodging or negating the damage and thus quickly turns the run into a waste of time if they haven't found a good enough environment or ideal items to take them on with. It does not mean those characters are entirely useless, they just have bad odds very early on unless playing with friends that can take out the boss much faster. Thankfully, the odds for seeing a even more cruel boss that fires electricity orbs on the first few levels are lower.
The game has considerable replay value, but there may not be enough variation for some. I can definitely recommend Risk of Rain to BoI fans and those who like games with similar gameplay structures.
