This game turned out to be a pleasant surprise, as I was getting a severely bad taste in my mouth due to the absence of early review copies being sent out and the general preorder brigading that has been going on lately. I bought a copy for myself and a friend mostly on a whim, and so far I've been having a blast. Point-by-point review to follow:
Pros:
+Graphics are extremely well done and the game runs quite well on my 970 (see one exception below)
+Combat system is quite nuanced, even if it seems simple at first glance. It is very much a risk-reward system, with stamina  levels being quite well-balanced and even nail-biting at times.
+Story so far has been enjoyable, although I've been getting pulled away by the innumerable side quests that become available with each progression of the plot.
+Crafting system gives you a sense of accomplishment when you manage to get the parts for that badass weapon you've been eyeing, while the limited repairs force you to continue scavenging for backup weapons at all times.
+Loading sequences are quite short, even though I have this loaded on a conventional 7200RPM HDD.
+Skill trees are infuriatingly well-balanced, insofar as I have had trouble deciding what skill to get pretty much every level, with the ever-elusive grappling hook taunting me from afar.
+Parkour allows for speedy travel while still maintaining an air of danger. Narrow ledges do not clip you to them, so if you accidentally walk off, you're toast, and the addition of destructible roofs and awnings that draw volatiles (freerunning zombies and the ilk, all of which are pretty much terrifying) forces you to stay on your toes at all times.
Cons:
-Online multiplayer, while fun, gets a bit...weird at times. Zombies will phase through walls when you're not looking at them, overrunning a previously secure area with zombies that have no right being there. Can probably be hotfixed with relative ease, so I'll see what happens with this in the coming weeks.
-Perhaps it's due to the fact that I have this game loaded on an HDD instead of my SSD (no more space, unfortunately), but the first 2 seconds or so of cutscenes usually freeze up for me, making a rather jarring transition between game and cutscene.
Overall, a great game, even though it was riddled with speculation about review embargos and such. Worth the buy at full price, especially if you're a sandbox fan like I am.

Enter a world where physical laws as you know them don't apply. Antichamber is a weird and wild ride in an alternate reality where what you see isn't always what you get. The chamber itself is relatively small compared to large open world games, but from the inside it seems vast and complex.
Your only equipment is a device which allows you to store cubes, assemble them into larger objects, and then manipulate them as you see fit. Along the journey, you acquire upgrades which further enhances this fundamental ability.
Antichamber never fails to challenge. It is a never ending saga of brainteasers that will leave you scratching your head. The game provides an adequate training pace, but early on, the game can seem overwhelming because things just don't make sense and you may have to ponder several puzzles at once. As you advance further and learn the rules, things certainly become more clear, but the difficulty remains.
Learning the ropes of matter manipulation is quite enjoyable. The more you practice, the more you realize that there are multiple ways to approach a puzzle. Once you acquire the final device upgrades, you actually become quite powerful and early puzzles that seemed difficult become quite easy.
On the downside, the graphics are pretty basic, and it doesn't seem like the sound and music was a priority for the developers. But the originality is what makes this game good. It's definitely a puzzling journey.

I have had some mixed feelings about this game, but then again this happens for a lot of horror games I've played. I'm not a big fan of jumpscares as I feel them being a cheap way to enthrill. Then again I've played this game through 3 times and the reason for that is that this game has a very good gameplay. It has some mediocre issues in storytelling and atmosphere that prevents this being an outstanding game. Instead, this is just good.
I have played all parts of the series, except third installement is still uncompleted. Then again the third one didn't seem to have anything to do with the first one so I though I might as well review this now.
The plot of the game is pretty generic. In space no one can hear you scream. Weird monsters invade space ship and the protagonist must fight back after their immediate escape possibilities are cut down. Plot starts immediately and isn't very surprising at any point. Player travels back and forth in the ship doing stuff while other characters in the game stand still and cry. Kendra Daniels is one of the most annoying side characters I've so far seen or heard in a game.
The part where this game excels is that it makes the playing part fun, although the plot is uninsteresting. By giving the possibility to cut limbs instead of just shooting aliens, this game makes the fights somewhat more interesting and more pleasing. In a fight with multiple enemies, one can shoot their legs off before move to finishing them with another weapon. Also by making playable character a walker instead of a runner, the game is much better paced than some other horror games. Sure he can run, but he cannot shoot while running and running usually ends in a situation where a necromorph is close enough to hug Isaac.
Then again even though the pacing excels, this is yet another example where I think the game could've used a real director(like movies have). Though the game tries to be a horror game, it rarely excels in it. Most of the enemies are given away by loud roars or sudden violin sounds. Basically player just turns to where ever the sound came and shoots. Some jump scares are not enough to call it a horror game. It's a jump-scare-game. I'm not afraid of jumpscare, I just don't like them, like sewage. The game loses a lot of atmosphere by doing this. Games scaries part are the vacuum scenarios where no sound is played, so one must stay alert all the time for the enemy. Also there are occasionally so many enemies that I felt like playing a shooter instead of atmospheric horro game.
The game is really cheap today(2,5eur in sales) so no hurt trying. Easiest difficulty setting is enough to take any challenge out of the game if one feels like going it just for the story, although some atmosphere is lost by doing this.

Also playable without v-sync but some say they've had problems related to one door not opening. Also playing without any kind of vsync might cause coil whine in gpu with FPS running over 200 with better cards(2012 enthusiast ->)

Until recently, I was somewhat reluctant to recommend this game. I enjoyed Dead Man's Switch, but, like many people, found it to be more of an interactive novel (with tactical interludes) than a role playing game. Playing around with the editor has been a blast, but I know that this isn't for everyone, and neither is playing through User Generated Content (though there's some excellent stuff out there).
After the launch of Dragonfall, however, I can post the positive review with confidence. Aside from implementing the much needed save-anywhere system, Dragonfall is a much more engaging campaign on so many levels. It's what Dead Man's Switch should have been, but wasn't. While the main hub is relatively small, you really do feel like the leader of a team of Shadowrunners, and are able to take on a variety of jobs, and complete them in the order that you wish. The jobs themselves, more importantly, feel a great deal more open, with tough choices and multiple objectives, including optional points of interest. The literally two side quests you got in DMS felt like afterthoughts ("oh crap, we forgot to put side quests in and the game launches in a week!"). Here, everything feels lovingly attended to. This is, perhaps, a major advantage of text based story telling. If you're inclined to pick up the relatively robust editor that comes along with the base game, you'll not that your storytelling capacity is only limited by your writing ability and your imagination (the scripting and map building aren't that hard to learn). If you've got the desire and the ability to write, you can craft beautiful and interesting adventures, whether side quest or main, to your heart's content. And that's what HBS has done this time around.
In fact, the one thing that hasn't changed is the excellent writing. This isn't high end literature, but it's engaging and interesting all around. It draws you into the world and, in some cases, really captivates you. The charachters, especially your crew members, the fixer, and the occupants of your little slice of berlin, are memorable and interesting to a person.
It's unfortunate that this had to be released as DLC. The base campaign had the writing down, but it didn't have the wow factor or the, well, interactivity. If only it had...The setting and the charachters of Dead Man's Switch could have really shone with a similar treatment.
Still, better late than never.

"South Park The Stick of Truth" is an Turn-based RPG where you take the role of the "New Kid" who moved to South Park. You travel around South Park... and Canada and meet people who also become your friends through Facebook. It is a game full of excitement, comedy, and adventure. I personally loved it. There is a few bugs I found; that being controlling the character in the world. Sometimes, it will only allow me to move up and down. That may be my controller's fault though. There are a lot of references to episodes in the series. Do note that if you are a completionist, there is some missable content in the game like: friends, Chinpokomon, and 1 side quest. Missing these can result in being unable to get achievements, so be aware if you are like me. Another thing, this game contains nudity and lots of vulgarity (I know it's South Park but just letting you know). There are also a lot of offensive things in the game like: the KKK, homosexuality, and Judism. Xbox and playstation remotes are also usable on here as well. All in all the game is great and I would recommend it to any South Park fan. Things I really hope they add in this game as dlc are: more quest, more characters, friends, and party members, a post game, and more summons. The game is short and gets boring after you complete it. not to mention one of the biggist difficulty spikes I have ever seen in a video game. The game starts to feel empty the more quest you complete and the more collectables you get. The game doesn't include all of the characters from the South Park series. Characters like: Towlie, Satan, and other famous characters in the South Park series. I would like to see The creators and devs continue to work on this great game.

For lovers of South Park this is fantastic; it's like playing through an interactive version of the series. The satirical and tolet humour of the series are captured brilliantly and feels like its been put together with care and attention to detail.
I played this with a controller and feel this would be the best way to appreciate the gameplay.
The combat is 'reactionary' turn based (i.e. reaction events to attack and defend, and extended sequences for some abilities) with simple equipment and skill tree bonuses improve your character (there are also a tonne of customisation options to change your character appearance) so isn't a 'hardcore' RPG by any means, but is enjoyable none the less.

Although quick time events feature, and I normally dislike these immensely, they didn't cause me any massive irritation, presumably as most of the combat is based around reactions. However some of the training segments felt oddly difficult.
Completionists beware there are a lot of 'missable' items/events, so consider using a guide.
Regardless I can't recommend this enough for any lover of South Park. Bonus points if you have the uncensored version.

I replayed HL2 after 10 years. It took me four days to finish it, against the month took 10 years ago. That reassures me more than a little about my memory and learning ability, apparently not yet completely devastated by age ... The game is still very good, and when you start it is hard to stop (a bit like with cigarettes). Certainly the astonishment felt the first time, for graphics, physics and gameplay today is no more, but the fun is still yet assured. The obligatory paths, the puzzles never too complicated and very good chances of saving make the game always smooth and never frustrating. The HDR made even more realistic graphics (for a ten years old game, of course). A little slow the loadings, and saving often produced momentary jamming, particularly annoying to hear.
It is in any case a crucial game, a milestone not to be missed.

Easily one of the very best games in my collection, and one of the least expensive. As a guy who hates going through a game a second time, I am working towards the end of my second playthrough on classic iron-man and looking forward to my third one (on impossible, hopefully).
The blend of micro- and macro-management is really fun and forces you to plan your funding strategies ahead (at least until you get full satellite coverage). The turn-based combat in itself is quite awesome, the action camera proving itself really immersive. Gameplay is both simple and ramified while the level design is well thought (while randomly generated). The entirety of the game is focused on making the fight for earth *your* fight for earth, and you can customize everything (even more with the dlcs) for your own enjoyment (and perhaps easier recognition of your soldiers while on mission).
Understanding all the game mechanics can be hard at first and requires a lot of thought, but is well worth the time spent.
Perhaps the only con I see for this game is the lack of real choice you have to make on the scenario. You can research all projects, complete the foundry, obtain full satellite coverage, have all your soldiers fully upgraded and geared all in the same playthrough. If I were to ask for an addition, it would be to force the player to make strategic choices (not only on what to research first, but on what to research at all), and challenges (why not adding some sort of automated earth defense system that you would have to deploy on earth, and the possibility to save countries that have left the X-COM project). XCOM : EW seems to deal in some way with this, I can't wait to buy it !
Unlike most games, the challenges offered (classic/impossible mode, iron-man, and second wave options) are both challenging and not irritating. However higher difficulty modes are mostly based on modifying in-game values such as your soldier's base hp, costs of items/research projects... etc (even if the ai is slightly better) which basically force you to use overwatch more and be more cautious. I've yet to see a game showing additional mechanics and forcing the player to swap for totally different strategies on higher difficulty modes.
In two words, GET IT !

I've loved Shadowrun for a long time. It was my first tabletop rpg, and it helped foster a love of the happy that is going strong today.
For those who don't know, Shadowrun is a setting that takes place in a dystopian cyberpunk future. Corporations are more powerful than governments, and most people are either wretchedly poor or corperate wage slaves with no freedom. But there is a twist. As this dystopia began to develop, magic returned to the world, bringing with it Elves, Dwarves, Orks, Trolls... and Dragons. Think Bladerunner meets Dragon Age.
You play as shadowrunners, mercenary criminals who live off the grid and do jobs that are too dirty or difficult for the corporations. You are a theif, assasin, or bodygraud on any given day, operating in the shadows and outside the law. I've always thought that this would make a great setting for a video game, but Shadowrun hasn't had too many adaptations: and the ones we did get weren't great.
But Harebrained Schemes thought they could deliver, and took to Kickstarter. And deliver they did. I kickstarted Shadowrun Returns, and the end product was worth the investment. It was a good turn base strategy rpg, along the lines of, say, Fallout, though the setting conjures up comparasions to Arcanum: of steamworks and magick obscura (also recomended). The combat was fun, the graphics looked excellent, and importantly to someone like me, the developers clearly understood Shadowrun, a sense that could not be gained from the poorly received X-box shooter of some years ago.
But it was good game, if there were several issues that kept it from being great. A save system that didn't work well, and a story that was a little too linear and static for Shadowrun's traditional style. These issues were tempered by a promise of mission packs and expansions, and a robust editor for the community to create missions of their own.
Now they've released the first of those mission packs, Dragonfall, and playing it convinced me to write this reveiw. Because where the original game faltered, Dragonfall soars. A rational save system is finally in, and there is more variety to the weapons, cyberware, and other combat options to make things a little more interesting. And, most importantly, the new campaign is exactly what shadowun should be.
It's got interesting characters to talk to, both in your team and in the hub where you go in between missions. It's supports player agency, from the runs you choose to go on to the way you solve those runs. Runs themselves are interesting and often dynamic. Each one has signifigant choices, and I had to think hard about seveal of them. While I could have seen more room to roleplay, for the most part I never felt that my character wasnt' represented in the dialouge choices. And while I like the story of the main game, the story in Dragonfall is much better. It made me care about the characters and the situation far more than the orignal.
But most of all, it feels like Shadowun. The runs played exactly like runs I might have written myself for the tabletop game, far more so than the first game. And the balence between story based missions and those just for case works much better than the previous as well. All in all, playing Dragonfall felt just like playing a real Shadowrun game. That is what I wanted when I kickstarted, and I will buy whatever DLC they release as long as they maintain that feeling.
So, I heartily recomend Shadowrun Returns, but strongly recomend you buy Dragonfall too- in fact, you should probably start with it over the original games campaign, espeically if you are familier with the setting, but thats a personal choice.
But is it right for those who don't know Shadowrun? I still think so. The setting is interesting enough to draw people in, and no previous knoweldge is needed for the actual gameplay, which is entertaining even without feeding into that Shadowrun feedback loop I have. That said, the Berlin Free State setting of the game might be a little bit bewildering, as the game doesn't explain all that much (That said, most shadowrun players probably don't know much about Berlin either - Me included- but at least with the background its easier to get up to speed). For those who don't know anything about Shadowrun, and are willing to put up with the weaker (but still good) story, starting with the first game's story might still be better as it is probly friendler to those who are going in blind.
tldr: Shadowrun Returns is a good game, but Dragonfall is even better, doubly so for anyone who knows the setting or has played the tabletop game. If you were on the fence before, Dragonfall makes it a good bet.

This is a surprisingly delightful, long, and non-linear RPG that rewards exploration and experimentation, has lots of worthwhile and fun side-quests and achievements, all wrapped around an excellent story that is full of unexpected twists.
It is also a ridiculously funny South Park episode, which is centered around a parody of the fantasy RPG genre. Note, though, that you won't find any new components: all the characters, gags, songs, and themes have already been used and abused to death on the TV show. I guess it's inevitable that a TV show that has been running for so long has to get so self-referential. But, well, some things are always funny. Like farts.
To fully enjoy this game, you MUST play it with a gamepad/controller, as it makes ingenious use of its physicality and vibrations. I played with an Xbox-compatible one, which was recognized without any configuration.
I say "surprising" because I was expecting a casual gaming experience with the South Park story at its center. But it's actually a very sophisticated game, with loads of cool loot you can find, sell, and buy, worthwhile abilities and spells to upgrade to, and a diverse set of companions to assist you in battle. And it's not too easy, at least on the default difficulty level. Note, though, that if you're a serious RPG player, you'll probably indeed find it easy: as soon as you level up enough and get good gear, somewhere in the middle of the game, combat because boring and repetitive, because you've already figured out how to win in every situation. I found a combination that could win almost every battle in two rounds. No problem, just increase the difficulty level, which you can do anytime during the game.
I had so much fun with this. :) I don't see much point in a sequel (every single South Park theme I can think of was shamelessly shoved into this game), but I hope this team of devs and creative folk get together on a similar project in the future. Kudos to everyone involved, it's a triumph, and one of my favorite gaming experiences of 2014!

Revised 11/21/2016
So, I wanted to redo my review since the last one really didn't do it any justice.
To start off, I never played the original XCOM games, but I had a feeling I'd like this one, so, let's dive in.
Graphics:
First and foremost, it's what everyone initially cares about, and while the graphics are a bit on the cartoony side and very much a product of the time (2013), they are still decent, and hold up 3 years later. Every now and than, you'll get your usual graphical glitches, or some clipping, but they've done a good job. It isn't going to break records, but it's very easy on the eyes.
Gameplay:
Ah, the gameplay. So this is an interesting one to describe, since you essentially have two different games (think the Total War series). The one everyone sees and loves, is the visceral and unrelenting turn-based combat. The turn based combat, with the lack of a guarantee you'll hit your enemy, coupled with the perma-death system, is actually quite the nerve racking mechanic for gameplay. You may think that you don't care about this soldier or that one, but when you've had the soldier for 10+ missions, fully decked them out, upgraded heavily, and even spent 40 minutes figuring out how to make them look awesome, them dying hurts not only your mission and your capability to win more missions, but your ego as well.
At times though, it's not just your tactical acumen that can get you in trouble, sometimes the game just has it out for you. During gameplay when your team is deployed, shooting at enemies is not a guaranteed hit, each attack takes into account a multitude of different things, like the elevate (if your soldier or the enemy is on higher ground), the cover that is being used, and pure luck and/or chance, and all of this is represented with a hit percentage. Sometimes you'll be mere feet away, with a 90% hit chance, and you'll still miss. While this might seem unfair, keep in mind, this is XCOM, a game that has built it's legacy on it's brutal difficulty and learning curve.
On the other side of the coin, you've also got your base management, which sort of includes a few mini games (in a sense) as well. First, you've got to dig areas in your base in order to build more rooms. The further you go down, the more expensive it is to dig, and you need to build power plants as well. It just snowballs further from there, you've got to keep a balance with all the countries that support the XCOM program, and each time there's an incident, you need to select between 3 choices, which are 3 different countries. Each has a benefit that you'll get at the end of the missions, whether it's money, scientists, or engineers. However, when you select a country to help, the panic in the countries you ignored go up, while the one you helped goes down. It's a very delicate balancing act, and when the panic peaks in a country, that country withdraws funding from the XCOM program, so you get less and less money each month.
This is just the tip of the iceberg, this is a very in depth game, and you can get very involved in it. I whole hardheartedly recommend it. I haven't played multiplayer, so I cannot comment on it.
Mods
Keep in mind, there are not a lot of mods for this game, because apparently this game is VERY hard to mod for, the game wasn't designed with modders in mind. That didn't stop the more skilled people from messing around with it though, and there is a mod I would definitely recommend, but it makes the game even harder, and that mod is "The Long War". I haven't tried it yet, but I have read a ton of good things about it. The devs for The Long War did such a good job, the Firaxis contacted them directly for input when designing XCOM 2 as to how to make it easier for modders to do their thing on XCOM 2.

Revised 11/21/2016
So, I wanted to redo my review since the last one really didn't do it any justice.
To start off, I never played the original XCOM games, but I had a feeling I'd like this one, so, let's dive in.
Graphics:
First and foremost, it's what everyone initially cares about, and while the graphics are a bit on the cartoony side and very much a product of the time (2013), they are still decent, and hold up 3 years later. Every now and than, you'll get your usual graphical glitches, or some clipping, but they've done a good job. It isn't going to break records, but it's very easy on the eyes.
Gameplay:
Ah, the gameplay. So this is an interesting one to describe, since you essentially have two different games (think the Total War series). The one everyone sees and loves, is the visceral and unrelenting turn-based combat. The turn based combat, with the lack of a guarantee you'll hit your enemy, coupled with the perma-death system, is actually quite the nerve racking mechanic for gameplay. You may think that you don't care about this soldier or that one, but when you've had the soldier for 10+ missions, fully decked them out, upgraded heavily, and even spent 40 minutes figuring out how to make them look awesome, them dying hurts not only your mission and your capability to win more missions, but your ego as well.
At times though, it's not just your tactical acumen that can get you in trouble, sometimes the game just has it out for you. During gameplay when your team is deployed, shooting at enemies is not a guaranteed hit, each attack takes into account a multitude of different things, like the elevate (if your soldier or the enemy is on higher ground), the cover that is being used, and pure luck and/or chance, and all of this is represented with a hit percentage. Sometimes you'll be mere feet away, with a 90% hit chance, and you'll still miss. While this might seem unfair, keep in mind, this is XCOM, a game that has built it's legacy on it's brutal difficulty and learning curve.
On the other side of the coin, you've also got your base management, which sort of includes a few mini games (in a sense) as well. First, you've got to dig areas in your base in order to build more rooms. The further you go down, the more expensive it is to dig, and you need to build power plants as well. It just snowballs further from there, you've got to keep a balance with all the countries that support the XCOM program, and each time there's an incident, you need to select between 3 choices, which are 3 different countries. Each has a benefit that you'll get at the end of the missions, whether it's money, scientists, or engineers. However, when you select a country to help, the panic in the countries you ignored go up, while the one you helped goes down. It's a very delicate balancing act, and when the panic peaks in a country, that country withdraws funding from the XCOM program, so you get less and less money each month.
This is just the tip of the iceberg, this is a very in depth game, and you can get very involved in it. I whole hardheartedly recommend it. I haven't played multiplayer, so I cannot comment on it.
Mods
Keep in mind, there are not a lot of mods for this game, because apparently this game is VERY hard to mod for, the game wasn't designed with modders in mind. That didn't stop the more skilled people from messing around with it though, and there is a mod I would definitely recommend, but it makes the game even harder, and that mod is "The Long War". I haven't tried it yet, but I have read a ton of good things about it. The devs for The Long War did such a good job, the Firaxis contacted them directly for input when designing XCOM 2 as to how to make it easier for modders to do their thing on XCOM 2.

I'll get straight to the point:
The Good:
It's official campaign Dead Man's Switch is pretty good so to speak. The story it has justifies the linearity of the game's design as it's pretty much like reading an interactive book (like some of the older RPGs of the 90s). The game is practically friendly to almost any PC considering that it relies on the cyberpunk aesthetics to make the game look pretty. In terms of combat, it's basically a simplified version of Xcom: Enemy Unknown and if you like that game, you are going to be fairly familiar with how the game works. And even if you are done with the main campaign, there's still more to offer from the community itself through UGCs which can be downloaded through Steam directly or through the Shadowrun Nexus (especially if you own the DRM-free version on GOG) And by the time of this review (which is the same time as when the DLC Dragonfall first came out) you can actually save without relying on the autosave feature.
The Bad:
Due to the fact that the replayability of this game past Dead Man's Switch (and Dragonfall) is dependent on the UGC of the community, you will probably have to take your time to look for custom campaigns that are actually complete, let alone any good. Most of the complete ones are usually the shortest or the simplest of campaigns. In addition, the Dead Man's Switch campaign doesn't seem to give much options to have a players who want to play a Face or a Decker as they are either very few instances to begin with or doesn't truly payoff. I don't like the fact that I have to actually rely on hiring more runners for a particular mission and they feel restrictive in which you cannot give them suitable gear or even have them hold on to an medkit if your inventory is full. Also, there are certain dialog choices that are greyed out if you don't meet the required stats to qualify. I'd rather have them hidden to keep me surprised. On top of that, I know that the idea behind this game is to make the player the main protagonist, but the problem with that is that this is Shadowrun, and the reason you have a variety of runner archetypes in a team is because you can take advantage of what they are capable of inside and outside of combat. Instead, that variety is only restricted to combat and combat alone save of you being able to appoint a hired/companion decker to hack into the Matrix for you in case you are incapable of such a task.
Overall: Shadowrun Returns has it's flaws but I like what Harebrained as treated it so far. It's not an amazing game and it's hardly going to be the "best RPG EVAR!!!11!" but if you appreciate a good cyberpunk story with a touch of magic with a potential for more to come whether by the devs themselves through DLC or by the Shadowrun community, then I'd say this is a very safe purchase.

Ever wanted to test your reflexes? Enjoy catchy chip-tune music? If your answer is "yes", then look no further: Super Hexagon is indie game which is all that and more.
In Super Hexagon, there are no easy ways out: you must challenge yourself to one of the three available difficulties available right from the bat. The game developers were greatly self-aware of their product's difficulty; the easiest route you can take is 'Hard', followed by 'Harder' and 'Hardest'. So what's the catch?
You control a small triangular shape around, surprisingly, a hexagon. Your objective is to make it through a course of randomly generated (to some extent) and ever-changing stage layout for 60 seconds. No checkpoints: you either make it there or you will have to restart all over again. Sounds easy? Believe me when I say it's not: the words "Game Over" and "Begin" will ring in your head for the hours to come. However, at no point is the game unfair in difficulty. You have a split second to choose the right route, and another one right after it. It's a gauntlet that you'll be glad to start, and even happier to finish. After making it through the stage, you'll be treated a harder, faster version of the same level. You won't have to retry the same, slower version to again to access this new faster level: it comes available to level select for you to master. This goes for all of the 3 stages, so that means you have 6 stages to tackle for, and it gets harder. FAST.
For such a simple and relatively short game, Super Hexagon is truly an immersive experience: you'll notice having already spend hours on it, and still chasing after that 60-second-mark on all of the stages. But you WILL learn it, and you CAN master it. That's enough to keep you going. So, what comes after you beat the 6 stages? I can tell you It's not cake, but rather something eeriely satisfying. Super Hexagon is an experience, something videos fail to capture: so go out there and get it for yourself already!

[Objective]
The player controls the survivor of a space freighter crash on a strange
planet. As the player progresses through levels, selected randomly and
with some procedural placement of objects within the level, they attempt
to survive by killing monsters and collecting items that can boost their
offensive and defensive abilities. The game features a difficulty scale
that increases with time, requiring the player to choose between spending
time building experience and completing levels quickly before the monsters
become more difficult. The game supports up to four cooperative players.
[Gameplay]
At the start of the game, each player selects one of twelve characters.
Initially, only one character is available, but as the player completes
various in-game objectives, more characters become available.
Each character has various statistics and a set of unique moves;
for example, a sniper has the ability to hit creatures from a long
distance for large damage but their firing rate is slow, while a common
soldier can do rapid, moderate damage at close range.
Within all but the last level of the game, the goal is to locate a
teleporter, placed in a random location. As the players hunt for it,
they will encounter monsters; upon death the monsters will drop in-game
money and will also provide the players experience. As the players gain
experience they will increase the player level, gaining more hit points
and stronger attacks. Money can be used to open various chests, buy items
at stores, activate attack drones that aid in combat, or pray at shrines
that have a random chance of dropping items, described by game lore as
the space freighter's cargo. These items include passive bonuses that
improve offensive or defensive capabilities, or a special weapon.
Players can only use one special weapon at any time, but they can
collect many passive items, including multiple versions of the same
item, stacking the benefits of these items. The location of these items
is randomly determined through roguelike procedural generation.
Once the players have found the teleporter, they activate it, starting
a 90 second countdown which the players must survive. During this time,
many more monsters, including at least one boss character, will appear.
After the countdown is over, no new monsters will appear but the players
will have to defeat all remaining monsters before they can use the
teleporter and proceed to the next level. At this time, any remaining
money the players have is converted to experience points. At the
penultimate level, the players have the option of taking the teleporter
to the final level (the crashed ship), or to use the teleporter to run
through additional levels as to gain more experience and items; when
this latter option is taken, the teleporter on these levels will allow
the same choice to either proceed to the final level or continue through
additional levels. On the final level, the player must fight a final boss
character which if they survive, they are able to escape the planet and
win the game.
The difficulty of the game is determined by a timer. The difficulty level
increases every 5 minutes up through 10 levels, with newly spawned
monsters having more health and stronger attacks. Additionally, boss
characters may spawn before the players have found teleporters. If
playing alone, the game is over when the player dies. In multiplayer
mode, a player that dies must wait until the other players survive to
the next level, upon which they are brought back into play.
The item drops are based on the various progress the player has made in
the meta-game through repeated playthroughs. For example, defeating
certain boss characters for the first time will unlock an item that can
then drop in future playthroughs. Other items are based on completing
certain goals, such as winning the game a number of times, or
performing specific goals with each of the characters. Monsters will
also drop log books that describe the monsters, this itself is used to
unlock more items.

Ever wanted to test your reflexes? Enjoy catchy chip-tune music? If your answer is "yes", then look no further: Super Hexagon is indie game which is all that and more.
In Super Hexagon, there are no easy ways out: you must challenge yourself to one of the three available difficulties available right from the bat. The game developers were greatly self-aware of their product's difficulty; the easiest route you can take is 'Hard', followed by 'Harder' and 'Hardest'. So what's the catch?
You control a small triangular shape around, surprisingly, a hexagon. Your objective is to make it through a course of randomly generated (to some extent) and ever-changing stage layout for 60 seconds. No checkpoints: you either make it there or you will have to restart all over again. Sounds easy? Believe me when I say it's not: the words "Game Over" and "Begin" will ring in your head for the hours to come. However, at no point is the game unfair in difficulty. You have a split second to choose the right route, and another one right after it. It's a gauntlet that you'll be glad to start, and even happier to finish. After making it through the stage, you'll be treated a harder, faster version of the same level. You won't have to retry the same, slower version to again to access this new faster level: it comes available to level select for you to master. This goes for all of the 3 stages, so that means you have 6 stages to tackle for, and it gets harder. FAST.
For such a simple and relatively short game, Super Hexagon is truly an immersive experience: you'll notice having already spend hours on it, and still chasing after that 60-second-mark on all of the stages. But you WILL learn it, and you CAN master it. That's enough to keep you going. So, what comes after you beat the 6 stages? I can tell you It's not cake, but rather something eeriely satisfying. Super Hexagon is an experience, something videos fail to capture: so go out there and get it for yourself already!

Cons:

Risk of Rain is a Rouge Like Action Indie Role Playing Game from developers  HOPOO Games.  A small three man Indie games development company. The publishers of Risk of Rain are Chucklefish, the company that published games like Starbound and Halfway. The focus of Risk of Rain is its fandom platform levels filled with monsters and loot, with each play though different from the last.
Risk of Rain only allows for one life each play thought and yes it sounds a little scary at first but this one life one game mentality makes the players think in different ways. Every time you die it makes you think what you could do better next time and no one death ever feel cheated and like the game was just out to get you. Risk of Rain all around feel even and balanced but can become increasingly easy the longer one session last for with the increase of items you collect, but having only one life makes you causes and only taking risks when it allows for great outcome. And Risk of Rain is all about that high risk high reward. Going back to  that one life one game look, it makes the players think about each action and in implemented in a way the player does not even know it is happening to them. They just want to do better than they did last time, want to get further in the game.
The music of Risk of Rain is what immerses the players in this 8 bit world of death and monsters, with the art style and music blending perfectly to fit the style of play that Risk of Rain offers. With the 8bit style art allowing for a wide verity of landscapes and beautiful backdrops, from frozen tundra's to lava underworlds. Each pixel looks gives a feeling of life to the players.
The music of Risk of Rain is there to only increase this feeling of a living and futuristic world. Making it feel like you are in danger on this alien planet that is out to get only you and that you could die at any minute. Giving the feeling that this planet you are on really is alien.
Each play though of Risk of rain I felt like I was only getting better and better at not dying. As simple as it sounds its true, and yes when you are not dying on the first level you can have lots of fun with Risk of Rain. With the amount of items you can obtain and the increasingly large number of enemies that keep rising you never feel like you are completely out of danger. Power yes but not in the clear to take a breath, for every moment in Risk of Rain. Even if it was my first time playing or my 100th. I always felt like I was in the edge of my seat, waiting for the next time I would be able to learn from my mistake and love it.

I still hold that the game is great and a must have. The combat is fun and it does look great. I want to sort of change my opinion about the story though, and make a comment about the quests. The story started off strong then tapered off. The final boss battle is incredibly underwhelming and will leave you wanting. I have never seen a game more blatantly set itself up for a sequel or dlc. There is no real conclusion and that's disappointing. The side quests get kind of old after awhile. I didn't want to believe what people were saying about being an "errand boy," but that is the truth plain and simple. The game quests lack that level of creativity.
Those are the primary negatives. So that being said, the game does more right than wrong. The combat is fun, the graphics are beautiful, the world feels very alive and is very detailed. I like the little effects like how safe zones are complete with guards and bright UV lights to keep the volatiles away. It looks really great from a distance. At night, those blue lights will be what you frantically look for as you're sprinting away from hungry zombies. The progression feels very natural. You start off kind of wimpy and evolve into a bad♥♥♥♥♥ It doesn't really make sense given the story, but it feels cool for the game.
The multiplayer is kind of shallow, I can't believe it was going to be a pre-order bonus. It's a fun little mini game but you're not really invading someone's game. If you leave the game open to matchmaking, people can join you and this mini-game will automatically start. It is fun, but it's not really what they made it out to be.
This game is best played with a friend. I've also found it more fun to just sort of wander around and explore setting yourself small custom objectives. For instance, when I was still weak, I discovered that the main bridge in the slums had a large nummber of police vans which generally contained high level weapons, like fire arms. The problem is that the bridge is infested with zombies. It was really fun teaming up with my friend to try to frantically loot these police vans. There's plenty to uncover within the world itself.
Overall 7/10

The sound design and weapon design are both top notch but every other part of the game is mediocre to downright bad. The games few high points come in a few clever environmental puzzles and a few fights where you have room to maneuver and aim. Unfortunately, there's a lot of just boring traversal and extremely cramped fights where you just dump ammo to avoid getting stun locked and killed. The story is very poorly written and told, it tries to be immersive but there's just no depth to it and the game tries to pull multiple twists that don't even make sense or carry any weight. The final boss fight might be the most frustrating part of the game as there's a lengthy unskippable cutscene at the start AND an even longer unskippable cutscene if you die.
Add to all that, you need to tweak the game to even use the mouse like a mouse and no FoV and the game is exceedingly awkward at times. I played with a controller and the sensitivty was either too high for precision or too low to move and turn efficiently. I didn't feel the game was more suspenseful due to the controls, it just felt poorly made. This was especially prevalent in bossfights and certain sequences when you were grabbed and had to free aim while being jerk around. I died a number of times because both your firing point AND the spot you're shooting are snapping around with no fluidity at all. Certain enemies have animations where they're invincible and you have to wait for them to snap to another animation for them to be vulnerable again which looks awful and is tedious.
The only way I would recommend this game is if you absolutely love suspense/horror as everything else it tries to do is done better somewhere else.

Was soll ich sagen?Das Spiel macht Spaß.Die Grafik ist absolut in Orndung und die Schauplätze liebevoll designt.Es macht Spaß mit seinen Soldaten den Sektor zu erkundne und gegnerische Aliens auszuschalten.Doch was gibt es taktisch her?Man beginnt beim Avenger, der einen zum Schauplatz gebracht hat und inflitriert das Gebiet mit seinen Soldaten im Rundenmodus.Es gibt verschiedene Klassen an Soldaten.So gibt es den Sturmtrupp mit Sturmgewehr, den Sniper, der auch von hinterletzten Winkel Aliens plattmachen kann, Supporter und Psi-Soldten, die den Mind-Krieg betreiten können, ganz bewährt im alter X-Com Enemy-Unknown-Manier.Die Schlachten machen Spaß und sind zu keinem Zeitpunkt unfair.
Das Spiel ist eine gelungene Adapation des Klassikers, einzig alleine (achtung Spoiler!) die Tatsache, dass es nicht zum Mars/Cydonia geht um den Endboss kaltzumachen stört mich.Stattdessen wurde hier ein "Tempelschiff" generiert, auf dem der Kopf der Alienbande ist und den es auszuschalten gilt.
Ansonsten ist eigentlich alles beim alten geblieben..die Forschung, die Werkstatt und der X-Com-Rat, der einen subventioniert, wenn man erfolgreich Terrorangriffe tilgt oder Ufos-Abschießt.Das Spiel ist sehr linear, aber das ist nicht weiter schlimm.
X-Com Enemy Unknown macht Spaß, wenn man auf Taktikspiele steht und abgehärtet ist gegenüber Niederlagen.Kauft es und vielleicht sieht man sich ja mal im Multiplayer, um gemeinsam ein paar Projektile in die Gehirne der Aliens zu treiben.

Fisrt, I want to say that I didn't had any technical issues with the game. My computer is a bit below the recommended specifications, but the game runs smoothly when I reduce some graphics settings. I finished the game, and it never crashed or freezed.

Killing Floor 2, after what seemed as much too long a period for being labeled as beta, continuing its presence as an early access game for over a year, has finally been given an official release date of November 2016.  Having sunk many hours into the original Killing Floor, many of the early edges have, I feel, finally been ironed out.  Initially I returned to KF1 and complained bitterly that the creature animations were jerky, hit boxes and weapons fire felt 'off', leaving impression of dissatisfaction and a stale level of gameplay.  The new weapons were a novel idea, but often were over powered or unimpressive.  The game was lacking seriously in balance and polish.  Today, KF2 offers, in its current state (September 2016) a worthy slow-paced levelling system for 8 classes (originally a scanty 4) with a measured reward of experience points modelled on how well you play and which weapon type you use to deliver death to the undead in what is mostly a Coop Survival Shooter.  The height of satisfaction gained in levelling up an off class, such as the Sharpshooter which specializes in proficiency in accuracy (headshots), can be buffed and ranked up while playing as any of the other classes simply by attaining headshots, is just glorious.  Now with the recent addition of the old Sharpshooter and Swat class, the game has finally reached a nice bit of special content that destinguishes it apart, in a favorable way, to KF1.  Nail bombs, trap doors (rigged explosive welded doors), freeze grenades, and adjustable perks all offer a huge amount of variety that was lacking in its early stages.  IMO, this game is ready for release now.  It is fun in its difficulty that even failure can feel rewarding on a great run.  It is once again equally funny and frustrating almost every time to witness a solo completed/failed run of a Wave by a solo player that could bring your team back from the brink of a failed late Wave game.  Few shooters have reached the level of satisfaction when I am that player, and how often it is achieved. The added content feels like it will give KF2 a long life, while the DLC is mostly cosmetic without giving away the edge or upper-hand to golden DLC weapon/ammo/buff packs.  Enjoy the great jokes with friends when 'Fleshpound' becomes a byword that evokes nervous cackles and shouts for the heaviest firepower.  Also, the ending bosses are once again just as cheap as all heck as they've ever been in KF original. Oh, and saying that, the Patriach is back too.
::edit:: You can only advance a class by using any one of their specialized weapon set or special skill (i.e. welding doors as Support Specialist).

A South Park game true to the show's spirit. A story heavily influenced by last season's three part Game of Thrones parody, as well comedic references to popular RPGs like Skyrim (even the main battle theme is a parody of the Dragonborn song!)  and even the Witcher (yes, it's in there! Look carefully). In short, your character (the new kid or, as he will come to be known, the "Douch3 bag") gets involved in Cartman's medieval live-action RPGing and the battle between the two factions (sans the PS4/XBOX war).  At the same time, cataclysmic events (as always) will happen in South Park, and it will be your task to sort them out and save the entire world. All this in classic South Park toilet humour and pop culture ridicule, in a game that is riddled with references to the show's greatest hits! Everything is in here!!! From the recent Game of Thrones parody to Al Gore and ManBearPig, to Tom Cruise locked in Stan's closet, to Lemmywinks, to the Ginger Kids and Crab People, to Chinpokomon, to Canada (presented in 8-bit pixelized style!) to the good old alien antenna anal probe! Fans of South Park will feel right at home. It will feel like playing an actual episode of the show!
Which is one of the game's main problems, i.e. it is, much like a South Park episode, too damn short! In "Normal/medium" difficulty this game will take, on average, 13-15 hours to beat (the main story and all sidequests, not all achievements won necessarily) which, for an RPG, is too little!  It's not that you don't have things to do; there are many side quests to complete, chinpokomon to collect and hobos to beat up (plus, you get to find Jesus). However, all this will be quickly over, and you'll find yourself thinking "What? Already???"
The Stick's gameplay is, essentially, that of a turn based RPG, a bit like Final Fantasy. On the whole it is implemented nicely. It must be noted that the PC version of the game has been designed carefully with the PC gamer in mind, and controls are optimised for keyboard/mouse. In other words, you won't need a gamepad to play this game. However, the minigames are BAAAD!!!! Stupid bad. From the farts training to the dreadful abortion sequence (which cost me 1 of the afore mentioned 13 hours till I figured out how to not destroy Randy's equipment), these minigames and puzzles will only cause you needless irritation.
Despite these issues, the game remains a great South Park experience.  SP fans, if you haven't already, dive in!  All the others, watch some previews first, then play the game, then binge watch South Park.
Pros:
+Really good cartoonish graphics, in South Park style.  Just like watching the actual show
+Nice music, often a parody of GoT, Skyrim, Lord of the Rings etc. Plus, the Lemmywinks song!
+Controls optimized for PC and keyboard/mouse! No real need for gamepads (unless you can't otherwise function...)
+A hilarious story, in true South Park spirit, and very interesting side quests.
+Princess Kenny. Nuff said!
+The entire South Park town, as well as the nation of Canada, all yours to explore. Obsidian really did a great work for the world.
Cons:
-Too short! Will take you at most two days to complete.
-Some graphics issues. In a few cases, your character flickers or disappears during cut scenes.
-The minigames, specifically the annoying abortion bit.
-No appearance of Satan whatsoever. No, Damien doesn't count. No Shaddam Housein either.
I would give this game 7.5 / 10.

Let's set this straight: Antichamber is two things at once. On the one hand, it's a Metroidvania in non-Euclidean space, deliberately and often deliciously confusing to navigate. On the other, it’s a surprisingly traditional puzzle game with some great ideas, but also some extremely clumsy mechanics. Those two things rarely intersect; while there are puzzles that utilise all the freaky geometry, most of them do not, which seems a shame. If anything, the game feels a bit too easy considering the brain-melting potential it had.
It’s definitely worth picking up just to experience all the funky corridor spaghetti and the occasional good puzzle, but I also feel the need to warn about the game’s often frustrating and pigheaded determination to not tell the player anything at all – particularly early on, it’s very hard to tell if you’re making any progress or just running around in circles (or indeed, if running around in circles doesn’t actually mean making progress). It’s not a particularly difficult IQ test, it’s just that someone took away the instructions sheet.

Killing Floor 2, after what seemed as much too long a period for being labeled as beta, continuing its presence as an early access game for over a year, has finally been given an official release date of November 2016.  Having sunk many hours into the original Killing Floor, many of the early edges have, I feel, finally been ironed out.  Initially I returned to KF1 and complained bitterly that the creature animations were jerky, hit boxes and weapons fire felt 'off', leaving impression of dissatisfaction and a stale level of gameplay.  The new weapons were a novel idea, but often were over powered or unimpressive.  The game was lacking seriously in balance and polish.  Today, KF2 offers, in its current state (September 2016) a worthy slow-paced levelling system for 8 classes (originally a scanty 4) with a measured reward of experience points modelled on how well you play and which weapon type you use to deliver death to the undead in what is mostly a Coop Survival Shooter.  The height of satisfaction gained in levelling up an off class, such as the Sharpshooter which specializes in proficiency in accuracy (headshots), can be buffed and ranked up while playing as any of the other classes simply by attaining headshots, is just glorious.  Now with the recent addition of the old Sharpshooter and Swat class, the game has finally reached a nice bit of special content that destinguishes it apart, in a favorable way, to KF1.  Nail bombs, trap doors (rigged explosive welded doors), freeze grenades, and adjustable perks all offer a huge amount of variety that was lacking in its early stages.  IMO, this game is ready for release now.  It is fun in its difficulty that even failure can feel rewarding on a great run.  It is once again equally funny and frustrating almost every time to witness a solo completed/failed run of a Wave by a solo player that could bring your team back from the brink of a failed late Wave game.  Few shooters have reached the level of satisfaction when I am that player, and how often it is achieved. The added content feels like it will give KF2 a long life, while the DLC is mostly cosmetic without giving away the edge or upper-hand to golden DLC weapon/ammo/buff packs.  Enjoy the great jokes with friends when 'Fleshpound' becomes a byword that evokes nervous cackles and shouts for the heaviest firepower.  Also, the ending bosses are once again just as cheap as all heck as they've ever been in KF original. Oh, and saying that, the Patriach is back too.
::edit:: You can only advance a class by using any one of their specialized weapon set or special skill (i.e. welding doors as Support Specialist).

Anfangs war ich skeptisch, weil ich das gute alte X-Com damals auf Amiga 500 gespielt und geliebt habe.Es war perfekt für mich, wenn auch heutzutage nicht mehr grafisch up-to-date.Ich kaufte mir also im Sale dies Game für zehn Bucks in froher Erwartung, ein echtes X-Com mein eigen zu nennen.
Was soll ich sagen?Das Spiel macht Spaß.Die Grafik ist absolut in Orndung und die Schauplätze liebevoll designt.Es macht Spaß mit seinen Soldaten den Sektor zu erkundne und gegnerische Aliens auszuschalten.Doch was gibt es taktisch her?Man beginnt beim Avenger, der einen zum Schauplatz gebracht hat und inflitriert das Gebiet mit seinen Soldaten im Rundenmodus.Es gibt verschiedene Klassen an Soldaten.So gibt es den Sturmtrupp mit Sturmgewehr, den Sniper, der auch von hinterletzten Winkel Aliens plattmachen kann, Supporter und Psi-Soldten, die den Mind-Krieg betreiten können, ganz bewährt im alter X-Com Enemy-Unknown-Manier.Die Schlachten machen Spaß und sind zu keinem Zeitpunkt unfair.
Das Spiel ist eine gelungene Adapation des Klassikers, einzig alleine (achtung Spoiler!) die Tatsache, dass es nicht zum Mars/Cydonia geht um den Endboss kaltzumachen stört mich.Stattdessen wurde hier ein "Tempelschiff" generiert, auf dem der Kopf der Alienbande ist und den es auszuschalten gilt.
Ansonsten ist eigentlich alles beim alten geblieben..die Forschung, die Werkstatt und der X-Com-Rat, der einen subventioniert, wenn man erfolgreich Terrorangriffe tilgt oder Ufos-Abschießt.Das Spiel ist sehr linear, aber das ist nicht weiter schlimm.
X-Com Enemy Unknown macht Spaß, wenn man auf Taktikspiele steht und abgehärtet ist gegenüber Niederlagen.Kauft es und vielleicht sieht man sich ja mal im Multiplayer, um gemeinsam ein paar Projektile in die Gehirne der Aliens zu treiben.

Fisrt, I want to say that I didn't had any technical issues with the game. My computer is a bit below the recommended specifications, but the game runs smoothly when I reduce some graphics settings. I finished the game, and it never crashed or freezed.
Speaking about graphics, they are amazing, even on the lower settings. All details, movements and effects, everything is perfect. Someday I will have a more powerful computer to play it on the highest settings.
The story is really interesting and creative. There is a lot of villains. Even Joker appear on the game in a very creative way. The DLC's adds more villains to the crew.
About the DLC's, the only ones I really didn't liked are those that adds new skins for the batmobile. You can only use them on the AR trainings, not on the city map, unless you finish the main campaign, but there is not much left to do at this point. But if you want all the achievements, you will need to buy all DLC's. I recommend buying the Season Pass, since all of them are included, and the price is lower than if you buy each one separatedly.
The map is bigger than Arkham City or Origins, but I find it easier to travel, thanks to the Batmobile and the Grapple upgrades. I thought that I would miss the fast travel using the batwing, present on Origins, but it isn't really necessary.
The batmobile adds an entirely new layer of playability to the game. Although some people state that you are forced to use it extensively, I don't share this opinion. The developers made a very good job on the batmobile design and its own combat system. I think it is very fun and sometimes challenging to play with it, but totally worth the time.
Now for the combat system. It remains almost the same, with some additions. As you progress on the game, you get all the gadgets back (from the Arkham City, not Origins). The combat received many improvements, like using the environment, get assisted by the batmobile and new movements.
The only modification I didn't like, was the change on the special attack buttons. Now you must press [alt + a number] to performe those attacks. Pressing two buttons is not the problem, but the position of the buttons are. But it is not a big deal, I really get used to it. Anyway, and you may change the layout of the keyboard if you want, or use a controller, if you have one.
I had more than 300 hours of gameplay on Arkham City, my favorite game from the series until now. I think this game will easily surpass this number.
I highly recommend buying this game, and the Season Pass DLC.

I'm not someone normally prone to hyperbole, so believe me when I say that this is possibly the greatest game every made.
Yes, it's a TV show spinoff game, and previous examples to make games of TV shows have met with mixed results. This one manages to make reference to an already establish canon universe, but then transcends it, becoming something much greater as a result. The boys are playing a fantasy game with the other children in town, and you, as "new kid", join in.
It's an RPG, so in terms of play mechanics, you won't be doing anything here that you haven't already done in similar games. It is very well done though,  and it continually adds new techniques and new genres so it never becomes tedious.
The game does an amazing job of reconstructing what it was like to be 10 years old and playing with your friends. It feels like the best LARP ever.
But at the same time, it is South Park - so it is chock full of amazingly over-the-top sequences that aren't just laugh-out-loud funny, but more howl-out-loud. Your own laughter becomes part of the soundtrack of the game. Note, however, that this is South Park free of all censorship and content restrictions, so it is South Park turned up to 11. Maybe 12. It does its level best to find something offensive to everyone and it is *very* good at it. This is not a game for anyone under 18 under *any* circumstances.
My only point of complaint is that, unlike most RPGs in recent memory, there are quests and items that are time-sensitive and cannot be revisited later on in the game. If you are a 100% completionist, the game will require at least 2 playthroughs - one, as an unfettered, virgin experience, and one with a Game Guide open to warn you about upcoming limited opportunities.
If you love RPGs, are not easily offended (and can recover from it when you are), were 10 years old once, have a sense of humour, and are old enough to vote, you MUST MUST MUST play this game.

First off i freaking love(d) this Game, i played it when it came out and wasnt even available in Steam, i had Hours of fun with this Game i even beat the freaking End Boss over and Over.
So why do i not recommend it? Thats easy.... or should i say hard?
Because thats what this Game truly is, or atleast it gotten so hard that its gotten freaking Impossible for any non-Hardcore Risk of Rain player.
I wouldnt go as far as saying im a casual seeing how "good" i once was but its not fun to me anymore. (Ill probably continue playing this Game though, trying to get better because i want to Love it again as it can be really fun if you have a good run)
The Items you get in this Game which make it Interesting are almost always Random and even though some Combinations of Items can be Overpowered later on it depends extremely on Luck.
If you get the wrong items at the start you cant deal with the Enemys that come and as the Games difficulty increases with the Time you play per run by the time you might get a few decent Items the Enemys have already become unkillable for you.
Since the Positives of this Game can be found in any of the mostly Positive Feedbacks im not going into detail about those... It does have a bunch of Positives so read a good Feedback for that but i will concentrate on the bad stuff.
- If you dont have Luck with the Items the game becomes nearly Impossible and this takes the fun
- Leveling Up gives you rea-eaally low Bonuses compared to how fast the Enemys get stronger
- Even with an Item that increases your Max life for Kills you cant tank anything and even if there are items that reduce damage give armor and Health Regeneration they dont help much, in fact even if you'd only get Tanky Items a Mobgroup takes you down in almost an Instant unless you are lucky enough to get the "Health on Hit"-Item which doesnt help you much if you dont continue getting it as the effect is not percentual but 2 HP/Per Hit/Per Item
- Because of the rapidly increasing Strenght of Mobs and the more Powefull Versions of Mobs that exist, youll find yourself Kiting most of the Time which leads to wasting Time making the Mobs even more Powerfull, because you need to be moving most of the Time Melee Classes are at a Heavy Disadvantage and almost unplayable (Though there is one that can Block all damage coming from one directions youll get too slow and mobs start moving around you and once you are in a group disabling that Ability will almost always kill you instantanously)
- Since Levelup bonus doesnt give you the Power to fight back youll find that most of your Damage is depending on your Items, since those are Random and the Activation aswell you need to bash at even a single Mob for quite some time with all your skills before it eventually dies.
"Hey theres a Casual difficulty Option" I hear you say, but since that doenst save your Progress you cant unlock any Characters or Items with it and most people arent very fond of playing the One Character you can play in the beginning with just a handfull of Items to Collect.
As much as i want to Love this Game its gotten so hard for me that its not fun to play anymore and because its so incredibly Luck based there are few rounds that i can actually collect some stuff before i get overwhelmed by the Enemies that not only have like 10 Times my Health but also Spawn so fast that they form a Group that bursts me down in an Instant.
If you can play this Game, and dont have trouble with the Difficulty and Random Items as much as I do than i totally recommend this Game for you but this is not a Game everyone can have fun with (anymore)

[EDIT]
I still hold that the game is great and a must have. The combat is fun and it does look great. I want to sort of change my opinion about the story though, and make a comment about the quests. The story started off strong then tapered off. The final boss battle is incredibly underwhelming and will leave you wanting. I have never seen a game more blatantly set itself up for a sequel or dlc. There is no real conclusion and that's disappointing. The side quests get kind of old after awhile. I didn't want to believe what people were saying about being an "errand boy," but that is the truth plain and simple. The game quests lack that level of creativity.
Those are the primary negatives. So that being said, the game does more right than wrong. The combat is fun, the graphics are beautiful, the world feels very alive and is very detailed. I like the little effects like how safe zones are complete with guards and bright UV lights to keep the volatiles away. It looks really great from a distance. At night, those blue lights will be what you frantically look for as you're sprinting away from hungry zombies. The progression feels very natural. You start off kind of wimpy and evolve into a bad♥♥♥♥♥ It doesn't really make sense given the story, but it feels cool for the game.
The multiplayer is kind of shallow, I can't believe it was going to be a pre-order bonus. It's a fun little mini game but you're not really invading someone's game. If you leave the game open to matchmaking, people can join you and this mini-game will automatically start. It is fun, but it's not really what they made it out to be.
This game is best played with a friend. I've also found it more fun to just sort of wander around and explore setting yourself small custom objectives. For instance, when I was still weak, I discovered that the main bridge in the slums had a large nummber of police vans which generally contained high level weapons, like fire arms. The problem is that the bridge is infested with zombies. It was really fun teaming up with my friend to try to frantically loot these police vans. There's plenty to uncover within the world itself.
Overall 7/10

One of the most unique and entertaining first-person puzzle games I've played, I rank this game right up there with Portal and Spacechem. Antichamber offers some really unusual and mind bending puzzles in a non-euclidean world: where the rules often change depending on your frame of reference. The entire pace of the game is similar to that of Portal, in that you can go at your own pace. The atmosphere is simplistic, yet vivid enough to convey the objectives in the world. The soundtrack is a peaceful ambiance that nicely complements the calm tone of the game. Antichamber also introduces new mechanics at a reasonable pace to keep the game entertaining. The “simple wisdom” posters, I feel, is also a nice touch.
Where it differs from Portal, however, is it's complete lack of a story. Rather, it's more of an “experience.” Obviously, some of the puzzles can be a bit unintuitive, but only a few I would chalk up to questionable design. Overall the puzzles are very challenging and the exploration factor in this game is very entertaining.

There is no free roaming - this game is on rails.  It's more like an interactive William Gibson novel than Fallout Tactics.
But it's the writing that really stands out,  that and the the RPG setting.  After playing this, I think if i ever did pen and paper again I'd like to try Shadowrun.  It reminds me a lot of Traveller (all-time favorite pen and paper RPG) in some respects.
The music is good and fits the game well.
The art is unique - be sure to zoom in occasionally to check out the details.
In some of the levels, you will have a character jacked into the matrix and running alone,  while the rest of the team defends the access point (and the helpless cybernaut).  The game does a good job of creating a genuine feeling of urgency in these situations.
Save points:  the game saves for you.  if you screw up a level you have to play it over again.  Did not care for this.
I did not find it possible while on a mission to drop out of combat (when no enemies were visible) to move easier -  either i just never figured out how,  or it's not possible.  It should be automatic.  Did not care for this.
I found the early game fights weak & easy.  Later scenarios were more difficult.
Many reviews I have read lamented that the game is too short.  If you were expecting an open world roamer,  it is -  but if you are expecting a good novel,  it's not.   And ultimately, i think that's what this game is - a good novel.
Speaking of good novel,  i found after playing  - being curious about some of the characters -  that i had met a very famous (in the milleu) dragon,  and an immortal - both subtly and (believe it or not) *realistically* portrayed.  another example of good writing.
More side quests and missions would have been nice -  but it would have detracted from coherence.
If you like cyberpunk novels, or gritty film noir,    you'll probably like this game.   I picked it up on sale for ~7.00$  and it's Definitely worth that.

Finished Shadowrun returns last Monday.
From my blog:
Played fully on Linux with Steam (native, no Windows Emulation).
You play a character in the Shadowrun universe which is on the hunt to bring down a friend’s murderer. Time is around 2057 but due to the Awakening, the world is filled with science fiction high tech and fantasy elements alike. You have genetic modification, cyberplants and hacking warfare along with elves, orcs, dwarfes and trolls hurling magic bolts. A rich and fascinating universe.
… you have to work trough yourself. The game can be summed up by the phrase “too less”. At first there is too less background for the setting, the story. You just start off creating a character, like an orc, with cybernetic implants. Yep, no explanation to this. If you want to find out more about the Shadowrun world you have to look elsewhere but not the game.
Then there is too less RPG. Seldom you find something useful to pick up and equip. Also stats and skills are presented in a very sober way in a plain matrix. No introduction, no nothing. All at once, on page. Also you likely will spend points on attributes and skills you don’t need in future. Sorry, there is no turning back.
Then there is too less adventure. The story is nice, but you got not real decisions to make. The storyline is very linear. There are some side-quests, but guess: too less.
Then there is too less of a challenge. At the first two thirds of the game. I pimped my elf with quickness and assault rifles and the game was no real match at “normal” level. Strategic fighting is nice and … easy. Yeah, the games picks up some pace in the last third and starts to get harder. This is were the fun really sets in. But up to then it is playing a nice story …
And someone always has the idea of something missing. Something’s missing at the RPG, at the adventure, at the combat game, at the grafics, animations.
E.g. Harlequin is one of the coolest elves I’ve come along in playing games, but when he wields his sword he is animated as if someone had stiffed a broomstick right along his “back”. The in-game representation is missing the charisma and style this elf has in dialogues.
Finally the save game mechanics are just bonkers. Actually you just can save at the start of a level, better: the game (hopefully) autosaves at this stage. Making a wrong decision at the end of a level requires to replay to whole level again.
The pro: once you’ve delved into the universe the plot is great to play and the dialogs are really nice written, the combat is fun after all. It remains a nice game. Hopefully they fix this bad savegame mechanics and give more universe background information in the DLCs and patches to come.

I got 30+ (and counting) hours on this game, so why not make a review about it?
This game basically starts you off with either a random leader or you can choose your own leader. It starts you off in the ancient era (you can choose which era you wanna start off in) and you have to progress up to the future era (which I think is the last era.) As you progress, you will meet more leaders, you can also download more leaders in the workshop to play with. Anyways, these leaders will either be your allies or your enemies, or sometimes, your allies turn their backs to you, and they turn into your enemies. This game is highly addicting and you will need some good strageties to take over a city. Download the demo to learn more.
Onto the cons and pros.
Cons:
-Highly addicting; This game is seriously addicting, it will make you play for more then 10 hours.
-Multiplayer; Multiplayer is actually pretty cool to be honest, its like singleplayer, but a lot more fun (if your playing with friends, that is)
-Steam Workshop; The Steam Workshop has some pretty amazing content that you can download by clicking a simple button.
-Highly fun; This game is seriously fun, its even more fun with the atomic nukes, heheheh...
-Scenarios; The scenarios in this game is seriously challenging, but fun at the same time.
-Advantages; Either you have the advantages, or someone else does, for example, higher technology, the better.
-Gameplay; The gameplay changes throughout your gaming, like how your city changes to a modern city once you reach to the modern era.
Cons:
-Texture Glitch; I dont know if anyone else has expirenced this, but the textures glitches whenever I load into a game, where its just all grey, but then the textures pop back in.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, this game is great. With its multiplayer being seriously fun, and this game being higly addicting and fun, I seriously would recommend this game to you. This game is a beautiful art from the gaming industry, and I hope I seriously see more like this in the future. Get this game when its in sale, its seriously worth it when its on sale. One of the most unique and entertaining first-person puzzle games I've played, I rank this game right up there with Portal and Spacechem. Antichamber offers some really unusual and mind bending puzzles in a non-euclidean world: where the rules often change depending on your frame of reference. The entire pace of the game is similar to that of Portal, in that you can go at your own pace. The atmosphere is simplistic, yet vivid enough to convey the objectives in the world. The soundtrack is a peaceful ambiance that nicely complements the calm tone of the game. Antichamber also introduces new mechanics at a reasonable pace to keep the game entertaining. The “simple wisdom” posters, I feel, is also a nice touch.
Where it differs from Portal, however, is it's complete lack of a story. Rather, it's more of an “experience.” Obviously, some of the puzzles can be a bit unintuitive, but only a few I would chalk up to questionable design. Overall the puzzles are very challenging and the exploration factor in this game is very entertaining.
