I'm not someone normally prone to hyperbole, so believe me when I say that this is possibly the greatest game every made.
Yes, it's a TV show spinoff game, and previous examples to make games of TV shows have met with mixed results. This one manages to make reference to an already establish canon universe, but then transcends it, becoming something much greater as a result. The boys are playing a fantasy game with the other children in town, and you, as "new kid", join in.
It's an RPG, so in terms of play mechanics, you won't be doing anything here that you haven't already done in similar games. It is very well done though,  and it continually adds new techniques and new genres so it never becomes tedious.
The game does an amazing job of reconstructing what it was like to be 10 years old and playing with your friends. It feels like the best LARP ever.
But at the same time, it is South Park - so it is chock full of amazingly over-the-top sequences that aren't just laugh-out-loud funny, but more howl-out-loud. Your own laughter becomes part of the soundtrack of the game. Note, however, that this is South Park free of all censorship and content restrictions, so it is South Park turned up to 11. Maybe 12. It does its level best to find something offensive to everyone and it is *very* good at it. This is not a game for anyone under 18 under *any* circumstances.
My only point of complaint is that, unlike most RPGs in recent memory, there are quests and items that are time-sensitive and cannot be revisited later on in the game. If you are a 100% completionist, the game will require at least 2 playthroughs - one, as an unfettered, virgin experience, and one with a Game Guide open to warn you about upcoming limited opportunities.
If you love RPGs, are not easily offended (and can recover from it when you are), were 10 years old once, have a sense of humour, and are old enough to vote, you MUST MUST MUST play this game.

There are a lot of great ideas in this game. The turn-based combat is really fun, character development is deep and interesting, the characters are fun and memorable, the dialog is well-written, and the graphics are a nice modern take on the original game. Unfortunately, some flaws keep it from being the classic that it could have been. Combat is not as deep as I would have liked, especially compared to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The linear nature of the game limits your ability to acquire money and experience, which makes the game tougher than it should have been. The lack of a quick save feature feels like a major oversight in the land of PC games. Luckily, the developers could easily fix all of these issues, possibly in a sequel, and finally give us the perfect reboot of this classic game. I still recommend that fans of the genre or series give this game a shot, despite the flaws.

Batman: Arkham Knight PC has come a looooong way from its initial release that resulted in unconditional refunds and eventual pulling from Steam. If you're concerned yet of how it runs, allow my legacy and mediocre rig explain a bit:
-Intel E8400 3.0ghz OC to 3.6ghz
-8gb Crucial DDR2 RAM
-Radeon R7360 2GB w/ some custom OC'n
Obviously I don't run 60fps, but I manage a steady 30fps with settings all set to low, or off, and the game STILL looks amazing! The only frame rate dips I noticed were the occasional car chase of an APC general, but in particular, when the city (spoiler alert) is filled with fear gas and you have to glide across the city to grab a device to allow your car to run in the gas. (/spoiler alert)
Here recentley I've noticed freezes that last roughly 3-5 seconds (always in the car under heavy fire) but it comes back smoothly.
As far as the game: It's an excellent end to the Arkhamverse that Rocksteady so brilliantly created. The freeflow combat is taken even further with FEAR takedowns allowing multiple enemy takedowns in one attack. The ability to beat the enemy as he lie on the ground rather than always having swoop onto him and do a punch takeout that always left you vulnerable to an attack that you can't counter.
The 'tank' batmobile. Yes, the batmobile is equipped w/ a 60mm cannon and a vulcan machine gun and it transitions from driveable to tank flawlessly. Yes, towards the end, the use of the tank features feels more like a chore than a fun missle barage fight, but the ending scenes will have you forgetting all about that very quickly!
I picked this up during the Summer Sale for just $30 and it includes the season pass content and updates that have made the game funner to play in NG+ and the challenge maps.
Verdict:
You've seen my specs for hopeless, but manageable game rig. If you can run this, and you've loved the other Arkham games in the series than I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game to you.

There is a lot of good and alot of bad in this game. Let's start with the good:
I can confidently say that the gameplay mechanics are very much improved. Combat feels smoother, the upgrades are cooler and more numerous, there's all kinds of new tricks like fear takedowns, and of course the batmobile, which is awesome. In fact the biggest difference I noted was that the counter-blocks seemed to *always work*, unlike Arkham Asylum or City where they almost never did. That alone made the game much more fun to play. They also made it so you can knock enemies out easier, so that you don't have to rely on doing ground knockouts in the middle of a melee and being constantly interupted. Instead, you can punch enemies out on the ground to finish them (left click).
A few things could've been better. They still throw hordes of thugs at you, so the brawls get super repetitive just like in Asylum or City. I would've loved to see more predator encounters. With the new edition of the batmobile, there is also a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of vehicle combat, which honestly got old super fast and made me feel like I was playing CoD and not a Batman game. But it is an action game, you're primarily there to beat up enemies so, whatever.
The bad part for me was the story. There are some moments that are super contrived and awkward, as well as blatant plot holes. It's as if they threw common sense out of the window just to ramp up the drama factor a bit more. The story got so overly theatrical that honestly I was getting bored. A more down-to-earth realistic approach would've been much better IMO. Don't get me wrong, there are some really badass cutscenes and such, but they're few and far between.
The worst part of the entire game is the ending. Up until the last 5 minutes, it's great. Better than I expected or could've asked for, even. But the game comes to a close on an extremely sour note, which is the fact that *you have no idea WTF just happened*. Not only that, but you have to finish 100% of side quests, including collecting more than 200 riddler trophies in order to even see the super secret real ending in the first place, which as I've just said is a confusing mess anyway.
Oh and not to mention that most of the side quests are repetitive tasks anyway, like taking out militia towers or vehicles over and over again. Bleh.
Last but not least, the game is really glitchy as well. It randomly crashed over and over for no apparent reason that I could discern, even after I raised the fps limit to 60 (which is BS that you have to do it manually). Several side quests bugged out. Frequently I would have things not trigger correctly, such as not being allowed to push a button I need to press. Batman also got stuck quite a bit for me.
This game seriously stretches the limits of what I can consider good. I'm giving it a tentative thumbs up because it's not half-bad if you just want to beat up lots of bad guys and you like Batman. But don't expect a batman masterpiece.

Before continuing to the review, I should mention that this game is not for the kiddies, the easily offended, the faint of heart, or the faint of flatulence. HERETOFORE BE WARNED.
For hardcore residents of South Park and (thick-skinned) fans of turn-based RPGs alike, this game shows a surprising amount of love for the genre while still poking and prodding fun at every trope and cliche with its pointed stick of truth. From the moment you hit the title screen, you know they've done it right, and it only gets better from there. Character customization is on par with many of its more graphically advantaged counterparts. You can make it so that you literally feel as though YOU have entered this bizarre-yet-familiar world. Combat is fine-tuned and well-balanced (except when it doesn't want to be). Everything feels like it actually has a point and purpose to exist in the game (except when the point is to be pointless and utterly no help). Best of all, exploring the world feels like a true joy, even for a mere casual South Parker like myself. They've given us the full extent of the quiet little mountain town of South Park, and there's always something to do somewhere. Much as with its modern brethren, it is somewhat marred by monotonous questing, but even that is made enjoyable by its spot-on, hilarious characters and absolutely bonkers situations. Never before did I think I would ever... oh, but that's the fun of it. You'll just have to see it for yourself. If you enjoy South Park, or if you can tolerate it and love a good RPG, buy this and don't look back.

Visually it's great. I am not a fan of controls, though: I believe it's not really convenient to run always holding left stick (I use gamepad) and using RB instead of A to jump.
Now... Comparison with Dead Island. There is actually one main difference between the two: level of seriousness. Dying Light takes a realistic-ish approach. Whole atmosphere is made to make it feel as real as possible: zombies are few compared to Dead Island, they are a bit more sluggish, but yet more bulky, you can feel their weight when hitting them. The colors are more grey, making the world look sterile and lonely, while Dead Island was bright, reminding you, that a few hours back it was brimming with life.
You also get into zombie fighting here, when other are fighting it for a long time already. Dead Island showed the start of infection, lack of knowledge and skills. Dying  Light, shows what becomes of such fight in a few months, when it becomes a routine. It reminds me of Metro and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games in this regard.
But then there is a dissonance. Secret agent infiltrating an organization on the matter of (yet?) incomplete cure? Come on, they all need the cure, so any concerns regarding it should be discussed openly, no? And where in real world does a noob prove himself in an organization as if it's an old-school RPG?
Overall, if you prefer a post-apocalyptic zombie game with a serious look and can ignore some minor issues with the story and story-telling - you may try this. If the above does not really appeal to you, skip. I am skipping it, because I'm just not in the mood for such seriousness at the moment.

Highly recommended. This game requires a meta-strategy that is both thoughtful and hopeful, as luck is a large factor. The moment-to-moment action is definitely a micro management  RTS, from the perspective of scace captain. There is much pausing-to-issue-commands here, where unpausing sets multiple commands in motion, in an Incredible Machine sort of way. WIth perma-death giving a sense of weight to every encounter, there are some truly awesome moments. Every square you visit is a dice roll though, and a lot of the success of a campaign (which lasts about three hours) is dependent on how lucky you were when you took each fifty/fifty shot to the next section of space. It's all about learning to adapt to what the random universe gives you, and it often ends in tragedy...but yeah. there are lots of extra ships to unlock and a ridiculous array of strategies for each type of ship/variant you manage to get. play on easy first.

I had this game when I was 15 on PS2, almost completed it but due to my file on the memory card being corrupted. I couldn't complete it.
So I found GTA VC on GMG for £1.20 and the 15 yo self demanded it to be played and completed. It was hard to not look at it from a 2014 perspective, because I was playing sleeping dogs at the same which is far superior in every way.
First of all, use cheats, otherwise you will run out of money buying armour and weapons all the time.
Also, as it is an old game, there is no load option in the pause menu. You have to drive to your home to save or load a game, which can get frustrating every time you die or get arrested and want to save money by not spending it again on weapons and armour.
The graphics are average, it is an old game so we will let that pass. The physics, however, are absolutely horrible, you fall immediately off a motorcycle from the slightest of touches; using planes and helicopters are a drag, and some cars are just impossible to drive with.
OK, the game. Tommy Vercetti is your lead character, and he's come to Vice City to take it over. You do missions for various gangs, businesses, and mafia type bosses.
One tip, after a while you'll notice you don't have any missions to do, even though the story is clearly not finish. You have to buy the printworks, and 5 other businesses (Not Homes!) and complete the missions for all of them. To know if you completed the missions, the businesses will generate money for you which you can collect often. DO NOT BUY THE PORN STUDIOS! The missions for that one are absolutely dire and no fun at all. Best ones are the Kauffman cab, and I heard the Malibu club is pretty good too.
After a while you're old mafia boss comes after you and you have to kill. It's pretty basic mafia story that is clearly inspired by scarface. It's a good story and you do enjoy watching the cut scenes due to the array characters involved.
GTA VC is still for me the best GTA game. The size of the  map was perfect and the story was pretty decent1The radio shows are also perfect, playing the best music that represents the 80s feel of the game.  Small things like physics of vehicals and graphics are a negative, but they won't be too much of a hassle. I recommend playing with a mouse just so you can shoot better. If you want to use a controller, I suggest you look online to find forums that help you with that as this GTA VC doesn't support controllers very well.
Overall, I'll give this a 7/10

As someone whos played nearly 1900 hours in KF1 now and runs a KF1 community (or clan, whatever wording you want to use), and also was a veteran of the UT2004 mod versions, I felt the need to leave a review for the game that just singlehandedly ruins the entire KF experience in exchange for lots of your hard earned cash.
First off, the developer's ethics are terrbile with this game. First they release it as early access, and claim it will last six months. That was well over a year and a half ago now. The first major update they push out, they incorporate microtransactions (Yes, in an EARLY ACCESS game). They lied about how the difficulties will work, "The zeds will not increase in health but instead have different abilities". Guess what, they had more health.
Speaking of zed health, last I played they incorporated "damage resistance". It ruined the game right there. If a stalker needs 4 shotgun shots to be put down, then you are doing something wrong. They overcomplicated the game, which took away from the experience that made KF1 so great. KF1 was simple, thus more fun.
The inclusion of sprint also makes the game really easy. Its possible to outrun almost everything now. The one thing I will give credit to it is that the game encourages kiting (running around the map) instead of just camping. I always love kiting, and it was very difficult in KF1. However, in KF2, the kiting is just way too easy.
Another thing that was very annoying was that zeds could throw you. So if a gorefast or crawler hits you, you get pushed. This is really annoying when there's a lot of zeds around you, and it also makes no sense. But no worries, just heal  yourself and sprint away, you'll be just fine.
Lastly, lets talk about content... So before Early Access the devs promised 10 perks, well they just announced that the 10th perk is no more. They are failing to deliver on promised content, and that is just wrong. The other thing is maps. They are literally making almost no maps, but instead incorporating PLAYER CREATED maps into the game. So not only did people have to pay for this horrible Early Access experience ahead of time, but they also had to help FINISH the game? And the other thing, each perk only has 4 guns for the most part. So theres no multiple ways to play a perk when its OBVIOUS you just have to work your way to an AA12, Scar, or Microwave gun. I really would like to know what the dev team is ACTUALLY doing in all this time. Oh wait, thats right, they are out spending all the money that they are making off of the weapon skins and keys. No need to finish a game when its brining you money, right?
Honestly, as a KF veteran, this game is completely against what KF should be, simple and fun. Instead we have to complicate things and be lied to by the devs. I really wish I could get a refund on this, because I'm boycotting it and refuse to play it, and I hate the fact that I had actually supported the devs by buying it.
KF1 is just fine, plenty of content, and none of the zeds have a ridiculous amount of "damage resistance". Feel free to take a look at my KF1 hours versus how many hours I spent in this, that will tell you exactly where I stand on this matter. If you want to play Killing Floor and play it right, wait for KF1 to come on sale for $5 (very common) and get that instead. Just trust me on that.
PS: I will not be surprised if this review gets massively downvoted (since the people who play this game worship the devs) and I end up getting banned from the game (rumors have been going around that the devs are banning people who have negative things to say about the game, I will definitely report back here if I do end up getting banned for this review).

It's very Firaxis; pared down to just the decisions which are "interesting". I missed the original, but this one never really opens up all that far---certainly not compared to usual replay-heavy games like the Civs, or management-y/sim types---you're constantly on the hook of the next scripted plot event, and the tutorial takes a frankly obnoxiously long time to take the handcuffs off. But when it lets you play the battles yourself, it's a solid turn-based tactical shooter, with a solid sense of soldier progression.

Frustrating? Yes, at times, but the rewards of playing are always there.
Difficult? Yes, at times, but it becomes a question of, "what can I do better next time."
Items? Each unique, different item, with their own little charms, backstories and effects, giving a nice depth to the game.
Artifacts? Difficult to earn, each one providing a deeper level of play, often a double-edge sword perk, but some are just downright cruel.
9 Artifact Run? "ded" -Risk of Rain
10 Artifact Run? "rekt" -Risk of Rain
Possible to do a run in under 40 minutes? Sure. You'll probably farm some gold on each level, so you can access all the shrines, chests and other available objects, but otherwise, should be beaten in under 90 minutes per average game.
The game will taunt you.
The game will laugh at your misery.
But the game is rewarding, there is a small learning curve, but it's the difficulty curve that is your greatest challenge.
Overall 9.5/10; minor bugs and stuff that doesn't really matter, it's a really good game.
Soundtrack 9/10; extremely fitting for the game, decent playlist for listening to while not playing the game.
*Some users have reported some difficulties with Multiplayer, but isn't that normal with anything online?

Super Hexagon can be a lesson to people who believe they can never do something. If you take the game and its "Easy" difficult, which is aptly named 'hard' It may seem difficult but if you keep trying and building up your memory and reaction time, you can achieve it easily. After you play for as long as I did the patterns start to merge together and you subconciously know what is going to happen, you predict the random generation.
As you feel your way through the first three levels you start to learn that the game has a few tricks that you won't expect your first hour or three, but as the advisor speaks its single words to you "Line" "Triangle" Square" "Pentagon" "Hexagon" you feel empowered after each of these dauntful yet encouraging quotes. And once you begin to get higher scores like mine on the 'Hard' difficulty of 5+ minutes, everytime you reach a new minute you here "Awesome" like you have finally accomplished a goal and milestone. But as the adventure continues to the final levels, you start to feel a shadow looking down on you as you reach an impassable barrier on your quest to 60 seconds.
With every minute passing you feel more and more frustrated by the lack of progress until you finally feel your way through the patterns that you haven't yet seen, you being to make the progress you wanted and are on top of the world, then at 50+ seconds the game pulls a trick and you are back to zero. The cycle of time starts again and you are stuck there. And once you beat the game the milestones only continue to grow, forever and eventually into 5, 10, 15 minutes of Hexagon.
This is the Super Hexagon way, a challenge and a frustration, but also a accomplishing task. The six-sided figure will always bring light in a rough day if you are determined to take the time to sate its thirst for a challenger.

Before continuing to the review, I should mention that this game is not for the kiddies, the easily offended, the faint of heart, or the faint of flatulence. HERETOFORE BE WARNED.
For hardcore residents of South Park and (thick-skinned) fans of turn-based RPGs alike, this game shows a surprising amount of love for the genre while still poking and prodding fun at every trope and cliche with its pointed stick of truth. From the moment you hit the title screen, you know they've done it right, and it only gets better from there. Character customization is on par with many of its more graphically advantaged counterparts. You can make it so that you literally feel as though YOU have entered this bizarre-yet-familiar world. Combat is fine-tuned and well-balanced (except when it doesn't want to be). Everything feels like it actually has a point and purpose to exist in the game (except when the point is to be pointless and utterly no help). Best of all, exploring the world feels like a true joy, even for a mere casual South Parker like myself. They've given us the full extent of the quiet little mountain town of South Park, and there's always something to do somewhere. Much as with its modern brethren, it is somewhat marred by monotonous questing, but even that is made enjoyable by its spot-on, hilarious characters and absolutely bonkers situations. Never before did I think I would ever... oh, but that's the fun of it. You'll just have to see it for yourself. If you enjoy South Park, or if you can tolerate it and love a good RPG, buy this and don't look back.

In a nutshell:
Overall,  first impressions 6 hours in are Techland have outdone themselves and I can't wait for the performance issues to be fixed so this becomes a true GOTY contender.
In-depth:
Rig:
Gigabyte GTX 660 2GB OC Edition
i7 2600k 3.4ghz (Not OC'd)
8GB DDR3 RAM
2TB Seagate HDD
This combo runs the game a bit worse then it should in all honesty, currently on all medium settings with HBAO/SSAO turned off, everything else on. I wasn't expecting miracles with this aging setup but I was expecting a bit better when I can almost max Shogun 2 and Metro with better FPS for example.
I get quite a few frame drops and the game does feel a bit choppier then I would of liked on these settings, doesn't detract from the fun of the game though. Even though I was hoping to get atleast Texture quality to high the game still looks absolutely amazing at medium. BIG props to the environmental artists or whatever you would call them, as the game is atmospheric as all hell and every nook and cranny of the city oozes of detail and little untold stories. You'll see destroyed quarantine zones, highways full of abandoned cars, rotting corpses and destruction and huge vistas of the flaming city. It's all very immersive and draws you in. I have spent probably an hour of my playtime just soaking in the environment.
Story is good so far, enough to feel me compelled to go on in finishing it and doing the main quest to see what happens, so better then Dead Island's. Combat is much better then Dead Island's without those damn immersion breaking health bars, Instead you rely on the much improved visual damage system to see how close a zombie is to death. Weapons feel satisfying as ever and very meaty.
I'd give it an 8/10 as it is now, maybe buy on discount if you're a patient scrooge but the current price wont leave you feeling shortchanged.

This review might ruffle a lot of feathers, bashing a classic as such, here goes anyway. I played the original way back in the day when it first came out.  Decades ago it was, and still sits in my mind as the best a FPS could get.  For some reason, it took me about 15 years to play Hal life 2, after picking it up on sale.  While I enjoyed parts of it, overall this seemed like an overly short, overly gimmicky and overly half-baked game.  Let me elaborate...
Half life 2 definitely has its positive points, the gravity gun being chief among them.  It is revolutionary, and I enjoyed using it very much. Second, the puzzles, while not too taxing, were very enjoyable and helped pace the game.  Thirdly, when the game is on, these amps go to 11 with some crazy firefights, satisfying weapons and good scripted events.  The first time you down a strider with your rpg, you'll want to renact the victory kiss photo with anyone within arms reach.
However, I have a lot of bones to pick with HL2.  For starters, it only took me about 13 hours to finish, and the slow story had just started to get interesting when the game ends without a satisfactory conclusion.  It felt too short I wanted more, but not in the good way.  Second, the driving levels (2 of them) seemed to drag on forever, and they didn't have enough interesting things to keep them exciting. Third, your allies  have such limited screen time with you that it's hard to care about them.  I was very meh when things happened to the main characters because the game didn't build up any attachment to them.  Fourth, the game feels very gimmicky.  For example, one level you get to command giant bugs, which is cool, but it only lasts a short while.  Next, you get to drive a jeep, but it only last a short while. Next, you get to fight with some buddies, but it only lasts a short time.  Then, to my great frustration, the game strips you of all your weapons in the final level, forcing you to use the gravity gun.  Again, it feels like a gimmick, and it makes the final part of the game boring.  You spend the whole game building up an arsenal of weapons and learning how to use them only to have them taken from you when you need them most.  Not to mention the fact that you've got a super gravity gun which basically makes you invincible. Boring... Lastly, large portions of the game lets you fight alongside rebel comrades.  You'd think it would be cool, but they stick to you like glue, and thus always get in your way, be it causing endless frustration by blocking your dodging of enemy fire, or reducing you to a crawl as you all shuffle through thin corridors.  These are design flaws I wouldn’t have expected from the team that made the first game.
Overall, despite my pedantic whining, I did have a nice time playing through this. That said, I expected a much, MUCH better game than this.  There are so many cool things, like the physics and the gravity gun, but so many school boy errors at the same time.  History seems to have already deified Half Life 2, and who am I to challenge that? Call me an iconoclast, but it could have and should have been a lot better, and Bioshock wipes the floor with this.
This is a game for people who enjoy having no clue what the ♥♥♥♥ they're doing, and that's precisely why it's brilliant.

Incredible game fluidity. Intuitive user interface. Impressionable graphics. XCOM: Enemy Unknown pulls all the right stops in all the right places, successfully streamlining and vastly improving upon the old-school retro XCOM which was one of the hallmarks of the turn-based genre.
XCOM: EU has simple core gameplay divided between base management and combat missions. Base management is very fluid and simple to understand but requires careful manipulation of resources to reach the overarching goal. Combat is incredible responsive, and punishing in the nature which one wrong miscalculation could end up extremely costly. Both are done to exquisite impeccability in graphics, interface, and core design.
The elephant in the room is, of course, how well it stacks up against its predecessor. Yes, it's simplified in a sense. Yes, some of the micromanagement has been taken out to elucidate the game for more casual audiences. But, in a general sense, the game retains most of its strategic depth. Tactical deployment still requires careful maneuvering and calculation of dispositions. Base and resource management still play a large role in grand strategy.
P.S. Definitely check out the iOS equivalent.

Super Hexagon can be a lesson to people who believe they can never do something. If you take the game and its "Easy" difficult, which is aptly named 'hard' It may seem difficult but if you keep trying and building up your memory and reaction time, you can achieve it easily. After you play for as long as I did the patterns start to merge together and you subconciously know what is going to happen, you predict the random generation.
As you feel your way through the first three levels you start to learn that the game has a few tricks that you won't expect your first hour or three, but as the advisor speaks its single words to you "Line" "Triangle" Square" "Pentagon" "Hexagon" you feel empowered after each of these dauntful yet encouraging quotes. And once you begin to get higher scores like mine on the 'Hard' difficulty of 5+ minutes, everytime you reach a new minute you here "Awesome" like you have finally accomplished a goal and milestone. But as the adventure continues to the final levels, you start to feel a shadow looking down on you as you reach an impassable barrier on your quest to 60 seconds.
With every minute passing you feel more and more frustrated by the lack of progress until you finally feel your way through the patterns that you haven't yet seen, you being to make the progress you wanted and are on top of the world, then at 50+ seconds the game pulls a trick and you are back to zero. The cycle of time starts again and you are stuck there. And once you beat the game the milestones only continue to grow, forever and eventually into 5, 10, 15 minutes of Hexagon.
This is the Super Hexagon way, a challenge and a frustration, but also a accomplishing task. The six-sided figure will always bring light in a rough day if you are determined to take the time to sate its thirst for a challenger.

Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002. It was set in 1986 in Vice City (Fictional name for Miami Beach, Florida, i guess it's not hard to tell). A game that is still one of the greatest games of this era, in 2003 everyone was crazy about it. You can judge if this is a masterpiece or not by just looking at it's popularity even nowadays, how many games that are 11 years old are still played today? Not many.
The atmosphere you find in this game is perfect, your ears are delighted with great tracks from: Michael Jackson (Never liked him, but he had some great tracks), Megadeth, Anthrax, Cutting Crew, The Whispers, The Outfield, Bryan Adams, Iron Maiden, Loverboy, Slayer, Judas Priest, even Frankie goes to Hollywood, and the list goes on more of course.
The graphics were absolutely amazing at the time of release. Gameplay was, and still is great, the mechanics are friendly. You ave a variety of weapons to choose from when it comes to slaughtering random people on the street, including hookers and old ladies.
The cars you find in this game, are mostly sport ones, you also can find scooters and motorbikes.

As for the technical stuff about this game. It works on Windows 8.1 flawlessly, without any compatibility options set, or any patch or modification. It recognizes new resolutions (1440x900 user here).
A perfect game that gave me hundreds hours of fun many years ago.

Buy this game.  Play it at night, alone.
The first half of this review is a defensive measure against all of it's haters and critics here on Steam.
Notice how all the negative reviews have either or both of two complaints: 1) the game doesn't run well, or 2) the controls suck because the port sucks. These people never thought to realize that maybe, just MAYBE, it's not the game that doesn't run well but it's their PC that doesn't run the game well. NEWSFLASH: If your PC blows or is outdated then you have no room to complain when a game any more demanding than Minesweeper runs poorly. There, I said it. Next up, the controls do suffer a bit at first but alas, we are humans, and we overcome and adapt to a new control scheme and feel for new games. Or at least some of us. Seriously, within an hour the controls felt fluid and fine. "Unplayable" they said. Seriously guys? Every game has a different feel, so why are you complaining about the mouse acceleration. Some people say it takes several seconds to turn around 180 degrees... Maybe turn your sensitivity up higher than 1%? I can turn around and have my gun drawn in less than half a second. These same people probably don't have the other half of their brain to even appreciate that slightly clunky controls actually makes this game better. Allow me to elaborate: You're Isaac Clarke, a man looking for his woman, stuck in a massive planet cracker starship infested and overrun with an unspeakable danger. You're scared. You're outgunned. Outnumbered. MAYBE, JUST MAYBE, having a "slow" response time and realistic movements makes the game feel better because it adds to the desperation and hopelessness of the atmosphere of the game. Not being able to instantly whip around or aim perfect head shots in 0.0065 seconds makes the game scarier. It really does. It takes away your control. It makes you feel like you are in just as much control of your situation as Isaac is, which isn't much. Having to take an extra half second to gain your bearings and wait for your body's momentum to stop in order to aim at your targets neck actually makes the game feel real and much more human. You feel vulnerable, and THAT is exactly why the controls and the feel of them make the game FEEL scarier.
With that said, this game is a masterpiece. I loved it. It mixed many different aspects of good storytelling, music, environment, horror, action, violence, and character development and put it into a unique universe. A hostile, bloody, dark universe full of cults and aliens. It kept me wanting to uncover more and more of why exactly things were happening and other character's motives. I was LEGITIMATELY scared at times in the game, namely in the beginning when I still had no clue the health, tactics, and potential that my enemies had. Everything was scary and mysterious. I kept to the wall and checked every corner with my plasma cutter drawn. Most of the scares are jump scares. But other times hearing whispers coming from the vents and the absolutely insanely eerie music made me want to take a break and come back when it was daylight. Eventually though I became more bold as I realized my enemies weak spots, becoming terrified for a moment upon seeing a new enemy type and trying to figure out how to avoid or kill it. It kept me on the edge of my seat the entire time, never growing bored of it throughout it's about 12 hour campaign.
PROS:
-The music. Oh the music. Terrifying.
-Sound effects were spot-on. Pipes clanked as I passed a vent, making me check them again. And again.
-Ragdoll physics, though exaggerated, made ripping things to shreds so satisfying.
-The graphics, for a 2008 (I believe?) title, were EPIC.
-Details like writing, stains, blood, rust, etc... made the atmosphere creepy, dirty, and overall immersive. No corner-cutting here. I found an in-game alphabet decoder for alien writing, and while I've yet to see if it works, the effort behind each and every room is amazing.
-Enemy types were fairly numerous. Some of them probably took a nightmare to think up. Fetus octopus zombies? No thanks.
-Voice acting was phenomenal.
-The HUD, or lack of, added the the feel of the game that I'm sure the developers wanted. When something did pop on screen, like a video call or map, it was never paused. I got attacked while upgrading my weapon at a weapon station. You are never safe unless you are saving or fully paused. The HUD was for Isaac, not me. We watch Isaac take the video call or look at his map, and there's something cool about that.
-Movement, as I said before, is slow and clunky but it adds to the game's scary theme. You are supposed to be scared running, not a badass Duke Nukem liberator. Act like it.
-Weapon variety was good too, although after trying a few, I stuck with the first mining tool, the plasma cutter. Upgrade that fully and it's the best gun in my opinion. I didn't even choose to unlock the later ones.
They seemed to pricey to fill up with ammo.
-Awesome story and a really spooky ending, even to the very last frame.
-Dead Space gave me a very different experience than any other game I've ever tried. It had a story, a twist, and characters that I won't soon forget.
CONS:
-They say in life, you either have money, time, or energy. As a child, you have time and energy, but no money. As a middle aged man, you have money and energy, but no time. As an elder, you have money and time, but no energy. Well... in Dead Space, it's very similar, except instead of time, money, and energy, it's health, ammunition, and credits. Except you only have one of each at any given time. I was CONSTANTLY either out of ammo and no credits to buy more but with full health. Or I had tons of ammo but no health or credits to get upgrades. I was always lacking one or two major requirements for a gunfight or boss battle. If you run out of ammo in a boss battle, there's nothing to do but die and backtrack and look for a couple more rounds of ammo. Or if you have no health but are forced to go to a boss battle anyways. Is it enough this time? Probably not. I get it, having sparse ammo makes the game feel scarier because you have to choose when and where to shoot instead of ripping people to shreds and having a lead finger on the trigger. But it really killed some parts of the game where you NEED lots of ammo and enemies just aren't dropping it, crates just don't contain it, and I don't have money for it. Dilemma: Spend all of my hard-earned credits on a new suit and be bankrupt or spend it all on enough ammo to get to the next chapter? The struggle is real gentlemen.
-Character development on Isaac could've been better. He never spoke a single time. Is that good or bad? I felt like it's a bad thing because with his suit he seemed like a robot and it was hard to sympathize with him.
-Puzzles got repetitive at times and seemed too easy. Although the meteor-radio transmitter puzzle stumped me for an hour. That one was rough for me because I was expecting it to be easy and kept looking past the obvious.
-No way to re-read text logs. WHY? I love immersing myself into the story and being able to do that would have been so cool. I guess with video logs you could but still... Having them to re-read directions or to understand the story would have been welcome.
-The tasks got repetitive. "ISAAC! The ship's parts are working again. I'll stay here where I'm safe and you go get 20 parts scattered across the ship with dozens of cannibal necromorph creatures that desperately want to chop your legs and face off in order to restore power to the ship's components so that we can repeat it all over again in the next chapter." I guess you have to go with this formula but it still got a little old in the way the tasks were presented.
Overall this game rocked. It is not perfect, but it's shortcomings are highly outweighed by it's strongsuits. Definitely gave me chills and made me jump a few times. For that alone, I give it 9/10.

Rig:

This combo runs the game a bit worse then it should in all honesty, currently on all medium settings with HBAO/SSAO turned off, everything else on. BIG props to the environmental artists or whatever you would call them, as the game is atmospheric as all hell and every nook and cranny of the city oozes of detail and little untold stories. I'd give it an 8/10 as it is now, maybe buy on discount if you're a patient scrooge but the current price wont leave you feeling shortchanged.

Dead Space is a 3rd Person, Survival Horror game unlike any other I have previously experienced. In many other horror genres I'd be able to call all the pop-up scares and gruesome mishaps...but not dead space. You can still see some coming, don't get me wrong, but there will be more times in which you just feel like screaming "NOPE NOPE NOPE NOPE NOPE" the entire time something comes flying out to kill you when you are not looking.
In Dead Space, you play as the engineer known as Isaac Clarke who boards a deep space mining vessel to try to fix it up. However, just looking at the title, things do not go according to plan, and soon Isaac and his two other companions are having to fight for their lives aboard a vessel of the living dead. These creatures are not your normal run-of-the-mill zombies...they come in a variety of deadly shapes and sizes, all wanting your flesh. Oh, and when I say you and your two companions must fight, I mean YOU (Isaac) must fight; they provide you with objectives to the next area where things that want to kill you in the most gruesome ways imaginable reside.
Dead Space is a disturbing, gore-filled game that mainly the mature should purchase and play. It possesses an enthralling and suspenseful story as you must try to put together all the pieces to a nightmare brought to life. I cannot wait to play Dead Space 2 now as a result, and I highly recommend purchasing this game if you are up for a good scare every now and then. I must say that the game probably lacks some replay value (unless you play on the higher difficulty for the challenge). Not because it is a bad game by any means, but because the "scares" are never quite as good as your first runthrough of a horror game, especially when enemies have set spawn points and are not randomly placed. That being said, Dead Space constantly introduces new enemies, various weapons, upgrades, and fast-paced life-or-death scenarios throughout the entire gameplay that will keep you wide awake with a twitchy trigger finger.
I'd easily give this game a solid 9 out of 10. So pick it up in the steam sales the next time you are up for experiencing something new or would just like a good scare. Oh, and I do hope you enjoy your stay aboard the USG Ishimura if you do:

Not many horror games use space as the backdrop and the few that do, usually do so with raving success. Dead Space is part of that. It's terrifying, but like any scary game, the longer you play it, the more desensitized to the fear you get. That and paired with the fact that you eventually (should you choose to) upgrade your weapons to a high degree usually means the monsters that scare you die in embarassing fashion.
The method is in which this game does go out to scare you is cheap as well. There are a lot of jump scares and set pieces. Any time you enter a large enough room, you know there will be an ambush. Eventually, you can start predicting when the scares happen. Monsters come out through vents and the predictable blind corner will usually have one waiting for you. Vents are scattered throughout the ship you're stranded on, so when you instinctively feel like an ambush is going to happen, it's easy to set yourself up and defend the waves.
Good game overall. Scary games of this type should be shorter though because you can feel that the developers themselves know that you're no longer scared so what they'll do with ambushes is just increase the waves, turning what's supposed to be scary into a full blown shoot out with paced rumbles that can sometimes last longer than you have patience for.
The Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star rendition was sp00ky though.

Every square you visit is a dice roll though, and a lot of the success of a campaign (which lasts about three hours) is dependent on how lucky you were when you took each fifty/fifty shot to the next section of space. Port Doom 3 to the consoles, then port it back to PC with non-rebindable controls and a laggy mouse, and the result is Dead Space. The game starts out in the survival horror vein, but soon suffers an identity crisis, locking the player in arena-like spaces with dozens of fast moving monsters attacking at once, which is dubious considering that the character is as agile as a pregnant potato and takes up at least a third of the screen. Choosing a third-person perspective for a game with a silent protagonist is another strange design decision that removes any sense of immersion, especially when the character just stands over a dying woman like a manikin with no trace of emotion. Add highly repetitive and mostly predictable gameplay involving completing two to three objectives per level, some of which are recycled later on, and there is no surprise that Doom 3 ends up a far superior game, with near identical visuals and storyline, but no artificial handicaps, better immersion, action, and horror. It's a shame, because Dead Space has a unique dismemberment system and would have made a great survival horror game.

An excellent puzzle game that uses non-euclidean geometry and a minimalist art direction to form what is probably the best puzzle game I've ever played, next to Portal.
I never really found myself getting stuck or annoyed at a puzzle as there's always something else to be explored and a lot of the time, puzzles can be solved be just stopping for a moment, taking a step back and questioning things more thoroughly.
The game also feels very personal, the tiles that are used to communicate to the player seem to tell part of the designer's life story as well as give small pieces of advice which serve to give subtle hints to some of the puzzles. Secret rooms in the game also feature pieces of concept art and even museum like sections that showcase previous versions of the block gun you use, giving a greater appreciation of how much work was involved to create something like this.
All this being said, it's still a short game with not a lot of re-playability value due to the nature of its design, so I'd say it's best to pick this up at a discounted price.

I have a lot of respect to guys who worked on the cool artworks of the game. As a RPG fan, I really wanted to like Shadowrun Returns, but the game kept disappointing me on so many levels and I constantly failed to find RPG features that make me love RPG games.
The story is very weak. Just compare the plot with Fallout series, the story of Chosen One, or Planescape Torment, the story of nameless one who wakes up in a mortuary one day and tries to find his forgotten past. Imagine Baldur's Gate's story, Candlekeep attack, Gorion's death, and the hunt for Saverok. Not to mention Kotor. This story doesn't give you any excitement or mystery in the storyline, and I constantly felt like the whole thing was written in a few days after the artwork was designed, although I am sure it is not true.
There is no freedom of open world environment. The game dictates where we should go, what we should do to complete a quest. There are no random encounters, locations or rare items. The game doesn't reward you when you succesfully accomplish a mission besides karma points.There are certain areas where you can buy your supplies, have information on your investigations and you can't miss them. There is no puzzle that players can possibly struggle with.
We are very limited with NPC options as well. Instead of choosing among several NPCs who have different POVs on matters, we have to choose no-name mercenaries for each battle. Think about Might and Magic series, Baldur's Gate, KOTOR, or Fallout and imagine how NPC choices were changing the gameplay, and how each character had different point of views on your actions.
If Shadowrun Returns hadn't described itself as an RPG game, I wouldn't write any of this, but I think this game does not even  deserve to be in the same category with all of the other RPG games. I would even go further and say that even GTA IV, or Diablo is more RPG than Shadowrun Returns because of all the reasons explained above. I think the game tried to accomplish a lot and failed miserably because of this, and I hope they won't make the same mistakes in the future titles.

This review might ruffle a lot of feathers, bashing a classic as such, here goes anyway. I played the original way back in the day when it first came out.  Decades ago it was, and still sits in my mind as the best a FPS could get.  For some reason, it took me about 15 years to play Hal life 2, after picking it up on sale.  While I enjoyed parts of it, overall this seemed like an overly short, overly gimmicky and overly half-baked game.  Let me elaborate...
Half life 2 definitely has its positive points, the gravity gun being chief among them.  It is revolutionary, and I enjoyed using it very much. Second, the puzzles, while not too taxing, were very enjoyable and helped pace the game.  Thirdly, when the game is on, these amps go to 11 with some crazy firefights, satisfying weapons and good scripted events.  The first time you down a strider with your rpg, you'll want to renact the victory kiss photo with anyone within arms reach.
However, I have a lot of bones to pick with HL2.  For starters, it only took me about 13 hours to finish, and the slow story had just started to get interesting when the game ends without a satisfactory conclusion.  It felt too short I wanted more, but not in the good way.  Second, the driving levels (2 of them) seemed to drag on forever, and they didn't have enough interesting things to keep them exciting. Third, your allies  have such limited screen time with you that it's hard to care about them.  I was very meh when things happened to the main characters because the game didn't build up any attachment to them.  Fourth, the game feels very gimmicky.  For example, one level you get to command giant bugs, which is cool, but it only lasts a short while.  Next, you get to drive a jeep, but it only last a short while. Next, you get to fight with some buddies, but it only lasts a short time.  Then, to my great frustration, the game strips you of all your weapons in the final level, forcing you to use the gravity gun.  Again, it feels like a gimmick, and it makes the final part of the game boring.  You spend the whole game building up an arsenal of weapons and learning how to use them only to have them taken from you when you need them most.  Not to mention the fact that you've got a super gravity gun which basically makes you invincible. Boring... Lastly, large portions of the game lets you fight alongside rebel comrades.  You'd think it would be cool, but they stick to you like glue, and thus always get in your way, be it causing endless frustration by blocking your dodging of enemy fire, or reducing you to a crawl as you all shuffle through thin corridors.  These are design flaws I wouldn’t have expected from the team that made the first game.
Overall, despite my pedantic whining, I did have a nice time playing through this. That said, I expected a much, MUCH better game than this.  There are so many cool things, like the physics and the gravity gun, but so many school boy errors at the same time.  History seems to have already deified Half Life 2, and who am I to challenge that? Call me an iconoclast, but it could have and should have been a lot better, and Bioshock wipes the floor with this.

I managed to pick this up on a steam sale a while back. My friend suggested I just pirate it because the game wouldn't be worth 15 euro. How wrong he was! I've just come off finishing this entire game in one sitting, and the reason for that is because the game is that good.
The game comes with one campaign which is called 'dead man's switch'. This is the campaign the developpers made and is a very good showcase of what you can do in Shadowrun returns. The story sucks you in and the entire realistic atmosphere gives off a gritty blade runner feeling. You actually feel the grime that exists in the world and the parallels to our world are scarily frequent.
The gameplay itself is a blast, you play the game using a self constructed avatar which you assign a 'class'. Which can be broken down into a fighter, monk, mage, summoner, hacker and trapper. The game then divides the points into the needed categories and from there you are free to specialise your character how you see fit. This gives you an insane amount of customisation as far as your character is concerned. Besides yourself you can hire help to go along on the runs (missions), you can preview their stats and items before picking them and during the mission you are free to control them as you see fit.
The game also contains a lot of dialogue which helps to flesh out the living and breathing world. You sometimes get choices which you feel will have some impact later on along the line, sadly you generally don't see any effect from your choices besides alternate ways of attack something or something being worth more or being more expensive.
I suggest anyone to atleast give shadowrun a try, the game is really fun, able to pull you into it's world and the challenge it provides is just right in my opinion. Despite in the last mission the two 'superior' characters being weaker then my own dwarf.

Awesome game for fans of the show. Few things you should keep in mind:
The game is short, easily beatable in 10 hours, and a few hours of side quests as well. It is a turn based RPG, very similar to Paper Mario, but much simpler. There's only one 'buddy' (side kick) at a time allowed, although several main characters can be used. You can use melee, mage, ranged weapons, and there are usable items as well. Having played all of the Paper Marios, it felt pretty similar but also unique since its based on South Park and feels like a real episode of the show.
Overall, I enjoyed the game. There are very few things wrong with the game, mostly due to it being an obvious console port (so controls are not modifiable, unless you mod the game). It is clear Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote the main story line, as it feels like the Black Friday episodes they did back in November 2013.

Excellent action-horror game.
In the search for my 'horror' cravings I came upon Dead Space, a third person horror game created by EA. Boy was I satisfied...
The story starts off with you (Issac Clark) an engineer that is part of a crew sent to respond to a distress beacon sent by a ship that was long thought to have been missing. One of the missing survivors from the ship is your girlfriend. Things aren't as they seem on the ship, as you get attacked by alien life forms called 'necromorphs' and have to work with the survivors to escape the ship. The story is good and has a few twists.
The sound is great. You can hear the clanging of metal, sounds of engines and necromorph movement which adds to the tense atmosphere. The voice acting is good as well from the suporting characters who are great at setting the scene.
Gameplay involves third-person combat. You get a variety of weapons which you can buy or find as you play. Weapons include the plasma cutter, shotgun, pulse rifle etc. You can upgrade weapons by finding upgrade nodes. The upgrade nodes are rare so you need to use them cautiously, preferably only fully upgrading one or two weapons. You can also upgrade your armor to increase health, carry more weapons as well as improve oxygen levels for space exploration. The game is seperated into chapters, with each chapter taking part in a different area of the ship. You move slowly (similar to Resident evil 4), but you can also sprint for a duration. Also there is no hud in the game, instead you have a healthbar which is shown at the back of your suit. Finally, opening your inventory doesn't pause the game, so you can still be attacked. Aside from combat you may have to do some puzzles where you have to move items around.
Your enemies are necromorphs. These horryfying monsters need to be de-limbed in order to take them down quickly. They move exceptionally fast and some have range attacks as well. One of my favourite moments was being surrounded by necromorphs and pumping dozens of pulse rifle rounds into them, it literally felt like I was one of the marines in 'Aliens'.
The graphics hold exceptionally well for today's standards. The lighting is dark and gritty, which helps to make the player feel tensed up as they traverse the ship.
One of the problems I have with this game are the mouse controls. I suffer major mouse lag when turning my character around and aiming my guns, even after maxing out mouse sensitivity. This makes it difficult to aim for limbs on the enmey hence, making combat unecessarily complicated and difficult.
I highly recommend this game to fans of action-horror games.

- IMPACT WHEN FALLING. This was a huge disappointment for me, and always will be until they polish it up. When jumping from a high height and landing on something that absorbs your impact (garbage, bodies, cars, etc.), you literally land flat on your feet, and it looks terrible. When I jump from a 5-story roof into a dumpster, I expect my character's legs to bend to absorb impact, or even roll if the fall is high enough. Perfect example of this is FarCry 4, they got the fall impact down perfectly. Fix this, and the game is almost perfect.
- Depth of Field. The DoF is a bit off, mainly when kicking. When you are directly facing a wall and kick it, your leg extends out fully, making it look kind of silly.

So I liked all the Arkham games, including this one.
In terms of gameplay, this is not a great departure from the last three games. You are Batman and you alternate between jumping from rooftop to rooftop beating up random dudes and then having fisticuffs with crowds of jerks. Like Arkham City and Origins, it's still an open world sandbox game wherein Batman fights to protect a city that seems to be populated exclusively with dudes who are lining up to rob a bank or knock over a jewelry store. Seriously, besides one building of cops, a couple of firefighters and Batman's assorted sidekicks, the entire city is just a pack of dip♥♥♥♥♥. It makes you sort of wonder why saving it is even worth it in the first place.
Anyhow, that aside, the main innovation is you have the Batmobile, which is a tank thingie that's fun enough to use. Nothing groundbreaking, but it's not like the Batmobile segments aren't fun or whatnot.
The story meanwhile is pretty strong, although due to the comic book origins of the series it pulls a lot of punches. I think this is supposed to be the last of the Arkham games, so you'd think that the creators would be more willing to kill characters. I mean, it's not like if you kill them in this game they're deleted from the comic book forever guys. But in spite of that, there are some incredibly good scenes and I was very interested from start to finish. Some plot twists are  presented a bit too obviously (the identity of the Arkham Knight is painfully obvious for about three hours), but most of it  still comes together pretty solidly.
Until you get to the ending.
Or well, I should say "Until you see what the ending involves". Because in order to actually see what happens at the end you've got to collect every single mother♥♥♥♥ing Riddler trophy. All 250 or so of them.
I don't understand Rocksteady's obsession with those ♥♥♥♥ing things. Is it just a petulant idea that if you go through all this trouble making a big sandbox city that you ought to put♥♥♥♥♥♥around to make sure the player goes around appreciating all of it? Ugh.
I ended up watching the ending on Youtube. It was alright. But the fact that the game locked it behind tedious collection quests is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Still, beyond that it's a good game. I'll probably play some of the DLC.

Excellent action-horror game.
In the search for my 'horror' cravings I came upon Dead Space, a third person horror game created by EA. Boy was I satisfied...
The story starts off with you (Issac Clark) an engineer that is part of a crew sent to respond to a distress beacon sent by a ship that was long thought to have been missing. One of the missing survivors from the ship is your girlfriend. Things aren't as they seem on the ship, as you get attacked by alien life forms called 'necromorphs' and have to work with the survivors to escape the ship. The story is good and has a few twists.
The sound is great. You can hear the clanging of metal, sounds of engines and necromorph movement which adds to the tense atmosphere. The voice acting is good as well from the suporting characters who are great at setting the scene.
Gameplay involves third-person combat. You get a variety of weapons which you can buy or find as you play. Weapons include the plasma cutter, shotgun, pulse rifle etc. You can upgrade weapons by finding upgrade nodes. The upgrade nodes are rare so you need to use them cautiously, preferably only fully upgrading one or two weapons. You can also upgrade your armor to increase health, carry more weapons as well as improve oxygen levels for space exploration. The game is seperated into chapters, with each chapter taking part in a different area of the ship. You move slowly (similar to Resident evil 4), but you can also sprint for a duration. Also there is no hud in the game, instead you have a healthbar which is shown at the back of your suit. Finally, opening your inventory doesn't pause the game, so you can still be attacked. Aside from combat you may have to do some puzzles where you have to move items around.
Your enemies are necromorphs. These horryfying monsters need to be de-limbed in order to take them down quickly. They move exceptionally fast and some have range attacks as well. One of my favourite moments was being surrounded by necromorphs and pumping dozens of pulse rifle rounds into them, it literally felt like I was one of the marines in 'Aliens'.
The graphics hold exceptionally well for today's standards. The lighting is dark and gritty, which helps to make the player feel tensed up as they traverse the ship.
One of the problems I have with this game are the mouse controls. I suffer major mouse lag when turning my character around and aiming my guns, even after maxing out mouse sensitivity. This makes it difficult to aim for limbs on the enmey hence, making combat unecessarily complicated and difficult.
I highly recommend this game to fans of action-horror games.

Rig:

This combo runs the game a bit worse then it should in all honesty, currently on all medium settings with HBAO/SSAO turned off, everything else on. I wasn't expecting miracles with this aging setup but I was expecting a bit better when I can almost max Shogun 2 and Metro with better FPS for example.
I get quite a few frame drops and the game does feel a bit choppier then I would of liked on these settings, doesn't detract from the fun of the game though. Even though I was hoping to get atleast Texture quality to high the game still looks absolutely amazing at medium. BIG props to the environmental artists or whatever you would call them, as the game is atmospheric as all hell and every nook and cranny of the city oozes of detail and little untold stories. You'll see destroyed quarantine zones, highways full of abandoned cars, rotting corpses and destruction and huge vistas of the flaming city. It's all very immersive and draws you in. I have spent probably an hour of my playtime just soaking in the environment.
Story is good so far, enough to feel me compelled to go on in finishing it and doing the main quest to see what happens, so better then Dead Island's. Combat is much better then Dead Island's without those damn immersion breaking health bars, Instead you rely on the much improved visual damage system to see how close a zombie is to death. Weapons feel satisfying as ever and very meaty.
I'd give it an 8/10 as it is now, maybe buy on discount if you're a patient scrooge but the current price wont leave you feeling shortchanged.

Pro:
- Steam Workshop.
- No other modern "Shadowrun" options.
- Still in active cycle of development (for now, anyway) and getting support.
Con:
- Story is short and linear: 7-10 hours of gameplay per campaign.
- Many spells require stat dumps in disadvantageous areas.
- No character will ever reach "Full Power" in its own area.
- No system of Stealth!!
Overall, this is a very "to-the-point" type of game. There is no open world, in "Dead Man's Switch" you have a bar you can return to in between missions, in "Dragonfall" you have a neighborhood.  Each map is a "level" and you move from one to the next.
The Game included is called "Dead Man's Switch", which is about 8-12 hours in length for most people on their first playthrough. The expansion is a campaign called "Dragonfall", which has about 9-14 hours on the first playthrough. The replay value has increased due to fixed issues, and the game continues to recieve support from the developers.
There will not likely be new content ever released.  This game is over, and it failed the hype.

Overall, Half-Life 2 is one of those games.

In FTL you are in the command of a ship and its crew and must travel through space facing random events and battles. This game is about management skills rather than maneuvering skills. There are 9 unique ships total, each with 2 different layouts, 7 different crew races with unique traits, and tons of weapons, including your crew that may be used to board enemy ships. But what makes FTL unique is how brutal this game is. One single tiny bad decision may turn a so far good run into a nightmare.Battles can get really hectic and will keep you on your toes. Pausing the game to think your way through a fight is the rule. The fear of death, always present. Once you're dead, either start a new game or cry. No second chance. All of this, plus the fantastic soundtrack, makes FTL a very emotionally engaging, tense game. Its random nature makes every run unique. The unlockable ships and the variety of ways with which you can specialize them gives the game a great replay value. FTL is amazing.
It's like dive into twisted reality of Rorschach (vessel from Blindsight novel by Peter Watts). You can't rely on your vision or common sense. This game always tricks you.  :)

Despite the humble purchase price, this was a very disappointing title.
Engaging storyline and atmospheric setting is quickly strangled to death by an awkward combat system, awful user interface, entirely linear gameplay and a long list of other clunky game mechanics. It felt as though I was stepping back in time about two decades, but without any of the nostalgia.
Make no mistake: I really wanted to like this title. As the setting happens to be one of my favourite genres, I persevered; investing a number of additional hours into replays using characters who focused on different skill sets in an attempt to see if I'd inadvertently missed something worthwhile.
No matter my choices however, the entirely linear design and frustrating in-game systems once again railroaded me into more of the same punishment.
The only positive I can offer is that the provided campaign wasn't any longer than it's humble 10-12 hour play time, as I found myself gritting my teeth in frustration quite early on. The strategy component was virtually non-existent and the gameplay most tedious.

It's a tricky endeavor to build a game mainly on story and narrative - but Shadowrun Returns handles this with success.
Shadowrun is a lore-rich cyberpunk/fantasy mashup universe which has been explored since the 90s. There are more than 40 novels in English, 5 video games and countless table-top campaigns. There is also an MMO being developed. Having it's back on this lore, this game offers a very compelling story, rich characters and and immersive game play.
One downside, however, is the linearity. Even though character and class variations are well balanced and of satisfactory variety, the playthrough is linear. This wouldn't necessarily be a downside if this game was an action/adventure game; but over the years we've come expect at least some sort of openworld gameplay. I hear, however, the upcoming expansion will be addressing this.
The additional plus for this game is its workshop. You can download user made content (which exist, and are pretty good) from new classes to new campaigns.

Roguelike space adventure game with a lot of detail and depth.
The upsides:
* Easy to pick up and put down - even successful games only last an hour or so, but you'll always want to play more.
* Many winning strategies that reward clever management of your ship, crew, and weapons.
* Randomized galaxies and events make having the same game twice impossible, which adds dramatically to the replayability and suspense.
* Many different ships that encourage different playstyles.
The downsides:
* The difficulty tends to snowball, either in your favor or against you. Randomization can be a cruel mistress, especially early on - one lucky weapon can make the game easy, and a few bad breaks can make it near unplayable within the first few minutes.
* Unlocking the final ship. SERIOUSLY. Total overkill compared to unlocking everything else.
The final word:
Indie and small team game design is very much alive, and FTL proves it. Great game for a low price. You shoot lasers and burn rebels. What's not to like here? HIghly recommend.

So I liked all the Arkham games, including this one.
In terms of gameplay, this is not a great departure from the last three games. You are Batman and you alternate between jumping from rooftop to rooftop beating up random dudes and then having fisticuffs with crowds of jerks. Like Arkham City and Origins, it's still an open world sandbox game wherein Batman fights to protect a city that seems to be populated exclusively with dudes who are lining up to rob a bank or knock over a jewelry store. Seriously, besides one building of cops, a couple of firefighters and Batman's assorted sidekicks, the entire city is just a pack of dip♥♥♥♥♥. It makes you sort of wonder why saving it is even worth it in the first place.
Anyhow, that aside, the main innovation is you have the Batmobile, which is a tank thingie that's fun enough to use. Nothing groundbreaking, but it's not like the Batmobile segments aren't fun or whatnot.
The story meanwhile is pretty strong, although due to the comic book origins of the series it pulls a lot of punches. I think this is supposed to be the last of the Arkham games, so you'd think that the creators would be more willing to kill characters. I mean, it's not like if you kill them in this game they're deleted from the comic book forever guys. But in spite of that, there are some incredibly good scenes and I was very interested from start to finish. Some plot twists are  presented a bit too obviously (the identity of the Arkham Knight is painfully obvious for about three hours), but most of it  still comes together pretty solidly.
Until you get to the ending.
Or well, I should say "Until you see what the ending involves". Because in order to actually see what happens at the end you've got to collect every single mother♥♥♥♥ing Riddler trophy. All 250 or so of them.
I don't understand Rocksteady's obsession with those ♥♥♥♥ing things. Is it just a petulant idea that if you go through all this trouble making a big sandbox city that you ought to put♥♥♥♥♥♥around to make sure the player goes around appreciating all of it? Ugh.
I ended up watching the ending on Youtube. It was alright. But the fact that the game locked it behind tedious collection quests is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Still, beyond that it's a good game. I'll probably play some of the DLC.

The story didn't have enough explanation at times, and there are definitely other GTAs with more things to do, but GTA Vice City is a great, solid section of the GTA franchise.
It's the 80s, the time of colorful pastel suits and track outfits that just never seemed to go out of style. The music industry was entering a new age with all of the technology, and the development of the metropolis became official. But what do I know.
GTA VC had a lot of content, but compared to the other GTAs didn't have too much innovation compared to previous titles (and future GTAs for sure) but it was a solid, fun, enjoyable game. The story was gritty and solid, not the best by far but it is still great and important to the GTA universe as it's contribution in the Miami Vice department.
In terms of personalization, there isn't much, but you get to be a crime lord, spending money on property and what not. While I think the future GTAs were better, as expected, this is still a classic you will have a hard time putting down.
I played the crap out of this for years and have nothing but respect for the game, but if you aren't buying it to grow your GTA collection and be a completionist for the series, there are probably other GTAs you should be prioritizing first to maximize your experience.

Worth buying at at least 66% off via my "Never buy games at full price" motto and "Percentage-to-hours" hypothesis (accounting hours played and enjoyment in regards to the absolute lowest percentage that I would consider buying it at if I suddenly lost the game and had to rebuy it).
Pros:
The story is incredible: the main protagonist doesn't speak or react to events, so it honestly feels like you're in the seat, which is perfect for a horror/survival shooter like this. The NPCs are vital to the story (there's 4 major ones, and a fifth person who appears every now and then and is a key part in the backstory) and feel realistic, and they add to the game experience unlike many games out there these days. The game's mechanics are timeless and the graphics are splendid, even if the game is generally dark. I felt emotionally attached to this game (more than any other, at least) because of how well the developers created the events in the story; stuff felt like it was happening to me, and that's the sign of a well made game. Save points are everywhere, checkpoints are well placed before major events, stores are crucial to the development of the character, and benches are your best friend who only turns up once a month (or in this case, chapter) but are a blast to hang out with (you upgrade you gear here with power nodes). This game was clearly designed with a lot of thought.
Cons:
The lack of gamepad mapping was kind of annoying at first, but the controls are still good. Sensitivity is downright poor sometimes, especially with the mouse. The bosses were not hard: the one in the middle or just past the middle was harder than the last one, and took way longer. Ammunition is very important in this game, which made it super annoying that enemies that dropped ammo before would often not the later on in the game it got. The story towards the end felt a little forced, but if it was planned with Dead Space 2 in mind, then it's fine, but it just felt like it happened because they did not want **START OF SPOILER** an unhappy ending **END OF SPOILER**. however this does not affect how I feel about the game. The game had some annoying glitches in it, like getting stuck in places in zero gravity and not being able to get out, and also falling through lifts into space and dying if you were not properly on the lift when you activated it. The machine gun-type weapon you use two times to clear asteroids had bad controlling, but it wasn't hard to beat that bit anyway. There's not much in terms of weapon variation, and you can very easily beat the game by just using a Plasma Cutter, maxing it out with the power nodes in the bench, maxing out your RIG the same way, and buying plasma energy all game.
Overall, I give this game a rating of 9/10. You could tell that this game's multiplayer could be incredible if done right, but unfortunately it doesn't come until Dead Space 3 (EDIT: Dead Space 2 has a nice 8 player, 4v4 mode that's actually not too bad). The game's single player is a top 5 best campaign in shooter gaming history, with Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, Halo, Half-Life and maybe Half-Life 2. The controls on the PC port are pretty unresponsive with the mouse, but with the controller it's basically solved, though there seems to be no remapping, which is off putting to some. Because of this, I got the full experience of this game (dark setting, headset on, XBOX 360 controller) and enjoyed it immensely.
Handy tip: when you reach the Target Practice minigame, I have a feeling that if you play it enough, you will not have a credits problem/deficiency for the rest of the game. So when you reach it, play it a lot and you will have all the money you need.

Good turn based strategy game. 8/10
Combat is fun. Hitting is based on accuracy % so there is a bit of luck in "hitting" enemies, but how you move on the field will greatly impact the outcome of a fight. (aka understanding of game mechanics is needed). They don't do a good job of explaining the mechanics so if you are new to the genre it may be a bit tricky. I'll just say this, use cover :).
Story has some twists and is fairly well developed. Not anything you are going to see from a AAA title but decent. There are usually a few different ways through areas which is nice.
Customization for main character is great. My only real complaint about this game comes from party customization, or lack there of. There is very little. The thing I enjoy the most in turn based squad games is tailor making my squad. Min maxing it
and scultping a design like melee death ball, ranged power, crowd control, etc... You "hire" squad members when you go on shadow runs and they come with pre-set builds. Like why the hell do I want a mage with 6 magic, 3 casting, and 3 gun skill? I want 6 magic, 6 casting. He is a mage and I use his spells, not his freaking gun. There are mods which I believe let you make a full patry, but for the story that comes with the game this is my main complaint.
Biggest value is probably that this game has mod support. I haven't had time to go through any of them yet, but there are always some user created jewels out there to extend the life of a game.
**Be prepared to read a lot of diagloue. Also there are moments where you have to put in some detective work with pen and paper if you don't have the right "skills" with your character to bypass X obstacle. **This is not a complaint**, merely a warning to those used to voice dialogue and the game doing the work for you with "mission clues".
Final Words: 8/10
If you are a fan of the genre this title is totally worth buying. If you are seeking to get into the genre I personally have to recommend XCOM over it as a first because I feel the combat was more polished.
