I really want to come up with one of those hilarious joke reviews that my oh-so-clever fellow gamers employ, but my love for this game makes this impossible....
God, where to begin....well, for starters, lets take into account that this game is now well over 10 years old, and still looks and runs fantastic! Part of that can be attributed to Valve sticking to their guns, and keeping the Source engine up to date and well optimized, unlike other engines of the time (e.g. id Tech 4).
Also too is its fantastic story. Its not the most revolutionary, in terms of plot or plot progression (Half-life never has been; SPOILER ALERT Aliens invade, you kill aliens. 'Nuff said). But its the way this story is told, and how attached you get to the beautiful characters in this game, such as Alyx Vance, her father Eli Vance, their fellow Scientist Dr. Issac Kleiner, and the like.
The gameplay is also rich and varied. For those who have played other shooters but for some reason haven't yet played Half-life 2, it has the standard suite of weapons (SPOILER ALERT), such as pistols, shotguns, smgs, etc. It also has more long range weapons, such as a crossbow, a rocket launcher, and hand grenades.
But one of the strongest selling points to the game, is the Zero Point Energy Field Manipulator, or the Gravity Gun. Thanks to Valve's beautiful implementation of the Havok Physics engine, you are granted the ability to pick up, move and throw objects with realistic reactive physics, aided in part by the Gravity Gun. The gun helps you solve puzzles and also aids in combat.
Its more than just a gimic though. Instead of just having a few arbritrary points where it can be used, a la Call of Duty, the Gravity Gun can be employed, to great effect, almost anywhere in the game. Sure, you could mow down that sqaud of soldiers with your pulse rifle, but thats BORING. Why not flip that car on top of them instead? Overwhelmed by a group of zombies? Cut them in half by flinging a buzz saw at them, or perhaps launching an explosive barrel at them.
All in all, 10/10, would play again.

The Enhanced update just came out so I'm going to update my review for that and flip this review from a thumbs up to a thumbs down.
When I got this game when it came out I said "If you like Dead Island you're gonna love this game". Well, I still stand by that comment except that I didn't like Dead Island. LOL
There are two main problems with this game. The first big issue is this game lacks replayability. Sure there is a hard mode and stuff to drive you crazy looking all over the map to collect but once you've finished all the quests and leveled your character theres not really much else to do and the game gets boring really quick. You could mess about in the game with mates but even that only gets so far. You can't really interact with the objects in the game world to mess around with them, everything is fixed down in place, even the shopping trolleys can't be moved. To add to that, the developers are strongly anti mods. In order for 2 people to play a modded game both have to have exactly the same ones. So if you have 20 mods installed, your friend has to have exaclty the same 20 mods or they can't join your game. And the chances of a complete random joining your game are exactly 3720 to 1.
The other reason is technical. This game is really beautiful. The world is lushly populated and detailed.. but then they ruin the graphics with silly post processing effects that you CANNOT disable. The worst one of these is chromatic aberration. It is a silly effect that degrades the image and should not be in games because its a limitation of film reels and analogue photography. Our eyes do not experience chromatic aberration so it should never be added to games where you are looking out at the world in first person. Chromatic aberration is a abomination because it takes away the sharpness of the image and makes it a blurry mess. It actually makes my eyes hurt and the game hard to play for long.
Lastly, I will add this one in as well, they added VAC to this game. Normally, VAC is good because it keeps out cheaters but in this game where all multiplayer games are local hosted, that is just silly. The host cannot be trusted to be running in a unaltered environment and there are also reports in the forums of people getting VAC banned for using mods. in a single player game.

Shadowrun has been a massively underutilised franchise when it comes to the world of video games. There are countless Dungeons and Dragons titles but only four set in the murky shadows of mega corps and monsters.
Of the four games, one of them was a Japanese only Mega CD title and another is a team based shooter which doesn’t really keep the ethos. The ones fans will remember are the excellent SNES version which saw Jake Armitage taking on a Dragon and the Genesis title that never made it to European shores. To say gamers have been starved of Shadowrun fun is somewhat of an understatement but that could all be about to change.
Shadowrun Returns is a turn based strategy game set in an isometric viewpoint and is about as old school feeling as a new game gets. It’s very close in mood and graphical style to the SNES game and benefits immensely from it. The areas of the city are dank and polluted and neon tinged signs cast light over the many citizens that walk the streets in this imagining of a dystopian future.
Conversations are carried out via dialogue trees with pictures of the characters face to the side of them. There is no voice acting or animation here but it doesn’t really detract from the game and if anything adds to the retro feel.
The story goes that your friend has been murdered and now it’s up to you find out who the killer is. At first it seems a fairly standard tale but there are a few decent twists to keep you on your toes and what starts out as a neo-noir thriller will soon go off into all sorts of strange and gruesome directions.
You can build your character from scratch from five races and a host of different class types which at least on the surface adds some depth and replay value to the game. In practice we found the classes that deal with robots or computers had their skill sets somewhat underused (especially in the beginning), with the combination of magic and guns often the best way to proceed. We’re hoping future instalments will flesh these classes out a bit more as the basic rule set is solid.
The game is split into three different sections. There’s the part where you run around the area talking to people and looking for clues, the turn based combat sections and parts where you enter the matrix. The first part plays out like a point and click adventure, all be it in a confined area.  Combat can occur quickly and it’s always nest to be prepared and ready. When combat does occur your characters are given a number of action points to move, shoot and cast spells. It’s not ground breaking but it works simply and effectively enough. You also have to keep an eye on characters strengths with Trolls and Orcs better at taking damage than Elves for instance.
Most of the time you’ll have a team of four and you’re missions will generally be to get into somewhere, retrieve a person or object and get out. Sometimes you just have to kill people but it becomes a step by step process of running to cover, concentrating fire and carefully moving forward. Mistakes can be costly and if you die you’ll start the whole sequence again. This is one of the flaws of the game as missions can be around an hour in length and you’ll often have to go through all the dialogue and adventure part of the game again if you die.
A quick save would have been pretty useful as well in case you need to step away from the PC, but as it is we only have the auto save which kicks in at the start of each new area. Just make sure you are sensible with your gear as being auto-saved into a difficult place means there may be no way to get out alive if you haven’t brought the right supplies or team. This can be somewhat frustrating considering you won’t know what you need until you get there.
The matrix sections of the game are also a little dry. They play out in much the same way as normal combat with the Decker moving around a virtual system setting up combat programmes and fighting drones. It would have been nice to distinguish this more from the normal combat but it works.
The game also comes with a detailed level editor and this is what is going to keep it going in the long term. The rule set is solid and there are already a ton of levels available that users have created. There are dedicated projects to bring both the SNES and Genesis games into the game as well. The standard game is a round twelve hours long and it’s likely you’ll be left wanting more so it’s well worth digging into some of the mission packs out there.
Overall, Shadowrun Returns is a positive return to form for the series. It’s not perfect but everything is in place for a bright future. The game as it stands now is solid, well written and will provide a good few hours of gameplay. A few more side quests and a bit more variety wouldn’t have gone a miss but it’s an easy world to get drawn into and any fan shouldn’t be disappointed. It’s a streamlined turn based strategy game set in an interesting world and we can only see it getting better and better in the future.
Overall 7/10

Total evaluation is 10 on the story. 4 on the graphics. A must-play for true roleplaying fanatics like myself.

TL;DR
I would probably have put this at a 7.5 or 8 out of 10 overall, but the ending and their incredibly annoying reliance on really bad mechanics at important points drop this down to a 5. Mediocre. It's not terrible, it's not the worst game in history, but man it's disappointing compared to the glimpses of a great game you can see underneath it.
You'll all no doubt notice my relatively brief playtime. I got as far as getting past the (reasonably well executed) tutorial, and then it ground to a halt (though audio continued), then crashed.
I reloaded the game, picked up a small bit before I left off, nearly crashed again, walked outdoors for a few minutes, and the game crashed again.
The game was preordered for me as a christmas gift, and I gotta say this♥♥♥♥♥♥is exactly why I don't preorder things. I really, really, REALLY wish developers would finish products before shipping them.
I turned down the graphics a bit, shutting off Vsync as I do in every game, motion blur, and even the antialiasing (even though I beat almost all the recommended requirements, and match the ones I don't beat; I wanted to be sure that wasn't the problem) between the first and second crashes, which didn't make the game look bad but definitely didn't make it look as good as I'm sure the devs intended.
Honestly I desperately want to like this game, but it's incredibly frustrating that I knew even before I loaded it that there would be issues. I know it's difficult to program for every system, and I'm not trying to be a hater.
In its' current form: don't buy it. In fact I'd say don't buy it until it goes down in price AND gets fixed if you're the type who prefers to send a message with your purchases.
System specs:
CPU AMD 1100t X6 3.3 GHZ
GPU Nvidia GTX 760
RAM 8 gigs 1600 hz corsair something-or-other DDR3
UPDATE:
So I built a new computer (pretty close top of the line), and on that the game runs great. I can do a real review.
Gameplay:
The mechanics of freerunning can take a bit to get used to, but once you do it's a good bit of fun. There's a great flow between running and fighting that is pretty unusual in games overall. The only real gripe I hear about the combat is that the zombies take FOREVER to die, and that's something I can vouch for. Personally I'm not looking at that as a bad thing though, because it makes them more threatening than they otherwise would be. There are a few places where doing tower climbs or other parkour things gets a bit tedious, and the non-zombie people are way harder to kill than they have any right to be.
The story is decidedly boring, which is surprising since it's about a secret agent getting dropped into a zombie infested hellhole. The two main characters seem "inspired by" characters from Far Cry 3, and there's a lack of ability to choose what your response to a lot of situations will be. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but I do like having a bit more choice (not necessarily moral choice, just choice) in what I do.
The performance on my new rig is great, but that comes with the caveat that it ran like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on my prior rig which wasn't exactly a slouch.
All in all I'm having fun with this, but I don't know that it'd be worth the $60 price tag (especially with digital distribution, come on guys) to most people. $40 would be a good price, and $30 would be a total bargain.
There are occaisonal bugs (for example my freerunning got me stuck in a shelf somehow), and they reused a lot of textures and things, but overall the game is pretty solid.
The voice acting is pretty solid for the most part, but the dialogue itself is hackneyed as all hell in a lot of places.
There's loads of content, but that content is pretty repetitive. Past a certain point that's to be expected in any sandbox style game, and they do a remarkably good job of providing reasons for the people not to perform a given task (usually bitey, smelly reasons).
Also the game gets a whole lot more entertaining once a certain ability is unlocked, so play through for a while if you already bought it before you write it off.
As far as the new computer goes:
Intel core i7 5820 (OC'd to 4 ghz)
16 gigs DDR4 2666
GTX 980 card
running from a samsung 850pro SSD
Update 2:
So I finished the game, and it wasn't worth it. The idea behind the story at the end isn't terrible, but the mechanics are nothing short of abysmal. The entire last segment from beginning to end is one long exercise in frustration, boredom, and memorizing exactly what comes next or getting lucky. They also have a really bad habit of arbitrarily deciding some of your abilities no longer work, which says to me that they knew those abilities were overpowered. Several times I lost my equipment, sometimes without actually having any part of the game explain why (always in a "boss fight", because god forbid they make a boss difficult on its own merits, and robbing the player of equipment and abilities is a cheap as hell way to increase difficulty) Honestly the only reason I finished it is stubbornness, and I doubt very much if I will be playing this ll the way through again.
What they could have done better:
Most games make the end sequence a test of all the skill and abilities you've built up til that point, and  for good reason. Doing otherwise leaves the player feeling cheated.
Give me some goddamned options for how I want my character to behave! Seriously, this game was BEGGING for a branching plot tree. Not necessarily a moral choice system, because those tend to be way overdone, but just giving one faction a benefit over another or allowing my character to side with one group (have good sides and bad sides to each option, instead of making it all one or the other). Mind you that would require removing some of the cartoonish mustache-twirling villainousness from the main bad guy, but they had the setup to actually make the guy someone who could be empathized with. They tried so hard to make their villain into Vaas from Far Cry 3 that they may as well have just called him that, but they also tried to make him have some tragic backstory for some confusing reason.
Seriously, I would probably have put this at a 7.5 or 8 out of 10 overall, but the ending and their incredibly annoying reliance on really bad mechanics at important points drop this down to a 5. Mediocre. It's not terrible, it's not the worst game in history, but man it's disappointing.

Unlike portal where the bending of physical space is purely under your control, in this game the spatial loops and areas that are bigger on the inside are purely under the control of the game designers, and it feels almost chaotic while still, somehow, following some kind of pattern. At first it feels frusturating when all the solutions are of the "who would ever think of that?" variety, until you understand that, well, that's the *point*, and you start to get more into the swing of things. You start to wonder "Am I supposed to solve it this way?" then realize it doesn't matter. You suspect you're doing the puzzles out of order, then realize that's part of the game.
The one major downfall is when you start to grok the game (which happens fast) all the unexpectedness falls away; "If this were a normal game I'd expect the solution to be X, but this is antichamber so it's probably the opposite"
All in all, well worth a few bucks and a day's worth of play time (plus or minus depending on how flexible your brain is.

I honestly can't say enough good things about XCOM: Enemy Unknown, or its expansion Enemy Within. It's by no means perfect, and there are some legitimate criticisms in terms of replayability and other areas, but it's a damn fine game, and a damned fine re-imagining of a classic franchise.
It's got a fairly linear core story to it, which starts strong but sadly tapers off towards the final hour or two. The journey up to that point though is nothing if not wonderful - the varying mission types, and maps you can fight on, the new technologies you unlock to help you fight the alien menace... it's an emotional and compelling experience strategy fans shouldn't miss out on, and there's an expertly crafted personal element to everythign with perma-death and the consequence of choice.
If you haven't played it before, I definitely recommend getting both Enemy Unknown and it's expansion, Enemy Within. EW is more of a content expansion, and you won't be missing out by going straight to the upgraded version.
If you already own EU, well, you either agree with me or you don't, but you may still be unsure as to whether or not to pick up Enemy Within. I would say do, but bear in mind that you're still fighting the same fight, and the core narrative keystones are the same. They don't even change the ending, which is a shame, but the new content and how it changes the flow of the game is worth it, I'd say.

Now that I've officially warned you, let's get into the nitty gritty of what I think makes this game a failure in my eyes. Hi, I'm Cel, and I played both of the Shadowrun games on the Sega Genesis (Mastersystem) and Super Nintendo back in the day. Jake Armitage was one of my favorite badass cyberpunk heroes in my childhood and the music in the SNES game blew me away and I still own mp3's of those 16-bit goodies. I know Shadowrun was a boardgame first, but we were promised a spiritual successor to the console games with boardgame flavoring, and that is not at all what we got. We can completely forget the disaster that was the Xbox / PC game Shadowrun before we go on.
Early shots of this game were really promising. The 2D isometric view fit perfectly and the early gameplay demos of combat showed promise. The UI looked awful and big at first and no one knew why, until it was evident they wanted to make a UI they could easily port over to fu*king TABLETS and ANDROIDS it became evident how cheaply these developers were going to cut corners to push out a product with their kickstarter money. When you see 2D worlds, hear it's an RPG you instantly think it's going to be open world (hey, if the SNES Shadowrun that appeared in fu*king 1993 let you run loose in an open world and that came out in the fu*king 90's, why can't this do that in a bigger scale?) you'll instantly be disappointed.
They even showed pictures of Jake Armitage the fu*king protagonist of the SNES game fully polygoned and he even had his own artwork. This is another "clever" way of enticing idiots like me who loved the SNES game into thinking this is going to be like that. Like, holy sh*t this could be good! NO! NO IT WASN'T!! Jake Armitage in the actual game is nothing more but some tutorial dude who tackles along with you and does nothing but teach you the dry basics, for about 10 minutes and then he's gone. Whoopie fu*king doo, right? Who cares? Well, I do. Why?
Well, imagine if Squaresofts FF7 got remade years from now into "HHD" or whatever sh*t they'll have then by some basement group of as*holes with high pictures showing Cloud with new models and brand new promising artwork. Then you start the game and Cloud guides you through how to assfu*k 7 Korean "women of the night" at the same time for 10 minutes and then disappears, because fu*k you, would you not be disappointed? Yes, yes you would.
I bought into the hype of the game since I booted up my old SNES (lol, emulator) and finished Shadowrun in anticipation. The game still held up and I was ready. Holy crap can nostalgia make you so blind. There were warnings everywhere, on forums, on the kickstarter page itself. Everyone was saying avoid this piece of sh*t but I didn't listen. Screenshots looked promising and combat wasn't so horrible.
So you boot up the game and bam, it begins without any intro. Nothing. Just a background artwork (that looks good, all the artwork is great if I'm honest) and a big tablet / android like button to start the game. I mean, nothing is even animated. It's barren and boring. If this was a video review I'd show you the fu*king SNES startup screen that has great great music and animation and a fu*king intro to the title and even a cutscene on how the game starts. This game, in 2013, made by "super enthusiastic super fans" of the series, has NOTHING! NOOTHING!!
After selecting classes and sh*t (you'll still be anticipating something good at this point) you're instantly put into a combat situation. The UI still looks like it was made from iPads and it has no animation or character to it. Everything in the game is non-moving and dead to look at. If animation isn't something that you care for, there isn't anything else to look at. All the enviroments look "handcrafted" which knowing the games origin you'll quickly realize how few of these areas will be in the game. Since there are no building blocks that means there's less areas. For an RPG to be insanely linear is a kiss of death. Look at how insanely hated Final Fantasy on the PS3 was for being so boringly linear. Handcrafted look is fine and it looks really impressive, but you quickly realize even on the first battle, on the first screen, that this is to the detriment of the game. The area is a clusterfu*k and for the first 20 minutes of boring text, text and text your characters don't move an inch. Why don't they move? Because someone spent weeks "handcrafting" that one spot so there literally isn't other areas to go to.
So you do your first combat scene and advance forward hoping perhaps it gets more interesting later on. Now it begins. The roleplay. The dread. The boring.
From the very get go at the start you will be bombarded by a books worth of dialog (text) about every inch of the game. Too much so, because you literally don't leave your own room until there's been dialog thrown at you about everything and everyone. The main problem with this dialog is that it's the core game. No joke. The dialog is all the game is. You just bought a digital novel meant for iPads and you realize how much your childhood game has been rap*d for easy dollars by as*holes who don't care. This is even before you meet Armitage and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ his character gets.
Skip the dialog? Sure, go ahead. Skip everything. If you do, all you'll be left with is the same 2D enviroment you've been backtracking for 2 hours being lost as to what to do. If you don't read everything everyone says in the game you won't know what to do next. This is not a bad thing necessarily, but for christ sake there's just so much of it! It never ends! I passed on buying this game when it first came out because it looked a bit odd. It wound up in my library through a HumbleBundle, and I decided to give it a play. I instantly regretted passing over this game all those years ago. The gameplay is great. Getting used to the control scheme and view point is not automatic, but it quickly becomes second nature. Characters are well thought out, and are developed excellently. Im a big sucker for a good story in video games, and Dead Space absolutely delivers. The story is fleshed out, and develops nicely as the game progresses. The atmosphere is excelent. I cannot stress this enough, the game keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. The environment is littered with potential threats, keeping you constantly scanning. The designers didnt stop there though. They paired this trecherous environment with a "weapon" collection that some how just never has enough ammo, and a character that just cant ever get his hit points back up to full. Exhaustive scavenging and ammo conservation are essential to success, but then that just loops back to an environment that is trying to kill you 100% of the time. All in all, the game is absolutely amazing, I couldnt get enough of it, and if you dont buy it now, you will forever regret it.

A story about an engineer fighting zombie aliens!  And cutting things!
Graphics:
The game is quite dark, which really helps the mood of the game.  Normally, this would make it hard to find items, but thankfully, all items and item boxes are lit and easily found.  The game also uses shadows really well to highten your fear.  The character models are all very good looking and well animated and the enviroments are also detailed well done.  Let's not forget the way the game messes with you sometimes.  Also, I like how the abscence of the hud, instead placing your health/air on your back and each weapon has it's own ammo counter.
Also, there are some good options for changing resolutions and gfx settings.
Sound:
The sound is excellent.  There is a slight absence of music, but that is a credit to the game.  It silence makes you feel uneasy and worried that something is gonna get you.  The random noises in the ship only add to it.  And when you're in a vacum, the sound muffles to make it feel like you're actually in space.  The voice acting is also good, though the constant silnce of the protaganist is annoying.
Controls:
The controls are a bit slow, but that gives realism to being in a suit and also gives all your attacks weight.  The weapons are very easily selected and used and all have a secondary ability/firemode.  You can play this eith either keyboard/mouse or gamepad and both feel right and well programmed.  Accessing the menu is also nice and easy.  The inventory is easily navigated and having a button to use health items without going into a menu is great.
Gameplay:
The game moves purposely slow to keep your fear up, wondering if you are about to be attacked.  Depending on the difficulty mode, the game hands you many items to keep you going. Save points are scattered nicely, though I remember a few being too close by, but it was rare.  Enemies mostly come in groups and will keep you on your toes since they will come from all directions!  There are some times when you have to backtrack into previously explored areas, but usually they are FAR different than when you were first there.  But I didn't like that some deaths felt cheap and annoying.
Still I would reccomend this game highly for it's scare factor and fun.  This is how a sci-fi horror game should be!

The reboot of a highly regarded franchise is no small task, but Firaxis outdid themselves. XCOM is an incredibly well put together piece of software, save for some odd framerate issues tied to one of the enemies.
The game just feels right. There's no other way I can explain it. The graphics are good and the way combat is designed makes every encounter a different set of challenges to face. Combined with research progressing only as you scan for activity, you will see hours fly by as you combat aliens in an attempt to complete research on plasma technology or get that extra satellite uplink built.
The story is not half bad and, while it doesn't drive the game as much as panic level, resources, or research, adds enough to make XCOM's world feel decently fleshed out.
The game's combat is quite intense. I know, it's a turn based game, but I've had my adreneline pumping through more engagements in this game than I can count. This is in part thanks to the soldiers. Sure they don't have too much personality on paper, but the fact that you can customize them, including their names, really helps you want to keep them alive. It also doesn't hurt that each soldier has their own level and abilites that get upgraded as you use them. These two features make losing a soldier feel like a crushing defeat each time it happens, especially if you don't load a save to fix your mistake.
This game is truly worth the money at full price. I picked it up on sale for $10, but after finishing my first 30 hour playthrough, I would have happily paid more for it.

An interesting platformer infused with some roguelike elements.
In each map, you need to find the teleporter, activate it and then destroy all enemies before being able to go to the next map. Until you manage to activate the teleporter, enemies will keep spawning endlessly. Worse, the overall difficulty of the game will go up every five minutes (a clock on the top right is here to show you the current difficulty). And the game features permadeath, so any mistake could be the end of your run.
Your only hope are the random chests and store dispersed across the map. Each contains a random item. Most items will give you a passive ability, and a few provide active abilities, but you can only carry one of theses. Items are the main source of power in this game, so figuring out how to best use your current combination of items is the only way to survive the hostile world of Risk Of Rain.
The game aims for a "short and sweet" vibe. A successful run should take you about 1h. After the first 2 or 3 minutes to get your bearings, things will start to heat up, and the action will be frantic from that point onwards.
One downside of the game is that the game push you towards a certain way of doing things. There are too many monsters and they usually run as fast as you, so it's usually best to flee and damage them from afar. It's a bit disappointing as you're encouraged to use cheesy tactics, rather than go into the thick of combat and pummel monsters to death.
The overall difficulty is not too high. If you're an experienced gamer you should be able to finish a normal difficulty runs after a few hours, once you figure out what is your favorite class and your favorites items. Once you've managed to finish the game for the first time, you will still have many opportunities to come back to it.
There are many things to unlock : new classes with radically different gameplay, items to be added to the random pool, artefacts that change the rules of the games. How much fun and gameplay you will find from playing with all theses new combinations will be a matter of personal taste. It will depends on how you like to replay the same game over and over again. Some will drop the game after 10h, others will continue for 30 or 40 more hours.

TL;DR
I would probably have put this at a 7.5 or 8 out of 10 overall, but the ending and their incredibly annoying reliance on really bad mechanics at important points drop this down to a 5. Mediocre. It's not terrible, it's not the worst game in history, but man it's disappointing compared to the glimpses of a great game you can see underneath it.
You'll all no doubt notice my relatively brief playtime. I got as far as getting past the (reasonably well executed) tutorial, and then it ground to a halt (though audio continued), then crashed.
I reloaded the game, picked up a small bit before I left off, nearly crashed again, walked outdoors for a few minutes, and the game crashed again.
The game was preordered for me as a christmas gift, and I gotta say this♥♥♥♥♥♥is exactly why I don't preorder things. I really, really, REALLY wish developers would finish products before shipping them.
I turned down the graphics a bit, shutting off Vsync as I do in every game, motion blur, and even the antialiasing (even though I beat almost all the recommended requirements, and match the ones I don't beat; I wanted to be sure that wasn't the problem) between the first and second crashes, which didn't make the game look bad but definitely didn't make it look as good as I'm sure the devs intended.
Honestly I desperately want to like this game, but it's incredibly frustrating that I knew even before I loaded it that there would be issues. I know it's difficult to program for every system, and I'm not trying to be a hater.
In its' current form: don't buy it. In fact I'd say don't buy it until it goes down in price AND gets fixed if you're the type who prefers to send a message with your purchases.

UPDATE:
So I built a new computer (pretty close top of the line), and on that the game runs great. I can do a real review.
Gameplay:
The mechanics of freerunning can take a bit to get used to, but once you do it's a good bit of fun. There's a great flow between running and fighting that is pretty unusual in games overall. The only real gripe I hear about the combat is that the zombies take FOREVER to die, and that's something I can vouch for. Personally I'm not looking at that as a bad thing though, because it makes them more threatening than they otherwise would be. There are a few places where doing tower climbs or other parkour things gets a bit tedious, and the non-zombie people are way harder to kill than they have any right to be.
The story is decidedly boring, which is surprising since it's about a secret agent getting dropped into a zombie infested hellhole. The two main characters seem "inspired by" characters from Far Cry 3, and there's a lack of ability to choose what your response to a lot of situations will be. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but I do like having a bit more choice (not necessarily moral choice, just choice) in what I do.
The performance on my new rig is great, but that comes with the caveat that it ran like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on my prior rig which wasn't exactly a slouch.
All in all I'm having fun with this, but I don't know that it'd be worth the $60 price tag (especially with digital distribution, come on guys) to most people. $40 would be a good price, and $30 would be a total bargain.
There are occaisonal bugs (for example my freerunning got me stuck in a shelf somehow), and they reused a lot of textures and things, but overall the game is pretty solid.
The voice acting is pretty solid for the most part, but the dialogue itself is hackneyed as all hell in a lot of places.
There's loads of content, but that content is pretty repetitive. Past a certain point that's to be expected in any sandbox style game, and they do a remarkably good job of providing reasons for the people not to perform a given task (usually bitey, smelly reasons).
Also the game gets a whole lot more entertaining once a certain ability is unlocked, so play through for a while if you already bought it before you write it off.

Update 2:
So I finished the game, and it wasn't worth it. The idea behind the story at the end isn't terrible, but the mechanics are nothing short of abysmal. The entire last segment from beginning to end is one long exercise in frustration, boredom, and memorizing exactly what comes next or getting lucky. They also have a really bad habit of arbitrarily deciding some of your abilities no longer work, which says to me that they knew those abilities were overpowered. Several times I lost my equipment, sometimes without actually having any part of the game explain why (always in a "boss fight", because god forbid they make a boss difficult on its own merits, and robbing the player of equipment and abilities is a cheap as hell way to increase difficulty) Honestly the only reason I finished it is stubbornness, and I doubt very much if I will be playing this ll the way through again.
What they could have done better:
Most games make the end sequence a test of all the skill and abilities you've built up til that point, and  for good reason. Doing otherwise leaves the player feeling cheated.
Give me some goddamned options for how I want my character to behave! Seriously, this game was BEGGING for a branching plot tree. Not necessarily a moral choice system, because those tend to be way overdone, but just giving one faction a benefit over another or allowing my character to side with one group (have good sides and bad sides to each option, instead of making it all one or the other). Mind you that would require removing some of the cartoonish mustache-twirling villainousness from the main bad guy, but they had the setup to actually make the guy someone who could be empathized with. They tried so hard to make their villain into Vaas from Far Cry 3 that they may as well have just called him that, but they also tried to make him have some tragic backstory for some confusing reason.
Seriously, I would probably have put this at a 7.5 or 8 out of 10 overall, but the ending and their incredibly annoying reliance on really bad mechanics at important points drop this down to a 5. Mediocre. It's not terrible, it's not the worst game in history, but man it's disappointing.

I've always heard great things about this game, and the hype is right! I've finished the game and can barely wait to start the sequel!
It's an over-the-shoulder shooter (much like Resident Evil or Mass Effect), and the immersion is incredible. There's no HUD blocking the screen, ammo displays are on weapons and your health is displayed on the back of your character's suit. All the in-game menus (Maps, Inventory, Journal, etc) as well as video and audio communication are displayed with holographic projections from your suit. The game also has areas of zero-gravity where you must navigate your way by flying across the rooms, and hopefully not plunge into deep space.
The player takes the role of Isaac Clarke, an engineer and space ship systems specialist sent as part of a repair mission to the USG Ishimura, a large scale mining vessel. Upon arrival you quickly realize that disaster has struck the Ishimura and spend the game trying to get out alive. Throughout the game you can upgrade the space hazmat suit you wear, as well as buy and upgrade various weapons. The majority of the weapons you acquire are improvised tools, such as plasma cutters and buzz saws, reflecting that you're primarily an engineer, and not a soldier.
All in all it's a great buy; solid gameplay, a gripping story, and an incredible soundtrack. I highly recommend it.

Summary:  This is probably the best ShadowRun adaptation to a video game I've ever played.  Fun RPG sci-fi experience packed into a small game.  Gameplay and innovation over pretty effects and graphics.  The game also has a toolset you can use to create your own adventures, which is a bonus.  Even better, you can use the Steam Workshop to download cool stuff other people have made to add massive replay value to the game.  For the price, this game is definitely worth it.
Cons:  Short.  I think it took me less than 20 hours to finish.  The graphics are unimpressive, and there is no voiceover or flashy effects that you see in most modern games.  This definitely has a "shoestring budget" feel to it.
Pros:  Great story.  Great storytelling.  It had a very nostalgic feel, and I liked it.  The gameplay was a lot of fun, which trumps everything I listed in the Cons section.  It doens't matter how pretty the game is if it's not any fun to play.  I love turn-based strategy and RPG, and this game blends the two together very nicely.  Lots of latitude on how to shape your character, and multiple ways to finish challenges in the game.  The Shadowrun universe was nicely represented.

I always liked the gameplay of roguelikes but was never really into the typical fantasy setting they were framed in. This, though, this is neat. A space roguelike. Over half a dozen ship types all suited to different playstyles, randomized galaxies so no two playthroughs are ever the same, and a difficulty very much in-tune with the genre it comes from -- it's quite easy to get killed misjudging a situation or taking too big a risk.
Travel from encounter to encounter is turn-based (the enemy fleet pursuing you only advances when you choose to warp to the next system), but combat and ship operations are real-time. To avoid being overwhelmed by the concerns of surviving a fight in space, the pause feature (Spacebar) allows you to queue commands to execute when you unpause.
It's a fairly small game which won't offer you 8-hour playthroughs or awesome graphics, but what content it does have is well worth the price tag.

Six years is a long wait for a sequel, but it was well worth it.  In that time, Valve created their own game engine, known as Source, and with the Gravity Gun quickly became THE game to copy.  Like ClassicDOOM before it, most FPS games that came after Half-Life 2 valiantly attempted to copy the in-game physics engine that allows to to catch and repel in-game props.  Many of them succeeded, but Half-Life 2 was the first to do it, and gamers know where to give credit where credit is due.
Once again, you play as Gordon Freeman, mute savior of humankind.  Reawakened by the G-Man from the previous game "some time later," you find that the world as you know it is no longer.  The Combine have successfully invaded and subjuated humanity, and it's only a matter of time before Man becomes just another X-stamp on the Combine's evolutionary whiteboard.  Unless you can rise up to the challenge of liberating your very species, that time will approach far quicker than you'd like.
One of the first FPS games to introduce drivable vehicles, adding the Gravity Gun is just icing on this cake (that's a metaphor, not a lie).  Chock full of references and easter-eggs, Valve should be proud that their title has continued to successfully carry the FPS banner.

RoR is a platform-based rougelite where you are marooned on a hostile alien world. Collecting items to mutate your body and enhance your abilities are key to surviving the never-ending horde of incoming alien hostiles. Time is of the essence, as the horde becomes more and more aggressive as time passes.
Immediately the context is given for the game: you are alone, your goal is to survive. Depending on how you play you can be aggressive or passive in how to address the game's starting stages, but more often than not you will have to resort to running away and picking off targets before you acquire the experience and upgrades you need. Before too long you'll be strong enough to decimate colossal threats with ease -- at the aptly-named difficulty "HAHAHAHAHAHA."
Now to me, this was where there was a divergence. The startup always felt sluggish to me; kiting enemies for 20-ish minutes before becoming powerful enough to take them head on didn't feel like it was worth my time invested into it. Some may find this fun, I didn't personally. Once I'd get over that hump, the game's pacing and goal changed from survival into a killing spree. This is something that the game is self-aware of with the higher difficulty levels being "I SEE YOU", "I'M COMING FOR YOU", and "HAHAHAHAHAHA" as well as the endings for each character making mention on how they have lost their humanity/sanity during their spree.
Overall it's a challenging game to get into due to its slow and downright-disadvantaged start. However that nuance is exactly what was intended to give the player that feeling of being overwhelmed, and it exaggerates just how powerful you become when you reach lategame when you contrast it to how weak you started out.

A return to to Shadowrun is like coming back to an old friend. I used to play and love "Shadowrun" for the SNES - never played the P&P RPG - but I was too young to fully understand the world and lore. Getting back into it now, the memories have come flooding back to me, along with the old enjoyment I felt of exploring a cyberpunk world full of corporate elves and shadowrunning orks.
This is a game without voice actors, without an advanced 3D engine, and without amazing particle effects. It is, however, a game with some fantastic and moody writing (and benefits from no voice actors because of this, IMO), a memorable story, and an ending with great closure. Before I get into pointing out a few things I liked and disliked, if you're a fan of RPGs with a focus on story and setting, this game is for you.
I played once through the Dead Man's Switch campaign, and I'm still a little undecided on how I feel about the leveling system. It seems, to me, a little bit simple. It could definitely benefit from some type of "perks" system that you could put points into that allow the gameplay to vary some. As it stands, it's all a bit too straight-forward for my liking, without any real hard decisions to make. if you want to use SMGs and be a decker, you just put karma points into those two stat lines, and that's about it. It's not bad, just not great.
The story, however, is wonderful, along with the characters. Coyote is memorable, and I hope to see her appear in the next expansion as well, and it was nice to see Jake Armitage make an appearance early. It really helped ground the game in the Shadowrun lore. There was a bit of a running red herring throughout the story (at least, I'm pretty sure it was), and I was genuinely happy to see the villain turn out a bit differently than I thought.
The actual combat is a bit like a simplified version of X-COM. It's turn-based, it utilizes a rudimentary cover system, and it includes magic along with gunplay. It's fun enough, but, along with the leveling system, seems a bit on the simple side, without much variation. This could be alleviated some, I feel, by using scripting to make the combat encounters more interesting. The shoot-out in the cemetery, for example, was easily, IMO, the best encounter of the game as it added variety and surprise in the middle of the fight.
And, of course, the editor! I dabbled in this for a number of hours, and it seems perfectly robust and easy to use if you've ever modded games in the past to any extent. I have experience creating modules for Neverwinter Nights, and the Shadowrun Returns editor is mercifully easier to use when scripting, as it gives you the language to select from, instead of you having to discover it yourself.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game to those who are either Shadowrun fans, RPG fans that love a good story (and aren't afraid to read as it seems a lot of gamers are these days), or want to create your own stories using the editor. I would give Shadowrun Returns a 7.5/10.

"Shadowrun Returns" is a kickstarter funded RPG based on the cult table-top board game by FASA (who also fathered the Battletech/Mechwarrior series), but is more of a homage to it's 16-bit off-spring on the SNES. You're dropped into a futuristic world of Japanese conglomerates, and a "high-tech, low life" subculture where 80's cyberpunk ascetics have merged with old world magic. The main campaign has you playing gumshoe for your dead partner, trying to figure out who killed him (there's a hefty 10,000 NuYen reward in it for you, so how could you refuse?), and running various other side missions along the way.
The gameplay (typical RPG fodder) is padded out with a very well developed story, engrossing characters, and decisions that only affect the world around in you in small, certain instances. The graphics are nice for what they are, sprawling urban landscapes, lovely character portraits, and 3D Models that a lot of people seem to hate on (think Torchlight, but with a lot less graphical detail)
There have been some complaints made about how long the main campaign is and I guess that's fair considering how the game is a bit on the pricey side, but think of it as an investment for all the free content you're getting on the Steam Workshop. Yes, the editor is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to work with (and this is coming from somebody who doesn't know the first thing about making a game), but the amount of fan-made campaigns is growing and a lot of them are really solid and really do show the game's true potential.
Is this a game for everybody? That's hard to say. If you're a fan of the legacy that FASA left behind, RPGS, and Cyberpunk in general, then yes (whether or not you played the SNES game makes no difference). If not, then you might need to look elsewhere.

To write a review about this game (orginal dead man switch campaign) is really difficult for me. On the one hand the game is not bad and on the other hand I can't recommend it to someone who expects an RPG. Many aspects of this game are good and are a solid foundation for an RPG but the campaign is way to limited for an recommendation
+ The Charactersystem: It allows lots of different builds. Unfortunately they are not balanced and some skills won't be needed too much.
+ The interface: It was created to also work on touchpads so it can feel a bit "clunky". However I did not have any problems navigating the menus.
- The save system: The game only saves on the beginning of a map. This can be annoying but it is not the reason why I can't recommend the game to RPG gamers.
- The story/campaign: This is the my main problem with the game. It is way too linear. Don't get me wrong the story is good in introducing the world too you but all the time when I played the game I thought: "Surely after the next mission I will have more freedom to explore the world, have some more banter with companions or get better gear" In my opinion the story ends to fast, dialogues with the few interesting NPCs is very limited, no decisions which could affect the story... well the important stuff besides a good character system.
+ The graphics: I liked the graphics the only bad thing: The resolution-settings: define how far you can zoom into the game.
Long story short: The base game itself is good but I can't recommend the game with the "dead mans switch"-campaign. I hope I can recommend the game after the release of the next (dlc) campaign because as I said the game is not entirely bad it just needs a good official campaign.

I always liked the gameplay of roguelikes but was never really into the typical fantasy setting they were framed in. This, though, this is neat. A space roguelike. Over half a dozen ship types all suited to different playstyles, randomized galaxies so no two playthroughs are ever the same, and a difficulty very much in-tune with the genre it comes from -- it's quite easy to get killed misjudging a situation or taking too big a risk.
Travel from encounter to encounter is turn-based (the enemy fleet pursuing you only advances when you choose to warp to the next system), but combat and ship operations are real-time. To avoid being overwhelmed by the concerns of surviving a fight in space, the pause feature (Spacebar) allows you to queue commands to execute when you unpause.
It's a fairly small game which won't offer you 8-hour playthroughs or awesome graphics, but what content it does have is well worth the price tag.

If you enjoy tactical strategy games, you'll really enjoy this one. The story isn't bad, it actually plays to the game style very nicely.
In the field, you have access to several unit types, each with their own unique weapons and skills. You kill, or capture, aliens while doing a number of other tasks (e.g. escort) and take the information, and corpses, back to your home base. With this info you can research new equipment and abilities. While in your base you'll be able to upgrade units, build new sections of your base, order research tasks, launch satellites, scan the world for alien activity, shoot down UFOs and lots more. There's LOTS of data and information to read, though you are not required to. It is just interesting to read it all, and realize just how much work and imagination the writers and developers put into this game. It's rather amazing. Your decisions are permanent, you'll have to load a save-game to change them, and the missions can get difficult, but the overall gameplay is very relaxed. I highly recommend this title to any fan of tactical strategy games, and of the series.

text:
It plays like Dead Island during the day. In fact it's so exactly like Dead Island it's almost indistinguishable, with the exception of the parkour. At night everything goes to hell and the difficulty gets ramped up. You can unlock safe zones to sleep in, there's lockpicking, all in all it comes off as sort of a Assassins Creed (parkouring around) meets Bioshock (the macho-jerk character and storyline) meets Dead Island (gather/quest/craft/kill zombies), while your character does dumb plot-related stuff that you probably won't agree with but can't really control.
There's a skill system with many branches to unlock, and your at-first clumsy character will soon be flipping over zombies like a pro.
My only gripe, aside from the storyline being on rails (which I don't personally care about because I'm more interested in gameplay, which is solid), is that you can kick a zombie 1000 times and your foot will never wear out, break, whatever. Hit a zombie with a metal pipe 10 times and it's broken, and if you don't quickly repair it, it'll soon break. Your foot, meanwhile, outlasts pipes, knives, table legs, shovels, you name it. If you're going to put weapon durability in a game (which I don't like; do you have any idea how freaking hard it is to break a metal baseball bat? Especially with bones?) then you need to extend it to everything, and fists should sprain, tendons pop, all that, and your foot would break long before a metal pipe. Because of this, until you upgrade your skills the endless kicking and punching can make your character come off like some kind of inexhuastable, but physically very weak, Bruce Lee.

RoR is a platform-based rougelite where you are marooned on a hostile alien world. Collecting items to mutate your body and enhance your abilities are key to surviving the never-ending horde of incoming alien hostiles. Time is of the essence, as the horde becomes more and more aggressive as time passes.
Immediately the context is given for the game: you are alone, your goal is to survive. Depending on how you play you can be aggressive or passive in how to address the game's starting stages, but more often than not you will have to resort to running away and picking off targets before you acquire the experience and upgrades you need. Before too long you'll be strong enough to decimate colossal threats with ease -- at the aptly-named difficulty "HAHAHAHAHAHA."
Now to me, this was where there was a divergence. The startup always felt sluggish to me; kiting enemies for 20-ish minutes before becoming powerful enough to take them head on didn't feel like it was worth my time invested into it. Some may find this fun, I didn't personally. Once I'd get over that hump, the game's pacing and goal changed from survival into a killing spree. This is something that the game is self-aware of with the higher difficulty levels being "I SEE YOU", "I'M COMING FOR YOU", and "HAHAHAHAHAHA" as well as the endings for each character making mention on how they have lost their humanity/sanity during their spree.
Overall it's a challenging game to get into due to its slow and downright-disadvantaged start. However that nuance is exactly what was intended to give the player that feeling of being overwhelmed, and it exaggerates just how powerful you become when you reach lategame when you contrast it to how weak you started out.

Six years is a long wait for a sequel, but it was well worth it.  In that time, Valve created their own game engine, known as Source, and with the Gravity Gun quickly became THE game to copy.  Like ClassicDOOM before it, most FPS games that came after Half-Life 2 valiantly attempted to copy the in-game physics engine that allows to to catch and repel in-game props.  Many of them succeeded, but Half-Life 2 was the first to do it, and gamers know where to give credit where credit is due.
Once again, you play as Gordon Freeman, mute savior of humankind.  Reawakened by the G-Man from the previous game "some time later," you find that the world as you know it is no longer.  The Combine have successfully invaded and subjuated humanity, and it's only a matter of time before Man becomes just another X-stamp on the Combine's evolutionary whiteboard.  Unless you can rise up to the challenge of liberating your very species, that time will approach far quicker than you'd like.
One of the first FPS games to introduce drivable vehicles, adding the Gravity Gun is just icing on this cake (that's a metaphor, not a lie).  Chock full of references and easter-eggs, Valve should be proud that their title has continued to successfully carry the FPS banner.

Killing Floor 2 is a great co-op shooter which pits up to 6 players against a horde of a variety of different "zeds", genetically engineered monsters that wish to tear, grind, stab, burn, and pulverize you and your friends. This isnt just another FPS however, the 2004 mod was one of the first to introduce classes (called perks in the game) to the co-op horde genre. The classes all focus on filling special niches in team composition and use specific weapons to fill them. Some of the more unique ones include Demolitionist, a class based around stunning enemies and delivering explosive damage; Beserker, a class that uses only melee weapons and utilizes the parry and block skills to negate damage and stumble large zeds; Firebug, a croud control class that has access to fire and microwave weaponry, and at this point those are only 3 of the 9 available unique perks in the game. Weapons feel powerful and fun to use due to being animated at extreme framerates, this done to display incredible amounts of detail when the game goes into slow-mo, or "zed-time."  At this point in Killing Floor 2's development, the game is polished, fun, flashy, full of depth and replay value. As you go up in difficulty, you'll see zeds do new moves such as utilize their weapons in different ways, block and evade, and even spawn as champion versions which spice up the gameplay and keep even the skilled player on their toes. Even after you max out all your perks to the highest level (which will net you at least 300 hours) you'll find yourself still coming back for more of that visceral action. I definitely recommend this as a top tier cooperative shooter which is all too hard to come across these days.

At it's launch, Arkham Knight was teeming with bugs and glitches that made the game near unplayable due to such an abominable port. Since then however, the game has been patched and through my experience is near bug-free at the time of this review.
The story is well-written and executed as it gives the phenomenal series closure in an thrilling and entertaining way. The series is especially nostalgic for fans of the Batman comics as well as the previous games as it reminds you that this is the conclusion of something bigger than an individual game and truly serves the Batman character justice.
Combat is extremely entertaining and engineered in a way that simply prevents it from ever becoming boring as is but is complimented with numerous special moves and takendowns as well as a massive arsenal of gadgets to aid you in your endeavors.
The city is unimaginably expansive and thoroughly designed which makes free-roaming really enjoyable but at the same time, incorporates a story that has you fly from building to building to progress onto the game. You will almost never feel that you are confined to a linear hall-way as this game forces you to get out there and explore the city around you which is bustling with life and thugs just waiting to be taken down.
The incorporation of the Batmobile is anticipated but rather forced as there are certain enemies and puzzles in the game that require you to use the Batmobile to defeat them which becomes stale fast.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to newcomers and fans of this series alike as this is the definite superhero video game experience and has raised the bar high for others to come.

Risk of Rain is a 2D platforming shooter that puts you on a hostile planet full of alien creatures. The enemies are randomly added and spawn in. While the game has random levels, after 7+ hours of play, you start to recognize that there are random levels with extra frills on them to make them feel as if they were generated. The object of each level is to make it to the teleporter that is randomly placed somewhere on the map. Once you activate it, you need to survive for 90 seconds. A countdown clock appears and soon after a boss emerges and you get swamped with enemies that spawn into the area. A lot of times they spawn on you. Once the 90 seconds are up, then you need to kill the remaining creatures including the boss before you hop in the teleporter to the next level.
Along the way you'll find plenty of items and power ups that do some interesting and fun things. Some give you a chance to make enemies freeze, bleed or slow down. Others help with regenerating your health. Another will a barbed wire shield around you while others turn dead enemies into ghosts that will fight for you. There are dozens of these items. You don't just keep one, they stack, so you can end up with a dozen on you and not just that, but if you get the same one on the same play through they increase the effectiveness. Two feathers means you can now jump twice in the air instead of just once.
Its more than just passive items, there are usable items that will do things like shoot a cluster of missiles, replenish your health or unlock all the treasure chests on screen. These items have a very long cool down timer, usually around a 45 - 60 seconds. You can even spend money to repair drones that either shoot bullets, lasers or heal you with a green beam. They're so nice to have, especially two of them.
You'll find these items from beating bosses, in treasure chests, stores, imp statues and chance statues. The stores give you a choice of three items. Once you buy one, all three disappear. The treasure chests give you a random item and cost gold to open it. The chance statues and imp statues also cost gold. As you get to higher levels, the amounts increase. The chance statues are just that, a chance to get an item. Sometimes these statues cost you health. The more you try, the higher the price. The imp statues release five imps that simply run away from you and you need to kill them all to get your prize. These are all ways to keep the game interesting.
The controls are simple, you can move left and right, climb up and down on ladders and jump. Each character has four abilities. Three of which have cool downs. So you have unlimited ammunition, just a timer before you can use them again. To start, you've got a standard fire button that shoots a short burst each half a second. Its not like a machine gun, but at least you can hold down the trigger. Rapidly pulling the trigger will shoot faster, but only if the gun animation has gone away. So not all characters will shoot faster. Depending on the character you have all sorts of range and damage output.
From there, you've got a defensive move. The commando has a combat roll to go through enemies.  The enforcer has a shield that he will drop down making him incredibly slow, but protected  from the front. The Bandit has a smoke bomb that makes him invincible for three seconds. Enemies stop chasing you and so on. There are 9+ other characters, but well after 7+ hours, that's all I was able to unlock. These different characters really feel a lot different from one another.
What I really don't like is a few times if I want to quickly turn and fire. I'll turn enough so my character will start moving the other way, but when I fire, he will turn around to shoot, then keep running the way he was directed. It seems to happen pretty consistently, especially as the bandit. Even dropping the guardian's shield he will turn around to drop the shield. It is just odd. It has cost me lives and wasted abilities, not to mention special weapons that I need to wait 45 seconds to reuse.
You have a good amount of health and it regenerates very slowly over time. Of course every enemy has a good amount of health too. This makes weapons feel pretty powerless. It takes several shots to take down lesser enemies and with larger enemies that have more health, I found myself sitting there just waiting. Perfectly safe, but waiting far too long for my character to kill them. Luckily there is a leveling up system that will give you more health and damage output, but as the clock ticks away, the enemies get stronger and more powerful. Its just really dull having to kill a clump of five strong enemies all batched together. I could put a rubber band on my 360 controller and walk away for a minute. The game just feels like one big grind. You can always get items that add a chance of homing missiles or a chance of mortars, but even then it doesn't help all that much.
The game feels slow getting from point A to point B. I'd dread knowing that I'd have to go back somewhere. The character feels like he moves slow, the weapons feel powerless. Its not quick action like Contra or Mega Man. Its all deliberate to prolong the experience. You have a nice wide view of the area, so you get a better sense of where to go, because your character is so slow that if you zoomed in on the action, it would take that much longer to find where you're going. I'm just happy that the experience and gold that falls from enemies automatically flies to you from wherever it is. Having to pick it up would be painful.
Like in the real world, you only have one life. When you die, that's it you need to start over, but hopefully you've made it far enough on your previous play through to unlock new items that you'll find in future play throughs. It always drives you to keep going like oo a new thing. Now all I need to do is play again and hope to randomly find it somewhere.
The enemies are pretty brainless, that's what allows them to just let me shoot them. I think because they all have so much health they need to be brainless. There are some enemies smart enough to jump up onto platforms to follow you and chase you around, but they're not smart enough to jump over gaps. Floating jellyfish will seek you out, fly through platforms and dart toward you at some point. The bosses are pretty iffy as well.
When you get to the teleporter and enemies start transporting in, I found myself getting randomly overwhelmed, because the foes would spawn in on top of me. So then I'd have to run away and keep moving for the 90 seconds or I'd quickly be dead. You don't get brief invincibility when you get hit. Enemies can keep right in you attacking unless you're fast enough to run away or use one of the defensive tactics like roll, smoke bomb or drop a shield. Even if you get good at running away, at some point, there are enemies that can teleport straight on you. Just poof, they're now in you. Do you shoot left or right? Well you occupy the same space, so your guess is as good as mine.
As for the music and graphics, both are great. The music excels at being something spacy and other worldly. The graphics look small and old school. I think these two came together to improve the experience I had and made me want to stay in game, because I know it was a struggle against the grind.
If you want to play cooperatively, you'll need to have a friend with you, have a LAN connection or an IP address. There is no play through Steam. I'm not sure if I enjoyed the game. Even playing with a friend, it wasn't that fun. I hate to be the only person that didn't enjoy the game. I don't feel like I had fun playing the game, when this game should be right up my alley. I like random stuff, I like good combat and somewhat random levels, but I just feel like I would have enjoyed it more with a faster pace.

It plays like Dead Island during the day. In fact it's so exactly like Dead Island it's almost indistinguishable, with the exception of the parkour. At night everything goes to hell and the difficulty gets ramped up. You can unlock safe zones to sleep in, there's lockpicking, all in all it comes off as sort of a Assassins Creed (parkouring around) meets Bioshock (the macho-jerk character and storyline) meets Dead Island (gather/quest/craft/kill zombies), while your character does dumb plot-related stuff that you probably won't agree with but can't really control.
There's a skill system with many branches to unlock, and your at-first clumsy character will soon be flipping over zombies like a pro.
My only gripe, aside from the storyline being on rails (which I don't personally care about because I'm more interested in gameplay, which is solid), is that you can kick a zombie 1000 times and your foot will never wear out, break, whatever. Hit a zombie with a metal pipe 10 times and it's broken, and if you don't quickly repair it, it'll soon break. Your foot, meanwhile, outlasts pipes, knives, table legs, shovels, you name it. If you're going to put weapon durability in a game (which I don't like; do you have any idea how freaking hard it is to break a metal baseball bat? Especially with bones?) then you need to extend it to everything, and fists should sprain, tendons pop, all that, and your foot would break long before a metal pipe. Because of this, until you upgrade your skills the endless kicking and punching can make your character come off like some kind of inexhuastable, but physically very weak, Bruce Lee.

I've played the series since they first appeared and I'm an X-Com fan, you may take my recommendation with a grain of salt :)
The first one (UFO Defense) was a blast. It is one of my most treasured games of all time. It involved a LOT of micromanagement, from the "which kind of ammo" for certain weapons (explosive, incendiary, armor piercing...) to buy (yes, you need to actually buy ammo), to the soldiers selection based on the stats (recruitment involved). You even have to hire scientists, engineers and so on. And then you have the "proper" game, the action. OMG, it was difficult, but really addictive.
XCOM EU is a different game, not just the same one with better graphics, easier interface and "dumbed down" micromanagement. No. A different animal. A beautiful and different animal. Is more focused on the action (TBS)... and its really well executed.
I like to play it on a slow pace, enjoying every bit of it. Right now, I'm around 30 hours, and maybe 50% complete... and I'm not tired of it AT ALL... can't stop playing it. You have to understand that 30 hours is a lot to me, because I can only play about an hour per day (if I'm lucky)... and add my backlog to that... 30 hours is really good, I really have to love the game to reach that.
If you liked the original X-Com, trust me, you'll love this one. Maybe you'll miss some aspects, but you'll like all the new perspective. If you don't know the originals, don't worry, you'll love this one even more

Finished Dead Man's Switch and I really enjoyed myself. I am new to all things Shadowrun and this experience made me very interested in researching some of it's older lore from it's table top stuff.
The idea of building a up character in a main campaign then being able to continue their story with mods like skyrim is just awesome to me.
I must admit the story for Dead Man's Switch was... good and bad. Good being detective story with a few really good plot twists. Bad being how they represent a certain native/american and black man.
Parts of the story felt a bit racially awkward in not just character design but in execution of the way they acted. I get they are going for stereotypes with elves being rich♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bags and Orcs being big and a bit derp but when it extends to magical native/american or black man it just feels wrong. But at the same time this game pushes for racial equality. A Troll in your hub will talk your ear off about it from time to time.
It's like when you watch a popular movie from the 80s or early 90s and they have the overly stereotyped exchange student in an all white cast. It is super cringe worthy and I believe that at the time it wasn't made out of hate but out of ignorance and how different = silly or at least entertaining. It felt lazy and bad. I am not sure how this made it into the final game but there it is.
Why am I recommending this? Well a lot of the first story should have never happened, but the game play is well designed and the combat is fun and challenging. I look forward to playing modded original stories from this engine and I may make content for it.
Also the save system works but is just clunky and bad... and at 80% and in their face how the ♥♥♥♥ do my shots keep missing?!?!? F%@#$%@ing seriously?!?!!!!!
TL;DR
"Dead Man Switch Campaign"'s story includes racist bits that echo early 1980s writing and decision making in media. F##$ it! get it anyway for the Mod community and the game design. PC master race.

Awesome turn-based fun!
If you compare this to "Classic XCOM", then yeah, this game is streamlined and feels almost arcadey. But if you are able to look past the changes from the classic formula and view this as a spiritual successor, even with all it's flaws and bugs (and let's be honest: there are a lot of flaws and bugs in this game), then what awaits you is a tactical turn-based game that is addictive, fun and challenging.
The basic premise is: Aliens attack Earth & you are in charge of THE one and only supranational organization to fend them off.
You research technology, build a secret undergound base and command squads of soldiers on battlefields with various objectives against tactically diverse monstruos foes.
If you fail on the battlefield then your carefully trained and equipped soldiers are doomed. If you fail too much, then the entire earth is doomed.
Why can you only have one single dropship to deploy one single squad of soldiers out of a choice of multiple simultaneous threats?
Well, because choices! Choices are hard. Choices have consequences! Choices are fun! And it's awesome.
When you groom your soldiers for greatness and then are forced to watch them die horribly on the battlefield you are instantly greeted by the gravity of the consequences of your own terrible decisions (unless the game screws you over, as it does, sometimes, as you may or may not find out).
What? You thought your sniper could make that 70% shot and survive his bout with an angry hulking brute carrying heavy weaponry? Well, tough luck, Commander! Sometimes XCOM will be harsh to you.
Other times, though, when all hope seems lost, the day is unexpectedly saved by a carefully placed rocket and an unlikely shot that miraculously hits against all odds!
So even with all of this game's flaws (of which I've actually mentioned none in particular - but trust me, the game has them) it's a hell of lot of fun, and for $10 - $15 this game is a bloody bargain.
If you can even imagine yourself playing a tactical turn-based game then I recommend you give XCOM: Enemy Unknown a chance.
Actually, there is a DEMO available for this game. Try before you buy, if you are unsure.
The basic game should last you a couple dozen hours and you do not necessarily need the DLC's if you're just trying this game out.
However I would highly recommend you also buy the brand-new expansion pack XCOM: Enemy Within as soon as you find out that you enjoy this game and are willing to throw much more cash at the developers, as it adds much more content and replayability to the main game by adding gameplay-balancing changes, a new hostile faction, many many new maps, new items, a new resource, new abilities and cybernetic robot-suits for your own troops!
Be aware that Enemy Within consists of  and adds content to the same campaign from Enemy Unknown, but you will have to start an entirely new game when you decide to play it.
It is NOT possible to transfer over your progress (research, resources, troops) from an earlier EU campaign!!!
The "Slingshot" DLC is also nice to have, as long as you buy it cheap. All it does is add 3 extra missions that give you a highly trained squad-member and a massive resource- and research-bonus once you complete all 3 missions.
Are you still reading this? Stop it. Stop it now. Get out there and stop them aliens, Commander!
P.S.: if you think that the changes made to the Classic XCOM formula are absolutely horrible and you demand complex micromanagement then may I suggest you take a look at XENONAUTS (find it here on Steam), which I haven't played and which is still work in progress, but is an actually faithful unofficial remake of the Classic XCOM / UFO game.
