Risk of Rain is a 2D platforming shooter that puts you on a hostile planet full of alien creatures. The enemies are randomly added and spawn in. While the game has random levels, after 7+ hours of play, you start to recognize that there are random levels with extra frills on them to make them feel as if they were generated. The object of each level is to make it to the teleporter that is randomly placed somewhere on the map. Once you activate it, you need to survive for 90 seconds. A countdown clock appears and soon after a boss emerges and you get swamped with enemies that spawn into the area. A lot of times they spawn on you. Once the 90 seconds are up, then you need to kill the remaining creatures including the boss before you hop in the teleporter to the next level.
Along the way you'll find plenty of items and power ups that do some interesting and fun things. Some give you a chance to make enemies freeze, bleed or slow down. Others help with regenerating your health. Another will a barbed wire shield around you while others turn dead enemies into ghosts that will fight for you. There are dozens of these items. You don't just keep one, they stack, so you can end up with a dozen on you and not just that, but if you get the same one on the same play through they increase the effectiveness. Two feathers means you can now jump twice in the air instead of just once.
Its more than just passive items, there are usable items that will do things like shoot a cluster of missiles, replenish your health or unlock all the treasure chests on screen. These items have a very long cool down timer, usually around a 45 - 60 seconds. You can even spend money to repair drones that either shoot bullets, lasers or heal you with a green beam. They're so nice to have, especially two of them.
You'll find these items from beating bosses, in treasure chests, stores, imp statues and chance statues. The stores give you a choice of three items. Once you buy one, all three disappear. The treasure chests give you a random item and cost gold to open it. The chance statues and imp statues also cost gold. As you get to higher levels, the amounts increase. The chance statues are just that, a chance to get an item. Sometimes these statues cost you health. The more you try, the higher the price. The imp statues release five imps that simply run away from you and you need to kill them all to get your prize. These are all ways to keep the game interesting.
The controls are simple, you can move left and right, climb up and down on ladders and jump. Each character has four abilities. Three of which have cool downs. So you have unlimited ammunition, just a timer before you can use them again. To start, you've got a standard fire button that shoots a short burst each half a second. Its not like a machine gun, but at least you can hold down the trigger. Rapidly pulling the trigger will shoot faster, but only if the gun animation has gone away. So not all characters will shoot faster. Depending on the character you have all sorts of range and damage output.
From there, you've got a defensive move. The commando has a combat roll to go through enemies.  The enforcer has a shield that he will drop down making him incredibly slow, but protected  from the front. The Bandit has a smoke bomb that makes him invincible for three seconds. Enemies stop chasing you and so on. There are 9+ other characters, but well after 7+ hours, that's all I was able to unlock. These different characters really feel a lot different from one another.
What I really don't like is a few times if I want to quickly turn and fire. I'll turn enough so my character will start moving the other way, but when I fire, he will turn around to shoot, then keep running the way he was directed. It seems to happen pretty consistently, especially as the bandit. Even dropping the guardian's shield he will turn around to drop the shield. It is just odd. It has cost me lives and wasted abilities, not to mention special weapons that I need to wait 45 seconds to reuse.
You have a good amount of health and it regenerates very slowly over time. Of course every enemy has a good amount of health too. This makes weapons feel pretty powerless. It takes several shots to take down lesser enemies and with larger enemies that have more health, I found myself sitting there just waiting. Perfectly safe, but waiting far too long for my character to kill them. Luckily there is a leveling up system that will give you more health and damage output, but as the clock ticks away, the enemies get stronger and more powerful. Its just really dull having to kill a clump of five strong enemies all batched together. I could put a rubber band on my 360 controller and walk away for a minute. The game just feels like one big grind. You can always get items that add a chance of homing missiles or a chance of mortars, but even then it doesn't help all that much.
The game feels slow getting from point A to point B. I'd dread knowing that I'd have to go back somewhere. The character feels like he moves slow, the weapons feel powerless. Its not quick action like Contra or Mega Man. Its all deliberate to prolong the experience. You have a nice wide view of the area, so you get a better sense of where to go, because your character is so slow that if you zoomed in on the action, it would take that much longer to find where you're going. I'm just happy that the experience and gold that falls from enemies automatically flies to you from wherever it is. Having to pick it up would be painful.
Like in the real world, you only have one life. When you die, that's it you need to start over, but hopefully you've made it far enough on your previous play through to unlock new items that you'll find in future play throughs. It always drives you to keep going like oo a new thing. Now all I need to do is play again and hope to randomly find it somewhere.
The enemies are pretty brainless, that's what allows them to just let me shoot them. I think because they all have so much health they need to be brainless. There are some enemies smart enough to jump up onto platforms to follow you and chase you around, but they're not smart enough to jump over gaps. Floating jellyfish will seek you out, fly through platforms and dart toward you at some point. The bosses are pretty iffy as well.
When you get to the teleporter and enemies start transporting in, I found myself getting randomly overwhelmed, because the foes would spawn in on top of me. So then I'd have to run away and keep moving for the 90 seconds or I'd quickly be dead. You don't get brief invincibility when you get hit. Enemies can keep right in you attacking unless you're fast enough to run away or use one of the defensive tactics like roll, smoke bomb or drop a shield. Even if you get good at running away, at some point, there are enemies that can teleport straight on you. Just poof, they're now in you. Do you shoot left or right? Well you occupy the same space, so your guess is as good as mine.
As for the music and graphics, both are great. The music excels at being something spacy and other worldly. The graphics look small and old school. I think these two came together to improve the experience I had and made me want to stay in game, because I know it was a struggle against the grind.
If you want to play cooperatively, you'll need to have a friend with you, have a LAN connection or an IP address. There is no play through Steam. I'm not sure if I enjoyed the game. Even playing with a friend, it wasn't that fun. I hate to be the only person that didn't enjoy the game. I don't feel like I had fun playing the game, when this game should be right up my alley. I like random stuff, I like good combat and somewhat random levels, but I just feel like I would have enjoyed it more with a faster pace.

I've played the series since they first appeared and I'm an X-Com fan, you may take my recommendation with a grain of salt :)
The first one (UFO Defense) was a blast. It is one of my most treasured games of all time. It involved a LOT of micromanagement, from the "which kind of ammo" for certain weapons (explosive, incendiary, armor piercing...) to buy (yes, you need to actually buy ammo), to the soldiers selection based on the stats (recruitment involved). You even have to hire scientists, engineers and so on. And then you have the "proper" game, the action. OMG, it was difficult, but really addictive.
XCOM EU is a different game, not just the same one with better graphics, easier interface and "dumbed down" micromanagement. No. A different animal. A beautiful and different animal. Is more focused on the action (TBS)... and its really well executed.
I like to play it on a slow pace, enjoying every bit of it. Right now, I'm around 30 hours, and maybe 50% complete... and I'm not tired of it AT ALL... can't stop playing it. Awesome turn-based fun!
If you compare this to "Classic XCOM", then yeah, this game is streamlined and feels almost arcadey. But if you are able to look past the changes from the classic formula and view this as a spiritual successor, even with all it's flaws and bugs (and let's be honest: there are a lot of flaws and bugs in this game), then what awaits you is a tactical turn-based game that is addictive, fun and challenging.
The basic premise is: Aliens attack Earth & you are in charge of THE one and only supranational organization to fend them off.
You research technology, build a secret undergound base and command squads of soldiers on battlefields with various objectives against tactically diverse monstruos foes.
If you fail on the battlefield then your carefully trained and equipped soldiers are doomed. If you fail too much, then the entire earth is doomed.
Why can you only have one single dropship to deploy one single squad of soldiers out of a choice of multiple simultaneous threats?
Well, because choices! Choices are hard. Choices have consequences! Choices are fun! And it's awesome.
When you groom your soldiers for greatness and then are forced to watch them die horribly on the battlefield you are instantly greeted by the gravity of the consequences of your own terrible decisions (unless the game screws you over, as it does, sometimes, as you may or may not find out).
What? You thought your sniper could make that 70% shot and survive his bout with an angry hulking brute carrying heavy weaponry? Well, tough luck, Commander! Sometimes XCOM will be harsh to you.
Other times, though, when all hope seems lost, the day is unexpectedly saved by a carefully placed rocket and an unlikely shot that miraculously hits against all odds!
So even with all of this game's flaws (of which I've actually mentioned none in particular - but trust me, the game has them) it's a hell of lot of fun, and for $10 - $15 this game is a bloody bargain.
If you can even imagine yourself playing a tactical turn-based game then I recommend you give XCOM: Enemy Unknown a chance.
Actually, there is a DEMO available for this game. Try before you buy, if you are unsure.
The basic game should last you a couple dozen hours and you do not necessarily need the DLC's if you're just trying this game out.
However I would highly recommend you also buy the brand-new expansion pack XCOM: Enemy Within as soon as you find out that you enjoy this game and are willing to throw much more cash at the developers, as it adds much more content and replayability to the main game by adding gameplay-balancing changes, a new hostile faction, many many new maps, new items, a new resource, new abilities and cybernetic robot-suits for your own troops!
Be aware that Enemy Within consists of  and adds content to the same campaign from Enemy Unknown, but you will have to start an entirely new game when you decide to play it.
It is NOT possible to transfer over your progress (research, resources, troops) from an earlier EU campaign!!!
The "Slingshot" DLC is also nice to have, as long as you buy it cheap. All it does is add 3 extra missions that give you a highly trained squad-member and a massive resource- and research-bonus once you complete all 3 missions.
Are you still reading this? Stop it. Stop it now. Get out there and stop them aliens, Commander!
P.S.: if you think that the changes made to the Classic XCOM formula are absolutely horrible and you demand complex micromanagement then may I suggest you take a look at XENONAUTS (find it here on Steam), which I haven't played and which is still work in progress, but is an actually faithful unofficial remake of the Classic XCOM / UFO game.

Killing Floor 2 has gone through an Early Access hell, it was done very poorly, thankfully a while after the Gunslinger was added, Tripwire finally got their act together and made this game the amazing gory HD Sequel that it was meant to be.

All the original perks have returned along with some new ones to help wipe out the Zed hordes! These include the SWAT, the Gunslinger and an upcoming perk! It was originally called the Martial artist, sadly it has been scrapped and being reworked to a new perk, what will it be? We will find out soon.

The original KF1 XP system was horrid, Sharpshooters and Berserkers got a huge advantage since you started with a pistol which gives XP to the Sharpshooter perk, while the knife gave Berserkers XP, and no other perk started with their own weapon until level 5 which can take ages to reach, plus some perks required you to do objectives to earn XP, like Commandos had to kill stalkers in the thousands ontop of doing a ton of damage to level up.
In KF2 there's none of that, you do get bonus XP for doing certain things like healing, but thankfully everyone starts with a perk weapon, the knife and pistol are Perk Neutral, and gaining XP from kills is the main way to level up.

All of them are back and they look awesome! They all look scary and hearing a Fleshpound/Scrake spawn sends shivers in my back, and seeing them makes me run for the hills even faster then in KF1. The best normal looking Zed for me is the Husk, in the original they looked alright, but here they glow, and blast you with flames violently to get a kill! We also get 3 new Zeds, two of them are variants of the Clot. The third is a boss who I won't spoil for anyone c: Plus we are getting another boss soon, meaning we will have 3!

Ever since I bought this game back on it's EA Release Day, I was amazed by the guns, they look amazing, they sound brilliant and they feel real. People say CS:GO's guns are good, but that statement is crushed by KF2's guns, they are just soooooo good!

And that's the best bit, while some new mechanics like sprinting and melee bashing are introduced, it feels like I'm playing KF1 again, but in sexy HD along with some badass guns! Tripwire kept it safe and didn't change the gameplay too much, so old fans will hop in KF2 quite easily!

From every class having a unique knife, to playing with your weapons by pressing the reload key, to the Zeds locked up in pens and messing around, the fires burning a broken Eiffel Tower, this game has a lot of small details!
From doing the training course, drop system, and doing certain achievements, you can get yourself a nice inventory quite shortly, just don't expect to get super rare stuff from buying nothing.
This is understandable since KF1 has been out longer, but right now KF1 has more weapons and event themed Zeds, which this game will hopefully get as time passes.
While we do have a nice cast of characters, a lot of them from the old game are missing, so if you enjoyed playing as the Steampunk Characters or D.A.R or the Chikenator, then you’re gonna be sad, they might return though.
KF2 takes place all over Europe instead of just being confined to the UK, so all the British Charm and voicelines are gone from the first game, thankfully if you own KF1, you get 2 Classic characters who have the infamous voicelines we all know and love!
At least Ash Harding is gone, that stupid ♥♥♥♥♥ makes me want to rip my ears off from her horrible voice.

A brilliant re-boot of a classic franchise, XCOM: Enemy Unknown puts players in charge of a shadowy mulit-national task force charged with defending Earth from alien invasion. There are essentially two games here; the first layer tasks players with strategic base management. From here, they will research technology, diplomacy, base and equipment construction, and personnel. The second layer of the game is the tactical turn-based squad battles. Some battles give the player certain assignments, such as escorting a VIP or capturing rather than killiing a hostile. Each shot counts, and failure could mean the permanent loss of agents. Each decision made, whether in the strategic map or the tactical battle map feels genuinely compelling. If you are a strategy fan, you don't want to miss out on XCOM.:EU!

FTL manages to be fun and cruel at the same time.  You have the highs of blasting an automated ship to dust in a single salvo, and of having your Mantis boarding party wipe out the crew of a pirate ship so you can plunder some much needed fuel. FTL.  I recommend it.  It just hurts so good.

This game requires you to think ahead short term and long term. Where does this missile go? Do I use this missile and drain the total number of missiles I have in order to do more damage? Do I buy upgrades for my ship now, or wait for a shop to have the possibility of getting mind-blowingly over powered weapons and augmentations? Half-Life 2 is a classic that set itself apart from the rest of pc games near the end of 2004 when it was released. I've had the pleasure of diving back into the world of Gordon Freeman and I must say that it still holds up. For a game that has aged over ten years, the nostalgia is definetly inescapable. After pressing the "New Game" option, I was happily reinvited by the notorious, mysterious, and ethereal like G-Man who was only so happy to see my return aswell. At mine and Gordon Freeman's expense, we were allowed to rediscover the world of Half-Life where humanity has been enslaved by a super advanced race of extra terrestrials who entered our world through the means of teleportation that humanity had previously uncovered and prescipitated the resonance cascade event during Half-Life 1.
The graphics and detail are still appreciated and admired by this reviewer. Although dated, it's easy to understand why Gabe Newell (Half-Life's creator) was happy with his Source engine. Even today I can lose myself in well mapped areas and enemies that will stop at almost nothing to bring down the Freeman. The sounds of gunfire and explosion still hold an amazing level of quality, especially when you're in the midst of a firefight against Combine forces and the human/vortigaunt rebels who seek to take back their worlds from their oppressive overlords. The feeling of dropping enemies in their tracks with a shotgun or any of the others assortment of weapons is memorable and satifying. You truly feel like a force to be reckoned with.
Vehicles and other mountables are implemented very well into the world, and rarely do you find any issues with them. Sometimes you may find the occasional hiccup where your boat or buggy will hit some innocuous object in the ground or sticking out of wall, but it's negligible since it's so much darn fun. However, transitional maps can ruin that intense feeling of speed and chases with loading times that seem to come far too often. Half-Life 2 is a game from over a decade ago, so it's forgivable. Ai also does has it's ups and downs. At most times they can coordinate well and truely give you a formidable fight, but at other times they just seem so daft when they have issues navigating their way through a doorway or any other bottlenecked areas. It's funny to see enemies push through areas like the Stooges having a bad day sometimes.
Half-Life 2 holds itself together well in an age where games are being pushed out faster and faster through the factory belt. We can only hope for a sequel and give it many praises for being a foundation of many other successful games.

- It sometimes forgets units that haven't acted
- The AI is slightly pathetic, starting wars against someone several hundreds of years of research ahead of them.

- The game gets long-winded after a while. It usually ends with me fortifying all units and going for the scientific victory
- Why can't I do blind research?
Here are a few things that Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri does way better
* Whilst simple, I don't feel that the AI is as stupid as in CIV V
* The unit designer! I always skip the regular Terraformer (Infantry chassis) for a rover-based terraformer with more movement. How does "Clean Planetbuster" sound? (Not possible in the expansion).
* Topography clearly visible in the maps.
* Blind research within 4 major fields. This is one of the key points I really like this.
* A few different automation modes for your terraformers.
If you can accept that Alpha Centauri is getting on in years (1999) and its graphics, sound and design is very simple, then I'd recommend you play that instead.

They did fix their mistakes with the quality of the programming so it is a playable game.  Things look good.  You do have controls that are usable with controller or with mouse and keyboard.  It is kind of good from that viewpoint.
But I am unhappy with a good portion of the story.  I just doubt the characters would do certain things that happen in the story.  I also feel that far too many convenient events happen to be reasonable.  The oddities beging to seem a bit silly after a while.
As for the actual gameplay, it generally works pretty well but at times gets a bit glitchy and foolish.  Having to try three or four times to jump off a ledge and glide.  Pushing one direction and batman goes a different direction for several moments.  Throwing punches that land on the target but don't hit the target so it gets it's free punch.
The little things build up small annoyances and frustrations all to be topped off with needlessly annoying and frequent taunting from enemies in the open areas.  Can't go to an area to gather riddler trophies and riddler taunts you for being too stupid.  Getting insulted could be character background if it wasn't so stupid and constant.  It was put in as a sort of hint towards where to find stuff, but it's just insults so it was done very badly.
Then of course any failure screen takes about a minute of time to get from the fail to the restart.  Other scenes where they deny you control of your character for a ridiculous amount of time even though you know exactly what you want to do.  It all adds up to be a frustrating game.  Pretty good and playable.  Something that most players can complete pretty well, but it really will pile up the annoyances on you.
It's okay, and a continuation of the Arkham games, but they are getting pretty lousy at making games.

Dying Light, breathes life back into Zombies. Maybe. From the get go I personally ran into frame rate issues and huge lag spikes. But, whether or not that's just ol' bossy needing an upgrade or the actual game time will tell. The first thing I did was turn motion blur off; no one needs it, and no one wants it. The story, at the outset, is believable; starting off with a run in with bandits- because of course there are bandits- and then meeting the good survivors.
The combat is visceral and strongly reminds me of Condemned. Messy, brutal combat is made only better by having a strategic element. One of this games boasts, the free running mechanic, runs like Mirror's Edge, except less nausea inducing. I rolled my eyes when the game brought in weapon degradation but was drawn back in when the game told me that you can't just constantly repair your broken weapons, instead you have to have certain parts to repair certain weapons and certain weapons can only be repaired a certain amount of times. One of the notable bits are the 'special preorder exclusive' buildable weapons. But they don't appear to be game breaking, just an extra option you get for preordering the game.
Pros and cons taken in, Dying Light reminds of what Dead Island was going to be before it became Dead Island. The game has it's bugs, various zombies becoming one with cars and in a two hour game time I feel through the world map once. But this is forgivable, given how much fun and generally interesting the game and story are shaping up to be. For some reason, despite all sense of good sense the jump button on the controller is mapped to the right button instead of A, like in most other controller supportive video games. And it doesn't appear that you can change the lay out, so, that's something that might need reviewing. All in all, I'd recommend Dying Light to anyone who likes zombies, free running around an open city, and brutal Condemned-esc combat.

So here is what I have to say after a night with much less sleep than I should have got.
Dying Light is going to get compaired to Techland's previous title Dead Island a lot. And it is fair that it is, because a lot of thing, big and small, feel so similar to it. However, don't let that part put you off. Really. Don't.
In Dead Island, much of the combat felt like a bunch of little one on ones, with no real interaction with "the mob". While it feels like I don't have the reach I would think I do, the free running feels great. It may be quite easy to fall off a pipe you run on, at least at first. After a bit, you will have the motions down a bit more like second nature.
In summary, what I am saying is this is five times better than what Dead Island was.

A fun throwback to the isometric RPGs of the past. Shadowrun Returns (SR) can be very enjoyable so long as your expectations are set at a reasonable level. Even though the main campaign is relatively short (8-10 hours), I did not have high hopes for the game and ended up sinking over 50 hours into it, thanks to some good writing, simple but fun combat and leveling mechanics, and player-made modules.
Visually, the cartoony art style is distinctive, detailed, and the colors are vibrant. This is really a matter of personal taste but the graphics have this old school quality that I like. While that’s great, one aspect I didn’t really miss about old school RPGs are the static environments. Unfortunately, SR’s environments, while nice to look at, definitely lack interactivity and life, serving as little more than pretty painted backdrops, which extends to the NPCs as well, most of whom are just standing there like cardboard cutouts. Audio wise, the music can seem generic but does fit the setting, and the combat sounds are often recycled but still feel satisfying.
I did appreciate how you could customize your character, even if the choices are limited, but it's a shame the world isn’t more responsive to your selected race and/or gender (at least in the base campaign). When you do interact with NPCs though, the dialogues are generally well-written, sometimes genuinely funny, and the descriptions are the appropriate length, never becoming needlessly long and tedious to dig through, and are fleshed out just enough to easily evoke images in your head.
The overall story of the main campaign is okay. It's linear, but that's not necessarily what weakens it, if anything it gives the game a better sense of focus and direction. The story is on to a great and intriguing start but looses some of its appeal after the somewhat cliche twist and ending. What saves the narrative experience from being boring is the unique and fascinating world of Shadowrun itself, which I didn't know much about before playing this game, but I am definately looking forward to learning more about it.
The core combat mechanics are simple and easy to get a handle on, which might be a pro or a con, depending on how long you want your learning curve to be. It’s safe to compare it to a dumbed down version of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, which is not necessarily a bad thing as it’s a very solid system. The controls only really require a mouse, but at times even just clicking on things can feel clunky and unresponsive, which can be annoying but not game breaking.
There are enough character skills to make some interesting combinations but given you can hire other team members with varying skills during story missions (called "runs"), you're never really punished for trying different character designs. Still, it's rewarding to try different approaches and find a concept that works for you, and reducing reliance on team members means you can have more money to buy better equipment.
Overall, Shadowrun Returns was one of my big surprises of 2013. It's certainly not perfect, but I suspect the game will only grow and get better with time, as the developers intend to continue their support by giving players the tools needed to make their own stories. While I haven't tried my hands at making my own content, I have played modules that have been made by others and was impressed by the level of quality that's possible.
I look forward to the official expansions and DLCs, and what the players have in store for the future of Shadowrun Returns. This is ultimately why I don't plan to uninstall this game for a long time to come.

It's the eighties, do a lot of coke and vote for Ronald Reagan.
Almost everything about this game is perfect, even on PC. Despite being one of the earlier PC ports of the 3D GTA titles it's relatively easy to control. There's a surprisingly large amount of graphics options for such an old game and especially one to come out in this time period when consoles were king in developers' eyes, so kudos to Rockstar for actually thinking this out.
I really think that the 80's are the perfect decade for GTA. The decade of decadence. Crime was getting more common, drugs were getting harder and easier to get, and the media was getting more violent. It was a time of total unhindered immoral activity. It basically screams Grand Theft Auto.
The soundtrack is amazing. I'm really into heavy metal and new wave, so I'm very biased when it comes to this kind of thing, but trust me, there's nothing like running over pedestrians in a muscle car while listening to Iron Maiden's "Two Minutes to Midnight" or fleeing from the police in a taco truck while blasting "Video Killed The Radio Star" by The Buggies.
There's a wide variety of melee weapons, and while the guns are nice I think the wide variety of weapons such as the chainsaw (straight out of Scarface) and a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥really set the tone for the game.
Tommy Vercetti is also a great character. He's beautifully two dimensional and the writers didn't try to ♥♥♥♥♥foot around that. He's a cold blooded Mafia hit man who's been released from prison after killing 11 guys and he's still♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. He's not an Anti Hero like Niko Bellic who's just trying to get the American Dream, nor is he an Anti Hero like CJ who's trying to protect his neighborhood from drugs and rival gangs. He's just a really bad guy. If you cross him, he will kill you. If you mess up a job he's on, he will kill you. If you don't pay him, you guessed it, he will kill you. It's that simple. His American Dream is making others' lives a nightmare.
However, there are two things I don't like about this game though. One is the graphics. The models, especially the character models, are terrible. They haven't aged well, and the game was obviously made in 2002. This is especially noticeble when the various "sexy" female characters are onscreen, because while they are obviously human, they basically look like they had their breasts and hips glued on. The wacky 80's hairstyles have a simaler problem, as do the brightly colorerd clothes that the majority of the main characters (and Tommy himself) wear. They look as if they've been painted or nailed on to some kind of puppet or mannequin. I honestly think that the models in System Shock 2 looked better than this.
The second thing is the lack of multiplayer. Add the fact that MultiTheftAuto is terrible and you have a huge problem. I understand that when Vice City came out, the main focus was on the PS2, which at that time still didn't have online multiplayer capabilites, so it is forgivable, but still, it's disappointing.
Overall, I think this is the greatest Grand Theft Auto game out there. Yes, even better than San Andreas. It's just totally tubular.

At the time of writing this, the game is still in early access but lets ignore that and get into the reasons why a recommend this game.
To start lets talk about the graphical enhancement between this game and the first game, the difference is astonising with lighting, cleaner and sharper textures and the well improved animations.
This games perk system is way better then Killing floor 1s as it allows us to customize between two options when hitting a certian level, those being 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25. Ranking up is perfect as in the beginning it will take about a game or two to rank up and as you have a higher and higher rank it will take more time to earn more XP than the last rank.
There is a variety of weapons for each perk but at times I feel that there is not enough for most perks as you start out with the weakest weapon in your selected class and save up till round 4-5 and you already have the most powerful gun in that perk. A great example of this is the support as the starting weapon is boss and can be used up to a high round giving the player the ability to buy the AA12 just before round 5 in a 10 round server. However in the recent update Tatical Response a survey was added talking about whether new guns for perks should be added.
Zeds in this game are all the original included newer one which are mostly clot remakes with their own unique attack.
Maps in this game so far are perfect and I don't have a problem with them as there is a wide range of maps with unique themes and sizes.
Now I have not touched upon the suicidal difficulty too much and for that reason i can not give my opinion on that or Hell on Earth at all but I can tell you this. Normal on solo is too easy piece of cake, Hard is quite challenging on the boss on solo whether that be the Doctor or the patriarch. Normal and Hard depending on your level can be hard on multiplayer as depending on the amount of players in the server will boost the bosses health higher and higher. Also in games such as Hard, Suicidal and Hell on Earth enemies have new and unique attacks which don't occur in normal mode.
What im about is nothing to do with the game but has to do with Tripwire Interactive and that is the communication between the community and them. Now through the recent month updates and word from them has been quite, but with the recent update these surveys released be Tripwire them selves have been very promising as this allows us to give our opinion on something.
So my final thoughts on this game. I would'nt say it beats the first game over all but definitely improves on aspects from Killing Floor. As the review sais I strongly recommend that you play this game, early access or not it's still great. A 9/10 and for a early access game that is impressive. I'm very compassionate about this game and decided to take and hour of my day really thinking of this game, also being able to write this review is amazing, thank you for reading, and seriously play this game :)

Batman: Arkham Knight
Having owned this game for about a year I can tell you I am supremely disappointed by this title and Rocksteady. I have waited until July 2016 to release my opinion on this game.
Batman: Arkham Knight isn't a bad game per se, it just falls short in some crucial spots like game performance, which has impacted my review.
+ Nice graphics, good lighting and rain effects.
+ The concept of combat remains solid, with lots of different attacks. It's fun, albeit difficult to combo.
+ Lots of unique gadgets to use, some that make a return from previous iterations of Batman and others are entirely new.
+Very intriguing characters and a great story.
+ Riddler trophies and mini puzzles are quite enjoyable.
- This point is entirely dedicated to the batmobile which is over-used throughout the game, becoming extremely tedious. Endless drone, cobra and APC hunting in side quests with extra tanks thrown in during the main story, make batmobile involvement beyond excessive.
- Combat hotkeys are badly implemented into the game and they are unnecessarily complex...There's a crouch toggle and then a 'hold down' crouch button which makes no sense.To hide in grates I need to use the "hold down' crouch + middle mouse, but I never use 'hold down' crouch usually, since it's outdated and pointless with a toggle crouch. So I'm basically using one key for a very particular action. The game is not streamlined at all. It's the same story for combos in fights. I don't use WASD for movement, I changed this to the arrow keys - but I still need to press the 1,2,3,4 keys to execute combos, which are half way across the keyboard.
- Big technical issues at launch, which I let slide as I waited for patches to correct the problems. 6 months passed and the game still didn't run efficiently. With a Nvidia Geforce GTX 970, 8 GB of RAM and an i7 CPU, I expect Batman: Arkham Knight to work smoothly on a relatively high setting, but minor and severe FPS drops occur during batmobile pursuits and in certain areas of the game world to this day. This is a killer for the experience and very irritating.
Overall score: 7/10
Disclaimer: I've scored this game 7 because the content is fantastic, it really is. It'd be a 9/10 if it simply worked. But it doesn't, so it takes a hard hit of 2 points. It's still playable, but it should be better than what it is performance wise.

Here are my initial impressions of  the newly released game - Dying Light.
Although a "fetch this" type of game in the early stages it is clear that there are 2 main elements that are done really well.   The first being the sense of tension that come with being alone in the dark during a zombie apocalypse the second being so fearless that you can run jump and parkour your way around it all.   Of course that fearlessness subsides at night fall....
Once you get used to the way Crane handles you really do feel the sense of both horizontal and vertical freedom similar to that of an Assassins Creed game, but in a more active sense - so unlike the "remote controlled guy" its feels like you re actually a well conditioned parkour practitioner.  Its a very liberating feeling versus that of games where you often say - I could totally make it over that wall, or I could survive that fall without dying.  Cranes movement is a bright spot in the game that makes you want to just jump from place to test your limits!
It also appears that the skill trees will complement your play style and the leveling up system rewards the player for doing what they enjoy the most.  So keep hopping from rooftop to rooftop and you'll find that your agility will increase at a steady and rapid rate!  The risk/reward  of the night vs day play also adds another wrinkle to the leveling system - actions done at night earn you bonus "XP" applied to whatever skill path your action falls under.
The melee weapons also provide a good thud and if you are use to melee type games like 7DTD, Condemned, and even Skyrim there should be much problem getting used to the initial sampling of melee weapons at hand.  Sorry but I have not got a gun yet so I can't comment on the gunplay (atm)
It will not be a spoiler to state that the main protagonist is sent to this living hell with ulterior motives, but I find myself liking his character as he appears genuinely concerned with those around him.
As you can tell, right now my initial impressions are very positive and I look forward to immersing my self deeper into its fiction and its visceral first person view.  Definitely in the vein of open world shooters such as FC4, and especially Dead Island series, but with the ability to jump and scratch your way out of danger.  It's not really funny like Dead Rising, nor is it overly serious like the Evil Within.  Basically if you like run-and gun FPSs and enjoy the zombie genre I really feel this game will be right up your alley.
I'm playing this game via K&M on an R9 295x2 at 1920x1200.  to get the best frame rate turn down the draw distance and keep motion blur on.. You can also try to reduce your shadows and eliminate the AA.   Dying Light will look best with Vsync on, but it is also very playable with it turned off, just expect to see screen tearing.  I am currently running stock clocks on the GPU and stock on an i7 3770k.  I run 16GB of RAM and use a P8Z77-I DELUXE mainboard.  Its all stuffed in a Cooler Master elite 130 Small Form Factor PC case with a custom mounted EVGA 1300W! G2 power supply.   I would say the game is very playable and achieves about a 50+ FPS average.  AMD users will want to keep a close eye on future updates and user recommendations via youtube and AMD forums as there may be ways to get better frame rates by adjusting the application settings under Catalyst Control Center.    The game also includes some Nvidia features - HBAO+ (supposedly "free" zero-cost ambient occlusion)  and Nvidia Depth of Field, but my guess is that in order to get 60FPS at MAX settings you'll need the most powerful HW your money can buy.

Half-Life 2 is a classic that set itself apart from the rest of pc games near the end of 2004 when it was released. I've had the pleasure of diving back into the world of Gordon Freeman and I must say that it still holds up. For a game that has aged over ten years, the nostalgia is definetly inescapable. After pressing the "New Game" option, I was happily reinvited by the notorious, mysterious, and ethereal like G-Man who was only so happy to see my return aswell. At mine and Gordon Freeman's expense, we were allowed to rediscover the world of Half-Life where humanity has been enslaved by a super advanced race of extra terrestrials who entered our world through the means of teleportation that humanity had previously uncovered and prescipitated the resonance cascade event during Half-Life 1.
The graphics and detail are still appreciated and admired by this reviewer. Although dated, it's easy to understand why Gabe Newell (Half-Life's creator) was happy with his Source engine. Even today I can lose myself in well mapped areas and enemies that will stop at almost nothing to bring down the Freeman. The sounds of gunfire and explosion still hold an amazing level of quality, especially when you're in the midst of a firefight against Combine forces and the human/vortigaunt rebels who seek to take back their worlds from their oppressive overlords. The feeling of dropping enemies in their tracks with a shotgun or any of the others assortment of weapons is memorable and satifying. You truly feel like a force to be reckoned with.
Vehicles and other mountables are implemented very well into the world, and rarely do you find any issues with them. Sometimes you may find the occasional hiccup where your boat or buggy will hit some innocuous object in the ground or sticking out of wall, but it's negligible since it's so much darn fun. However, transitional maps can ruin that intense feeling of speed and chases with loading times that seem to come far too often. Half-Life 2 is a game from over a decade ago, so it's forgivable. Ai also does has it's ups and downs. At most times they can coordinate well and truely give you a formidable fight, but at other times they just seem so daft when they have issues navigating their way through a doorway or any other bottlenecked areas. It's funny to see enemies push through areas like the Stooges having a bad day sometimes.
Half-Life 2 holds itself together well in an age where games are being pushed out faster and faster through the factory belt. We can only hope for a sequel and give it many praises for being a foundation of many other successful games.

Dying Light is what happens when Dead Island and Mirror's Edge had a baby, although anyone could expect that from the first game trailer. What I didn't expect is that Drying Light took the best of both games to make something that feels more like a true zombie game that almost any other.
From Mirror's Edge, it takes the parkour, and given that I didn't like Mirror's Edge, I didn't expect to enjoy it, but it's become one of the defining reasons I'd give for why the game is good. What this game got that Mirror's Edge sadly missed was the first person platforming doesn't work in closed environments. Everything is nice and open so that you can stretch your legs, and almost anything that you can see can be climbed on top of or used to be climbed on top of other things, all while zombies can only shamble around as you dart past them. It's fluid in a way that few games are, and the sheer joyful fun that comes from the freedom to hop around is unmatched on this scale.
This does somewhat contradict the established tone of the story, but the story itself isn't worth mentioning and not what I think we're here for, anyway.
What is worth mentioning is that even with all of my run and jump prowess, I never stopped behind afraid of the zombies. Combat as rather frantic, as you have weapons that degrade and a small stamina bar for fighting  that makes it hard to take out even one of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Legging it is the better option most of the time, but it's not an option that comes without its own risk. Zombies can be almost anywhere, and while staying above the streets tends to be the better option, getting up there after you've fallen down can be tense if you're in a jam and don't have the time to check out what you're climbing on top of for the undead. Still, it never feels unfair. The game's controls are built around the freerunning mechanics and--for once in a game--surprisingly useful dodging controls. If you die, it's because you weren't prepared enough or cocked up a jump or didn't know how to handle yourself, 100% of the time.
What I had wondered going in was how the game would handle its horror elements, The elements I've just mentioned make it tense, if nothing else. It does an adequate job at this with its atmosphere. That alone doesn't make it for me, though. If that was all the game had, I'd question the use of the horror tag.  What sealed the deal for me were the story missions. They take advantage of all the tools in the box to make you scared. In one mission a little ways in, for example, you need to hop into a sea of zombies and set up a few traps inside the hood of some cars. All you can do is throw firecrackers in the general vicinity of where you wanted the zombies to go towards and cross your fingers as your character turned away from the hoarde for a few precious seconds. Moments like this make the game shine, and there's enough in here to recommend. I don't know if I'd call the game horror with those story missions, either, but it's close enough that horror fans will find something to love.
Still, I can't help but feel like the game is unrefined, somewhat. Scavaging is a chore and sometimes parkour can be frustrating with how fast you move. With the combat restricted as it is, the game can be somewhat of a bore at times, as you stick to the rooftops and prance above the town, more or less safe from danger. Once you get used to how to move around and get yourself out of a jam, there's not much the game does to spice things up to shake the feeling of security you begin to develop, which is disappointing. The ingredients are here, and the game does what it can to make use of them, but it doesn't come together in a truly wonderful way due to a lack of polish.
What is Dying Light, then? Dying Light is unique, fun, and better than the games that inspired it, and what more can you ask for from a game? I'd recommend a price drop before picking it up if you're lukewarm, but if you're not bored of zombies and the parkour looks fun to you, it's an easy recommendation at full price.

Though not as deep as it's DOS predecessors, XCOM: EU is a great little turn based strategy game that offers dozens of hours of suspenseful and satisfying gameplay. I never played Shadowrun but I'm really digging this game. It's a turn-based RPG essentially. The amount of activities you can do is fairly limited but there are side "quests" you can take during certain parts of the game to gain Karma (skill points) and nuyen (cash).
The game doesn't seem like it's a full-fledged RPG with multiple quests and I wish you could manage a party. Instead you hire runners for each job but you can't really customize them or buy new weapons for them or anything. I would say that's a good description for the entire game as it stands--limited. Is it fun? Definitely. Could it stand for more features and content? Definitely.
The feel of the game is pretty cool, sort of like Blade Runner. I like the writing, it's all text-based, no voice-acting. The story is interesting and I like the exploratory aspect (again, it's limited as it's pretty linear).
The battles are fun but a bit limited (and over too fast IMO)... there's a sweet mode called Decking where you jack into the Matrix and battle digitally. I really like it but it only makes an appearance a few times (so far). Mostly you'll want to focus on ranged combat; I chose Pistols and Shotguns. Mages seem limited, if I did it again I wouldn't put any points into Willpower, instead I'd go full Cyberware. Quickness and Intelligence seem to reign supreme so far with some Strength for HP/etc.
Savegames are a bit weird... essentially you need to reach the next area (loading screen) and the game autosaves. In big missions, you access a new floor/area and then it saves. It's just the right amount of time between autosaves, about 30 mins. I do wish they just added quicksave or some other save mechanism (not during a battle, mind you, but while outside battles).
Overall it's good; it was worth the sale price I bought it at... I would love to see more content, quests, and items, so here's looking forward to expansions!

Dying light is definitely a unique game. It takes Mirrors Edge style parkour and mixes it with the good mechanics from Dead Island to make an amazing experience. The environments, enemies and effects all look absolutely fantastic whether you are jumping from roof to roof, staring at the sun setting over the distant landscape or chipping away at a zombies skull using an adjustable wrench, you will always be stunned by how realistic it looks.
The game also runs relatively fine with some FPS drops, but disabling the Depth of Field and Motion Blur fixed (I really dont care for those video options anyways) makes for a steady 60 FPS experience. The View Distance also has no real effect on the graphics (at least I did not notice), rather it just cause severe crashed in FPS.
The single player campaign, although I have not completed it yet, is quite the experience so far. Sure, some of the lip syncing from the AI and the not so relative replies they give you can be irritating at first, but even though annoying, these little things do not take away from the immersion of the game. I would just prefer they would react to situations a little more efficiently.
The "Be the Zombie Mode" is fun but could definitely use some adjusting. The UV lights the humans have can affect the zombie from such a great range that it becomes fairly annoying to pounce the enemy because you need a full energy bar. To further build on the annoyances of being the zombie, the human players can continuously mash the "survivor insinct" button, which reveals the location of the zombie on the minimap, making it ever so easy to be able to flash him with the "long range" UV light preventing him from pouncing. Even if he does try to pounce, you can easily turn around and quickly prevent it because of the "survival instincts". The UV flashlight one human is equipped with also has a seemingly infinite charge (recharges quickly, does not drain very fast), imagine when 4 are in a group. Another issue is that the humans spawn faster and right beside the hives they have to destroy, so if they ever kill the zombie, they can practically destroy a hive for free. Don't get me wrong, the mode is still very fun, it just needs some tweaking.
There are quite a few weapons in this game, both one-handed and two-handed, which can be modified into deadly zombie killing machines. Theres a variety of bluprints to add electricity or fire or just straight up make the enemy bleed. The best part is, you no longer need to be at a crafting table to mod or repair weapons, it can now be done in the character menu, which is awesome. But there is a drawback to the weapons, they break really easily and can only be repaired a certain amount of times before they become useless. This can be annoying at first, but really just adds to the immersion of the game.
Pros:

- Good size map
- Spot on Parkour
- Fun coop and mulitplayer
- Weapon mod variety
Cons:
- Multiplayer needs tweaking
- Some bugs
- FPS drops

Shadowrun Returns is an isometric RPG set in a noir styled future-meets-fantasy world.  The backgrounds for each area are terrifically well detailed and the music, though not ascending to any great heights, appropriately sets the mood.
For me, the biggest draw was how well the writing and atmosphere nails the noir setting the designers are after.  I'm a sucker for it, and the excellent descriptions of grimy slums and neon-yellow corporations is addictive.  The dialogue is consistently clever and snappy.
The simplicity of the gameplay is in contrast to the complexity of the worldbuiding, but I mean that as a good thing.  Every mechanic is very clear and fun to use.  I felt encouraged to try different builds.  This is a game that mixes guns, swords, and magic, so a cover mechanic, very similar to the XCOM update, is utilized effectively.
If I did have a criticism, it's that gameplay skills outside of combat are lacking.  In only one level do you have a lot of ways to use your hacking, speachcraft, or strength and maybe some other options) to progress.  It was reminiscent of Deus Ex and made me briefly feel like a real Shadowrunner.  However, that level was an exception, and for the most part the game is linear and has a sharp divide between its combat and the exploration/speaking bits.  Prospecitive owners should consider this for any purchase.
However, the game also comes with a complete level editor.  Many custom campaigns have been created, some of them quite good.  One of them, Nightmare Harvest, has excellent writing and a hub-based design that corrects issues that some may have with linearity.  With more great fan missions on the horizon, buying Shadowrun Returns is potentiall giving you acces to many more hours of great content (and the chance to create your own).
I finished my time with Shadowrun Returns intrigued by the world and eager to play its upcomming expansion.

At the time of writing this, the game is still in early access but lets ignore that and get into the reasons why a recommend this game.
To start lets talk about the graphical enhancement between this game and the first game, the difference is astonising with lighting, cleaner and sharper textures and the well improved animations.
This games perk system is way better then Killing floor 1s as it allows us to customize between two options when hitting a certian level, those being 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25. Ranking up is perfect as in the beginning it will take about a game or two to rank up and as you have a higher and higher rank it will take more time to earn more XP than the last rank.
There is a variety of weapons for each perk but at times I feel that there is not enough for most perks as you start out with the weakest weapon in your selected class and save up till round 4-5 and you already have the most powerful gun in that perk. A great example of this is the support as the starting weapon is boss and can be used up to a high round giving the player the ability to buy the AA12 just before round 5 in a 10 round server. However in the recent update Tatical Response a survey was added talking about whether new guns for perks should be added.
Zeds in this game are all the original included newer one which are mostly clot remakes with their own unique attack.
Maps in this game so far are perfect and I don't have a problem with them as there is a wide range of maps with unique themes and sizes.
Now I have not touched upon the suicidal difficulty too much and for that reason i can not give my opinion on that or Hell on Earth at all but I can tell you this. Normal on solo is too easy piece of cake, Hard is quite challenging on the boss on solo whether that be the Doctor or the patriarch. Normal and Hard depending on your level can be hard on multiplayer as depending on the amount of players in the server will boost the bosses health higher and higher. Also in games such as Hard, Suicidal and Hell on Earth enemies have new and unique attacks which don't occur in normal mode.
What im about is nothing to do with the game but has to do with Tripwire Interactive and that is the communication between the community and them. Now through the recent month updates and word from them has been quite, but with the recent update these surveys released be Tripwire them selves have been very promising as this allows us to give our opinion on something.
So my final thoughts on this game. I would'nt say it beats the first game over all but definitely improves on aspects from Killing Floor. As the review sais I strongly recommend that you play this game, early access or not it's still great. A 9/10 and for a early access game that is impressive. Overview: 2d Rogue-Action/Platformer
The Good:
+10 characters each with their own unique attack and abilities.
+Randomized levels every time you start a new game.
+Over 100 items ensuring lots of variety
+Plenty of things to unlock. You first start out with only one character: the commando and a handful of items. As you play and complete challenges, you unlock more characters and items making it easier to get to the end of the game.
+Every good rogue game I've played has a nice sense of pacing. What seems like an impossible task in the beginning slowly becomes easier once you start understanding the mechanics. Making it to the last boss is a very satisfying feeling.
+ One of the main premises of the game is that as time goes on, the harder enemies become. This creates somewhat of an interesting balance to the game. Normally you may think that you should just complete each level as fast as possible however this may leave you underpowered in the next level. Take too long in a level and you may find the enemies too hard to defeat. Finding the right balance between killing enemies, collecting as many items in a level and staying above the difficulty curve is part of the strategy.
+ I love the music. Fantastic soundtrack.
The Average:
Although there are 10 character to choose from, some of them are not that good compared to others and some were designed with multiplayer in mind.
Online multiplayer community is dead
Conclusion
This is one of my favorite rogue games on steam. It has an addicting quality to it. Playing each character, getting rare items and having a good run is one of the hallmarks of a great rogue game.

THIS is how you adapt a media property into a video game. The plot is befitting of a South Park movie.
The look, feel, and mechanics of the game are identical to what you see on television series... This is how such a story would play out on television, no question.
It plays upon the tropes of RPGs, something the creators of South Park a very skilled at satirizing on the show. There were several times I just dropped my game controller and sat there laughing for several minutes.
Because of the visual style South Park has always had, it can be tricky at times to spot certain things on screen. This is not a game where you can pan around for a view of the landscape... you're IN South Park, moving around in pretty much a 2-D world like on the show. That said, the characters move and act EXACTLY as they should in such a context. So, the limitations of such perspective work perfectly.
Had this tried to be a FPS or some other 3-D setting, the game would have likely suffered for it. By keeping the same style you know, they made something darn near perfect for what it set out to be.

You are on a standard government space ship, with 2 crew members.You must take the helm of your ship and take it through the dark depths of space. The other 2 take place where ever they need to be, one maning your shields so your haul doesn't get a hole in it, The other mans your missles and lasers so you can put holes in others. Your mission? Get to the other end of the galaxy and deliver critical information about the Rebel Fleet, and bring their reign of terror to an end. Through the first sector, you gather scrap and missiles from the pirates and rebels you destroy. You saved a slave from a life of servatude and he became your engineer. You are boarded by a rock man, and have a shoot out in your ship while being threatened to burn due to the extremly close sun.
Upon your entry to the 2nd sector your haul is half stable, so you upgrade your shields and direct all the extra power you have to power them. To bad the next enemy you face has missiles that go right through them. Sadly, your mission ends there. Peace and Order is destroyed. The Galaxy is lost and enslaved. You now have to try again.
This is what your experince in FTL is going to be like for a while.
FTL is a Rogue like ship managment game where you have one shot to get your crew to the other end. On the way you will gather more crew, scrap, missiles, and ship parts. You can use scraps to upgrade energy caps in parts of your ship like shields, weapon and how much energy your ship generates.
The most compling part of this game to me is how you deal with energy. At the beginning you have enough energy to power your engines, your shields, and one of your weapons. As the game progresses, you'll more then likely upgrage something. You then have to power down something else to get the new thing powered, until you are able to buy more energy to power everything.
The combat is basic but satisfing. There is a few type of weapons here. You have Lasers, which deal massive damage to the haul, but is stopped by any shield. Then there is a basic laser burst gun, which can take down a shield and hit the haul for some damage, and some have more then one burst. Energy shots take down shields and knocks out a system for a short time which can turn the tide of the battle. Missiles go right through shields and hits for great damage, but miss often and require ammo. A bomb teleports inside the enemy ship and blows up, but these often miss and can even hit you.
You can also attempt to use drones to help you, there is everything from a boarding droid that attack the enemy ship, healing droids, laser droids, etc. You have this randomized map with ineresting quests to be found. You can make your ship unhittable for a short time and so much more. There is a lot more to be found in this wonderful game that Im not typing in, as long as you can stand the 1-life only gameplay and the amount of luck it takes to win sometimes. It is a very satistisfing expericene that is rarly found. Its one of the best indy games I've ever played, and its well worth the price of admission.
You will learn how to progress as you fail and suceed at each puzzle.  Be persistent but do not try the impossable unless you think it will work.

Batman: Arkham Knight
Having owned this game for about a year I can tell you I am supremely disappointed by this title and Rocksteady. I have waited until July 2016 to release my opinion on this game.
Batman: Arkham Knight isn't a bad game per se, it just falls short in some crucial spots like game performance, which has impacted my review.
+ Nice graphics, good lighting and rain effects.
+ The concept of combat remains solid, with lots of different attacks. It's fun, albeit difficult to combo.
+ Lots of unique gadgets to use, some that make a return from previous iterations of Batman and others are entirely new.
+Very intriguing characters and a great story.
+ Riddler trophies and mini puzzles are quite enjoyable.
- This point is entirely dedicated to the batmobile which is over-used throughout the game, becoming extremely tedious. Endless drone, cobra and APC hunting in side quests with extra tanks thrown in during the main story, make batmobile involvement beyond excessive.
- Combat hotkeys are badly implemented into the game and they are unnecessarily complex...There's a crouch toggle and then a 'hold down' crouch button which makes no sense.To hide in grates I need to use the "hold down' crouch + middle mouse, but I never use 'hold down' crouch usually, since it's outdated and pointless with a toggle crouch. So I'm basically using one key for a very particular action. The game is not streamlined at all. It's the same story for combos in fights. I don't use WASD for movement, I changed this to the arrow keys - but I still need to press the 1,2,3,4 keys to execute combos, which are half way across the keyboard.
- Big technical issues at launch, which I let slide as I waited for patches to correct the problems. 6 months passed and the game still didn't run efficiently. With a Nvidia Geforce GTX 970, 8 GB of RAM and an i7 CPU, I expect Batman: Arkham Knight to work smoothly on a relatively high setting, but minor and severe FPS drops occur during batmobile pursuits and in certain areas of the game world to this day. This is a killer for the experience and very irritating.
Overall score: 7/10
Disclaimer: I've scored this game 7 because the content is fantastic, it really is. It'd be a 9/10 if it simply worked. But it doesn't, so it takes a hard hit of 2 points. It's still playable, but it should be better than what it is performance wise.

Half-Life 2 is a classic that set itself apart from the rest of pc games near the end of 2004 when it was released. I've had the pleasure of diving back into the world of Gordon Freeman and I must say that it still holds up. For a game that has aged over ten years, the nostalgia is definetly inescapable. After pressing the "New Game" option, I was happily reinvited by the notorious, mysterious, and ethereal like G-Man who was only so happy to see my return aswell. At mine and Gordon Freeman's expense, we were allowed to rediscover the world of Half-Life where humanity has been enslaved by a super advanced race of extra terrestrials who entered our world through the means of teleportation that humanity had previously uncovered and prescipitated the resonance cascade event during Half-Life 1.
The graphics and detail are still appreciated and admired by this reviewer. Although dated, it's easy to understand why Gabe Newell (Half-Life's creator) was happy with his Source engine. Even today I can lose myself in well mapped areas and enemies that will stop at almost nothing to bring down the Freeman. The sounds of gunfire and explosion still hold an amazing level of quality, especially when you're in the midst of a firefight against Combine forces and the human/vortigaunt rebels who seek to take back their worlds from their oppressive overlords. The feeling of dropping enemies in their tracks with a shotgun or any of the others assortment of weapons is memorable and satifying. You truly feel like a force to be reckoned with.
Vehicles and other mountables are implemented very well into the world, and rarely do you find any issues with them. Sometimes you may find the occasional hiccup where your boat or buggy will hit some innocuous object in the ground or sticking out of wall, but it's negligible since it's so much darn fun. However, transitional maps can ruin that intense feeling of speed and chases with loading times that seem to come far too often. Half-Life 2 is a game from over a decade ago, so it's forgivable. Ai also does has it's ups and downs. At most times they can coordinate well and truely give you a formidable fight, but at other times they just seem so daft when they have issues navigating their way through a doorway or any other bottlenecked areas. It's funny to see enemies push through areas like the Stooges having a bad day sometimes.
Half-Life 2 holds itself together well in an age where games are being pushed out faster and faster through the factory belt. We can only hope for a sequel and give it many praises for being a foundation of many other successful games.

The first time I heard of the Shadowrun roleplaying game (the tabletop rpg that is), I found the entire concept pretty silly. Cyberpunk with elves and dwarves? I mean, come on! The abysmal video games of the last years (apart from the SNES game, but that is just so much hearsay) didn't do much else to entice me.
Then this game came along.
A lot of people complain that this game plays like it was made ten years ago, and that it would've been a bad game even by those standards. I disagree with that notion.
The game is based on the ever so versatile Unity engine. 3D character models act in front of 2Dish backgrounds, with the player overlooking everything from an isometric perspective. Personally I find it pretty neat. The background is drawn with a lot of attention to details and the character models show enough of the same to tell them apart and still look unique. Sure, it doesn't have the same graphical power as a triple-A game, but it doesn't need it either. For an indie game straight out of kickstarter, it looks more than good.
Soundwise it has background music appropriate for the scenery, with a mix of upbeat and eerily haunting techno. The dialogues are not voiced, but simply text-based. Which is not a dealbreaker in my opinion.
The biggest complaint people seem to have about SRR is that you can't save whenever you want. The game autosaves after every scene transition. Didn't bother me one bit. It actually made the entire action even more tense. But the developers have already announced a manual save feature for the upcoming DLC.
So, do I recommend Shadowrun Returns? Yes, I do.I recommend to those people who want an easy introduction into the setting. I recommend it to the fans of Shadowrun for it finally being a decent adaptation. And I recommend it to everybody else on the grounds that it is just that: a pretty good game.

Vice City is probably the best GTA that has been made to date. Obviously, as a PC gamer, this opinion does not include GTA V as that one was never released by Rockstar on my favourite platform. I personally liked GTA IV a lot and the reviews on the latest installment were very promising - I just think Vice City was more captivating than the rest.
Vice City looks dated, yes. Please bear in mind that this is an eleven year old game and considering the capacity of our smart phones this game is accessible as an Android application as the game's engine can easily be handled by our phones' hardware. Its atmosphere, however, is still captivating even a decade after its release so playing such an "old" game on a widescreen monitor with next-gen hardware is no shame!
You play as Tommy Vercetti (voice by Ray Liotta) and you are in the '80s. You have cars, music and even film references from this era. Some scenes remind you of Miami Vice while others are clearly a nod to Pacino's character in Scarface. How cool is that?
You have dozens of missions available. Some continue the main story while other are just side missions. Each includes a cutscene with amazing voice acting so it is a crime to skip any of the available missions. Oh, you don't want to do any of these? No problem: Vice City allows the player to just cruise in the city, steal cars, crash these cars, harass citizens (with these cars, too). You can drive a cab and earn some money at your leisure. Or steal a police car and become the terminator of vigilantes.
There are tons of things to do in GTA. And while Vice City is certainly an outdated game nothing else out there can remind you how cool the '80s were than this piece of treasure.

I find it easier to write reviews in a Pro and Con list style, as I find it's a more effective way to get my meaning across, so please bare with me if it's not to your tastes.
-Good graphics, even with things like AA and other advanced settings off.
-Great atmosphere, especially with the music score at its full intensity and also by letting your imagination wander while playing.
-As I just touched upon, the sound design is fantastic, constant bangs, clunks, moans, and rattles give the effect that you are indeed aboard a decaying ship, with monsters moving throughout it. Fleshy bits make an appropriate "squish" when shot, and guns have an appropriate "oomph" to them.
-Good variety of enemies, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. For example, Slashers are fast, but have exposed legs, Pregnomorphs are slow, but hard to take down without spilling their "cargo" all over the floor, etc. Other types of enemies have other weaknesses.
-The A.I. is pretty good. Enemies will charge you if you turn your back, pop out of vents that are close to you, swarm you all at once rather than one at a time, etc.
-The story is good, but it does have its issues, as I will state in the Con's section.
-Voice acting is good, none of the actor's sound like they "phoned it in." While the main protagonist Isaac Clarke doesn't talk, he does make grunts, yells, and appropriately heavy breathing noises when necessary.
-Environmental design is great, cargo rooms and mechanical stations are open, crew rooms are more enclosed, with tighter corridors, etc. Rooms are in places that make sense (i.e, no engine room on the opposite end of the ship from where the engines are.)
-They story is pretty decently lengthed, I've beaten this game several times (mainly on console) and it still takes me around 8 hours or so. I'd imagine it would probably take a newer player around 10-12 hours to beat.
-Character design is good, no one is stereotypical, and each character is decently memorable.
-I enjoyed the audio and video log collecting, which helped expand on the backstory and helps determine just what happened aboard the
(the name of the ship you board.)
-There's a good variety of weapons, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. There's also different suit levels you can get, which work well and look cool at the same time.
-You can upgrade your weapons, armor, Statis unit (slows down enemies and objects), and kinesis unit (pick up objects from a distance) using "Power Nodes" you find throughout this ship or bought through the Store aboard the ship.
-Each weapon also has an "alt fire" mode to it. The plasma cutter changes from horizontal to vertical shooting (more useful than you might think) the Pulse Rifle fires in a circle, etc.
-Anti-gravity areas are cool, but could have been done better. (They are done better in Dead Space 2 and 3.)
-There's more positive aspects, but that covers most of the main bits.
-The game also likes to mess with you in small ways, areas that were safe most of the game may not be safe anymore, some enemies come out of unexpected areas, the game tenses you up for a scare that doesn't happen (but it's done well, and on purpose.)
-Aiming is a bit iffy with a mouse and keyboard, turning of V-Sync helps, which you have to do both in the in-game settings and in the .cfg files for it to actually work. However, I'd recommend playing with a controller if possible, if not, you can still play the game quite well with a M/KB.
-While I stated earlier that the story was pretty good, it's not without flaws. For the most part you are the secondary protagonists *itch for most of the game, doing something or other for them, sometimes when it's something they could do themselves. Not to say they sit on their butts all game, but still.
-This game also follows the horror game trope of magically seperating you from you allies when a situation arises. Granted, it doesn't do it as often as other games and sometimes you even meet up with them. (Who'da thunk it?)
-As I said, this game has a cool variety of weapons, but for a more skilled player, they are unnecessary. I can make it through this game with just the Plasma Cutter and the Pulse Rifle as my weapons, not even touching the others. On console, I've even done an entire run through of the game with
the Plasma Cutter.
-The A.I. is good, but it does have its..... moments. I've seen Necromorphs pop out of vents, only to hop right back in and pop out somewhere farther away from me. I've also seen the A.I. not want to walk through doorways that lead out of the area, but are willing to hop in a vent and pop out of a vent that
in that new area, for reasons I assume that involve the games pathfinding.
-The game also can get repetitive after a while, not that it's not fun, but some Necromorph encounters do get predictable (mainly entering a new area and Necromorphs almost immediately showing up.)
-The game has puzzles (not that I mind), but almost all of them are pretty basic and easy (at least to me) and don't offer much challenge.
-Controls are tanky (much like Resident Evil 4), which is fine, but in some areas of the game (mainly anti-grav and space areas) these controls can get semi-annoying and cumbersome.
-The game just isn't that scary for me, it's pretty decently thrilling the first time you play it, and its got its tense moments, but I was never crapping my pants in horror or dreading to go in the next room. I am also hard to scare however, while some people are quite the opposite.

-The amount of settings are decent, but nothing to write home about, and I was disappointed by some options that were missing.
-The game isn't very optimized, I can play Dead Space 2 with higher settings than this one and run higher frames, yet I play this game with the same settings and get noticeably lower frames per second.
-Another reason to turn V-Sync off (as if there weren't enough already) is that it causes a noticeably annoying "dragging" feel to your mouse, this is especially present in the Main Menu and the Pause Menu.
-This isn't an annoyance, but playing this game with headphones is a good idea, it helps you find enemies easier, helps you get more enthralled in the atmosphere, and just makes it an overall better experience.
If I had to give this game a number review it would probably be a 9/10. (It'd be higher without the wonky V-Sync and mild control problems.)
And finally: TL:DR -MUST PLAY, BUT 2 SPOOKY 4 ME.
