You are on a standard government space ship, with 2 crew members.You must take the helm of your ship and take it through the dark depths of space. The other 2 take place where ever they need to be, one maning your shields so your haul doesn't get a hole in it, The other mans your missles and lasers so you can put holes in others. Your mission? Get to the other end of the galaxy and deliver critical information about the Rebel Fleet, and bring their reign of terror to an end. Through the first sector, you gather scrap and missiles from the pirates and rebels you destroy. You saved a slave from a life of servatude and he became your engineer. You are boarded by a rock man, and have a shoot out in your ship while being threatened to burn due to the extremly close sun.
Upon your entry to the 2nd sector your haul is half stable, so you upgrade your shields and direct all the extra power you have to power them. To bad the next enemy you face has missiles that go right through them. Sadly, your mission ends there. Peace and Order is destroyed. The Galaxy is lost and enslaved. You now have to try again.
This is what your experince in FTL is going to be like for a while.
FTL is a Rogue like ship managment game where you have one shot to get your crew to the other end. On the way you will gather more crew, scrap, missiles, and ship parts. You can use scraps to upgrade energy caps in parts of your ship like shields, weapon and how much energy your ship generates.
The most compling part of this game to me is how you deal with energy. At the beginning you have enough energy to power your engines, your shields, and one of your weapons. As the game progresses, you'll more then likely upgrage something. You then have to power down something else to get the new thing powered, until you are able to buy more energy to power everything.
The combat is basic but satisfing. There is a few type of weapons here. You have Lasers, which deal massive damage to the haul, but is stopped by any shield. Then there is a basic laser burst gun, which can take down a shield and hit the haul for some damage, and some have more then one burst. Energy shots take down shields and knocks out a system for a short time which can turn the tide of the battle. Missiles go right through shields and hits for great damage, but miss often and require ammo. A bomb teleports inside the enemy ship and blows up, but these often miss and can even hit you.
You can also attempt to use drones to help you, there is everything from a boarding droid that attack the enemy ship, healing droids, laser droids, etc. You have this randomized map with ineresting quests to be found. You can make your ship unhittable for a short time and so much more. There is a lot more to be found in this wonderful game that Im not typing in, as long as you can stand the 1-life only gameplay and the amount of luck it takes to win sometimes. It is a very satistisfing expericene that is rarly found. Its one of the best indy games I've ever played, and its well worth the price of admission.

This game had an excellent sense of immersion in to the world of Shadowrun. I have enjoyed playing both the released main content of Shadowrun Returns as well as many of the player workshop campaigns. One of the biggest selling points was in shipping a very useful editor that put the power of creating these campaigns in the hands of the player community.
That being said there are a few rough spots. The current save system (which appears to be replaced in the next DLC Dragonfall) only provided save points at the start of a map, which means in order to save ones progress you would have to complete the section you were on and move to the next load in area for it to record your progress.
The replayability was also argueable. While I enjoyed some of the subtle changes each class could bring to the different dialogs and oppertunities that would arise, the game is unfortuantely very linear. Even with those subtle changes the overall story will progress the same way.
The linear story did, however, showcase many different aspects of the Shadowrun world and in my opinion was successful in introducing players to different creative aspects they could explore while making their own content for the game. You have sections of story running through the matrix, attacking a corporation and even fighting through zombies.
For 20$ I found the game to be worth my expectations and have played a total of 58 hours so far between main story and workshop content. I have no regrets with my purchase.

THIS is how you adapt a media property into a video game. The plot is befitting of a South Park movie.
The look, feel, and mechanics of the game are identical to what you see on television series... This is how such a story would play out on television, no question.
It plays upon the tropes of RPGs, something the creators of South Park a very skilled at satirizing on the show. There were several times I just dropped my game controller and sat there laughing for several minutes.
Because of the visual style South Park has always had, it can be tricky at times to spot certain things on screen. This is not a game where you can pan around for a view of the landscape... you're IN South Park, moving around in pretty much a 2-D world like on the show. That said, the characters move and act EXACTLY as they should in such a context. So, the limitations of such perspective work perfectly.
Had this tried to be a FPS or some other 3-D setting, the game would have likely suffered for it. By keeping the same style you know, they made something darn near perfect for what it set out to be.

Early on in Antichamber, you will come across a room comprised of large floating letters that state "W T F ?". This pretty much sums up the experience... but that's not necessarily a bad thing. It's quite refreshing, actually. But let's start at the beginning - what is Antichamber exactly? It's not easy to explain. It's a puzzle game, but the puzzles you solve are not exactly of a traditional nature. The game is set in some sort of nondescript facility, comprised of interconnected hallways and chambers. Visually, the world is quite simple, made up mostly of bright white walls with a spattering of color here and there. You explore in first person and must figure out how to solve each room in order to progress. And that's where it gets even harder to explain. The solutions are far from clear-cut and there is no one main mechanic that is used from start to finish. You just have to think, experiment, and explore. Eventually you will find a tool that is able to manipulate small cubes that are scattered throughout the facility. But unlike in a puzzle game like Portal for instance, the cube "gun" is not the only component of the puzzle-solving experience (though it does become so later on). Rather, at first, you will likely just spend a couple of hours exploring, getting lost, and trying to figure out just what the hell is going on. It takes a little while to adapt to how the game wants you to think, but once you have learned how to solve certain problems, it opens up more of the world for you to explore. I know this explanation sounds very vague, but it's almost impossible not to be when trying to explain this game - it is very... unconventional. That said, I thought the game was really cool, though I can definitely see that it would not be for everyone. If you like games that have a clear goal, explain their mechanics well, and don't require much thinking, then this is most definitely not the game for you. If, on the other hand, you are curious to try something that is vague, never provides anything in the way of explanation, and has some truly "out-there" puzzles to solve, you just might find Antichamber to be a breath of fresh air. All in all, this is a worthy experiment in the puzzle game genre, and unlike anything else I have ever played. Check it out if you think it may interest you - just don't hold me responsible for how much hair you end up pulling out of your head in frustration.
Final Grade: B+

(Writing this having played part-way through the game, estimating six or seven hours.)
On the one hand, Shadowrun Returns is actually Shadowrun, versus the letdown of a shooter that came out a few years ago. On the other hand, it's small and has very little of the style that's so important to Shadowrun. The atmosphere is right, but not enough is done to draw you into it.
Gameplay is competent, but not terribly exciting. Some of the possibilities have to be lost in the translation to a $20 video game, but so much of it is reduced to a simple trope that it's hard not to feel disappointed. Decking amounts to an occasional small alternate battlefield, with none of the intricacies or intrigue of the pen-and-paper's Matrix. Riggers get to be a pet class, and it's just that simple. Cyberware is over-simplified to essentially a few pieces of stat-boosting equipment (no claws/spurs, if you were looking for them, either). Possibly the biggest letdown is that stealth and planning are not really options; you might get a turn or two to get the drop on your enemies, but there is no opportunity to plan a run with a minimum of conflict or risk. You start the mission, you kill all of the opposition, and that's it.
The story is decent, but extremely linear. Linear isn't necessarily bad, but there's next to no exploration at all, meaning even fewer opportunities to take advantage of the setting and your skills. Graphics are serviceable, but animations are stilted and awkward-looking. For a setting where style is so important, it's disappointing to see so little visual customization.
Player-created content is an option, though I haven't tried any of it yet. The main campaign, though fairly well-written, is not a great showcase for Shadowrun. The gameplay is okay, but nothing terribly special. I'm having an okay time with the game, but I can't really recommend that anyone snap this up.

Risk of Rain is a quirky and fun 2D action roguelike, which is a lot more fun when played with other people.
The minitaure-sized sprites all look great and have their charm, and the timer-based difficulty setting was a really interesting touch that forces you to balance going around the maps to collect much-needed upgrades with not wasting too much time in any given area to avoid raising the difficulty too much. The different character specializations are fun to experiment with, even more so when playing co-op, since you can mix and match them to cover each other's weak points.
As negative aspects, I'd say that the lack of enemy and level variety coupled with cryptic conditions for unlocking new playable characters make this a game that is best played in short bursts. Enemy variety is limited to a few level-specific ones, and the challenge comes more from the game spawning lots of them and giving them ever-increasing stats than actually learning their attack patterns and how to overcome them; then, the levels themselves seem to have a few basic layouts that are repeated often, making them quite predictable after just a few runs. I only wish you'd start with more characters or the conditions for unlocking them were simpler, since having to play with the same ones over and over wasn't as fun, especially in co-op mode.
In spite of its shortcomings, I'd definitely recommend Risk of Rain to anyone who likes co-op action games, as the short-ish average play sessions means you can have fun and experience some crazy and fun situations without a huge time commitment, and playing in short bursts means you won't get burned out by the relatively shallow enemy and level variety and will be able to enjoy it a lot more.

There isn't anything I can really say about this that hasn't been said before so I'll just throw out what I didn't like about this game. Shadowrun is a great IP that was thoroughly wasted here.
1) No save system. This is 2014, a real save system in an RPG is kind of a no-brainer.
2) Combat was boring.
3) Investment in skills didn't seem to pay off very much. I tried out a few different skills in an arena module and was very underwhelmed. Lots of karma (skill points) needed to progress for minimal returns.
4) Magic system was clunky and dull; poorly implemented.
5) Campaign was short yet somehow tedious. A truly inspiring combination.
6) Lack of diversity in weapons and equipment. All gear gives only very minor, incremental bonuses that don't justify the amount of money your character has to spend on them.
7) No loot system. At. All. Really, really DUMB.
8) Sometimes the writing is very cheesy.
9) The expectation that the developers expressed, that the community should finish their unfinished game through user-generated content. Because why should you finish making a game when you can include an editor and tell people you're done (when there are all kinds of issues with the game's engine).
Bottom line, if you invested in this on kickstarter you should see about getting your money back. If you somehow actually LIKE this game, I just don't know what to say to you. This game is crap.

I was introduced to Shadowrun, the tabletop game nearly ten years ago when I met my boyfriend, and have since fallen in love with the series, so I was eager to play Shadowrun Returns when I'd heard about it considering Shadowrun the 2007 fps proved to be a failure of expectations and representation of the franchise.
Shadowrun takes place in an alternate reality where magic flourishes on Earth, humans have mutated into subspecies resembeling Elves, Orks, Trolls and where society dissolves, corporations take the role of Goverment, and technology and magic flourish.
Think "Blade Runner" mixed with D&D.
Shadowrun Returns manages to capture the atmosphere of the tabletop game near perfectly.
You take the role of a mercenary known as  Shadowrunner, a body for hire. You are given missions to complete, oppertunities to raise your skills, and the choice of whether or not you are performing out of moral obligation, or simply because you need the cash.
Returns offers a tactical rpg setup where choice of team and how you ask them to perform is crucial to your survival. If you cannot afford the people you need, you best prepare for a tough fight ahead. The game pulls no punches. You must think of strategy and execute it without fail or you will die.
If the mission fails you forfeit your pay, making it harder to purchase the neccesarry weapons, upgrades and ability to hire quality teammates.
Knowledge of the franchise prior to purchase isn't neccesarry. Certainly helpful, especially where Shadowrunning jargon is concerned, but you will not be stuck in the dark if this is your introduction to Shadowrun.
If you have played the Shadowrun tabletop, or perhaps the old SNES game years ago, there are nods and cameos that will be appreciated, including Jake Armitage, Dodger and Harlequin - the soundtrack from the SNES game has received an upgrade and sets the mood beautifully!
If you are a fan of the tabletop game, this is a must have purchase. It is faithful to the franchise and represents it accurately all the while providing entertaining gameplay and story.

Half-Life 2 is a singleplayer FPS set in the far future. Fighting large arrays of enemies ranging from antlions, to zombies, to the combine. There are many levels and chapters that never stop changing the gameplay. All the weapons have a purpose (with the exception of the 9mm pistol, late game.) The maps are very well decorated and the A.I. is very smart. The game is truely gameplay inspired since there are 2 cutscenes in the whole game. (beginning and end) Looting is a big thing, i found myself looking for crates to find ammo and health. The physics are amazing and the gravity gun isnt as OP as thought. There are vehicle sessions allowing you to drive with very well done driving mechanics. ( the airboat gun is so OP ) Theres also a compeling story. Though it may get confusing for those who havent played the first half life since there are so many references to the first game. Its also fun to just play with the gravity gun, ( i made a cooking show in the sandtraps chapter ) There are 14 chapters, each about 1-3 hours long. There is alot of content, unless you are a fan for multiplayer or co-op which is not featured here. (which was kinda obvious considering this is a half life game after all.) Thankfully there is a great save system that lets you save anywhere. I mostly used it when i died and got to where i left off, after being set back a little. There are puzzles in the game you must solve to get past a point or to get some much needed loot.
HOWEVER, this game aint perfect. Because theres no minimap or more cutscenes its hard to tell us where to go. I got confused and where to go and had to look to tutorials on how to progress because the maps fail to tell you where to go. The game has its share of glitches but not too many. One of which, stopping every scripted event (including a door opening -.-) The game IS challenging but to me, i felt that it was too much at times. *SPOILER* There is a part where you fight striders and then a combine base. But the strider would see you if you tried to attack the base of combine, the striders couldnt die because there wasnt enough rockets spawned in the map to kill 2 striders. So you had to fight the base with a strider on you with combine shooting at you ALSO. *END SPOILER* Loot in the game becomes more and more futile as you get better guns because you really will only use the AR and shotgun the most and therefore you will look for AR and shotgun ammo. The 9mm pistol NEVER gets used (late game) unless ammo for another gun is a problem.
Overall, a great game. Alot of good things about this game with not too many downsides ( but rly, the maps are really WAY too confusing ) So i can recommend this to someone who enjoys a challenging FPS,Puzzle,Adventure,Action game. I give this a strong 8/10, Great game!

I'm reviewing "Shadowrun Returns" as is, without any modules or steam workshop content.
Well, here are my two cents.
I've never really liked the idea of a game that relies too much on the community to create most of the gameplay, I think this is kind of cheap of developers to do so, especially seeing that, in my opinion, this game was made with much less capital input than was raised at its kickstarter profile, and it shows.
So, basically it is a top-down Vampire: The Masquerade meets Fallout meets Deus Ex meets Syndicate. The idea to merge Cyberpunk and Fantasy isn't new, and it is something I would have done a long time ago, frankly I am surprised why as of now only few settings with magic-meets-guns exist.
Anyway, the graphics, sound, animation and presentation are on the level, maybe not something I would expect for a game priced thusly, but they are just enough to represent the basics of every action and/or event in the game world. Nothing too shabby. The only three-dimensional objects are characters, albeit with low quality detail and rendering. The backgrounds are well drawn, but it isn't something an average photoshop-skilled designer can't do overnight. I honestly don't see how this game could cost over $100,000 to make.
The first part of the story is very well done in terms of dialogue and logic, but the narrative quality as well as story progression and any kind of common sense just gets trashed by the mid-game. One second you are a cool cybermancer dude with glowing neon weapons, cruising through the streets of Seattle mesmerised by the night lights, fighting street scum with cunning speech choices and awesome magic spells, and in the next you are dwelling dungeons in a grind, shooting spectral fauna in a quest and narrative that would belong in a poorly made C-class sci-fi/occult thriller movie whilst choosing dialogue options that make your character seem either very high on something or extremely immature.
Either way, the game delivers some entertainment value for the 10-12 hours it takes to beat it, but I do see how it was meant to be more of a construction kit, rather than just a full game. Your character does not even approach a fraction of his/her potential by the time you see the end credits. I'm just not make-your-own-adventure type of gamer, but I do recommend it for those that are into "Bladur's Gate" or any other kind of party based isometric cRPGs.
P.S. For those that believe this is as close as you'd get to cyberpunk and that it honours work of W. Gibson, this is what he himself said of Shadowrun in general:
"…when I see things like Shadowrun, the only negative thing I feel about it is that initial extreme revulsion at seeing my literary DNA mixed with elves. Somewhere somebody's sitting and saying 'I've got it! We're gonna do William Gibson and Tolkien!' Over my dead body! But I don't have to bear any aesthetic responsibility for it. I've never earned a nickel, but I wouldn't sue them. It's a fair cop. I'm sure there are people who could sue me, if they were so inclined, for messing with their stuff. So it's just kind of amusing."
P.P.S. Thanks to Talint for gifting me this game :)).

Playing this game on and off since it's release, I can say without a doubt I will not be regretting this purchase. Having played the original quite a bit I feel as though this game far exceeds the originals quality. While I do enjoy this game and find that it has a lot to offer, the negative aspects of this are a glaring sore spot keeping a lot of people from enjoying this game so to adress them;
Microtransactions - As someone who has participated in the cosmetics race this game is pushing, I partially regret the dollar I put into it. The only purpose they serve is to have a different looking gun to stare at while you kill Zeds, it's not quite the CS:GO system where it's a point of bragging considering the fact it's impossible to show them off. I like the one skin I bought but I should have just downloaded and equally acceptable mod from workshop.
Lack of content - Classes feel wholly unfinished, they don't have enough weapons to allow variety, making having more than one of a class (other than the berserker) a detriment to the team, this could be a design choice but if so it's awful and limiting.
I still can't turn off ♥♥♥♥ING ZED TIME - I've had this complaint since the first Killing Floor, I understand that a lot of people like it, and therefore in online servers it is likely going to be turned on. However I still can't disable it in a hosted server, or in a solo game and it pisses me off.
Why poll the community if you don't actually follow the popular results? It irks me that after following development, and seeing where they were going they almost seemed to be ignoring the general public and fans. This is a major 180 from "Killing Floor 1" in which the game was almost exclusively run by fans, creating new content and interfacing with the devs on what they wanted. The original has workshop as paid DLC, you can still find the packs of the mods, and download them but if you'd rather support the game and mod developers you can buy the DLC. If this sounds farfetched feel free to go look for yourself.
What I enjoy about KF2 is the gameplay, on it's own this is a really finely tuned piece of the Zombie Survival genre. As a Killing Floor game it feels disjointed and disconnected from it's roots, it has a long way and I urge you to watch carefully, but as it stands unless you have some friends to play with, wait until the full release. You'll get the full picture of what the Developers had in mind, and you can make your choice as well informed as possible.

Before I get into review, I should mention that I am playing on a fairly beefy PC rig; as such Most of the common cons to the game (i.e. stuttering graphics) don't apply to me very often or even at all.
MAKE SURE YOU UPDATE YOUR DRIVERS BEFORE PLAYING
Review:
First of all, you don't NEED to have played the previous Arkham games to play this one, however some previous knowledge will definitely fill some plot holes. With that said, though, the game does a decent job at bringing you up-to-speed with the story so far.
Pros:
- Smooth, natural combat (like 99% of the time)
I say 99% of the time because sometimes extensive combos don't register.
- Batmobile
- Massive, beautiful open world
- Solid story with several SEVERAL side quests to do (DLC missions are also a lot of fun)
- Skill trees are extensive and allow for growth in several different playstyles.
- Scripting is awesome
- Graphics are fantastic
- Gotham truly feels like it’s at war
- Detective mode is OP

Cons:
- Detective mode is OP (you can literally find anything so easily that it feels kind of cheap at times; players aren't forced to problem solve very much)
- GRAPHICS (I don't have these problems nearly as much as most other people due to my rig, but they are still there to some extent, and to a much greater extent for several other players)
If you aren't playing on a very strong rig, I would recommend you either pass on the game, or get it on sale and try it out on low settings. No sense in wasting your money paying full price for a game that doesn't work on your computer.
- Repetitive
Side missions in a nutshell: "Go find this" "Go meet So-And-So" "Go chase down this guy." They are very 'rinse and repeat' like, if you will, and the rewards aren't all necessarily worth it considering you just spent 30 mins trying to find a specific person without any reference of where to go.
- Story is relatively predictable. No spoilers, but I called like 90% of the endgame in the first hour of play.
- Batman can kill people
There are walls up to prevent you from actually killing people, but if you really want to you can. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as it gives more power to the players, but it just isn't Batman.
- Enemy AI is pretty stupid.
"Don't mind me, while I just casually choke out the person who is talking and standing 2 feet away from you bro..."
- No skill is required to do the hardest difficulty
AI is a bit smarter, but you can block and counter literally anything instantly and beat the game without much problems if you know what you're doing.
Conclusion:
It's a fantastic game, and I would definitely recommend the game to any Batman enthusiast. Just be warry of the fact that there are graphics bugs that do exist, so be careful of that. Other than that, the story is great and will keep you going, whether it’s trying to solve Riddler’s conundrums or trying to advance the main story.

This game was captivating. From the beginning, I was dropped into this simplistic world with little detail or instruction. The game branched off quickly and there were numerous hallways and rooms to explore. It had some intricate puzzles and some more straightforward puzzles. There was a definite sense of progress as more of the map was uncovered and as the gun-like device was upgraded. There was no distinct story, but there was still a sense of identity and purpose in this peculiar world. Object permanence was frequently overlooked in lieu of shifting hallways and rooms that changed at a glance. By the end of the game, the changes were not erratic, however. I began to get a sense of the machinations of this labyrinth as I struggled for escape. The signs along the way were my only guidance. This game is one of my favorites of all time. You should play this. I'm sharing it with all of my friends.

This game... Oh man this game... This is, by far, the best game I have ever played. I'm 15, but I still love this game, and I could play it a million times over if I could. This game definitely deserves a full sequel, not by "episodes", but by a full game "Half-Life 3". This game is the pinnacle of Valve's creations, and shame on the people who pirated this amazing game, just because they can't save up some cash to support the development of a (hopefully even more amazing) sequel to this masterpiece. The ending to this game is amazing, and the ending to the episodes are just BEGGING for a sequel.
If I were to rate this game, released only 6 years after Half-Life, I would rate 10/10 overall.
11/10 for graphics, especially for its' time.
10/10 for gameplay. My god is the gameplay amazing.
10/10 for creativity. A nuclear physicist, armed with only a crowbar and gravity gun, deserves high praise.
9/10 for game types. Multiplayer would have been a nice feature, but Half-Life 2: Deathmatch, and the length of single player definitely makes up for it.
10/10 for sounds. The sound effects in this game are phenomenal, and the voice acting is spot-on perfect.
Overall, this game is hardly debatable as the greatest game ever made. Anyone who always reads reviews before they buy it, I say BUY IT RIGHT NOW! Play the game, or be left in the dust with all the others who haven't seen the beauty of Valve's greatest achievement.

Mazes and hallways with impossible infinite loops, whole areas contained in deceptively small spaces and portals that allow you move you from room to room simply by changing your perspective are all common place here. The addition of a Matter gun that lets you manipulate special material, various traps, secrets and testing apparatuses make for a complex and often confounding experience. At the same time, the game's unique sense of pacing keeps it from ever getting too frustrating. You can't die - instead if you get stuck you're able to instantly warp back to the main hub at any time. The main hub acts as a map where you can revisit any room you've discovered thus far, so you're able to tackle whatever area you want when you're ready to solve it and you're very rarely forced to do any excessive backtracking. There is a timer, but (without spoiling what happens if it runs out) there isn't much sense of urgency. Along with a rather pleasant ambient soundtrack that slowly builds as you progress, Antichamber is a unique experience that can prove to be just as serene as it is mindbending. Highly recommended.

I made that review was when I just started playing this game, and looking back at it, I feel like it does not do justice to this game. So here goes:
XCOM is a strategy game that, although turn based, keeps you on the edge of your seat, will leave you cursing your mistakes (especially in ironman mode), and challenge you to think on your feet almost all the time.
Things I like most about this game:
- It is a game where you have to think before making your next move, as going in blindly will not win any battles. A great contrast to games where you just go about shooting and hacking everything in your way.
- Also unlike other games, this game does not have a level where you can restart if you fail (except in some rare special cases). So usually, even if your whole squad dies, you must carry on with whatever you have left. And if you cannot, Game Over, and restart from scratch.
- Lastly, the base customization is great. You only have tech you research, equipment you built and upgrades you have bought. It really helps make the game feel like one whole big experience rather than a collection of levels
So, again, BEST STRATEGY GAME EVER!!!

My experience with Arkham Knight on PC was vastly different from others, I hardly had any crashes or graphical hiccups. The real problem is that this game does not have a gratifying resolve, regardless of gameplay or story. It is just lukewarm. There is so much here that could have made it the best Batman-game on the market, but it is arranged so poorly that it resolves into being “just another” Arkham-style game.
Pro:
01) It’s another Arkham-style game**
02) The Batmobile is kinda fun
03) Harley Quinn’s “booty sequence” and well-designed V-cut top
Cons:
X1) It’s another Arkham-style game, but it gets outclassed by Shadow of Mordor in comparison.
X2) Scarecrow is supposed to be the Main Villain, but “you know who” and Emo-Kylo Ren’s twin brother hog the spotlight; but thank god because Scarecrow says “Fear” more than all of the Scooby-Doo-films combined in saying “Scooby-snacks” (and they’re synonymous)
X3) Everything is poorly arranged and feels jimmy-rigged together. Wasted characters and gameplay opportunities, 2nd-rate story arcs, not to mention the overuse of a unique concept (Batmobile) just render the game as “lukewarm”
X4) The underusing of Harley Quinn in this game is ludicrous. Rocksteady knows how to make micro-campaigns, a  “Blood Dragon-esque” campaign for Harley Quinn-fans would have easily made shovel-loads of money and saved the game from its lukewarm reception
To Fellow Harley Quinn-enthusiasts:
Rocksteady made a big deal about our favorite psychiatrist in black & red tights being playable, but she is vastly underused to the point that I asked myself, “Why even give her a ‘Story Campaign’?” She is fun to play as in AR Challenges; but this is no Mega Man X’s ZERO Micro-campaign, rather a cheap, unfulfilling promise to many of us who want to play a Harley Quinn starred Action-game (even if it is a Micro-campaign)
Verdict:
If you want to play another Arkham-style game, this is an option. It is no magnum opus like Arkham City or well-crafted experience like Shadow of Mordor. If this is your first Arkham-style game, you may love it; but to other fans of the genre it really is just indifferent when compared to the other titles

The addition of a Matter gun that lets you manipulate special material, various traps, secrets and testing apparatuses make for a complex and often confounding experience. At the same time, the game's unique sense of pacing keeps it from ever getting too frustrating. You can't die - instead if you get stuck you're able to instantly warp back to the main hub at any time. The main hub acts as a map where you can revisit any room you've discovered thus far, so you're able to tackle whatever area you want when you're ready to solve it and you're very rarely forced to do any excessive backtracking. Pay attention, everyone. THIS is how you adapt a tabletop system to a videogame. Shadowrun Returns is what that looks like.
The game is mechanically sound and tactically interesting. The combat is straightforward enough to pick up easily, but as you upgrade your character and progress through the game, your options and strategies become more complex. Character progression is also quite well-handled; although you have tremendous freedom in choosing how to spend your "Karma," the game seems to do an excellent job of keeping all your choices balanced and avoiding game-breaker builds.
All of this is backed up by a lovely, slick interface (with just the occasional hiccup or quirk), an excellent soundtrack, and a content editor so that users may make their own campaigns. I have not tried the editor, but there is no shortage of custom content in the Steam workshop right now, so I presume it works.
The default campaign is quite solid, itself. It acts as a perfect introduction to this universe, and features exceptionally strong writing- something I can't say about nearly as many games as I'd like. A good portion of my enjoyment of Shadowrun Returns came directly from the strength of the setting and story. (The final twist is a bit of a letdown, but in the context of everything that has already happened, it feels alright and is easy enough to overlook.)
Make no mistake, if setting and story aren't your thing and you'd rather play something more strictly gameplay-oriented, this is really not that game. I say that not because the gameplay is lacking, but because the story is given such high priority. You will spend a lot of time talking to people. Interesting, well-written people, but not everyone cares for that.
If that doesn't sound like a problem to you, then I would absolutely recommend this game.

Playing this game on and off since it's release, I can say without a doubt I will not be regretting this purchase. Having played the original quite a bit I feel as though this game far exceeds the originals quality. While I do enjoy this game and find that it has a lot to offer, the negative aspects of this are a glaring sore spot keeping a lot of people from enjoying this game so to adress them;
Microtransactions - As someone who has participated in the cosmetics race this game is pushing, I partially regret the dollar I put into it. The only purpose they serve is to have a different looking gun to stare at while you kill Zeds, it's not quite the CS:GO system where it's a point of bragging considering the fact it's impossible to show them off. I like the one skin I bought but I should have just downloaded and equally acceptable mod from workshop.
Lack of content - Classes feel wholly unfinished, they don't have enough weapons to allow variety, making having more than one of a class (other than the berserker) a detriment to the team, this could be a design choice but if so it's awful and limiting.
I still can't turn off ♥♥♥♥ING ZED TIME - I've had this complaint since the first Killing Floor, I understand that a lot of people like it, and therefore in online servers it is likely going to be turned on. However I still can't disable it in a hosted server, or in a solo game and it pisses me off.
Why poll the community if you don't actually follow the popular results? It irks me that after following development, and seeing where they were going they almost seemed to be ignoring the general public and fans. This is a major 180 from "Killing Floor 1" in which the game was almost exclusively run by fans, creating new content and interfacing with the devs on what they wanted. The original has workshop as paid DLC, you can still find the packs of the mods, and download them but if you'd rather support the game and mod developers you can buy the DLC. If this sounds farfetched feel free to go look for yourself.
What I enjoy about KF2 is the gameplay, on it's own this is a really finely tuned piece of the Zombie Survival genre. As a Killing Floor game it feels disjointed and disconnected from it's roots, it has a long way and I urge you to watch carefully, but as it stands unless you have some friends to play with, wait until the full release. You'll get the full picture of what the Developers had in mind, and you can make your choice as well informed as possible.

Narratively and game-flow speaking this is perhaps one of the best video games of all time. Working on a playthrough for the first time in 5 years and it's holding up really well. The bulk of the game has stood the test of time magnificently. A lof of the graphical elements are stil quite strong, particularly the facial textures. I've done several playthroughs over the years (2004, 2005, 2008, now 2014) and the only element that has degraded relative to other FPS games is the gun play. It's fairly clunky feeling. But all in all, the narrative, actual action sequences and story pacing are STILL second to none.
So is it still worth it? If you simply want a gun play FPS - no. If you want a stand out narrative action adventure, it is definitely worth it. Overall Half Life 2 stands the test of time and is STILL better than the vast majority of narrative-driven FPS games coming out today.

(4/5 stars)
Shadowrun Returns is a classic example of a game for “fans of the genre”.  It doesn’t have the budget to blow you away, but its solid implementation of gameplay systems and cool setting are more than enough to make for a very enjoyable experience.
The game’s story follows a single character, a “shadowrunner” that you create from scratch.  During character creation, you choose one of six starting archetypes: a mage, street samurai, decker (hacker), shaman, rigger (drone combat), or physical adept (magic & martial arts).  These archetypes give your character an initial boost in a certain direction, but don’t lock you out of any other path if you should change your mind afterwards.  After a certain point, it won’t make sense to be dropping points into lots of different upgrade paths anymore, but there are enough upgrades to spend some time early in the game trying out the different paths.  Once you do decide, you’ll want to stick with it since there’s no re-spec option that I saw while playing the game.
In retrospect, this may be why the game starts out a bit too easy.  I didn’t spend much time messing around in different upgrade paths, so almost all my points were going towards Rifle and Decking competencies.  Perhaps because of this, the first half of the game wasn’t very challenging at all.  In fact, about 5 or 6 hours into the game, the initial storyline seems to come to a conclusion.  Unsure how long the game was, I was ready to be a bit disappointed.  Fortunately, this turned out to be a false ending, merely the halfway point in the game.  From there on, combat got a bit tougher and more strategic and the game wrapped up really well.
Before going into combat, you’ll have the chance to hire your team.  You have a fixed group of runners of all types to choose from, although this list grows over the course of the game.  A couple times I forgot to save money for my team, and spent all my cash on weapons and armor for myself.  I ended up taking on one optional mission totally solo, and barely escaped with my life.
Choosing your team is very important.  Another time I picked a team that worked really poorly together and got wiped out on one of the late-game areas.  Luckily, there is a “Rewind” feature that lets you reload your save to any previous checkpoint, even if you didn’t make a distinct save.  I chose my new team more carefully and smashed through the previously difficult mission.
Combat works similarly to XCOM: Enemy Unknown, although it’s not quite as polished as that game.  Cover doesn’t seem to have a huge impact on hit percentages in Shadowrun Returns, and some actions seem to take one more click than should be necessary.  But the variety of powers for the different types of characters is fun, and there are plenty of opportunities to play with different strategies.
The game’s story itself is fine, but some of the characters you meet over the course of the game are even better.  Visually, the game has a very nice, clean 2D art style.  I played the game on PC, but I can imagine it probably works just as well on iPad or Android tablets, where it is also available.
By the time it was over, I quite liked Shadowrun Returns.  If you enjoy a good turn-based strategy game with a bit of map exploration, dialogue trees, and a wide variety of character progression, I can definitely recommend it.

This is a new review written 03/23/17. I deleted my old review because it was out of date.
.....I am giving it a positive recommendation now which I didn't previously. But I still don't like it as much as I liked KF1 and there are a lot of issues I'd like to see changed or fixed.
.....It is a good game compared to others but KF1 was better. The devs spent too much time on bells and whistles and not enough time making sure they retained the core feel and features of the original game.
Pros:
.....Basic gameplay:
Choose a class, a difficulty level, and a map.
Spawn into the map with up to five other players.
Kill zeds to earn cash and survive to the end of each round for bonus cash.
Use the cash between rounds to buy ammo, armor, and better weapons for the next round.
Survive all of the rounds to face one of the bosses.
Kill the boss and you've won.
Rinse and repeat.
For more details about what I like about the game see my review of KF1.
.....All of the stuff in the "details" part of that review still hold true here.
Here's what I don't like about the game.
Dark palette and a lack of basic visual controls:
....The new game is dark. I mean very dark. In the original game you could control the brightness, gamma, and contrast. In the new game you have only one option. And all of the maps are very dark, at max brightness I still can't see ♥♥♥♥. Why are basic visual control options missing?
Lack of depth:
.....While the graphics are good, they lack depth and definition. Combine this with the black color palette and you get a muddy, eye straining experience. Even the nuclear cloud looks two dimensional and flat.

.....Specifically there are zeds called crawlers that are black and scoot along the ground. In most dark areas they can't bee seen at all. The only way you know they are there is because you start taking damage or can't move in one direction or another because they are in the way. So you have to shoot blindly at your feet in all directions.
.....If there are multiple crawlers they're just a black blob of legs and you can't tell if you killed one of them or all of them.
.....Other items like bushes, cars, barrels are simply black outlines or blobs with no depth.  or detail. Some interiors have black holes where shadows make seeing interior details impossible.
Anemic weapons:
.....While some of the top tier weapons which were carried over from the first game are quite satisfactory, most of the newer weapons look and sound puny, don't have enough ammo, or scatter their bullets all over the place. KF1 had first rate weapons. Each one looked, sounded, and behaved as you would expect. And they were lethal.
Too many classes:
.....There are now ten classes in the game. In KF1 the commando class was one of the best all around classes. in KF2 it has been butchered and it's perks and abilities spread across three classes leaving the commando and it's step children in limbo as they no longer excel in any area or serve a clear role on a team.
.....The same can be said of the Sharpshooter. It's stepchild is the Gunslinger. They share a lot of the same weapons and similar perks while both are weaker than the original KF1 Sharpshooter.
.....The firebug class still suffers from low damage and not enough ammo to be useful at higher difficulties. Although they gave him a super cool microwave gun which is fun to use at lower levels.
Too much leveling:
......There are now ten classes in the game. Each class has 25 levels. That's 250 levels.
If you assume an average of an hour per toon per level, that's 250 hours of play time just to get all of your toons leveled up.
.....KF1 had levels. But I never felt like I was "grinding" just to level up a class. You just played the game and it happened. KF2 doesn't feel that way.
Too much dev time spent on bells and whistles that don't matter:
.....Skins, gun reloading animations, stumble mechanic, ragdoll bodies, and the gore mechanic. All fine and good. But the speed of the game has been ramped up. Enemies come at you faster and move around like spastic meth addicts. All those bells and whistles quickly become wallpaper (something you ignore) as the number and speed of your attackers increases.
.....Strangly enough your own characters movement still feels clunky and slow. A carry over from KF1 that I thought would have been fixed.
.....The ragdoll bodies combined with the stumble mechanic is particularly annoying. Because the ragdoll bodies keep moving around even after their dead.
.....So you shot it, but it's still moving. Is that the ragdoll body wiggling around on the ground or did I or just stumble it and it's still coming? Or is that another zed behind it that I can't see because the body is still wiggling around?
.....On some occasions you shoot a zed, it falls down, and you think it's dead but it just gets back up. See a zed blown across a room? Don't ignore it, it may still get back up and come at you from behind.
.....At this point I just shoot everything until it stops moving. But In the highest difficulties ammo and cash for kills are reduced so ammo management becomes important. At that level wasting ammo on something that's already dead is a bad idea.

That number above me? Ignore it. I've played through Dead Space more times than I can count. That was on the PS3 version which I feel to be technically superior, despite this being a somwhat shoddy port. To start out with the PC-specific stuff, it's a little messy. Most noticable is the framerate being locked to 30FPS, at least on my nVIdia card. To fix this, all I had to do was change the Vsync option to "adaptive" and the game ran at a smooth 60FPS from that point on.
Now, unlike the console versions of this game, there is no DLC support for this title. Personally, I'm fine with this, because all that the downloadable content amounted to was overpriced pay-to-win re-textures of existing weapons and armour. The PC version may lack this content, but depending on your view, it may just be better of for it. What the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions of this game lack however, is any way of improving the frame rate. If you ask me, having twice the frame rate is enough to consider this the definitive version of Dead Space.
But what is Dead Space exactly? Well, if all the spooky screenshots didn't already give it away, it's a sort of horror game. On the horror action spectrum, I'd say it falls under "Action Horror" akin to Resident Evil 4. with some survival horror trappings to keep you on your toes. In terms of structure, BioShock is the most apt comparison. The levels aren't exactly open-ended, but aren't totally corridors, either. The routine is as follows: you get an objective, fight your way to said objective, and flip a switch which causes a slew of enemies to ambush you in a hectic, almost arena-like battle. After completing that objective, some other part of the ship will break down in an almost comical manner, forcing you to play repairmen across several hours. Seriously, this should just be called Murphy's Law: The Game (In Space).
The characters can honestly be pretty forgettable, especially silent protagonist space engineer Isaac Clarke, who struggles to be endearing and badass at the same time without having to say a word. The worst part? I think it actually works. If you're a fan of the mute hero trope, you'll probably will enjoy slipping into Isaac's boots, though some players might understandably find it jarring. The narrative can be sparse at times, but does feature a pretty decent twist that sees some expansion in later games, as the universe opens up.
Combat is frantic, clunky and intense. Though I compared the game to Resident Evil 4, it leans closer to survival horror than that game. You have melee attacks, but they really don't want you to use them. You have telekinesis, but it's not always super effective, unless you're hurling an explosive. All of this comes together to create a system in which you are forced to fight back, regardless of how bad you might be at fighting. If there's one thing Dead Space manages to pull of extremely well, it's putting you in the shoes of the game's protagonist, an inexperienced engineer who's forced to survive in a horrifying situation. You CAN and MUST fight the Necromorphs to survive, but you aren't very good at it.
Okay, there's another thing Dead Space accomplishes that few others can: a sense of seamless immersion. There's no true heads up display present in the game, only contextual holographic pop-ups that are very much a part of the game world. Your health and statis meters are displayed on your back, allowing you to get a clear idea of your status without constantly breaking your immersion with an ugly HUD. It's honestly my favourite thing about the entire franchise, and it's something I wish more games did.
If you're a fan of science fiction movies from the 70's and 80's, you'll probably appreciate this game like I did. Visually and thematically, the Dead Space franchise has been heavily influenced by the Event Horizon and Aliens, along with an assortment of other sci-fi flicks.
At its core, this is a very strong entry into the horror genre as a whole. It's UI is a bit clunky, and it's age as an early seventh generation title certainly shows, but these issues are more or less cleaned up in the later iterations. Still, you can beat the purity of the original Dead Space game. Though it has a heavy emphasis on action, it still creeps me out with its oppressive atmosphere and horrifying monster design. If you're looking for some spooks, you've come to the right place.

As a Killing Floor player since the Unreal Tournament 2004 mod, even I was hesitant to write this review at some points in Killing Floor 2's roller coaster of an Early Access cycle. Early Access in itself is very tricky. Tripwire stated that they wanted to "Do it right" for early access. They failed that promise for the 1st half of the Early Access cycle, and scared away a lot of Killing Floor 1 veterans as well as newcomers. To help summarize what happened, here is the complete development cycle compiled to the best of my abilities:
*Killing Floor 2 was officially announced on May 8th 2014 surprisingly by PC Gamer. It was confirmed to being worked on since 2011, and many fans had expected that it was in development shortly after KF1, in 2010. It was slated for full release in "minimum" 2015. On December 6th 2014 it was announced for PS4 as well.
*On April 21st 2015 Killing Floor 2 was anxiously released on Steam Early Access.
To start, only 4 of the 10 perks(Commando, Support, Medic, Berserker) would be in Early Access, 1 boss (Hans Volter) and a measly 3 maps (Biotics Lab, Outpost, Burning Paris). To say the least, this got old fast. Despite the massive graphical improvement, excellent gameplay mechanics and impressive tech features(covered below).
*In May 2015 1 map (Volter Manor) was added to try to keep players at ease with the promise of new perks and an old favorite boss was announced to be coming soon.
*In June 2015 we saw the first glimpse at my favorite NVIDIA feature to date, GameWorks’ PhysX Flex. This physics based engine is without a doubt a game changer in a shooter that focuses in Blades, Bullets and Blood. Pooling blood, puke, squirting headshots.......its worth buying a new NVIDIA card just for that.
*In September 2015 Incinerate 'n Detonate was released as the first real content pack. Adding in an array of new features including two new favorite perks (Firebug, Demolitions). And 2 new maps (Catacombs, Evacuation Point). Catacombs perfectly amplified the firebug's "bright" nature of burning everything and the demolition's perk made my Nvidia Flex bloodlust even more intense on Evac Point. With zed's guts floating in the pools of blood and decorating the walls like confetti and beads on mardis gras....except it was intestines and gore. Seriously, Evac Point is a good map with the RPG-7. :Fleshpound:
*In November 2015 the Trading Floor/ZEDconomy was added to the game. Adding in microtransactions. Once again splitting the community. While only cosmetic, this set off a bad vibe for an Early Access game. Remember, at this point we only have 6 perks and 6 maps. At this point, the game would obviously not be finished in 2015.
*To remedy this massive blowback, The Return of The Patriarch content pack was announced in November 2015. Becoming the second massive expansion adding in 2 new maps (Black Forest, Farmhouse), 1 new perk (Gunslinger) and 1 boss, the return of the big man himself, the original Patriarch boss.
*And then silence.........minor tweaks, no content. New microtransactions, no content. Minor hints at the next favorite perk, no content. This deafening silence, fractured the community as a whole and sent even the most loyal fans into disappointment. Many of these issues were caused by a lack of communication and some nasty false rumors being spread about Tripwire Interactive.
*In January 2016 Tripwire turned things back around and admitted that they wanted to better communicate with their fanbase. They immediately hosted a livestream to answer questions, showed off the Revenge of the Zeds update in which players can play as the zeds, hinted at the Bullseye update, talked about more future content/ideas, as well as apologized for mistakes made. Still, they could not provide any content. Stringing along more minor tweaks and perk balances.
*In March 2016, Tripwire updated the game to include support for Steam Workshop.
*Shortly before The Revenge of the Zeds update in April, Tripwire hosted another livestream to answer questions and show off the new mode.
*In April 2016, after almost 5 months of near dead silence, The Revenge of the Zeds content pack was FINALLY released. Adding 2 weapons for the upcoming Sharpshooter perk(Crossbow/Lever Action), 1 map (Prison), a crafting system for The Trading Floor/ZEDconomy and a surprise release of the new PVP VERSUS mode. While PVP was criticized for being something no one asked for, it ended up being surprisingly fun and unique. Despite the resources that should have been used towards core development.
*In June 2016 the Bullseye content pack was announced, completely adding in 1 perk with its other weapons, the most anticipated (Sharpshooter), 2 maps (Contamination Station, Hostile Ground) and an impressive amount of balances to 4 out of the 8 perks, UI changes and new gameplay systems(Resistance/Weakness System/Game Difficulty Modifier).
*In July 2016 the 3rd Q&A livestream was held by Tripwire. This showcased the next perk, new content and addressed that over 30 updates have been made since the release of the game in Early Access. Once again they stressed that they are paying close attention to feedback and are getting faster at updates. A new boss was hinted at as well. They officially announced that the game would be fully released in Holiday 2016.
*In August 2016 1 perk (SWAT) and 1 map (Infernal Realm) was released in a beta update. In addition to this second to last perk, new gameplay mechanics for the zeds(Evade,Block,Rage) were added, heavy refinements on existing player mechanics(Parry,Poison,Panic,Stun,Knockback,Knockdown,Freeze), refinements to the other 4 out of previously 8 perks(now 9), adjustments to the in game difficulty modifier, 2 new versions of zeds(Alpha Clot and Poison Crawler) and major sound/UI/quality changes. This update was huge and fundamentally solidifies how perks should feel.
*In August 2016 it was announced that Killing Floor 2 would be released on November 18th 2016 on PS4 and PC.
So where does that leave this review then? Well, considering the massive amount of content that has been released in the last 6 months, we now have at this moment:
-9/10 Well Balanced Perks(Medic,Berserker,Commando,Support,Firebug, Demolitions,Gunslinger,Sharpshooter,SWAT)
-12 Unique Maps(many more in testing at the moment including Nuke from workshop)
-Steam Workshop Support
-Cosmetic Microtransactions(for better or for worse)
-6 Player Co-op Survival(with endless survival coming)
-12 Player Versus PVP with Playable Bosses(for better)
-2 Bosses(with a 3rd coming)
-14 different zeds(excluding bosses, more zeds hinted at)
-An overhauled resistance/weakness system
-Slomo Zed Time is better than ever
-Crisp audio, with improved weapon sounds and animations
-In game difficulty modifier that rivals Left 4 Dead's "Orchestrator"
-Cutting edge technology such as NVIDIA Flex, 4K support, A genius system that leaves blood on the map the whole game, Advanced PhysX options that strings giblets across the map,the M.E.A.T. system which controls how many ways zeds are eviscerated, NVIDIA HBAO+ Ambient Occlusion, Depth of Field, Bloom and industry standard lighting/shadowing.
-Server Browser, Drop in/Drop out support, Server Takeover, Dedicated Servers, Achievements, Trading Cards, Crossover DLC and Gameplay balanced around the perks.
After seeing the SWAT update's perk attunements in August, and seeing the PS4 version at E3 in June(which had up until the Gunslinger update (7/10 perks implemented)), I have no doubt in my mind that the last perk should be out before October and the game finished by the November 18th date for both PC and PS4. There is plenty of time to finish refining the game until then. As it stands, I would say there is more than enough content now, to keep you playing for a VERY long time. Hell on Earth difficulty is brutal, the AI is smart and BOY OH BOY is it a bloody, gory, puke filled good time.

This game is amazing.  The construction is close to perfect.  You're constantly deciding between continuing and staying to get all the items on the level.  Both have their merits, and finding the balance between the two is enough of a challenge to keep you going for hours.
The upgrade system is great.  You have to earn every item you receive, on the micro and macro levels.  To unlock new items in game, you need money, which you can't get without fighting.  Overall, you can't find items unless you complete the corresponding achievement.  To do this, you need to master skills and classes, which means you have an incentive to play as all the characters, giving tons of replay value and preventing the game from getting boring.
Continuing on the replay value trajectory, there are plenty of game- and self-imposed challenges that you can employ to give the game a whole new experience.  You can try speed runs or you can hunt for the in-game Artifacts.  These artifacts, when employed, put new effects in place that alter the pace and difficulty of the game in new, exciting ways.
Finally, if you thought you had tried everything in the game, try playing with friends! There's local multiplayer, allowing up to three gamepad-users to play on your computer screen (this probably works best with two or more monitors), or there's internet multiplayer.  The online MP is a little tricky to set up, but I think it's worth it for the new collaborative experience.
All in all, the game is a constant challenge, with essentially infinite unique games to be played out.  High replayability, and it keeps you guessing every time.  Just when you think you've mastered it, the game humbles you by kindly ripping you to shreds.  With a great soundtrack, and sharp wit thrown in when you least expect it, this game will keep you entertained for days on end. 10/10.

What can I say? Yahtzee's review comparing this to Paper Mario is pretty spot on.
It's an RPG, simple to learn, easy to master, almost too easy. I cranked the difficulty up to hardcore knowing it was an easy game and it STILL provided only a mediocre amount of challenge if only because I was playing to maximize the amount of achievements I got in a playthrough. But I suppose it is nice to do that because then subsequent playthroughs are faster and easier. Seriously you can attach upgrades to weapons and armor and remove them at will with no penalty, it's very easy to become OP and makes combat trivial and time consuming (which I guess is why the main story almost entirely consists of Paper Mario style dungeons where you want to use the environment to instakill enemies in interesting ways to skip past combat).
Mechanically the game has different status conditions (stunned, asleep, grossed out, on fire, and bleeding) but given how bosses are immune to stun, sleep, and grossed out, not to mention a more frequently recurring enemy 'type' that's always immune to grossed out it can be very easy to accidentally gimp your character (offset by the game's ease, I guess). Respec-ing doesn't exist so yeah, have a plan for a character.
Plotwise it's solid (for South Park) right up until the end. No, seriously, you will know the point at which Matt Stone walked into the dev team's room and said "Alright, gimme what you got cuz we're releasing this tomorrow." But the stuff before the ending is really good. Without spoiling, they effectively recorded voices for multiple characters for every scenario, placing bits from the show in at all kinds of points to really make it worthwhile to explore.
Overall pick this up while it's on a 66% sale. I did and I got a lot out of the game (3 playthroughs worth of entertainment). Just be aware that this game does have missables, and missables make you playthrough again to get achievements.

Kind of a mixed bag for me - I'm a big fan of both the genre and the gameplay, and was familiar with Shadowrun back in the pencil-and-paper RPG days, so i was a little biased to get this. Overall, it was a fun game - but had two big flaws. One was the lack of meaninful decisions in the storyline - the story was very much on rails here; many have described it as less of a game and more of an interactive novel, with you playing out some of the action scenes (and I'd have to say that's a pretty accurate description). The other, related, complaint is lack of meaningful choices in your character. Don't have a slicer? No problem - the game gives you one. Your character is a bruiser? A smooth talker? It doesn't matter - the game will allow pretty much all paths to succeed in essentially the same ways. While I understand this from a gamer perspective (no one likes to feel like they're missing out on content as thay play!) for me this really hurt replay value.
Still, overall I enjoyed the game. It was a little less than I'd hoped, but still enjoyable.

Narratively and game-flow speaking this is perhaps one of the best video games of all time. Working on a playthrough for the first time in 5 years and it's holding up really well. The bulk of the game has stood the test of time magnificently. A lof of the graphical elements are stil quite strong, particularly the facial textures. I've done several playthroughs over the years (2004, 2005, 2008, now 2014) and the only element that has degraded relative to other FPS games is the gun play. It's fairly clunky feeling. But all in all, the narrative, actual action sequences and story pacing are STILL second to none.
So is it still worth it? If you simply want a gun play FPS - no. If you want a stand out narrative action adventure, it is definitely worth it. Overall Half Life 2 stands the test of time and is STILL better than the vast majority of narrative-driven FPS games coming out today.

Killing Floor 2 is a wave-based, co op shooter. It is truly an incredible game and well worth re-writing a review for.
This is the game that truly got me into gaming at all. It drove me to upgrade from Intel HD graphics to an 560 ti, to finally building a new beast machine from scratch.
There are just so many things that this game got right. First, the gun play is fantastic. I've never seen better gun animations and models, barring perhaps the Battlefield franchise which is reknown for it's realism in weaponry. The BLAST of a double barrel shotgun or the whistling of an RPG rocket are all done to perfection.
Next, the co op is where this game truly shines. While a very fun experience playing solo, when you play with 5 other people all with different weapons shredding, exploding, blasting, and slicing through zeds (this game's "zombies) it feels very epic. Especially to the pounding metal which I already listened to before even getting this game.
Probably one of my favorite aspects of this game is the developers (which can't be said for a lot of games). Tripwire has been so loyal to this game and I can't really give them enough praise for all the continued support they give to Killing Floor 2. Every few months out comes a new weapon, map, or game mode, so don't feel that if you buy this game you are buying a dead end, dying product (quite the opposite).
If you have the rig to handle it, I highly suggest turning all settings up to maximum for this game (including Nvidia flex). While a massive performance hitter, the gore is just ridiculous. I've never seen any other game that has such explosive and in-your-face gore, besides Doom 2016. It makes it pretty satisfying to blast zeds when they fall into pieces and blood flows into a puddle at your feet. Yikes.
In summary, you can't go wrong with this game, especially on sale. As you can see I've put way too much time into this game and it will only go up as Tripwire adds more content. You can make or play on custom maps, jam to metal music, and slay monsters with your friends. It's awesome!!!

Risk of rain is really simple game about finding cool stuff that do cool stuff, stacking as much as possible, then using said cool stuff to annhilate hordes of nasty things... all to a really cool sountrack!
Seriously though, this is as close to the binding of isaac people are going to get without having to play the binding of isaac. Which for some people is a god send, especially because top down games can and do give people huge headaches to play, myself included a few years back. Nowadays though, I will suffer through any rogue-like if it promises gameplay even half of what risk of rain offers.
The graphics to begin with are really, really small and that's awesome. Your character will look like they are miles away, which only gives scope to how big some of the enemies are. Every little thing in the game is made up of pixels, sometimes individual ones if it adds a level of depth to the creation. Most of the characters have single pixel big arms and legs, while the bosses you're trying to kill are a hundred times that and really, really beautiful to witness.
The soundtrack is, like the graphics, superb in a very specific way. The music doesn't change during a level, doesn't get more complicated based on your situation, it just plays out nicely in the background, awaiting your demise. Chiptune and ambient layers fall on a framework of chill-out techno, perhaps even straying into the realms of trip hop once or twice. Each level is perfectly fitted with a piece of music, each boss has a brooding track that makes you regret touching the damn teleporter and the tiny sounds here and there that give you information such as an item picked up, an enemy kill or an enemy spawned fit perfectly. The sound world of risk of rain is a complete one and should be downloaded along with the game.
The game itself is a mixture of two things. It has the character selection, unique stats and abilities as a MOBA, the item collecting of a classic sega megadrive platformer (each one stacking for added damage/% chance/chance to poison, etc...) and the difficulty of a middle of the road title, somewhere between zelda and dark souls, not childish by any means  but not frustrating either. You will die a lot, but it will always be your fault and not the game throwing some unavoidable crap in your face.
You kill enemies to acquire money, then spend that on chests and shrines in the hope of getting an item (chests always, shrines not so willing to help you out). That item might make you faster, or increase your chance of doing double damage. It might also allow you to spawn a butt-ton of rockets when opening any chest from then on, or add a piercing shot to your third attack from then on. They stack of course, giving you increased chances each time. Bosses may drop their own unique items too, adding to your arsenal. As you become stronger, the clock ticks away and the longer you preserve yourself, the harder the difficulty becomes. When you reach the penultimate level and beat it, you can either tackle the final level now, or teleport back to the beginning with all your collected items intact and the difficult such that only bosses spawn... a lot!
Along the way you'll encounter rune stones that change how the game is played and even make some characters you thought we terrible amazing. Glass for example gives you 10% of your normal starting health but allows you to deal 500% of your normal damage, making the otherwise poultry, accumulative effects of Acrid's special attacks now pull down juggernauts from their cities in the sky.
Either playing the game normally, adding some rune stones for variety, changing your character for each day of the week, you'll have so much fun with this game I cannot recommend this enough. When you become good, the rune stones will bring you back down to earth, especially because most of them reduce your new found skills to the childlike button mashing you experienced when first you played the game. I would expect more updates in the future, but even if there aren't, the value for money is absolutely amazing.
10/10 - Even if the game finds no new dlc in the future, follow the guys that made it and show them some love for their efforts. Most of them are still learning! Why, when they can make games of this quality, I will never know...

Downside: no half-way-through-a-puzzle save. So if you spend an hour on a puzzle and quit without having it solved, that gets added to your time twice effectively since you'll need to start over.
I wouldn't say I've "completed" the game since there were quite a few "hidden areas" and sort-of easter eggs I've yet to find. Plus I didn't find all the weapons.
Is it worth your money? Yes. If you're a true puzzle fanatic looking for a challenge. If you intend to play this game just to get to the exit / credits, wait until it's on sale.
Other remarks? Sure;
+ Awesome sound track/ambience
+ Simplistic graphics, complicated puzzles
+ Feels of being able to "hack" the game
- No in-between saves
- Fairly straight forward puzzles (i.e. no 5 step-ahead thinking required)
- Didn't have any "Eureka" moments
So. Worth a shot, worth a replay, but wait for it to be on sale.

Dead Space is a wonderful game combining many genres, third person shooter, survival, action, and horror, all into on. While some games fail when trying to do too much, Dead Space is able to do all of these parts well and deliver a satisfying experience from start to finish.
Dead Space progresses very nicely from start to finish. The story is intriguing and, while horrifying space creatures is nothing new, presents a well rounded and detail/lore filled experience that took some thought to follow. The opening sequence leads very nicely right into the action, immediately making you want to find out just what happened to that ship.
As far as firefights go, this game offers some intense sequences. Whenever I overcame a hoard of enemies I felt like a badass, but I always hoped that an engagement like that wouldn't happen again. This may be what Dead Space does best: present you in an environment that makes you uncomfortable, leave you feeling exposed at all times, and give you just enough to get the job done if you do it right and think on your feet.
That being said, I found the biggest flaws in the game to also center around the combat situations. While there are plenty of action sequences in the game, it is not as smooth as other action games, which is of course fine as this isn't the initial purpose. However, some sequences and enemies felt cheap to me when you meet them. The enemies are varied, challenging, and interesting as a whole, but some sequences are downright frustrating. Often this happens when an objective is not fully clear or your purpose is not adequately explained. I don't expect a game to hold my hand, but when it isn't clear what that button you just pressed does, but swarms of enemies come out of the vents, it can become exhasperating. Fortunately, this doesn't happen too often.
The progression system in Dead Space is very good and rewarding. You can build your loadout to your playstyle and upgrade equipment to suit your strengths. Dead Space offers a variety of weapons to use and tactics to implement to keep battles fresh and fun.
I would definitely recommend Dead Space, even though it is a few years old. It is still a great game, and at a discount during Christmas or summer for $5 simply can't be missed.

An overambitious, overcomplicated, disappointing entry in the Arkham series.
The combat, which was so fluid and satisfying in Arkham City, now has too many bells and whistles thrown in. The controls, which were much refined from Arkham Asylum to Arkham City, seem to have devolved again into more fiddly and annoying (seriously, who can switch to Alt+number keys in the middle of a combo??). Combat controls for the Batmobile ensure you'll have cramped fingers within a few seconds, as you're either holding down "W" to accellerate or the RMB to stay in 'battle mode' during a battle - apparently toggles are out of fashion.
The story takes itself far too seriously, unable to decide if the tone should be dark psychological horror (the oh, GODS so annoying unskippable Joker crap), or confident and inspiring tale of victory against the odds. The twists are telegraphed from a mile away, we're forced to once again sit through the illusion of choice as Batman makes mind-numbingly stupid decisions throughout, and never learns a damn thing.
There are good things in here. The refinements to Predator combat, especially the varied use of the disruptor weapon and the 'fear' takedowns, are a joy to play, but you don't get to play with them anything like enough to put up with the rest of the crap.
Avoid this bloated, self-indulgent misery-fest, and just play through Arkham City a few more times.

Ever look at history's greatest leaders, and conquers and think "Hey I bet I could do that better!" Well now you can prove it. Civilization V lets you take your pick of famous civilizations and guide them from a tribe of nomads with some stone axes to a space capable world super power that can rain death with nuclear powered death bots. While mastering the mechanics will take experience, having a working knowledge good enough to make it in your first game is easy. Want to be warrior race that dominates your neighbors? Do it. Want to play nice with your city-states? Watch as when Attila starts a war you fight back with your whole coalition. I haven't found a culture win to be very viable, but science, military, and science are all fun to compete for. Cultures are programmed to act like the leader they're based off of. Attila will usually be a war-monger that conquers any city-states in their reach. George Washington will be a diplomate-general, and the Greeks will typically act diplomatically. Play enough games and you will learn the patterns of most of the AI. My advice, when you are selecting a faction, have the victory you want to pursue in mind. Unless circumstances dictate otherwise, you'll have a hard time getting science victory with Germany, or A diplomatic victory with the Huns. Also try not to grow too fast.
