Bottom line: this in an INCREDIBLE game with a DULL ENDING.
What happened with the PC version of this game is almost tragic. It's been infamous because of its terrible port to PC, but if you are able to run it and play it, you'll discover probably one of the best AAA games ever made.
If you like Batman as a characters of have enjoyed the previous Arkham games, you'll probably love this one as well. Its story is spectacular, to say the least, with several memorable moments and conversations between Batman and his close associates.
I played the game on a PC with a Gigabyte GTX 770 4GB GPU, an I7 3770 CPU and a Sandisk SSD. When I capped the game FPS at 60 or 90, I experienced wide variations in performance, like many users, and it was very noticeable during the game. However, when I capped FPS at 30, the game never fell under 29 fps and performed steadily with that framerate. I know that for many players, that's unacceptable, but since I played the other Arkham titles on my PS3 at 30 fps, I could play this one with that framerate without any trouble.
That said, there are two aspects of the game that I didn't like that much: the Riddler challenges and the ending.
Somewhere I read that this game had a "good" ending and a "bad" ending, and that in order to get the "good" ending you had to arrest all the main enemies, including the Riddler. And to be able to fight and capture the Riddler, you have to finish all the Riddler challenges.
I love side missions and I even loved the Riddlers challenges which were part of the game story. But in order to complete all the additional Riddler challenges, I had to literally spend days tracking and solving them -many of them were pretty clever- but it totally drove me away from the main story during that period. I would have put all those additional Riddler challenges in a DLC or something. There's also not a "good" or "bad"ending; apparently, they are the same, one is just "complete" and the other one "incomplete".
Many players probably liked the ending, just like many people liked the Batman movies' ending. I didn't like either. I don't like open endings. But that's just a matter of opinion.
Many players have complained about the overuse of the Batmobile. I actually enjoyed many sections with the car, but I agree it was probably too much. There are parts when you HAVE to use the Batmobile to advance in the main story. I would have probably given a choice, as a developer, to use the car or find another solution with Batman for the people that didn't like to use the Batmobile that much.
I know that the car is a very big thing in American culture, but it always made more sense to me that Batman -as a character based on a flying creature- should resort more to the Batwing. Sadly, that flying marvel is used in the game just as a delivery and multipurpose drone.
So, to wrap this up, if you liked the previous Arkham games and you manage to run this one, you'll very probably love it!

If this game is ever under $10, jump on it. It is definitely worth it for that price, but I bought it on the Summer Sale, with all the DLC for about $18, and I feel a little salty about it. I'm a huge fan of the Arkham series, so my review is mostly comparing Arkham Knight to the others. Look, this is, in every aspect, another Arkham game. That said, it has a base level of quality. It looks pretty good even with the graphics set to low across the board. But compared to the rest of the series, it is far away the worst of the bunch.
The batmobile was a nice thought, but the controls are terrible. You feel like you're driving on ice the whole game, and I'm sorry, but with the big♥♥♥♥♥tread on those tires, Brucie isn't sliding anywhere unless he wants to. And even with the addition, I STILL had more fun zipping and gliding around Gotham. There are some interesting things to see from the Batmobile, but roof/air travel is still the only efficient means of getting around the city quickly.
My biggest issue with this Arkham entry was the combat. The Arkham Series' minimal button combat, which rewards timing over mashing, is among my favorites in action games. But the combat just seems. . .  off in this one. The timing is so picky compared to City and Origins, which caused me to fight around the edges of a mob rather than jumping right into the middle of the fray (as I believe Batman would in similar scenarios). As a result, it signifcantly limited the way I could fight, navigate within the group, and even the moves I could use. In larger fights I found myself reverting to the basic "pinball" fight mechanics, because all the fancy moves and gadget techs I had acquired were more dangerous than efffective.
An mechanic addition I REALLY liked was the Fear Multi-Takedown. This is an incredibly useful tool in predator situations, and I think it's a super fun way to start off a fight. Your FEAR guage is refilled by silently taking out enemies, or over time. If you have full fear, and you can sneak close enough to a group of enemies, you can initiate the Multi-takedown, highlighting enemies and beating them down one by one in a bullet-time style interactive custcene. It's intensely gratifying. Trust me. However, I have a feeling the developer didn't intend it to be used for combat as extensively as I did. It's not a big deal, I guess, I just would have liked more flexibility with how I exercized the option.
As for the story, (**NO SPOILERS HERE**) this is obviously the last game in the Arkham Trilogy (whatever that means). Fans of the series knew it before the release, and the plot makes it painfully, hurtfully clear about a gillion more times. But, even with that in mind, the ending is flat out dumb. It's anti-climactic, and it was a very serious let down for me personally. Until then, the story was a pretty standard Arkham affair. Just another night in Rocksteady's version of Gotham, which is to say: good, not great. But that ending. . . awful. There is a secret/additional ending if you 100% the game, which means finishing the side quests and collecting all those damn Riddler trophies. I am including that ending in my assessement of its stupidity.
Full disclosure: I bought the game and all the DLCs at once, so I can't really distinguish them all. But, there is some DLC that added a few more side quests to the vanilla game. These lead to some additional famous faces from Batman's extensive rougues gallery popping up in the main campaign. They essentially add an additional Most Wanted list to the base game. These DLCs, I loved. Anything that can make the story longer and more compelling, I'm on board.
The DLC AR missions, which are the stand alone combat and predator scenarios, are lame. Only because they focus so heavily on combat, which I was frustrated with from the get go. If you end up liking the short timing windows and extended counter animations, you'll love the extra AR missions, and more power to you.
Then there are the Arkham episodes. These are "story" driven mini adventures featuring some of Batman'sa supporting players (Nightwing, Robin, Catwoman, etc). They're. . . just. . .  dumb. Each one is basically just an excuse to take away certain fight moves and gadget abilities. (Which vanilla combat already does anyway.) For instance, every character in the game has a Scorpion-style grappling move that allows you to traverse the battlefield quickly, deal damage, and maintain your combo score. Oh, but Catwoman doesn't. SHE HAS A FREAKIN WHIP! Dumb.
I'm a huge Batman fan. A huge Arkham series fan. I was disappointed by this game, and I didn't even have to deal with any of the mess when it launched. (or when it re-launched and still sucked apparently.) Even if you feel an undeniable compulsion to play this game. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE excerize patience. One day it will be $9.99. Then, and only then, will it be time to play Batman: Arkham Knight.

I've played quite a bit of Shadowrun in my day, and I am thankful that there is now a game that actually embodies the feeling of running in the shadows of Seattle in the not to distant future.  For any of you who do not know, Shadowrun Returns is based on the tabletop RPG Shadowrun, a world in which magic has come back after being dormant for many years, and yet technology still remains, still marches forward.  Part cyberpunk, part fantasy...punk.  It is a great game.  This takes the game and translates it very nicely into a computer game, much the same way Baldur's Gate did for D&D.  It has a lot of the same feel as BG, and plays very similarly, just in a very different world.  And enough wonderful things can't be said about how great it is to have Workshop incorporated with this game.  There is a single, extensive story for the main campaign.  But because of Workshop, there are now dozens, maybe even hundreds of new stories that the community has built and you can now play.
The one con is that there is no multi-player aspect to this game.  It would have been fantastic if I could buddy up with my friends online and we run the shadows together, or even through a lan party.  Otherwise, this is a great game for any fans of BG, Shadowrun, or RPGs in general.

On the playstation 2 I absolutely loved GTA:Vice city. Before I get into particulars i'll broad-stroke the premise. GTA: Vice city was launched for the PS2. It can best be described as a sandbox adventure game. Youre given various missons and objectives by people and advance the game by completing these missions. Theres not a whole lot of missions aside from the main story but who needs sidequests when you are wreaking havock at every turn?

A large part of this game is the fun you make for yourself. Walking into this I was very excited to relive some old memories with crispy graphics, tiny load times and nearly endless draw distance. What I found was just that, except for a few small details that ended up being big problems. Remember on the good ol' PS2 when you would boot up Vice City and you had the time to walk away, get some snacks, maybe use the bathroom and sit back down and only have to wait a few moments more for the initial load? No more! Load times and load zones are no longer an issue here.
So was pretty stoked. I couldnt wait to see all(or most) of vice city rendered as once in the highest of resolutions. And this game delivered that for me too. It was a wonderful trip down memory lane, that is, until I had to take control of the main character. Unfortunately, the controls dont translate well to mouse and ketboard. At first it wasnt a problem, I used a ps3 controller. There are too many commands that have to be mapped to too many buttons, it wont let you have the same controls that you did on the PS2 version. I tried many different control schemes and ideas but none worked the way I really wanted them to. Eventually I gave up.
There ARE programs and doodads that you can use that should give you a better expierience with the controls. Also, vice city is very playable as is, out-of-the-box. I just couldnt get comforable with any controll schemes I tried.  If youre looking for a GTA game you can play on an older computer I'd reccomend GTA:San Andreas. It's slightly more easier to play on mouse and keyboard. If you are looking for a little bit of nostalgia, you would be better off booting up you PS2, and digging out your old copy.

This game makes me feel like I am the Batman even more than the prequels. There definately is something great about having the Batmobile that makes the Batman experience more complete. Although I enjoyed Arkham City very much, this game has more of that fighting, rescuing and detective stuff only better. As well as the Riddler puzzles, this time incorporating the Batmobile in them in a very fun way. I enjoy these new puzzles more than the old ones that were designed only for the Batman and not his car.
Lots of meaningful side missions this time round and they all have a sense of urgency for you to complete them, for example there is one where Catwoman is captured and fitted with an explosive collar which you must find a way to disarm but at the same time you are on the main mission to rescue the Oracle. Another example is a mission where you must find a killer that is killing innocent people and displaying them in public. Then there is one where you need to find a giant mutated bat creature that is terrorizing the city. All these side missions are pretty memorable in comparison to the side missions from Arkham City.
The city is much bigger and more detailed in this game and feels much more alive and believable, even though the city from Arkham City was already pretty good. More importantly, the Batmobile runs silky smooth on the roads of Gotham City and it is definately the predator of the road. I liked every moment with the Batmobile. One thing though, I would like to see the cockpit view of the Batmobile when i switch camera view. I think that would be so awesome being able to see the cockpit. Fortunately we do get a glimpse of the cockpit view in cinematic sequences, so I guess it is there just maybe need to enable it with a mod?
This is definately the best Batman game to date and I hope they make more. Nevertheless, one thing i don't like about the Batman games including this one is how difficult it is to target the exact bad guy i wanted. I wish they can find a way to make targeting easier, which would make melee combat much more enjoyable and not so erratic. Perhaps use an over-the-shoulder view during combat and include some form of crosshair for targeting purpose?
I mean lets face it the combat system is getting old and need a bit of change to make it more personal, up close, and visceral. The QTE button smashing follow by series of flashy animations has been fun to watch for a while. But now it just gets old and I find myself avoiding melee combat as much as possible by using the Batmobile to gun the bad guys down. Hopefully we see a new melee combat system in the next game and not just the same old QTE.

Risk of Rain is a platformer/sidescroller/survival game that puts you in control of one of a few survivors of a crashed spaceship. You will have to fight enemies and earn money to purchase upgrades and progress to the upper levels. The game's difficulty scales with the time, adding an incentive for players to use their time efficiently. In each individual "run" - or single playthrough - there are six levels, each with harder monsters and more expensive upgrades. Boss monsters appear at the end of a level or sometimes in the middle of a level if the difficulty is high enough. Risk of Rain will require several playthroughs to fully explore what all of the upgrades do and how to play each of the survivors.
Read more for an in-depth look at Risk of Rain.
This game's story is largely told in the beginning and end cutscenes, as well as in monster logs - information about enemies that randomly drop when you defeat one. Some of the descriptions in the item log also hint to background story events.
Risk of Rain [ROR] is a 2D pixelated platformer game. The art is excellent and each of the characters and enemies are unique. Each of the survivors has 4 unique abilities that are fairly balanced. Each one has their own forte and shortcomings, so experiment a little with all of them to figure out which one suits you. You only start with one character unlocked (the Commando), so you'll have to unlock the rest.
Items/upgrades are found in chests which unlock for a price. Monsters drop money and experience when killed, and both can also be found in small amounts within canisters. There are four ranks of upgrades - white (common), green (uncommon), red (rare) and orange (use item). The first three ranks are items that are either passive or triggered by events, while the fourth are items activated by the player. All use items and skills (except for the primary basic skill) have cooldowns. There is also an artifact hidden within each level. Artifacts do nothing in the run they are acquired in, but after that playthrough a new artifact's effect can be chosen in the character selection screen. Each one adds a different game element (only elites spawn, 500% damage but 10% health, etc).
ROR also has an incredible soundtrack, merging genres from electronic to trance to ambient to rock. Each level has its own exclusive background music, giving it a unique atmosphere. The sound effects are very believable and yet are alien enough to convince you that the planet you are on cannot be Earth.
Risk of Rain is an incredible platformer with solid gameplay mechanics, excellent replay value and an addicting arcade-style structure. Online multiplayer is also available. A solid game all-around. Definitely worth purchasing if you enjoy a good thrill.

Better than Binding of Isaac.  Yes, you heard me.
After consideration and playing for awhile now, I feel that Risk of Rain is a better rogue-like game than Binding of Isaac, perhaps even Rebirth.  Yes, you read right.
The reason why I feel this way is that BOI:Rebirth punishes players for using things like generated seeds by locking out achievements or forcing players to rely on random dumb luck to unlock things.  Risk of Rain on the other hand rewards players who ferret out the special artifacts that alter game play and do not penalize players for using them when it comes to unlocks.
Some people will feel that unlocks should not be the point of the game, but even without unlocks taken into consideration the artifacts allow players to really customize the feel -- from making things even harder than hard through using specific artifacts, to eliminating some of the randomization of drops so surviving as specific characters is less reliant on getting a good item early.  It makes the game feel less restricted in play.
At the heart of the game, there's still a tremendous amount of strategy involved in using the items you find to the best of your ability and class, with each class having drastically different play styles.  On top of it all, those who like the ludicrous over-powering of BOI:Rebirth should be satsified as it's quite possible to create that same feel using a combination of the right artifacts and items (and those who don't -- well you're covered as well).

I've played quite a bit of Shadowrun in my day, and I am thankful that there is now a game that actually embodies the feeling of running in the shadows of Seattle in the not to distant future.  For any of you who do not know, Shadowrun Returns is based on the tabletop RPG Shadowrun, a world in which magic has come back after being dormant for many years, and yet technology still remains, still marches forward.  Part cyberpunk, part fantasy...punk.  It is a great game.  This takes the game and translates it very nicely into a computer game, much the same way Baldur's Gate did for D&D.  It has a lot of the same feel as BG, and plays very similarly, just in a very different world.  And enough wonderful things can't be said about how great it is to have Workshop incorporated with this game.  There is a single, extensive story for the main campaign.  But because of Workshop, there are now dozens, maybe even hundreds of new stories that the community has built and you can now play.
The one con is that there is no multi-player aspect to this game.  It would have been fantastic if I could buddy up with my friends online and we run the shadows together, or even through a lan party.  Otherwise, this is a great game for any fans of BG, Shadowrun, or RPGs in general.

In another game named so generic that it has to add the developer's name to the title, "Sid Meier's Civilization V" is the fifth entry in the turn based hexigrid strategy game series. In Civilization series, you are always competing and aligning yourself with various other leaders on your way to world domination through several means. The game lets you grow your empire through conquering cities, settling new ones, through trade and other forms of diplomacy.
Civilization V feels and plays almost the same as previous entries in the series with a few upgrades, combat tweaks and a fresh coat of paint to make it feel modern. Is there anything wrong with having an updated game to a beloved series? Nope. Does it make me want to play it when I played previous iterations of the game twenty hears ago? Nope.
The game begins in ancient times and you will work your way up through the millennia so any Civilization takes a long while. You select a leader each with their own perk, select a map size and your desired type of map. Then the game generates a new and unique map making every play through unique. There are eight difficulty settings and four paces for how long you want the game to last. My play through on normal difficulty with a standard pace with a small map has surpassed six hours.
You start with a single city. Each city lets you produce something, either a unit to move around, a building to increase resources or a wonder. Over time the population of a city will grow depending on your food and the happiness of your population. Have too little food and the citizens starve and the city shrinks. With more citizens, the faster you can produce something.
Creating one building in town will unlock other building choices. Its a level of micro management that gets old when you have a dozen big cities with short production times that you are always producing stuff for them at every turn. Plus someone thought it was a good idea to have the produce button on the right side away from the list of stuff to produce on the left side.
Units have two major types: military and workers. Workers enhance the area around your cities. They can make connections, roads, mine, farm and you can chose to let them do the work automatically. If a worker is captured by a military unit, they are lost and become the enemy's worker. Military units have three forms, ranged, melee and siege to use against cites. Each unit has its own move distance of one or two tiles, attack distance, attack strength and so on. Creating specific buildings unlocks new military for that city.
Once you've unlocked the appropriate technology, most units can set sail in ships. The only catch is they're vulnerable to attack. Combat ships and long range attacks can sink the transports.
You can set a unit to move across the map, and see how many turns it will take them to get there. Then they will automatically move each turn unless you have them stop. You can have them do nothing, stand alert or go to sleep which in some circumstances is good as deleting them because I'd usually forget they exist for a few centuries. Military units can garrison cities and gain their defenses. Like other games of the genre, there is an automatic explore, which is good for scouts.
Combat takes place on the hexigrid world map. Simple battles play out between two units and you have no control, just the strategy of having ranged units can attack from two tiles away rather than one tile away. All units have ten health so when a unit takes damage they can fortify themselves which wastes a turn, but heals them a single point of health. Any fight will give the unit experience and leveling up gives a choice of certain perks such as better damage against enemies on rough terrain or clear terrain. Others gain one hit point per turn or 50% better defense.
Conquering cities is quite a task and requires too much effort. It can slow the game to a halt at least on normal difficulty. First you need to bombard the city with ranged attackers and mainly catapults or cannons. Then once the city has been weakened, you need to send in your melee attackers. Its a process that benefits the defenders. Taking cities turns into tedium as you can amass a giant army, then just go from one city to the next. Cities have a ranged defense mechanism that does little to deter my troops. I just have one troop take a beating and fortify themselves while other troops pummel the city. If the fortified troop gets down to one hit point left, take them away and replace them.
As you're playing, you acquire science points and gold from each city. Gold lets you quick buy units or buildings rather than taking the time to make them. Science lets you research technology quicker. Technology enhances one thing or another and can unlock new buildings or units.
Everything in the game is designed to unlock something else, to build something else to make it faster to build. With that in mind, the entire game is a grind,but its a grind that is just easy. So easy that its engaging because you're just making choices with some combat to give the game some diversity. Even the combat requires a only a small amount of thought.
There are heroes and several types of them with their own uses. A battlefield hero can increase effectiveness of those around him, and he can also make a citadel at the expense of his life. Science heroes can expend their life to get an instant technology. Another type of hero gets a project done instantly.
You also gain political points that let you unlock certain theologies and then perks that come long with them. Just another choice to keep you entertained. Engaging in war hurts your political points, but in return, its easier to bully your opponents. On the other hand starting a war may get several nations to hate you. Gandhi in my first game started out as a friend, then he wanted me to declare war on some nation he had a hatred for. When I asked him to wait ten turns, he agreed. Then when the tenth turn was up. I went to war and so Gandhi ended up going to war with me because I went to war with the one he wanted me to be at war with.
Some leaders will buy a peace treaty with you for X amount of turns. Agree to the terms and you never have to leave their borders. However, when I stocked up and surrounded cities of a nation I had a treaty with, once I declared war they threw everyone out of their territory. That took a lot of time and coordination across ten turns to get them put in and the game just nullified that. Oh but that never stopped my victory and that's a problem with the series, you know when you've won long before you've conquered the world, just as you know when you've lost long before the end.
To make the world feel more alive, there are barbarian tribes which have no alliance. They spawn soldiers and archers until you destroy them. Its interesting coming across a tribe of barbarians int he 1800s. In fact a lot of things are interesting in the 1800s like how a city still needs a coliseum, but I suppose its a fancy way of saying arena.
Its a toss up to recommend a game that is so easy there's no challenge, but its so easy that its relaxing. Its just a big grind that throws never ending choices in your face while you're conquering the world. Its fun for a play through, but after the daunting task of painting the world with my empire, its a journey I never want to take again. When all is said and done, its still the best looking hexigrid turn based strategy out there with over twenty years worth of depth and choices that keep you occupied and make each time unique.

Addictive as hell and hard to master. This game forces you to walk the line between making your character stronger with item farming and progressing to the next level of the game. If you move too fast, you'll be too weak to survive. If you move too slow, the difficulty scaling will overwhelm you. You will die... a lot... but restarting the game feels fun instead of a drudgery.
The combat is fun and fluid. The music is absolutely incredible (props to Chris Christodoulou). There is enough randomness to keep each play-through exciting. The items all make a difference and each of the characters (of the four I have unlocked so far) feel completely different to play as.
One drawback - and a minor one (I try to include one with every review) - as you get into later levels with loads of items/drones to help you and loads of enemies attacking you, it's hard to see where you are. There is a platforming element which gets obscured with the sheer amount of chaos that's going on on-screen. But if you're at that point, you likely don't have to move too much anyways. Sometimes a tactical retreat is in order though... this is where it gets a little tricky.
That said, this game is a MUST OWN. For $10 it's a steal. I've gotten more enjoyment out of this than almost all AAA games.

The aliens have invaded Earth and XCOM, a secret project created by the Council of Nations, becomes our planet's last line of defense. As its commander, you will have to manage everything, from research, recruitment, building projects and deciding where to intervene in the world against the invaders.
I never played a previous XCOM before, so that shouldn't be a problem if you haven't either. On the other hand, I must warn you that this game is very hard and pretty unforgiving. Getting your team completely wiped out for a little tactical mistake is a common thing.

There is also an ironman mode, where everything you do is irreversible, giving it a rogue-like experience, plus with the permanent death of your squad members and excellent soundtrack, the grid turn based battles can get pretty tense.
In the end, XCOM is a serious candidate for game of the year! Everything in it is great, from the tactical and engaging battles, to the base management and world affairs and the difficult decisions it presents to you. A must buy!

The game was surprisingly good. It had the feelings of a South Park episode and had some good jokes. However, the game does have some sections based on shock humour. For example the anal probes in the UFO, the abortion mini game (frustratingly hard with a controller), and the nazi zombie fetuses... These sections of the game got old quickly.
The gameplay itself is a turn based RPG. However, it suffers with being too easy. Combat is easily broken if you get a multihit weapon with bleeding (such as the bouncy ball) or a bow with bleeding and fire then you will never use a fight. Couple this with the special moves and the combat does not give any real challenge. The main problem with special moves is the intro video for each plays everytime... and you end up using the same moves. Butter's professor chaos special attack was one of the most useful, but the intro got old quickly and I just wished I could skip them.
The parody of Lord of the Rings was amusing. The interaction with the main characters really was the highlight of the game. The special moves intros were entertaining (Princess Kenny with the unicorn attack for example).
Overall, this is worth picking up if you enjoy South Park. If your looking for a turn based RPG then you are better off looking else where.

An odd sort of first person puzzle platformer.
This game might appear at first blush to be a very mind-bending game but in actuality it is not.  The game basically boils down to either puzzling with block switches and portal-esq emancipation fields or figuring your way around teleports between room transitions.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing though, as the effect it tries to convey is fairly effective.  The teleports are very nicely seamless with no hitching or obvious breaks or transitions.  Its just that the two are rarely mixed and it does not stray far.  The game also does not carry over teleport mechanics between rooms, so while it fits the theme it means it feels a little thrown away.  More often I feel shunted rather than truly lost.
This game has the odd trait of being mostly optional.  Room progression is very fluid, but it means that finding where you need to go next can be a bit of a difficult task.  A few more of the hint arrows telling you the way to go would be helpful, especially at the end of the game when the second acquired power has no less than 4 access rooms but the fourth power has only 1 and finding that one proved difficult amidst my many other options.
The aesthetics work well for the game. I can't comment on story.  There are many story-irrelevant placards in the game which mostly work as pre-puzzle hints or post-puzzle commentary.  The ending implies some deeper setting it seems, but it is not really comprehensible.
8hrs almost full clear (extras too), not a bad game and definately breaks the mold.  I'd reccomend it!

To my mind, there's never been a more likable anti-hero than Tommy Vercetti. Brilliantly voiced by Ray Liotta, the player takes control of Tommy after a big money drug deal goes tragically wrong. From there he embarks on a brutal path of crime and destruction in a steady rise to power within Vice City's underworld - because it's the only way he can survive. To this end, the player must take on varied missions as favours to allies, cement friendships with some excellent characters (again, superbly voice-acted), purchase properties, gradually gaining influence and wealth, in preparation to deal with Sonny....
Rock Star developers have created a vast city environment vibrant with colour, life, and crime. There's alway the opportunity to break off from the story missions and pursue other ways of making money....Earn cash as a taxi driver, pizza delivery guy, or even a cop. Locate and retrieve drug packages hidden about the city. Perform wild stunts on motorbikes, screech around the streets being relentlessly pursued by vengeful police in hair-raising, exciting car chases, or even fly over this sprawling metropolis in a helicopter!  There's also the option of navigating Vice City's coast in a yacht or speedboat....All of this, while listening to some classic 80's tracks over the radio (check out some of the comments on Youtube, you'll find these artists have found further fame from this game).
For those with a taste for mindless killing of innocents, search around for the 'rampage' icons: Tommy must massacre a certain number of people within a given time. Or, if a chance to prove your driving skills springs to mind, then watch out for certain vehicles dotted about the city. Personally, I enjoy a simple bike ride cruising along the city streets lit by neon lights, a balmy breeze blowng in my face, then park and lose myself in some fantastic tunes.
Killing bad guys is one thing - heck, they deserve it! - yet must confess at times the unbridled violence of this game I found quite distressing; 'Kill the Wife' mission (her panicked cries still haunt me) and accidentally running over innocent pedestrians particulary guilt-wracked what good nature I possess. However, if you reassure yourself this isn't real but instead digital destruction at it best, GTA: Vice City  presents some great challenges and promises hours of fun exploring a hectic urban jungle whichever way how!

Dead Space follows some control conventions that are common in Third Person Survival Horror games, the character is slow, the aim is sluggish, you are limited in the amount of equipment and ammo that you can carry. The goal is to make you feel unempowered and weaker than the monsters you face. Given that your character is a mid-forties system engineer wearing a bulky, armoured space suit, it doesn't seem far fetched.
The story is not unusual, a ship is in distress due to system malfunctions (and has your wife as its medical officer) and your team is sent to fix the problem. You arrive and monsters have infested the ship. You get seperated from your firends and have to navigate to them, find survivors (however few there are), regroup with your team and put a stop to whatever is happening. There are some twists to make the plot interesting, but they aren't mind blowing.
You start out with very little weapons and resources, but by a quarter in you will have been introduced to several weapons, as well as the abilities to throw objects and slow enemies. Your weapons are various pieces of mining and engineering equipment that have been weaponized and fire in specific patterns, which are represented by the weapon's firing reticles. The reticules are not just for flavour but try and covey where the shot his when you pull the trigger. Aside from the sluggish aiming, your shots are accurate and will not stray from the reticules. This is important because the name of the game is conserve ammo by killing enemies efficient.
There is a wrinkle in that part about killing enemies efficiently through. Unlike the classic zombie convention of shooting in the head, the monsters in Dead Space are weak to limb damage. These critters are shambling around, often in unconventional ways and as such it may be difficult to hit said weakspots. Severing a limb often rewards you with the enemy stopping for a moment, allowing you to line up another shot. Most enemies go down after two to three limbs are destroyed. The game tries to make you panic by having enemies show up in groups and in different configurations, keeping the enemy at bay with well placed shots, throwing objects with telekinesis, and occassionally slowing a target down allows you to manage fights and win. Sometimes added pressure is given by giving you a limited oxygen supply, environment dangers, poor lightining, or mid-boss enemies which can't be killed by gunfire.
There are relatively few puzzles in the game, most of which rely on you using your telekinesis and time slowing powers to navigate a hazard. There are zero gravity sections which will call have you moving on a surface you are standing on and able to aim and jump to other platforms to stick to. Enemies tend to float around and you'll need to have good spacial awareness to get a bead on them somtimes.
As the game progresses you will have the opprtunity to upgrade your suit and weapons. If you are thorough in exploring and selling excess ammunition and wepaons you don't like, you can fully upgrade your suit and one to two weapons by the end of the game. Once the campaign is completed, you can replay on a different difficulty and your suit and weapons upgrades carry over.
The game is satisfying when you play well, clearing encounters with cool calculating actions, and getting to stomp on a monster's guts after a battle can take the edge off if it was a particularly harrowing fight. There's a part with asteroids and a cannon which is unfun, and one of the boss fights can be a pain, but other than that it is smooth sailing.
Highly recommended if you are not bothered by gorey horror, intentionally sluggish controls, steady power progression, and playing a game that challenges you to stay in control of the situation.

This is a game where they nailed almost every aspect of its design and fine-tuned it to perfection.
It's a survival horror set in space with clear inspiration from the movies like Aliens and Event Horizon.
You play as a space engeener on a mission to repair a mining vessel after the communications went silent, but you have a personal stake in it- your girlfriend of part of the staff working on that ship. The mission is off to a bad start even before you set foot on the ship, when you and your team have to emergency land the shuttle in the hangar bay. And as your typical horror story goes from there on it gets from bad to worse- your team members get killed by some mysterious creatures, you get separated from the rest of the team and have to survive on your own and unfolding the mystery of what happened before your arrival using only your wits and determination. And a badass arsenal of limb cutting tools. See the Ishimura (the ship you're meant to repair) isn't a military ship- other than the assault riflle you will be using mining gear to dispatch enemies. And thats good, because the nemies can be best and most effiecently killed by removing their limbs, so things like buzzsaws, plasma cutters, and line guns are best suited for this purpose. And it's a good way to convey that you are a technician and not some army grunt out for blood and naked women.
Issac Clarke (You) is the silent protagonist type, but he's far from a mute person. Although he doesn't have a single line of dialogue, the groans, moans and other sounds that come out of his shielded mouth when he's being hit, when he swings his arm in a desperate attempt to save himself from being stabbed in the chest, when he stomps crates while searching for supplies or when low on health more than make up for it. And it sounds great. His walk/run cycle even changes the more he is damaged so at critical health you can almos see him tripping on his own feet and collapsing to the ground as he wheezes through his helmet.
The game has no on-screen interface- every information the player needs to know is somehow integrated in your suit, whether it's the health bar on your back, status windows projecting in front of Isaacs face or the ammo couter for your weapons displaying on top of them. Early in the game you aquire new abilities for your suit enabling you to slow down enemies or certain objects and to move objects out of your way or into your enemies. You can also buy new suits that offer better protecion and inventory as well as new weapons at shops provided you found schematics for them beforehand.
From the gameplay standpoint the game would seem like a typical third person action game with the over the shoulder camera, but the devil, as the say, is in the details. First of all shooting enemies in the head or body isn't advised as 1) it will take more shots to kill them, and 2) can enrage some enemies so that they start flailing their limb making them harder to target and risking wasting ammo and depending on the difficulty level can be hard to come by (untill you find a store where you can resupply provided you have the cash). I strongly recomend playing on hard on your first playthough- it provides a good challenge and isn't as difficult so you'd fling your controller (or K+M) at the screen to vent your rage. As I wrote earlier the best way to deal with the enemies is to shoot their limbs off, it not only conserves ammo, but by cripling it's legs yor exapmple you slow their advance giving you time to reaload or finish it up. All guns have an alternate firing mode, for example the plasma cutter has a rotating barrel to alternate between horizontal and vertical shots or the line gun, which fires a mine that sticks to walls. All weapons can be upgraded with nodes found in the enviroment or bought from the store- each weapon has it's own upgrade path and you'll have to fill it with nodes from the starting point to the desired stat boost. The same can be done with your suit (or RIG) and ability modules (stasis and kinesis, respectively).
It's a good time to mention the enemies, you'll be facing called the necromorphs. They're mostly mutated human coprses having their bodies unnaturaly twisted with blades sticking out of their hands, but there are some grotesque variations of this concept to keep combat interesting. A good example is anecromorph based on a human baby, that walks on walls and sprouts appandages from its back that shoot projectiles at you. All in all the bestiary is varied and filled with imaginative and equally disturbing creatures which are fun to battle and equally fun to watch as they rip you to shreds, should you fall to one of them.
When not in combat you engage in a multidude of puzzles most, of which require previosly mentioned abilities. You'll be replacing damaged tram cars, arrainging objetcs to clear a path forward, alligning communication dishes or fixing the centrifuge to restore gravity etc. You'll also be doing some item fetching to enable progress in some way or the other. There are also the Zero G sections where you'll be jumping form platform, to platform while sometimes while evading attacks from all diretcions thanks to those baby monsters and other baddies. This can be further made more difficult by the vacuum of space where all sounds are muffled and, you can only hear Isaac breathe and you also have to keep watch on your oxigen supply so as not to suffocate mid combat. There are text, audio and video logs to collect, that explain what happened on the Ishimura as well as fleshing out the game world with extraneus information.
With the gameplay covered it's a good time to write a couple of words about the games presentation. Tu put it simply it's stellar. From Isaacs suit which is so well designed and full of detail, that it's almost amazing how well it looks even in this day and age,  to the Ishimura, with every deck having it's own distinctive fell with locations that look and feel believable due to how much care went into designing them. I especially love the lighting which while soemetimes produces some low res shadows. it blends perfecly with the level design and with the acompanying sounds creates atmosphere so thick you can almost touch it. First hand experience- the game has a run button, but 90% of the time I'd rather walk with my gun up than to risk bumping into any of the creatures stalking the corridors (it also has a build in flashlight, so there's that). And the sound design may be the crown jewel of the package- sounds of footsteps, weapons, enemies and enviroment packed with rather minimal and mostly contextual musical score takes what I already written and amplifies it tenfold. The cast hired to do the voices does their characters justice with few known names like Peter Mensah and Keith Szarabajka. The direction and performances are very good.
It's not all sun and roses though, as this game like every other is not perfect and has some issues.
First of all DO NOT enable in-game vsync. It creates input lag so severe that it's almost unplayable as well as massively extending load times. Force the vsync using your video driver, because screen tearing in this game is horrible.
Some of the textures can be a little blurry and low quality and I wrote how shadows can be sometimes ugly.
Even though earlier I recomended playing this game on hard once you get a full grasp of the mechanics it still can be a bit on the easy side. Thanks to the greatly overpowered stasis ability which lasts waaaaay to long on enemies, encounters can be a cakewalk.
To conclude you get a houghly 12 hour game split into 12 chapters with excellent atmosphere and design and even new game plus mode with some bonus unlocks after completion (you can't change the difficulity however).
Couldn't recommend it more. Thanks for reading (if you managed to get here:P)

It's a South Park game, and they don't hold anything back, so expect tons and tons of crass toilet humor, references and metahumor.
Of course this alone wouldn't hold interest in a game for more than a half hour, if the gameplay itself, and story, are crap. But in this case they are superb.
They could have gone the lazy and cheap way, and tack the toilet humor on a crappy game, but instead they have clearly put a lot of work on both the gameplay and the story, and it shows. The characters are actually interesting, and playing the game is very engaging. The game mechanics might not be chess grade, but really well done for casual play.
I play lots and lots of games, and I would actually classify this as one of the most enjoyable I have played in a long time. In fact, it makes me want to re-watch the entire South Park series, just so that I can understand all the references.
Crass toilet humor and somewhat simplistic turn-based combat might not be for everybody, but personally I enjoyed it. I highly recommend.

This is a cool tactics game, but not for the tactics. The game itself rewards you strongly for using a plodding, careful, and methodical approach to every mission -- trying to pull some kind of gambit rarely turns out well, and is never really necessary.
What's cool about the game is the connection it manages to build between you and your squad. Your dudes level up from useless to Rambo as they go on more and more missions, but when they die in combat they're done for good. The squad members even get random nicknames when they reach a certain rank, which is fantastic.
This connection brings a lot of tension into each mission, especially on ironman mode (no reloading saves), and as you focus so much on your squad you see amusing little storylines emerge between them. You notice that your assault guy "Hardcore" always manages to stumble neck deep into trouble. You notice that "Roadblock" has godawful aim, even if he uses the same random number generator as everybody else.
And then once you've already written you're own storyline, an actual scripted storyline peeks up out of nowhere and manages to instantly disappoint, but that's easy to ignore.

This is probably one of my favorite RPGs/tactical turn based shooter of this year: mainly for the fact they're knocking the dust off the old Shadowrun RPG. The Shadowrun world, in a nutshell, is like putting "Cyberpunk: 2020" and "Dungeons and Dragons" in a blender and hitting frappe. It's a good mix of high technology and high magic in a Future Imperfect world where corporations pull the strings. But the game itself plays out like original XCOM or Jagged Alliance games: you have a turn, you pick your actions, you do your actions, your enemies respond. I think the execution on this game was solid. My only critiques would be I'd like to see a "real" initiative system, where maybe you don't get the first chance to act in a combat round. I'd also like to have seen deeper modifiers for the cyberware and a better implementation of the "Physical Adept". But these are really just holdovers from my experience with the Pen and Paper game.
Anyway, if you play this game like a turn based tactical shooter, you'll be pleased with the options the game offers. The combat is fun. The story is good and very fitting for the setting. User content is coming out and is decent. Plus they have a DLC coming out next year. Check it out.

In another game named so generic that it has to add the developer's name to the title, "Sid Meier's Civilization V" is the fifth entry in the turn based hexigrid strategy game series. In Civilization series, you are always competing and aligning yourself with various other leaders on your way to world domination through several means. The game lets you grow your empire through conquering cities, settling new ones, through trade and other forms of diplomacy.
Civilization V feels and plays almost the same as previous entries in the series with a few upgrades, combat tweaks and a fresh coat of paint to make it feel modern. Is there anything wrong with having an updated game to a beloved series? Nope. Does it make me want to play it when I played previous iterations of the game twenty hears ago? Nope.
The game begins in ancient times and you will work your way up through the millennia so any Civilization takes a long while. You select a leader each with their own perk, select a map size and your desired type of map. Then the game generates a new and unique map making every play through unique. There are eight difficulty settings and four paces for how long you want the game to last. My play through on normal difficulty with a standard pace with a small map has surpassed six hours.
You start with a single city. Each city lets you produce something, either a unit to move around, a building to increase resources or a wonder. Over time the population of a city will grow depending on your food and the happiness of your population. Have too little food and the citizens starve and the city shrinks. With more citizens, the faster you can produce something.
Creating one building in town will unlock other building choices. Its a level of micro management that gets old when you have a dozen big cities with short production times that you are always producing stuff for them at every turn. Plus someone thought it was a good idea to have the produce button on the right side away from the list of stuff to produce on the left side.
Units have two major types: military and workers. Workers enhance the area around your cities. They can make connections, roads, mine, farm and you can chose to let them do the work automatically. If a worker is captured by a military unit, they are lost and become the enemy's worker. Military units have three forms, ranged, melee and siege to use against cites. Each unit has its own move distance of one or two tiles, attack distance, attack strength and so on. Creating specific buildings unlocks new military for that city.
Once you've unlocked the appropriate technology, most units can set sail in ships. The only catch is they're vulnerable to attack. Combat ships and long range attacks can sink the transports.
You can set a unit to move across the map, and see how many turns it will take them to get there. Then they will automatically move each turn unless you have them stop. You can have them do nothing, stand alert or go to sleep which in some circumstances is good as deleting them because I'd usually forget they exist for a few centuries. Military units can garrison cities and gain their defenses. Like other games of the genre, there is an automatic explore, which is good for scouts.
Combat takes place on the hexigrid world map. Simple battles play out between two units and you have no control, just the strategy of having ranged units can attack from two tiles away rather than one tile away. All units have ten health so when a unit takes damage they can fortify themselves which wastes a turn, but heals them a single point of health. Any fight will give the unit experience and leveling up gives a choice of certain perks such as better damage against enemies on rough terrain or clear terrain. Others gain one hit point per turn or 50% better defense.
Conquering cities is quite a task and requires too much effort. It can slow the game to a halt at least on normal difficulty. First you need to bombard the city with ranged attackers and mainly catapults or cannons. Then once the city has been weakened, you need to send in your melee attackers. Its a process that benefits the defenders. Taking cities turns into tedium as you can amass a giant army, then just go from one city to the next. Cities have a ranged defense mechanism that does little to deter my troops. I just have one troop take a beating and fortify themselves while other troops pummel the city. If the fortified troop gets down to one hit point left, take them away and replace them.
As you're playing, you acquire science points and gold from each city. Gold lets you quick buy units or buildings rather than taking the time to make them. Science lets you research technology quicker. Technology enhances one thing or another and can unlock new buildings or units.
Everything in the game is designed to unlock something else, to build something else to make it faster to build. With that in mind, the entire game is a grind,but its a grind that is just easy. So easy that its engaging because you're just making choices with some combat to give the game some diversity. Even the combat requires a only a small amount of thought.
There are heroes and several types of them with their own uses. A battlefield hero can increase effectiveness of those around him, and he can also make a citadel at the expense of his life. Science heroes can expend their life to get an instant technology. Another type of hero gets a project done instantly.
You also gain political points that let you unlock certain theologies and then perks that come long with them. Just another choice to keep you entertained. Engaging in war hurts your political points, but in return, its easier to bully your opponents. On the other hand starting a war may get several nations to hate you. Gandhi in my first game started out as a friend, then he wanted me to declare war on some nation he had a hatred for. When I asked him to wait ten turns, he agreed. Then when the tenth turn was up. I went to war and so Gandhi ended up going to war with me because I went to war with the one he wanted me to be at war with.
Some leaders will buy a peace treaty with you for X amount of turns. Agree to the terms and you never have to leave their borders. However, when I stocked up and surrounded cities of a nation I had a treaty with, once I declared war they threw everyone out of their territory. That took a lot of time and coordination across ten turns to get them put in and the game just nullified that. Oh but that never stopped my victory and that's a problem with the series, you know when you've won long before you've conquered the world, just as you know when you've lost long before the end.
To make the world feel more alive, there are barbarian tribes which have no alliance. They spawn soldiers and archers until you destroy them. Its interesting coming across a tribe of barbarians int he 1800s. In fact a lot of things are interesting in the 1800s like how a city still needs a coliseum, but I suppose its a fancy way of saying arena.
Its a toss up to recommend a game that is so easy there's no challenge, but its so easy that its relaxing. Its just a big grind that throws never ending choices in your face while you're conquering the world. Its fun for a play through, but after the daunting task of painting the world with my empire, its a journey I never want to take again. When all is said and done, its still the best looking hexigrid turn based strategy out there with over twenty years worth of depth and choices that keep you occupied and make each time unique.

SPOILER-FREE REVIEW:
It took a while for myself to try and get through this game...I never felt like I very drawn to get back to the game and finish it. I could not find the motivation.
I don't think the game is THAT great nor do I think it is bad, but I think it is good. The game started pretty nicely...You begin to care about characters, bringing you into the action, although, things quickly seemed to fall short as the game progressed. Unless you read those written documents you can pick up that is, then there sure is a fair amount of story to jump into, but besides that, it seemed to be an alright story in my opinion.
The horror in this game is really not as close to as scary as people say it is...at least for me. I think that the atmosphere and music is fantastic. The screeching of the orchestra and eerie drums are fantastic at setting the mood. Along with the atmosphere in this game, they both work together very well. The enemies are pretty freaky I will admit, but I freely ran down corridors and twisting hallways with no worries because this game did not really seem scary to me. I played this whole game through with surround sound and a 50 inch HDTV in the dark most of the time, it just was not very scary. I think the people that talk about the horror in Dead Space is just too ridiculous at times.
The gameplay was interesting but very slow in my opinion. Aiming and moving seemed so unresponsive. I was flicking the joysticks and Isaac doesn't even move or look. It could be the controller support being bad but the buttons seemed quick and responsive. The controls on the controler which I am very sure are the same on the Xbox, I think they just are not that good. Reloading is LT+A, jumping in zero-gravity is LT+Y, using a health pack is X, etc...
The shooting is pretty fun, the way you have to dismember enemies and the different weapons you get to use is a blast. Dismemberment is always awesome to see in a game and in this game, it is most certainly well done. Dismemberment is a huge part of this game.
A part of the game I very much enjoyed was the zero gravity. The zero gravity had parts that seemed pretty memorable and the level design for all of those events in the game were actually very cool and creative. What is also creative is the HUD. Isaac's life meter displayed on his back and his ammo projected above his weapons is really cool and fitting with the game...It just does not feel out of place in attempt to save space on the screen.
With the beginning and ending of the games, I liked but hated them at the same time because the whole game inbetween the beginning and ending seemed to be only gameplay and nothing else but somewhat repetitive missions. Do this, do that, and then story comes to a close with tons of ingame animations and sequences I wish were there throughout the entire game...Meh...You feel like you are being used by everybody in the campaign, but I guess that is how a lot of games are so it's not a big problem in my opinion.
I also hate the extremely long death sequences. When you get killed by something in this game, there are quite literally 20 second long death animations you just cannot skip. Every time I was stuck watching one of those, all I can think is that the developers were probably bragging about how cool their death sequences are. Anyways, when you are stuck in a part of the game, you will constantly be getting killed and have to watch and wait through entire death scenes...it is so annoying.
To wrap up this review the game is pretty good. The shooting is fun, the RPG elements motivate you to play, the atmosphere and music work well together, etc... Although, the game has a lot of shortcomings and mistakes, but it is a very solid horror game.
If you love horror shooters, play Dead Space!

FTL is an entertaining, very replayable and murderously RNG-dependent roguelike-like. Good for space captain fantasies, even if you will likely be violently disabused of them.
You control a Federation spaceship transporting intelligence that must make its way through sectors of space being chased by the Rebel fleet, for the intel points out their fleet's weaknesses. This plot is lightly described yet more than serviceable - more on this later.
Gameplay consists of turn-based jumping between FTL beacons and fighting enemies in pausable real-time combat involving charging and aiming weapons & drones, and/or deploying your own crew to board or defend against boarders. There's a fair amount of micromanagement you can do to get the most out of your ship, up to opening and closing individual doors. Ship systems and additional items can be bought & upgraded using scrap metal, which can be found or salvaged from defeated enemies.
You must also manage your fuel supply, as well as missile and drone supplies if you use either of them. If your ship's hull takes enough damage, or your crewmembers die, your game's over.
Sometimes, multiple-choice events happen - they don't change between playthroughs with the exception of different choices being unlocked with upgraded systems or crewmembers of different species. You might come to remember some of the right choices after encountering them multiple times, but the Advanced Edition seems to add enough events that this isn't as big an issue.
You can also unlock quite a variety of ships between playthroughs, some of which are better than others, but most of which provide new and interesting playstyles.
While you have a lot of variety between upgrades, as well as offensive and defensive strategies to choose from, apart from your starting equipment you are quite simply more dependent on random chance than usual for a game like this. That means you usually have to work with what you have, and that won't always be enough. This is compounded by the fact that on difficulties above Easy, you receive less resources
the game generates tougher enemies (in exchange for increased score of course). You can and will go from doing pretty well to barely limping along in the space of one jump. The difficulty wouldn't be so bad if you had more of a guarantee of receiving the tools to deal with or run away from it if you need to.
Which is to say nothing of the final boss. It's grossly overpowered and pretty unfair even for a roguelike-like, especially when you never found enough resources to upgrade your systems enough to even stand a chance - or never got the chance to use them to upgrade in the first place because you were taking so much damage. To say nothing of how it turns FTL's metagame on its head with how
the final fight is. With all of this in mind, new players should therefore start on Easy - while I can respect its presence, it's kind of baffling why people thought the game needed a Hard mode in addition to Normal.
I think there's a
bit of a bright side to the difficulty, though. FTL is not only a quite fun and quite polished game, but a quite involving game, and if you become involved it makes the near-deaths and actual deaths that much more intense. On that note, you can re-name your ship and its crewmembers, and giving them personalized names only adds to the immersion. The touch of the plot is light to allow the players to fill in the gaps with their imagination, and experience their own space adventures. This isn't as much of an advantage when you simply want to win, however.
At least the devs' handling of the Advanced Edition is stellar. It features additional content in almost every area, including events written by Chris Avellone of Fallout fame, and you can even turn the additional content off for the vanilla experience.
Of mention is the mod community. The official forums are host to an easy-to-use mod installation tool, and
user-created mods that you can pick & choose from. They range from minor event/cosmetic additions to new ships to entire new campaigns, and can greatly extend the life of the game. Just make sure you're on top of your game and mod updates.
If you like your spaceships and your roguelike-likes, pick this up -
- but be prepared to die and die again.

- Autosaving seems to be the only way to save your game, and doesn't seem to happen often enough to be able to stop in the middle of a session.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn based strategy game that has a heavy emphasis on resource management, be it your soldiers you manage or your weapons or even the pieces of alien research parts.
XCOM shines fairly brightly among a sea of FPS games and even holds it's own against some of the better strategy games of times past. Cover is heavily emphasized and the AI in the game is very solid.. The damage from weapons is very impactful and certainly maintains a solid aesthetic. I find myself objecting to the requiring of DLC to put helmets on your troops though.
The objective of XCOM is to investigate the recent alien activity on earth. It quickly becomes apparent the aliens are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and want yo dough so you gotta give em a good slappin. In other words, save the world. Nothing special. What makes XCOM better than most is it's ability to pull you in, making you want to keep going and constantly having you manage your resources. The game actually makes you think about what you would like to buy and doesn't just say 'you can research all this stuff when you want'.
So what are the good and bad aspects of this game?
Good:
A constant sense of purpose and direction.
Resources are actually valuable and meaningful and not just another means to an end.
A large assortment of maps that can take multiple playthroughs to see all of them.
Good aesthetics. (The rainy flood mission is the best)
Solid controls (up and down levels can ♥♥♥♥ themselves).
Strategically destructible terrain.
Bad:
There's multiplayer in this game? (It's competitive EYUCK)
Ironman is bypassable by alt +f4ing.
Skill trees are kind of 'yawn'.(except in the zone. single handedly the best skill in the entire game)
Not much variance in environments (forest, city, forest, city, crash site, city, crash site, city, forest, city, crash site, city.)
Overall this was a pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good game. I def recommend it. Grab it for somewhere between 25 and 40. It's good, but not ♥♥♥♥ing 50 dollar material. Also don't be an idiot and buy the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 'bureau' to get this game unless you like generic♥♥♥♥♥♥shooters. Too bad I can't reveiw games I don't own!

Having role-played and been into computer games for over 30 years I was aware of the Shadowrun system, but somehow the computer game version passed me by, so this is my 1st experience of it.
Having role-played for so long the Fantasy genera has been a bit dull for a few years and I have been looking towards others such as horror and cyberpunk. Shadowrun is a nice combination of all of these themes winding cyberpunk and fantasy together in a nice adult themed game, with several good horror elements in the mix.
The game plays like many older RPGs, with real time movement while your exploring dropping to a turn based system when in combat, kind of simulating the pen and paper experience, all done in an isometric style.
The story is fun and compelling, but a little text rich in places for someone with dyslexia and would defiantly benefit from some voice acting in places. Despite the game being fairly linear in nature there were a few areas that I didn’t get into on my first run so will likely play through at least once more to try and open them. Because the story and the game were very good I felt the main campaign was a little short and left me wanting more!
But never fear the steam workshop has that covered with many more campaigns listed. Although my experience of the user created content has been a little ropey, with the 1st one I played, “Milk Run” being over before it started and the second basically crashing after over an hours play without any auto saves. The editor included seems good enough to create fully functional, none bugged campaigns so assuming someone puts in the time to do this, yes this is now on my bucket list of things to do, there should be plenty of hours left to play. But personally I would like to see an official DLC to extend things.

Shadowrun Returns, although not exactly like the previous versions, is a great rendition of the series. The combat system is simple, using a style that resembles XCOM: Enemy Unkown, and brings cover into play. The Karma system is very well done, although more description of the spells before buying them would be nice instead of having to go to a shop to find out. Also there is a lack of major use for a decker in the main game besides a few points. The Sega Genesis version allowed deckers to be of great use and it is sad the main campaign did not really use them. Also the saving system is not forgiving as you cannot manually save, but it does autosave for every section you enter. This is a problem because the main game is not open world, meaning if you forgot to do a side quest or buy an item, I forgot a spell once or twice, you had to continue on anyway. The positive side is the workshop games that can be added, bringing lots of extra play time and different stories to explore. The workshop games are bringing in more weapons, which was desperately needed on the melee side, and greater use for the decker. The main game is fun and very interesting, but I believe the real value lies in the user created workshop.

Alien meets The Thing in 'Dead Space'. It doesn't escape horror cliche through its narrative, but its execution is brilliant - the immersive HUD, chilling sound design and music and grotesque monsters are a compelling combination. There are some memorable low gravity sequences too and, generally speaking, the pacing is consistent enough to allow the finale to pay off.
Weapons are fun to use and I liked the emphasis on skill shots to limbs, rather than dishing out the firepower arbitrarily. This is all rounded up by a basic but effective upgrades system and the ability to slow objects and enemies down with Stasis, as well as move objects around with a Kinesis module.
That said, it wasn't as frightening as I hoped it might be and was overly reliant on jump scares. Nothing really made me fear going round the next corner like other titles have. Tension failed to build as the game went on as the Necromorphs' tendancy to jump out of vents and stand behind doorways became predictable and noticeably scripted as the game went on. I think I only visibly flinched a couple of times during my 11 hour playthrough.
Nonetheless, I had a lot of fun with this game and could really tell that a lot of very talented people were behind its creation. Would definitely recommend.

Antichamber? More like crash-chamber-because-I-filled-the-room-with-blocks
But seriously, this game is all about discovery. There's not much of a story here, just you experimenting with the physics of this world and that of the gun. The parallels with Portal here are obvious, except this one focuses on fairly difficult puzzles, whereas Portal has far more story. Largely the puzzles are difficult because of the non-Euclidean geometry and some of the gun functions not introduced terribly well. There are tutorial levels, it's just one is either after you learn about a function (on the green gun) through trial and error or I just missed, and one assumption I made (with the yellow gun) was never challenged fully until the end.
The biggest problem, if I'd call it that, is coming across unsolvable puzzles without the appropriate gun upgrade. As you work through the game you get better upgrades (more block moving power), but the puzzes for each are interwoven. However they might be colour coded to help now that I think about it (blue, green, yellow and red). If the blocks match your gun or one you've picked up, you're probably able to do it.
So if you're a puzzle nut, pick this one up. Otherwise, oblique life lessons tied into the chambers aside, there won't be much to keep your interest. Unless you like stress-testing the brick engine :p

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn based strategy game that has a heavy emphasis on resource management, be it your soldiers you manage or your weapons or even the pieces of alien research parts.
XCOM shines fairly brightly among a sea of FPS games and even holds it's own against some of the better strategy games of times past. Cover is heavily emphasized and the AI in the game is very solid.. The damage from weapons is very impactful and certainly maintains a solid aesthetic. I find myself objecting to the requiring of DLC to put helmets on your troops though.
The objective of XCOM is to investigate the recent alien activity on earth. It quickly becomes apparent the aliens are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and want yo dough so you gotta give em a good slappin. In other words, save the world. Nothing special. What makes XCOM better than most is it's ability to pull you in, making you want to keep going and constantly having you manage your resources. The game actually makes you think about what you would like to buy and doesn't just say 'you can research all this stuff when you want'.
So what are the good and bad aspects of this game?
Good:
A constant sense of purpose and direction.
Resources are actually valuable and meaningful and not just another means to an end.
A large assortment of maps that can take multiple playthroughs to see all of them.
Good aesthetics. (The rainy flood mission is the best)
Solid controls (up and down levels can ♥♥♥♥ themselves).
Strategically destructible terrain.
Bad:
There's multiplayer in this game? (It's competitive EYUCK)
Ironman is bypassable by alt +f4ing.
Skill trees are kind of 'yawn'.(except in the zone. single handedly the best skill in the entire game)
Not much variance in environments (forest, city, forest, city, crash site, city, crash site, city, forest, city, crash site, city.)
Overall this was a pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good game. I def recommend it. Grab it for somewhere between 25 and 40. It's good, but not ♥♥♥♥ing 50 dollar material. Also don't be an idiot and buy the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 'bureau' to get this game unless you like generic♥♥♥♥♥♥shooters. Too bad I can't reveiw games I don't own!

I enjoyed many of the sci-fi elements of Dead Space. Zipping around in zero gravity and performing repairs on an enormous mining ship were quite fun.
That said, I found it impossible to take this game seriously. Its world has no internal logic that I could find. The number of times something happens solely BECAUSE SCARY are too many to count. After the third time I found a can of flamer ammo in a wall box conspicuously labeled "EMERGENCY SUPPLIES", it became clear that this was a very traditional survival horror game with a sci-fi coat of paint. Horror games absolutely rely upon your immersion in the gameworld, so constantly breaking my suspension of disbelief by putting momentary thrills ahead of the world-building was a dealbreaker.
Lost its charm somewhere around the 1400 hour mark.

This is my #1 favorite game.

I can't fully describe my affection for the features in this game, because it has everything I could want. It has:
Innovation (The entire game is completely hudless, all critical information can be seen around Issac.)
Fun gameplay (literally cutting the limbs off of your enemies one by one)
Atmosphere (dread and danger around every corner)
Visuals (Every deck of the ship has its own style. I swear I could tell where a player is with one screenshot.)
Aesthetics (There are so many details that help you believe that the Ishimura was a place where people lived, along with other stuff that helps makes the experience more interesting. I mean, every container in the game has a logo that glows green when you shine a light on it!)
I've played this game far more than it was ever built for simply because it's something worth re-living. It pains me deeply to know how the series declines with the 2nd and...... 3rd game (which is terrible).
If you're willing to take the time to get it working and want a quality horror game where you don't have to hide like a baby, I strongly recommend Dead Space.

First and foremost:
This game is as crude, if not more so, than the show.  If you don't enjoy the South Park brand of humor you won't like this game.  This is also not the kind of game you play where someone not "in the know" might walk into the room.
That being said, if you're even a casual fan of South Park you will find a lot to love here.  The game plays out pretty much like an episode of the TV show, including so many homages to the show that I recognized dozens of things from only the couple dozen episodes I've seen.  The game is on the short side clicking in at around 16 hours, but in my opinion that just means it doesn't overstay its welcome.  The ending comes at just the right time and you never feel that drag that kicks in during the last act of a game when you're just ready to be done and its trying its hardest to pad the playtime.
Gameplaywise this plays like a more sophisticated Paper Mario.  Quick timing based battles and a nice sized town to freely explore, with secrets gradually becoming accessible as you gain new abilities.  If you like Paper Mario you will definitely enjoy this gameplay.
This was quite a surprise for me, honestly one of the most interesting new games I've played this year.  I don't usually go for some of South Parks cruder themes, but the overall humor and tight gameplay really made this shine for me.  If you like South Park, Paper Mario, or just fast paced RPGs in general you will find a lot to like here!
